While I don't think the turn-based gameplay is bad, it does often come across as very stiff and can sometimes feel repetitive. One thing that I also consider as really well-made is the progression system, which consistently gives you new upgrades and small things to do throughout the whole game. I would rate game length and content A as well. I cannot talk about the English version, since I went with the Japanese synchronisation.

This game is currently in early access, but as far as I'm concerned, it's finished (besides a few rarely occuring bugs). If you have a friend or three, this is a perfect party game. Let me try to explain this game to people who aren't completely sure what it is. Basically, there are four runners, and you have to try to stay on the screen. If you fall too far behind and go off-screen, you're out and the screen starts shrinking. I don't mean that the screen resolution decreases, I mean that the border of the screen closes in, making it easier to go off-screen. Eventually, the screen gets so small that stopping just for a second could mean a loss. There are also powerups that could either help you and/or hurt others. It sounds stupid, but it really gets your heart racing.
- Customizable controls with a console controller.
- Very fast-paced.
- Custom levels, ranging from silly to amazing.
- Easy-to-use level editor.
- Great powerups.
- Very balanced; you never feel like another player has an
advantage.
- Bots actually know what they're doing.
- Fun features besides running (grappling, wall jumping, etc.)
- Some very rarely occuring bugs (ex. falling through the floor and out of the world)
- Bots usually won't work on Workshop levels.
There's no reason not to get this game. Even if you don't have any friends to play with, the community is surprisingly great, and the bots work great on the official levels. Also great for killing time.

This is a very unique game and very well executed as well, I highly recommend it.
The unusual mixture of genres leads to incredible mechanical complexity and the games employs said mechanics in a way that truly makes you feel invested, makes you care about knowing the game, to the point where knowing the cards, particularly the bosses, is key to a great advantage.
As a consequence of this, you might want to turn difficulty to easy (this is done in the deck builder, counterintuitively) if you plan on playing the whole game in over a week. If you, like me, find yourself firmly grabbed by the desire to explore the game, the immense variety of cards and their associated stories will give you an abundance to explore, expect however to have to read the majority of information.
The combat is carefully tutorialized and some of the weapons and artefacts feel amazing to use*, but the deck building aspect of the game requires a lot of cunning to truly get the hang of, recommended decks leave quite a bit to be desired, yet are enthusiastically pushed on the player.
*I played with an XBOX One controller and it worked flawlessly, would recommend using it.
The length is satisfying and there are modifiers and additional (so far) free content for good replay ability.
The story, lore, and the narrator truly are the crowning jewels of this game (no spoilers ahead).
You know very little about where or who you are, or about what's happening...but throughout the game you get clues, delivered by the dealer, whose comments (delivered by excellent voice acting) left me interested in the world of this game of cards like I never thought possible!
Excellent writing overall.
Get this game. Play this game, listen to this game, read what it has to be read.
It is a unique experience that everyone can enjoy, but that will speak personally to you if you share my great love of games.

This is a very well-executed port of one of the PS3's earliest exclusive masterpieces, the most creative and innovative strategy game of last generation.
If you've played it previously on PS3, this is the same game, but with a few upgrades and additions: the inclusion of all DLC, a better framerate, achievements, and keyboard+mouse controls.  It's worth noting that this same port is now on PS4, but I chose this version simply because aiming with a keyboard and mouse is a bit easier than with analog sticks.  This version does support the XBox controller layout right out of the box, though, so you can use that if you do prefer analog sticks.
That's what's new in this version.  If you've never played the game, read on:
This is a turn-based strategy game with some innovative twists to the mechanics.
Half of the gameplay is familiar: you deploy units onto a map, and then order them to move and attack, one-by-one, until you've exhausted moves for your turn; then, the enemy does the same.  Repeat until your objectives are met or failed.
What makes the game unique is what happens while you're ordering each individual unit.  The camera shifts from the overhead map to a third-person camera, and you control the character in a way similar to a third-person shooter.  Your shots aren't fired in real-time, however; it still maintains the strategy custom of lining up your shot and pressing a button to execute your attack, at which point the attack process happens automatically, factoring in elements like cover and angle.  You must be quick and focused while moving your characters, however, as enemy units positioned along the map can still fire at your character in real-time (and the opposite is true as well, so it's on you to position your units in ways such that they can take shots at advancing enemy units during the enemy's turn phase).
This blend of turn-based strategy with semi-realtime interaction makes for a unique and creative style of gameplay that's never been previously seen, making Valkyria Chronicles one of a kind.

I was looking for a new game to play when I stumbled upon this little Gem with a friend of mine.
I played three seprate rounds, and I don't think I "won" any of them, nor did I lose.  The instructions are vague, or just lacking, but that said... Well, it's a charming little game.  I'd like to see more of its ilk in the games pool.  I wouldn't recommend playing it without at least on person interested in playing the intended game, though for this little beauty, leave the voice chat at home, I think.
The unfortunate fact of the matter is, this game is susseptible to trolling even more so than most others, because absolutely nothing can be done without the participation of at least one other player.  So you could easily get stonewalled, and trapped by someone jusy using the test-to-speech to make their character say stupid stuff.  I got lucky when playing, and ran into only one such person.
It's at least worth playing one or two rounds of, I'd say.  Unique, and charming.  It's like everything the murder-mystery dinner packs want to be, but with the added element of true anonymity making it that much easier to lose yourself in a little.

Don't let my time played fool you; I was playing this game before it was introduced to Steam. If you don't believe me, go ahead and check my two or three Archeage screenshots. This is why I felt I needed to suck it up, download it one last time and share with you my experience with this game. I will admit it is a beautiful game with an interesting battle system, a highly customizable class system and a justice system that I feel should be explored in other games. It also has boats, gliders, personal housing, trading, farming, etc. So why wouldn't someone want to play this game? For those of you who don't like to read, think of this game as Farmville, mixed with Candy Crush with a generic MMO skin. You want to own land? You need to buy the premium membership (15 dollars a month) and even then, good luck trying to get some with all of it bought up by other players or owned by hackers. Want to pvp? Have fun zerging, which is excusable I admit. Want to upgrade your equipment? Better hope that it doesn't randomly break. Sorry, but just like SWOTR, if you are going to put out a "F2P" game, make sure you give access to all of the features to everyone without putting them behind a paywall. I do not recommend this game to anyone until they either go to a pure subscription model, buy to play or free to play with a cash shop sans buy to win.

Look at any screenshot and it's instantly obvious the nine year development cycle went to good use. Every background asset and stage looks impeccable--even sharper as they actively transition from day to night before your eyes. An orchestral soundtrack of live instruments from TEN different people brings this world to life. I had to occasionally stop just to soak everything in.
However, this game is host to a few glaring issues that I have to address. For a platformer, this game is very story heavy with plenty of lore to uncover. You'll find a lot of fascinating history, and a ton of character interaction. As you examine the characters more closely though you'll realize that their motivations are typically unexplained and often times complete nonsense. This is painfully apparent as the game and its story come to an end.
If the game weren't so good at building up the characters and the lore then the ending and final leadup to it wouldn't have felt nearly as dissapointing.
-----plot spoilers
------
Even on a basic level the plot fails to deliver. Why bother having the protagonist be mute if one of his partners always speaks for him? Wouldn't it be better to have him speak to establish stronger bonds among your party?
The game shoots itself in the foot by refusing to answer any of the meaningful mysteries it presents, offering at best vague clues buried behind 3 hidden gold coin macguffins in the overworld (bonus: you can't access all the gold coins to read all the vague clues until after you beat the game).
So much effort goes into building up both the plot AND the villain. He's a hulking, Darth Vader-esque titan. The screen trembles as he walks and every npc and ally cowers in fear as he approaches. There's a brilliantly animated cutscene that establishes just how absurdly strong he is halfway into the game and that's when♥♥♥♥♥♥really hits the fan. I was legitimately awestruck, mashing f12 as hard as I could.
-----final boss spoiler
-----
Much like the writing, the gameplay is a mixed bag. The Metroidvania exploration elements are very, very light, almost nonexistant. The levels and dungeons may as well be linear with a big hub world. Dungeons mix up the puzzles and gimmicks often and the cutscenes are a decent length (but unskippable, so forget about replaying it). Throw the big guy on the big switch to open the door. Hide behind the crate for stealth-lite sections. These are all gameplay elements you're familiar with. It's not revolutionary but it is servicable.
You spend almost the entire game flying. Projectiles are nearly auto-aim so just focus on dodging rather than precision aiming. If you're close enough, you won't miss your shots. Flying and dodging a lot benefits bosses since now they can attack anywhere on screen but hampers the level design. It's not much of a platformer when you never step on the platforms.
Dying is uncommon, but the punishment for death is almost nonexistant. You'll probably succeed on your first attempt against every boss since you're already free to focus entirely on not getting hit.
Most people take about eight hours to finish this game, with another one or two in post-game collecting anything they missed. The reward for gettnig everything is a real let-down though so I'd recommend against doing that in retrospect. Keep the unusually hgih pricetag in mind as you mull over how long this game will satisfy you.
This game is for relaxing. Load it up one weekend and submerge yourself in exquisite backdrops. Just don't expect much of a challenge. Try not to think about how many plot elements are left unresolved, or how the characters don't always make sense, or how the game's ONLY ending feels like a typical game's bad ending you get for not doing 100%.

I don't normally take the time to write reviews, but I thought it was important you understand ArcheAge. So you can think long and hard before investing your time and money.
ArcheAge could have been a very amazing MMO, but it is completely ruined by the cash shop and Trion's money  grubbing. You have no hope of getting anywhere without the payed account statis. Which you can pay $15 a month for (Which I have no problem with, MMO developers should make money off their product, just not expect to suck an endless amount out with broken cash shops.), or buy two Apex items off your servers auction house. My server Apex was worth 500-600g. Now apex can only be bought through Trion's webpage for $10. Meaning anyone using apex for a payed account, will be feeding Trion $20 a month instead of the normal $15.
With this being stated, the majority of players pay money for their monthly account. Despite this Trion still forces cash shop purchase with regrade charms, that only come from the cash shop and can not be crafted.
End game bosses are unoriginal and boring. Each boss shoots out some form of area of effect one shot magic attack. Which is countered by standing together the whole fight and casting a spell, that makes all of you immune to magic damage. The only exception to this is boss ship battles.(They are fun.) Bosses are open World, where only one guild gets to kill and loot it. Each with a one day repawn timer. Your faction or the opposing faction can grief you while you fight a boss. Even if you get boss loot, you are still forced to regrade it.
Regrading is a JOKE and is the "hidden" end game in ArcheAge. I've never seen a MMO punish their players so much before for simplely upgrading their equipment. It is a system based only on luck and cash spent, where 99% of the players fail time after time, while the 1% get impossible success after success. Enough so where you just assume they are cheating.
You regrade an item by using a scroll and spending gold each attempt. Charms can be added to this to increase your chance of success. Each success increases the grade of an item, giving it a stat boost. Once you reach a certain grade, your item can not only explode and destroy it, it can fail and fall three grades. There is NO WAY to prevent this, leaving you with only wasted time and money.
I am very sad because ArcheAge could have be great game, but at it's core ArcheAge is built to milk money from your wallet.

The content is somewhat limited. There is a reasonable tutorial, several challenges, and versus mode has a regular mode and a "rush" mode - in which both players run forward until they clash. That being said the game has enough content to be enjoyable, it would just be nice to see more.
The art and music is simple and fits in well with the game.
Kiai Resonance feels like it could be great with more content, however it is still fun as it stands. The price tag is very reasonable.
You're not likely to face any surprises - if the trailer looks appealing then you will enjoy the game.

Kiai Resonance is a 2D samurai fighting game developed by Absorb Reality. In Kiai Resonance you play as a samurai and take part in quick fights and difficult challenges requiring fast reflexes as one hit kills in Kiai. Kiai Resonance is made up of singleplayer fights, multiplayer fights and challenges but my review is focusing on challenges and singleplayer only.
+Cool painting-esque art style
+Simple combat that's relatively easy to get to grips with
+One hit kill combat makes the fights interesting and short
+Three different combat stances to utilise, each with giving you a different advantage
+Interesting challenges
+There's a rush mode which makes you and your opponent charge towards each other at the start of the fight, makes things a little more interesting
+Good tutorial
+Full gamepad support
+Great soundtrack and soundeffects
-Kiai Resonance has a serious lack of content. There are only two characters to choose from. There are only three maps (four if you complete all of the challenges). There's no kind of upgrades or unlocks which doesn't exactly help its replay value.
-The multiplayer is completely dead
-Serious lack of graphical and audio options, all you get is Fullscreen: On/Off, Sounds: On/Off and Music: On/Off
-The singleplayer AI doesn't provide much of a challenge once you've got your head around the controls
Verdict:
6.5
Kiai Resonance is a good samurai fighting game with a nice art style and simple combat that currently suffers from a serious lack of content.

When you first pick up the game, there are 3 stages available. If you play through all the challenges, you unlock a 4th. There are 2 playable characters, both of whom are also the only available opponents. The only graphics option is "fullscreen: on/off", and the sound options are "sounds on/off" and "music on/off".
This probably sounds like a game which is lacking in content, and realistically, it probably is. That said, everything the game has is incredible. The music is simple, and helps set the mood. It's well-done, and not over-done like it very easily could have been. The menu and each stage have unique melodies that play, all fairly understated, and suited to the stage. The shouting voices of the fighters stands out against the music, as do the rare moments where blades clash. The hissing of blades cutting the air is audible as a counterpoint to the music, and the cound of a successful strike stands out as well. Turning the music off puts a measure of extra emphasis on the sound effects, making them seem to stand out more, and somehow giving the game a slightly different tone.
As for the gameplay itself, it's definitely "easy to learn, hard to master" - there are two buttons for movement, forwards and backwards. You can't jump, and the fighters only swap sides when you cross in a climactic final blow. There's also only one attack button, but you have 3 buttons to switch between stances, each of which has its own style of attack. This game doesn't involve complex combos or strings of attacks. There are no healthbars. You strike, once, and your opponent is dead. It's possible to clash a few times, it's possible to jump backwards and avoid a strike. But one hit will decide the fight. Sometimes two fighters will rush into one another immediately, and within a couple of seconds, there's blood-red ink dripping around the fallen as the victor sheathes his sword. Other times there will be a tense standoff, a few quick rushes where the fighters push one another back, or their blades clash, each testing the other's reactions before the decisive blow.
If you've watched a few samurai films or anime swordfights, you'll have seen times where two fighters dash past one another, both slashing with their weapons. There's a moment of sudden stillness where it's unclear who won, before a spray of blood and one of the fighters drops. This game's more intense fights frequently end that way. When you're one of the fighters, you can often pick the winner as the two fighters cross paths, knowing that your blow wasn't the one that landed. Even then, you know it was close.

First, let me say that this isn't an awful game.... there is some genuine fun to be had here (though it requires significant grinding to find). But given Mass Effect 2's spectacular reputation and my high expectations coming into the game, the gameplay experience I had just doesn't warrant a recommend. Maybe more of a "meh" as opposed to a 'No' but definitely not a 'Yes'.
I've been hearing about ME2 for several years now so I was excited when I picked up ME1 and ME2 in a recent Steam bundle. I played both within two months time... ME1, though dated, impressed me so I was excited to install ME2 (as I had heard it was the superior of the two). What I found, however, was not the game I was expecting... instead of a reimagined sequal of ME1, I got what seemed like a poorly designed expansion pack which actually removed more gameplay elements from the original game than it added. Though there are significantly more missions, ME2 felt like a smaller world than ME1 due to its linear level design and removal of certain "open world" elements. The graphic engine seems to be the same as used in ME1 so the only "newness" is a few extra skins and some new minigames (which predictably get old after the 5th time you play them). Buggy gameplay from ME1 was fixed (which was nice) but many gameplay elements - such as RPG elements, open world planet exploration and MAKO gameplay - were completely removed, which I just cannot understand why as those were some of the best parts of ME1.
I still found myself enjoying certain missions and storylines but, honestly, given the total package I just don't understand all of the hype around this game. ME1 is a profoundly better game than ME2. And considering that ME2 came out in 2010 (a year after  Fallout 3, seven years after KOTOR, and almost a decade after GTA 3), I am astonished that this game was met with anything but disappointment by the Mass Effect community.
Overall, I enjoyed about 20 hours of this game (mostly storyline elements). This would normally be great except that it took me 3 times as long to complete all missions (which translates to a lot of grinding to make it to the end). Ultimately it was my OCD and the thought that "I must be missing something here if so many other people liked it" that forced me to finish this game. Otherwise I would have walked away after 15 hours. If you, like me, loved ME1 but are one of the few left who hasn't yet played ME2, the storyline here is worth going through... but I'd recommend watching the ME2 storyline on YouTube as opposed to forcing yourself through this mediocre gameplay. 6/10
Pros:
+ Companion mission storylines and gameplay are superb (this was my favorite part of the game)
+ Level skins are much more diverse than ME1 (with less reused textures and level design)
+ Some of the later missions are genuinely fun (with timed run-throughs and level-specific minigames)
+ Email System and NPC conversations add to the atmosphere
+ Various bug fixes from original game (Companion pathing during combat works now, which is nice)
Cons:
- New Mini-games are just awful (Poorly designed, repeat minigames was one my cons in ME1 but it seems that BioWare decided to double down on this adherence to low-quality puzzle games for simple actions in the game)
- Re-used material from ME1 (About 2/3s of the Codex is a direct rip-off of the original game and they even reused a couple of cut-scenes which cheapened the feel of the game)
- Lack-of or boxy furniture made for empty levels (this just felt like lazy art design)
- Linear Level Design/Removal of Open World Elements (ME2 is much larger of a game than ME1 but it doesn't feel that way due to poor design choices by the developers)
- No Mako gameplay (or any vehicle gameplay for that matter)
- Menu Systems are still awful (and were clearly designed for consoles)
- Removal of what little RPG elements existed in ME1  (I was hoping to design my characters like in ME1 only to find out everybody has only 4 qualities now)
- Pathing Bug that drops or raises Shepard from the level floor forces a revert to the last saved game  (This got me about a dozen times throughout the game)
- Save Feature didn't work in combat and on certain levels (In combination with the pathing bug this forced me to restart entire levels on a number of occasions)
- Character Models are hit or miss (Some of the characters body types aren't consistent from scene to scene which made the game feel very cheaply made, others are just creepy - like when Shepard or Jacob "smiles")
- Main Storyline is weak in comparison to ME1
- Planetary Probing was a neat idea but gets incredibly old after a short while (I wish they would have spiced up this mini-game somehow as I felt like this had a lot of potential)
- Mediocre combat means that missions a actually become the low point of the the game
- Upgrade/purchase system have been dumbed-down (Now instead of having different purchases to equip your character, each vendor offers maybe 3 things to sell and all other upgrades are dependent upon you finding and researching)
- Ship upgrades are a nice idea but poorly executed

A great strategy game similar in many ways to Xcom, but set in a WWII type scenario instead. It also adds its own unique additions to the various mechanics. The class upgrading is done across the board, so when you upgrade a character class(Scout, Shocktrooper, etc.), all characters of the scout class get upgraded to the next level. Same with upgrading weapons and unlocking new ones, everyone that can use it can equip it immediately without having to pay for it. And the game is very story rich.
Whey it comes to the actual combat, it's turn based, where you have a bar that depletes as the character moves, and can shoot once per phase. You get a certain amount of 'Command Points' per turn, and you use that to make character act. So I can select Character A, in which I can now move and attack(or use an item). Then I can select another character and do the same until I finish using my Command Points. But I can also select Character A again if I wanted, but each consecutive 'selection' lowers how much movement points they get.
Valkyria Chronicles has full controller support, however the Keyboard/Mouse controls are also wonderful, which is practically unheard of with PC ports. It also has 60FPS support too.
If I had to desribe it in short, it would be like an Anime XCOM with far more depth and set in an alternate World War II. All in all, I definitely recommend this game, especially to Turn Based Strategy fans. Amazing game.

this game is the definition of wasted potential. sure it's fun for the first couple hours. you'll breeze past the first half of the content in about 2-4 hours, but once you get about two thirds of the way through, the game takes a massive difficulty spike. the game starts reusing old boss fights, but they use them along side other groups of enemies, in addition to the ones that that the boss comes bundled with. see every time you fight a boss they summon 2-4 enemies to fight along side them at the start of the battle. it's impossible to fight *just* a boss. this wouldn't be a huge problem, except that in addition to fighting the bosses again, with more enemies this time, the bosses and their mooks are all powered up, they have more health, and more (and more powerful) moves. now all of theses things combine would be challenging, but managable if not for one major flaw: the arenas in which you fight get smaller and smaller as the game progresses. at the start of the game you fight 1 boss and about 2-3 enemies in a REALLY big arena making it possible to divide and conquer, and avoid attacks. by the end of the game, you can wind up facing about 10+ enemies including 2 bosses in an arena about a quarter of the size in which you found the original boss encounter. oh by the way the second to last boss is in one of the smallest arenas in the game, spawns with 4 ranged units with shields, has undblockable attacks, can block attacks himself, AAAANNNNNDDDDD his minions can't be killed until AFTER you kill the boss. oh and his unkillable minions (seemingly intentionally) position themselves between you and the big guy, and even when they aren't in your way, sometimes your character just seems to ignore him. the autoaim on your attacks seem to prioritize his unkillable minions for some reason, and even when he's alone, it will just ignore him entirely.
all of this only outlines the problems with the combat encounters. most of the other encouters in the game are strictly luck based, and rely entirely on you winning a 25% roll, or you lose most of your equipment/health/provisions.
all I can say is, I hope the devs look at this game, figure out all the stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t they got wrong, and make an awesome sequel, because if not for its compeletly unforgivable, unignorable, experience ruining flaws, this game would be in the running for the greatest game I've ever played. that said, don't buy it. it's not worth you money because you'll never be able to actually beat it without getting incredibly lucky and I mean that literally, no matter how well you play, no matter how clever you are, most of the game comes down to situations where you have a 75-100% chanace of immediately dying a completely unvoidable death.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Response to developer's comment:
the graveyard deals a ton of damage (I think I lost like 45 health most of it in max health reduction) to you if you are cursed, and you are always cursed passed the first wing if I'm not mistaken (100% chance for a negative, potentially run ruinning outcome especially on levels like the king of scales where you lose health/food/gold randomly and can easily starve). also the treasure chest goes from being a nearly garunteed free gain to a nearly garunteed chance to lose most of your health to gas and a mimick (again, often in permanent health reduction). those are the ones that come to mind right now, but I know there are others.
basically some cards like the graveyard have a garunteed negative outcome if you don't know what they do ahead of time and put them in your deck at the wrong time, and others go from being really good during the early stages of the game to just being a death sentence later like treasure chest.
now don't get me wrong, I don't mind that the cards change as the game progresses, I mind that they change completely *without any warning.* if the game told you ahead of time that certain encounters where going to get more difficult that would be one thing, but when an important part of my strategy for getting a good run going with decent gear arbitrarily decides to kill me with out warning... that's when I get a bit upset.
my reccomendation would be to put a level indicator on encouters similar to the monster cards to warn you "hey this has a much bigger chance to go south, you sure you still want it in your deck?" but instead you have to learn that it can screw over your entire run by having it screw over your entire run, and that really sucks.
all that said, I love the ideas you guys put into the game, it's really REALLY cool, it's just that the luck vs. skill could use a little bit of balancing more towards skill --or at least informed deck building-- and the arenas just get way to small and crowded to fight in later on and both those things really ruin an otherwise ingenious game.

The controls are simple and the game seems easy at first; the first few levels have easy challenges, battles with slow counter-attack times, and weak enemies. But then it ramps up. I'm about halfway through the game and it's gotten challenging, but not so much it's just annoying to play. Counters are more difficult, if not impossible at some points, and enemies take a bit more strategy to beat. The storyteller is sarcastic in the best way, often getting annoyed if you wait too long or making fun of your resources if you're doing poorly. The only issue I have with it is there are required cards for every mission, and some of them get old after using them again and again. But they do change up after you get the token for the card, so that's good at least. Overall, it's been a fun experience and I definitely plan to buy the expansion (and any more that come out).

This is a wonderfully made indie card game/action game.  This game is something I don't think has quite been done before.  You build your deck to determine what happens during a round and the mysterious dealer (who is wonderfully animated and voiced) lays traps and misfortunes for you, but he's not your enemy outright.  He plays more of a dungeon master role and lays out the game's story for you.  A lot of time was put into him, as he remembers what cards you used on previous playthroughs and remarks on your playstyle.  If you rely on the same card too often, he will laugh at you for using cheap cards as a crutch.  If you make the enemy deck too easy, he might add a few difficult cards to keep the game interesting.  He has a series of around 16-ish foes for you to challenge, each one harder than the last.
You move your token and land on dealt out cards which determine the environment; then the environment comes to life and fights you in a fighting style remniscent of Arkham Asylum.  There are also trap sections you run through.  The animations during this sequence feel a little mechanical and the default difficulty is MUCH too forgiving.  You can just tap the attack button and win.  I recommend upping it to hard mode ASAP.  It causes all the run and hit animations to move faster, hiding some of the awkward motion during action sequences and keeping you engaged in the battle.
The game has a great soundtrack with SFX that mirror what the card's effect on your character is.  The voice acting and animation of the cards and the dealer is fantastic.  A single game takes around 15-20 minutes depending on how fast you click through the UI, but there are challenge cards that you can throw in to handicap your character, adding to the replay value.
An original idea executed better than any game on the Unity Engine I've seen thus far.  Worth playing.

Update (1 Week Later):
In the week I've been playing around with Conan Exiles I've been extremely impressed with the Dev support this game has gotten.  Funcom has gone above and beyond somehow managed 6 patches and a wide vareity of fixes in short amount of time.  It's seeing support like this that makes me feel like buying something in early access is worthwhile.
-----------------------------------(Original Review)----------------------------
Conan is a little rough around the edges, as should be expected from early access games, but also the most promisng of the survival sandbox games I've played with (RUST, The Forest, Ark).  Unlike those three Conan actually feels a bit more like it could turn into a complete polished game at some point.  It has some things that those games definitely lack but it's also at a much younger and jankier stage of development than they are.
What Conan have going for it?
- The foundation of a story (Needs a lot more but what's there seems pretty good)
- Interesting world and setting
- NPC's (should be a big plus for those that prefer singleplayer or just want an army of slaves)
- A consistent and interesting art style
- Better UI than it's competition.(though the HUD interface needs improved)
- Dong Slider (worth $30 just for that really)
What's working against it?
- This is not a polished build, expect bugs and missing features.
- This is not an optimized build, expect it to perform below your hardware capabilites.
- This has not had the 2 years in early access to be tweaked and impoved yet the way Ark and it's contemporaries have.
- Combat could be a lot better.
I like Conan Exiles.  I think it's a good game that stands a pretty solid chance of being better than it's competition after some polish, optimization, and refining of mechanics.  In fact a year from now I think this game may even be one of the best games on steam.  It's not there yet though and it probably won't be for quite some time.  If your not cool with that DON'T BUY it right now.  If your fine with it being a work in progress and like survival games I'd say pick it up,  It at the very least works better and has more features than both Ark and Rust were when the first showed up on early access.
This game is good looking, fun to play, has great voice acting, and an awesome story.

The singleplayer mode is for practice, since there is no story mode. There is also a local multiplayer for 2 players.

The visuals are beautiful, how some parts of the maps are animated, and some other are in a front layer, not all in the background, it really looks like a "living painting" with the warriors fighting. By the way, my favourite map is "Water" based on Tani Buncho's "Grasses and Moon" painting.

There is one unlockable map, making them 4 maps in total.
To sum up, entertaining game, with more options than it may seem at first, it's a lot of fun when you learn "distracting techniques" and defeat a player with such tricks. The price is maybe a little high for the lack of content, but I do

text:
If you enjoy a deep economy, crafting system, tons of content, and a great community, play ArcheAge.
Still here? Great. The rest of this review will be dedicated to the pros and cons of Archeage, and analyzing how it holds up in the oversaturated MMORPG genre.
Why ArcheAge is good:
-You are immediatly given a huge number of character customazation tools, making it easy to really personalize and come to love your in game sprite.
-Graphically beautiful. Everything from the in game models to the backgrounds and environments feel alive.
-Deep class system. Through the patented "pick 3" class system and the option to change classes at any time, you should never feel bored or disappointed with your role.
-Economy nuts will have a blast. Through a deep player driven market and well designed trading system, wealth is just a couple minutes away.
-Deep and interesting universe. Each area feels aesthetically different and holds its own lore. About 60% of the quests, including side quests, have some deeper meaning in the in game world and give you the opportunity to immerse yourself.
-Gear and loot tends to be pretty well balanced.
-Combat and pvp are intelligent. Mashing buttons isn't going to do you any favors. Play smart.
-The community is, generally speaking, supportive and enthusiastic. Of course, it's up to you to find a guild and make friends, but I doubt anyone would have trouble finding a friendly group to work with.
-Gaining skills feels rewarding. I genuinely looked forwards to each level up because it signified one step closer to something awesome (nothing feels as satisfying as your first meteor or tiger strike)
-The game really did feel like a sandbox. I never felt like I was being pushed one way or another. The story quests act as a sort of guided tour of each area, but other then that the game is more then welcome to let you do as you please.
-Building, owning, and maintaining in game property is intuitive and immensly satisfying. From the smallest cottage, to a mantion or castle, every home interior is fully customizable and ready to show off to your friends.
Why ArcheAge falls short of greatness:
I had a few major issues with ArcheAge, but they mostly all boil down to two thing: Accessibility and Respect for the Player.
So what do these big words mean? Don't worry, I'm here to help. Basically, for much of the time I spent in ArcheAge, the game neither felt easy to use or even that fun at points. Here's why.
-ArcheAge is hard to understand.
Trying to craft or perform higher level trade runs (essential at higher levels) is a bit like trying to hit a pinata. If the pinata was the size of a penny. And your hands were tied behind your back. Basically I'm saying it's really not easy to do. There are a few vague and confusing extra curricular quests you can attempt to learn the most basic functions of these mechanics, but in the end you're still left confused and unsatisfied for most of the process.
-ArcheAge is hard to use without payment.
The so called "pay to win" model people often accuse Archeage of having is, while exagerated, somewhat factual. The game funtions on a "Labor" system, where the player regenerates points while playing, and then spends those points on in game actions. Come the later levels, it is enfuriating to constantly find your self without Labor points. ArcheAge functions on a subscription basis, but unlike other MMORPG's, the subscription is less of a luxury and more of a necessity, as it doubles your maximum Labor and allows Labor regeneration while offline.
-ArcheAge does not respect your time.
ArcheAge has a deep dungeon system and great end game/pvp content. It's a shame you won't see a sign of any of this for the first 150 hours of play time at least. This game does a good job of rewarding players who stick around past the 250 or so hour mark. Not ready to dedicate that much of your time? Sorry, you're missing half of what the game has to offer.
-ArcheAge does not respect your desire for progression.
Grinding, or playing repetative quests for the sake of progression, is a staple for MMORPG's. This is understandable, and can even be fun as a way to fill up your time between more important tasks or quests while leveling up your character. However, in many places ArcheAge falls pray to excessive ammounts of padding and side questing that feels boring, unrewarding, and generally leaves the player dissapointed at the game. I found it really saddening that, although I was surrounded by beautiful environments and interesting lore, most of the time the questing broke down to "Go click F on 4 NPC's, kill 50 monsters, go click F on the same 4 NPC's. Rince and repeat."
I had a bit of a dysfunctional relationship with ArcheAge. Every time the game annoyed me or wasted my time, and I was sure I was going to quit right then and there, it managed to rope me back in with the little things. Have you noticed that when you play music in a dungeon it echoes? Have you ever ridden a snow lion through a rain forest with a friend? Beautiful environments, brutal enemies, and exotic upgradable weaponry system combine to deliver a very solid shooter. Health packs, skippable inbetween-level cutscenes and spawn triggers will bring you back to a different age of PC gaming.
Personally, I purchased Hard Reset on sale and after finishing the game, feel guilty I didn't pre-order it. If you are looking for a challenge, play through this on Insane - while it feels impossible at times, the feeling of triumph you have after completing difficult sections of the game is uplifting. Secrets are abound in this game, some tougher to find than others, but each one gives you currency used to upgrade your weapons or unlock new ones.
While it ends a bit abruptly, the ride there is full of gunplay. Some of the AI is simplistic, but the volume and strength of the enemies provide difficulty. Loved it.

Its amazing how presentation can spice up a simple game.
This is a rouge like where you guide your hero through various challenges, slaying enemies and defeating the boss at the end of each level.  the twist is everything is depicted as card wielded by a mysterious stranger playing across from you.  each encounter is a card thats flipped over and revealed when your peice lands on it and it can be anything from an enemy abush to helping a wandering priest.
most of chanllenges will be simple text scenarious where your given a choice of what to do. depending on your answer you'll sometimes auto succed or fail or four cards with fail or succed will be revealed (how difficult the challenge depends on how many of the cards are success and how man say fail)  the cards are flipped face down and suffled and you pick one and pray.  your rewarded with supplies, equipment, and gold and punished with curses, injuries, and loss of provisions or fights.
Various events will lead to the drawing of monster cards and suddenly your in an arena fending off enemies with arkham city style combat controls.
Then comes another clever twist. often completing challenges will unlock new cards at the end of the round.  you see the challenges you face and the equipment you might earn come from a deck that you can alter.  each round has a requires your equimpent deck and enconter deck to have a certin number of cards and you can swap out encounters or equimpent you don't want to chance coming across in favor of ones you like so you have some conrol of what you'll run into during the game, though the dealer will always shuffle in a set of his own cards to try and trip you up.
And all the while the dealer taunts teases and converses with you.  He's really one of the main highlights of the game.  Its like playing a card game with Ron Peralman dressed as a masked wizard (no its not him but thats what the dealers voice reminds me of)
This game reaks of charm and personality and i highly recomend it. The game play is simple but how its presented makes it into a unique experice.

9/10
Overview RPG/Third Person Shooter
The Good:
+ 6 Character builds to choose from: Soldier, Infiltrator, Vanguard, Engineer, Biotic, and Adept. Each one specializes in different abilities, skills, weapons and each class feels distinct.
+ The combat is excellent as each weapon feels different, the controls are tight and the third person cover and shooting mechanics are solid.
+ Both artistically and technically the game is visually appealing especially when you visit outdoor locations. I particularly like how each of the major cities in the game feel distinct from one another. The bright/light colors of Illium contrast the dark red hues on Omega for example. Just by the appearance of certain locations you can easily get an understanding of what the place is about and what to expect.
+Like the first mass effect, the scope of game is equally impressive. Everything this game has to offer, the characters, races, locations, missions, cities, etc is designed to make you feel like you are part of an epic science fiction adventure.
+The story is more self contained than the first and third game, it certainly doesn't feel as big in scope to the other entries but that doesn't make it is any less interesting or fun. The story focuses more on individual characters rather than a grand narrative and because the characters are so good it makes the overall game better.
+Bioware's strength is writing detailed, interesting characters and this game is no different. The NPC's that you find and join you are some of the most interesting characters you will find in the entire series. Speaking to them and learning about their lives is interesting and adds an extra layer of believability.
+Arguably the single greatest improvement over the first game is the side quests. This time around they are varied, fun , provide interesting back-story to many of the characters and locations and overall make you feel like you are part of a much larger universe. Side quests come in two types. The first is loyalty missions for your crew aboard the Normandy. These missions flesh out more of the characters history and most of the time involve you shooting many enemies. The second type involves you scanning planets to find an anomaly which leads you to the planet's surface to investigate. Most of the time these mission are self contained, however sometimes these types of missions will lead to other side missions.
+Soundtrack and special effects.
The Average:
Probably one of my bigger disappointments with the game is the lack of rpg elements. Rather than improve some of the mechanics of the first game (inventory, UI, exploring planet on vehicle etc.) Bioware simply removed them completely. Even the character classes themselves have been streamlined with each class only have 4-5 skills. The game could be considered a third person shooter with some rpg elements rather than a full blown rpg.
Its great that your choices from the first game carry over. It adds a bit of continuity to the story. The problem however, these choices don't really amount to anything other than a few changes in dialogue. In would have been nice if the choices you made had a much bigger impact in the following games.
The citadel is suppose to be the major hub of the galaxy where all the trading and races come together, yet the design of the citadel feels small and cheap compared to the first game. The citadel is a few floors consisting of shops
The series STILL lacks of controller support
A few crashes
The Bad:
- This is more a fault on EA than the game. Under normal circumstances, when you buy a game on Steam with any dlc or bonuses everything gets downloaded at once, at least that is what I thought. Not with this game. In order to get any of the DLC, you first have to create an account with EA, log into the bioware social website, download each individual piece of dlc and then install each one separately....Thanks EA.
- The game introduces planet scanning to find resources. These resources are used to upgrade weapon damage, biotic powers, upgrade the Normandy etc. This itself would not be a problem except for the fact that scanning planets is repetitive and boring. You are commander Shepard savior of the galaxy, speaking to different races, saving people, exploring planets, fighting dangerous missions... and all of that comes to a grinding halt when you have to stop and scan planets to upgrade anything. It sounds like something that was good on paper but failed in execution.
-I found it odd that the only way to compare weapons is by reading the weapon description. There is no way to compare weapon damage, rate of fire, reload speed, etc.
Conclusion
This is a worthy sequel to an already great game. I just wish they didn't have to sacrifice so many RPG elements to make it.

Ok so this game is really clever. The storytelling makes it. Sharp writing with an incredible flow that you could only get from an interactive experience. I love the way the stories play out across cards that you find, and that completing one card encounter, gives you the next part of the story in a card that you may draw next time you play. The dealer is wonderfully voice acted – something that is sorely missed when it comes to your average indie title. The only negative is that the real time combat is a bit clunky. It obviously draws from the Arkham series’ “Free Flow” mechanic, but is not executed with the same finesse. However, the combat does have some real weight, and seeing your gear materialise from their cards when the battle starts is ultra cool. This is a minor gripe, and something that will no doubt be addressed in Defiant’s future titles.
Seriously – Hand of Fate is ridiculously good, and you should play it.
Also it’s totally heart-warming to see such a great piece of entertainment come out of my home town. Well done!

Hand of Fate is a card game, yes, but not exactly.  It's also an action rpg, and that's what's so unique about it.  Not only that, but the game is totally randomized, like an actual card game.  You choose a few cards from your deck, and the card-master stuffs a few surprises in your deck, and you play the game.  You have absolutely no idea what comes next, and it's not always in your favor.
Not only that, but there are quests in the cards themselves.  For example; you have a card (Let's say Desert Storm) and you find that card in the game.  If you "play your cards right" then you'll be able to get the coin of the card and get the next encounter card, which is Lost in Desert, and so on so forth.
I completely recommend this game.  It is worth every penny, and if it's on sale you buy it without a second thought.

Elsword is an MMORPG that, obviously, has pay to win factors in it, but aren't needed. They are very helpful though. I have spent money but that's for  a e s t h e t i c s. The only thing worth paying for in this game, if you don't care about a e s t h e t i c s, are buying the item slots (increases item quick slot from 3 to 6) and skill slots (increases skill slots from 4 to 8). Even then, I got those for free from events.
I found it to be very fun and there are regular updates with events going on. It's time-consuming like every other MMO mostly because of level grind. Especially from level 90-99.
For a 2.5D scroller, it's actually pretty fun. Smooth animations/frame if you have a good internet (it's an MMORPG, so even if you have an amazing PC setup, this game will not run smoothly without good internet). Very flashy and lots of visuals. Personally, I think it's become very easy for new players to level up lately. Events have given them level boosts, equipment boosts, etc. Later on you'll need to party with others practically all the time. Stages like Secret Dungeons and Heroic Dungeons are difficult.
Sounds for this game is what I'm unsure of. I keep my own music running in the background since I do that for every game.
Be careful about breaking equipment from upgrades. Armour and weapons can be upgraded to +6 but has a chance of breaking onwards to +12.
Learned that the hard way (Rip +10 drones)
Infinite Stamina Weekends have been removed, so grinding will be annoying without stamina potions.
With more characters added lately, new players have a nice range of playstyles to choose from. I joined when there were only seven characters, but now there's 12 characters.
One of the things I don't like about this game is the economy. Unless you buy costumes then sell them on the marketplace, create Secret Dungeon Armour sets and sell them on market (which takes awhile), there won't be any easy way to get money. There's no fixed price for items on marketboard (Eg. BDO has a marketplace and items cannot be sold below or above a certain price. A weapon for 90m silver cannot be sold for 80m or 100m) and costumes pieces usually start at 50m all the way to 700m depending on the item.
Another thing I don't like is the inventory slots. Really compressed and barely able to keep many items at once. You can store it at the bank, but there's almost no space to store anything. You need to buy inventory slots to, well, get more slots. It did teach me what's worth keeping or not.
Take note I don't PvP, therefore this review is mainly PvE.
TL;DR: Good game. Time consuming. Good internet needed. No need to pay for anything to get good. Small inventory/bank space. Broken enhancement system.
EDIT: After checking out Elsword again (Oct, 6, 2017), I found out why I stopped. It got stale for me. No incentive to play anymore. I've most likely ran my time with this. I'll still recommend it, but be wary. Also, get friends to play with you. Even with only one friend. It's much more enjoyable that way especially if you can talk to them through calls.

I have to give Hand of Fate credit. The presentation and style, as minimal as it is, is impressive. The game itself offers a unique and potentially engaging experience. The mysterious dealer sets the perfect mood with his appearance and narration. The only problem is HoF is one of those style over substance sorts of games. The flow of the game is entirely determined through cards as they're flipped over, and its this.... hand... that determines your fate. (eh? eh? that's the pun in the game's title)
Most of the time the game itself never goes beyond making a choice based on the card flipped and then selecting a shuffled card to determine if your action is successful or not. This in of itself isn't bad, but if you're looking for an action-y graphically intense RPG experience with deep lore, you won't find it here.
Infrequently, there are action-y bits. Usually in the form of a fight. Sometimes as an obstacle course. They're good place holders and don't do anything particularly wrong, but the AI is typically predictable and easy to overcome if you're a well seasoned gamer even on the harder mode. The action areas are also cramped looking and claustrophobic feeling.
Playing off its card based mechanics, the more you play and beat the game, the more and different cards you unlock, and the longer the new games you start become. Longer games translate into higher difficulty. This is one of those games where moves are a resource represented as food. Running out of food typically means you lose HP until you die and starving is typically how you fail in Hand of Fate.
Hand of Fate does come together very well though. It works as a game and, most importantly, is enjoyable and fun. The only major complaint I have is there isn't enough content or variety to justify the $25 price IMHO.

Recettear brings a combination of video game genres to the table that I thought I would never see.
It is an RPG, business simulation, and dungeon crawler all in one game.
At first, I was skeptical about how well this combination would play out, but after going through two weeks game time, I'm incredibly happy I spent my money on it.
The game brings a simple but engaging story of a young girl who is forced to pay her father's debt to a loan shark since her father has disappeared for three months (and was last seen about to duel a dragon to the death atop a volcano). Rather than just take your home and everything you care about, the loan shark offers to help you open an item shop and let you make ever-increasing payments on your loan each week.
It is to that end that you begin running your cozy little establishment and learning the basics of capitalism. You can get goods from several different locations throughout town and, as you sell more items, you become able to do more advanced things, like purchase items from customers or mix some items together to get better things to sell.
The dungeon crawling element comes into play through the adventurer's guild, which lets you hire people to raid dungeons for loot. You pay them a lump sum of cash and then take control of them as they hack their way through whatever dungeon you've decided is worth running them through. Provided your adventurer makes it out, you have sweet new merchandise to set on your shelves for sale.
Aside from the store mechanics, where you actually get to haggle with customers for the price they pay (or you pay if you are purchasing an item from them), the storyline of the game gradually evolves and there are neat events that happen sometimes when you're in town that add some flavor to the characters and their personalities.
Altogether, I have to say that I am impressed by this game and would recommend it to others in a heartbeat. The developers took on a difficult task putting this many (and these particular) genres into one game and it did a great job.

Anime. RPG. Shop simulator. Capitalism. Loot. Crafting. Level up awesome characters. What isn't there to like about this game? I've sinked a lot of hours to this game, and the game is anything but short. However, it's replay value is IMMENSE.
General overseeing:
Graphics: 6/10; Not the best you can ever see. However, you can get so attached to the game is doesn't even matter.
Gameplay: 10/10; This game offers you a chance to step into the world of capitalism. Learn the consequences of charging too litttle or too much. While, at the same, time, build badass characters to go dungeon raiding with and craft even better items that go for huge prices. It becomes even better when you can buy stuff to customize your shop: new floors, walls, and carpets. There is no way this game can bore you unless you suck at dealing with Japanese dubs and repetitive selling of apples and cakes.
Story: 7/10; A unique, but casual storyline. Each hero is different in good ways, and there is a lot of option for new dialogues as you replay the game. Anime people may have no problem and love the storyline, but others may refute it. That is fine.
OVERALL: 9/10
It is an awesome game despite it's lolicon looks. (Not that I have a problem with that.) You adventure, get items, sell items, make money, and spend money on better equipment for heroes. You learn to run a shop. And you have fun while doing it. Gameplay is innovative and suspenseful, storyline is a good emphasis on pressure for a child left with debt by her far-away father, and graphics are mediocre and good enough to appeal without making the game look bleak. If you are a stickler for sharp and extreme panoramas and amazing looks, you'll be disappointed. However, most will dismiss it and appreciate the game's excellent play. This game is a ++ for anime lovers.

Played for a few hours today and I must say, very impressed thus far.
Graphics are above average, had some FPS drops to 7 in the beginning, but I screwed around with the options and am at a steady 40/45 FPS on average with some drops to 30 inside my little hut.
Pros:
- Ability to play SOLO.. I absolutely hate the fact that many games FORCE you to play MP, especially PVP. I do not want to work for hours and hours, only to have my base looted by a gang of bored people with nothing better to do.. Personally, that drives me away from many games that look like fun such as ARK etc.
- Great UI.. very smooth, easy to craft, easy to see what you need unlike other crafting/survival games where it takes 5 minutes to make a fireplace (DayZ)
- Smooth and easy placement for crafted items
- Great snap grid for walls and foundations
- Large playable area
- You aren't going to die of thirst or hunger in the first five minutes
- You can set your server to whatever play style suits you and when trying to figure out the game, this can come in handy.
Cons
- Would like more enemies, which I am sure will come with updates, currently there aren't a huge variety
- Would like to run into NPC for quests.. although the foundation suggests this may happen already, have seen some NPC's but they tried to kill me
- More interaction between the AI in game, none at all currently
- Would like to see some villages with both hostiles and friendlies, I understand you are alone, but even in a wasteland there will be a few villages to trade with, as of now there is nothing like this that I have seen
- Currently no ability to settle an amount of land, thus getting rid of the spawners (Built a small hut and it is surrounded by turtle creatures)
- No a sneak/crouch option and it is definitely needed
- My avatars hair whips wildly around in circles, which can get annoying
- Very similar landscape, easy to get lost
Other than that, I think the game is great, the price is a little higher than I would normally pay for a brand new game, but I think it has potential to be amazing in the future.

Nine  years is a large chunk of anybody’s lifetime, for those of us lucky to see a century, it’s almost a tenth of the precious, finite time we get to spend on this planet. I’ve been following the progress of this game since the first few morsels were public and admit to having forgotten about the game several times until inevitably finding more little delicious crumbs to follow until arriving at the 1st of November and a metaphorical cake, responsible for the delicious line of crumbs that preceded it waited to be eaten.
I sat there like a mad man, refreshing the store page every five seconds until I was finally allowed to pick up my fork (controller) and dig in (buy and play the game!) Until at last some wonderful music and gorgeous pixel art made way for the menu buttons, the new game started and I started to take the first bite.
After a brief and somewhat emotionally uncomfortable introduction to basic mechanics, the game proper began in a lush, warm room, I stayed here for five minutes mesmerised by the level of mastery the artist had shown through animation, colour palette and precision of pixel placement. Everything looked as it should, as the artist had no doubt spent hours meticulously on this single interior, this prospect left me feeling both excited and somewhat flabbergasted as to what might be waiting for the majority of the game that was waiting for me.
Outside, the incredible visuals began to be accompanied by some understated but catchy music, fading and acquiring new layers to its depth as the area was explored, and explore I did. I spent a good hour just playing, interacting with objects, smashing pots for the glittering coins within and hitting flowers before watching them grow back. It might be an overstatement to say that small details like this are what make good games great but what it shows is a deeper level of understanding of the symbiotic substance that is a video game. Video games  are a composition of audio, visual and active interaction; the greatest challenge of any game designer or indeed, member of any games design team is to anticipate player action, it may seem stupid but by placing a seemingly small and insignificant flower for me to repeatedly lop the head off of is testament to the level of thought that has gone into building this lush, interactive world to explore.
The devil is in the details, when you move slightly a cloud of dust forms at your feet, when you flap and roll, the air visually moves behind you and it all contributes to making the movement feel dynamic.  Audio, visual and interactivity composed to make even the simple act of movement fun and engaging, which is a relief because as this is primarily platforming and exploration you’re going to be doing that a lot!
Quite a few critics have, in my opinion, unfairly described OwlBoy as having a “retro pixel art aesthetic”. There is no appeal to retro-activity to be found in the sublime pixel pushing of this artist but simply a love, understanding and desire to show the gaming community the brilliance of pixel art as a form of visual art in and of itself. There were so many occasions where I sat there in sheer awe of the level of detail being presented to me in one of the harshest, most technically difficult mediums to present such things. Any person can pick the pencil tool in paint and draw an isometric cube, provided they clicked one pixel at a time this could be described as pixel art but that would be the same as getting someone to paint a portrait of their dog in oils and calling them Rembrandt.
OwlBoy is a master-class in pixel art; it is the interactive equivalent of going to see the finest works of art at La Louvre in that it showcases the medium of pixel art in a manner so far unmatched in any indie game thus far and I would put it on a level equal to some of the greatest pixel work done in video games, ever.
As mentioned earlier the visual is accompanied by some of the most whimsical, brilliantly executed musical pieces that I have heard for some time, everything is meticulous here, considered and there’s no better way to understand that to simply play it yourself. The visual and audio contribute to making each and every area feel unique, hand crafted and a pleasure to explore.
The ability to fly is such a huge and wondrous ability, usually limited to the final parts of many action-driven platformers, so it is such an ingenious twist to  gimp the main characters abilities in the realm of combat very rarely can you do anything but dodge or defend when playing as Otus (the titular owlboy) alone. Luckily the designers were kind enough to supply you with three very different (mechanically and characteristically) friends to grab hold of your feet and offer their projectile shooting abilities, each has their own uses, from providing a piercing rapid fire to cover most basic enemies and weaker structures; to huge bursts of musket fire to incinerate. Not once do you feel like a character is merely there for the sake of it, they have been designed and the world and all of its dirty little secrets has been designed around both your ability to fly and their ability to help you to.
Speaking of dirty little secrets, there’s quite a few, hidden walls to find that usually contain some point of interest such as chests or coins. At one point I discovered a secret, only to return later and realise it held and even bigger one. Discovering these things always feels organic, as though you were meant to and that speaks volumes of the game as a whole to be honest, everything feels as though it was MEANT to be that way, it feels crafted, designed out of a labour of love. There will never be coins you can miss, they’ve been placed in areas that you can access after exploring an area; such is the level of foresight possessed by the creators.
The narrative, story and plot are all wonderfully executed; you’re always kept guessing and there’s enough mystery to fuel a fan base who will inevitably be making discussion threads about why certain things are said or done. The pacing feels tight and considered, not once did I feel the story was rushed or there was too much exposition thrown at me at once. Ultimately, once more, everything felt like it had a purpose, as though it belonged for a reason greater than simply “because it can”.
I’ve spent 20 hours exploring in this game and I don’t feel like single second of my time was wasted in terms of the main content of the game, there’s one mini game whose inclusion seems rather odd and out of place but this would be the singular negative in an otherwise brilliantly executed piece of art. OwlBoy rewards you for exploring, for interacting and provides some of the greatest pixel art I’ve ever seen in a game together with some top notch music.

Last Light is 4A Games' follow-up to the also excellent, but not as polished, Metro 2033. If you've played that, then you mostly know what you are in for. Being able to step back in to the world they have created is in itself a treat. Although the narrative structure and level designs are very linear, it shares much in tone and atmosphere with its Ukrainian sister series STALKER (and, arguably, takes place in the same universe). It's one of very few games to replicate STALKER's truly immersive environment and oppressive post-apocalyptic world, where you never really feel safe. Despite not being able to explore much outside the bounds of the level path, the world feels organic, living, breathing, and full. For once, antagonistic wildlife in a game actually feels like wildlife, instead of just more enemies thrown at you. Creatures run in packs, scavenge remains, and keep to themselves unless you step in to their territory (which often can't be avoided, or is offered up as a risk/reward for loot areas). This world is showcased via some absolutely gorgeous graphical work, which also performs very well in spite of its high fidelity (at least, in the Redux version, which includes graphical tweaks and updates). Adding to the immersion is its wonderfully minimalist HUD, most parts of which are integrated organically in to the game world.
The story and characters aren’t particularly deep or original, but its method of delivery, and the content and message at its core manage to make it compelling none the less. You’ve no doubt seen other fictional works about war that cover similar thematic territory, but  this game’s unique presentation makes revisiting those ideas a very worthwhile endeavor.  The world of the game may be bleak and cruel, but there are always bits of earnest humanity that manage to shine through.  There are a couple binary moral player-choice moments baked in to the narrative, but aside from those most of the game operates in a moral grey area that doesn’t seek to beat you over the head with a “right” point of view. This isn’t unique to Ukrainian games, but it feels much less prevalent in western games, which can often come off as preachy, or undercut their moral outlook with things like tone-deaf jingoism or sappiness.  The only real complaint I might offer up in this category is that nearly all of the women characters are sex objects, and even the one that isn’t eventually turns in to a cliché romantic story beat. This is a problem a great deal of games and media in general suffers from, though, so I’m not going to dwell on it here.
The gameplay experience is a harsh and unforgiving one (particularly on the more difficult Ranger or Spartan modes), in fitting with the game’s world. You will die a lot. This can be viewed as favorably adding to the immersion, but unfortunately it also leads to multiple instances of trial & error gameplay, where you must repeat a section until you finally intuit what the game wants you to do (or give up and watch a guide video). In several instances, mechanics that the player has not been introduced to, will be sporadically inserted in to the game and then never seen again.  In addition to this frustration, the autosave system can sometimes leave you stranded in a seemingly impossible situation (eg, you’ve run out of gas mask filters for an outdoor area). Because the levels are so linear, almost to a fault (with several environmental cut-off points in each mission), this generally means no backtracking for missed items. The occurrence of these design “faults,” be they intentional or not, are not so frequent as to detract from the game as a whole, however.
So yes, it’s a bit buggy, a bit rough around the edges, and most certainly not for everybody. But the experience of this game as a whole is so rewarding in many ways that it will remain among my absolute favorites of the genre.

Kiai Resonance is a 2D, 2 player (local and online) where timing and 'stance' is everything.
The game has a fantastic ambience to it, traditonal Japanese music and backgrounds: you do feel like you are playing hand drawn characters on cloth - I think the presentation for what is really a simple premise of a game is excellent.

Each stance is either a defence, counter strike or strike.

The solo play is IMHO only available so you can get a feel for the stances and movement. There is also a section with challenges that will assist in your quest to follow Bushido and become the ultimate Samurai - these challenges, actually are quite challenging.
If you like these sort of fighting games, get it. However it may be prudent to wait until it has some online action, as the solo and challenges will bore quickly.

GAMEPLAY: The gameplay of Kiai Resonance is, difficult to describe. It is a two-player, two-dimensional (2D) duelling game. Basically, you have two players in a 2D plane fighting with the same weapon, to the death. Speaking of Death, it's a one-hit kill system. If the sword as much grazes you, you instantly die, making the game very tense. It also makes it, in a sense, strategic.
In my experience, most matches last less than a minute if they even reach thirty-seconds. This was how duels were in real life, very quick, brutal affairs. The player has many tricks to use against AI and Humans alike...
The player has three stances, high, middle, and low. Each stance has it's own advantages and disadvantages. They have different purposes and different uses. Unlike Nidhogg, where each strike did the samething. Players can also parry, lock swords, and even charge/jump backwards.
-
GRAPHICS: The graphics of Kiai Resonance are not 'impressive' according to the current standard. However, they are in my opinion, amazing. It is in imitation of traditional Japanese art and fits the game's theme and feel perfectly. It is as if watching an animated painting, objects in the environment move as well.
Also, unlike Nidhogg, this game already has working multiplayer. Complete with a ranking system.

9/10
Overview RPG/Third Person Shooter
The Good:
+ 6 Character builds to choose from: Soldier, Infiltrator, Vanguard, Engineer, Biotic, and Adept. Each one specializes in different abilities, skills, weapons and each class feels distinct.
+ The combat is excellent as each weapon feels different, the controls are tight and the third person cover and shooting mechanics are solid.
+ Both artistically and technically the game is visually appealing especially when you visit outdoor locations. I particularly like how each of the major cities in the game feel distinct from one another. The bright/light colors of Illium contrast the dark red hues on Omega for example. Just by the appearance of certain locations you can easily get an understanding of what the place is about and what to expect.
+Like the first mass effect, the scope of game is equally impressive. Everything this game has to offer, the characters, races, locations, missions, cities, etc is designed to make you feel like you are part of an epic science fiction adventure.
+The story is more self contained than the first and third game, it certainly doesn't feel as big in scope to the other entries but that doesn't make it is any less interesting or fun. The story focuses more on individual characters rather than a grand narrative and because the characters are so good it makes the overall game better.
+Bioware's strength is writing detailed, interesting characters and this game is no different. The NPC's that you find and join you are some of the most interesting characters you will find in the entire series. Speaking to them and learning about their lives is interesting and adds an extra layer of believability.
+Arguably the single greatest improvement over the first game is the side quests. This time around they are varied, fun , provide interesting back-story to many of the characters and locations and overall make you feel like you are part of a much larger universe. Side quests come in two types. The first is loyalty missions for your crew aboard the Normandy. These missions flesh out more of the characters history and most of the time involve you shooting many enemies. The second type involves you scanning planets to find an anomaly which leads you to the planet's surface to investigate. Most of the time these mission are self contained, however sometimes these types of missions will lead to other side missions.
+Soundtrack and special effects.
The Average:
Probably one of my bigger disappointments with the game is the lack of rpg elements. Rather than improve some of the mechanics of the first game (inventory, UI, exploring planet on vehicle etc.) Bioware simply removed them completely. Even the character classes themselves have been streamlined with each class only have 4-5 skills. The game could be considered a third person shooter with some rpg elements rather than a full blown rpg.
Its great that your choices from the first game carry over. It adds a bit of continuity to the story. The problem however, these choices don't really amount to anything other than a few changes in dialogue. In would have been nice if the choices you made had a much bigger impact in the following games.
The citadel is suppose to be the major hub of the galaxy where all the trading and races come together, yet the design of the citadel feels small and cheap compared to the first game. The citadel is a few floors consisting of shops
The series STILL lacks of controller support
A few crashes
The Bad:
- This is more a fault on EA than the game. Under normal circumstances, when you buy a game on Steam with any dlc or bonuses everything gets downloaded at once, at least that is what I thought. Not with this game. In order to get any of the DLC, you first have to create an account with EA, log into the bioware social website, download each individual piece of dlc and then install each one separately....Thanks EA.
- The game introduces planet scanning to find resources. These resources are used to upgrade weapon damage, biotic powers, upgrade the Normandy etc. This itself would not be a problem except for the fact that scanning planets is repetitive and boring. You are commander Shepard savior of the galaxy, speaking to different races, saving people, exploring planets, fighting dangerous missions... and all of that comes to a grinding halt when you have to stop and scan planets to upgrade anything. It sounds like something that was good on paper but failed in execution.
-I found it odd that the only way to compare weapons is by reading the weapon description. There is no way to compare weapon damage, rate of fire, reload speed, etc.
Conclusion
This is a worthy sequel to an already great game. I just wish they didn't have to sacrifice so many RPG elements to make it.
