The bad:
Well the biggest problem that I've noticed is the lack of content and variation.  All opponants look exactly the same and for all I know use the same AI. There's no kind of storymode that one might traditionally find in a fighting game. I haven't tried local versus mode, so I'll assume that functions, however the online competition has been a ghost town every time I've made the attempt.
Final thoughts:
Kiai Resonance feels like a great alpha build game. The core gameplay is beautiful and working as one might expect, but where's the content? Where are the different modes to offer some variety? I would be hopeful if this was an early access game that we might see the polish that this game deserves, but I see no indication that developement will continue. As of the time the I'm writing this review, Kiai Resonance is on sale for $4.49 and may be worth it just to enjoy the traditional styled Japanese art and get a small taste of some fun gameplay. For me, the lack of being able to do anything other than face the same AI over and over really takes away from the experience, so I don't see people really getting much playtime out of a title like this.

My overall rating for Hand of Fate: 100/100
Hand of Fate is something I was missing for a long time. Card deckbuidling game mixed with RPG-games, all hidden in a rogue-like coat. The game is hard, shows no mercy, yet is enjoyable as hell. Let's see why.
GAMEPLAY
+ Card game base
+ Real-time fights
+ Roguelike board game
+ Various encounters
+ Cards are changing and getting more difficult
+ Strategy needs to be changed a lot
+ Well made DLCs!
o Sometimes clunky controls (training is needed :-D )
- Luck is needed (lack of it can be potential game-ender)
Gameplay is based on solving cards, either through choices, or you have to deal with threat personally in combat. As you progress further, game becomes more and more difficult, but there is one thing that has to be cleared. Game is rogue-like, so if it seems unfair to you, then it is right and you have to try your luck.
That can be frustrating sometimes, because hardly defeatable encounter with full gear can be your first card in dungeon! Anyway, both DLCs added some cards and new strategies to defeat upcoming challenges. Still, with all possibilities, the game is a step ahead. Bugged achievements got fixed, so good luck!
VISUALS
+ Marvelous art style
+ Formidable combat
+ Backgrounds and battlefields
- Minor bugs and glitches
There is nothing I can complain about visual style. Cards are stylish, they are looking like an old card game played in some mysterious temple. The atmosphere is mystical and full of tension and expectations. Combat is also perfectly created, though, some creatures might get bugged after hits, but that seems more funny than annoying to me.
CHARACTERS
+ Dealer and Warrior
+ Story
It is a game of life and death. Just the Dealer and unknown Warrior. Nothing more or less. Perfect.
SOUNDTRACK
+ Arabic-style songs
+ Credit song
Jeff van Dyck showed us many excellent performances and this music belongs to one of his best. Arabic-themed songs are adding its piece to whole impression of this mystical game. My favourites - Life and Death, Welcome to the Game, Deal of the Millenia, Dead Skin, Dune Storm, Hand of Fate (Instrumental) and Hand of Fate.
SUMMARY
Card game with real fights, what more can be desired? With music of that kind and perfect voice-acting it was a pleasure to play and discover the secrets of this game. And also to return to it again. Many mysteries were revealed and more are awaiting to be. But is it possible? Let's find out. Perhaps ;-)

After waiting a long time, SCS brings their truck simulator franchise back to the United States and I'm really enjoying the time spent in it.  While it may be only a couple of states covered, there is a lot of potential of having the entire country mapped out, even if that means multiple DLC map expansions.
If you're a recent truck sim player, you may or may not be aware that the developers of Euro Truck Simulator 2 and ATS have developed the 18 Wheels of Steel series during the 2000s decade and it has been a while since the late time they focused on American trucking in 18 Wheels of Steel: American Long Haul.  Since then, the map scale has increased a great deal, focusing on more American cities than ever before.  While some have noticed that the scale is a bit more compressed in comparison to ETS2, it doesn't seem to bother me as I understand that there is already a daunting task from the small development team as it is.  The same goes for the number of trucks because of their focus on wanting only licensed trucks in the game.  You can count on the modding community to address these shortcomings quickly and new official trucks get added in for all players at no charge, as was the case in ETS2.
It is generally the same basic gameplay as ETS2 and there is nothing wrong with that.  A couple of new features have been added to set it apart: weigh stations and multiple parking spots.  The latter adds some of the more challenging parking trials to the player and tests your skills. Or you can skip those challenges if you want to keep things simple.
In spite of the smallish map, there is some nice attention to detail from the silly billboards in Vegas to the amusing amount of burger and donut places,  A few faults with how some of the intersections are laid out, particularly with the less than ideal traffic light situation for cars wanting to turn left. Having a left turn only light would be helpful.  Police presence are rather plentiful and some have complained about frequent tickets, but it really helps to pay attention in advance to when the speed limits change. Just expect some inconsistency with speed limits.
For the price, it's really worth it regardless of if you're an old veteran or a newbie wanting to know what trucking sims are all about.

If you've ever wondered what it would be like to play a card game against a mysterious wizard, then this is the game for you. Just by sitting at a table to play cards against this man, the game does a wonderful job at world building. It creates the impression you're in some sort of Arabian Nights tale, or perhaps one of the Call of Cthulhu back stories. Either way, I was quickly sucked in.
All the card game's rules are handled by your wizard friend, who is both your opponent and your friendly dealer. The learning process for this game was quick. The tutorial is a natural part of the game and a natural part of story progression, which I thought was well done.
The wizard lays out a series of face down cards connected like a road. Your little chess hero starts at one end and has to jump from one card to the next to reach the Big Bad at the other end. Each card you land on is turned over and will result in a random event. Sometimes it will mean combat (that will take you into 3rd person combat mode) but many other times it will be games of chance, or decision making that may affect you later, or risky opportunities. In the end, you reach the Big Bad, enter combat and fight to the death. Victory means you win new cards to add to your deck and a chance to play again to fight a new Big Bad. Defeat means the wizard reshuffles and deals again. You keep your victories over the previous Big Bads though.
Fighting is all about building up hit streaks and finding a rhythm. Mouse and keyboard controls are slightly
'janky' but not bad enough to get in the way or make you lose a fight. There are many cards that enhance the things you can do in combat - they add weapons, equipment, spells, and so on. The combat mechanics are simple and could be improved, but the simplicity of the combat is also what allows this game to be a "pick up and play" type of game. I like the starting animation when your hero enters combat and puts on his gear, it's clever and it's an excellent in-game way to remind the player what cards he or she might be able to use in combat.
Each time I won a game I unlocked new cards which I could add to my deck and play in the next game. The cards I unlocked were random, but also related to my wins and losses to the little battles and tests of luck against the wizard during the game. It made me feel like I had earned them.
If you know that the next card game is going to focus heavily on undead, for example, then you may want to tailor your deck in that direction. The deck builder is straightforward, but if you don't want to bother building a deck, the game will build it for you and it does a good job. I never unlocked too many cards per game, so I never felt swamped, so I always made my own deck. Just to add some spice, the game hid the precise details of new cards until I landed on them in a game, so if I added them to my deck it was a gamble, but a necessary one.
These cards are the bulk of the game and they are what make it so much fun. They are surpisingly varied, and you can even encounter the same card you've seen before and get a totally different experience from it. These cards, coupled with the dialogue from the Wizard, who was talking directly to me, made the game feel personal and turned every victory or loss from these cards into a fun wager.
There is some lore surrounding the Big Bads and there's some lore present in the description of the various characters you meet while travelling, but overall it is light. All the atmospheric strength and character of this game emanates from three places: The first is the wizard and his desk. His hands and his eyes are expressive, I just dig him. The second is the Wizard's voice. I found him wry and sarcastic at times but also dark when he needed to be. And the third place is the deck of cards. I thought the art on the cards was well done and perfectly suited to this type of game.
A single game might be 15 to 30 minutes. So it's perfect for that moment of downtime. I'd say that during that harder difficulties you're more likely to spend 30 minutes on a game than 15, because you'll try different strategies or try for more cards, or get more combat. It just depends on your luck. Except for combat, the game runs at your pace.
- This is a game for someone who values their time, enjoys Call of Cthulhu, M:TG (3rd Ed, Ice Age, or Tempest), watching tv and playing a computer game at the same time because they don't really want to concentrate, and graphic novels.
- It's probably best with a controller, good with a keyboard and mouse, definitely not with a trackpad.
- Works on low-ish settings on my Lenovo Yoga 2 Pro.

Hiya! I'm uh, rather new to this whole review thing, but I'mma give it a shot anyway!
Ah, Elsword. A game I've gone on and off playing constantly (Which right now I'm currently in the on stage), with characters I've grown to love such as Add, Eve, Elesis, Lu/Ciel, and so many more. To be honest, if I wrote this review when I first started playing it would be negative. Plenty of reasons why, all of which I'll go into. As you can see, though, I'm giving this game a positive review, which I will also go into! Don't worry, don't worry, TL:DR will be at the bottom. :P
Now lets start with some negatives.
-Let's start on matchmaking for PVP. Holy crap is this bad! Like, completely unranked level 25 goes agaisnt a S rank level 90? How's that fair? What chance do I have? I haven't even earned my first rank, yet I'm stuck against people of a rather high rank! What do I do against that? Well, besides be either Rena or Rose and spam X. (I do not hate either character by the way, I've seen skilled players for both that don't only hit X. It's just that most do the X strat.) KoG seems to have this problem of "Let's rebalance the characters guys!" Rather than "Let's fix the matchmaking!" The characters are fine! Yes, there are a few that are pretty strong, or nigh unbeatable in PVP if played well. There are characters like that in big tournament fighting games too! The big problem isn't the characters at this point! The characters have been buffed/nerfed enough for people to live! It's now the matchmaking that needs to be fixed! I'm sick of trying to get into pvp with my level 45s or such and getting stuck against S+ ranked max levels that roflstomp me in the ground.
-On to one of the biggest issues of this game now, the cash shop. Holy crap is the cash shop an issue. Not only are the costumes pretty damn valuable (I mean have you seen their buffs?), but their almost necessary for PvP! Not to say you can't win without em, but they're pretty worth while, and more often than not those with a costume will beat out those without one. Plus all the buffs and boosts you get using K-Ching? It gets ridiculous. Now, I get that you can sometimes get costumes and such from the big bad board, but those get sold for like, over 100,000,000 ED each piece. For a whole set (That's being sold cheaply mind you) you need about 400,000,000/500,000,000 ED? That's kinda ridiculous! Now, I may be speaking out my booty here, I don't have a max level who gets whatever ED a max level gets, but for us lower/medium levels that seems pretty hard to reach!  Then the free costumes we get? They aren't permanent most the time! And when they are they're those pretty bad outfits, like the Steam Halloween Pumpkin hat, or the new Thanksgiving outfit you can earn. It just kinda sucks how much good stuff is in the cash shop you just can't get otherwise.
- Okay, okay, I may of said that the characters weren't thaaaat bad, but I may of pushed past one little thing...Or a lot of little things. Certain characters can spam a liiittle too much honestly, or are just too hard to really do anything against. Lets see some examples! We gat Nightwatcher Rena and her endless traps! All of which she stands on so you can't combo her! And all the while she's pressing X! Then we got Rose and her auto guns! Pew pew pew! That's all there is to that! We got Blade Master and his Slicy Dicy tricks which give him super armor! Speaking of Super Armor, Infinity Blade Elsword! Not much needs to be said about that lil rascal and his endless Armor!  What about Iron Paladin and his inability to be damaged due to his damage mitigation, all while having super armor? Yeah, it can get pretty bad. However, realistically, all these strats CAN be countered or beaten out. I've not only seen it (Using super armor effectively against Nightwatcher traps, or taking advantage of the Auto Guns mana giving.) but I've also done it plenty myself! (Dodging Raven's initial slashes when he starts up his Super Armor combo leaves him pretty open for counter attacks, and IS Elsword isn't impossible to deal with against his super armor, it's just pretty damn annoying.) However IP Chung? Naw, that guys a jerk.
Okay! That may not be all the negatives, but let's just move on to the more positive aspects!
-The characters! Oh my god I love the characters of this game! Their personalties are so wonderful it's not even funny. Well, okay, it's a little funny at times. I think I'll only go into my favorites, I don't wanna explain the whoooole cast. So we have Add, the mentally and emotionally scarred Nasod obesessed scientist with a horrific past that drove him to the depths of madness! Then we have Elesis, the serious yet bubbly Red Haired Knight and the older sister to the games main character, Elsword! Then we have Rena, the bubbly, happy, motherly figure of the group! The personalities are all so different, and sometimes the clash rather greatly. For example, we see Aisha and Elsword bump heads plenty, and we see Add's difference in views compared to the others when he finally joins the group. The characters are just so much fun, and watching them all interact in the little quest dialogs is a lot of fun.
- The combat is actually pretty dang fun honestly. Yes, it can get repetitive, but so can anything really if you do it enough. It's all about taking it in strides and not just over saturating yourself to the point you feel sick of it. The combat is pretty easy to grasp. Arrow keys to move, Z and X to attack, A S D C to use abilities (With added QWER if you get the medal thing), and different attacks depending on your motion, from running to jumping to double jumping. However, to actually be good at the game? That takes a lot of practice. The combos can get pretty intense honestly, and learning how to string different attack patterns into a long running combo is both challenging and pretty satisfying. It takes practice and work, just like any other game that you wanna be good at.
- The job change system is absolutely wonderful. I know this isn't the only game to have it, but none the less in this game particularly it's beautiful. Each character has a choice between 3 jobs  (Besides Rose who has 4) which then get a second job change to a more advanced version. Like Add goes into Time Trace at level 15 which upgrades to Diabolic Esper at 35, or Rose goes into Bloodia at 15 which then turns to Crimson Rose at 35. Of course not at those levels, unless you buy the cash shop items, since you gotta do quests to reach them. The reason this is so wonderful though is for one simple fact. Each job change technically has its own personality, even if the lines don't fully change. Like Grand Master Elesis is technically one of the lead knights of the Red Knights. Meanwhile, Crimson Avenger led the Red Knights into an ambush that led to them being killed and her being corrupted by Dark El to survive. While GrM is far more bubbly yet serious, CrA is far more dark and agressive.  I think that makes the characters more interesting, simply because you see how they do/react in different situations.
Okay, that really wasn't everything, either good or bad, about Elsword. It's just that I write a lot, as you saw, so I didn't have room. So, for TL:DR Negatives are really the PVP matchmaking, some character issues and the Cash shop, while the Positives are the Character personalities, the story, and the combat.
Honestly, I do recommend this game. I think it's wondeful, it just has plenty of issues that need to be worked out or changed. I don't think it's for everyone of course. If you want to be competitive without spending a dime then you got a lot of work cut out for you, but if you just wanna be a casual player who doesn't care too much (like me) or you wanna see interesting characters interact, then this game can provide a lot of fun and can be one great time killer. So this game gets a thumps up from me!

Last Light is 4A Games' follow-up to the also excellent, but not as polished, Metro 2033. If you've played that, then you mostly know what you are in for. Being able to step back in to the world they have created is in itself a treat. Although the narrative structure and level designs are very linear, it shares much in tone and atmosphere with its Ukrainian sister series STALKER (and, arguably, takes place in the same universe). It's one of very few games to replicate STALKER's truly immersive environment and oppressive post-apocalyptic world, where you never really feel safe. Despite not being able to explore much outside the bounds of the level path, the world feels organic, living, breathing, and full. For once, antagonistic wildlife in a game actually feels like wildlife, instead of just more enemies thrown at you. Creatures run in packs, scavenge remains, and keep to themselves unless you step in to their territory (which often can't be avoided, or is offered up as a risk/reward for loot areas). This world is showcased via some absolutely gorgeous graphical work, which also performs very well in spite of its high fidelity (at least, in the Redux version, which includes graphical tweaks and updates). Adding to the immersion is its wonderfully minimalist HUD, most parts of which are integrated organically in to the game world.
The story and characters aren’t particularly deep or original, but its method of delivery, and the content and message at its core manage to make it compelling none the less. You’ve no doubt seen other fictional works about war that cover similar thematic territory, but  this game’s unique presentation makes revisiting those ideas a very worthwhile endeavor.  The world of the game may be bleak and cruel, but there are always bits of earnest humanity that manage to shine through.  There are a couple binary moral player-choice moments baked in to the narrative, but aside from those most of the game operates in a moral grey area that doesn’t seek to beat you over the head with a “right” point of view. This isn’t unique to Ukrainian games, but it feels much less prevalent in western games, which can often come off as preachy, or undercut their moral outlook with things like tone-deaf jingoism or sappiness.  The only real complaint I might offer up in this category is that nearly all of the women characters are sex objects, and even the one that isn’t eventually turns in to a cliché romantic story beat. This is a problem a great deal of games and media in general suffers from, though, so I’m not going to dwell on it here.
The gameplay experience is a harsh and unforgiving one (particularly on the more difficult Ranger or Spartan modes), in fitting with the game’s world. You will die a lot. This can be viewed as favorably adding to the immersion, but unfortunately it also leads to multiple instances of trial & error gameplay, where you must repeat a section until you finally intuit what the game wants you to do (or give up and watch a guide video). In several instances, mechanics that the player has not been introduced to, will be sporadically inserted in to the game and then never seen again.  In addition to this frustration, the autosave system can sometimes leave you stranded in a seemingly impossible situation (eg, you’ve run out of gas mask filters for an outdoor area). Because the levels are so linear, almost to a fault (with several environmental cut-off points in each mission), this generally means no backtracking for missed items. The occurrence of these design “faults,” be they intentional or not, are not so frequent as to detract from the game as a whole, however.
So yes, it’s a bit buggy, a bit rough around the edges, and most certainly not for everybody. But the experience of this game as a whole is so rewarding in many ways that it will remain among my absolute favorites of the genre.

First things first: It's a sequel underground arcade racing game from Rockstar San Diego, released in the 2003. And it's working on the Windows 7 and Windows 10. At least, in the most cases.
What's good about? Well, basically this game is really like the first Midnight Club, which was the honored hit of the underground arcade races a good time before Need for Speed catch up. It's quite original, both in single and multiplayer... And it's working on the current OS, unlike the first game, so, if you want to scratch some dust and look at the roots - don't turn it down! The price is not anything high, there are regular sales, bundles or even free giveaways from time to time.
Originality goes mainly from the "open world" pattern, with three big cities to explore (LA, Tokyo and Paris), and "cruise mode", where you drive around the city looking for an opponent, then chase him, then race him, and finally pink slip him. Or her. Each of the riders you challenge is a colourful distinctive character (or, at least, supposed to be). Also, there are the many multiplayer game modes like "capture the flag" and "detonator"... Or the races with checkpoints not ordered in line but scattered around, where you need to find your own better way. Also, there is some damage system for your car, only visuals involved, though.
On the other side of coin... The game is far from obligatory to see, if you're not recollecting, say, all the Rockstar-produced titles on the market, or all of the famous underground racing games. It's dated. It was obvious right in the 2003, with the awkward visuals from early PS2-era, with the gameplay, which was not developed much since the first Midnight Club and was left behind by NFS Underground and other racing titles released in 2003 and around.
There's is no car tuning. The difficulty is either too low or too high, too event-scripted and has little to do with player actions. The cars aren't any special, there are too few of them, and they are mostly feels the same (which makes pink slips kinda stupid, except from the first one, when you getting a nitro).
The music is too bleak mostly, the usual: some rap, some electonic tracks - but almost all unnoticable and uninspiring. Except, maybe 1-2 tracks, And yeah, I'm still holding in my player many tracks from 90' and early 00', so I'm not just some kid with dubstep-killed ears, who can't notice a good rhyme or good tune. It's just a dull playlist. The first Midnight Club had a better choise of noticable tracks, which were good to accompany a fast lane. Not talking about other racing games of the time...
Finally, the feature with the stupid pedestrians, jumping under your wheels, which you can hit at your leasure... But without fun, or some points, either for applause such road kills (as in Carmageddon or GTA 1 or 2), or to punish you somehow and prevent that reckless driving... No. Human models on the streets of Midnight Club aren't even counting as obstacles. You'll not loose you speed or get a "wretched car" texture, as it goes there with crushes. You just drive through the corpses unconscionably, which sounds normal only unless you've seen some splattered bodies in real life, on your street, around your home. I'm very far of general fake moralizing that "games provoking people to violence", no, that's bullthing. But there, that "freedom", it's kinda unpleasant experience. Of the same kind, as trying to sell some "Plague Inc Evolved" to the family member of the victim of some deadly flu outbreak. Not everything in games are alright, if you catch my drift.
Overall, with all positives, like originality, somehow decent engine (even if looking dated even at the release date), big cities to cruise around... and downsides, as very scripted-events-based AI, the feel of speed, which is really eluding with each race, with mostly unnoticable cars which you can't enhance anyhow... With the dull soundtrack... Well, it's 6/10 on my scale. The game certainly made its way in the history of arcade races, but... that credit goes mostly to the first Midnight club. The follow-up was too late, and not so good in the comparison to other titles around. And no, I'm not an NFS fan, unless it's Porshe 2000 Unleashed. I'm just a guy with some tastes and opinions, which could be far from yours.
Peace, people.

Everything you do ingame costs Labor points: to open pouches from enemies, cut down trees, mine ore, crafting, etc. If you play for free, you get 5 points every 5 minutes ONLY if you are online. If you pay however, you get 10 labor points every 5 minutes even if offline.

If you want to play it for free, the only way you can do stuff is by leaving your game open to stack labor points.
On a last note, everything in the cash shop is way overpriced to be worth your while.

If you've ever wondered what it would be like to play a card game against a mysterious wizard, then this is the game for you. Just by sitting at a table to play cards against this man, the game does a wonderful job at world building. It creates the impression you're in some sort of Arabian Nights tale, or perhaps one of the Call of Cthulhu back stories. Either way, I was quickly sucked in.
All the card game's rules are handled by your wizard friend, who is both your opponent and your friendly dealer. The learning process for this game was quick. The tutorial is a natural part of the game and a natural part of story progression, which I thought was well done.
The wizard lays out a series of face down cards connected like a road. Your little chess hero starts at one end and has to jump from one card to the next to reach the Big Bad at the other end. Each card you land on is turned over and will result in a random event. Sometimes it will mean combat (that will take you into 3rd person combat mode) but many other times it will be games of chance, or decision making that may affect you later, or risky opportunities. In the end, you reach the Big Bad, enter combat and fight to the death. Victory means you win new cards to add to your deck and a chance to play again to fight a new Big Bad. Defeat means the wizard reshuffles and deals again. You keep your victories over the previous Big Bads though.
Fighting is all about building up hit streaks and finding a rhythm. Mouse and keyboard controls are slightly
'janky' but not bad enough to get in the way or make you lose a fight. There are many cards that enhance the things you can do in combat - they add weapons, equipment, spells, and so on. The combat mechanics are simple and could be improved, but the simplicity of the combat is also what allows this game to be a "pick up and play" type of game. I like the starting animation when your hero enters combat and puts on his gear, it's clever and it's an excellent in-game way to remind the player what cards he or she might be able to use in combat.
Each time I won a game I unlocked new cards which I could add to my deck and play in the next game. The cards I unlocked were random, but also related to my wins and losses to the little battles and tests of luck against the wizard during the game. It made me feel like I had earned them.
If you know that the next card game is going to focus heavily on undead, for example, then you may want to tailor your deck in that direction. The deck builder is straightforward, but if you don't want to bother building a deck, the game will build it for you and it does a good job. I never unlocked too many cards per game, so I never felt swamped, so I always made my own deck. Just to add some spice, the game hid the precise details of new cards until I landed on them in a game, so if I added them to my deck it was a gamble, but a necessary one.
These cards are the bulk of the game and they are what make it so much fun. They are surpisingly varied, and you can even encounter the same card you've seen before and get a totally different experience from it. These cards, coupled with the dialogue from the Wizard, who was talking directly to me, made the game feel personal and turned every victory or loss from these cards into a fun wager.
There is some lore surrounding the Big Bads and there's some lore present in the description of the various characters you meet while travelling, but overall it is light. All the atmospheric strength and character of this game emanates from three places: The first is the wizard and his desk. His hands and his eyes are expressive, I just dig him. The second is the Wizard's voice. I found him wry and sarcastic at times but also dark when he needed to be. And the third place is the deck of cards. I thought the art on the cards was well done and perfectly suited to this type of game.
A single game might be 15 to 30 minutes. So it's perfect for that moment of downtime. I'd say that during that harder difficulties you're more likely to spend 30 minutes on a game than 15, because you'll try different strategies or try for more cards, or get more combat. It just depends on your luck. Except for combat, the game runs at your pace.
- This is a game for someone who values their time, enjoys Call of Cthulhu, M:TG (3rd Ed, Ice Age, or Tempest), watching tv and playing a computer game at the same time because they don't really want to concentrate, and graphic novels.
- It's probably best with a controller, good with a keyboard and mouse, definitely not with a trackpad.
- Works on low-ish settings on my Lenovo Yoga 2 Pro.

A flawed gem, but a gem nonetheless.
Overall I really like the game but it really has some issues that can make the game really annoying. I think I’m about ¾’s through the game. The game has a beautiful aesthetic and makes you really feel like you’re sitting at the table with your sleep deprived and vindictive DM, along with some very cool music to fit the mood.
The narrator/ DM/ creepy old guy in a weird crypt has a pretty amazing voice, and has a lot of interesting things to say. It’s cool to hear what he has to say when you reveal a new card, or his quip before the boss fight.  I also like the “choose your own adventure” vibe you get between making your deck, and the multiple options some cards have. It gives the game a great amount of replay ability.
The game does have something in it that I find very frustrating when playing. When you unlock cards for your deck, some stay in your deck until you defeat them on a level. This itself isn’t that bad, but one card in particular makes this a nightmare. After beating one of the bosses three copies of a card called “Ratman Hunting” are put into your deck. These fights can be anywhere to an easy-ish fight to a nightmare, and very rarely gives you any reward. The worst part is to get rid of it you have to use a different card, and pay 50 gold, which is a silly amount. I have not been able to both find this card on the field, and pay for it, even if I sell all of my equipment. These cards are pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Another big issue for me is that sometimes cards rules seem to change on you and that seems like it kinda defeats a large point of this game. I’ve had the probability of card change on me for seemingly no reason, and I’ve gotten encounters on cards that I hadn’t before, without so much as a witty one liner from the DM about patching the card.
Also the arena’s get really cramped really quickly and are too small, and later on when they become booby-trapped it becomes a nightmare. Especially with the plague rats that poison you if you go by there body after you kill them. It makes what little land you have even more of a mine field. Overall the combat is serviceable but too clunky for the amount of precision it demands.
Overall I like the game and it is a lot of fun, but there is some frustration factors. I would recommend it if you love tabletop games, and “choose your own adventure” style games, but avoid it like a plague rat if you were interested in it’s combat.

An adventurer walks into an item shop.... in the typical JRPG world, you know where it goes from here--you sell off all your unwanted junk and buy the nice upgrades you've been eyeing.  In Recettear, however, you're a plucky young heroine Recette charged with making enough dough running an item shop to pay off the massive debt your dear old dad left you with (thanks, Pops!).
The visuals are nothing stunning or groundbreaking, typical JRPG fare here, and the musical is a tad forgettable, but the unique game-play really shines.  Recettear essentially is like two games in one--a rouge-like action RPG as you dungeon-crawl your way through various randomized maps gathering loot, and the entrepreneurial world on the other side, where you attempt to make a tidy profit off the baubles you acquired in said dungeons.  It makes for a unique formula that helps prevent fatigue from either one of the two activities.
If you're up for a light-hearted JRPG with a cute characters and entertaining game-play that switches up the typical formula, give this one a try!

First, It's Early Access, if you don't accept that you're going to have problems.
Pretty good for an EA launch.
Performance:  The dev team is shipping out updates daily to fix bugs and server issues. Server lag under control enough that enemies now work and can properly attack, I've experienced no crashes in 2 days of play and single player runs perfectly fine.
Crafting: Your typical survival game crafting, cut down trees, grab rocks, slay beasts and rip their hide from their still warm corpse, etc. Granted, ingredients are a bit more exotic than most survival games.
Building: ARK-like, but with all of your complaints addressed. You can rotate objects on any axis using your mouse wheel and ctrl, alt, or shift. Foundations and walls can be put a pretty far into the terrain, allowing building on narrow or otherwise uneven areas.
Combat: I'm not a fighter, so I haven't figured out fighting quite yet, but it uses a combination of blocking and dodging, or just shiving the crap out of something with a sword and a dagger. With lag being fixed (or single player) archery is viable, though the first bow has terrible range.
World: I've explored a third of the world and it seems well crafted so far. I haven't encountered any stuck spots yet, and even found a few hidden caves.
Overall pretty good for the first few days of an Early access and I look forward to how the game progresses.

There are very few games which can be described as having truly perfected their formula. One could say that Mario and Sonic perfected the platformer, that mario galaxy perfected the 3D platformer, perhaps even that games like GTA: San Andreas perfected the open-world formula. Mass Effect 2 is a game that has created its own formula by delicately fusing RPG elements with third-person shooter gameplay, and the result is simply pure perfection.
The game picks up a few years after the first Mass Effect game and revolves around the protagonist from the first game, John (or Jane) Shepard, who after waking up from a coma and being essentially brought back from the dead by a shadowy organisation named Cerberus must stop an invasion of deadly aliens known as the Collectors, who are abducting entire colonies of humans for some unknown purpose. To do this, he must assemble a team and travel beyond the Omega 4 Relay, from which no ship has ever returned. As he recruits new allies and old friends for his suicide mission, Shepard makes new discoveries which reveal more and more of the mysterious Collectors' nature and goals.
The story in this game is absolutely amazing. How the plot progresses depends partly on the actions that Shepard took in the first Mass Effect, so I highly reccommend playing that first before this. The rest is decided through the game's morality system - "Paragon" choices make Shepard a much more noble, just character, whereas "Renegade" choices make him bolder, harsher and colder. This allows for a different experience and different character developments for Shepard depending on what choices the player makes throughout the game and its predecessor - anything that you do could change the course of the whole game. And when you reach the ending, I absolutely guarantee that you will be on the edge of your computer chair with tension. Also returning from Mass Effect 1 is the ability to start a romantic relationship with one of the characters on board the ship. This has little effect on the storyline itself but it's kind of cute to see Shepard finding love.
As for the gameplay, Mass Effect 2 builds upon the starndard third person shooter formula with some innovative features, for instance Shepard and his team can use various abilities in battle, including various technological abilities, different weapon ammo types and "biotics" - psychic-like abilities which can be used for both offence and defence. This seems to make battles flow much more as you swictn betwnn shooting and using your powers to find the best way of dispatching your enemy.
The game has a "loyalty mission" system, wherein you can gain special missions from particular characters, and if you complete these missions you will unlock an extra outfitm and extra power and that character's "loyalty" - in the endgame thhis will become very important, so after you start receiving these missions, try to avoid other missions until you have recruited everyone and completed all of their loyalty missions. Shepard can also purchase upgrades for his allies and for his ship, the Normandy - these will also be much needed in the endgame.
All in all, Mass Effect 2 is hard to describe with any other word other than its own title. With an awe-inspiring story, action-packed gameplay and endless replay value, no self-respecting gamer should pass it up.

If you liked Mass Effect 1, odds are you'll enjoy this one, since it mostly improve on the previous episode. Still, the game remains a rpg/shooter/dating sim hybrid, with all the flaws that implies.
+ The firefights are cooler and much more enjoyable than before.
+ The individual dialogues make more sense; it is now impossible to romance someone by mistake.
+ The secondary characters are more interesting (and fleshed out) than in the first opus.
- The rpg part is far from what it could have been. The scenario is pretty bad, and while you can go everywhere on the map, there is no real point to it.
- Hunting ressources feels like a chore. It's rare to have such a boring crafting system.
- The cover mechanism could have been improved upon. Sometimes your character will just jump over a crate/rock instead of taking cover, resulting in his death.
The Mass Effect franchise is great for people looking for their science-fantasy fix, but it suffers from a number of problems.

I know a lot of people complain about different parts of this game, and the game probably would be a lot better if they listened to those complaints and fixed the game accordingly... but honestly, even as it stands now, and even for someone like me that's too cheap to put money into a patron subscription (....my money goes to Hearthstone packs instead...) the game is still a blast.
It's done so much that I really haven't seen anywhere else (such in-depth systems for flying, sailing, driving, diving, trading, etc.) and for that, I still can't help but have fun with this game.
Given, I haven't fully explored the end-game stuff and many people have been complaining about the way obtaining end-game gear works, so I haven't run into those frustrations firsthand yet. Nonetheless, fun is fun, and I've had a lot of it so far (don't mind my low play hours here, I didn't play it through Steam before).
Also one final note: I do think the labor system is kind of brilliant. Not terribly brilliant, but kind of brilliant. Only because thus far I haven't come across any better way to combat complete market destruction by bots. At least there's one more obstacle in the way, since just to gather or craft things, you have to pay labor which is only accumulated over time, and is not a tradeable resource. I think that puts a nice balance in the economy (compared to something like, say, Runescape, where it's ridiculously easy to bot, and where bots just completely overproduce and destroy the economy).

Without spoiling the story the adventure you go on is full of thrills, twists and moral choices that you can make, and an elaborate dialogue selection that influences the story. I was suspect at first, but so far this is a really great game.
I haven't sunk in as many hours as i'd like, but i'm over half way through the story mode.
Basically, its a rogue-like, and the fighting portions are a mix of Fable and Arkham Asylum.
Your character will develope each session in a table-top game kind of style. Encounters will often present in a "pick a card" luck based system. You're not completely subjected to the luck system. You can take note of the winning card before hand and try to follow it as it shuffles.  Sometimes you win. Sometimes you get bit hard.
Make no mistake, a single RNG luck-based encounter can kill your character. I had a character with extra life, food and gold, and awesome gear. Then I bumped into a Devil, and he took me down to 8 health, gave me extra tough monsters, and I died in one hit.
But this isn't a bad thing. It's not a huge loss. If you lose a session you'll likely still unlock something. You'll never lose hours of progress. The setbacks are very minor, and the potential progress always outweighs the loss.
You will get frustrated every now and then, you'll get back-to-back sessions of getting your♥♥♥♥♥spanked by RNG and bad luck. But you won't reach that Dark Souls level of rage where you want to throw your computer across the room.
Endless Mode is very unforgiving.  The RNG seems very slanted against you in it, but it provides a legit challenge, and you will need some luck to get far.
This is a great game. It's a high quality rogue-like, with elements of a table-top game. The graphics in fight scenes look great. The sound is great, especially when listening to The Dealer doll out cards as your session progresses.
The game is worth the money. I was fortunate to pick it up on the summer sale.

Google "The Forest inventory" if you want to see how its done right.
I could live with all that if the game was fun though, but its not. You and every moving entity in the world (NPC too) are jittering arround from constant lag. Every five meters you see an identical looking hut or camp built by another player, usually named "M1ck L0ngd1ck" or equally childish anti-roleplayers. The genitalia-slider only goes one way, which means  the  s c h l o n g  of every dude you meet is as long as their legs and bazongas on the--usually nude--girls come with a mandatory weapons license. If you don't constantly eat something like an obese american office drone, you die within a minute. Clever sidenote: Eating bugs gives you about 10 seconds to live.
Killing something is a bit of a gamble with the server. NPCs generally love to teleport arround, sometimes take 20 hits, sometimes 5, sometimes they just stand still until they drop dead. Same goes for simple travel. If you like rubberbanding, Conan Exiles is your game. And let's not forget how you can die of thirst while standing in water and hammering your waterskin button. At least the game gives you a map with GPS right at the start, because who wants to explore anyway, right?
The only ways to communicate are global, guild and local chat within close proximity. No personal chat like tells of any kind, no groups, no parties, nothing. You either create a guild with your friends (good luck finding each other), or you broadcast to the entire server of Dr L0ngl0ve's.
I understand this is early access, but early access does NOT mean early alpha state. Compared to DayZ and The Forest, Conan Exiles is a DayZ copy with rudamentary features and a netcode from the 80's.
Windowed fullscreen works, that's a plus. Performance-wise its smooth sailing on my 4770K@3.5Ghz, GeForce 1060, 16GB RAM. Loading times are okay from my SSD. Also the character creation is pretty good for a survival slasher.

I can remember when this game first came out on steam, I saw it on the sales page and thought 'eh, this looks cute, and it's fairly cheap, why not', I got it on a whim. What I DIDN'T expect was for this game to be a gem among all the indie games on steam.
So the premise - you are a Recette Lemongrass. Your father ran off to go adventuring, left you with all his debts. and the loan Fairies are after you to collect. What's the logical solution to this problem? OPEN AN ITEM STORE. Cue the start of the day-to-day antics of trying to repay your debts, hiring adventurers to beat up giant crowbar-weilding mice, and selling a book that comes with free Alcohol to small children.
When it comes to the buying/selling system, the mechanics are easy to pick up and the game gives you plenty of information on which items are hot and which are not, and even if you do fail to pay back an installment, your only punishment is a CG of Recettes new house (THE BOX) and then you are thrown back to the start with all the items you had when you Game Overed, which makes it easy to get going again.
My only issues with the shop part of the game are that as you might expect, there are certain tactics you can employ to rake in the cash far faster than the game really intends, removing all challenge, and the way you can more or less ruin your file by playing badly and have no idea that you've done wrong, as the story often requires you to have certain characters visit your store to trigger story events or unlock new dungeons, and if you end up giving your store the kind of atmosphere that a character you need doesn't like and/or annoy them by failing to provide them orders or overvaluiing items so they leave without buying, you can end up getting stuck without any indication that you're stuck.
It's also not really a criticism per-se, but it's a little annoying that you can't directly offer equipment to your adventurers-for-hire - it's annoying when you spend hours hunting down all the ingredients to craft an ultra-laser cannon, then having to sit there hoping that the character that can use it comes into your store, then hoping they want said cannon and not one of your 10 ham sandwitches, THEN hoping that them and not one of the 20 generic villagers in your shop decide to buy it...the randomness factor there is a bit of a pain.
As for the dungeon sections of the game...I would say they are good, but a little bit standard. Each adventurer plays a lot differently to the rest, and most are fun to play, but you'll probably end up using Charme or Tielle for most of the game when you unlock them, since they're much better than the rest. You do get an extremely versatile character that some might consider the best, but only after clearing the entire game, so I can't really count that character in there.
The dungeons themselves are as I said, fairly standard rougelike affairs. Each dungeon has a set number of floors, and there are different themes throughout most of the dungeons, with randomly generated maps, loot and traps (BEWARE THE TUNA). There's a decent variety in the bosses even if they are a little simplistic for the most part, but the game does  repeat a little bit (Like King Slime? Now fight TWO King Slimes!). There's also a good range of enemies throughout the dungeons, enough to keep things fresh, but your enjoyment here really depends on whether you like these kinds of 'Rouge' mechanics. There isn't permadeath, but dying in a dungeon means you lose all but two items of your choosing, which means you can end up losing items that you brought into the dungeon if you fail.
Overall, the game is a unique little adventure. The story is cute and amusing for the most part, and the mechanics are generally quite fun overall. At the time of writing, the game is £12.99, which I would say is a reasonable price for what you get, easily worth it if you do end up enjoying it. If you still aren't sure, there IS a demo available, which should give you more of an idea if this game is worth the asking price for you. Just be warned bargain hunters, this game deosn't go on sale very often.

Asphyxia is a very difficult game to review.   It is clearly, by far, the most interesting VN on steam and easly one of the best values.   However, it isn't for everyone.
Fist, the story isn't really about depression, drug addiction and all of the other stuff you read in most of the other reviews. Since the chracters are all based upon very damaged writers, there is depression, drug references, and there are images showing death by drowning like in Hamlet.  But, that isn't really what the story is about.
The stroy involves Sam as she trys to regain the friendship she lost of her best childhood friend.   As you read, you will learn, like any good famous author, Sam has a lot of issues and is obsessed.   You probably shouldn't read past here if you don't like a few spoilers... but the few negative reviews need a proper resposne.
If you play all the routes and really think about things, you will start to see that even the "good" ending has very dark overtones. People who think the game is just about depression, are being far too literal.  The game has more to do with the way several characters (including our hero Sam) tend to love people in smothering ways. Nothing good comes from that. In the "good" ending Sam gets the "friendship" of the person she loves back, but if you really think about the conditions imposed, you will realize that ending could end up being nothing short of a living hell of sorts. The whole point is to get you to think about the relationships, how damaged each of these character is, and to think about things. The "good" ending may not be the best, it is better than the implied suicide one, but it may not be the best. For Sam, it might be best to let go and move on.  If you ever messed up a relationship, and did your best to put it back together again... it is almost an attempt to show that might not be for the best... even if worked.
In short, I think the title has more to do with every single aspect of the novel. The author was trying to recreate the stifling atmosphere of a book of the time period of the names of the author's characters of the book are from. And the novel does an amazing job of that.  Not so much Hamlet (depite the image) but more like the Awakening.  Unlike the novel the Awakening where the lead character drowns herself, in our book (if you go with the "good" ending) she finds out that the character she loves is secretly more damaged than anyone else (even herself) and Sam agrees to something (that if you think about carefully) will be very painful. Drowning in another sense.  It will likely be far (FAR) more painful than not being that person's friend in the long term.   Tragic in a way.  Sometimes, a false hope may be worse than no hope at all!
So, Asphyxia isn't a game about just depression.  The author was going for the kind of story you debate over in college, and they succeed brilliantly. It is the kind of VN you think about and then reread parts to soak in the true weight of what people are saying. But, that dosen't make for a happy book.   It is really cool how the tragedy of the whole thing sinks in... and that is for the "happy" ending.
This VN isn't for anyone who really didn't like English in college, the books they asked you to read then, or for anyone who really screwed up an important relationship and is still depressed about it.  While I think the author really has some helpful things to say, it may be too painful.
However, if you want to read something that will make you think about what you read and its full implications, this is probably one of the few games on Steam that will ever fit that bill.  Enjoy!

This game is a major part of my teenhood. I remember a friend of my uncle's let me borrow it for a week or however long I had it for and let me tell you, the story is very engrossing, there's lots of witty humor and charm to it. Sure there are other games that outclass this one in terms of gameplay mechanics, story, characters, and graphics, but this game was considered to be ahead of its time way back in the day. I bought this when it was on a sale a year ago and I don't regret it. I loved returning to Albion for the first time in 12 years and it still felt refreshing and the game itself was enjoyable.
Although almost everything about this game is outdated and outclassed, i have to say the best thing about this game is the many ways you can play this game. You can commit evil deeds and morph into an evil looking dude or do good deeds and be renowned as a hero. You can play the game with only melee weapons or magic or using a bow and arrow only. The possibilities are endless!
Of course, what really drew me to this game was the story. While you can spend countless hours exploring the not so open world of Albion and fight monsters for experience constantly and even for gold, you don't have to keep grinding for experience. You don't have to complete all the side quests. As a matter of fact, you don't have to be completely evil or completely good. You can be neutral and you'll still be the celebrated hero of Albion. Somehow despite being good, evil, or neutral, your alignment doesn't affect the overall story, which is kind of sad, I mean there are some key plot points that will be affected by some of the choices you make (marrying Lady Greystone(?), Killing or sparing Whisper at the Arena, releasing the women at the brothel in the dark woods, etc), but overall, there were no serious changes. At least none that I can see.
The worst aspect of this game would have to be graphics. While they're not the worst, they are terribly outdated, but it's not enough to drive me away from this game. Even after all this time, I still enjoy experiencing the Lost Chapters over and over again.

The P2W isn't what drove me away. It's the god-awful crafting system. Crafting is tiered and requires the previous version of something in order to craft a better version of it.
Want that level 50 staff? First craft a level 20 staff, then upgrade it to the level 25 staff, then to the level 30 staff, and so on and so forth. Each new version needs a bunch of different hard-to-get materials and it's obnoxious. Now imagine doing the same thing for all your different armor slots.
To compound the problem, you can't just harvest everything you need for crafting. Some things can only be gotten from trade runs. Other things have to be crafted from other professions. The prices for everything are so inflated that oftentimes buying the oil you need to make that leather armor negates the profitability of crafting it yourself. You might as well just buy the armor of the AH.
It's just uselessly complicated and absurd. If I could harvest everything I needed, and didn't need the 10 previous versions of a piece of gear to make that gear, I would love this game. But the crafting system as it is right now just enrages me. I can't take it anymore.
It's a shame because I enjoy most other things about the game. With MMO's it's always that one boneheaded design decision that ruins it for me, and in ArcheAge it's the crafting.

Mass Effect 2 is a masterpiece. It features some of the best combat, interesting missions and by far one of the biggest and most compelling stories that has ever been told in a video game. From the original they continued the story of Commander Shepard and his/her role in one of the biggest sci-fi universes ever seen. The game instantly sets out being darker than the previous game with the immediate destruction of the Normandy and Shepards death. Fortunately Shepard is reconstructed pro-human organisation Cerberus. They outfit Shepard with a new crew, a new ship and one mission. Deal with the Collectors.
Without spoiling the story the adventure you go on is full of thrills, twists and moral choices that you can make, and an elaborate dialogue selection that influences the story. There are numerous interesting characters to meet on the way who join your crew, each with their own background and personality, including the return of Garrus, Tali, Joker and Dr Chakwas to the crew from the first game.
The combat is extremely engaging and creating a new game upon the completion of an old save is worth it just to choose a new class an experience battle in a different way. The inventory and weapon management has been improved since the first game and it is now much more fun to use biotics and tech powers.
There is so much to this game it is hard to express in a small review so I shall use this closing statement.

BioWare’s first Mass Effect felt like a KOTOR clone, and not in a good way. The universe was a place we wanted to live, but there were too many systems and menus to dig through to get there. Still, it terrified us to hear that BioWare had streamed back so much and put more emphasis on the shooting mechanics. Turns out, it was for the better: Mass Effect 2 trims just enough fat to let you focus on what matters: the optional Loyalty missions for your team.
Instead of an exercise in galactic exploration, Mass Effect 2 plays out like a sci-fi Ocean's Eleven or Dirty Dozen. Recruiting a team to take on the Collectors puts the focus on small, interesting stories. Each Loyalty mission gives you insight into your companions’ motivations, making every member of the Normandy's crew an unusually deep character. Once you've grown to know and love them, the endgame suicide run is one of the tensest final missions ever. It's rare for a game to spend more time on character arcs than its central driving narrative, but Mass Effect 2 pulls it off. This is some of the best writing in BioWare's history.

A must-have sequel to original Mass Effect. Not that it is particularly great - in my opinion, it doesn't measure up to its predecessor nor to the trilogy's finale - but it's a necessary part of the story and it's definitely worth playing.
The second part of ME franchise puts greater accent on squad interaction. In fact, you can get as much as a dozen companions, and missions related to their backstories occupy most of the game. It might be a turn-off for some, but if you felt immersed in the first Mass Effect, you should find most of those characters and missions quite enjoyable, at least during the first playthrough. I promise you're going to love some of your new squadmates, who will make you laugh and cry, and it seems that your old friends haven't forgotten about you after all.
The main storyline is consequently even shorter than in ME1, though with all the other assignments it shouldn't be a problem. One's for sure - I'm not going to spoil the climax, but it's as epic as the battle with the Sovereign. Mass Effect series didn't lose its scale and there are still moments that make you turn up the volume and sit at the edge of your seat. The ground battles have a whole new quality to them (finally Mass Effect has elements of a proper shooter - ducking behind cover and shooting seems more real and exciting than in the first part of the series), though perhaps you're going to miss the Mako.
A few words about the equipment system - it's much simplier than in the first game and I personally consider it an improvement. If you enjoyed comparing stats, shopping, and painstakingly equipping every single member of your squad, you might be disappointed, but if not, here's good news. The whole equipment system has been replaced with several items of weaponry, a few customizable elements of armor for Shepard, and a variety of upgrades giving bonuses for Commander or the whole squad. You may like it or not, but it's definitely easier to deal with. Leveling system has been simplified as well - maybe even too much - but it's now more intuitive, and it doesn't take 40 levels to get you the skill you want anymore.
My biggest pain with this game lies within DLC-s, which cost more than the game itself (especially when it's on sale), but when you finally play them, they seem essential to the story. It might be a pain in your wallet, but the sad truth is that some content has been apparently cut from the game and sold in separate bundles. Mass Effect 2 is still a fairly good game by itself, but it feels somehow incomplete without that additional content.
That said, it's still Mass Effect, and thus it's a part of one of the greatest stories I've been immersed in. Don't forget to check digital deluxe edition available here for the same price... and have fun!

What a great game! There were some unfortunate changes to the gameplay over Mass Effect 1, in particular the addition of ammo and a woeful minigame to pick electronic locks. The addition of ammo made combat pretty much pointless in my preferred "first person" play style as a sniper - you only get a handful of shots at the swarms of bad guys then spend the rest of the time spamming stupid magic fireballs and hoping your teammates will finish the battle for you. And although the game plays smoother on a tablet than Mass Effect 1, the lock pick minigame is so jerky you will fail over and over until you randomly get an easy-to-pick setup. But man oh man is the dialog worth that tedium.
You start out tossed into a situation with a bunch of losers, but as you progress you get back some independence and the opportunity to build a team with some interesting characters and deep interactions. German translation is decent; the story definitely doesn't suffer. It's even worth disappearing off Steam for a few days to complete the trilogy, in a fabulous closer to the series that lets you say goodbye to (almost) all the wonderful people you met in the first two instalments. Truly epic space opera. Highly recommended if you like sci-fi drama and don't mind a somewhat underwhelming shooter experience on the side.

It took a lot of effort from me to uninstall this because I couldn't stop playing. It gets a tick in every department I can think of- gameplay, story, characters, art style, presentation, soundtrack etc. I like the refreshing take on tactical turn based gameplay done in real time 3rd person, allowing you to move, shoot, heal etc. There are other factors involved too which gives this system some good complexity and really spices things up. The story is simple on paper like most things out there but it's what happens along the way which keep you engaged. I felt attached to all the main characters in this and I really liked how the game explored these people's personalities and journeys, offering some really good character development and interaction. The only issues I have with the game is that there is a lot of dialogue at times (like how there is always a conversation at the start of a battle) and watching everything the enemy does in their turn can feel like a drag and overly long at times. Full review:
Since people reading these things love to blame the players for anything unflattering they read about a game, let me get my conditions out of the way. I've been playing on normal with the default fate or whatever and I'm almost exactly half way through the story mode. (one card over half) If that makes me unworthy to have an opinion in your opinion then stop reading.
This game feels like a good indie game. This game is rather fun but it is in no sense an RPG. There is no real character building, even cosmetically. Everyone gets to be the same biker looking pirate dude and everyone gets the same starter garbage.
This game qualitatively defies genre placement. Roguelike would definitely be the closest fit in the sense that you have a near totally random set of contexts and events. But the deck building aspect, the essentially unchanging arcade beat'm up combat, with quicktime event counters (that I never ever get to execute because crowds), on top of a turn based almost board game layer, just moves you so far away from the typical roguelike and any other concrete genre definition, that you start to question all the labels.
Each encounter card is more or less trying to be a minigame, and the major story objective cards require a build up of power in order to have a prayer of victory, but since each card is trying to be a minigame you have some chance to fail at all of them incurring weakness, damage, loss, or simple failure to gain. That's fine in a vacuum, but the upshot of this at the larger scale is that you very easily fall into a rut where you are playing slots, just dying over and over hammering at token cards hoping they unlock stuff that will slightly improve your RNG odds at the deck building stage.
But still, even then, because each card is trying to be a mini game, and victory requires a string of RNG victories (unless you're just a total twitch kill/counter/stun battle ninja) progression basically becomes exponentially unlikely.
And that's the important distinction here, the difference between difficult and unlikely. Gamers generally I find don't understand the difference between challenging and difficult and unlikely. They also conflate various aspects of time investment, practice, luck, game play, micro management, actions per minute, command inflation, grind etc etc.
Difficulty is about making choices and experiencing varying levels of game response to them. Probability on the other hand is about pulling the handle till you get 3 in a row. But getting back to this game specifically, yes in theory I could train to become a battle ninja, and I could train to be a spreadsheet flow chart probability ninja when it comes to deck building, I could train to be a shell game card shuffle expert, but even if I did all of them the RNG gods are probably going to screw me a consistent percentage of the time.
What I'd like to see:
The main thing this game definitely needs is a character creation step, even if it's just a choice of prefabs and a name box. Something to emotionally invest me in and link me to the character. I picture something like so many points to spend and you can spend them on anything from cards to stats. Some cosmetic choices would be awesome as well. Nothing wildly complicated. Think Torchlight 2. Maybe some low intensity long term progression, like the badass points system in BL2.
I'd also like it if endless mode had everything in the game unlocked by default.

I find myself moving down this dusty corridor, dodging flame traps and a spike ceiling trying to crush me.  I catch my breath for a moment, roll past some arrow traps, and grab a chest!
And my reward is some cards.  And the man across the table from me makes some cryptic statements about my past, or the history of that card, or something vague and menacing.
This is the sort of thing that happens in this game, and its amazing.
Hand of Fate can be best described as a Deck Building Action RPG hybrid.  You are a nameless someone, who has decided to play a game of life and death against a mysterious Dealer.  Your goal is to defeat the 12 members of the Dealers Card Court.  Your weapons, tools, and even dungeons are the very cards being used in the game.
I have not played for very long as I don't want to spoil the game for when I do a video playthrough of it, but suffice to say what I have played has my interest piqued.  I want to know who I am, where I came from, how I got to this place, and why this Dealer is such a snarky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Recently, the devs put out a Free content expansion, which adds another little mini story to the game.
The basic gameplay is that you have a deck of cards that you have built.  Well 2 actually: Equipment and Encounters.  The dealer then spices things up by adding cards to them, cards you have no knowledge of.  He then lays out a dungeon face down on the table, made up of cards.  You then move a token around from card to card, and experience a variety of things.  One card might be an Ambush of Skeletons, another might be meeting an Elf Lass, another might be a dangerous ravine, or a trap room.
In the case of combat, or trap rooms, the game switches to an Action RPG setup, using a combat system very similar to the new Batman Arkham games.  You can dodge, roll, attack, and eventually should you find the gear cast spells or special powers.  One power I had early on let me cause all my attacks to generate cash on the ground that I could pick up.
The devs have said the main campaign takes about 12 hours to get through, so about an hour per court member.  There is also Endless mode, which is of course Endless.
Hopefully more content updates come down the pipe as I can see myself playing this for quite a while.

Deckbuilding is the neatest of the features I liked in the game because as said it let you make your own Dungeon. While in Endless Mode you dont have deckbuilding because you use all unlocked cards , in Story you have to build your deck, matching the required number of cards for Encounters and Equipment. While you have complete freedom in your Equipment deck, in the Encounters one you will  see locked cards ( one of them is the end boss of the dungeon). Some of the locked cards can be removed by completing them but often leads to new locked cards.
Cards are being unlocked by receiving card tokens. And you receive card tokens when you complete an encounter for first time. And you harvest the rewards at the end of the dungeon ... or after you die( its cool that you arent being punished for dying since a lot of card unlocks can end up terribly for you) . Different cards got different requirments to be completed and gest the best of RNG doesnt mean you will get the token. Once you get to the part where token breaks to reveal cards you will be welcomed with a neat animation. From the token you can get new equipment, encounter cards or gain cards. There are several "quest" chains that are worth doing. The newly obtained cards contain no information until you encounter them in-game so you can only guess what may happen.
Once your deck is ready  the party starts. Dealer will setup the board with separating the different decks in piles and then he starts drawing encounter cards to form dungeon levels. Once everything is setuped you start hoping from card to card till you reach the end... your end or dungeon's end. During story every dungeon comes up with bonus ... curses which will improve your game experience(or make you rage) . Every dungeon in story mode ends up with a boss fight(if you find it before you die) that will unlocks new cards, including the next level. At the end you will unlock new cards(hopefully) and will be able to increase your deck variety. While in the dungeon you have to take care of your supplies: Gold and Food. Food is beiung used on every turn and heals you.
One of your deck is filled with equipment that you can use during your adventures, if you get lucky to find it. You have Weapons,Armored,Gloves,Helmets,Rings, Artifacts(skills) and Blesses/Curses. While you can hoard all the equipments, you can change your active items before fights so you have to be picky and hope for the best. You can have only 1 active item from each category apart from Rings and Blesses/Curses. Encounters can remove any kind of item without blessing/curses(unless its stated otherwise). There are a lot of different items with their own pros and cons.
Ah the Encounter Deck, no matter how many good encounters you put in it, there will be always some that will screw everything. There are different kind of Encounters, from straight fights to short text-based adventures. Almost every encounter comes with a lovely RNG that features cards and there are 2 kinds of RNG : Success/failure that are represented with Huge Success,Success,Failure and Huge Failure cards. The amount of cards you can pick is 4 but they depends on the encounter themselves but you always have at least 1 success/failure card and the amount of cards you have to pick from is 4 ; Enemies are also represented by cards . You have the 4 basic enemies Skulls(skeletons), Dust(bandits), Plague(rats) and Scales(Lizardmen) . Each of them got melee and range model which puts the enemy count to 8. While playing you can unlock additional enemies( I got so far Mages, Liches and Lava Golems) which put the enemy count up to 11 . And the Iceing on the cake is the boss cards. Once you beat the boss its being unlocked in the monster deck and with 12 bosses to unlock you put the enemy count up to 23. So enemy variety is quite big for this kind of Game.
Last but not least, the Combat. Combat is pretty straightforward. You have Melee attack, Weapon Skill,Artefact Skill, Counter, Stun and Dodge. So you can say that the combat is similiar to Batman or Kingdoms of Amalur but with lower budget. Enemies attack are slowed most of the time so you can react accordingly. If you have shield you can counter melee attacks or reflect projectiles but thats only if the prompt for attack glows green... if its red you better get the f* out of there.  There is a friendlyfire so you can use this to your advantage with good positioning so you can let enemies tank the range attacks. Now.. one thing that I noticed is often so long leaps when you counter enemies at distance or being stuck in animation with no time to react. My main issue with the combat is the camera. You cant rotate it so at times you have no idea what are you gonna face or where exactly the enemy is. Apart from that combat is fine.
Story is pretty simple : you are an adventurer who stumbled upon Dealer's home and you are invited for a game but you are free to leave whenever you want. In the said game you have to defeat the Dealer but before that you must defeat his strongest warriors(on every warrior's level you will meet new challenges so GL). Simple yet well presented thanks to the strong Narration. Voice actor did his job superb but there is still something more to be desired from the writing. Still even when Dealer repeats himself is often in the mood of the situation and there are just a view occassions when the line will not be fitting the situation.
Now this is more about the DLC "Wildcards" . Fates lets you change your playstyle. In base game you have 3 fates that serve as Easy/Normal/Hard difficulty in other games but if you have the DLC you get access to 9 more fates with different stats that affect your playstyle. It's a neat addition but there is still room for improvment.
Once you are done with the story, Endless mode seems best option to play it .. but I personally didnt like it since it kills Deckbuilding. In Endless Mode you play with all the unlocked cards you have and on every floor the Dealer gets stronger and stronger.

Its a neat roguelike with forgiving RNG and superb quest design and narration. Its good for short playsession and for people who like to unlock all cards.

I had thought about playing this game for awhile, and for the price, I finally caved and got it because I wanted something short and quick.
Other reviews warned me of the game dealing with mental illness and dark themes, but I didn’t think they were that severe, and I say that as someone who struggled with depression as a teenager. I thought it was pretty realistic at times and didn't try to glorify unhealthy relationships. Rather, it really highlighted just how bad they are. To me, that's a plus. So that being said...
Pros:
-beautiful art
-good dialogue
-moderate amount of choices
-some interesting characters
-being able to skip read text quickly
-decent handling of what depression feels like and how it’s hard to listen to rational advice
Cons:
-rather short (finished everything with breaks at 4+ hrs, but the cost is decent)
-vague motivations of other characters (no real backstory, just bits and pieces here and there)
-only a handful of characters to interact with, (only part of the game that really changes is the ending scene/s).
-the characters can be grating and always seem to have some sort of conflict (given the nature of the game and the fact it takes place over the span of a day, a lot of it seems crammed in like the snippet of a scene instead of the whole novel).
It was a pretty enjoyable game if only for the art and figuring out how to get the “good” ending. The game does a decent job, as I said, at handling the heavy topics in a realistic way without seeming as if its preying upon them for shock factor. For the price, it’s work a pick-up if you like morbid, non-gore based visual novels. I liked it, and I'd recommend it if you like this genre and beautiful art. Unfortunately, if you’re looking for a true happy-ending visual novel where everything is resolved neatly- even through unrealistic or unhealthy glorified means- I wouldn’t recommend it.
