So, I think it's about time I finally made a review on this game.
Quick warning, I am going to be writing a book.
Letme preface this review by saying I have been an on and off Warframe player since the game first released. I never really bothered getting too deep into it until recently however. Recently being the last few months.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Warframe is honestly my favorite game currently at the moment. I was hyped for Destiny 2, but when that "shockingly" turned out to be a dissapointment, I moved on over here full time. I am currently Mastery Rank 10 in the game which is by far nowhere near the crazy levels other more experienced players are at. I am by no means a great player, I would say I am barely above average.
That being said, this game has me absolutely addicted. I cannot stop playing this game even when I'm bored and just sitting in my Orbiter I am STILL entertained. Whether it be just listening to the radio chatter or just hearing Ordis blurt out one of his many insane quotes, I find entertainment and value everywhere I look in this game.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Gameplay
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Where do I even begin. The gameplay is fantastic, if you couldn't already tell by the fact that, you know, you're literally a ninja.... in space.... that can do crazy flips and glide and cut people in half while simultaneously casting insane abilities bestowed upon you by the Void.... you cannot tell me that doesn't sound amazing.
This game feels wonderful, it controls amazing, and everything is so smooth and clean. It is satisfying to just run around, whip out your sword, slide and cut a Grineer soldier in two. It honestly will never get old. The gun controls are also amazing in this game, I'm normally not a big fan of third person shooters but this game does a damn good job at it.
There is very little I have seen that is bad about the gameplay, the only big things I've noticed are the occasional bugs and glitches that are sadly present in every game, however these are very far and few between.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Graphics
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ok, the graphics and textures in this game, aren't really the best. If you watched the developer's latest devstream, you would have seen that the models are getting a major overhaul, so this part of the review may change later on down the line. However, for a free game, the graphics are amazing. The effects look beautiful, the lighting is good, and the models and textures are pretty amazing as well, especially the Warframes.
I have noticed very bad texture glitches where they were either stretched really bad, or rendered wrong, etc, but these are generally fixed next time I run through the mission.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Story
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
First, three words.
OH. MY. GOD.
Alright, let's begin. The story in this game is INCREDIBLE. Like, this is a FREE TO PLAY GAME, may I remind you, but it has AAA level writing and story telling. There is even really deep, rich, lore that puts Destiny 1 to shame. It is so beautifully writen and intriguing and I just want to know more. The lore and story is what really hooked me in this game and made me keep playing. It hooked me as hard as pre nerf Roadhog. I won't give any spoilers, but The Second Dream and War Within story questlines are by far the best in the game. Seriously, if you play this game, and don't like it, atleast get those 2 quests done before making your final decision.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Premium Currency/Paid Content
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I wanted to save this part of the review towards the very end. I want to start off by saying NOTHING in this game has to be paid for. You can get everything you want/need just by playing the game. Even the Prime Warframes that are Vaulted go through a cycle of being unvaulted and vaulted again, it's just another reason to constantly play.
I personally only buy Platinum (the premium currency) to support the developers over at Digital Extremes, and that is what I encourage anyone to do, only buy the currency if you feel like you want to help out. Because get this, even the game's paid, premium currency can be earned 100% free. You can sell mods, prime parts, blueprints, etc, to other players in exchange for Platinum. I personally have made somewhere around 1k platinum just by trading (you can earn a lot more the later in the game you are). And even the devs themselves constantly give out 1k Platinum during their Prime Time or Devstreams on Twitch.
The game also allows the use of a tool they call TennoGen. This tool is used by players to create their own custom skins for items in the game which can actually be added to the ingame Market and then other players can buy them.
In my opinion this game has the best Premium Currency/Content model I have ever seen in a game, and I wish more games imployed something like this.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Final Thoughts and Rating
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This game is amazing. I encourage everyone who has never played to atleast try it out for about and hour or so, I mean it's free so why not. I have almost no issues with the game besides the little bugs and glitches that are bound to happen. So, my rating of this game is:
Gameplay: 9/10
Graphics: 8/10
Story/Lore: 10/10
Premium Currency/Content: 9/10
Overall I give Warframe: 9/10
Great work DE, and please continue to make this already fantastic game even better.

Owlboy is a fantastic 2D action adventure that combines flying with platforming in the world floating among the clouds.
You play as a mute owl named Otus. Owls are a highly intellectual species, and you are a complete and utter failure in the eyes of your mentor. You’re constantly failing to live up to expectations, and always letting others down. With the imminent threat of pirates attacking, you manage to make a few friends with other misfits that believe in you. Together, you and your friends embark on a grand adventure to try and help save the world.
There is a lot of action and combat throughout the game. Combat is interesting, and I like the mechanics. You fly around, spinning and dashing to avoid taking damage. You can pick up objects to throw at enemies, or heal yourself, and you can also carry your friends. While carrying a friend, you gain access to their unique weapon and ability.
You switch between your companions to progress through obstacles, and defeat boss encounters. Changing from one companion to another is easy to do, and it’s often very clear which ally you should be using. At first, I was worried that I would have to monitor the ally’s health while in combat, and keep them safe. Fortunately, they can be thrown around and shot at while they aren’t being carried, so you don’t need to micromanage them. While you’re carrying them, you have to be more careful. If you or them get hit, you take damage, suffer a brief daze, and your friend falls to the ground. It’s not too inconvenient to drop your ally though, since you can immediately teleport them back to you with no cooldown on the ability.
The game is open-world. You can venture back and forth between the different areas as you please. There is a fair amount to explore, and you can find hidden treasure if you want to. You collect these coins to obtain items from the shop, some of which increase the size of your health pool.
Owlboy took me over 8 hours to complete, and I loved every minute of it. It’s not a game I feel the need to replay, but if I wanted to go back and collect everything, I could load the save right before the final boss.
Some people may think that the price is a bit too high. At first I was a bit concerned with the price tag as well, but after finishing my playthrough without a single complaint, I’m completely fine with it. You can tell that a lot of hard work and passion went into creating Owlboy. It’s such a wonderful game, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a well-crafted 2D adventure with unique combat mechanics, charming characters, and an engrossing story. It’s truly an excellent game.

What seemed to be just a little indie game with over 9 years of development, Owlboy is an adventure to behold. I finished this game two days after the game had released. Why? I absolutely fell in love with the game. There's a lot of things that really hold this game and make you just want more. While there are many MANY good things about this game. There are, however some spots I really was disappointed in. Now I won't be spoiling the whole ordeal on what I am talking about, but I will make reference to it so this review does HAVE SPOILERS AT THE END OF THE REVIEW ON ITS OWN SECTION BUT IT WILL BE SPOILER FREE!!!
Owlboy is an Indie adventure game where you control Otus, a mute Owl who apparently has a lot on his shoulders when things don't really go his way. He and his friend Geddy are tasked with watch over their village when a huge group of bandits known as the Pirates invade, taking an Owl relic that is stored in the village. And off we go on our adventure to get that back and stop the Pirates and their plans.
One of the first things I've noticed in game is the presentation along with the soundtrack. Holy crap this game has detail in its animations. Props to the devs and animators for a very polished game. The scenery looks beautiful and it sets the mood in the beginning as a light-hearted adventure. Otus himself is a mute, but the amount of detail in his responses, whether he is twiddling his thumbs when he's nervous, he covers himself with his cloak when he's sad, its all there and I wasn't expecting how I would feel for the poor guy. One effect though I had with the looks of the game were at some points, textures didn't spawn (which were resolved by resetting the game) and there are some weird bugs like if you eat a healing item and get hurt at the same time, it produces some weird result. Nothing gamebreaking, but I think that needs to be addressed.
Speaking of feeling, this game can really tug on your heartstrings. You can get attached to these characters and then suddenly the feel train will hit you. I remembered that I at least teared up or even flat out cried at some sections because what was happening and how I didn't want bonds or spirits to break from the main cast. This story is very well done and the pace is very fluent. There weren't times I wanted to put down the game because I was just done. No, like I said before, I wanted more. When it finally ended, I was pleased with what I got. The game's difficulty isn't that bad either. It's very easy to get into and the game will test your knowledge of when to use certain partners, There are some hard spots, but it isn't too bad.
Now lets talk about that gameplay huh? So Otus, as a mute owl, he really can't attack. He can stun people with is little spin, but thats all he can really do other than his little dash (which I'll get to in a minute). So the game pairs you up at first with your best friend Geddy, Geddy has a gun, which Otus can carry him and he can fire at enemies. This is an interesting mechanic as you need to manage having your partner on you while also dodging enemies, solving puzzles. The whole game would be a boring cake walk if Otus can attack. Because of this, there are special sections were Otus is alone and he has to sneak past enemies. There are a number of stealth sections in this game and they are handled pretty well. I never got bored of them as they went by pretty fast. Not to mention you have a great source of movement. Oh my god the movement. I mentioned Otus can dash either in the air or on the ground. As a speedrunner, I absolutely love games with amazing movement, and Owlboy is no exception. Sure there are a lot of times I spammed the dash to get point A to point B in a timely manner, but I never felt rushed. The regular flight speed that Otus has is very optimal. At no times when I was exploring a dungeon that I needed to move around by dashing, only when I needed to backtrack or dodge incoming fire. There is even an upgrade you get that makes your movement even better so that in the later parts in the game when you have more freedom to backtrack and collect any of the game's currency to buy the extra goodies.
Overall, the game is a gem. It was worth the wait of 9 years of development and polish. I didn't hear about this game until youtuber VideoGameDunkey where he had said he had a really good feeling about this game. I looked into it, and gave a lot of hope. Owlboy is a must play if you like adventureous games with a story that really likes to hit your soft spots. I absolutely loved it and am looking forward to speedrun this game!
Owlboy gets a 9.5 out of 10 for me. ~LuckPercentSRL

The combat is akin to the more recent Batman games. Not the same level of polish, but still very good. Combat is at a moderate pace and the variety of equipment (and their effects) make combat a more thoughtful endeavor, asking you how and in what order you will deal with the steadily growing variety of opponents and their abilities.
Outside of the combat the game is somewhat of a choose-your-own-adventure game with each step being a new encounter of some sort. There's a decent variety of encounters with new ones added each successful playthrough. In some cases the ways to deal with these encounters can be equally as varied. And thankfully I've yet to see any encounters of the 'Rocks fall, everyone dies' kind. Every encounter can be dealt with potently even turning a bad encounter into a total gain. Even those based on chance have ways to tip chance in your favor. Again the lack of time limited choices allow content to be handled at your own pace.
Overall the game is almost relaxing to play. It doesn't throw any cheap shots, but it also doesn't pull any punches. That and the well versed DM that is the mysterious dealer across from you makes it a +5 game of goodness.

Hand of Fate is a unique and refreshing blend of a few great genres. It pits you in a game of life or death (though really there's not much risk to you aside from a few broken knuckles) against "The Dealer", who is a mysterious and actually pretty solid character.
Mechanics: Basically this game you play with the dealer is a kind of choose your own adventure/board game where the tiles on the board are random cards which either come from your deck or the dealer's deck. I'm paraphrasing Total Biscuit here, but your cards (usually) serve to help you gain some leverage in the form of gold or weapons, where as the dealer's cards are there to mess your♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Occasionally you'll land on a combat card which will transition the game from a top down boardgame into a 3rd person hack and slash fight which is comprable to a very simplified Darksouls.
Overall, I love how dynamic the mechanics are and everything just feels right on.
Pros:
Solid combat
Interesting tarot esq theme
Great sense of RPG progression
Plenty of cards
Very dynamic
Fresh incorporation of collectible cards
Cons:
Difficulty progression isn't on point
Replayability is questionable
Some of the quests seem too much like a chore
Not many game modes
Classes seem a bit unbalanced, as do items
Overall it's a great game. I'd love to see multiplayer somehow implemented, maybe 1 player 1 dealer, 2-3 players AI dealer, I'm not sure, but this game has tonnes of potential to take it one step further and I hope the devs know that.

So, after spending 47 hours exploring the world of this dreary, bleak, yet oh-so-wonderful world, and getting every achievement for it, I can definitely say that Metro: Last Light Redux is a great game... with some caveats:
First, I'd like to say that this game still looks amazing, even though it is technically a HD retexture and relighting of the original Metro: Last Light game that came out in 2013.  Character models are well detailed, clothing is a bit off but is very serviceable nonetheless, weapons look amazing, and the world looks just... breathtaking.  I'm running it as high as it can go with my setup, and it looks superb.
However, to go with that statement, for a game that is essentially a 2014 HD upgrade to a 2013 game, this game has some massive framerate dips in several levels towards the end of the game.  I don't know if the original game was like this, but Redux is now almost 3 years old, and these frame drops are certainly annoying on my setup, which is more capable than the 4A Games recommended PC requirements.
Certain graphical glitches are prevalent.  At points in the story where there is heavy amounts of rain or rivers, graphical errors consisting of blue light in a lightning bolt streak; this is in areas where there is no thunderstorms, so it is not an envrionmental feature.
The final thing I take issue with is the games use of Nvidia GameWorks.  Personally, I don't like the idea of gimping my framerate for better looking environments.  My PC is powerful, but Nvidia's software makes my rig take a dump on the frames when I enable the options.  It looks good, but it's not my cup of tea.
A good game, with some graphical errors, but the negatives do not overshadow the game itself.  It is a great atmospheric, story-driven, post-apocalyptic game set in a unique setting in Russia, and I cannot wait to play the next title in the Metro series.

if you're never liked history in school, you're just like me. Random dates, random dudes, random wars... It just seemed so boring at the time, and memorizing all this data was excrutiating.
But the thing is, human history is one hell of a story, you just have to look at it differently. Don't ask what, or when; ask why — that's the most interesting question. Or, even better, what if? What would my life be like if I'd be an english duke right after norman invasion? Well, turns out that whoever I'd be, it'd be a series of endless clashes with weak kings, and uprising after uprising. I still don't remember all the stuff that happened there in real life, but know I have something much better — a common sense that there was just to much power in arms of all the individual lords, and with scottish menace to the north, normans to the south, and norwegians to the east, England couldn't have possibly have a single year without some kind of violent conflict back then. A lecturer could've told me all about it a hundred times in a disty classroom, and I still wouldn't get it as good as then.
It's not a game about conquering the world, or getting the best top score — at least, not for me. The real world is unjust, unbalanced, and it isn't a competition that you just measure by raw scores. But it's a game about much more interesting challenges.
Would you be able to stay independent as a King of Iceland, when all you have is a couple of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ provinces and couple of pretty powerful neighbours that want to become your lords, by piece or else? Can you build an Israel state a thousand years before Ben-Gurion? Bringing Roman Empire back to it's glory may seem like a worthy task — but is it harder or easier than just surviving as a tiny Novgorod?
History is ♥♥♥♥ing interesting. Come play with it.

I usually don't play games from studios that i've never heard of buttook a chance with this game. I was a bit shocked with the basic start up menu and was expecting something bad because of how simple it was but i was even more shocked when i discovered how fun the game was. You start your first 4 quests as tutorial type missions where they introduce the elements of the game and do very well explaining how it works. The Narrator who is also the man you see in the game cover adds a great element to the game. I really enjoyed his comments to make the game interesting and they did a great job focusing on his animation.
Too sum it up its a game of randomness on every quest you go to making them slightly unique. As the game progresses you unlock cards that can add to the randomness and even add more difficulty of the game. The game is indeed a bit to easy in the medium and easy setting. The hard setting can get difficult because the odds are stacked against you but to me it adds to the fun.
The combat is done similar to the Batman games where you have attacks and counters. Some opponents attack faster and some can not be dodge which adds a bit more difficulty because usually you're out numbered. You get random weapons and armor through out the game based on the "helpful" cards you have in the deck that you can create making the game easier or harder. Their is also a recommended setting in case you don't want to tinker with it.

This is a fun game to play as long as you're willing to put some money into microtransactions. One thing that honestly astonished me was some of the pricing of just outfits, some outfits, in order to buy the complete outfit you're looking at an average of $20, which is just ridiculous. Gameplay is very entertaining in the beginning however later game it is extremely repetitive.
After level 30ish it's just hours of grinding by playing normally just to gain one level, in order to gain levels at an actually decent rate you have to be willing to solo dungeons on the hardest difficulty over and over and over without break.
The game itself are pleasing to look at, however, this game rewards pay-to-play players significantly more than the average free-to-play player. That in itself doesn't make the game bad, it's just a heads up to any free-to-play players out there.
The combos are a little complicated but can be learned and memorized after playing the character over and over.
The PvP NEEDS to be re-done completely. The balancing is just awful, level 15 players are paired against level 72's more often than not, and there's no excuse for that.
The interface itself is a little painful, not confusing just not very pleasing to look at.
Crafting items can be very confusing to new players, so I reccomend reading up on some crafting guides before hoping into the game.
The game runs pretty well on potato PCs, as long as all the video settings are on low.
My conclusion? If you're into grinding dungeons and being a masochist, this game is for you.

This game...oh this game.  It's adorable, it's fun, it's interesting.  Recettear is indeed an Item Shop's tale; you take on the mantle of your father's incredible debt as Recette, an earnest and sincere young girl who's eager to preserve the house in the name of her father and facillitate the alleviation of said debt by turning it into a nifty little item shop at the behest of
Tear, the fairy representing the people Recette's adventurous father owes all her money to.  To do so, she needs to sell items and make weekly payments while balancing other economic decisions, such as buying stock, and time itself is also a commodity.  There're truly different faucets of gameplay to this wonderful gem: dungeon crawling and making dough (not literally, she isn't Alicia and thus doesn't work in a bakery.  There is another guide for that kinda thing.)
Time is important as it determines what you can do.  You only have X amount of time to do things each day, and certain activities, like going to the pub (no the girl won't get drunk, don't even think about it) for some reason or another, or going dungeon crawling, or operating the shop, or going to the park; interactions with other characters will often happen in places that don't serve an obvious purpose.  Operating the shop involves managing the general ambience, as well as determining item placement (window shoppers should be taken advantage of folks), and involves attracting customers to investigate your stock and then haggling with them to get a better price.  People will come in and ask for things you have set out, as well as things you have in storage.  They'll also try to sell things to you, in which case you haggle for a lower price.
Successfully haggling and other things improves your rank and what not, increasing your access to X benefit and Y item, etc.  Haggling in and of itself is mostly intuitive; you'll quickly realize that different people, like in real life, are malleable to different degrees when negotiating price, and they'll let you know if the price you selected bothers them (or walk out flustered.  And beware of the little girl, she's stingy).  The items themselves come in a wide variety, from food to clothing to weapons
.  It's a blast to run through a cave picking up all these weird things and assembling your flying circus of a collection at the store to reintroduce them to society via CAPITALISM HO!
To get items, you can buy stock, but it's best to get it through dunegon crawling; over the course of the game, Recette will encounter various characters, many of whom will become available as dungeon buddies who will slaughter hordes of strange bouncing goopballs to get you chocolate (and a plethora of other items; there's some RNG thrown into the whole thing).   You crawl the dungeon, hacking and slashing and using special abilities and picking up items and eventually finding doors to let you exit the dungeon, for if you succumb to the horrors within your ability to leave with all the nice loot you got is severely limited.  Boss fights are interesting and fun and the integration of action adventure hack and slash combat with the rigors of running the weirdest store ever provide a unique and delightful game play experience that actually, despite being a mashup of entrepreneurship and super spelunking, works quite well and delivers something I haven't really been able to compare to anything else.
TL;DR
Adventure RPG with hack and slash mechanics, as well as business simulation.
Loli kawaii shopkeeper and friends slay baddies to get goodies and sell them for $ to save
her livelihood.  Cute, fun, unique, I totally recommend this, it's a great experience for me, and hopefully it will be for you too ^_^

text: This is the type of game where, if you are good enough, you can singlehandedly defeat 10+ players charging at you. It's the type of game where enemies occassionally just turn and run if they see you gazing at them. Once you surpass that point, its the type of game where people still remember you... a legend... after not logging on for a year. If you give up easily, I don't recommend this game for you as there is a steep learning curve. Otherwise, prepare to have a head-chopping blast making your way to the top.

WARNING: Its era is called ROMANTICISM! What does that mean? Grim, dark, and utterly unjust are just a few symptoms. You will be traveling to (cute) girls impersonating the greatest poets of this era. And as poets usually are, not the happiest of folks, so is romanticism especially a dark era. Be advised. Heavy stuff. It might actually best to stray entirely from it if youve never suffered from depression or know how utterly alone a human can be, because all they say will be nonsense to you.
This game in one of the most important in my life. It changed me so much. Yet this game gave and gives me hope.
I suffered from quite a manic depression. And as depression are, they are alienated to be a "bad thing" in society (for good reasons as well, depressions are terrible undoings). I felt lost, as my way got worse and worse. Even though I had people to talk to, they were friends of my age (puberty mostly) and just as lost, either in a way of trying to help me or all on their own as well.
Now, Ive met people whose depression was way way worse than mine (eg. I was never suicidal) and still, I never felt like I could talk to them openly. No one seemed to suffer from what I was suffering. I strayed from professional help, I was far too "Not-worth" for that. In general, my self-esteem was a mess and I often sat on my bed, wondering that, if I were to die now, why none would miss me.
Then I stumbled upon Samantha. A fictional character, but that never bothered me. She suddenly took words directly out of my soul. Things like "Im just a constant burden to them" or "If I were to disappear now, none would care". The list goes on, of couse. Ive never bonded so much with a character in a game as much as I did with her.
Im not saying she cured my depression. If you play this game, youll see why. But, it did gave me 2 very important things: Reason and Acceptance.
Reason. I suddenly felt like I knew why I was so apparently different: Because its just me. Not because I am a weakling or am a failed creation. These things may still be true or false, but they all stem from being me. I could SEE why things did entangle in my mind as they did. I was not lost anymore, trying to search for the constant "WHY" of it.
And Acceptance. It was always alienated to be "Depressed", as mentioned before. Sadness is, socially speaking, unaccepted and should not be pursued. And telling a person, who are in a bad state,  that they are, for whatever reason, a bad being because of something they are unable to change, will only amount to their list of things they hate themselves for. And this. As I was finished with all routes (respectively in condescending order), I felt like being miserable isnt so bad. Its just part of me. Its just part of what makes my personality complete.
Nowadays, Im much much better. I give a lot of credit to this game. Certainly not all, but it was a keypiece in helping me become decent. Not saying that I am free of relapses, but whenever they come, I know its not a bad thing. It makes a part of me, and that is good.
So this a thank-you to the Devs/Writers/whoever helped to give birth to this game. Its been a blessing.
And for every person who still reads and hasnt yet played the game: If you feel lost, try this game. Dont expect wonders from it, a miracle is called one because it is so rare, and my case was maybe one. But just maybe... maybe it works well for you.

So, things that are unrealistic in this hyper-realistic truck-driving simulator:
*The traffic in LA, and Las Vegas is not anywhere near as bad as it is in real life. (This is a good thing)
*The intersections of freeways/highways are logical and identical and sane, and not anything like reality. (Also a good thing)
*The AI car drivers use their turn signals approx. 10x more often than actual CA drivers. (Thank you lord)
*The roads are reasonable in the towns and not anywhere near as maze like as reality. (I've been in a lot of industrial parks in California, the one's in the game are so much saner)
*Every single traffic light has a camera to catch you when you "accidentally" run a red light. (Annoying, but okay, I guess)
*A lot of the major cities are far less impressive and picturesque because of the downscaling. Admittedly, there is stuff in the distance in towns to add depth, but you can't drive there, and I'm usually so busy paying attention to the speed limit I don't notice. (LA didn't bother me much, but Las Vegas was super disappointing compared to the real thing.)
Things that are super realistic and awesome:
*That moment, where it's 3am and you're driving around Las Vegas looking for a place to sleep and you're staring at your GPS and next thing you know you've plowed straight into the back of a car while going 50mph? Yeah, that was me.
*The first time I drove into Primm in game, I was so amazed at how much it was exactly like the real thing that I missed my turn, over-compensated, drove straight into a wall, and caused about 5 car accidents. Seriously, the Primm in-game is identical to the real thing, it's a little creepy.
In short, you'll either love this game, or hate it. I find that it's great to play when I've had a long day, I can just turn on some dance music and zone out and drive. That being said, if you don't enjoy the thought of having to follow the speed limit, and follow the basic laws of the road, this probably isn't for you. I'm really hoping and looking forward to future DLC that adds more states, because while I enjoy the fact that I know all these towns, it's a little uncanny.

I first saw this game in the Winter Sale and didn't think much of it until I saw the price ($2.99). I don't usually go for third person detective/puzzle games but it was 90% off. I told myself awhile ago I need to broaden my gaming horizons (I have a bad habit of just playing the Bioshock series over and over rather than moving on to something else) and this seemed like a good option. This was the first non-FPS that looked really fun; mostly for the camp-y story plot.
It takes place in Salem, Massachusetts. You are a murdered cop and your unfinished business on this earth is to solve your own murder. The town is small and you basically just run around town looking for clues. While your objectives are clearly laid out you have the luxury of running around the central part of town working on side (cases) quests that are easy and short, between pieces of the larger case whenever you choose. You can also pick up bits of information about your past and historic facts while in town. During the location parts of the main case (when you are inside buildings) you can collect ghost stories. Fun antidotes that have nothing to do with the main lot but are great ammo for the next time you are camping around a fire with friends.  Very plot driven, but also informative.
I bought it and finished in around 15 hours, most of which are cut-scenes, but thankfully you can skip those if you choose. I’m serious about the cut-scenes; it might as well have been a movie. I like games with good immersive stories but sometimes it got a little much. I wish there was more game play as a whole, because I really enjoyed looking for clues and fighting demons. The sleuthing set up was quite fun and your inventory backpack has great organization so it is easy to go back and review information, mixed with some demon battles that draw upon my love for running  around killing things.
The investigation was a lot of the "eye-spy" type. Run around your crime scene interacting with objects and guessing if they are important or not. Sometimes you have to put clues together to get the rest of your clues (there is a tally at the bottom left-hand corner of the screen that will tell you how you are doing). Analyzing details were really multiple choice word problems that described the seen. A little bit of point-and-click. Demons were ambush attacks, got to work on your sneak skills.
Overall I loved it. It is a light game with all the ambience of something deeper like a noir, but the game play goes by too quick get very in depth. The ending is a little hurried but ends very much like a noir which I like since it is being faithful to the genre. It is something fun to play in between serious or time consuming games like Fallout 4. If you want a good distraction with some cool history and quick play through, this is the game for you!!

is a history lesson in the lives of the Romantic poets told through the medium of cute anime girls. Emphasis on the word "lesson." It's also a visual novel about one girl's quest to find a way to continue living through her crippling depression, either by convincing the friend she's become dependent on to return to her side or by trying to forget same said friend.
For the most part, I have no idea who this is for. The visual design of the game makes you think this immediately that this is going to be your bog standard waifu simulator/school girl on girl fantasy for typical straight weebs (though classier than most examples). It doesn't take too long into the game though for the meticulous amount of research and knowledge of the characters of the Romantic poets whom each of the girls represents to start weeping into the narration and the dialogue. The bizarre accuracy and heavyhandedness of the speech patterns, the philosophies, and the temperaments attuned to each writer being channeled into their respective moe moe girl is really something to behold. It makes for a much heavier read than you might expect from what the game looks like.
On the other hand, as dense and referential as the writing may be compared to some visual novels, the characters are much more vivid and fleshed out because of a committment in their basis as real people. Though it isn't necessarily realistic for teenage girls to treat one of their peer's depression as a serious disease or wax poetic on the very nature of misery and happiness. At the same time, the VN doesn't stick so close to the history books that it can't pull a gag about a cellphone falling into manure.
I like this game, mostly because I saw a lot of myself in its depressive protagonist. I saw a lot of my loved ones in its vicious, verbose, and lovable cast of mean girls. It made me rethink Coleridge, who I always felt was soppy. I still hate Wordsworth though. Her ending in the game felt the fakest too.
Anyway, I'm giving this a thumbs up, despite my apprehensions. Not like a little hard reading ever hurt anybody.

Elsword the game with a unique charm similar to Smash Brothers, but with the faulty advertisements of a dedicated fighting game. In terms of specs to run this game, you can nearly hop on any computer and start playing.
You join the game, select your first character. A unique cast that charms you by the beauty and elegance of their fighting styles and chibi-like looks. As you start off you may go on solo or with your new found playmates. From the combination of side-scrolling gameplay like in Mario Brothers, and light and heavy attacks similar to Smash Brothers you may be fooled into believing it's a fighting game.
But sadly the more you attempt to play arena, the more you attempt to hone your skills, the more you attempt to dungeon, the more you attempt to strive to become stronger in PvE or PvP. The more you quickly realize how difficult it is to get by without throwing your cash at this game. But with a few hours to spare you want to experience the full experience, the challenging experience. So you press on without spending a single dollar.
So with a keen interest in PvP you begin. You begin to practice and practice and practice. You go from a nobody to a noticeable foe. Practicing in spar rooms, and taking on the dangerous Arena. With your technical skills honed you realized, this isn't a fighting game. It's a beat-em up game. And despite your efforts you get trumped time and time again by simple tricks which you have no counterplay to.
So with all the pain and suffering, you think maybe you should pursue this "gear" everyone talks about. So with your technical skills honed to perfection you struggle onwards.
With hard work and much grinding hour by hour, day by day, you've accomplished difficult feat for Elsword. You've spent hours doing daily quests leaching off the "strong", and doing event quests acquiring much needed assets to your "gear." You've done it you're fully accessorized and you even look pretty damn good.
Gear the major determining factor to your stats, you've increased your stats to your ideal, using your RPG knowledge you've put it together like a puzzle. Each piece that took you hours upon hours of your time and effort.
Now with your new found power you are respected for your clear speeds in dungeons, your friends respect your hard work and your power. So you tackle PvP once more.
Now you have become what you thought was impossible to defeat, you have become one of the "strong." Only to be hated in PvP. Only to give your opponent the experience against fighting impossible odds, with little to no counterplay.
You soon find yourself bored time and time and time again. You've honestly done all you've wanted in your solo adventure, with your free2play spirit in a harsh monopoly of a pay2win game.
So you think back and ask yourself. "What have a really accomplished?" I've made friends along the way I see them come and go. Your closest friends have quit the game. The community dwindles to near emptiness at night. When the community is awake the topics is always the same. Complaints about the game, complaints about PvP. When someone asks you to teach them you simply laugh and show them the one trick that works 9/10 games. When you try to style your combos many will not notice and only few veterans will praise you. You've reached a level of strength that one would not think is possible without spending at least a couple hundred dollars.
"Is there something more? Is there something more to experience?" You ask yourself. With only the feeling of empty accomplishment and many regrets. "Did I actually enjoy playing?" Yes, yes you did for awhile. But soon it became a disappointing grind everyday, soon it became a hassle a simple desire to see how far you can push the limits. At times you showed anger, frustration, and then you took it seriously and in the end... You've hurt your friends, and you've hurt the one that you held dearest to you, a game taken too seriously.
So you decide to slow down, you decide to see "What more does this game offer?" Taking the time to sit down and read and watch the story. Reading up on the lore. You quickly discover the plot is incoherent, sometimes unfinished, misleading, counter-intuitive, but comedic and random.
With so much hours put into this game, with many accomplishments one after another. Sadly this is the disappointment in the end.
This is my lonely and disappointing adventure in Elrios, in the game of Elsword.
----------
Despite this. You log on, to talk and meet old friends that still have stuck with you for all this time. This is the true value you found. I have mixed feelings about Murdered: Soul Suspect. I enjoyed the game with it's very unique style, and the story full of twists and turns, so I do recommend it, but there are a few issues that prevent this from being as good as it could have been.
Some of the puzzles require you to choose "most relevant" clues, so you might pick 3 from 10, but it often feels like guesswork. Not guesswork into your character or the story, but guesswork into the developers minds. This can lead to frustration, but doesn't prevent progress.
If you miss a clue earlier in the game, even though you can return to that location, the clue isn't always there. A lot of people get stuck on the 15/16 issue with Apartment 4A, for example, and that was the one clue preventing me from a perfect score.
The final area does give you a warning message, but once you enter it, you cannot return to a previous save to hunt down any remaining clues. As soon as you enter the area, you are either choosing to give up on side quests, or planning to replay the entire game again.
Those issues aside, it's a great experience and worth playing if you can pick it up on sale.

This is a game for those that have A LOT of time on their hands
it is an enjoyable experience so long as you are on a well populated server, population in my opinion creates slight balancing issues when it comes to the game so choose your server wisely, too few people and you'll find the game quickly becomes boring after level 55 since there will be little challenging your free reign, however, too many and you'll find that the game becomes pretty much impossible limitting you to a portion of the map unless you find yourself a guild to travel safely with.
Some people call this game "pay to win" and I can see where they are coming from (to an extent). The game uses a labour system and once you have used your labour you cannot craft, mine and do various other tasks that would be possible in other MMORPG's (say WoW), buying a membership or the in game currency will allow you to receive MORE labour points in a quicker space of time, or allow you to replenish labour points instantly with labour potions. This clearly gives the pay out population of the game an advantage over the free to play members, I wouldn't say this makes the game a "pay to win". You see whilst you cannot mine/craft you are still able to quest and complete dungeons, meaning that labour is not the only way for you to level/grind quickly in the game, however it does mean that paying members will be able to craft higher level equipment a lot faster than free to play members. I wouldn't agree the game is fully pay to win because the free to play members can get the same grade equipment and stats as paying members, this makes the end game (the bit that really matters) fair to the entire server.
Until you reach level 50-55 you WILL spend your time grinding and questing, there is little else you as a player can do at that level without getting killed by the opposing faction/pirates, I think the game needs a bit more variety than it currently has in the early and mid game scenarios because it only really opens up to the player when they get the to higher levels.
I hope this is explained well enough, I do recommend the game especially if you have friends interested, it is a lot of fun and a great pass time. It is a very good game but like all games it does have flaws and there are some improvements I think Trion should make.

This is absolutely gorgeous. This apparently has been in development for nine years. I've never heard of it until yesterday, but this is what a game that looks like it has been worked on for almost a decade. The sprite art is stunningly gorgeous, but screenshots don't do it justice because the animation, well, I could say it's the icing on the cake but I would rather call it the cake on your other cake.
So many little details are in the environment and character animations. I don't mean that in the same way modern triple A games get praised for adding basic details that Nintendo 64 games had. There was clearly genuine effort put into these animations. Triple A games tend to look good in screenshots and from a distance, but up-close you can see just how robotic the characters act. This game looks fantastic from a distance and in screenshots, but gets better the closer you look.
Pixels seldom remain still on characters and environments that would logically be moving. It is not necessary for the game to inform you by text what emotions characters are feeling, because you can see for yourself. Characters will stand with a different posture appropriate to their expressions, they twiddle their thumbs, shake their knees, sweat, avoid eye contact, get red in the face, and many more subtle ways of conveying emotion. No need for a giant thought bubble with an emoticon. The protagonist may be silent, but I understood everything he wanted to say.
The gameplay isn't bad, either. It's smooth, perfectly responsive, and has a lot of remapping options, although the default controls are perfect anyway. Gamepad, at least. I don't know how good the keyboard controls are but platformers and keyboard controls have never got along well.
Just get it now, even if it's not on sale. It's also on
, which I would recommend over Steam because it's DRM-free. If I had known it was on GOG, too, I would have gotten it from there.

TL;DR:
Disgaea PC is a very strong port of a well worth your time game that started a great series of SRPGs, if you are looking for a solid SRPG that has several hours of content or a single player rpg with quite a bit of leveling/farming/bossing to do after the story is over, this game is that.
What it does well:
+ [ Humor ]  Over the top voice acting and a whole lot of complete nonsense is what makes the story mode engaging and worthwhile.
+ [ Soundtrack ]  The kind that you hum to/beat box to while playing. In the case of the Dark Assembly; doo doo doo comes to mind. Hear for yourself:
+ [ Level Over 9000 ]  Has a fair amount of post game content. Expect to grind though if you are doing post game, but if you ARE doing post game you probably don't mind grinding atleast a little, right? RIGHT?
+ [ "The Dark Adonis" ]  Memorable characters, pushed by the fact that the voice acting is stellar.
+ [ Gameplay ]  Fast paced for a turn based when animations are turned off, when they are on expect to see Dragon Ball Z levels of spectacle carnage.
+ [ Puzzle Elements ]  Geo panels setting different rules for tiles according to color, making maps a bit more interesting.
What it does not so well:
- [ Story ]  While it has its few good serious moments, its overall pretty weak but still not too badly written atleast when the humor comes in.
- [ Camera Angles ]  In the story mode camera angles arn't much of a big deal, the maps are designed around it and rotating the camera will solve any visual issues you may experience. This isn't true for the item world. In the item world, you will sometimes not be able to rotate the camera enough to be able to see ceratian tiles that are obstructed visually by being in dips in terrain elevation. This can be a problem when dealing with locating the destination panel, or trying to relocate the base panel.
The other things it does:
* [ Power ]  Through enough grinding everything will become a complete pushover. You will eventually be able to one shot everything in the game if you grind your stats out enough. Through the master/pupil system there is no cap [known?] to the amount of stats you can farm.
* [ Majin ]  There is no real reason to use other classes than the "majin" once you unlock it, except for stealing as a thief or for teaching the majin spells through mages using the master/pupil system. Though you don't need to worry about majins during the main story as you won't unlock them until you grind some post game content for a while.
* [ Item World ]  Items level up as you progress through each floor of their own dungeon. This is the place you will need to spend a lot of time if you want to get some good gear. Your gear is very important when determining the overall power of your characters thus meaning that if you want to have the most time efficient power gain for post game; you should be using the item world. The maps are procedurely generated and they have random geo panel effects on every floor. You will need to go through 100 floors if the item is legendary and defeat multiple item bosses that reside in every tenth floor to get the most out of your items. 100 floors of leveling items can be very time consuming if you are trying to kill everything on every floor, so the popular method of progression is to stack up rogues that have good throwing ability, and use them to travel accross the map in a single turn to reach the destination panel. Which makes the item world more of a puzzle game than a SRPG for the large majority of it.
TL;DR: The item world can be very tedious but gives very high rewards.

First off let's get the biggest negative out of the way. This game is grindy. This is the grindiest grindfest I have ever grinded and in this game grinding isn't a by-product of difficulty or a way to make money via exp boost micro-transactions no no, in this game grinding is  a mechanic in itself and that just annoys the hell out of me. If you want to get the most out of this game, prepare for a lot of grinding.
With that being said though the game is great. It's an old game so visually it's not going to be the best but that doesn't mean the visuals are off putting. I don't have a problem with them at all.
Disgaea is a very unique feeling tactical RPG with many mechanics to learn. From team attacks to the grid-based geo panel effects there's a lot you need to learn in order to master the combat to not only come out on top, but end each fight earning the best loot you can. Speaking of loot, there is a lot of it.
Story wise the game doesn't take itself too seriously. It's full of humour and the characters are just as ridiculous. I really love the writing here, no negatives from me in terms of the story and the humour.
One negative would be that fullscreen just doesn't work, like at all. Even with fullscreen set in the options I'm still forced to play in a bordered window. It's really annoying to a certain degree but as you go on you learn to look past it.
This is the sort of game that I recComend NOT playing constantly. A few hours each day maybe to keep it fresh otherwise you most certainly will get tired of it because the grinding is tedious. Still, even without grinding there is plenty to do so you'll likely get a lot of hours out of this title. Not really sure if it's worth the full price but if it goes on sale I'd certainLY say it's worth giving a go.

The story was lackluster and poorly written. Molstrom just dies without you ever fighting him, despite being the ultimate war machine built by the Owls, and Solus never confides into Otus his reasoning for using the relics, despite saying that he considered Otus to be his only friend. There were too many unnecessary, irrelevant things to the story that were communicated while tons of other more pertinent questions to the story were left unanswered. For example, what does the engraved stone with the Roman numerals on it mean? Why are there plants overgrowing in some areas, and how did no one realize that they broke the wind machine in the Owl Temple? Who wrote the Book of Nocteus, and why was it prophetic?
There may be more to the end of the universe, but this story did not do a good job of convincing me that there is.
I could go on about the oversight in game mechanics, but I feel as though they pale in comparison to the lack of effort put into the story.
However, I will say that this game is beautiful. There were many times that I was just awestruck by the detail put into it. I can't reasonably put my enamorment into words, but the art alone made this game worth it to me.
I would not recommend this game, though, because I believe great games have great stories. This, sadly, was not one of them.
(EDIT FOR CLARITY—11/5/2016):
I have taken the spoiler tag off not to spite anyone here, but to more easily make it understood how incomplete the story is.
The authors attempted to create many twists within the story, only to neuter it by creating major flaws in the character arcs of Solus, Molstrom, and the unknown Book of Nocteus author.
Taste is subjective, but the story is not written well on an objective level, and I had to create an argument with apropos evidence by stating such a thing.
A game with a good story should allow you to get immersed and lost within it. This game does everything within its power to prevent this, from the complete and utter destruction of Advent after Anne says to come by her house in Advent to learn more about her, to the lack of historical explanation of the Owl race. This game goes out of its way to make the story undigestible.
This will be my last update, as the story of this game is not worth discussing further.
My review is not against steam rules, and you are not required to read reviews before purchasing this game.
Should you find anger after reading my review, then I suggest you reevaluate why you sought out reviews in the first place.

Hand of Fate is something really quite special. Cards become a dungeon as they're laid out on the table before you. With each step another card is turned over to reveal another encounter, each feeling like they've been taken straight from the pages of a choose-your-own-adventure book.
The dealer sitting opposite you engages in amusing and intriguing banter, alternating between challenging and encouraging you, threatening to make the game more deadly at every turn, and hinting at the secrets behind the mysterious game you're playing with him.
It's a fantastic setting for a game, and quite a difficult one as the dealer keeps to his word and throws tougher creatures, harsher traps, cruel encounters and a seemingly endless array of painful curses to stop you in your tracks with every round you play
At times it can get a little frustrating. Being a card game, you can tweak your deck with favourable encounters, but sometimes that's not enough to prevent a string of bad encounters early on which can bring a game to a swift end. Couple this with some encounters being simple games of chance, and at times it feels like you've lost without really playing badly.
Thankfully this doesn't happen too often, and with each conquered challenge rewarding you with new cards, even a failed adventure can net you some new toys.
And if you really dislike having so much RNG in your game, you can stack the deck in favour of combat encounters to help limit the amount of dice rolling.
The combat, however, is probably the weakest part of this game. It's a straightforward affair, a watered down version of the free-flowing combat in the Batman Arkham series. It works just fine and can get quite challenging, and there's a vast array of weapons, armour and trinkets to aid you, but I feel like it needs a few more options to keep it interesting. All you can really do is attack, block, guard-break, dodge, and occasionally use a trinket or a weapon's special ability. I wouldn't expect the immense depth the Arkham games have but I think it's a little too simple here.
For the most part, the game looks and runs just fine. Personally I find the art style quite appealing and fairly unique, but I suppose some people might find it a little too simplistic for their tastes. I have encountered a few graphical glitches however, such as pink boats and monsters' limbs stretching like elastic, as well as a couple of freezes that forced me to restart the game. Nothing remotely serious or common enough to warrant a major complaint, but it's a very rewarding experience when you let yourself get immersed in the adventure, and those sorts of minor irritants draw you out from it.
In summary: A wonderfully entertaining card game/dungeon crawl/choose-your-own-adventure experience with a few minor issues. A little simplistic in its combat and sometimes a little heavy on the RNG, but these minor gripes are a small price to pay for such a unique game with a sinister, secretive adversary who raises the stakes with every round. It does get quite challenging as your progress, so don't expect an easy ride.

I'm on the fence about this one, because in some aspects, I would recommend it. But in other areas, I cannot. Overall though, I feel as if I can't recommend this simply because it's hard to empathize or connect with any of these characters, which is important in story telling. After all, this is a visual novel and that's really the entire point. These girls are all mean spirited, rude, inconsiderate, and even while trying to be nice - their ideas of being "helpful" and "kind" are still back handed and mean in nature.
It pains me to keep watching the main protagonist (Sam) try to trudge through everything on her own. She is a desperate cry for help who keeps getting walked all over. Sam is constantly trying to justify the other girl's actions and words. Always turning it around. Its "her" faullt, she deserves it, SHE should have done or said something different. The whole point is that Sam is trying to cure her loneliness and build friendships. But these girls? You're almost better off alone. They're not even nice to each other. It feels as if none of them have any sort of positive relationships with one another. No matter what outcome you get, no matter the decisions you make, it's hard to feel as if Sam's situation has improved in the slightest.
I will say though, that the portrayl of Sam being a young individual with anxiety/depression is very accurate. I just wish they would have put a better variety of characters with more supportive roles.
- You are a huge fan of all visual novels and aren't picky.. then by all means.
- You like cheap games. I bought this at 75% off for 1.62. But even at the full retail price of 6.49, it's a very decent length of a game to actually get your money's worth (assuming you read the whole thing).
- You like getting easy achievements or trading cards. This game has both.
- You enjoy a more mild "PG" type of game. There's no nudity, foul language, etc. The artwork is beautiful as well.
- You like a game that's well optimized. The game functions and works well. It has an skip function, auto read (eliminating clicking, allowing you to read it like a book), and all of the other options for volume, speed, and screen resolutions all work.
- The characters, like I said, are just awful.
- It just really put me in a bad mood. :/ I felt BAD when reading this. I felt as if I was reading a story mostly about verbal abuse.
- There's a lot of back story that's shoehorned in that isn't necessary, or well explained.
- Some of the endings feel as if they were rushed, leaving me even more dissatisfied.
- Although it is a longer game, I feel like a lot of the dialogue isn't necessary. I felt myself often saying "get to the point already". is probably the cutest worst game there is.
better covers it: you play half the game as a top-down dungeon crawler and the other half as manager to the eponymous item shop, with neither halves being properly implemented in the first place. I get the feeling that the developers,
, had very ambitious ideas for the concept of "Item Merchant Game" except that they've botched everything until what they made barely resembles a game anymore! I'll explain...
You are Recette, spunky little girl entrepreneur required by the faerie bond collection agency to raise enough money to repay her father's exorbitant adventuring debt. For this task you have your house located smack dab in the middle of RPG City, which you've converted into an Item Shop for the convenience of all. Sell items to the roaming adventurers, make a profit, repay your debt; simple enough, right? It all goes to pot with the whole bargaining system and the complete lack of player feedback other than win/fail.
Before that, an egregious crime in game development: having the tutorial LIE to you. When faerie sidekick Tear tells you that selling at around 121% of base price is a conservative strategy, she is flat out LYING to you. This is far above what many villagers can afford and will not increase important customer loyalty. This is especially villainous considering there is no other way than trial-and-error to determine a customer's comfort range.
The process of selling and bargaining for optimal profits and customer loyalty is stupid and punishes experimentation. Any experimentation in bargaining reduces important customer loyalty which reduces the overall money pool they're willing to invest in your products. Worse, it's all so incredibly MOOT!!! When you buy goods from the guild merchant, he sells it to you marked down from base price. Therefore if you sell those goods at base price, you make a (small) profit. Base price is a perfectly good baseline for most customers and you can repay your debts out of this practice! Otherwise, use a strategy guide to know optimal salesmanship builds as there's no rhyme or reason to the whole process!
Dungeon crawling is the second half of the game and although mostly innocuous, doesn't introduce any elements anyone would deem "fun". You hire an adventurer from the pool of friends you've made and go down randomly generated levels, looking out for monsters and treasures until you discover the exit. Inventory space (bag space) becomes the most annoying aspect as you're stretched between saving space for treasures at the expense of bringing food, rings and adventuring gear. Because the adventurers don't bring their own gear with them; no, that would be too simple! You have to sell them the stuff from your store, except you have no control over what they ask for and you can't "suggest" goods either. Egregious crime in gaming #2!
All that said, the Main Story is fun enough. You have likeable characters, humorous dialogue... You really can't fault the English publishing company
for anything. It's New Game + that becomes a pain because the challenge comes from grinding for rare items (in multiples, for completion of the Fusion Recipes) and the fact that the dungeons are just longer with cheaper boss fights. Oh, did I mention that you can't save inside of a dungeon? There's really nothing to gain from the New Game + experience except an increase in frustration and
two characters. I put a point in saying
because if you do unlock the final character, you've already defeated all the monsters and bosses the game has to throw at you. That's bad pacing right there.
The main problem with
is that the item shop game, billed as its selling point, just doesn't work. It fails from lack of options for the player, lack of interface telling the player what he's doing right and wrong and arbitrary levels of contentment amongst the customers. It's not
, far from it! It's that there's no
related to the experience. Recettear might as well be a visual novel with a dungeon crawler tacked on to it. It's cute and endearing but it fails at being a game to begin with. And I'm the idiot who gifted this product to so many of my friends. Just enormous waves of regret all around, don't be like me and get suckered in by a cute exterior...
PS: I really wished that there were more "Adventurer" customers and less normal looking villagers, so you could really make this game about an ITEM SHOP SET IN AN RPG WORLD. As it is, you're really more of a goods store selling general products and knickknacks.

As someone who suffers from depression (and anxiety), I absolutely adored this visual novel. It conveys the struggle of keeping friends while having a mental illness very, very well. I could relate to the protagonist more than I have with any other in a VN. People tend to be unkind to those with a mental illness, especially chronic depression (not to be confused with situational depression). The characters that interact with the protagonist do an excellent job of showing how friends and people in general react to someone with depression. "If you don't like things, change it" is so much easier said than done. People don't believe you when you tell them that you're trying to get better. People call you needy, clingy, and desperate, when you just want reassurance from them in order to ease your suffering a bit. People act like being friends with you is a chore in the same moment they claim you're not a burden. People do/say all sorts of cruel things rather than try to actually understand someone's pain.
I do have a complaint though. I considered what I feel was supposed to be the "bad ending" as the best one. I don't think any of the endings that involved being friends with any of those cruel, patronizing characters were good, especially not the one that involved the protagonist's romantic interest. I felt all the things that were said during "Georgia's ending" (I'll call it that so there aren't too many spoilers) should have inspired the opposite of what happens in the end.
The characters had no racial diversity, but I'm not surprised. Some of the characters, including the protagonist, were insinuated to be queer, so there's that at least.
Nonetheless, I do recommend this visual novel. Beautiful artwork. Excellent portrayal of depression and dealing with other people while having said mental illness. Lovely, poetic writing.

I used to be a big skeptic of this game. Quite a few hours of gameplay have changed my opinion. There is a main story but I hardly paid any attention to it due to the almost overwhelming amount of optional things to do. Typical to any MMO there is a fair amount of character customization to start, then when you get into the game, you can buy your gear for a relatively cheap in-game price or you can scavenge for it or you can quest for it, already you have several options. There are infinitely more side-quests than story quests, and while there are some pre-requisites that are unclear to me, I'm sure if you do all the side quests in your alotted spawn you can find a million other things to do. Want to run trade missions across an ocean or continent? Go right ahead. Want to own a house and live off the land? It's up to you. Want to pull your riches from the ocean through fishing? It's up to you. Want to claim other people's riches as your own as a pirate? Don't let me stop you. You can live life however you see fit in this game, anywhere from a life of crime, to calling the largest castle your not-so-humble abode. It does take a bit of a pricey PC to run on higher graphic settings, I wouldn't even consider this game for Mac users, sorry, you're definitely missing out, but most desktops can run this on fairly decent settings. AI can be 5 feet away from you and still hit you, you can either dodge left, right, or backwards, and it has zero effect. I am not a nice person.
I judge things by their faults, not by their strengths. It is a system of subtraction. For everything that displeases me the game needs to have something equal or greater in order for me to enjoy it. Games that are "flawed but good" do not get my recommendation. I am hard, I am critical and I find little pleasure in things anymore. I have prejudged them all and found them wanting. I tell you this so that you might understand the weight of what I say next.
Owlboy is a masterpiece unlike any I have seen for a long time. It is not only a joy to behold, but to experience.
I am not one for graphics making the game, but the screenshots and whatever video you have seen of this game does it no justice. It is stunning from start to finish. The characterizations, the movement, the attention to detail, the colors and the vivid landscapes. Everything is uniquely designed and is so amazing you won't be able to take it all in through a single playthrough. As you play, keep your eyes open and attentive and you will be endlessly rewarded.
The music is a marvel. I am going to go and buy the soundtrack. Its really just that great. There's flow and character and mood and melody. Everything is weird and different but it all fits together. Character themes and areas and even the sound effects just flow seemlessly to set the tone of the adventure. If you love old soundtracks for the classic game of bygone then you will not be disappointed.
Story and writing are not what I would expect out of this game nor did I anticipate it to be such a high point. It has epic adventure without feeling forced. The characterization is excellent. There's comedy, which is genuinely funny and light hearted, but its only a pause from the rising gravity of a situation gone extremely wrong. There's intrigue and development and those who are careful to watch it unfold can notice some very interesting things early on that will pique your curiosity.
Its a fun game to play. The controls on keyboard and mouse are simple enough that you don't struggle against a steep learning curve but certain segments will have you hammering away at keys in order to switch up moves and having you scramble during some of the faster paced segments... but the game is very forgiving. It will throw you into a situation, but its not guaranteed instant failure if you mess up. You get multiple chances and if you've worked on what the game has taught you then you will easily fall into the reflex of knowing what to do. The areas feel good, feel smart. They're crisp and never requiring pixel perfect jumps or for you to count frames in order to succeed. Its fun.
There's a few minor bugs to the game. I've had to deal with one, but honestly I can't blame the developers; its a problem with XNA and I daresay anyone developing a title like this one would have been bit by the same thing. They're working on it, and I've had no issue with performance outside having to reinstall WMP.
Its worth the money new. And that's high praise.

This is game is a complete masterpiece. I had never heard about it until a few days ago, and I instantly fell in love with the artwork. I had no idea what the game was supposed to be like, I bought it purely because it LOOKED nice. I was very pleasantly surprised to find that it also has a great story, unique and loveable characters, amazing music and sound design, superb animation, and of course fun and interesting gameplay.
I've played for about 3 hours so far, and am just now feeling like the adventure is really getting started, though I've enjoyed every minute of it. I was a little worried that it might be short with not a whole lot to it, as these visually impressive 2D games sometimes tend to be, but every once in a while you get a true masterpiece like this, where everything from design to gameplay is spot on, and isn't too short and gives you a lot to do.
This is not a multiplayer or open world sandbox with endless replayability game which seems to be the strange requirement for a lot of people in games these days. It is fairly linear with some exploration in areas, finding coins to unlock upgrades, with secret rooms and hidden chests. I honestly miss games like this, that aren't overly complex with upgrade trees and skill sets. It's quite simple, but does a really good job at being simple, fun, and intriguing. I can definitely see myself being satisfied with a sense of completion when I manage to finish it.
With all that being said, I think the price is completely justified. This isn't a short random indie game with nothing much to it, it's a full blown story and adventure with puzzles, boss fights, numerous and unique creatures and characters, secrets to uncover, and has amazing artwork. You can definitely tell that a lot of skill, hardwork, and time went into making this. I want more games like this, so I'm willing to help fund the cause of bringing back games with the magic and creativity that we just don't see so much anymore.
If you feel nostalgic it's the perfect game for you.

Hand of fate is an interesting game.  The combat is kinda simple, but the real meat of the game is in the 'meta'game.  Playing the cards and messing about with the decks you want to build to equip and fight against is a ton of fun, and there's a lot of anticipation and foreplanning when it comes to exploring each floor.
A good portion of the encounter quest cards lead to more encounters, often in a narratively sense as well as a strictly unlocking sense.  Making your way through a boarder town for the first time, for instance, will open up new frontier lands (in the form of new encounter cards) for you to adventure forth to.
I am also very fond of the main character.  While he is a bit of a silent protagonist, you do get a lot of insight to him from the cards and the encounters, which are based off of his past life and/or memories.  I also like that he's not just a generic sort of a guy; he's got an interesting but not overdesigned look, and clearly isn't afraid to do what he desires.  This is also somewhat shown through gameplay, as while you often get several choices of how to respond to some encounter prompts, only one of them will progress you to future encounters.  It lends a sense of "this is how it actually went" to thing.
At the same time the other main character, and your opponant, the Dealer, has his own story, some of which you unravel as you play.  He is voiced very well, and manages to capture one's attention as he comments on both your gameplay choices and the narrative happenings in the plot.  It's like you are both playing a game with him, and yet telling a story with him through your actions.
The system is also very expandable, so it's fairly safe to assume that there'll be some DLC in the works for this game.
Overall, this is a very solid game, and one well worth throwing a fair few hours at.
I would recommend a controller, if you have one, as it makes the combat feel a little better.

Summary: Great game with a few rough patches... Well worth the purchase.
Good: This game's combat, while pretty easy to wrap your head around, is surprisingly gratifying as your heroes level up. The abilities feel really fun, and dungeon exploring does a good job of being tense and challenging throughout the game. Combining a store style sim with an action combat mechanic is by no means a new idea, but it's executed very well here. The store management system is fun and very in depth. I had a great time tweaking my store's aesthetics and placement, choosing where each item goes based on how that will affect my sales. If you like store management games, action rpgs, or both, you're going to find something to love here.
Bad: In all honesty, I was unimpressed by the game's story. While some of the characters were interesting, the main plot and a lot of the side plots were kind of dull, and I found myself wading through text trying to get to the next part of the game. A good story draws you in, not forces you to skip it. Also, you have regular bills to pay each week, and the last one is suddenly, terrifyingly large.
Ugly: I only have one complaint large enough to be called "Ugly": To craft the really good items to sell in your store, you need material items, some of which are seemingly impossible to find. Any game that requires me to hunt down a wiki to complete is probably doing something wrong.
Complaints aside, this game was impressively fun and engaging. Definitely check it out.

Asphyxia is a realistic portrayal of mental illness - most convincingly, depression. A bit different from typical VNs that are more light hearted, it deals with heavy subject matter and doesn't have scantily clad women like many of the anime style VNs do. The art style is also quite different, opting for a more detailed painted look versus the traditional anime look.
Overall I found the game "ok." I thought the writer did a good job of showing the telltale signs of depression - suicidal, lethargic, impulsive, irrational, etc, but it is really over the top at some points. I know that in real life, depression can feel like that, but as a casual reader, it felt like many parts were repeats, over and over. Some people may like the more proper English and drawn up descriptions, but I felt many parts could be a lot more concise.
I thought the characters were very interesting, much more so than the typical anime sterotypical tropes. It kind of makes you think of whether you can identify with the personality of one of the characters. The game does a decent job of showing how each main character is multi-dimensional, and how there are positives and negatives to each person. I think it does a good job of explaining the inner motivations of people that may not be apparent.
I know not everyone is going to agree with me on this, but what I did not like is how the mixed up this very serious topic with a lesbian love triangle (granted with plenty of unrequited love). There are many facets of depression, and the massive focus on one particular part of it detracts from the rest. Because they set it up in such a way, I did not find the endings very satisfying, and even the 'happy endings' are not very convincing especially given the challenges of the protagonist. I guess maybe the endings are realistic!
