Let me just say that I haven't played many visual-novel style, indie-developed games. Life Is Strange is in my library, because who can resist time travel and the butterly effect colliding beautifully in a French-made game with beautiful indie music backing it? Yes, I compared it to Gone Home in my review, but that comes from its origins within the 3-D walking simulator type of game.
Basically, all you need to know is that Asphyxia is a game in which the major Romantic poets of the late 18th century are reimagined as cute schoolgirls. Does this work? I personally have to say that the author of the VN has certainly done his research, but also the characters are so beleiveable, so well-written, that there was hardly ever a moment where I thought, "OK this is where they are making reference to something, or writing, verbatim, what these middle-aged male authors said some 300 years ago," because the characters are so beleivable, the source material has been worked in almost seamlessly. The VN's writer, Ebi-Hime, is definitely on my radar now.
A lot of the reviews are coming from the, completely optional, I might add, lesbian romance side of things, again drawing a comparison to Gone Home. There seem to be multiple endings, and while there are subtextual references to how Samantha feels around Lillian, there are certainly many endings where they do not end up as a couple. I appreciate that the relationship, while somewhat forced at times, can certainly not come to fruition in what is certainly meant to be a melancholie game. I would not have purchased this game in the first place, if it was yet another teen/LGBT drama that was forced out of contrivacy such as Gone Home, however the author gave it to his audience to make of it what they will.
Samantha Coleridge is certainly a protagonist you want to root for, while she drinks energy drinks and absinthe to the point of vomiting, and stands freezing in the Scottish countryside wondering just how to win her friendship (Optional/obvious lesbian relationship) back with Lillian, you will be a part of her thoughts, which is why this is a good novelization, and you will struggle with her. Of course I have a particular affinity for redheads, and suffice it to say that Samantha is cute, like the other characters in this game, I wasn't wholly on board with all the avenues that she takes, for instance, the cigarette smoking, Someone I wanted to like smoking cigarettes I could have done without, and I parsed through the text referencing it.
Pros:
A writer whose dedication to his/her craft shows throughout, with numerous references to Romantic poets.
Cute, redheaded protagonist, who doesn't fall victim to gender steryotypes.
Cons:
Everything just has to be LGBT for some reason. Don't get me wrong I work with gay people on a daily basis, but few people realize that less than 5% of people (at least here in the USA) so for such a small minority, they sure are outspoken. I'm not sure if this is the author's perspective, or if they are trying to appeal to a broader demographic, but it always illicits an eyeroll from me.
It's an indie game, so I can hardly count it against the game, but I wished there was a cast of voice actors/actresses.
Final Verdict:
7/10: Cute animated girls, with clever references and writing alluding to the major Romantic poets of the late 18th century. If not for the repetitive RPG-maker music and shoehorned and completely unneccessary lesbian/LGBT ties, it would have been best in its class.

I was drawn to this visual novel entirely by the art, music and concept. The artwork is very different to the more traditional anime style usually seen in visual novels, with a watercolour look and more classical character designs, all accentuated by the multiple pieces of music that accompany each section. It was however that setup which really caught my attention, as we have here interpretations of classical English poets reimagined as adorable students. Despite the change in age and gender, it’s fun to see traits from the real poets show through, my favourite example being the flirtatious and crafty Georgia Byron who certainly lives up to her namesake.
Honestly I could easily recommend purchasing Asphyxia purely on these aesthetic choices, but there is actually a story beneath them.  It’s extremely well-written, with some great character development and quite a few humorous moments. However… it’s a heavy story. Our main protagonist Samantha suffers some mental problems, contemplates suicide and spends a good portion of the story in a state of depression that, depending on your choice, can either get steadily worse or be overcome or even denied. I confess that I struggled to get through the story, not because it’s bad by any means, but because I personally couldn’t get into Samantha’s mind-set most of the time and found it difficult to go and make those darker choices to get the other endings, and some of those left an unpleasant feeling afterwards. But as I said do not take this to mean it’s bad, I commend the writers for tackling this topic with such maturity and it is written incredibly well, plus those darker moments make the happy and funny sections all the more rewarding and heart-warming.
Overall Asphyxia is a beautiful visual novel, with gorgeous artwork, lovely music and a charmingly unique setup, all wrapping a deeply emotional story. I highly recommend that you give it a try, but do be aware that it can get very heavy at times.

Unfortunately, Condemned Heroes tarnishes the fair name of the "Men of War" series.This "game" was not developed by Best Way, but was instead whomped up by a large publisher's team of ham-handed developers. At its best, this "game" is nothing more than a mod with a small amount of graphical tweaks.
At its worst, this "game" is a bundle of bug filled, sometimes nearly unplayable missions.
Back when this game was just announced on one large gaming website, i remember my excitement. A dozen screenshots depicted updated models of Soviet and German infantry fighting in ruined trenches, large towns being overrun with battered looking tanks, and grim winter landscapes that forebode vast, fierce battles. The idea itself also caught my interest. Instead of commanding ordinary troops, Condemned Heroes promised to unfold World War II from an entierly different perspective. Players would command a Soviet penal battalion, a unit that consisted entierly from convicts and prisoners. This was a very interesting theme, one that was barely explored in WWII games before. But as it often turns out to be, the pre-release screenshots were better than the actual "game" itself. It can be concluded now with full confidence, that when making their product, the "developers" concentrated on the visual aspect of the game, completely ignoring the actual gameplay. The first thing that catches the eye are the updated infantry models. As soon as this game was announced, this new feature was shown literally in every screenshot, clearly acting as eye candy. And indeed, if "Condemned Heroes" has at least one positive element in it, its the new infantry appearance. Many players will agree, that the infantry models in Men of War look very simple, and soviet infantry just looks outright horrible (not because of their historical uniform, but because in Men of War, they have the least amount of detail, except those shiny big black boots). It's no surprise that the infantry was low in detail, because Faces of War (the predecessor of Men of War) came out way back in 2006. Condemned Heroes improves this part of the game by replacing the original infantry models with more realistic looking ones. The textures of the uniforms look much more detailed and sharp, and instead of clay little figures we now command tired, realistic looking ex-cons. Vehicle textures have also been improved with more realistic ones. Tanks are covered with rust and mud. The surrounding enviorment also changed a bit, with many new textures and structure models adorning the battlefield.
But be that as it may, a standalone game deserves to be called as such not only thanks to the visual content, but also gameplay (otherwise, it's nothing more than a mere mod, and those are usually free). The only two apparent gameplay differences that i saw in Condemned Heroes in comparison to Men of War is a dozen of poorly designed missions and some alleged tweaks (that are a change for the worse) within the physical parameters of the game. Specifically, heavier armor will usually explode upon being hit with AP rounds, while lighter vehicles will NOT explode at all when hit with HE rounds. This makes the game extremely annoying to play, because your damn tank (which is a rarity in the campaign, save for the first mission) instead of being damaged, will get destroyed, and thus the player is forced to reload the game. For the record, you never get reinforcements in any missions throughout the entire campaign, and will usually have to beat missions with two initial squads of soldiers. Any tank or vehicle that you find HAS to be captured and repaired, thus again contributing to the already annoying gameplay. Enemy AI isn't merely stupid, it feels like it's completely absent. Any enemy sequence or action that happens in missions is triggered by certain factors (like a completion of a secondary objective for an example). Otherwise, enemy soldiers and vehicles simply don't do anything. They just stand in place (usually trenches or buildings) and fire away, often not even aiming at your soldiers, but at your allies (computer controlled units). This gives the player a possibility to crawl and flank the unsuspecting enemy, destroying major threats like tanks and gun emplacements with grenades (if the player has patience to play at this point). Some missions are severely bugged and are almost unbeatable, and those several missions that ARE bug free still don't possess any real quality or complexity, instead being dull, boring trash that was seemingly made by a beginner mapper-modmaker. Instead of a tragic, fascinating storyline (like Soldiers: Heroes of World War II or Company of Heroes) with Stalin's political enemies in lead roles, players get a garbage campaign that has no plot value in it whatsoever. Additional content includes a useless reference about Soviet penal battalions during World War II that nobody is going to read anyways, especially amongst western players (and i can't judge them, instead of teaching the gaming audience about the horrors of the eastern front with TEXT, i suggest writing and designing a good in-game plotline instead). In short - you will not easily find an another such flawed game on Steam, and that's considering the fact, that there is a lot of crap out there.
Music in Condemned Heroes consists of about 3 tracks, 2 of which are so repetative, that it will make your head hurt. The other track played during a few winter missions late in the game is kinda smooth, reminded me of Warhammer 40k DoW's "Outer Reaches". The sound quality is pretty good. Most weapon firing sounds from Men of War were replaced with more realistic, dynamic firearm shots, again contributing to the overall feeling, that Condemned Heroes is more of a mod rather than a seperate game. After all, it ain't hard to change sound files.
"Men of War:Condemned Heroes" AKA "High Resolution Infantry & Lousy Mappack Mod" is a kick in the teeth to all fans of the "Men of War" series. During all my time writing reviews in Steam, i have never "Not Recommended" a single game, often even "Recommending" games that got mixed reviews, and therefore opinions. I always try to see something positive in any game, because i respect the time and effort that developers put into its making. But in the case of this here title, i'm going to have to make an exception. Fellow RTS and Wargamers, if you don't value your money, at least value your nerves and stay away from this "game"... Otherwise, you will just get dissapointed and will go for the uninstall button anyways.

Fable, to me, has a certain magic to it that completely distinguishes it from other RPGs. That magic is the balance of two opposing concepts: darkness and (sometimes crude) humor. Your hero in Fable battles monsters and demons throughout progression of the story while at the same encountering hilarious characters and situations. I can't tell you how relaxing it was, after finishing an intense main quest, to complete a silly side quest, like dressing up ridiculous for Beardy Baldy or participating in a chicken kicking competition. These features also showcase the options that Fable provides, most notably, choosing to side with good or evil throughout the game. While the ending of the game doesn't make your past choices relatively significant, I still appreciated having the option to either make or break one's day, sometimes even their fate, in the game. Some of the decisions I made were impacting enough to even make me feel guilty about them!
I would definitely give this game a shot if you're into RPGs or story driven games. Fable was a very unique game for its time. If you're willing to judge Fable by the standards of games during the Xbox era, maybe even later, then I believe that you will find one or more things about Fable special.

I liked the game, I really did, but honestly, I feel the updates come way too fast to earn any event prizes. I admire their attempts at bringing old players back to the game, but the rewards don't feel like a "welcome back" gift and more of a"Come back and we'll give you things". In the old days, Elsword had a skill system where players could choose to equip any skill out of an entire tree, that includes the hyperactive. Since then they changed it approximately thrice now; in one version, the original tree was revamped so instead of dedication sp to the skill to level it up in bundles, you had to level them up one-by-one as well as there being a passive-skill tree seperated from the rest, second and third versions being the ones available today. Something that hasn't change was the pay-to-look-pretty-and-still-somehow-be-better-than-everybody-else system. Ah memories, when people who took pride in their wallet dumped it into the game to get absurd amounts of magic stones to attribute their equipment with top of the line perks. The PVP is always the same though, you end up fighting another player within your rank or level range and get completely overwhelmed because of their dexterity. To those who want to play this, don't play a PVP mode. The ranking and matchmaking system is as skewed as WarThunders'. PVE is as equally skewed, but with the players being on the same side. Since I began playing this game, I admire KoG for implimenting the individual item drop thing, but alot of the game is repetetive. Scroll right, scroll left, kill everything, move on. I used to feel alot of competetition playing in PVE like I felt in PVP because everybdyo went straight for the mobs and ythen moved on. Yada Yada Yada.
tl;dr: I used to like this game when I started out, but as the game developed, it lost that special something that hooked me in the first place. PVP sucks, PVE sucks because everybody kills something before you do, it's repetitive, Everything in the Premim+Casual market is overpriced, the updates keep changing the game that it's hard to keep up. Gonna go ahead and give you the TL;DR at the beginning to save you from reading a rather lengthy review: Basically, right now, the game is nothing special. Its another early, early access survival game, and it plays like another early, early access survival game. If you enjoy other survival games like ARK, you would probably have some fun with Conan Exiles. At this moment in time, however, I wouldn't say there is any reason to play this game over ARK unless you really enjoy the universe of Conan. The game does some things well and it does show promise though, and it is worth keeping an eye on if you are a fan of the genre. So while I do give it a positive review, my viewpoint is better represented as a "Maybe", as "Mixed" feelings represents this game well.
Right now, I will say Conan Exiles is basically everything you would expect an early, early access survival game to be.
It's buggy. It lacks polish. It's laggy with lots of rubberbanding. You can literally find notes called "Placeholder Lore".
It's far from complete.
For the rest of this review, I am going to compare its gameplay to that of ARK, because the gameplay of Conan Exiles takes such heavy inspiration from ARK that I wouldn't say that the people calling it a ripoff are unjustified in doing so.
For all of its shortcomings, this game already does some things better than other survival games out there though, only one year into its development.
+Along with progression paths being more clearly laid out in Conan Exiles than it is in ARK, it is also much more satisfying. Conan Exiles is more difficult than ARK and the progression is slower, but that leads to the feeling of leveling up being far more satisfying.
+I would say the building and crafting system is better than what is in ARK: A) You can craft while you move/do other things without your movement being slowed or any other penalties. B) Repairing Tools is as easy as having the materials in your inventory and hitting the hotkey assigned to the broken tool (No wait required: It instantly repairs it) C) Buildings seem to snap to the environment far more easily than they do in other games, along with you being able to be more creative with buildings than you would in ARK. D) Being able to craft walls while I place them is also great. For example, if I have no walls in my inventory but I had a hotkey assigned to walls, it will automatically begin to craft them (assuming I have the materials) when I hit that hotkey (and as earlier, it will not slow me down or otherwise penalize me for doing so).
However, that is about all the game does well right now.
-As said near the beginning of the review, you will lag and rubberband. Alot. Especially if you are on a server of 30+ people.
-The combat is really nothing special right now. I mean this with lag/performance aside, it just is really nothing special. It has about the same amount of depth and complexity to it as Minecraft does, which is not an impressive feat at all. For example, Reign of Kings, for all the hate that it got/gets, had a good combat system. At least, better than anything Conan Exiles has right now.
-The AI is pretty bad, and often enemies will stare at you while you beat on them.
-Enemies of different types seem to ignore eachother for the most part. It's not uncommon for you to run through an area and have various enemies of different types chasing you without caring about eachother, even if it doesn't make sense for a Hyena to ignore a group of Exiles and chase you alongside them. Another example of enemies randomly ignoring eachother, and something I encountered alot was the unholy alliance of Hyenas and Spiders, working in tandam to make me ragequit the game. They spawn very quickly and in large numbers, have high aggro ranges, and have perfect synergy.  The Crippling Poison that Spiders have (which they spit at you from a range, which also stacks with each hit) in combination with Cripple that Hyenas apply with each hit actually ROOTS you, because Crippling Poision and Cripple are different stacking effects apparently.
-The progression, while satisfying, can be very weird and frustrating at times. One of the main sources of weirdness is the recipes that cost multiple points but are essentially bundles of recipes. For example, one of the most basic things you need in a survival game is a house. The most basic needs for this are basically all bundled into one recipe that costs a few points called "Stone Masonry" (or something like that), and it has Foundation, Walls, Ceiling, and a Doorframe. However, it does not include Windows, Stairs, Slanted roofs/foundations, and other things, which must be acquired individually and all cost valuable points to get. Another weird recipe is "Journeyman Craftsman" with most of the recipes being gated behind it, meaning you basically HAVE to get it. However, to get Journeyman Craftsman, you need to learn how to make a Furnace, a Tannery, and a Carpenter's bench, which all take 3 points (or basically an entire level) each. While this is not a big deal from a solo player's view point, it can be frustrating when playing as a group and trying to spread out who knows which recipes.

I am recommending this game as I personally like it. I will give my reader a huge
before purchasing : the game play isn't super immerse, it's more the genre of the game. The controls/abilities are a bit limited. The game itself, however is comparable to a beautiful painting.
Murdered : Soul Suspect follows a detective who was pushed out of a window and then shot repeatedly as he was trying to get up. The (bell tower) killer is an unknown assailant who has been attacking random individuals. After being shot, the detective is now a ghost and has to figure out why he's still roaming the Earth and hasn't passed on.
You are in third person view of Ronan (the detective) and have identical controls/movements (not actions though) to Hitman Absolution. What is probably the most outstanding feature in the game is the fact you can walk through walls. Of course, you cannot walk through any wall you wish. This will be made obvious with a solid white fill on a few walls or other "ghostly" objects will appear that will not let you pass. None the less, something completely different I have never been able to do in any game I've played yet. The combat is quite minimal. I should add if you are looking for a cop fighting action game, this isn't it. The most you'll be able to do is pull lost souls from demons that roam nearby areas. Demons are to be approached from behind when they cannot see you and soul extraction happens when you press RT. Again, not much to it but there is a rush associated with it. If you are seen, you will be chased and killed. You may hide in "ghost remnants" (small ghost cracks in levels) and can fast travel to each one in an attempt to evade the demon. There will be other obstacles in your way such as demon traps in which you require to possess a person while they walk across it. Being a ghost, you are able to possess literally anyone. NPC's will have general thoughts you can read while certain characters (usually for missions), you're able to "peek" (see what they're seeing) or "influence" (use a clue to job their memory in an attempt to force an action). They made jumping/possessing person to person quite easy to do. The game even goes as far as allowing you to posses a cat (with a purpose of course). Over time you will acquire new skills such as teleportation, poltergeist (setting a printer or phone off) and detect mode which lets you see through walls. You may also run in game but you do not have the ability to crouch or jump. Most of the time you will be free roaming until you come across a crime scene. Once in investigation mode, you will be looking around for clues and sometimes need to hit RT to reveal the complete evidence. Often times than not, you will need to find certain clues in order to find other clues (meaning intervention or possessing others to get a complete answer). Once you think you've found enough, you can conclude your investigation with the clues you've found. The game basically follows one crime scene to another and in between there are small side quests. Doesn't really sound appealing (which I'm sure is why people don't like the game) but it appealed to this extremely picky gamer.
The visuals are pretty good (not super fantastic but good). I have an AMD card and have tried to get more than 30 FPS. The graphics really resemble those of Hitman Absolution. They do have a lot of symbols and ghost writing that does pop up which enriches the environment. The sounds are suitable to the environment the game provides. It's not super over the top but I would assume it's hard to imagine what a demon would sound like.
Overall, I enjoyed the game. I think it's cool to play through but leaves the player with no replayability. I got this game on extreme sale in a bundle. I would say it was worth it for what I paid. I would highly recommend people do their homework before buying such a game. I like to play it, you may not due to it's lack of actual gameplay activity.
RATING : 7/10

I loved Disgaea when it was on PS2. That probably had more to do with my age and environment than anything, but... actually, I should start from the beginning.
Disgaea is a strategy-rpg from an era in which the market wasn't flooded with them. It was originally on the PS2 console, standing out among very few other titles of its time as a "niche" genre, and it came with a story that satirized anime and RPGs in general. You play as Prince Laharl, heir to the throne of The Netherworld who has just awakened from a two-year nap to find out that his father is dead and any of the vassals who aren't completely lazy have just up and split without a word. It is a story of betrayal, rampant theft of lesser demons' fortunes, mockery and defamation, and all the other fun stuff a childish cartoon character can get away with.
It is also a story partially told in an annoying high-pitched voice or three, which is one of the things that got me to never watch very much anime. I do love a good spoof movie though, and Disgaea fleshes out its characters a bit more than what I've come to expect from video games. But that might just be because video games since Disgaea's publishing just don't have a protagonist that isn't a blank slate very often.
There are countless ways to achieve an objective in a given battle. You might want to just murderize everything as quickly as possible, or chain up combos for bonus points, or destroy the coloured terrain for bonus points / damage potential, or just move on to the next floor without another thought. In Disgaea, you have *options.* Swords are the game-favoured option because this is an RPG, but axes get some much-needed love as well. But, with all the good things Disgaea has to offer, there are just as many things to make me hate it.
The repetition is painful. You're going to hear the same voice-clips every time a character attacks or uses a skill. When you use a skill, you're going to see the same lengthy animation that might cause slowdown depending on the particle effects. And then, just to make things as over-the-top and nonsensical as the story, the grind from one level to the next is obscene.
As a player, you are generally expected to be able to field ten units to a battle. But, you start under-equipped and the amount of kills needed to recruit units that aren't garbage-tier to fill party vacancies borders on ridiculous. And as your units get stronger, they unlock new character classes (which must also start at first level). And as you progress through the story, your party will need fresh (expensive) equipment upgrades.
Constantly.
As entertaining as the story is (and it gets a few genuine chuckles here and there), the story grinds to a halt every now and then because your party needs to catch up to the new enemies in terms of power.
And is it a decade after I first played this that I realize that this was the prototype model for "casual gaming." Sure, you might think you're hardcore because you've sunk in enough time to defeat the secret bosses and collect all the achievements, but at its core Disgaea is a game meant to be played casually. Battles only take a few minutes to get through, and you can save and heal up after each one. The story ties everything together to legitimize the game itself, but progressing through the story requires time spent slogging through maps you've already cleared for EXP. It's unnecessarily padded out, and even then it's more than plausible to finish the game at lvl 100. The secret content requires characters with several thousand levels under their belt though.
In the Steam version, you get Pleinair as soon as you start the game. She comes with a decent accessory and a weapon that costs roughly 2,000 (currency), and has a boost to her HIT and SPD stats that will make people who play the game drool. Also, bunny-bombs. Neat little addition.
Also, Etna has a new voice! Just in case Flonne's squealing wasn't annoying enough, now you have a pre-teen trying to be an edgy demon-girl instead of an actor who understood subtlety... but maybe subtlety didn't fit the theme of Disgaea? Somehow the Japanese voice-acting is less screechy, but I've yet to reach The Humans on this version.
Etna's story mode is also interesting, but the grind is not only worse but punctuated by starting at first level with only a few prinnies as backup. The story is shorter but the level advancement covers a much broader gap.
And then, just to screw with anyone who might want a go for nostalgia's sake, they took out that silly J-rock track that played in the original's fight with Maderas. I know it was a cheesy track, but it was good cheese.
But nostalgia's bad for you. Sometimes you gotta learn that lesson the hard way.

First of all I'd like to say all the reviews saying it's pay to win are completely exaggerated and more of, Over the top.
Also I'd like to point out I have more hours into this game than it says on steam. I was running the standalone but it's bugged a bit with windows 10 so I installed the steam version.
The game at first seems a bit standard normal mmorpg not entierly sure what you're doing or where you go. Boring quests at first but as you get a little farther into the game around level 20 or 30 things start to pick up. You get dropped into pvp zones where you can.
A. Kill people in your own faction
B. Get killed by people on the other faction
People complaining about the fact that they drop you in pvp zones is absolutely asanine. Plenty of mmo's do this. WORLD OF WARCRAFT is a prime example. A game that has lasted many many years and is still going to this day.
It's very easy to avoid fights. For example maybe glide away when you see a red name. Or... If you think you could handle it try and attack them! even if you're 9 or 10 levels below the player YOU COULD STILL WIN This game is heavily skillbased and is not 100% dependant on stats and gear. Those help but you can still do damage to someone significantly higher level than you.
Lets get into the "Pay to win" aspect. Not once have I seen something remotely close to be even called "Pay to win"
The only thing I've ever seen in the marketplace is workers compensation potions (Potions that restore labor) FUN FACT YOU CAN FIND THESE WITHOUT BUYING THEM. No one is seriously going to drop their damn money CONSTANTLY on a game just to get some labor. That's wasteful. You could easily buy patron and get a subscription to pay monthly OR stay free to play and leave it on overnight to gain labor. Once again I'd like to point out you CAN play this game free to play but if you want the FULL expirience. Buy patron. free to play is basically somewhat of a trial or demo. Not all the features are unlocked. Hey at least this game lets you play for free. World of warcraft MAKES you pay a subscription to even GET in the game.
Most of the "Gear" that you think is pay to win. Is usually gear that people have EARNED in game I haven't got that far but I havent seen anything in the marketplace relating to any kind of overpowered gear. I'm fairly certain you need to earn it with honor points. People EARNED this gear. Stop ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the game because you're getting rek't.
Now onto the mob's
The mobs are difficult later on. Around level 40+ it becomes VERY hard to solo things. But it is possible with a little skill and planning. It's not difficult in the sense that it's unfair. If you're not killing the mobs later on. It's because you are not playing the game right. Formulate a stratagy and learn how combos work, Learn how your class works, And don't just pick darkrunner because you googled "Whats the best class in archeage" and then follow some outdated guide to put your skills into. Pick one thats best for you. Because there is not just one skill rotation you can do. It varies depending on the situation. You have to think quickly otherwise you could mess everything up and leave yourself extremely vulnerable and possibly draw your last breath.

Bots.

This game is beautiful.
The controls are tight and responsive, even in flight where you'd expect them to be floaty. The story is great, even though some specific parts can be a little predictable (One specific part follows an overused action movie cliché that can be seen coming from miles away.) The soundtrack and pixel art is
and doesn't try for a nostalgia grab at all. The music isn't chiptune, and the color palette isn't restricted to a short, specific range of colors to emulate the NES, SNES, or SEGA Genesis art/sound styles. The music sounds like a full orchestra, and the art is about as detailed as pixel art can get. The game also runs at a constant frame rate of 60fps with little to no frame drops.
The gameplay is really unique, and there's really only one thing that I can compare it to.
Remember when you were really young and wanted to play "Sonic 3" with your older brother, but got stuck playing as Tails because that's who player 2 controls? Remember how Tails was actually really useful to control because he can fly and carry Sonic around to hard to reach areas? That's right, you're pretty much playing as Tails carrying your friends around, but this time
player one, you make the decisions now. When you're carrying any one of three companions, the game goes from a scrolling platformer to a twin-stick shooter with puzzle-platformer aspects. It really is a lot more fun than just being able to ferry the real protagonist around.
The characters are all very diverse, and though the trope of "silent protagonist" is there, its part of the character. Most games that follow that trope do so to help the player put their own personality onto the character they are controlling. In this game, Otus (playable character) is mute, and other characters comment on this. Instead of Otus' personality being expressed through dialogue, it is shown through his expressions and animations. Throughout the game, Otus will show his reactions to getting bullied with a saddened expression. He'll react to his teacher and father figure downright hating him for being such a disappointment at everything by crouching a little and covering his ear-slits (because he's an owl) with his hands to try to block out what's being said. When he drinks something that raises his max HP, he'll stand stock-still, stiff as a board with a wide eyed, surprised expression. At the end of the game is the only time we ever see him take on an angry/determined expression, but its easily identifiable.
The only gripe I have with this game is the price. I mean, I would have spent $25-$30 anyways so I could get the soundtrack, but $25 for the base game is a little steep. I don't regret spending the money at all, though. I'm not trying to justify the price by saying "I enjoyed it, so the price is worth it to everyone, anyone who disagrees can go to Hell." The price is a bit too high, and that
be a turn-off for some people.

Midnight Club 2, where to start with...
I've had this game on PS2, so that's old. Yeah, old, but frankly it's a jewel.
In terms of challenge, MC2 is quite a hard game. The "story" mode, featuring characters who incarnate clichees from the whole world, inside the street racing universe, will get you to face opponents in the middle of the traffic, following absolutely insane tracks. MC2 doesn't work with straight roads, instead you have to follow checkpoints which actually makes the track. Some races are even "freeways", which means you can pass the points in any order (and those will need more training to get out of them victorious, particularly near the end). Now one thing I loved was that every car has its own handling. You will feel a difference between each car you drive, that it be in speed, acceleration, handling, drift or even weight (I insist on this one, since sometimes the AIs can be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. I'm looking at you, Haley.) But the feeling of reward once you beat a racer has for only simbling the feeling when you beat a boss in Dark Souls. The police might also come during certain races, but other than just trying to get in your way while ordering you to pull over with a distinctive accent depending on which city you race, they don't do too much.
In terms of fun, MC2 has everything you need. Speed down the streets of Paris, Los Angeles and Tokyo at up to 402 km/h, driving from busy main streets to the catacombs of Paris, jumping over the Seine or drifting near the castle of the emperor; those things you can do, either in races or in cruising mode. Because yes, there is a freeroaming mode in which you can just drive freely wherever you want, traffic or not. You can even create races by placing checkpoints and play them with AIs! If it wasn't that fun enough, there's even a mode wherein you can activate items. You know, those Mario kart-ish things where you gain power-ups like machinegun, rockets and whatnot. Or you can just type savethekids in the cheat section to gain a machinegun on the light button as well as rockets on the honk command - unless they changed the codes on PC, I have no idea about that.
In terms of optimization, I've seen some complaints but for me, the game runs perfectly. However, I would strongly recommend a pad to play it. I had no problem playing with a xbox360 gamepad, and each control can be binded by the game menu (whatever some reviews said, this worked perfectly for me.)
So yeah. MC2 is a must have for anyone who's fond of racing game. So go ahead and keep racing, shrimp!

A really good strategy game for anyone that doesn't mind a serious challenge. To be blunt, you will struggle. You will die unexpectedly, at the worst possible time. Your heir apparent with all the right stats will get knocked over the head in battle and become a useless vegetable. His four year old heir will be completely useless and all of your relatives that were your strongest assets only a few minutes before will suddenly become pretenders intent on breaking apart your meager holdings while a pagan uprising obliterates your armies. Days' worth of work reduced to nothing in a matter of minutes.
But this is what makes the game endearing. While the odds of guiding a lowly count to the throne of France or uniting the empire of Brittania from a single county are somewhere between astronomical and nonexistant, this makes your victories feel like accomplishments in a way that most games just can't manage. Because when you do manage to beat the odds, assassinate your rival claimant, marry the daughter of your powerful neighbour, use your new ally to beat down the rebels and maybe even snap up that upstart kingdom on your border, you finally heave a sigh of relief. You look around. Realize there are no more fires to put out. And feel like your the greatest ruler in history.
And then you fall over dead and your powerful neighbour is laying claim on your lands... But its just one more round of hurdles to be overcome. Its a game of overcoming long odds, rolling with the punches, and eventually... going down swinging.

When I first saw Valkyria Chronicles on the Ps3, I remember thinking how lovely the artwork was. I remember passing this many times when I went into the shop, telling myself one day I would buy this game, often picking it up and just re examining the cover and blurb at the back, as I did with all games I considered bringing into my collection at some point.
A fun combo of the Sakura Wars series, Fire Emblem mercilessness, Skies of Arcadia and third person element gameplay – Valkyria Chronicles delivers to its audience a refreshing experience and take on RPG action – and even spawned an Anime based on the game.
For lovers of emotional, involving story games, Valkyria Chronicles will not disappoint. With many allusions to the second world war, your main character and his forces start off in a tiny nation known as Gallia. As much as this nation would like to remain neutral in the erupting war between two superpowers around them –  because Gallia is rich in the precious mineral that sparked the war in the first place –  it gets invaded by the main antagonist nation: the East European Imperial Alliance.
Through the exploits of Squad 7, you will follow an well constructed emotional story that hints to darker elements of history.
The Gameplay is a nice spin on normal tactical elements. The system used is referred to as BLiTZ, or Battle of Live Tactical Zones. Once you've gotten past the cut scenes you control a set amount of troops on the field, each with different abilities. You get to select your own troops in the recruiting menu. Each individual troop has strengths and weaknesses which add a nice personal element to the game, as you will actually end up being attached to some of your troops, despite their minor impact on the main story. In your Action Phase, where you can control the troops on the field, they have a movement phase and targeting phase. Your movement is determined by your AP (Action Point) Gauge. Once it runs out, the unit will no longer be able to move. So you will spend your precious AP trying to position your units in the best way possible, and take out the most targets. Positioning is absolutely vital because after you've finished moving all your troops, the enemy gets to do the same in return. So an out of position troop could get out maneuvered and targeted by several enemy units, and die because it was too far isolated, or unable to receive supporting fire from your nearby troops due to a bad location. Surveying the terrain and deciding which unit is best placed where will work to your advantage. You have: Scouts who are able to move very far, but are weak and lacking fire power. Shocktroopers who have less movement but more damage. Lancers who are slow, but can take hits and deal chunks of damage to tanks. Snipers who are also limited in movement, but have long range and can nitpick targets from towers. You also have tanks which are devastating to infantry and can knock down walls, but can't roll over certain terrain and have restricted controls. Engineers who can repair damage, barricades, disarm traps and replenish ammunition. These are just a few of the units mentioned.
Although the system is turn based, it does require a lot of forethought in what you do with your turn. The bad thing about the third person camera viewpoint is that even what should be dead accurate shots can miss, due to the awkward angles it can sometimes present the character in. I personally really like the tactical elements behind this – especially as wrong mistakes will punish you in permanent unit death, like Fire Emblem.
That's right. Start resetting those levels every time you lose someone you like. (Unless you play with a heart of iron and accept each unit death that occurs.) I don't have a heart of iron. So resets did indeed occur. :(
Graphics wise, I love the animations. Cel shaded games can be a bit hit and miss in my opinion, but this one has beautiful artwork, smooth and polished graphics with watercolour style backgrounds, with enough detail to keep you moving along. Although they're not stunning, they're well presented.
I find the music of the game great. There are sad melodic piano tracks, uplifting battle themes and tense tunes in moments of great strife. I loved sitting around and listening to certain tracks loop, because they were so well crafted. The voice acting isn't particularly memorable in my opinion, but bearable and good enough for what we're presented with. You have the option (At  least on my U.K version) to have it both with the English voice actors or the Japanese voice actors. I actually did it with the Japanese voice actors.
Honestly, I loved this game. I would happily recommend it to anyone that I could, especially as it combines the best of both worlds – a strong story, characters you become attached to, and an innovative battle system that will have you planning out your moves as best as you can, sometimes with the odds horrifically stacked against you.
Definitely get. Like, seriously. What are you waiting for?

I really wanted to like this game, and be able to recommend it, but unfortunately I did not and cannot. For everything I liked, there was a flaw holding it back.
I loved the art style, and it made for beautiful scenes. Unfortunately, the character design clashed with the descriptions of the characters. The characters appeared 12, yet their actions and activities put them in their late teens, and the school teacher looked the same age as the students.
I loved the writing style. Unfortunately, there was also too much writing with too little purpose. There were long sections of text that failed to advance the plot, develop the characters, or provide interesting interactions, and instead seemed like prose for the sake of prose, meandiring off into the land of self-satisfaction while the story was left to languish. So while I liked the writing style, I was left feeling bored more often than not.

The story starts off really... meh. But in the later parts your more eager to find out what's really going on. The story is intriguing, but there's not alot of growth between the characters. They stay the same thoughout the story regardless of choices. As a result the dialogue can get abit boring and you just skip ahead to see the secrets.
Pros:
-Clear choices that influence the story.
-The story reminded me alot of the great sci-fi series Space Above and Beyond.
-Lots of interesting twists, intrigue, and 2nd guessing yourself.
-Story was a good length.
-Fair character design. My character felt like the one I wanted to play, had realistic flaws.
-Lloyd, the ship's A.I. I would love to see another story with Lloyd.
-Don't have to remember what's going on, clearly reminds you what the mission is.
Cons:
-Most of the characters are pretty static, don't get opportunity to change their POV.
-Didn't like how you earn credits, but can't spend them in game. It's an end game score.
-Didn't feel very invested in the story. There's high stakes, but not at the personal level.
Final Verdict:
-I'd only get it on sale.

Where do I start... This game was great. I say "was" considering I haven't played for months, perhaps a year. The last time I played Elsword was during the final 3rd class release events and the time I decided that the community and structure of the game was at it's most unstable. Apparently I was wrong. I liked the game, I really did, but honestly, I feel the updates come way too fast to earn any event prizes. I admire their attempts at bringing old players back to the game, but the rewards don't feel like a "welcome back" gift and more of a"Come back and we'll give you things". In the old days, Elsword had a skill system where players could choose to equip any skill out of an entire tree, that includes the hyperactive. Since then they changed it approximately thrice now; in one version, the original tree was revamped so instead of dedication sp to the skill to level it up in bundles, you had to level them up one-by-one as well as there being a passive-skill tree seperated from the rest, second and third versions being the ones available today. Something that hasn't change was the pay-to-look-pretty-and-still-somehow-be-better-than-everybody-else system. Ah memories, when people who took pride in their wallet dumped it into the game to get absurd amounts of magic stones to attribute their equipment with top of the line perks. The PVP is always the same though, you end up fighting another player within your rank or level range and get completely overwhelmed because of their dexterity. To those who want to play this, don't play a PVP mode. The ranking and matchmaking system is as skewed as WarThunders'. PVE is as equally skewed, but with the players being on the same side. Since I began playing this game, I admire KoG for implimenting the individual item drop thing, but alot of the game is repetetive. Scroll right, scroll left, kill everything, move on. I used to feel alot of competetition playing in PVE like I felt in PVP because everybdyo went straight for the mobs and ythen moved on. Yada Yada Yada.
tl;dr: I used to like this game when I started out, but as the game developed, it lost that special something that hooked me in the first place. PVP sucks, PVE sucks because everybody kills something before you do, it's repetitive, Everything in the Premim+Casual market is overpriced, the updates keep changing the game that it's hard to keep up. I don't recommend it for people thinking they want to return to the game, but I do recommend it for first time players, just don't PVP..

*Note* I did not play Metro 2033, i went directly to Last Light as of writing this review.
+ Every level is so extremely detailed and visually stunning from beginning to end. This is one of the best looking first person shooters I've seen.
+ The Gameplay is a ton of fun. It's a great variety of stealth and shooting segments, and each level is unique to the last.
+ Very atmospheric and emmersive sounds, weather effects, lighting, and so fourth that really bring the game to life
+ Horror elements as you go through Spider infested catacombs, and dens full of oversized mutated creatures
+ Survival elements as you will be constantly low on ammo searching every body and every dead end for more as you desperately try to conserve as much as possible. (Bullets are also currency, so  saving ammo is critical)
+ Story driven with a lot of surprises which are very entertaining
+ Extremely intelligent AI.  This is one of the few games where I really felt like the AI was intelligent. The stealth segments especially felt amazing because it really felt like the enemies were alive, and you could sense what they could and could not see or hear. It was really something incredible. All the nemies in the game also don't run straight at you, they actually flank, use cover, and react to your movements
+ Nice variety of weapons which you can upgrade. (Loved seeing a Quad barrel Shotgun)
+ Bonus Content / DLC which actually provide A LOT of extra content and are a ton of fun! I believe there's 9 fully fleshed out extra levels, some that include missions where you play as other characters, while others are unique challenge stages with a lot of depth.
+ A handful of boss encounters which will have you on the edge of your seat
+ Plenty of Content, expect to spend ~ 8 hours on the campaign, and an addional 2-3 hours on the bous levels.
- The FOV is locked (at 60 I believe) which made me feel a bit sick at times
- The story is a bit all over the place at times. It reminded me a bit of Call of Duty, where one mission ends, and then suddenly you are in a completely different area.
- Having not played Metro 2033, it was a bit hard to grasp all the factions or groups in the game. There's The Order, the Red Line (Soviets), The Fourth Reich (Nazi's), The Dark Ones, and a number of other smaller groups.

Choice of the Star Captain is short in that it can be completed in just a few hours, depending on how fast you read. In terms of replayability, it mainly divulges into two distinct paths, pacifistic or bloodthirsty. The main theme that the story revolves over is contact with a spacefaring species and the ending practically allows you to decide what happens: humanity wins, the aliens win, or an uneasy but prolonged peace is found. Uniquely, CotSC actually has no romantic aspect of its relationships. The most important character interaction you'll make, however, is with your ships AI, Lloyd. So, the breakdown, considering the price, length of the story, it's quality and characters, all based on my opinions:
Grammar and Vocabulary: 5/5 - mostly due to having no noticeable errors
Story: 4/5 - considering the price, I think it's modestly long enough and it does explore human nature mixed with the concept of contact with another intelligent species though the length restricts it from going to deep our exploring other ideas like Human-AI interaction.
Characters: 3/5 - characters remain static due to the length of the plot but interactions with Salazar, Nagoop and Lloyd remain probably the most central of the interactions while Lloyd's interaction with you serve to be the only thing to grow (or shrink) in terms of how you react to his less than polite banter.
Replayability 3/5 - not too bad, not too good; for its length, you can probably squeeze three-fourths of a day from the choices and endings.
Overall Score: Meh

Here are some tips:
>Save spam.
>Use 2 rifleman 1 machine gunner in one squad and create two of them, with one supporting the other while it advances.
>Use stealth when you can, entire enemy entrenchments can be eliminated without firing a shot if you go behind the enemy and melee them.
>When encountering tanks, shoot at it with any weapon, retreat to a covered position and use your AT granades.If the tank is out of range flank it with another soldier.
>Special weapons such as Panzershrecks ,K98 snipers and MP 44's can be found on some enemy soldiers throughout the game. Take these and use them to your advantage.
>60% of the time your units will encounter entrenched enemies clustered together, take them out by lobbing in some grenades, grenades in this game have an extended range when compared to MOW:AS.
>The enemy is in a building and you cant hit him? take an AT granade throw it under him to collapse the building.
>Rockets, bombs, barrels of fuel and tank shells (such as ones found on planes, in crates or in destroyed tanks) can be used to make a trap for the enemy and create a big boom.

Ah, Fable. This one is another case where it could've had potential to be one of the biggest names in the gaming community (more or less), but since the developer went all crazy (Peter Molyneaux, in this case) it pretty much lost its wonder once the sequels got released. Now, while I did have a fun time with 2 and had an..... experience with 3, I won't be comparing TLC to those games, and instead just judge this game on its own merits. With that out of the way, let me start of with what the game does right:

+ While the story itself is cliched, everything else about the game has charm, and a fun sense of humor into it, as well as having a balance of being serious and just being laidback.
+ Combat is pretty fun. Standard hack n' slash action with your one-handed and two-handed weapons for your Strength attack, archery combat with bows and crossbows for Skill, and a nice array of spells in the Magic session. Not only that, but each attack from the three aspects will net you experience points in that respective area, while killing an enemy will give you general experience. While it can get repetitive at times, I still think the game's combat does well enough so that it doesn't get infuriating or annoying.
+ Even with the techincal issues (more on that later), I still think the environment themselves can get good-looking and even a bit atmospheric at times, though that's probably because it's accompanied by a relaxing OST.
- Might as well adress this now - this game has definitely shown some age. Not only are there issues with character models and textures, but sometimes even particle effects or simple glitches can pop up every now and then. There was one instance where it pretty much showed a glimpse of a boss.... before I was even able to activate the fight.
- The story and the choices in it honestly doesn't really change much, from beginning to end. Every single choice you make in it (besides maybe the endgame one) will just change one minor element in the game's world, that's it.
- The game is way too easy. Even without the use of exploits, it didn't take me long to get some of the strongest items and equipment in the game, more gold than you know what to do with, and make some my spells maxed out so that I can end fights with ease. I think the only time I ever got some sort of trouble was at the final boss, but even then I was able to readjust myself easily.
- There isn't really much to do after finishing the game. Sure, you got your sidequests, Silver Keys, and Demon Doors, but you'll more than likely finish up almost all of the side quests just by going through the game naturally, I never really found a reason to collect the Silver Keys (though someone else might, admittedly), and I found that, outside of a few occurances, most Demon Doors are not worth opening at all.
Even with the flaws and exploits, I still give this game my Recommendation. Maybe it's because I still have nostalgia from when I played this game religously when I was 6, but I still think there's enough charm and merit to this game that most can enjoy from it. While you can beat the game in a weekend, there's still (more or less) enough content to warrent an immediate replay session.

TL;DR Great Game, Buy it without a doubt.
I bought this game for the xbox when I was a kid and loved it. Ended up getting it for the 360 years later and the game was once again fresh and fun to play, especially as I have gotten older I began to notice there are alot of low key jokes and crude humour placed throughout the game that I had not realised when I was just a young lad.
So once again...years later I bought it for the PC and here I am going through the game AGAIN and I'm still not tired of it.
Gameplay is really good, the combat mechanics are pretty basic but it makes the game enjoyable as you will find yourself fighting ALOT further into the game and if it was a long drawn out affair then it would probably make the game pretty dull. The game also focuses around your alignment which is Good and Evil in this case, both sides have certain magic attacks and perks that go along with it. I found that achieving Good status has a bit of a challenge earlier on but once you are steady on that path then the game begins to flush itself out regarding two sided quests (for example you can attack a village or defend it, depending on which quest you take will give you good or evil points) and by no means are you weaker or anything in late game stages.
Side note: Your character also changes their physical appearance as you gain more alignment. So good characters get light skin, white hair, bright blue eyes and will eventually have a halo that forms above your head. Evil characters get black eyes, pale veiny skin, Devil horns, and flies will float around your character.
Evil is pretty easy to achieve and also makes the game pretty fun, You basically have complete freedom throughout the game to do whatever you want however there are always consequences to your actions so keep that in mind. Also once you because very evil then villagers will begin to fear you which can negatively effect things such as store prices on items however you can counter this little speed bump by upgrading your "Guile" which enables you to haggle and trade more efficiently.
As I stated above you also have a fairly large amount of upgrades you can give your character. They are divided up into three main categories Strength, Skill, and Will.
-Strength covers things like Health, ability to deal damage and ability to take damage. All of these have a passive effect on your character as well, making the hero larger and bulkier over time  which gives a physical view of how your hero is progressing.
-Skill covers Speed, Accuracy and Guile. Speed is how fast you can attack or pull a bow, Accuracy is well...accuracy, and Guile covers two aspects. First it enables you to sneak around better so if you are a theif then this is something you'll want to upgrade alot and eventually you can learn things such as lockpicking etc. Secondly it effects how you trade goods with villagers, so as you upgrade Guile prices drop lower (I have potions that started over $100 and are now $17 to give you an idea of how strong this skill is) and they also allow you to sell goods at higher prices meaning if you are smart you can make a good bit of coin just by buying something in one place and selling it at another. Shops will also provide a list of items that are "wanted" so keep an eye on those as that's where you can make even more coin by feeding a demand in a village.
-Will is magic in Fable. There are a ton of magic spells to choose from and upgrade so I won't go into too much detail but basically you have spells that are good for attacking (Lightning, Fireballs etc.) there are spells for defense (Summoning dead soldiers, Personal shields) and quite a few more that can be quite useful depending on your character build.
There is not a huge selection of weapons but just enough to keep things interesting. You'll have light weapons (katana, sword, cleaver) and heavy weapons (Warhammers, axes, etc.) and they all have pros and cons. Light weapons deal less damage but can attack quickly whereas heavy weapons are slow attacking but deal greater damage. The main difference comes in the quality of weapons so even though there are only a handful to choose from, they come in multiple stages and with the right amount of coin you can buy a very deadly weapon (My greatsword kills almost all foes in two hits) and you can also augment your weapons giving them even more lethal or stronger towards certain foes (Silver augment causes more damage to Balvarines and undead for example)
Clothing is pretty diverse, you have neutral armor, good and evil armor and they come in many stages and look drastically different. They also offer regular clothing for assassins, spell casters, bandits and most clothing that is specific such as this will give extra bonuses to your class of hero.
There are a few more extras in the game, Pub Games, You can buy and rent houses, trading with stores, Mini games, Fishing and digging up treasure, and you can even visit a brothel and "hang out" with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s!
Overall this is a great game and there is alot to keep you interested. The story line is decent for how old the game is and the graphics are also not bad for it's age. If you like RPG's definitely get it but this is not to say that this game only appeals to those kinds of people. Just about anyone will enjoy this one and it is definitely a classic and a must have in your library.

Fun game so far. Not finished but:
Combat might or might not get deeper than it is - counter/reflect projectiles, dodge roll, stun, and combo multipliers.
In many encounters the difficulty seems to be mainly from managing both the actual enemies and the arena itself which can be laden down with traps. Even at the start I find it taxing to manage both, but the game doesn't seem to expect you to be able to come out unscathed. The other part of the difficulty is managing resources as you move through grid dungeons.
The story itself is deliberately vague so far, it fits the setting and the delivery from the deckmaster really sells it. The game might be hinting at a deeper story involving the character's past, or it might just be dressing for the nature of the game, it's hard to tell. I'd condiser it a bonus if there's a payoff, but what's already here definitely nails the atmosphere.
I'd say the atmosphere is definitely the game's strong suit, and the developers did a really good job with the little details such as using expanding lighting on load, sound effects for things like the opening of the token bowl and dropping of items. The game also knows its exact limits in terms of graphics and animation, and utilizes those things very well.
If I have a complaint so far it's mainly just that the use of the game world load for merchant visits is a little bit pointless, though the location and appearance of the shop does change with respect to what kind of shop it is and (I'm guessing) what kind of dungeon you are running.
All in all an excellent game especially at the sale price.

I've only played a bit so far, but before the sale is over I wanted to get this out.  It's really a neat idea for a game, and I'm having a blast with it.
It's basically a procedurally generated game, but procedural generation is affected by a deck you put together and the AI puts together.  It plays out like a board game, where each card is a space you can move to.  Each game has several of these cars laid out.  Somewhere towards the end of this trail of cards is a boss to slay.  Each time you move. the card you land on is revealed.  You may have a choice to make, an oppurtunity to shop with gold, or end up fighting.  Combat will cause the cards to create a small arena and an opponent or opponents for you to fight.  Combat is simplistic, attack, stun, counter, or dodge.  It works though, and the enemies look cool.  Love the slow-mo effect on the finishing blow to the last enemy.  Speaking of face-crunching weapons, those come from cards as well, as do food and gold.  These are drawn whenever you receive items from a encounter card, or on display at the various shop cards.  Food is expended when you move your piece.
The narrator you play with has a lot of character, as someone else has pointed out.  I was genuinely enjoying listening to his commentary on my choices and the cards on the table.  His presence really makes you feel like you sat down to play a game with him.  Occasionally he'll tempt you into undertaking a card's challenge by offering you a token that will unlock other cards for your deck.  I can see this getting me killed eventually, but they are so shiny...
The variety in the cards from the get go is interesting.  Without spoiling anything (half the fun is in the suprise I think), I was suprised my many of the encounters.  They can be very creative, especially the ones that require decisions.
I've killed two bosses thus far, and if I didn't have real life stuff to do I'd be up for a while with this.
Long story short, the atmosphere and suprise in the game are amazing.  It's like sitting down and playing a board or card game, but being teleported into a fantasy location for combat.  It is absolutely worth the sale price if you think you would enjoy playing a mysterious game of cards with a good beat down session every thirty seconds or so.

I'm a sad man. I'm late-40s and I still like cute things. I also love RPGs, so you can see why I looked at Recettear and liked the look of it.
The game wasn't quite what I thought it was though.... but in a good way. I was pleasantly surprised.
You'd probably be forgiven for thinking as I did - this is a typical JRPG with the theme being centred somehow around a shop. Well, yes it is... and it isn't. The game essentially has two parts to it. The RPG part takes the form of a fairly typical top-down dungeon crawler a la Chocobo's Dungeon, Pokemon Mystery Dungeon and a host of other similar ones. That's about as standard as it gets though.
Recettear does things rather differently - you are a young girl who has inherited her father's item shop which serves the local townsfolk with equipment for their day-to-day use and more importantly, stuff to go a-dungeon-crawling with. You also have a guardian of sorts (who also turns out to be a debt collector too) who's a fairy. Well, this is a Japanese game - 'nuff said. The relevance of this is that Recette (you) have also inherted some burden of debt too, who naturally you owe to your ward. So, the crux of the game is to run the shop, and earn enough each day to enable you to pay off your monthly debt payment.
I know, that might sound a little boring, but it isn't. It's actually where the game really shines. Your day is divided up into a maximum of 4 sections, which you can "spend" by either visiting town for certain things, visit the adventurer's guild (more on that later), or open the shop. Your shop has certain shelf spaces laid out, and arranging the stock so your best stuff is visible from the window is an essential trick. Put the boring, common and cheap items in the window and you'll attract less passers-by. Put the really expensive stuff in the window and you'll also attract less passers-by. It's a balancing act.
Once customers come in, they'll flit around looking, and approach you with items they want to buy from the shelves. As with any real-world store, the trick is to maximize profit, while retaining custom. So, sell higher than you bought it, but low enough so they don't get annoyed and never return - another balancing act. Some customers will ask for certain special orders in advance, which you almost always never have the stock at the time to fulfil, so you make a gamble on whether you can acquire the stock they're asking for - accept and fail, and they'll get annoyed, but refuse and they'll get annoyed too. You can't please everyone...
So where does the stock come from? This is where the adventurer's guild and the dungeon crawling comes in.
Instead of opening the store, you can toddle off to the adventurer's guild where all the adventurers hang out. You can recruit them, for a fee to go and dungeon crawl with you.  There's a great element of risk/reward here, as at the end of each level, you can choose to duck out with the loot, or proceed onwards with the chance of more and better loot, but with the added risk of costly failure. As Recette, doesn't fight (well, she's only a girl), you take the role of the adventurer here. Her role is to tag along and store your part of the loot.
So, you fight, you level up your adventurers, you gain better loot to sell for better prices, you get money to pay off your increasing debt, and so on.
There's also some added little nuances such as it being wise to look after the adventurers you are hiring by selling them stuff cheap when they visit your store, as they'll use that stuff when crawling the not-so-murky depths. As the game progresses, you'll need to get a bit inventive in how you manage your stock and customers, but I won't elaborate on that as that would be spoiling things!
It's not an easy game to describe, and it probably sounds a bit dry on the face of it, but if you like the straight up old-school action-RPG dungeon crawler, I wouldn't hesitate to grab this - it does that part of it very well, but the light startegy side of shop management and how it dovetails so very, very nicely is what makes this game utterly unique. I can't recommend it highly enough.
So I have no hesitation in saying this is easily worth £15 on my value-for-money scale.

This game is... strange, in a good way.
It's all about running an item shop and crawling through dungeons for items to sell, or ingrediants to make better items. The start is a bit slow and the combat could be better, but it picks up quickly as the days go by. The story of the game is all about you being the daughter of an infamous adventurer who left a massive debt in his name, and you're the only one who can clear it. With the help of the business fairy, Tear, you'll work through a month to pay off the debt... or you'll have to sell your house!
Good things about this game:
+Good music
+Unique theme
+Various items to find and a unique system for equipping your adventurer with items
+Various characters to run through the dungeon with
+Dialog is interesting, if not a little childish due to the age of the main character
+Beating the game, or failing to do so, will allow you to 'restart' with all your items and 'Merchent Level' in tact. This lets you get up in money much faster than you would do so at the start, but you don't keep any of your money or your progress through events.
+Decent end-game content that makes it worth while to try and get what you need
+Haggling is a pretty neat concept, though it takes practice to get it down right.
+Characters are interesting and have their own unique style, in dungeons and just in general.
Bad things about this game:
-Combat could definitely be better, with hit-scan and certain abilities. Some characters are just notably better than others.
-Events are picky. You have to know when you need to go to places in town to get certain chat boxes, which can affect how you get items, characters, or unlock a new location. This causes you to lose a 'block' of time, too, and not all events do anything.
-One girl will come in and sell you something and refuse to buy anything. She'll always refuse to sell at 100% of the item's price, too. 200% is the minimum for her, and there's no way to get rid of her after she appears. You can refuse to buy it, but this messes up your combo and makes you level up slower.
-Getting the 'true card' for characters takes too long. True cards let you use your adventurer without having to find them in the story, which can be helpful for clearing dungeons again. But getting the True Card requires you to beat the game and use that adventurer the most. (More than any other adventurer, that is, for that month.)  To get another one, you have to play the game /again/ and use a different adventurer.
-There's little 'stats' to the game that you can see, at least in my experience. There /are/ stats, but you can't really see them except when your adventurer is buying an item that is better than what they have. You can't even see how much people like you to adjust your prices.
Despite the lengthy part of the 'bad stuff', I really just offered more explanation as to what and why it was bad. This game is still amazing to play, especially if you like dungeon crawlers. The 'bad' things are just my opinion, anyways, and the good things weren't as descriptive because I don't want to spoil anything!

I very rarely post reviews of the games I play because most of the time I stream my gameplay, first-looks and such on Twitch.tv.  But I need to express my adoration of this precious gem!  The characters are extremely well-developed, the story line touching and the game play itself spectacular.  You play the part of Ruh-Set (Recette), a girl in danger of losing her home due to her long-missing adventurer-father's massive debts.  The twist is that you do not just grind away money in dungeons, although that CAN be a part of the game if you so choose, but you manipulate economy and win the hearts of people in the adventure-boom of the growing city of Pensee.  Every playthrough is different (not entirely, but, well-enough).  Dungeons are adaptive and Rogue-Like Randomized, and to think this is a game released long before such elements started to become more popular.  Play control is SUPER-tight.  I mean...tight...like a TIGER, tight!!!  Each playable character (and there are quite a few adventurers whose hearts you win through generosity and honesty) has their own play-style and stats, and even personal gear.
If you love Anime, you will marry this game.  If you love a unique approach to the Zelda: A Link To the Past style adventure and exploration engine, you'll spend hours in the dungeons, trying to decipher the clues hidden from you by your Faerie friend, Tear.  The sense of humor is spectacular.
Do not be deceived, though.  Men act like MEN!  Women act like women!  Robots and ancient constructs act like...well...you'll see!!!  Or will you?!  Not every character comes into play each time through, unless...
Music and sound is wonderful, with lovely voice acting and totally believable fun, antics, character-origins revealed through game-play.

I had really been looking forward to this game... but after completing it, I'm sorry to say that I cannot recommend Recettear. You expect there to be more when really the game is pretty shallow.
The Ragnarok Online-ish graphics got me hooked at the start and I liked the no-nonsense dungeon crawling and the shop aspect.. but there's just not enough here to keep you engaged. Or if there is, the game is not organized in such a way that you can enjoy it without a guide.
First of all, the dungeon crawling gets really repetitive. Fighting doesn't require you to be clever, because you're OP all of the time. After you unlock your fourth and final skill on a character.. you switch to a new one because they just get stale.
Worse, dungeon crawling is actually detrimental to your progress, because you rarely find items worth the hassle, but you lose 2 units of ingame time that you could have spent selling stuff in your shop.
The shop system's got a tutorial that makes you haggle with your customers, although suggesting a price they'll like is the only way to get combo bonuses for selling, which are more useful than the extra buck from high sales prices.
I also found it very, very difficult to survive the debt cycle (someone in the comments even asked "So did anyone survive the first round?"). When you can't pay back your debt on time, it's not a complete gameover, but you start again from the beginning, only you keep the items you have in stock and your merchant level (that gives you access to more stuff on the market + other stuff that helps). The second time around is too easy. I finished the last ingame week doing nothing but killing time and still had 1 million pix when I payed off the final debt of 500k. This should be more balanced.
The crafting system is a nice addition, but suffers from a lack of menu integration. You literally have to write stuff down you want to hunt for in the dungeons. Would have been much nicer to be able to pull up a menu and see "Aha. I need 2 more pieces of X to make Y." That's why I ended up using it just to make stuff I had randomly collected the ingredients for. It's very inconvenient.
Sure, I could have played it smarter and looked into a guide to make lots more money by crafting. But honestly? When hunting for the items isn't fun.. why would anyone bother?
All in all, I don't really want to drop a huge pile of dung on this game. It has its enjoyable aspects, but as it is, I just don't think it'll be fun for you. That's why I'm not recommending it. If you like, you can play the demo. But don't expect much more than the content you see there.
