Story 8.5/10 - If you have the patience to wade through the tedium, there's an interesting story here.
Story execution 6/10 - Voice acting was good, usually.  The cutscenes were choppy and low quality.  The dialogue would bounce between statements in a way that made you feel like... like they were prerecorded then cut and pasted together.
Atmosphere 8/10 - I consider myself pretty judgmental when it comes to this sort of thing, cause I feel like people have to resort to cheap thrills to make something interesting and horror-oriented.  Although there are a few such cheap tricks, the majority of the game creates an atmosphere that is genuinely interesting, scary, and unique.
Unique Mechanics 7/10 - The puzzle aspect is nice, but not impressive.  It would be awesome, except that after a few minutes it starts to feel like a game of "Where's Waldo", in which you just look for little details that feel very pre-defined.
Gameplay 4/10 - The game feels sluggish and awkward.  Getting your character to face a clue can occassionally be problematic.  Much of the game felt like overcoming the tedium of moving your character through the environment in order to find hidden objects.
Level design 3/10 - The maps feel very chaotic and disorganized.  While the general layout may be right (Here's a church, up front there's a chappel, in back there're some other rooms), the execution of the specifics feels pretty awkward and staged.  It's made worse by the "ghost obstacles" that artificially block your path basically everywhere.
Graphics 6.5/10 - The main character has the best art of anything in the game.  The overall feel fits the atmosphere, but neither the graphics nor the art are particularly gripping.
Bugginess 3/10 - Had the game crash 5+ times in 10 hours of gameplay.  Once it required me to force-powerdown my computer, since even the task manager couldn't come up.
Overall 6.5/10 - The twisty, creepy story makes up for an otherwise poor game.  I bought it in the humble bundle, and don't regret the purchase.

Bloop is a quirky little physics based puzzle game, that isn't the first of its kind, but will most definitely not be the last, so what makes this little game so interesting? Let's dive in and find out.
Gameplay: 83/100 B-
Nothing revolutionary here, but that doesn't mean it isn't good. What Bloop lacks in innovation, it more than makes up for it with a polish in gameplay. It's not perfect and some levels are a bit of a pain to figure out, but they're not impossible, in fact, they're clever and often times will require the player to think outside of the box. It's a simple game, very few controls and a handful of concepts to master, but like any good puzzle game, it has a nice balance between simplicity and complexity.
Audio: 92/100 A-
Some folks might think I'm giving this game a little too high a score for the audio, but I'm a sucker for good sound development, but even more for jazzy/lounge soundtracks and Bloop is filled with it along with other tracks, but they are never distracting or overwhelming, taking away from your concentration. If the soundtrack was available to buy, I would most definitely buy it. Aside from that, the game's effects aren't anything unique, but like the gameplay, is well made.
Visuals: 84/100 B-
Speaking of distractions, the visuals are a bit messy. I don't mean it in a bad way, it's cool looking and full of little gags that made me giggle like a schoolgirl, but the faded watercolor look sometimes drew my attention away from the problem I was trying to solve (Or was that just Borderlands 2 vying for my attention again?). Anyways, back on point, Bloop isn't bad to look at all, the colors are all nice and the shapes and stylings are, well - bloopy.
Content: 75/100 C
There isn't really much here to talk about besides the gradual progression of puzzles and difficulty. You probably won't be blasting through the game in an hour or even two, but once you get done with it, that's kinda it. It's a good time killer, but once spent, it won't do much for you, so you're better off sharing it and letting others try it out.
Design: 77/100 C+
One of Bloop's selling points is it's organic and physics based puzzles, that said, this involves a good portion of open world problem solving, involving you the player to create your own solutions more or less, within the bounds of the stage in the form of number of moves, or pieces you can use. The game could definitely benefit some small zoom option, but it's really nitpicking. It does what it needs to do.
Performance: 79/100 C-
This would definitely be higher if it wasn't for the simple fact that on the highest resolution, this simple game seemed to lag on my computer. I couldn't figure it out. Of course on the lowest resolution, it was smooth as butter, but a bit harder to read. Overall, the game ran just fine. There isn't much you can really tweak and outside of the resolution, the other options didn't seem to affect the games performance by much.
Verdict: 82/100 B-
Bloop is nice. Bloop is friendly. Bloop isn't hateful. Bloop is just Bloop. It's a fun game for the most part and while it may only be worth one or two playthroughs per person, it is definitely a game you should give to another person, especially as a way to introduce someone to the physics based puzzler.

I'm not really into physics games, but I had to try this out and give it a review.
First of all, the game suffers from numerous technical issues. Sometimes the game doesn't start, cutscenes get stuck, alt-tabbing frequently crashes the game on windows 8. So you have to aware that there might (most likely) be some issues.
Secondly, the game itself. Difficulty curve is not well laid out, the first few levels are too easy, then the game gets too hard very quickly. (as I said, I'm not a big fan of puzzle games, so that could be related to my missing experience in this particular genre) The game mechanics are very simple to learn, and each level has multiple solutions. The game is proud of that, but that makes the game feel strange. You never know if that is supposed to be a proper solution or some kind of workaround or glitch. The same goes about the behavior of lifts and other elements in the game. Even if you find a solution, it just won't feel right.
Thirdly, the music and all sounds are just simply annoying. It makes you tear your ears out, and hang yourself. Yep, it's that boring. The art itself is somewhat similar to that too, generic, nothing special.
Fourthly, the texts. Asides the few grammar and composition issues the texts are the worst part of the game. The author tried to be cute and funny so hard, that they became irritating. It's like ponies on fluffy clouds. Makes you want to kill yourself the second time after you hanged yourself because of the music. And the third time. The fourth time. The fifth...
So in short, avoid the game.
However, if you still want to try out a game from the developer, and you are interested in the concept, check out Bloop Reloaded. That's definitely a big improvement over this one.
And there is something else I have to say here. I presonally don't like the idea of releasing a game, then release a better version as a separate purchase a few weeks later. I understand the circumstances of the releases (this version being stuck in greenlight for a long time), and that the products are separated by years of development. However I still think reloaded should have been free (or greatly discounted) for Bloop owners. "The right thing to do."

As prince of Nether world, take back what is yours, restore law and order. And don’t get stuck in the Item World forever.
Disgaea is an engaging game with lots of features, capable of pulling the player in for hundreds of hours.
Gameplay:
It's a tactical turn-based JRPG with visual novel elements here and there.
You have your tactical map, your character's party placed on this map, and enemies all around. Your goal is to defeat every single enemy unit on it and win. Pretty straightforward, but also pretty damn fun! Moving through story you will unlock better equipment, and new character classes to join your party, both common and unique. It needs to be said that there is really ALOT of characters in this game, and to unlock some of them you'll really need to break some sweat.
Story:
The game's story is self-aware, not too deep and not too serious, which is nice.
The premise is as follows: You are Laharl, the only son of ruler of the Netherworld. You've been asleep for two years, which sounds like a dream for some of us, but when you wake up first things you find out are:
1. Your father has passed away some time ago
2. His former vassals are now fighting over the throne
So your goal is to defeat everybody, reclaim the throne and become the next lord of  Netherworld.
As you probably know, Disgaea was originally developed for the consoles. Compared to the PS2 version, this PC release features updated textures and better art. It also has a bonus campaign from the PSP release included.
If you want a game that will remove you from your social life for a month, Disgaea PC is your choice.

More Men of War? Could this ever be a bad thing?
Well that depends, how many times can you capture a German trench? Believe me, by the time you get to the end of Condemned Heroes you should have pretty much mastered the art of assaulting an occupied trench.
Condemned Heroes can be difficult at times. Nearly every battle is a Soviet attack and as the game follows a Soviet penal unit, that means your guys are the tip of the spear. As grisly as that sounds, it's the counter attacks you have to watch out for.
No sooner have you shot, bashed or exploded the last German soldier must you begin to prepare for the inevitable counter attack. I bet you wished you hadn't thrown anti-tank grenades at the PAK or MG positions now, da, tovarich?
I don't think there was ever a counter attack where I wasn't just holding on by the skin of my teeth and hoarded anti-tank grenades [Hard difficulty]. You can begin to appreciate how soldiers felt in such situations when relief finally turned up and helped beat back the attackers.
Condemned Heroes is a visually pleasing and tactics intensive game that's only short fall is the focus on the Penal Heroes. Yes, they are the focus of the game but again, how many times must I assault a trench line then defend that trench line.
Other games in the Men of War series provide a more varied pallete of missions, Condemned Heroes should only be played by those wanting to truly test their infantry assault tactics.

Bloop is a physics puzzle game where you have to draw platforms so that liquid can come out of a faucet and flow along the platforms you created into a beaker. The levels aren't complete unless you can get a certain amount of liquid - "Bloopies", as they're called - inside that beaker, so you'd better make sure your platforms aren't an inch off of the beaker so that everything starts bouncing. After all, half of the game is physics!
Unfortunately, Bloop is terribly presented and horribly optimized. These issues are extremely off-putting, and it's why, even though the game is kinda cute at times, I have to give a negative review and warn other users to spend their money elsewhere on puzzle games.
First, the presentation. Bloop has an odd art style that I haven't seen much use of before. It's part abstract and part psychadelic. The colors are a little weird, the physics and motion of everything seems a little off, and it kinda made my head hurt to look at for too long. The soundtrack is immensely boring and will put you to sleep - not something that should happen during a puzzle game unless it's the puzzles themselves.
Continuing on about the presentation, the puzzles themselves weren't too confusing, but those really annoying pop-up "tutorials" were less helpful than my own mind putting together what the "Clear" button does. When an abstract mechanic came along - namely, the elevators in puzzle 4 - those pop-ups did nothing but infuriate me because they wouldn't go away. I did read them, and they did not provide any helpful information as to how I was supposed to clear the level. I ended up "rage-quitting" at that 4th puzzle, simply because I just couldn't be bothered to figure it all out.
Second, the optimization. Bloop is the only game where you have to double-click a level to play it rather than single-click. It threw me off for a good minute before I figured out what was going on. The framerate is terrible; I'm not going to say I was running a program that detects framerates, but the game was not running smoothly and seemed to almost freeze at times. I was running at 1920x1080, which other games have performed at with smooth as silk framerates. It's also worth mentioning here that a friend of mine was experiencing crashes when attempting to ALT+TAB, and could not even get past the introductory cutscene because the game would freeze at that point.
Oh, and to skip cutscenes, I think the input is SPACE + LMB. Which is weird, considering I can skip the game's intro developer showcase (the thing before the main menu) with just the LMB. Coupled with the weird double-click for level select, I'm curious to know if Studio 2SD has played any PC games released in the past 5 years.
I think some serious work needs to be done to this game before it can be considered a good puzzle game. Not to mention its short length, or at least what it seems like - the first three levels were not very in-depth, and only 42 levels makes this seem like a very short game. Regrettably, I cannot justify purchasing Bloop unless it's in a bundle. For 2D physics puzzles, there are probably much better alternatives.

Bloop is a really neat physics-based puzzle game in which you place platforms in an effort to guide liquids to their jars. There are also various obstacles and mechanics that you encounter and have to overcome, such as pendulums, elevators, etc. The art style is minimalistic, yet aesthetically pleasing, and suits the game quite well. To draw a comparison to another game, Bloop is sort of like Crayon Physics Deluxe, but with fluids instead of a rolling ball. Given the nature of this type of game, I feel that working with fluids, rather than a ball, allows for more flexibility and mechanical complexity (of which I am a fan of); the other side to this coin is that this causes a spike in difficulty that not all players will be able to appreciate. While I am a fan of difficult games, the quick spike in the transistion of difficulty between levels does cause a bit of frustration and can be a little off-putting at times. That being said, it isn't enough to turn me away from the game, just enough to cause me to take a break and come back later with even more determination.
When I first started this game, I had a small and inconsistent problem regarding it crashing a few times. I posted a review that stated my problem so that potential buyers could be aware of this. Whithin a mere minutes of my post, the developer (a SINGLE person) messaged me on Steam, asking what the problem was, and offering to help resolve it (the problem was resolved). This is a developer that TRULY cares about his work and his audience. These are the type of developers that are saving the gaming industry, one game at a time.
This game is enjoyable, difficult, and requires you to think outside the box, so to speak. I recommend this game to anybody who enjoys physics-based puzzle games that require deep and abstract thinking. The difficulty ramps up a little quicker than it probably should, but that's really my only gripe regarding this game. This gem belongs in any thinker's collection.

Recettear is essentially two games rolled into one, and neither is particularly deep, though the store management aspect is still pretty fleshed out. What it does, it does well (minus a few gripes) but somehow manages to both drag itself out and rush you to the "end" of the game. The problem with the end-game is that, while it has plenty to offer, it arbitrarily bars you from it with unnecessarily padded goals.
So the shop sim is the meat of the game. There's no point detailing the mechanics, so I'll just point out the failings and oversights I didn't care for.
Patrons have a finite amount of money when they enter the store. This value is influenced by how much they "like" you, or what "patron level" they are. The maximum amount of money they have when entering your store is a very important number and it is also
to the player. So when a patron says "I don't have that much money!" there's no option to say "Well how much do you have?"
Buying items: some patrons will sell YOU things. You have no option to politely decline; you either make a reasonable offer for something you may or may not want, or you make a terrible offer and♥♥♥♥♥♥them off. Patrons also have their own dialog style, and occasionally it is unclear whether you're buying an item from them or selling an item to them.
The goal is to do a capitalism until you pay off all your debts. This happens rather rapidly and they kind of rush you through this section of the game so that your time limit is over and you can go at your own pace. This is particularly good for the dungeon-crawling portion of the game, as entering a dungeon will consume most of an entire day and leaves little opportunity for vending.
The dungeon crawling plays very smoothly and each of the playable characters has enough uniqueness to their playstyle to give them all a wholly different feel. There's a considerable number of dungeon and environments. And they're all the same randomly-generated box rooms and hallways given fresh paint at regular intervals. After a short while, it gets stale, and as much as I enjoyed the gameplay, I did not feel compelled to complete even the Obsidian Tower. They just don't keep it fresh or interesting, and that kind of killed the game for me. There's lots of end game content and no motivation or reason to experience it.
All said, I'd still recommend the game if you can nab it for a few bucks because the first 5 to 10 hours are a pretty fun ride.

Okay the controls are well done, you can tell they've had plenty of time to polish everything out, including the interaction with the world, you can tell that the game was meant to be played with a controller so if you have one, I'd use it. The soundtrack is great, it's diverse yet it fits the theme of the game very well, every moment, every plot twist, the ambient sounds, movement, and combat sounds are also very pleasing to the ears. The deck-stacking aspect of the game adds a nice extra layer to the rogue like formula for me giving you a rudder to turn in the storm of RNG not giving you true control but enough that you can play to your preferences and have a sense that you are not just caught in the stream.
The developer support for the game is also amazing the 2 content patches have added a lot to the variety of the game extending the amount of time it offers just as you were getting ready to put it down.
So as long as you enjoy rogue likes and enjoy some timing based brawl fighting I recommend hand of fate.

Ahh, American Truck Simulator. What a great continuation to the Truck Sim legacy.
American Truck Simulator is a sequel of sorts to Euro Truck Simulator 2 (however more like a very large expansion), and a very similar game in fact. American Truck Simulator is, well, a truck simulator, where you must build your land shipping empire from the ground up. You start with nothing. No money. No truck. You also have a very limited amount of jobs you can do (low value, short distance, non-hazardous, and normal times only). From there you do odd jobs, getting hired by other companies and driving their trucks, and slowly start to build up your cash reserves. Once you get enough money, you can buy your very own truck, where you have to do maintenance, pay for gas, and all the other fantastic things that come with owning a vehicle. From then on jobs pay more, and you can upgrade your truck, and even hire drivers and buy trucks for them, and they start to generate income on their own, taking jobs and delivering.
(NOTE: You can take out a bank loan, instead of doing dozens of odd jobs, but the interest on the loan can be quite a weight on your shoulders)
Now, do NOT let the word "Simulator" put you off. This does not feel like a simulator. People generally think of boring, tedious, and mundane when they read "Simulator". This game is rather fun, sometimes tense, and liberating. Another point I must make is, I have no idea how, but they perfectly capture the feeling of driving, and the feeling of the open road.
As for the visuals, many textures up close look outdated and many would likely agree they could use a new graphics engine. However, in general the visuals are very satisfying, save for the occasional close-up of an NPC driver.
And then there is the world, which likely recieves the most criticism out of any aspect in this game. The world as of yet consists of California and Nevada. However this area is quite large, it is possible to have fully explored it within 10hrs, and many fans of ETS2 will likely be dissapointed at this, as that game had 16 different countries. Do not be worried however, as there is another state, Arizona, coming very soon. The devs plan to add all of Canada and the USA, and potential for a map stretching down to the Panama Canal, however it will be "vote with your wallet". Land will be sold in expansion packs after Arizona most likely.
One more dissapointing aspect is the number of trucks available for purchase at the moment. A grand total of
. This is not due to dev laziness however, but rather because licensing/negotiation with the actual manufacturers has been quite slow. More trucks are on the way.
All in all, this game is great, and I highly reccomend it. Even if you are upset about the lack of content at this moment, there is always ETS2 to tide you over until then. Buy this game, especially with the very low price $28.99CDN ($25USD?)

Asphyxia is a short visual novel with a handful of choices. Each choice has dramatic impact on the outcome of events. My first play through was completed in 2½ hours including some time alt tabbed while I searched for other games done by Ebi-Hime. The art and soundtrack are beautiful and fitting for the atmosphere of the game.
Asphyxia, at first, comes off as grandiloquent, however, this unifies with the florid motif of the rest of the game into a harmonious and concerted aesthetic.
If you're still reading after that last sentence then you'll be just fine with the diologue in this game.
Perhaps because I've been struggling, and losing, with exactly the feelings we see Samantha trying to understand within herself, having tried desparatly to reconcile these feelings in exactly the same ways she did, and am ultimately considering the same solutions she has, I may be not be as objective in my review. However, as each person, no matter how hard they try to avoid it, carries the baggage of their lives with them and has their view of the world coloured by their own experiences, it is impossible to be absolutely objective; why not indulge in subjectivity instead!
I don't feel that the subject matter in this game is particularly grim, rather, it is an exploration of the human condition. It addresses the fears and insecurities one faces when building and nurturing real relationships. It is a love story but not a love story in the romantic sense; It is about the idea of love as a basic need and what value it holds to us at our core. It is about our need for acceptance and how this is handled. You will not find a heartwarming story about overcoming trials and becoming stronger person. You will not feel the warmth and tenderness of a blossoming romance. What you will feel is the helpssness, emptyness, and fragile life of somebody who constantly wears a smile to hide their desperate stuggle to find even the smallest reason to live.
Asphyxia will leave you with a heavy sense of dissatisfaction. It is not a comfortable story and it does not leave you with a sense that everything will be okay in the end.
That is precisely the reason I love it.
Asphyxia is not a game for everybody. In fact, I think it's not a game for most people. Asphyxia is a game for people who feel deeply and often; those of us who interpret and communicate with the world through our emotions rather than thought even though we know, intimately, that we will get hurt in the end.

Great atmosphere and a great idea for a game, unfortunately ruined by a lot of bugs, terrible design decisions, poor AI and dumb scripted sequences. The lack of manual saves is the final nail in the coffin for this game. Ultimately not worth it if you value your sanity.
Strengths:
- Great atmosphere and setting - the game has a way of dragging in you into the story
- Pretty enjoyable combat against humans, even if they are dumb as a box of rocks
- Decent visuals if you don't look too closely
- Really good sound production
Weaknesses
- Lack of manual saves - this is by far the worst decision the developers may have made. In a game full of traps, instant deaths, possible stealth sections and tons of bugs, automatic checkpoints are beyond infuriating.
- Bugs, oh the bugs - and I don't mean the mutants you have to fight in this game. The majority of issues are of visual nature, e.g. broken animations, so it's possible to live with them, but the sheer frequency of these problems will take you out of the game's atmosphere.
- Poorly thought out scripted sections - be it defending against a pack of mutants while waiting for a boat or battling a giant shrimp, these sequences are frustrating and completely out of place in this game. The latter boss fight ultimately ended my playthrough, as immediately after killing the monster my gas mask was broken and I could not continue on. Remember the lack of manual saves? Well, the auto save was made exactly the moment my character had to take off the mask. Literally a progession blocker due to crappy design. Or it could be a bug, hard to tell in this mess of a game.
- The Ranger mode, while a cool idea, was really poorly implemented. Yeah, removing the HUD makes sense and adds to the atmosphere but why did you have to remove the weapons menu where you switch between throwable weapons? How the hell is the player supposed to know which item is where? QTE prompts are not displayed either of course. Which reminds me...
- QTEs - ♥♥♥♥ them
- Terrible human AI - It's extremely basic and laughably incompetent. The developers tried to hide it with some occasional additional scripting (e.g. an enemy investigating disabled lights) but it still shows. Every time I heard a startled NPC's saying that "a cold is a definite possibility" I wanted to bang my head against my desk.
- Frustrating fights against mutants - Mainly due to mutants being bullet sponges and the poor hit detection in the game. Especially annyoing on Ranger Hardcore difficulty where every received hit counts.
- Poor texture quality (on highest settings) and extremely janky animations
- They couldn't even make melee kills work properly. Half of the time, instead of a proper animation being triggered, the PC makes the stock melee hit animation and the enemy will just slump to the ground like a puppet. If he is killed that is, otherwise everyone in a 5km radius and their mothers will be alarmed to your presence.

At first, when I read the premise behind this game, I got genuinely angry.
I'm really sick of the Weeaboo obsession with school girls and anime art style. Like seriously.
And to besmirch the great Romantics by portraying them as bickering, simpering school gir--
Wait a minute....
The Romantics acted just like a bunch of adolescent school girls! In this instance, it works!
And does it ever! It is so gratiating, thought-provoking, and geeky to read this Romantic-themed visual novel that focuses on the troubled  Sam(antha) Taylor Coleridge's obsessive and dependent relationship with the conservative Wi(llian) Wordsworth.
I was also a bit respulsed to see a curator recommending this because of it exploring alternative sexualities. That isn't the point of the narrative. It isn't fan service. There is no Hentai. It is about the very real fascination and agrandizement that many of the Romantics had with William Wordsworth, and briefly mentions the rumours that Byron has bisexual relationships-- but not with any of the characters in the game.
So don't be fooled by the appearance of this game. It's not a perverted anime visual novel. It's a serious reflection on all of the major themes of Romanticism-- the innocence of childhood, the corruption of adulthood, and the nostalgia for the past. The game focues heavily on the issue of logic vs. feelings, the issues with excess, and takes place in an ideal and beautiful natural setting.
I recommend it for anyone struggiling with depression, too, as Samantha will be as mirror-like as still water in some ways.

I'm a huge fan of visual novels as a general concept, though I dislike the subject matter of most of them (mostly moe, fanservicey dating sims). So it's always a treat when a game like Asphyxia comes along that bucks the trend and offers something unique and interesting.
Asphyxia has a heavy emphasis on themes of depression and suicide, though it's significantly less depressing than its free quasi-prequel, "Dejection: An Ode" (just look at that title!). I thoroughly enjoyed the story and artwork, and after you finish one of the four endings, you unlock notes on the history of all the famous poets that the characters are based off of, which adds a whole new (often delightfully clever) layer of meaning on top of the game's proceedings. This is truly edutainment at its finest. :D
If you enjoy more serious/non-traditional VN's like

I have a tone of experience with the survival games and I enjoy the genre a lot! I have countless hours on ark and many on rust. This is not displayed on my account due to playing ark on a console since my PC really couldn't comprehend the intensive demand to play the game with it being so unstable.
- Downloaded and launched the game with no problems.
- Character customisation is brilliant (race & religion, facial hair, eyebrows, cosmetics, body features etc...) very in depth with more options coming later on. Hairstyles tessellate being a great feature giving the game more depth.
- The game has a great story to fall back on adding something more unique to what other sandbox survival games offer.
- Day time and night time cycles.
- Weather features such as intense sandstorms.
- Crafting / Building system is very easy to use and works very well from what I have experienced. With the addition of triangle foundations at launch bringing more creativity to your builds along with lots of furniture and decorations for your build to make it your own unlike some other survival games that have very limited decor. Its clear on what you need to make something and is easy to determine which side is the inside and which side is the outside face when placing walls, fences etc due to the small subtle label on each side when the position is highlighted before placing. If you have ran out of materials when placing your last structure and its on your hotbar you can automatically create another without having to go into the menus.
- Levelling up system is great and progressive unlocking new weapons, items, structures with freedom to take your own path in what you learn first with consideration. (Green items you have already learnt, yellow are what are next in the tier to learn, red cant be learnt until something else is learnt which is stated as you click on it.
- Graphics are visually beautiful and run perfect on my rig, not to the ultra standards but default to high with no frame issues at all. Currently run the game at around 70 fps and is probably one of the most stable games in this category.
- Combat is gory and simple enough with body severing. The ability to dual wield. The ability to use shields to block. Bows are simple to use. Normal w,s,a,d and left click right click. 1h and 2h weapons.
- PVE and PVP is great. I haven't done much PVP but from what I have experienced its pretty smooth and quite enjoyable usually ending up cutting your opponents body up after you have defeated them. PVE is interesting with the Thrall and clearing camps, the ability to bring them back to your base to use as slaves.
- I really like the server modes for conan exiles with the ability to choose from purist, relaxed, hardcore, roleplay, experimental. There is solo/coop offline play. They have a PVP normal which is a server with no wipe cycle. They have Blitz which is a 1 month wipe cycle with accelerated progression. And PVE pure servers.
- Clan size restrictions are built into the game. This regulates clans so there isn't just one clan dominating the server. This allows for new comers to have a chance and not just being destroyed as soon as they join the game. Clans are very important and give permissions to base share and have shared access to doors, buildings etc...
- Raiding I have not had much experience with yet but from what I have heard its like most other survival games but a little more smoother and is linked to the monsters to can get in game.
- Admin panels are brilliant, very clean and simple layout that's easy to use and I haven't found any need to type any commands in as its all generated through the boxes you click.
- Server settings can be changed very easily in game and out of game if you are admin.
- Nudity is hilarious and characters are attractive.
- Some servers are quite laggy apparently linked to battleeye problems with the 'rubberbanding' phrase.
- I have found every so often I get a huge frame drop which didn't help if I was fighting and the enemy is still attacking and I cant do anything while its froze.
- Controls feel slightly clunky with the swings of weapons being so delayed, so spamming click isn't really an option as their is so much time between swings and is not instant.
- Dodge feature I didn't find very useful as it worked sometimes and was very hard to achieve the effect.
- Trying to join or recruit someone into a clan is slightly a struggle, for people who haven't played any of the other similar survival games.
- Server favourites did not work.
- Server filtering from the top or bottom did not work.
- Trying to join the same server as a friend was a struggle as it wouldn't always show on both your lists and the steam join feature did not work.
- PVE ai is okay but sometimes they just stand there and do nothing.
- The community seems pretty immature about nudity and ive heard a lot of complaints about the nudity but what do you expect, if you don't want it then turn it off. The option is there and that's why its implemented.
- When playing with someone on a non dedicated server the range from which you can walk from the host player is very little, something around the 70 meters mark. Quite disappointing because of how small it is and should be increased.
- Dying after respawning was an issue.
- Items not decomposing leaving loot bags everywhere, even after server restart.
- Character launched across the map after walking out of a door that's just been opened ending up in death.
All in all I think this is one of the most stable games I have played at launch with very little game ruining issues. I have already had a lot of fun playing this game and will continue to.

Conan Exiles is an open world survival crafting game that is currently in early access on Steam. The game can be played solo, or as locally hosted online co-op, or on a dedicated online server. I experienced all 3 modes, and the online servers are the best option. It’s far superior to both the solo/locally hosted co-op mode. If you intend to play solo, I would strongly advise against that, as it gets very lonely and boring.
Using the player hosted co-op is better than soloing, but it’s also got issues that need to be addressed. I found the co-op experience not as enjoyable as it could be; the biggest issue being that the people you are hosting are invisibly tethered to you, and you can’t split up at all. Other people are dragged along wherever the person hosting goes, so I look forward to that being fixed.
Playing online multiplayer is definitely the way to go. Due to all the different server options, the gaming experience will vary from server to another. You just need to find a server that fits what you want to do at a pace that you like. Most importantly, you’ll decide whether it’s PvP or PvE, and how fast people are able to progress. Personally, I prefer faster progression with PvP. As is the nature with any PvP game, expect to be zerged, killed, and lose practically everything you own in the blink of an eye.
A major focus of the game revolves around gathering resources and crafting. You’ll need to make everything from weapons, to armor, to torture devices and shrines, to housing and decorations. There isn’t a whole lot to say about the story since most of it isn’t implemented yet.
Fighting players is much more satisfying than fighting the AI. Most of the combat is melee, but there are ranged weapons as well. All tools, armor, and weapons have durability. When items become completely worn out, you can repair them with a few materials instead of having to completely recraft them. Dying respawns you back at wherever you have a bed set up, and on most servers, all of the items you had are left on your body.
Performance wise, I’m able to run with all settings maxed, but there are framedrops every now and then (Win10, 32GB RAM, i7-6700k, GTX 1070). It wasn’t too bad though, and I could easily tolerate it. On more popular online servers, there’s more likely to be server lag causing problems rather than performance drops.
I’ve played the game for over 20 hours so far, and I’ve had the most fun while playing on the online servers PvPing and building up bases with others. I can see PvP conflicts between players and clans being a reason to encourage long term replay of the game, and that’s definitely something I look forward to doing more of.
Conan Exiles is in early access, so if you’re looking for a perfect, polished, and complete game, just hold off until the game develops further. Servers may lag, and it is something that is top priority for fixes, but in the meantime, you can use the lag to your advantage in many situations. After my experiences with Age of Conan, I admit was skeptic about Conan Exiles. However, there is plenty of fun to be had with it. I think the game is off to a great start, and I don’t understand all the hate that it’s getting. I have played a lot more than I thought I would, and I intend to play even more as the game develops.

Disgaea is your tile turn based rpg with plenty of levels and items. The story is much more humorous then serious in any way as you gather a rag tag team of many races and personalities on your way to become the overlord of the netherland. It is mildly difficulty  but that can be changed with how much you level grind. It is possible to play this game through with a horde of characters, a few select, or even just a single charcter you overlevel a bit making it possible to play to your preferance. Its a bit lacking in strategy in the main story play as the main strategic point in the game (geos) are quite one dimensional. They do make up for that a bit by having a randomly generated dungeon you can go into whenever that has plenty of depth of strategy whether you get to the end using a geo combo to kill everyone or just make it to the portal down (you can also just brute force kill everyone).  There is full voice acting in both english and japanese and its all well done and translated well. My main problems with this game are the lack of a large amount of strategic depth, the amount of level grinding, and the lack of much end game content.  Overall though the game is very fun and quite good 9/10
The end game content is different endings you can achieve a second story that plays the game in a different perspective and one specific ending is level grinding through the levels and unlockable maps which takes a long time.
Avoid this game if you dislike level grinding, tile turn based rpgs (duh) or want a game that you can play for +100 hours as even though i enjoy this game a lot and have played all versions id say i have about 120 hours worth of play time over 10 years or so.

Would I recommend this game to others?  Yes.  Would I outright tell people they need to play this amazing game?  Also yes.  Would I feel sad when I screw up and send my poor character to live in a box?  Absolutely, don't look at me cry.
The basics of this game are that you take on a parent's debt when they are gone, and you open up their shop to try to save up to pay it off.  You have to pay it off in chunks, and you will fail.  But that is where the good comes in, you get the ability to reset and keep going with all you've learned and much, if not all of your stuff.  The core gameplay is gathering goods and selling them in the shop to try to make the best profit you can.  You can buy, gather, and find goods to sell.  Other than shopping, much of your goods would come from the dungeons, yes, dungeons in your cutesy shop management game.  Of course your adorable little character cannot fight, so instead you go with a fighter, that you unlock as you play, and fight through a variety of dungeons, mainly to gather all the goods you can sell in your shop.  The harder the dungeon, the better the goods.  You will spend much of your time trying to figure out what it takes to earn the most money, then start to rake in the dough and have things be perfect, until some event seems to screw everything up for you, just for you to need to reset once more.
The art is cutesy and as far as I can tell, impossible to not love.  The gameplay is fun, and challenging.  The challenge is enough to make the better players still enjoy it, but not too hard as to alienate the lesser player.  The music isn't bad, the cast of characters are fun and funny, and it is hard to not enjoy everything this game has to offer.

Absolutely Epic in scale and with nigh unlimited amounts of depth and replayability CK2 is the kind of game that can consume your life if you let it. It really captures that "just one more turn" aspect that makes CIV games so successful but in a real time game. It definitely holds the spot of best strategy game in my steam library, its difficult enough that a hardcore gamer can feel like he has truly earned each measly County in his patchwork empire, but still remains accessible to those unfamiliar with this style of game assuming you are willing to put in the hours.
However this game is not for the faint of heart, While its interface does give you all the details you could possibly want, learning exactly where to go to find those details is not quite so simple. Managing anything larger than a Duchy can be a daunting task for those unfamiliar with the mechanics. Thankfully there is good wiki support for the game that I would recommend for all newcomers.  Similarly some of the intricacies of the various systems of realm laws and inheritance systems can be lost on those who dont have a background in medieval history or latin! Again the various wiki's provide reasonable assistance but it would be nice if the game was better at setting out the exact consequences of your various decisions. The best advice to new players is to take your lumps in those first few games while you learn the ins and outs and you will be founding the British Empire 600 years too early in no time.
Issues aside, this is an absolutely brilliant game, it has both heart and depth and really draws the player into its cutthroat world of assasination, regicide, backroom favours and the occasional spot of open warfare.  You will have to restrain yourself from boring your friends with stories of your latest internal crisis, family squabble or inheritance dispute or that time you had to brutally murder your wife and 3 grandchildren to make sure that the Kingdom of Bulgaria didnt pass out of the family line.
The base game alone is worth the time and money to any fan of grand strategy but the expansions open whole new realms of possibilities to you and I would highly recommend them particularly when they are on sale en mass which seems to happen semi regularly.

: ATS is a great game which captures the feeling of the open road, however is quite limited at this moment of time.
Ahh, American Truck Simulator. What a great continuation to the Truck Sim legacy.
American Truck Simulator is a sequel of sorts to Euro Truck Simulator 2 (however more like a very large expansion), and a very similar game in fact. American Truck Simulator is, well, a truck simulator, where you must build your land shipping empire from the ground up. You start with nothing. No money. No truck. You also have a very limited amount of jobs you can do (low value, short distance, non-hazardous, and normal times only). From there you do odd jobs, getting hired by other companies and driving their trucks, and slowly start to build up your cash reserves. Once you get enough money, you can buy your very own truck, where you have to do maintenance, pay for gas, and all the other fantastic things that come with owning a vehicle. From then on jobs pay more, and you can upgrade your truck, and even hire drivers and buy trucks for them, and they start to generate income on their own, taking jobs and delivering.
(NOTE: You can take out a bank loan, instead of doing dozens of odd jobs, but the interest on the loan can be quite a weight on your shoulders)
Now, do NOT let the word "Simulator" put you off. This does not feel like a simulator. People generally think of boring, tedious, and mundane when they read "Simulator". This game is rather fun, sometimes tense, and liberating. Another point I must make is, I have no idea how, but they perfectly capture the feeling of driving, and the feeling of the open road.
As for the visuals, many textures up close look outdated and many would likely agree they could use a new graphics engine. However, in general the visuals are very satisfying, save for the occasional close-up of an NPC driver.
And then there is the world, which likely recieves the most criticism out of any aspect in this game. The world as of yet consists of California and Nevada. However this area is quite large, it is possible to have fully explored it within 10hrs, and many fans of ETS2 will likely be dissapointed at this, as that game had 16 different countries. Do not be worried however, as there is another state, Arizona, coming very soon. The devs plan to add all of Canada and the USA, and potential for a map stretching down to the Panama Canal, however it will be "vote with your wallet". Land will be sold in expansion packs after Arizona most likely.
One more dissapointing aspect is the number of trucks available for purchase at the moment. A grand total of
. This is not due to dev laziness however, but rather because licensing/negotiation with the actual manufacturers has been quite slow. More trucks are on the way.
All in all, this game is great, and I highly reccomend it. Even if you are upset about the lack of content at this moment, there is always ETS2 to tide you over until then. Buy this game, especially with the very low price $28.99CDN ($25USD?)

Owlboy is a game that traditional platforming fans might find lacking,  as there is not much in the way of challenging platforming sections in the game's ~6 hour runtime. Most of the challenging platforming is concentrated in the last hour. The mechanics of the game (infinite flight for the protagonist) naturally make it difficult for the developer to create platforming sections that test the player's mastery of the game's physics. The platforming is not what I would call the game's strong suit, but it doesn't have to be- everything else is top notch.
The pixel art is jaw dropping and backgrounds are frequently gorgeously animated. The music is a standard orchestral affair, and there are plenty of strong tracks within the soundtrack. The characters of the world are great- Otus, the main player character, is established early on as a sympathetic failure of an owl whom most characters brush off as useless or disappointing, especially so Otus' teacher, Asio. Otus starts out almost friendless, but the band of buddies Otus meets along his journey keep him in high spirits. My favorite surprise of the game was how expressive Otus was- despite being mute, he has a litany of facial expressions that keep him from just being a stonefaced protagonist. Every character in the game has great dialogue, especially so for Geddy, Otus' best bro. Geddy is the star character of the game scriptwise. He says the right stuff at the right times.
The game does not last any longer than it needs to. It establishes the main conflict well within the first 20 minutes of the game and solves the conflict within a reasonable time period- should the game have lasted an hour longer, I imagine I would've started to feel the tedium of traversal in the game through the same areas weigh on me. The level design is about what you would expect it to be for a game featuring a flying protagonist- many floating islands in the hub-like areas and frequent linear sections limiting flight possibilities in the areas related to plot progression (though these flight limiting sections are often not as interesting as I would like them to be personally, but again it's not a dealbreaker). To that end,
. Look elsewhere.
, if you want a nice 6 hour experience with amazing presentation that tells an engaging story with a great cast of characters....this is the right game for you. Is the game worth the 25 dollar price point? I'd say the value I would put it at is closer to 20 dollars.... Though of course, if your game is in development for 9 years, I suppose you really want to get your investment back sooner rather than later, so I can understand why the devs put the price point where they did.

Asphyxia is a difficult visual short story. It's odd to hear games of this genre described as "difficult," since they're barely games at all, but Asphyxia packs an awful lot of terribly trying reading into so small a package. The story is driven almost entirely by its cast, and if the author weren't so adept at creating excellent, if not particularly likable characters, the whole effort would have fallen flat on its face. And that's really the trouble with Asphyxia: You don't like the characters, but that's what makes them good characters. The protagonist is morose, obsessive, and horribly depressing, and the rest of the cast spends much of the story being cruel to one another. The whole thing would have ended up very Dickensian if not for all of the moments where the facades get dropped and it becomes evident that the characters are actually three-dimensional...Well, that and the lack of mutilations through horrible industrial accidents.
I suppose I say all of that in order to say this: Asphyxia is worth your time, even though it's short, and even though it's utterly depressing. I was left with the impression that there was a ton of work packed into so short a story. Ebi-hime's knack for diction and characterization is difficult to come by in any medium, making it evident that they're a strong writer, if one that could benefit from an editor. I spotted quite a few grammatical errors in my playthroughs, and some of the petty squabbles between characters really just went on and on far longer than they needed to, belaboring the point that X and Y don't care for one another. Beautiful music and artwork contribute much to the story, making the characters and setting all the more engrossing. All things considered, Asphyxia isn't just worthwhile, it's really pretty good. It takes the reader through a wide range of emotions in a short period of time, leaving its audience exhausted and frustrated, but still wanting more.

I got much more value from budget games like Curse: Eye of Isis or Hard Reset than I did from this disasterpiece, yet Soul Suspect is enjoyable and I couldn't seem to put it down for the 8 and a half hours it took me to reach my goal.
I think the game performed so poorly with professional reviewers because it's simply not what you expect.  At heart, the game is like an old school point and click, detective adventure with some demonic combat and fetch quests thrown in.  In the game you play as Ronan O'Connor; a sleuth murdered at the hands of the Bell Killer...a sort of Jack the Ripper type serial killer stalking the infamous town of Salem.  The plot of the game is interesting if not somewhat predictable, mish-mashing together a bit of ideas from film (Seven, Silence of the Lambs) with the hard-boiled whodunnit atmosphere of LA Noire.  Some of the plot twists you can see from a mile away, but there's some that were at least somewhat of a surprise.  The story is told at a brisk place with cut scenes between present and past (the Salem Witch Trials) with the voice acting being strong enough to keep you involved and invested.  Ronan is voiced well enough, but sometimes the writing is a little untentionally cheesy.   Thankfully, in the context of a hard-boiled, noir style mystery it works and causes a chuckle or two without being too too flat.
Gameplay/atmosphere wise you run around the town of Salem which is setup as a mini-sandbox.  If Airtight Games had more time and money to put into the project, one could only wonder just how amazing this game could have been.  You can't enter alot of the buildings, leaving you to run around between finding various collectibles, taking on a scant few side quests and finally going to one of the city's main locations for the main action.  The graphical detail isn't overly impressive, but it's solid with decent characer models, appropriately dingy gothic design and some cool locales to explore.  Animation is stiff, the framerate is sometimes choppy and sometimes the items you need to collect will glitch in and out of existence making it a royal s.o.b. to pick them up.  The voice-acting as stated earlier was well-done although the ambient effects (besides the sinister demons you take on in stealth combat) aren't anything particularly special.
The gameplay slides between sleuthing, stealth action, fetching and exploration.  You'll come across numerous crime scenes and points of interests where your main goal is to search, examine and interrogate for clues.  Everything plays out like a stripped-down, beginner's version of L.A. Noire.  Sometimes your ghostly abilities will come into play such as possession to get inside people's heads, teleportation to get where you need to go, passing through walls, etc.  Initially, the gameplay is fun but as the game progresses you can see how basic it is.  You shouldn't need a walkthrough at all for this sucker because everything is laid out just how you need.  Once you've collected enough clues you can solve the crime scene by selecting the appropriate hints and picking the order of their importance.  It's a shame that your'e a ghost with such cool abilities but they feel second nature.  You will not be punished, nor will anything change even if you screw things up.  The game is linear to a fault.  Yet, these sequences are enjoyable enough in an old school point n' click style that it's fun.  If you can think past how the game always seems to cramp and rope you into doing what it wants you to, you'll be interested in how solving each puzzle advances the story.
To break things up you'll get the chance to possess a cat and use it to explore hard to reach areas.  The other main shake of the gameplay is stealth combat where you take on floating demons that look like monstrosities culled from Clive Barker's Undying.  They are actually pretty creepy in the way that they scream and hunt you down if they spot Ronan.  The only way to kill them is to engage them from behind, entering a quicktime button combo that will take 'em out.  Once alerted they can be tough to escape as your only means of protection is to hide in spiritual residue left behind from poltergeists.  You can jump from one residue host to another, leading to a cat n' mouse game where you try to get the upper hand on the beasties.  It's a fun addition to the gameplay variety but like most things in Soul Suspect it's awkward and feels undercooked.
By far one of the most enjoyable parts of the game were the sidequests, where you help dwelling spirits find out the manner in which they died.  These murders have somewhat of an emotional, human element to them (as stated by a few reviewers) that makes you want to help the poor schleps get some eternal rest.  Each quest is set up as a mini-mystery where you canvas a crime scene and put the clues together.  The only problem is that there's about 5 of them total.  If more were added it would have been a great thing.  Once again this represents just how much of a missed-opportunity Soul Suspect is across the board.  For those after Steam Achievements there's a ton of stuff to collect, but some of it's level specific, so if you miss it...too bad.  You have to start the game over again from square one and give it another shot.  Maybe some of you will but I sure won't.  I got 73% on a first try and I nodded afterwards saying to myself, "Good enough, good enough."  It would have been cool if you could start the game over as a new game plus.  I started it over briefly and it seemed to reset everything.
From a technical standpoint things aren't perfect either.  The game ran fairly smooth most of the time but several drops in framerate got me killed by demons about 2 or 3 times, I had about 4 game freeze crashes and I also got the end of cemetery level glitch.  None of these are game breaking, so you can get through them without losing too much progress.
To break it down:
Pros:
-Salem is a killer game setting.
-Involving storyline with great atmosphere
-Fun mix of sleuthing, adventure, stealth combat and pick a path gameplay
-Side quests and collectibles are a plus
-Strong voice acting
-Decent graphics and sound
Cons:
-Pseudo sandbox gameplay is too linear
-Easy puzzles and difficulty
-Cool ghost powers but all of 'em are quite restricted
-No branching paths for messing up the detective gameplay
-Can't carry over collectibles that I saw
-Some minor annoying glitches
-Undercooked combat
-Once you beat it, there's really no reason to go back
Though I have alot of qualms about what Soul Suspect coulda been, what's there is worth playing through once.  Somehow for all of its flaws, there's a charming veneer lurking behind the game's black tooth smile.  The story in and of itself makes it worth a playthrough.  Whether you'll want to pick it up a second time is going to be an iffy, p2p decision.  I'd say this game is worth no more than $15 if you're going to pick it up.  I got it on a holiday sale for a few bucks and it more than exceeded my expectations in terms of value.  I'm pretty sure I paid $5 and could have seen paying as much as $15 for it.  But for $30?  No way Jose!
Final score:  7/10

If you liked the first Mass Effect, you will probably love this one.
Pros:
-You have more squad members, and each one has more depth and complexity than the original. They have personal stories and views to share, rather than exposition. A lot more character development happens, and the romances are more satisfying.
-The movement and combat are much smoother.
-There is more variation between the classes, making each one feel truly unique.
-The weapons are varied, having different firing types and ranges, rather than just different stats in Mass Effect.
Not-Pros:
-The story seems to veer away from where the first game was heading. It’s still neat, but ultimately you’ll care more about the personal missions of your squad rather than the main campaign.
-You need to purchase a large amount of DLC to really get the full game, especially if you want to continue to Mass Effect 3.
-Thermal clips. In the first game, weapons heated up when fired, and you had to let them cool down. In this game, that mechanic has been replaced by thermal clips, which function similar to magazine in other shooters. This limits the “ammo” you have for your weapons. The old system was more fun, and made more sense from an in-universe perspective.

Ever since SCS announced ATS, I was counting down the days until it was released. When they told us that it was only going to come with California, I was still going to be okay with it, I just wanted to drive my Peterbilt 389 in the U.S instead of those tiny European roads. Now that ATS has released, I can say that I am greatly impressed by it. The amount of detail that went in to the states of California and Nevada is unbelievable. Even though its running on the same engine as Euro Truck 2, it still feels like a new experience for me. It is definitley a step up from the bland cities of Euro Truck.
Things I don't like:
1. The lack of long roads. One thing I enjoyed about Euro Truck was being able to stay on one highway for a long time and just enjoy the journey on the road. On nearly every journey on ATS, there are a number of turns on to different highways, usually dont stay on one for over 5 minutes
2. Only coming with two trucks. Yes, I know there are going to be a ton of new mods that are going to make up for it, but I was looking forward to driving more high quality trucks from SCS. I am looking forward to when they do put more in the game.
3. The weigh stations. One of the biggest things I was looking forward to was learning how to do the weigh stations and what they would be like. Well, as of now, they don't do anything. The ones at the rest stops literally do not do anything, no icons or anything. They are just there. The ones on the highway will randomly ask you to pull in for a vehicle inspection. When you get there, you just stop on the icon and press enter and they will tell you to continue. You dont get to know the weight of your cargo or anything. I am hoping they will put more into them as the game continues its development.
Overall I am still very excited to be playing ATS. I know the mods will make this game what we all wanted it to be. I am now counting down the days until we can be driving across the entire U.S!

How to haggle like a pro.
Usually, the hero of a video game is the representation of what society views as 'strong, courageous and tough'. This is why male heroes make up such a collectively large proporition of protagonists in video games and all mediums of entertainment; books, movies, lolcat memes (not the norm) are all forms of entertainment that attribute widely to the popular - and I emphasize popular- social stigma of society.
Examples are here:
Fifty Shades of Grey: Super hot stuff
White men can't jump: Self explanatory
Locat memes: Desire to anthropomorphize ourselves into kittens.
Now let's focus on Recettear again.
Let's say 'hypothetically' that Recettear is 'different' from the norm. Instead of a strong male lead, you now have a female lead who starts off relatively inept (Not an opinion against females, just what the character starts off as). Her only benefits being that she doesn't need to eat, or atleast from what we can see, and that she can follow a schedule better than any student or adult in the known world. Also, she's an anime girl: the truest and strongest form of feminist pro propagandanism.
So what gives?
How are we supposed to connect with this game if there isn't anything remarkably 'interesting' to connect to?
Well, that's the essential difference in video games; it doesn't need to because video games aren't all words or film.
Here's why:
Recettear is absolutely blossoming in charm from its art style (animesque) to the gameplay (finances 101). It's a mix mash of japanese tropes/culture,dungeon crawling and finances. Though, I wouldn't go so far as call it an RPG because it's remarkably hard to connect with the main character, but it serves well in its main drive of gameplay; the flesh of the gameplay is the retrieving and selling of products with a hint of dungeonesque elements, specifically you need to get sellable materials from the dungeon to sell. And boy, you want to sell, sell and sell because debts in game come in fast. In fact, never has procrastination on debt lead to such dire consequences where a little a girl gets evicted from her home to the doghouse, though if that's your thing...
However, in the end, the frantic nature of gameplay makes each decision a calculated decision to maximize profits from retrieving and selling. Thus, you will want to haggle everyone despite your best conciousness;
a little old lady, how nice! Sell the bagel at 500% mark up. It's a deal she can't refuse, literally! (Starving old lady)
It's a game that will teach you how exploitative you can be and you know what? That's the best form of video game.

Valkyria Chronicles is one of the hidden gems of the PS3 that everyone should play. The graphics are beautiful, the story and characters keep it entertaining, the backdrop has been used often (WW2) in games but never from this sort of rural perspective. This game involves military cadets at a small country caught between two warring powers- but while you may be used to brawny, muscle bound CoD war machines, the characters in VC aren't so war hungry. They have weaknesses, fears and personalities all their own, and it hurts if they fall in battle.
The gameplay itself is both unique and fantastic, a major draw of the game. It uses a mix of turn based strategy and active movement- where you'll come under fire while moving, where cover like buildings, trenches and sandbags can really save you. You can sneak through grass- and each class has special abilities, such as scouts to spot those in grass, snipers which can't defend themselves but can take out enemies from a distance, and machinegunners which tear up close enemies as they run by on their turn.
VC is what a strategy game should be- strategic, yet quick paced with every movement and position and action having meaning, and mistakes being very costly.
I'll happily endorse Valkyria Chronicles as the best game of the PS3, and those who didn't have the chance on console should pick this up. (That is- unless you're waiting the HD version on PS4)

I really wish I could like this game, but there are some serious issues that keep me from giving it a positive review.
I liked the main cast, they were funny in their interactions, albeit with fairly weak voice acting. The visuals are nice and there's a fair amount of content to the game.
Beyond that, it starts to fall apart. The game is pretty grind heavy. It might be that I was missing something obvious, but I found that I had to constantly replay through earlier chapters of the game to train up my units. This is made more frustrating in that the only way to gain EXP is for the unit to defeat an enemy. There's no EXP from healing your own units, which makes it frustrating to train up the clerics, who aren't known for their damage outputs.
In regards to the actual combat, the main issue that I had with it is that the levels don't really feel well-designed. There are a lot of walls and such that require rotating the map, which makes navigating and moving units feel slower than it should be.
All in all, I want to like this game, and perhaps there is something I'm missing, but it's too grind-heavy and clunky in gameplay for me to have enjoyed it.

I've enjoyed this game for a long time now. It was the first game I have ever bought on steam and is the main reason I came to steam in the first place, but after playing close to 230 hours of this game I cannot recommend it. Lets break this into Pros and Cons.
Pros:
-This game has an amazing combat system unlike any other game. It is increadibly fun to learn and takes time to master.
-Large variety of well done maps that really give of a medievaly atmosphere.
-The Ingame voices are fun. (Expecially taunting)
-There are multiple gamemodes.
-It has a good community... sometimes.
-There are servers for new players (Rank 15 and under)
-Graphics are pretty cool.
-Large but limited variety of weapons.
-Lots of content on the steam workshop for this game.
Thats about it for the Pros...
Cons:
-Very Buggy. Developers put more time into adding cosmetics than fixing very irritating bugs that have been in the game for a very long time.
-There are two types of people that play this game, Newcomers, and Veterans, nothing in between, so it eathier going to be too easy or way too hard.
-The community is sometimes pretty toxic. This doesn't mean you won't find nice players but a large amount of them are just straight-up ***holes.
-Rank 15 and under serves is pretty much a compitition to see who can swing their sword the most and the fastest.
-Most high rank players use an exploit called dragging. This takes away from the realisim of the game aswell as makes it impossible for new playes to adapt to the game. The high ranked players also refuse to recognize this as an exploit.
-As soon as you turn to rank 16 you are put with players of upwards to rank 40+ (Balancing is non-existent in this game) This results in a very steep learning curve, which, dont get me wrong, is not a bad thing, but it's just not for some people.
-Gamemodes such as Team Objective and Team Deathmatch are usually stacked, meaning that one team usually has the majority of the high ranks and the other team has low ranking players. (Just imagine a group Sumo Wrestlers going against some really nerdy kids) Only if you're lucky you will find a balanced server.
-This game is as optimized as a potato. You better have a good computer if you want to play this.
-The community is dwindling fairly quickly. When I started playing there was on average around 5000 people playing at a time, now its around 1500 on a good day.
-(For me personally) once I unlocked all of the weapons, the game started to go downhill. There was no challange or objective while playing.
Just a Few side notes:
-Don't get this game if you have anger management problems... just don't.
-Don't get this game if you do not have a very good computer... It will run like absolute cow dung.
-Get this game only when it's on sale... whatever you do, do not pay $25 for this. It's really not worth it.
-Get this game if you are going to play with frends. If you're going solo, you're gonna have a bad time.
-If you do get this game, never play after 11:00pm... Thats when all the super tryhards come out of their caves.
Peronal Note: Don't get me wrong here, I absolutly loved this game. There were lots of good times to be had with friends when I first started. There is just simply too much wrong with this game for it to be enjoyable anymore. But at the end of the day, it's up to you if you want the game. Go on and check out some other reviews and compare them to mine and see if you notice a common theme.
Also if you are thinking about commenting with something along the lines of dragging. Don't, you might get some of your nerd sweat in your keyboard, and we wouldn't want that now would we.

Beautiful graphics, novel gameplay, interesting (albeit clichéd and somewhat nauseating) storyline.
I wanted to play the game more, I thought it was a tactical squad game but with a beautiful anime story in place of a grizly, realistic war scene. But the game penalizes spending time to secure locations and advancing your squad safely, putting more emphasis on completing the objectives in the least turns possible. This means more often than not, the most efficient way to complete a mission with full ratings is for a lone scout (sometimes 2) to simply dash to the objective, ignoring the hoards of trigger-happy enemy soldiers in-between, while the rest of your squad just sit where they spawned like stunned cattles. That really broke immersion, and I haven't been able to bring myself to finish the game despite wanting to see the story progress.
I don't hate the game, it has a lot of promise aside from the major flaw in gameplay concept. But the way they want us to play it, it really encourages players to exploit the system for a high rating. That's where we see videos of a war effectively won single-handed by a lone over-powered scout. For tactical squad games, I really like the way X-Com implemented it. X-Com encourages you to put your squad members safety above completing missions in the shortest time for arbitrary reasons. And 'X-Com:Enemy Within' introduced melds which also required players to take risks for a time-crucial objective; but players decide if it's worth putting their squad members at risk for it or if the danger out-weighs the gain.

Visual novel is a gamestyle that I really appreciate, because it not only puts you right in the mind of a character, it also allow you to really influence the story based on your choices. With Amnesia, I was really surprised.
First, Graphics : The art direction in the game is just wonderful, you feel as if the whole game is happening in a romantic painting, each character is unique in itself, but it really is the background which stunned me visually.
Second, Story : In this kind of game the most important part is the story, the place where it takes place, along with the multiple events which allows you to see the characters evolving, Asphyxia does a pretty good job considering the game happens during a schooltrip and doesn't really have "action", or any other game cliche like this.
Lastly, Characters : In a Visual Novel, characters (and espescially the hero) need to be attractive, not in a physical way (even if the cute girls are kinda cute) but in an emotionnal aspect and this game really moved me here, Samantha and her struggles, her fears, her hopes, even her way of not understanding her own feelings felt really true, Not many games have had such an impact on me but I really cried and really wanted to make her feel good. The other characters, fit perfectly in the story, I can easily understand why they may (or may not) have a connection to Sam.
Finally, I will say that Asphyxia is really a wonderful game, after the first 5-10 min of gameplay, you will start to feel what Sam is feeling and you will WANT to see the end, to help her in her relationship. The ONLY complain I have about this game is that it doesn't have a really happy endings, sure the best one is pretty nice, but I feel like Sma deserves more happinnes in her life.
If I can give you ONE advice, play this game, you will understand pain, sorrow, despair and hope in a much different way than ever before...

For a visual novel about gender-swapped English poets as schoolgirls, the game felt surprisingly personal in the way that it discussed the heavy themes it brought up (suicide, substance abuse, depression, homelessnes, sexual assault, and many others). The characters felt very real in how they interacted with each other, and I often found myself thinking, "I've had these thoughts before," in response to the main character's bleak musings. Even in its gloominess, the writing still had many clever little lines that made me laugh. The few times modern world contraptions like phones and the internet are brought up in the narrative, it felt weird and out of place, but not enough to take you out of the game.
The art fits the implied aesthetics of the writing and is generally polished with the exception of some of the characters' awkward poses. The one thing that could use definitely some work is the UI; it got a bit hard to read the text when the backgrounds turned light.
Took about 5 hours to get all four routes, and funny enough, it made me want to sit down afterwards and learn about the Lake Poets. So, there's that video game edutainment angle for you, I guess.
Overall it's a great experience that's well worth the low price.

Both Asphyxia and its predecessor,
, are about gender-swapped versions of Romantic poets, and inspired by their real relationships with each other. I absolutely love visual novels with references to classic literature, and while reading Dejection, I was impressed with the writer's ability to imitate the style of that period without making it too dense for modern readers. I felt very empathetic towards both Samantha and Lillian, its only two characters, especially during one well-placed run-on sentence about Samantha's feelings. I couldn't wait to read more, and the next game managed to somehow exceed my already-high expectations.
Asphyxia makes the heroines of Dejection teenagers and sends them on a school trip in a semi-modern setting – there's modern technology, but still a very old-fashioned feel to everything – with several of their colleagues. This expansion of the world of the story doesn't seem to stretch the creator too thinly at all, however, as it is still beautifully written. And while the art in Dejection is very cute, the art in Asphyxia is downright gorgeous. It really fits the setting well, as does the lovely music.
Perhaps most importantly, Asphyxia really made me develop strong feelings for the characters – even more so than I had expected. I loved Samantha, and wished that I could help her overcome her problems, despite the fact that their similarities to my own would probably make that impossible. (mild spoilers:)
And while some of the other characters seemed irritating at first, they all grew on me as more dimensions of their personalities became evident. There were things I liked about them all, and the only thing I didn't like about their story was that it eventually had to end.
I recommend that anyone who's at all remotely interested download and read Dejection, which is both free and quite short, and then buy Asphyxia if they like it. Also, definitely read the notes in the “extras” section once you've played it. Even if you're an English major like me, there are bound to be some interesting details you didn't know that were referenced in the game! It's really a very well-researched project on top of its other great qualities. It's definitely on my list of favourite visual novels I've ever read.
