I don't know what to say about this game, I would give it 50% thumbs up and 50% thumbs down. Objectively it shouldn't be fun. It's tedious, frustrating and too easy at the same time. But the story and the gameplay still kept my interest through the whole game. So, I completed it in 6 hours.
I say this game is worth your time, but not necesseraly your money (if you would buy this full priced). The main gameplay element is investigation, which is basically pixelhunting in a 3D environment, then the game asks you a question and you have to answer by chosing one or more (usually 3) found clues. If you mess up, you can always retry. You can't fail an investigation, because you will repeat it until you succeed. This is why I said it's easy and frustrating at the same time.
There is one very annoying mechanic, which is the so-called "combat". It's a very basic stealth portion of the game where you have to hide from demons and possibly stealth kill them or avoid them altogether. It's not too hard after you get the hang of it, but because it isn't too sophisticated, the AI is very primitive, it can be very frustrating (for example when the demons are searching the same hiding spot the third time when you're waiting for them to give up the search).
Thematically it is a bit confusing: It seems like the devs couldn't decide in what era the game should take place. The main character is dressed like he's in a film noir and all the investigation is done and all the characters talk like we're in the '50s (there is no forensics at all in the game). But the "skin" of the game is present day: there are cell phones, modern cars, and all the living NPCs are dressed as from a modern day.
I bought it in a Humble Bundle and I had 5 hours of enjoyment and 1 hour of frustration, so it was good for me. It is an interesting game, but gameplaywise it isn't a very well made game.

Midnight Club 2 is definitely one of the better of the early-2000s arcade racing games. I originally played it on the PS2, and I must say it has aged well.
The graphics, to begin with, are definitely not bad. They're nothing to write home about of course, but the texturing is pretty nice, and the only thing that really stands out as being old is the rather blocky look of some of the buildings.
The controls for the cars & bikes are pretty good. It actually takes a bit of skill to deal with bikes [you will initially find yourself crashinf very easily]. And each of the cars available to unlock will have it's own quirks that you can use to your advantage, once you figure them out. One thing that stands out in this game is that you can actually flip your car in any direction [when it's in the air], and many arcade racers of this era had you stuck horizontal to the ground.
One of the areas this game is, maybe not bad, but definitely odd, is with the AI. Oftentimes the public traffic seems almost scripted in the way that a massive truck happens to come out of an intersection just as you turn the corner and slam right into it. Or it might just be coincidental. This seems pretty neat at first, but it soon gets a bit tiring as you know it's going to be coming, so you can plan it away in advance.
Also, the opponent AI is strange. They seem very apt to crash and swerve into traffic at when they go at high speeds [altough it's worth noting you can set the difficulty of the game manually, see the game guides and forums for details on this]. And in the "free roam" races, I find that regardless of which route you take, the opponents do worse if you're following them. Which makes me think that they're unaffected by traffic if you're not there to make it render. A bit of  ahandicap for you as the player, but I guess it just adds a challenge.
Also, if you're going to use a controller, you may have a hard time navigating the menus. If you're using an xbone|360 controller, hold DPAD L+D, and use X to select items. You'll know what this means when you get to it. Alternatively, look into xinput to keyboard mapping software.
So to summarize that, this is definitely one of the better "old arcade racing" games, but it's obviously got its problems. If you're only interested in newer stuff, then avoid it, but if you don't mind it being slightly dated, then go for it. You'll have fun.

One of the best sci-fi action games I've ever played.
This game feels like they put up a core concept, and then just started adding their favorite mechanics from AAA titles.  From most developers, I would expect that to be a flaw in their game design, but Digital Extremes has managed to pull off a cohesion between so many different game mechanics and systems that I genuinely wouldn't know where to start with breaking them down in a review.
The best part, THIS GAME IS FREE!  WHAT?!  There has to be over 100 hours of content just in the campaign missions!  you can spend money on guns and aesthetics to accellerate your progress through the earlier missions, but so far I have only spent anything on cosmetic items and I haven't had any issue making steady progress without feeling like things have stagnated.
Some critiques:  I shouldn't need to use a wiki to find out where certain crafting materials appear.  tooltips would be nice for a game with such a vast ammount of content and customizability.
Second, why do I have access to weapon blueprints which I cant get materials for until later in the game?  I know better now, but when i was brand new, i grabbed the Latron blueprint because i wanted a sniper instead of a bow, not realizing that one of the materials was unobtainable until I got to saturn.  I bought that blueprint around the 6 hour mark.  I'm now at 35 hours, and only just am getting access to the mineral i needed.  again, a tooltip may have prevented that frustration
These are small greivances, and the resources I wasted early on are pretty moot at this point.  So, honestly I cant reccommend this game enough.  I'm absolutely blown away by the immersion into this sci-fi world through small details they put in outside of missions, and just how fun the gameplay is.  the fact that this game is free and people still blow hundreds on DLC for destiny blows my mind.

Buyer beware:
Read all the other reviews for the glowing praise that I would only be repeating, I am simply giving a warning.  The "digital deluxe" version includes next to no DLC despite the misleading title.  Do not expect to be able to play Lair of the Shadow Broker, Arrival, or Overlord.  Kasumi Goto likewise requires a purchase to have as a follower and Zaeed Massani appears to be completely unplayable as a code is not provided with the Digital Deluxe Edition and a download/purchase is not listed on Bioware's website where the rest of the DLC can be purchased.
Similar to Xbox Live, purchase of Mass Effect 2 DLC for the PC requires purchase of "Bioware Points".  The total cost of all DLC listed above is 2480 points and once again similar to Xbox Live, these points can only be purchased in predetermined amounts.  This results in being able to purchase 2400 or 2800 points, leaving either a deficit or a surplus,  meaning you are forced toeither not purchase certain DLC or essentially throw away some money due to an inability to use the remaining points effectively.  Overall, purchasing game changing DLC costs $35 and all DLC costs $50.
Other DLC such as cosmetic changes and weapon/armor add-ons are also not included in this edition, but are not game changing and add no additional content beyond minor tweaks to the game.  Make no mistake, the full edition of this game costs an additional $35 to the $30 required for the base game, meaning the full Mass Effect 2 costs $65.  Buying the game while 50% off brings it down to $15, making the full game cost $50.
Despite everything listed above, I recommend the game as it is my personal favorite sci-fi RPG and the base game while on sale for $15 is definitely worth it.

Well done sequel to Euro Truck Simulator 2. If you're a fan of the first, this entry improves the experience abit in some areas.
+ Graphics seem crisper, smoother - though bottlenecks seem to occur on full settings near cities (a problem with ETS2 as well).
+ The trucks feel/drive live big 'ol American trucks should.
+ The randomized parking option is nice, a new challenge when completing deliveries (optional if you want it).
+ The RPG aspect adds a little interest to your character-building, though it never feels like it has a profound impact on the game results.
+ The roads look/feel like Southwest American roads.
+ Varied towns and companies
- You only have two trucks in this game at the moment, which is very limiting when compared to what was offered in ETS2.
- The map is small by ETS2 standards - covering just California and parts of Nevada. In just over 3 hours I've covered about a quarter of the routes.
- The developers still havent addressed certain aspects such as questionable driver AI and very-short on-ramps. These feel carried over from EST2.
- Some of the major towns/cities feel desolate at times and there are few people walking about. Others are just fine and feel teeming with life.
Overall, despite its inherent shortcomings, I'm enjoying my early days with this game. It's a nice respite from life that can keep you busy in 30-45min spurts (or all day if you want). For $20, it's a worthy successor to what ETS2 has already established.

Hand of Fate, at the most base level, is a card-based Roguelike with a focus on rhythm-based arena combat and the occasional coin-flip when asked to resolve anything else, but boiling it down to such an extent does the game a great disservice. It's perhaps one of the greatest examples of a game being more than the sum of its parts.
The central concept that underlies Hand of Fate is perhaps best described as "Luck of the draw" or any other kind of card-game term, signifying the idea that sometimes you get dealt a good hand, sometimes a bad one. It's a game that is centered around this very idea, of both luck and fate, that draws on a heavy mysterious atmosphere, a strong narrator and stories that are slowly uncovered with each run. It's this presentation, narration and atmosphere that sets it apart from other, perhaps better rogue-like games and that keeps me coming back to pit myself against the dealer over and over again.
The game has weaknesses here and there, the arena combat can sometimes be frustrating (damn scales), the trap-mazes are rather predictable and sometimes, the suggested decks aren't entirely up to snuff, but I am willing to overlook all of that, and would likely overlook more, for the delightful world and theme.
As it stands, I've sunk more time in Hand of Fate than I've sunk in many other games and the very idea of two players, playing a game like this for a mysterious reason, has kept me engaged both while playing and when not. The art-style, narration and depth of this game make it a no-brainer for me to recommend.

Almost everything about
is perfect.  There are no issues with the port from the original console version.  The painterly style of the Canvas engine gives it a uniquely beautiful look.  The setting - an alt-universe version of Europe in WWII with some fantasy elements - is refreshingly original.  The story's well-written, and the characters are deep and believable.  Even the rank-and-file soldiers in your squad who aren't important to the plot have names, backstories, quality voice acting, and personality traits that affect their combat performance.  And the core mechanic of classic turn-based strategy combined with real-time third-person controls that put you right in the action is simply brilliant.  It's even got plenty of replay value, with a new game plus mode and challenge missions.
So, what mars it?  Just two things.  One, the AI is incredibly stupid.  It's depressingly easy, for example, to get enemies to kill each other by drawing an enemy soldier's fire and taking cover behind another enemy.  And two, scouts eventually become overpowered - but that's only a big issue in new game plus.  Should you start thinking, though, that cheap exploits make the game too easy, you've always got the expert skirmishes and bonus missions in the DLC to give you the experience of playing with severe handicaps.

We all love board-games, don't we? The only problem with them is that there's too much left for the imagination. If only there'd be a game with board-game rules and visualization of, say, Diablo III or Torchlight, or something similar... If you ever had a thought like that (and I know that I did), you're welcome to buy Hand of Fate as soon as you'll finish reading this review.
is a game that's very simple to play, yet very complex to explain: basically, it's a card game, where you move your token from card to card, encounter monsters, treasures and various obstacles. At the end of each scenario, you fight a boss. Though, the complex thing is that when you encounter an enemy, the game turns in something or an action-RPG with you controlling your hero, using skills and items to actually fight your enemies in real time.
Graphics are good, I did enjoy both hacking and slashing, and browsing through on-board adventures (not all of the cards include you teleporting to the arena and fighting monsters, obviously enough). The dealer is a nifty masked dude with creepy yet charismatic voice (you might expect a new announcer with it in Dota 2, though), which follows his own rules and easily admits defeat if you slay his henchmen.
As you progress through the storyline, you encounter more powerful enemies and gather a stronger loot. Every scenario is unique, thanks to the randomizer -- you can even call these levels procedurally generated, rogue-like style: every time you start over, both scenario decks (yours and dealer's) are shuffled, and you're getting a new adventure each time you start over.
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
I'd strongly recommend this game to all of the RPG fans out there -- it's a breath of refreshing air on the modern RPG scene, really. If you're not into RPG, you might want to check the game out anyway -- it's well-done and interesting to play overall.

Very impressive - Said as a seasoned player of roleplaying games.
This has got me very excited about Dramagames potential!
My most immersive roleplaying experience yet.
I'd start by saying this game won't be to everyone's taste.
The basic premise is that you assume the role of a character, you must then pretend or roleplay to be that character and improvise as a story unfolds. The stories vary, often with different variables that change to create replayability and unpredictability. You are given a nice concise bit of information about your character with some extra details such as recent history you witnessed. This means you are given all the tools to roleplay your character and the backstory elements which often involve other characters too give you something to talk about right off the bat.
Most of these ideas however aren't something completely new or unimagined, I mean I've played many a roleplay game and many have dabbled in these devices. What really blew my mind was the immersion, I instantly felt a completely different roleplaying experience to any I've had before. All text is processed into a voice, each voice different to match the character. The quality of this dubbing is really good, I have no problem imagining these are real voices and while at times they do sound a little Hawking, most of the time they work great. The voices change in tone to match what you're saying depending on buzzwords and such, these are matched with animations too to get the point across. The visuals are great and the way the camera works is again really good at creating immersion. Conversations are managed well, allowing you to click to look to people in your convo as you talk to them and such.
I could now go on about the other features but you could read about that or learn it elsewhere couldn't you?
I think I covered my points enough, to summarise.
Very interesting, immersive roleplaying game.
To avoid any confusion this game grants you free access to one scenario that changes every month, to access the others you must subscribe. Very fair considering subscribing is only half the price of a sandwich anyways.
-Hint if you sub and want to find games (but it looks like no-one is online), hit the forums and join the steam group!

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to be a depressed teenage girl based off of a British romantic poet? No? Well, you should.
Asphyxia is a grim game that wholly deserves the attention of all its readers. Don't be deceived by the cute art, the game focuses on the worrying condition of the protagonist and the troublesome life she follows. Any fan of literature will enjoy this game, as it feels like a classic novel. But, whether you know the poets or not, the game does a splendid job of getting you into the characters. If you do know the poets though, you'll find your nerdy poetry loving heart a little tickled as there are a number of things you'll just /get/. In the extras, there are biographies of the poets that you can read for more insight as well.
The writing is great and it captures the condition of Samantha perfectly. Samantha is a realistic character and if you read through it and find yourself unable to relate to all her plights, know that I have. This game had me leaning over to see if my secret stash of angsty poetry had been invaded.
I can say that I don't regret this at all, and I don't think many people will. It's a wonderful piece of writing and it sweeps you along into all the emotions involved. It's grim, emotional, depressing and a great experience.

This is a visual novel with several endings. There is quite heavy subject matter, if you prefer to avoid that, this VN may not be for you. I've divided this review into two parts - gameplay and story/emotional impact of the game.
I feel the execution of this game was done quite well. I've tried 3 or 4 different routes so far (there seem to be more to discover) and the way new content is presented as you make different choices flows quite smoothly, in contrast to some games where extra/different routes may seem a bit clunky. I really enjoyed the writing, clearly a lot of knowledge and research went into this, and it's nice to see an 18th, 19th century British literature influenced writing style. That said, it may be a bit stuffy to read at first and the characters seem very pompous, but that is due to the influences and style the game has. The art is quite gorgeous, and while eerie I think it is perfect for this VN. I felt that my choices do matter, and in trying to please everyone, ended up turning everyone away (one or more of the routes).
You will be put into the head of someone who is depressed, quite literally. You'll follow her thoughts and inner dialogue. For me, I got irritated, but then reconciled in cycles, even if I knew that these thoughts cannot be controlled by the mind you are in. The dialogue hit me hard, because a lot of it was the eerily similar with conversations I would have with a friend, who would in real life, explain her mind like how Samantha does. The dynamics are captured very well, and hit me in a very personal, emotional spot. I've had ups and downs with said person, and the dialogue for both the good parts and bad parts are relatable and it hurt.
This game is amazing, to me. It made me feel emotions like The Cat Lady has been able to produce in me. It hits home and I relate to it from past experiences. I would try to find all the endings right this instance, if I didn't have exams. And I will - this game, after reading only a couple endings, has constantly been on my mind. [Edit: shortly before exams I found all the endings...] I know this game is not for everyone - if you don't like VNs, if you don't like depression and other heavy themes, please stay away. Subjectively, I highly recommend this game.

Let’s get one thing 100% cleared out of the way:
As the title may suggest, this is a pretty grim game.
Despite the fairly colourful visuals, there are some pretty heavy themes (one of which may or may not be clinical depression) going on, not to mention everyone seems pretty short with each other and prone to casually bringing up suicide and death.
That established, let’s look at this:
This game has a very interesting art style; like a water colour painting with some Lolita influences. Characters are sufficiently expressive, and there are some really beautiful shots and backgrounds to be seen. I don’t think this is going to be everyone’s cup of tea, but I can’t think of many other titles that had as distinctive art work.
The game also has quite a unique writing style, though not without faults. Clearly based on the writing that came out of the Romantic Era (or there about), the very formal and ‘proper’ pool of words used is entreatingly varied and vivid. It’s refreshing to read, and has some very effective descriptions. The game sometimes has an issue on delivering exposition, and can sometimes come on a little strong when hammering in a point, but overall, I would rate the writing fairly well.
As for the characters, there’s also some interesting things going on, but there are weaknesses. I thought the fact that every character was named after and KIND OF loosely based on old writers and poets was a nice touch, and fit the style of writing. There is certainly a varied cast, each carrying their own themes and touches, with a solid four romantic interests.* However, there’s a weird issue going on: everyone’s kind of short with each other. This makes sense for a lot of the pairings (Roberta and Georgina, for example, who are polar opposites), however everyone feels pretty quick to say aloud the faults they find in the others. Even when it’s meant in good grace and good fun, this comes up oddly often, and makes one or two characters straddle the line to being unlikeable (even if only unlikable for a single scene). Not sure if that’s got something to do with the writing style or anything, but it’s hardly a deal breaker, just an odd quirk.
Overall, I’d say the game was perfectly fine. It has its faults to be sure, and it was never going to be everyone’s kind of thing, but there’s a lot to like in there.
*Edit: I've been told it may not be straight up romance in all of the routes, or that it might be "heavy subtext" etc. Be warned.

Asphyxia is a game in which the major Romantic poets of the late 18th century (Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley et al. though sadly not Blake... though I guess he was kind of a movement unto himself) are reimagined as cute schoolgirls (or, since this is a British game and set in Britain, upper sixth formers :-p)
In this way the game bears some similarities to Ebi-Hime's earlier 'Mahou Shoujo Žižek-chan!' which did the same for Marxist Slovenian philosopher Slavoj Žižek (one kind of fears that the author would prefer a world in which all humans were cute schoolgirls, but it's good she's choosing educational topics!)
As a Brit it's probably a slightly difference experience reading this VN since the characters in the game are all based on poets you probably had to study in school or uni. I'm not an expert, but most people here in Britain will be familiar with Wordsworth's "I wondered lonely as a cloud" and Coleridge's 'Rime of the Ancient Mariner'. This means for me that reading the game can be quite an odd experience as I'm simultaneously seeing these characters as 16/17/18-year-old schoolgirls while at the same time being pretty constantly aware that they're actually a bunch of long dead guys in their 20s (ish). I don't think this would be an issue for most readers though! I quite liked trying to work out which stuff was autobiographical and which stuff is just invention. De Quincey's the only one of the writers who I have read quite a bit of for pleasure so it was funny to think that all the weird stuff concerning their character was pretty much based on truth (i.e. the troubling fetishisation of murder; the relationship with the violent older brother; the emotional attachment to a young girl who died - in reality, Wordsworth's daughter I think). De Quincey's probably the most entertaining character in the game though that might depend on your tolerance for zany, selfish, boundary-pushing and inappropriate characters like Excel Excel or Haruhi Suzumiya etc.
*SPOILERS* The only thing I felt unsure about (so far) is the stuff with
To my knowledge that never happened in real life and it felt like a potential slur against a long-dead poet... that said, De Quincey was kind of a jerk and behaved in lots of inappropriate ways so it wasn't exactly out-of-character. But yeah... it left me with an odd taste in my mouth I guess.
One of the other reviews said they felt the art was creepy because it is infantilising and sexualising. I don't think so myself... though I can see that De Quincey's outfits means that the character borders on the fanservicey. That said, 'Asphyxia' contains no sex scenes or graphic content whatsoever so it's already less creepy than a massive amount of other novels in the medium and I certainly wouldn't be put off buying it on the grounds of sexual infantilisation like I was with the similarly pretty, watercolour looking 'Littlewitch Romanesque' (a shame cause otherwise it looks good!)
Actually, I somewhat wonder if there is a bit of a cultural split going on here because the British age of consent (and remember Asphyxia is both set in Britain and written by a British writer) is 16 rather than 18 in America so it might seem slightly less troubling having a 17-year-old character like Coleridge talking about having had sex or a character like De Quincey wearing revealing outfits. That said, I can see that the art arguably makes the characters look even younger though TBH I find this with most manga / anime-style art and though it does trouble me a little I just kind of accept it's part of the visual style.
And the art strikes me as pretty damn assured - certainly there's a good grasp of shading and line-work and anatomy drawing etc. The art is certainly a step-up from Ebi-Hime's previous Steam game 'The Way We All Go', which was highly variable in quality.
That said, story-wise I found 'The Way We All Go' more dramatic and enjoyed the horror elements. 'Asphyxia' feels a bite more slice of life though the momentum really picks up once
Perhaps a weird comparison but it reminded me of that episode of
in which Mark and Jeremy get lost in the Quantocks, what with all the bickering! It's definitely a character-driven game though and I found the characters engaging and interesting and liked that there were secrets from their back-stories / pasts to discover.
Sometimes the game can feel a little static perhaps... though I know it isn't in the style of visual novels, I kind of wish the characters would have gestured when angry or just generally looked less composed. It suits the slightly formal and fancy writing style though - personally I didn't find it pretentious (I mean it all makes sense and there aren't any over-reaching or nonsensical metaphors) though sometimes it feels a little odd that this is presumably modern-day Britain but the characters still talk more like there were in the 18th or 19th century (save for Byron's modern-day swears). But I think it's just a matter of having characters based on real people from the past.
While the writing really excels is in its sly humour. There are lots of good jokes - though always laugh-out-loud, but often wryly amusing and clever. The tone can get a bit cynical, but I think the emotional earnestness kind of balances that out.
Overall it's definitely a strong and professional-looking game, especially worth your time if you like character stuff with a melancholy edge or have any interest in the autobio lives of British Romantic poets! Asphyxia aspires to be this groundbreaking, poetic piece of writing, but in doing so treads the same tired ground we've seen countless times throughout lgbt media. I ask you, writers of the world over, what about "happy lesbians" vexes you? Better yet, why are you so bent on sad gays?
While I'm not done digging at the writing, I'd like to pause to mention the art. The character models are designed to maximize loli-appeal, in that they're dually infanticizing and sexualizing. It's creepy, and also doesn't mesh with the narrative. Our protagonist is described every scene as an absolute wreck, but how am I supposed to believe that when her model is a perfect porcelain doll?
As for the writing in general, the piece can only be described as stylistically arrogant, too caught up in its own self-assured greatness to actually go anywhere. Imagery is used seemingly without cause or care. The characters are drawn too far into the pits of despair to be relatable to any but the most unfortunate of individuals.
The game fumbles with  a number of difficult, powerful themes; substance abuse, suicide, homelessness, mental illness, manipulative relationships, girl x girl romance, and other assorted feminist issues; in a display that comes across as mocking to each of those themes.
And that's another matter: there is no closure here. Zero. If you are twisted into some form of attachment to the plot threads or characters, you're bound to be dissapointed by how those are cut and forgotten, in a sort of meta-commentary about how the stories of the marginalized are discarded and ignored, though I can't imagine such insight was intended.

Metro: Last Light-Redux is a first person shooter and is the continuation of Metro: 2033-Redux and takes place after you launched the missiles blowing up the Dark Ones. Even if you got the good ending (didn't blow up the Dark Ones) this game takes place in the very near future as if you did launch the missiles killing all of the dark ones...or did you kill them all?! Soon after you start the game you find out that, at least, one Dark One survived..but its much smaller then the others were (perhaps a child?). Its now your job to find that "last" Dark One and kill it so their threat has been completely removed from this destroyed/dieing world that you live/exist in.

M:LL-R (Metro: Last Light-Redux) is very similar to the first game in that bullets are still currency and just about everything you come across either wants to kill you or kill you AND eat you! I must make this absolutely clear..EXPLORING PAYS OFF!! Its not without its own risks but usually the rewards out weigh (provided your aim/reaction time is good) the increased chance of injury/death. Search everywhere for keys and their safe counterparts so you can get some decent loot (generally a small cache of "Special" bullets with some ammo/med-packs).

If you want to play loud and proud (shooting without silencers/stealth kills) you can do that. Letting everyone know you're coming and their isn't a damn thing they can do about it!! If you want to play stealthly (my personal favorite style) that can pay off more as long as you're perceptive and patient. Stealth doesn't necessarily mean slow..it just means, as I said before, being PERCEPTIVE and PATIENT..waiting for enemies to path to the most advantagious areas for you to take out so other enemies don't find their bodies and ruining your stealth. Its a lot of fun going through a whole area knocking out/killing all the enemies while never raising the alarm..makes you feel like a badass.

I personally followed a 100% achievement walkthrough and it showed me where to go/what to do to get the most out of the game and makes it much easier to get those "easy to miss" items/achievements. If you don't like to use strategy guides thats fine. You won't need them to play/enjoy/beat this game. Its story is, imo, excellent and you can't help but feel for those who are suffering around you. You want to help them and doing so, usually, nets you positive morality points.

Morality is..somewhat important in this game. It affects how some view you but mostly it affects the ending of the game. Have a mostly positive morality and you get what the game has deemed a the "good" ending (usually less needless death is involved with that ending). If you preferred to be a mean/uncaring person and don't care about morality then..yep you guessed it..you get the "bad" ending. Many positive/negative morality points aren't exactly easy to find..as I said earlier..exploring tends to pay off. Some are easy to understand, steal a bullet from a beggars cup..negative morality point. Donate/give a bullet to a begger..get a positive morality point.

There are several different types of guns/weapons (including grenades and throwing knives) of which you can customize (limited though it may be) to your liking. Silencers, scopes, extended barrels, laser pointers etc can be added/removed from your weapons to help suit your play style. You can find most combinations of guns/attachments throughout the game whether its off of decaying bodies or enemies you knocked out/killed or you can get them from gun merchants (that option is going to cost you money....bullets).

I could go on for a decent amount more but I'll bring this review to an end with this last bit. The overall gameplay feels solid and is great experience. If you liked the first game you will like the second one. I'd give this game an 8 out of 10 if you are the type of person who likes seeing a number rating system and/or requires one to objectively view/review a game. Theres so much more I want to tell you but if I do it would ruin your emersion into the world/environment and you'd hate me for it. Purchase this game..you won't be disappointed (I sure wasn't..bought this game, and beat it, twice..once for the original games and again for the Redux versions).

Should you buy/play this game then good luck and have fun.

This game is the most breathtaking single-player story-driven FPS I have ever played in all of my life. Every time I play it, every time I watch gameplay from it, every time I
, I get chills that run up my arms.
This game throws you headfirst into the recovering wasteland of Russia, where there is still a political struggle for power in the Metro tunnels beneath the landscape. The Rangers have recently gained a valuable asset to use against the Nazis and the Reds, and everyone wants a piece of it. I'd rather you find out the rest of the beautifully-crafted story on your own, so I'll get into how the game works and how it runs.
First, it's extremely important to note that this is the sequel to Metro 2033. You shouldn't play one without the other. I made this review on Last Light mainly because it's my favorite of the two games (until Metro: Exodus hopefully!) With that being said, if you just bought Last Light, I highly suggest you get 2033 and play that through first. It's very important to the storyline!
Now we can get onto what makes this game so great. Metro: Last Light, like 2033, puts you in the place of Artyom, a Ranger who has some sort of strange connection to the Dark Ones, the main antagonists from 2033. I won't reveal anything past that. Artyom fights through the Metro several times to kill something, explore something, save something, etc. etc. I'm sorry that I'm not revealing anything more, I just really want you to experience it firsthand. You are greeted with a very immersive interface, a wide variety of customizable weapons, and some useful gadgets that you don't always see in games like this.
Artyom comes out of the box with a watch, a map, a lighter shaped like a bullet, a knife, a compass, a flashlight, a charger, a medkit or two, and your trusty gasmask. The struggle for filters in this game isn't nearly as bad as it was in 2033, but radiation is still present, so your gasmask will come in handy constantly. Occasionally, you'll be blocked by thick webs, or at least slowed down by a few in your path. The lighter can burn these cobwebs, freeing yourself in the process, or it can be used to ward off the spiderbugs, which think the sun is a deadly laser. The map itself isn't actually used, but there is a compass built into it and a piece of paper listing your objectives. To be honest, you won't be using this much. Your flashlight is great for times when you need a large gun out *and* a wide beam of light, but it needs charged at certain points in time. Luckily, this won't hinder gameplay at all, as it gets charged using your hand-powered charger. The hand-powered charger also helps unlock areas by providing power. Gasmask filters are limited in the game, but it's fairly easy to find them and stock up, and each filter lasts 5 minutes. You usually aren't in irradiated areas for more than 10, so you'll be alright. If you lose track of time, your watch will beep and remind you when to change filters. The beeping usually starts a minute before it runs out, so I usually wait until there are 15-20 seconds left on the filter in order to change it, as not to waste anything. In Ranger modes and Hardcore modes (correct me if I'm wrong), the watch does not tell you how much time is left on your filter, but it is a functioning watch, so when you change filters, check the time. Check your watch every once in a while and make sure you aren't running low. I shouldn't have to tell you what your knife and your medkit do.
Although this isn't a frightening game itself, you'll constantly find yourself worried, heart beating fast, as you try not to break stealth on lots of missions. It doesn't help that a lot of animated sequences look like a death animation, even though in reality it's just a plot point. Almost any stealth mission can be completed loud, but it is much more difficult in my personal opinion, and it wastes valuable resources that you could be using for the bosses that appear in Last Light. Oh, and just a heads-up: Last Light has a lot more bosses than 2033.
Also, there is always two ways to complete a Metro game. There is a good ending and a bad ending. Bad endings happen when you've killed lots of enemies when you didn't need to, or do something selfish rather than selfless. Good endings happen when you choose to knock out most of your enemies from behind, or save Rangers from certain death, or even something as simple as pressing F on an instrument in some town or giving a bullet or two (the currency, not your ammunition) to a beggar. I suggest playing the game through and experimenting with what gives you "karma", and then playing it through again with the other ending. I sort of ruined my experience by reading a guide right away, giving me the good ending in both games. I have to tell you, it was sort of a pain getting the good ending. But I liked it.
Last thing. Last Light Redux comes with every DLC available. Once you play through the game, go to the New Missions tab (it should be under Missions, and then you can press Q to see New Missions) and play through the DLC missions. The Spider Lair was my favorite DLC by far.

TL;DR: This might be one of the best Arcade Racers out there. However, the PC port is quite broken. If you play this version, use a 360 Controller, use a keyboard for the menus, make sure to remap the controls to something that makes sense, use driver settings to force AA/AF/VSync if you want them, and be prepared for the occasional crash. If you don't want to deal with these issues, then try to find a copy of the PS2 version.
Midnight Club 2 is the second and (in my opinion) best game in the Midnight Club series. The Midnight Club series has often been compared to the Grand Theft Auto series as they share the same publisher. However, these are two very different game series. Midnight Club is much more focused on being a racing game, whereas Grand Theft Auto is a much more open ended game with a lot more than just racing. This often makes the Midnight Club games a much better racing experience, as all of the development time has been put into making the racing as best as it can be.
The racing itself is very tight and controlled. There's never any time where you feel like the game isn't responding to your input. The game has you race at very fast speeds, but your turns feel tight and drifting is powerful and fun. Through the early game, you unlock different abilities that slowly increases what you can do in the races. Each of these abilities is simple to understand and is well balanced. All of the abilities, along with the games great control, makes for interesting and varied gameplay.
It's important to mention the unlocks system in this game. Some games use a shop system that allows you to buy and upgrade cars you like. Midnight Club 2, however, uses a linear unlock system where you unlock new cars by winning races and you don't upgrade cars. This is a different system from other racing games, even other games in its own series, but I think it helps to focus the game. Instead of trying to win races to unlock money to get better cars, you win races for the races themselves. Some people may not like that, but it's one of the reasons I think this game is great.
The races themselves are open checkpoint style. That means that while you're required to go through all the checkpoints in order, the game allows you to take any path you want between them. This means that finding the right path and shortcuts to take is just as important as driving fast. There are even a handful of races that allow you to hit the checkpoints in any order you want, opening up the game and letting you experiment on what route gives you the best chance to win. This makes it so that when you have to restart a race because you lost, you don't necessarily feel like you are stuck. With maps that allow for a lot of shortcut opportunities and varied routes, there is always another, possibly better route you can try.
There are three relatively large maps in this game, each one modeled after a different city. Los Angeles is probably the most varied in terms of road types, ranging from small, windy paths to city blocks to high-speed highways to construction sites with lots of ramps to jump off of. Paris has a lot of shortcuts that makes finding your path a lot of fun, along with the catacomb system and numerous large jumps that makes the city feel very open. Tokyo is a bit more mundane than the other cities, but since you get there late in the game when races go well over realistic speeds, you will be happy for the larger roads that makes it easier to dodge traffic and other racers. Each city feels unique, with different environment textures and building making them visually distinct and varied layouts making them play differently.
The characters in this game fall flat. Many of them are stereotypes from all over the world added in an attempt to make the game feel more worldly. However, this backfires in many places, with the characters often feeling more like caricatures than actual people. However, they really only play a small role in the game, with only short introductory scenes before each race and the occasional and ignorable quip during the races. Luckily, there is no player character, so there's no single annoying character that carries you through the game.
This game is very difficult, but isn't unfair. This is because the game has a very slow and approachable learning curve. If you've never played a racing game before, this game starts easy enough to get you into it. If you're already a good racer, than you can fairly easily blow through the first easy races and start getting to the more challenging races. If you're really good, then you might need some patience to through the easier races, but trust me, there is a challenge waiting for you in this game. The last few races are brutally difficult and require many, many attempts to beat, but the difficulty smoothly increases, so you never hit any real difficulty spike.
Midnight Club 2 is, in my opinion, the best in the series. Midnight Club: Street Racing (the first in the series) didn't really know what it was doing, having much slower races and no abilities like the slipstream turbo to make the gameplay more varied. Midnight Club 3: DUB Edition suffered in a lot of weird ways. The lackluster upgrade system, a poor sense of progression, and an unnecessary amount of motion blur makes it much less fun to play than its predecessor. Midnight Club: Los Angeles (the forth in the series) is one of the better racing games out there, but suffers from a fairly broken upgrade system that lets you get the best vehicle in the game by the time your half way though, leaving the rest of the game to just be a grind. Midnight Club 2 is also the only game to get a PC port, so none of the other games in the series is available on Steam anyways.
Speaking of PC ports, this game certainly has some trouble on the platform. First of all, this game needs to be played with a controller. The keyboard controls do not provide the control needed, and the mouse controls are just too awkward to use. However, the controller support in this game is kind of broken. I've had success with the Wireless 360 Controller, so I recommend using that. Some controllers (the PS4 controller for example) causes an odd bug where the menus think that the center of the joystick is the top-left corner, causing the menu selection to uncontrollably scroll. I can't say for every controller out there if this happens or not, so be careful before buying. In addition, the default controller mappings are quite broken, but you can manually remap the controls. Note, however, that it doesn't support "analog buttons", so you can't use the 360 controller's triggers as buttons. Additionally, it lacks many graphical settings, like AntiAliasing, Anisotropic Filtering, and VSync, so you will need to turn them on from your driver if you want them. The game also has a number of smaller issues that may not be worth naming, but can impact your playing experience (some of which is dependent on your resolution). If you want to play this game, but don't want to deal with this port's issues, then I'd recommend playing the PS2 version. There’s also an Original Xbox port, but there’s no compatibility for the 360.
In the end, I’d recommend this game. It’s one of the best Arcade Racers I’ve ever played, and is even the game that got me into the genre. I do highly recommend you pick it up, but do be weary of the quality of this port.

Unless you're interested in playing competitively, and learning every abstract technique in the book, just play it with friends. The swordplay is really crazy and fun, but the community mostly consists of veterans with thousands of hours. This makes the learning curve almost entirely vertical, as you'll never have the chance to test your mettle against people of similar skill. You will most likely die to veterans without fully understanding why, again and again. If you can overlook the skill disparity between veterans and newcomers, there is a really enjoyable and deceptively complex experience to be had.
Most veterans are beginner friendly, willing to teach anyone who is willing to learn. In fact, there is even a pinned thread in the Steam forums where players can offer/request coaching. That being said, there are a handful of high-level players who perpetrate a toxic environment by insulting anyone of a lower skill level than themselves. These people are best ignored, as they often get stomped by the more approachable veterans.
If you're looking for a Medieval swordfighting game with a high skill ceiling, and you don't care about "immersion-breaking bugs," buy at full price. It's absolutely worth every single penny.
If you're looking for an immersive online Medieval swordfighting experience, you might be disappointed. Wait until the next Free to Play Weekend, and try it before you buy.

Back then, when CD-ROM was the top notch technology that was available in the market, there was a day when I was going through a news stand and suddenly my jaws dropped on the floor. I've seen this game for sale for a bargain, and since I was a huge fan of FPS games, and most of titles that you'd find to purchase were often very expensive, I didn't think twice before investing all my savings into it.
So ok, I've got home as quickly as possible, installed the game and I was delighted with the beginning of the story (even though I didn't really know what was going on anyway). So I've played for a while, then for some reason I thought that the game was getting scary (even though it had such crappy graphics, it was like playing in Full HD nowadays), so I got into this part that I've got lost for some reason and I couldn't find a way to beat the level. Even though there were some walk-throughs available online, they were usually written in English, and since mine was something really basic back then, as it's not really my native language, and there was no YouTube available at the time, I suddenly stopped playing it. After a while, some other games came by and this one was forsaken in the past.
Well, many years passed by and now there's no more physical media, it's all about Steam. During one of the first sales that I had the honor of participating, I've suddenly noticed this game to purchase, yet again. I don't know why, it must have been because of some kind of nostalgia (or simply the great bargain that I could get), I decided to buy it again. Anyway, this time I decided that I should put an end to some unfinished business.
It can be kinda tricky to evaluate some old releases nowadays, because they can be surely seen as something outdated. Either way, in my opinion, I'd say that this could be a "Quake's poor cousin" kind of game. It's been a while since the last time I've played this, so I don't remember much about it, so I can't say much about the story. As for the graphics, they're not the greatest thing in the world, if you want to compare with the things that we have available today, but I don't really think that it's an issue. The music and sound effects are ok. As for the gameplay, it's basically an old school FPS, nothing else to say.
Ok, during my second playthrough, I decided to be much more tolerant than I was before. There were some parts that I really couldn't find my way out, and I tried really hard, only that this time my English had improved a little more, so I could check on some walk-throughs and watch some videos that really helped me out. There're actually many levels available; back then I didn't have the slightest idea that this was such a long game. There were times that I felt really bored while playing this, but whenever I'd see it on my to-do list, I'd take a deep breath before resuming the adventure. After all these years, I've finally managed to put an end to that story.
What are my final thoughts about it? I don't think that it's a bad game, but I seriously wouldn't like to pick it again to play nowadays. Even though there were some really tedious parts during the playthrough, there were also some moments that I truly enjoyed what I was doing, so I have no regrets. Life goes on.

Well done sequel to Euro Truck Simulator 2. If you're a fan of the first, this entry improves the experience abit in some areas.
+ Graphics seem crisper, smoother - though bottlenecks seem to occur on full settings near cities (a problem with ETS2 as well).
+ The trucks feel/drive live big 'ol American trucks should.
+ The randomized parking option is nice, a new challenge when completing deliveries (optional if you want it).
+ The RPG aspect adds a little interest to your character-building, though it never feels like it has a profound impact on the game results.
+ The roads look/feel like Southwest American roads.
+ Varied towns and companies
- You only have two trucks in this game at the moment, which is very limiting when compared to what was offered in ETS2.
- The map is small by ETS2 standards - covering just California and parts of Nevada. In just over 3 hours I've covered about a quarter of the routes.
- The developers still havent addressed certain aspects such as questionable driver AI and very-short on-ramps. These feel carried over from EST2.
- Some of the major towns/cities feel desolate at times and there are few people walking about. Others are just fine and feel teeming with life.
Overall, despite its inherent shortcomings, I'm enjoying my early days with this game. It's a nice respite from life that can keep you busy in 30-45min spurts (or all day if you want). For $20, it's a worthy successor to what ETS2 has already established.

Valkyria is a game in the vein of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, at least at first glance, with turn-based combat that emphasizes cover as well as permadeath for your units. While XCOM focuses on a series of randomized missions, however, Valkyria has missions that are hand-crafted, with enemy positions and events all being pre-determined.
This means that every mission is highly linear, though also that it comes with its own unique challenges. Each mission feels almost like solving a puzzle, figuring out how to optimally utilizing your units, reloading a save if things go badly (and trust me, you will want to save, a lot, even if doing so takes a chunk of the tension away).
Each mission, or chapter, basically feels like an episode of an anime. You get a series of cutscenes elaborating on the plot, followed by a single battle containing some unique gimmick to master or overcome, like traversing an exposed desert with little cover (which conveniently enough has sandstorms obstructing vision at regular intervalls).
While the linear nature of the missions can be seen as a detriment, i found it enjoyable to have each new mission throw something new at me, approaching it more like a puzzle than a strategy game. The game also keeps this up for around 30 hours, so you are in for a lengthy experience, considering it is all linear story. This also means that the story is what drives the game forward. Thus, if a story about the harsh reality of war, viewed through a light anime-lens (which takes away a lot of the shock and horror you'd expect) does not sound appealing, then the basic gameplay might get dull in the long run. If you
like anime-style storytelling and turn-based combat, however, this is a game i will highly recommend, especially for the asking price (even more so during sales).

Velvet Sundown has an interesting premise. Take a role as a member of a luxury yacht cruise and play your part while trying to acheive shady goals to appease one fo two rival corporations or simply your own pocket. Conversations are handled with surprisingly effective text-to-speech tech that gives players the ability to freetype their dialogue while remaining in character. Business cards are exchanged, drinks are drunk and tasers are used. It's fun for a while but clearly not finished.
The goalds are often very difficult as they involve either trusting others or getting others to trust you. If you have to find some information, for example, you basically have to speak to everyone and carefully try to find out if they have what you're looking for. There's a tight 30 minute time-limit too, making this even harder. Relying so much on every single player being totally into the game and willing to realistically trust or mistrust others is risky and often leads to dissapointment. If the player holding all the data disconnects, for instance, the round is lost, although no-one has any idea this is the case.
It also only takes one nutter rambling to break the role-playing immersion. In almost every game I played there was at least one person proposing sex, demanding passports for no clear reason or claiming to be Batman.
If the game was in Early Access the serve lack of balance could be forgiven but not only is this being shopped as a finished game, in order to play more than one small scenario a £4 per month subscription is required. Why anyone would subscribe is beyond me but the fact is the developers seem to think it's worth it.
I can't recommend the game at any stretch but I'm sincerely hoping the conversation techlology makes it into other games and the idea of the social multiplayer thriller is not confined to this one title. If you fancy a different experience to your usual shooters and RPGs, download this for free and give it a go with a friend. If anything you'll have a funny, if surreal, new experience.

Want more mana gain from your attacks or when you're recieving damage so you can you use more skills in a dungeon/pvp? Well you can just buy a mana necklace for 8$ more for a pernament version.
Want a nice pet? pay up. Do you want that pet to pick up all your drops from the dungeon? You got to pay even more on top of that. Anyways, the game is really repetitive/grindy.. no surprise for your typical Korean MMO. Endgame revolves around you repeating the same dungeons to complete daily quests. PVP is completely unbalanced starting from the characters and to the gear and bonuses some costumes give. The pay2win factor can really be noticed there.
Don't get me started on the economy. Due to inflation and like zero money sinks, this game's currency (ED) is pretty much considered worthless. I always wondered why Korea Elsword always had a better economy compared to their other region counterparts. It just makes me think that KOG and KOG GAMES (gamer's publisher/developer) doesn't care at all for the nonKorea servers and just sees an opportunity to squeeze as much money as possible from us. Also there's a stamina system in this game that limits how much you can play each day .
This game is indeed fun though with its combat, and I really do love the character designs also (especially Aisha's and Ara's) .It might be fun at first, but after reaching max level and grinding dailes to craft gear... I was like what's the point if I'm struggling to play this game regularly without using my wallet frequently. If you're not going to spend  money on this game especially for pvp, I wouldn't even bother playing it. The combat got boring after repeating the same dungeons over and over. I would say it's better to pass on this game and play something else.

So there's three "warfare" games, all Russian in origin but with some differences in who developed them. I've beaten this game two or three times, on normal to hard difficulty. After this one came "Warfare Reloaded" where you play as the Russians against the US in Afghanistan. I can't even review that one, because it's not sold on Steam, probably because it's AI is mentally handicapped and one mission won't end even after you complete the objectives. The third one is "Syrian Warfare", and I'll review that one next. This one is the first, the best, and the other two aren't worth touching.
Gameplay:
You get a limited force to start each mission with, you will sometimes get reinforcements mid-mission. How you perform in each mission affects what assets you will have available in the next. If a unit gains experience in a mission and survives, you get to use it as a more experienced and effective unit in the next mission. The more guys you keep alive and the more enemies you kill, the more command points you have available next time, which you can use to get new and better units. You can capture enemy vehicles as well.
If you're lucky, you'll have infantry, light and heavy armored vehicles to command, possibly even choppers, artillery, and rarely the ability to call for airstrikes. Ammo and fuel have to be replenished, so protect the vehicles that store these things. Your environments range from open desert to big cities. Your objectives can be as straightforward as taking over an area or as complex as search and rescue. You cannot Zerg rush your way through this game. Each part of your force must support and protect the others, and be on guard, because you can never be totally sure what's coming up the first time playing. There is some micromanaging of the troops involved, but not too much, Just don't send anything but the toughest units out unsupported.
Story: The Russians are no friends of ours, but they have zero love for jihadis, and they wrote an unintentionally pro-American game. By paying close attention to the "war journals" "news tickers" and cutscenes, I have surmised that the story goes like this: Spoilers in the next paragaph.
America won in Iraq and Afghanistan, and those wars came to a close. But then the
Saudi clerics, Al Qaeda and radicalized Saudi Arabian Army joined forces against the King of Saudi Arabia, aiming to create a Caliphate starting with the most oil-rich nation in the Middle East. The King, along with the Saudi police and National Guard, ask for American assistance. The King, like most petro-monarchs, is opulent and surrounded by sycophants, but with American help they survive, get their act together and govern after American forces drive the jihadis out. Russian writers were careful to ocassionally include the tropes of the "ignant" American soldier and "it's only because of the oil, maaaan" but they didn't change the overall fact that America was fighting against a movement of characters even the Russians couldn't love.
Was it Fun?: It sure was. You learn as you play; the tip screens come in the appropriate scenarios, but they don't hold your hand. Once you've learned to be careful of mines and the ATGMs off in the distance that might kill or incapacitate in one hit, you will soon have the hang of this game. It's fun, once you've drawn up your line of battle, to see your units at work, moving as you please and blazing away at the enemy. Play it with Five Finger Death Punch's "Bad Company" in the background, as your forces move on towards victory.
The explosions and gradual building destruction are gorgeous. Good attention is paid to unit detail. The Arab-accented voice acting is so bad that it's good. And this game won't empty your wallet.

This game is truly an incredible surprise.  It is only a card game in the sense that there are random elements and you get to pick some of the deck those elements are drawn from.  It is only an action game in the sense that you play the encounters you draw, but these encounters are not as tiresome and repetitive as in most 3D action brawlers.  It is only a RPG in the sense that you pick, sell, buy, and loot equipment with different properties and you can choose a "fate" for your character that changes the rules of the game.  But if you take those pieces and put them together, and add in elements of choose-your-own-adventure and rogue-likes, you get a unique, fun, changing game with beautiful presentation.  If you only tried it in early access, try it again.  I was shocked when I went back to this in my library.

This game is effectively Pay to play/Pay to win due to the following mechanics:
I can not use the auction house with spending money of buying a license off of someone with an excessive amount of gold.
I can not open any of the loot dropped without spending "Labor" which accumilates at a rate of 5 per 5 minutes only when logged online. Opening a green drop at level 20-30 costs 30 Labor. Labor is also used for almost everything you do in the game like crafting, harvesting, openning drops, etc... and your Labor cap is 2000. If you pay the monthly fee then the Labor cap is 5000 and it generates at 10 per 5 minutes online or offline.
Storage breaks this game also. Storage is fine until around level 20. You have 50 slots in your bag and another 50 slots in your warehouse (bank). Expanding this becomes the problem. It costs 300 credits to expand it 10 slots which translates to $2 every expansion scroll. Expansion scrolls can be bought in the auction house but the going rate is around 75 gold which I have yet to accumulate at around level 27.
Crafting is very extensive and normally I would consider this a good thing but with the issues of "Labor" and storage it makes having to craft extremely annoying.
I can not recommend this game mainly due to the greedy descisions made by XLGames and Trion. This game has much potential but ALL of the above issues need to be fixed.

This game...i am conflicted...the story isn't half bad,lots of kawai girls and all sorts of dudes to pick from,though let's be honest,you'll probably only end up using a handful of them,(*cough* 9 characters deployed with a 20 unit roster *cough*),anyways,my praises go to how the game is presented,in all forms,sometimes you get a cutscene,sometimes you got closeups of them talking,and even in cobat it gives you a feel of looking through a comic book(as best as i can describe it),as even when you shoot the word "bata" pops out of tank turrets,per bullet(bata-bata-bata-bata etc),each character presented has their own small piece of development put into them,and trust me,there's A LOT of them,and i didnt find the charater dialogue stupid at all(by this i mean: *main enemy pops out of nowhere with a grand entrance*,*some character proceeds to point out villain name several times because why not*),rather,it got to the point,here's the backstory,this is whats going on now,*insert small piece of character dialogue that shows you how 1 and 2 get along* and this is what you need to do,go do it.
My bone to pick with this game though,is wth the gameplay,its unique,of course,its fun,absolutely,but,more often than not i found my characters being completely incompetent of delivering a bullet when enemies were a 2 feet distance,i cant tell you how many times i had to mak a scout run all the way up a hill,simply to proceed carefully align the gun so the very end is practically pressed against their heads for headshots,simply because i wanted them to die without me having 4 characters shoot like a maniacs from only 10-15 feet away,at least for me,the tank controls are awful,just awful,see,you have this AP bar,let's call it stamina bar,it drains as you run only,you can shoot only a couple of predetermined couple of bullets depending on your class per turn,this includes the tank,your tank has this "stamina" bar,so,you think:"oh hey,i can simply move forward a bit,stop to take a shot at some enemies and then drive through the curve over there",welllllllll,you could,except your tank turn to face the direction you were aiming at,so,you drive up,you stop,you enter "aim mode",you take the shot,now proceed to have your tank try to automatically adjust to where you were just looking as you desperately try to get your ***** back together,at this point it's almost like your driver wants to lift the front portion like a bike,and congratulations,you just used up the rest of your "stamina" hopelessly strugling to get your tank to stop spinning,now if you're like me,and just so happen to have some bad luck thrown in there,this is the part where YOU WILL DIE,as this was your last turn,your tank's butt is exposed,and this one jack-*** shoots his equivalent of a bazooka from all the way across the map,miraculously hitting your one weak spot,and you tank blows up in only one shot,GAME OVER,yes,tank dies,you lose,at least in most cases.
it's a fun game,for sure,but i warn you,be prepared to get your butt savagely smacked on harder than when you played the dark souls series.

this is the best game in the franchise and EASILY one of the best driving games of all time. its one of the only games to exist that gives you that street racing feel. the cars all have such a tight feeling to them something that no game has been able to capture. i've tried lots of racing games but i find myself coming back to midnight club 2 time and time again. it really lacks the artificial street racing feel other games have by having you race on a set track that you can't leave with big invisible walls blocking your way. it truly takes away from the whole experience.  the beauty of midnight club is that the race is in an open city, it makes you feel like you're a real underground street racer dodging traffic, the cops, buildings/obstacles its fantastic. midnight club 2 takes you from the streets of los angeles, to the parisian back roads to the tight city streets of tokyo. 3 great open cities that really help enhance the experience. accompanied by one of the greatest eletronic soundtracks of all time midnight club 2 has everything you need for the ultimate street racing experience. after many years i truly believe this is the epitome of street racing racing games. its a shame the sequels are nowhere near as good. i highly doubt any other street racing game will ever be able to touch this game.

In a lot of ways, it's an incredible game. It got out in 2003, same year as NFS: Underground and 2 Fast 2 Furious movie came to light, ergo the highest point of the street racing hype. MC2 and Underground were the first succesful big ones to ride that tide.
In my social circles, at the end it all came down to "which one of the two translates 'dat Fast and Furious feel' better". And this question is a bit trickier than it seems at first. While Underground got that slick visuals and style, bullet proof design (advanced tuning + short but intense races), not to mention being succesful reboot of the huge NFS name, Midnight Club 2 offered much more intricate approach to, well, racing. Which lead to constant creation of different "oh,♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; moments and accidents. In my opinion, a lot of them added a bit more of the Fast and Furious franchise ferocity than an endless raw of drag racing showdowns from Underground.
Basically, every race in MC2 is a checkpoint rush. A twist - it all happens in a sandbox level. So your route from point to point doesn't matter while you've hit all of them and finished first. Throughout the game, this simple concept is being fumbled with constantly, presenting you each time a race with a slightly different freedom degree - from a "there's the only straightforward route you can take to win" to "here's a bunch of checkpoints on your map, clear them all as fast as you can, using any route or technique AND in any possible order". Dence traffic and AI racers (who also pick different routes) make sure that every race has some degree of chaos, typically. In general, that's it. And you'd be surprised how much fun it can deliver.
As I see it, there are two major additional points. First, semi-scripted events. Now and then, something happens: say, a truck blocks a way right after that checkpoint. It does that every time in the same way, but what do YOU do with that is, again, up to you. Evade? Drive under it? Make a U-turn and pick a neighbour street? Whatever, just finish first. That and some smart, tight level design (shortcuts, jump ramps etc.) and AI competitors together keep game's chaotic nature fit. No matter how good you know the map and that specific route, every time there's a chance something of the above will intervene, screw everything up and make you rethink your tactics. Such things also spawn those bright, memorable moments, like a car flying just over another car while jumping from the ramp - or crashing into each other and making a huge traffic mess.
Second, game has bikes and, subsequently, bikes-only and mixed "bikes-cars" races. They present a noticeable shift in gameplay mechanics, although it's more of an intermission for the main cars-only play. Still, bikes have their moments.
Sadly, openworld brings the most of MC2's cons, too. Naturally, it's just not that good-looking with all the resource hunger of the big spaces, especially placed near Underground (which is exactly the same age but looks way better). Also, more open space needs more complicated AI, therefore it will glitch, sometimes a lot. There are other problems (e.g. different vehicles are too similar to control, some arcade flicks like two wheels riding feel unnecessary and underbaked), but they are minor compaired to visuals and AI.
Still, in my opinion Midnight Club 2 is a decent game, that brought a lot of hours of fun to me more than 10 years ago. It's core gameplay is solid even now. And while its looks have aged not nearly as well, I absolutely advise to give it a chance. Doubt not, "she's still got it".
P.S. And yes, it works with Windows 7 just fine.

I'm nearing Act 3 as I write this so maybe it'll tank but:
Good:

♥♥♥♥ing custom instruments for your playthrough music?!
You get to make out with Skeleton men, Dwarf dudes, and Elf ladies.
Iffy:
The new armor system. Its good because CC on your guys isn't a total crapshoot. Its bad because once you get a ways into the game there's a TON of armor and you just HAVE to burn guys down ASAP
Moving around feels a bit slower? There's a mod for it though
Why are the achievements still so damn obtuse?!
Bad:
Bugs - apparently there's a big memory leak if you "fast travel" too much. It's a big RPG, if you want a smooth experience wait a month or two
The quest journal tries to be better but fails. It has limited quest markers but never gets rid of them. Updates with more information as you get it but still puts redundant info in there to hide what is actually important
Not terribly well balanced? Physical builds seem quite a bit stronger than magic this time, at least in the early and mid-game.
Overall: If you liked Original Sin 1, or just RPGs in general, this is 100% a no-brainer. If you want to co-op an RPG.... this is a 1000% no brainer.
If you don't like turn based combat - if you don't like having to explore - if you don't like to think outside the box for quest solutions - if you don't like to customize your character or roleplay at all - if you don't like 60+ hour games
Give it a miss.

About the game: Developed by DoubleDutch Games and Published by tinyBuild; SpeedRunners is a competitive-casual game (Yes, I just said that) that can be played with up to 4 players and is quite possibly some of the most fun I've had playing video games with my friends. There is a various selection of characters to play as and as these characters you compete against others to be the last "SpeedRunner" alive whilst using power-ups (such as "The Golden Hook", missiles, Bombs, and a lot more), boosts and the terrain of the maps to your advantage. As one character gets eliminated by going outside of the borders of the screen, the borders get smaller and smaller until there is only one "SpeedRunner" remaining. To win a game, you must win 3 rounds.
Pros:
- This game is extremely fun with friends, honestly some of the most fun I've had playing video games.
- Is very competitive but can also be casual, a strange sort of thing which really works for this game.
- A lot of replay ability because of how much fun it is to play
- Cool and unique characters with some characters you may recognise from other games + there are paid DLC character packs which contain popular YouTubers (and give no game play advantage, strictly cosmetic)
- Exciting fast-paced gameplay.
-Interesting maps that are fun to play on.
- Steam Workshop Support (Anyone can sumbit things onto the Steam "Workshop" and anybody can go and download these things and put them into their own game, at this time the only thing on the Workshop are maps).
- Active Developers who listen to what their community has to say and have been making great updates and additions to the game since 2013.
- Clean and simple graphics that look nice and go well with the game play.
- Although it is in Early Access it feels like a finished game..
Cons:
- Not very fun if you don't have friends to play with.
- Occasional connection issues (although they are very rare and in recent patches are barley present which is good).
- Can be rage-enducing.
Score: 8.5/10
Notes: THIS GAME GOES ON SALE FOR VERY CHEAP VERY OFTEN, SOMETIMES FOR AS LOW AS 3-4$ OR LESS! If you are going to get this game, get it with a group of friends, you won't regret it. This game IS an Early Access game but feels like a finished game. As I quote from Northernlion: "SpeedRunners is Mario Kart on foot, basically."

Ive played this for years, ever since Raven first came out( Before it came to Steam mind you). Things were great at first, fun combat made  my actions planned and less forced, nice mix of characters each with there own unique story, and having my character seem to actually age when i'd reach the next class made me feel like I was growing in the world.
But as time went on, things changed. PVE stayed the same (after some minor additions to help remove inactive players) But everything else began to seem wrong. PVP is broken, I've seen people play as Chung, and picked the class Tactical Trooper, and not even need to fight. I saw these 2 players, both level 70 at the time, face off, and while the other was busy attacking chung, he just sat there, gaining MP from the blows. When he had enough, he pressed ONE skill, dropped a nuke, and it was over, all of the other's HP was gone. And thats COMMON in PVP, just one example of thousands.
Next is the costumizations, yes theres alot to choose from, and most are amazing, but they cost way to much. The only reason people buy them is because if they don't they can't have that crutial edge in a fight, as the best costumes all have fairly decent,(if not overpowering) stat boosts. But to KEEP these little outfits you MUST PAY DOUBLE PRICE TO KEEP IT. If you dont specify that you want it permanently when you first buy it, it will disapear forever after only 30 days. Making you waste all that money is a low blow.
The community isn't to bad, I had a great guild and i'd been a member for most of my time there. But in the more competitive areas thats not really the case, PVP pits you against others based on Rank and not Level, meaning as a poor level 15 I may have to fight a level 80 De-ranker....Yes people derank themselves by losing to people on purpose, then fight there way back up for ammusment. I recommend not even bothering with pvp until your final job class is unlocked at level 35.
The last and probably the worst is what happened to my younger brothers account. He's young and naive so his password wasn't the most secure, and he was unfortunatly targeted by a hacker, after I appealled to costumer support on the issue they asked me to;
1. Have my previously used password
2. a SCREENSHOT of you playing as a character on the account
3. emal address
and so on... I was finally able to give the info and when things seemed to be looking up.
THEY DELETED HIS ACCOUNT, on the grounds that "Sharing your password to others is prohibited"
as if all the time he had spent on his character wasn't bad enough, all the items bought even with real money were erased. My brother was crushed and quit forever, myself shortly after when something similair happened to a guildmate. The support is poor when it really counts, and isn't afraid of quickly saying 'Theres nothing we can do'.
I'd go on but there are many other reviews you could read that have the finer details of the games issues, and to be honest i'm getting a headache remembering all this crap.
Try it yourself if you want, but for your own sake don't buy anything until about 3 months into the game, see if its right for you. No need to break the bank for that swimsuit costume that gives more stats than any armor set...Not even gonna start on THAT one.
