"Daddy, what's a 90s FPS?"
"Unreal, kid. It's Unreal."
Disclaimer: I love Unreal. I'll try and be objective. As tears roll down my face and I tremble before the screen as the adrenaline rush wears off, I'll try and be unbiased. No promises.
(First off, download the (Epic Games approved) 227i patch and you'll fix most problems. Then, you're good to go.)
Yeah, I'm the guy that discusses presentation first, so let's get this out of the way:
Unreal engine 1 is old, and it shows, but as with most well-crafted 90s games, it's mostly the character models and animations that haven't aged quite well. The texturework is great, the weapon models are great, the environments are amazing, imaginative, hell, even the skyboxes are gorgeous. The sound in this game is also top-notch, everything from the music, the gun sounds to the enemy grunts and roars and squeaks, everything is as it should be. Movement in this game is fine-tuned, hyper-responsive and smooth.
And it has to be. Because in ye olde times, some evil genius at Epic games designed the most relentless, punishing,♥♥♥♥♥kicking enemy AI the world has ever shaken a crosshair at. You know how, in some shooters, you kind of become immune to the event of seeing an enemy because you left-click and they disappear? Here, everytime someone jumps in front of your face, you will crap your pants, strafe, jump, shoot until they finally drop dead. Though the enemies are somewhat (*somewhat*) bullet-spongy, the way they move and attack you'd swear there's someone on the other side, sadistically cackling at your feeble attempts at victory. They dodge rockets and projectile weapons, some even use the same weapons you do, and they're hell-bent on splattering your guts all over the wonderful level designs. And you better pray you've managed your ammo well. Because the Dispersion pistol is like throwing beans at an ogre.
Speaking of weapons - no one does weapons like this anymore. THE F&$K HAPPENED, YO?! You've got a measly projectile-based Dispersion pistol, soon replaced by an AutoMag pistol, then things move up from ASDM (aka Shock Rifle) and Ripper (launcher of spinning discs of death) until you get your hands on the fabled Flak Cannon, the Rocket Launcher, the GES BioRifle, a sniper rifle, and two iterations of a Minigun. Every weapon is balanced perfectly, they all have alternate fire modes and ammo is distributed masterfully. That doesn't mean it abounds, it takes considerable restraint not to blow everything at once, but every time you seem to be running low on something, it shows up sooner or later.
We're missing one more piece of the puzzle, the level design. You wake up in a cell on a ship with your Dpistol and your trusty Universal Translator. This is a fairly genius way of slipping both lore and objectives to the player without annoying cutscenes and walls of text to read. The only downside here is that the last thing you looked at with your translator is what appears when you call it up - a "log" function would've been nice, because sometimes, you lose critical objective reminders. For example, you find an engineer's log that says there's a coolant leak and that you should activate the pump so you can access the power generator, which basically means "go here because you need to activate this system to open that door", but then you look at a door and all that useful info gets substituted for a simple door label (Main Hall). I sorta-maybe promised I'd be
objective, and here it goes: while the level design is awesome, the game can turn into a wander-fest fairly quickly if you're not aware of what switch you hit, what switch you have to hit and what your final goal is. I sometimes spent quite some time re-navigating a level if I left it unfinished and came back after a few days. Luckily, the levels have enough detail and polish so that navigation is hardly a problem, and the variety of the environments you move through as you progress the very simple story - get off the planet Na Pali alive and eliminate the Skaarj - also helps to keep you engaged.
Thus, when you combine the uncompromising enemies, the incredible arsenal and the outstanding level design, you have something as close to 90s FPS perfection as you could possibly get. Writing this on Steam feels like treason, but I never understood why Half-Life got all the spotlight and praise and not this exquisite piece. As I mentioned, the level design can get confusing and I'm not a big fan of the "touch switch to activate it" system instead of using a "use" button, but that's really the only thing I can find fault with.
There are certain elements in this game that have been sadly phased out as FPS games changed, for better or worse. If you want to see them showcased in all their glory, this is the title to pick up.

This game is not just not that fun to play. Everytrhing feels needlessly complex without a real payoff. The menus are a pain to slog through. I constantly struggled to get the camera in the right spot to see anything. And good luck findning anything. You have to press a key to see items and that doesn't show half the stuff you actually want to pick up. For such a complex game, you really need extensive intro to game mechanics to have the faintest clue what is going on and that is not present.
Just as an example, lets say you want to sell items. Great, so almost every NPC you meet is a vendor with some gold and items to sell. So that means you have to click on every NPC to see what theyre selling. And when you want to sell you have to move all the gear to the character with the bartering skill so you can sell it at max price. Theres a good chance that all your gear is actually on the character with thievery (because he steals stuff and opens chests) or the one with high wits that you use to spot hidden treause and traps. So have fun moving all your gear between characters that all have individual carrying capacity and inventories full of potions and scrolls.
This game seems to be meant for a small subset of gamers that like a really heavy story-driven rpg with super complex mechanics and don't mind all the difficulties that come with no limits on what you can do. There's a reason conventions like group inventory or merchant NPC's or skill trees exist - they save the gamer time so they can go do the fun stuff like exploring the world and story. Suffice it to say, I see the promise in this game and if some of its underlying gameplay was changed to be more user friendly I would gladly enjoy the story. Instead I feel set adrift among a host of unexplained, needlessly comlex game mechanics without direction as to where to go or if I'm doing something wrong.

I really like this game. It's a card game one might find on in a table top crowd but gives it new life as you are transported into the cards' world. For instance, you land on a battle card. Another thing I love is how engaging it is. It's very simple really, but somehow it's still enticing to play more. It might be the quips The Dealer says throughout the game or the atmosphere or even the achievement of getting more cards to play with after you beat a Path. It's probably all of these things and I love the game for them even more.
Speaking of The Dealer, he is a mysterious character but also a formidable opponent. I don't want to give too much away but if you find yourself having trouble with any of the minions or bosses you fight, best to make sure you're well and dandy to square them away before the final fight. Luckily, you can replay any part of your Journey which can be a big help.
So really, if you've been contemplating getting this game, do it. It's worth every penny.

This game is quite the clever idea, and an entertaining game most of the time. Its difficulty curve is quite puzzling, though. After the initial "tutorial" hands and you start the game proper, it gets quite tough. However, when you succeed at the quests on the cards you find, you unlock new gear and bonuses which you can acquire later and on future playthroughs, and you can modify your deck (a lot easier than it sounds and not at all complicated or annoying, and this is coming from someone who typically tries to avoid alchemy and crafting in pretty much every game it's possible to avoid). The difficulty isn't so bad when you do this...until you reach the last few sections of the game. The fifteenth boss/level you take on (King of Plagues) is simply unacceptable on the normal difficulty, which is what I had played up until that point, and it was quite a challenge all the way until that section became impassable for me.
Speaking of which, there is an "easy mode" you can access by going to the DLC menu (Fates) in the Deck Builder. While almost all of them are things you have to pay for, the normal difficulty and the easy mode (labeled as "Apprentice") can be chosen there, and it gives you a ton of bonuses/perks for your character to aid him in getting further. At that point, though, easy was far too easy on the fifteenth level, while I couldn't come close to completing it on normal. Beyond that point, I stuck with the Apprentice difficulty because it didn't seem to get any easier.
The combat is essentially like a simpler version of the Arkham games' combat, with a number of abilities you can activate (only 2 can be taken into any given battle) depending on your gear. The battles get truly ruthless and not particularly fun late-game on normal. Even if I could handle the battles at max health, the problem is that the cards you draw along the way will hinder you even further. While you do have cards which can aid you, the bad cards very often outweigh the good.
All that said, I was able to complete the game's last few bosses/levels on the Apprentice setting, and some of the late-game stuff is surprisingly challenging, even on that difficulty. Unless you like showing off, I would highly recommend playing the Apprentice difficulty because the normal one just becomes a chore to play. It's a good game, but the difficulty settings are pretty screwy, so be warned of that.
Oh...and the ending after you land the final blow is maybe 10 seconds long and only six words are spoken after that blow. If short/lame endings put you off, you may wish to take that into consideration.

Valkyria Chronicles is by far one of the best games i have played:
- The story: is amazing, sure you have your "anime 101" some enjoy it and some dont. The story is a reinterpretation of WW2, with fantasy added to the story. as Juck Fames puts in his review: you will enter looking for fun but will emerge with feels
- Gameplay: is a mix between 3rd person shooter and turn based strategy (3rd person x-com i've seen people call it). This sort of combat gets you in closer to the battle instead of just seeing everying from up high, and for me personally being able to control my Squad in 3rd person helped me feel more attached and bring the feeling of war far better. Unlocking special orders you can issue during combat for granting various bonuses is not only immersive but strategically important as you go along to put it in short: Your squad will die without orders from their commander.
- The characters: you as a commander of Squad 7 is put in charge of gathering a fighting force and there is easily more than 40 different characters you can recruit into your squad each with their own name, backstory, strengths and weaknesses. Each character will have set of "perks" showing strengths and weaknesses for example some characters might have "Sand allergy" and thus thinking about bringing that particular unit to a desert battle is not a good idea as it will result in damage over time for due to the allergy but brining a "City born" to a fight in the city will increase his/hers defense. These characters can die on the field of battle and thus you will have to replace lost soldiers.
- each battle scenario is scored with a grade A,B,C etc. and based on your grade the more XP and Currency you will recieve. I am not a huge fan of that as it temps the player to find the quickest way to complete a scenario(you dont have to look far on youtube before you can find a guide that shows which maps can be completed in 1 turn) but i can see the enjoyment of hunting A grades after completing the game therefor i would recommend when first playing this game to take it a bit slower and plan you moves.
10/10 - Im off to do a 2nd playthrough! Squad 7, Move out!!

I got this game recently during Steam's end of year sale for less than half its normal $20 USD list, and it's one of the few games where I can say that I (almost) wish that I had paid full price for, because the quality of the game deserves it.
About the only negative thing I can say about the gameplay is that its mission-scoring system (e.g. how much experience and currency you get for completing missions) emphasizes speed (number of turns played to complete the mission) way too much over any other element.  If you take your time to move your squad carefully through the encounter, minimizing your own casualties while simultaneously trying to inflict maximum damage to the enemy, you're likely to get a rather poor mission grade and not much exp/currency.  On the other hand, if you use the semi-exploitative "order-buffed scout" strategy to make a bee-line to the oubjective (e.g. base capture) you'll score high, even if actual damage to the enemy forces was minimal.  I started playing the game with the mindset of a prudent military commander, and found myself gradually getting outclassed by the enemy forces as I progressed throug the game because I was getting "C" and "D" scores on many of my missions, even though I was doing substantial damage to the enemy force and keeping my casualties low.
Another minor negative is that most of the game's settings, including key/button bindings and A/V settings are set by an application that runs outside the game.  You can't adjust game controls, sound or video settings within the main game.  Fortunately, the game does not have a huge number of controls, and the default mappings are for the most part intelligently assigned, so you probably won't have much of a need to change control mappings in-game.  However, when I'm learning a new game, I'll often use the keybinding UI as a reference,  and the split nature of the settings vs. game apps preculdes doing this.
Don't let my few negative comments dissuade you from giving  this game a try - they are just a few fairly minor negatives in an otherwise outstanding game.

I have to say i am a huge fan of this game. I enjoy commerce games, and games that have the ability to upgrade either your shop or your character. In this game you get to do both. You get to hack and slash, and then sell your wares.
Pros of this game are:
Quick to learn.
Easy.
Casual.
This is a fun game to just play around on while you're waiting for the rest of your gaming crew to get online, or just to relax before bed.
Cons:
There is a con to this game that drives me up the wall.
There is A LOT OF DIALOGUE in this game, and there's many examples of it where its completely unneeded.
A number of conversations are so back and forth without reason.
"Are you a dog?"
"No i am not a dog."
"But you look like a dog!"
"Maybe i am"
"But what if you aren't?"
Ugh, just get to the point already!
Luckily, you can hit escape to skip the whole scene, which is nice if you've played through the scene before, but you don't want to miss the whole scene just in case there is something important.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys anime games or commerce games.
Totally worth the money, but if you aren't convinced, leave it on your wishlist til it goes on sale.

This game...this game can be really fun, and it can be really BAD at the same time.  Not a whole lot of people play this game anymore, and I'm guessing I know why. Then you have the little kids....ahhhh, kids. Ruining video games 1 curse worded mouth at a time.  I can't tell you how many times I've joined a game and had someone spam letters at me, curse at me, pretty much bullying other people, racism across ALL races, spewing out garbage from their tiny little pea brain mouths.  I've also had many join just so they can disconnect purposely the moment they get in the game. This tends to ruin the game, especially if they have an item on them that you need, or if you need to hand them an item to complete a goal of yours.
I also think the fact that when you win or lose, there really isn't much of a difference. You don't win anything like costumes or new characters. You don't even get a "you win!" spammed across your screen.  So, winning doesn't give you that "YEAH!" feeling like other games do. I think that is why there are so many trolls on this game who can't keep their attention on the actual game. Then you also get a lot of people who try to cyber with you and use the game as a way to ERP. Gross.
Overall, I think it would be a great game if there was a way to weed out the kiddos from being able to get on, or even a report system to report people who purposely d/c or try and curse you out with every curse in the book.  Maybe if it linked up to your actual steam account and banned you through steam, maybe that would fix the issue, but then again...there is already a lack of people as it is, I feel like if that happened then  there would be even less.
PROS: It's fun when played as intended.  Good little time waster, fun little rpg, strategy based game. Text to speech. Who doesn't love text to speech??
CONS: The lack of missions, having to pay to be able to play the other two missions when nobody plays anymore, the kids, the fact that when a player d/cs it ruins your game (they should make it so if someone leaves and has an item on them you should have some sort of "D/c taser" that tases your items off their person. That way it doesn't snow ball and so people don't d/c shortly after that one person because, let's be honest, it always snowballs into that. =/ Did I mention the kids who play? Yeah...Let's not get me started on those guys.
Did I mention the kids that play? Oh, right. I did..........grrr.
If this game had more (enjoyable) people on it, or more people in general...and a report system...I'd say this game would be fun. There is a grinding element but it's mercifully short and never becomes a chore. Fun game.

The definition of a game that is enhanced by its presentation. While Hand of Fate may be a fairly straightforward arena combat game like most of the scenarios of what you would find in a Batman Arkham game without the open world exploration, it is carried by its stellar atmosphere, narrator, and a drive to discover all the possible cards that can be played in each deck and challenge thrown your way.
Despite being a pseudo roguelike having persistent upgrades but starting each round as a blank slate, the game supports difficulty options in the base game for those less skilled at the two button attack and counter system. For those more talented turning on hard mode and stretching your starting supplies to near limit provides a fun thrill of flipping over each card and hoping that fate will smile apon you like an adventure.
Flavor text for each event and card help to paint the world around you as you proceed through your quest to the boss monster of each challenge. A little imagination and a liking for a dungeons and dragon style atmosphere where the storytelling is your imagination will provide satisfaction with the snippets of info that come your way with each turn of the cards.
While ultimately a fairly simple game at the meat of the experience as combat is very straightforward and the game is quite generous in letting you get used to the mechanics compared to most roguelikes, Hand of Fate is a lovely example of a game that pulls you in with its performance and showmanship and wills you to carry on not because its the best game ever made, but because it legitimately has a heart and soul unlike any other game thusfar.

What a train-wreck let down this game is. Not only does it lack any recognizable RPG mechanics, it also strips down combat for the Gears of War crowd. Not to mention all the non-Mass Effect 1 characters are shallow as a puddle of♥♥♥♥♥♥ TWO characters with daddy issues? Isn't one plenty? What the hell are you doing, BioWare? Oh and we got characters with child issues too? ♥♥♥♥ you. Give me more conspiracies or past involvements with the wrong people or something. Far too many family crises. The only good loyalty missions are the ones with Grunt, Garrus and Tali.
And don't even get me started on the forgettable and tedious recruitment missions. Between them and the loyalty missions, this game was 80% entirely busy work for stuff that Cerberus should have had in place for you by the time you were woken. Speaking of Cerberus, what's the point of the Illusive Man? He's literally nothing but an evil messenger and it's far too obvious from the start that's what he is. If he stepped off his pedestal and did something that would actually effect Shepard in a way he would have had more purpose. The only time I enjoyed him was when I get to tell him to go ♥♥♥♥ himself and hope I never see him again.
I mentioned earlier this game doesn't have much in the way of RPG mechanics, the most obvious being the complete joke of a leveling system. in fact I didn't even want to level. It's that absurdly bad. When there's likely to be no difference in your characters abilities whether you manually leveled or you auto leveled, you know somebody ♥♥♥♥ed something up. The fact you don't get XP from enemies and you barely get any for doing misc tasks makes you not care about trying to do anything other than what you have to in order to progress. In short: they might as well not even have had a leveling system.
This game made me bind Fire to a key because it refused to recognize my left mouse click half the time. I literally clicked 50 times in a row once and not a single time did it register. I assume it was a sloppy port due to that along with some nagging graphic glitches on characters. I would like to mention I also own and played the PS3 version and was as disappointed with that version as I am with this version. I gave this game a second go on PC based on how much I love the original Mass Effect.
Another huge let down for me here was the crummy music. Mass Effect 1 had such a vibrant sound stage while Mass Effect 2 soundtrack was so dull I forgot it was there at times. One positive: I did like the credits music. It had a "It's over for now" feel to it and it was a nice listen as the credits flew by.
I was scratching my head why there wasn't an inventory to speak of in this game. BioWare must have went mad and listened to all the people who thought Mass Effect 1's inventory system was a chore (it was but it just needed a little rework, not to be completely removed). It had a trickle down effect that made virtually every new weapon in the game to be just straight upgrades you didn't have to think about. In short: absolutely no weapon or tactical variety. You are likely going to have the same exact experience with this game as everybody else.
Mass Effect 2's characters drove me up the wall so much I intentionally let most die in the suicide mission.  I would never do something like that in a game for fear of missing out on story unless I really disliked them to no end. I only made sure Garrus and Tali survived since they have memorable personalities.  I wanna throw in that I really liked the Aria character in Afterlife. I wish she was a squad member.
As a run of the mill Third Person Shooter I think Mass Effect 2 is a very good game. It's a notch below something like Uncharted, which is a high compliment considering how good those games are. However as an RPG (especially one from BioWare) this game is a "coulda, woulda, shoulda".
TL;DR: This game shattered my hopes twice. It should have been one of my favorite games ever and I'll be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at it and BioWare forever for it. I hope I enjoy Mass Effect 3 better.

I got this game recently during Steam's end of year sale for less than half its normal $20 USD list, and it's one of the few games where I can say that I (almost) wish that I had paid full price for, because the quality of the game deserves it.
About the only negative thing I can say about the gameplay is that its mission-scoring system (e.g. how much experience and currency you get for completing missions) emphasizes speed (number of turns played to complete the mission) way too much over any other element.  If you take your time to move your squad carefully through the encounter, minimizing your own casualties while simultaneously trying to inflict maximum damage to the enemy, you're likely to get a rather poor mission grade and not much exp/currency.  On the other hand, if you use the semi-exploitative "order-buffed scout" strategy to make a bee-line to the oubjective (e.g. base capture) you'll score high, even if actual damage to the enemy forces was minimal.  I started playing the game with the mindset of a prudent military commander, and found myself gradually getting outclassed by the enemy forces as I progressed throug the game because I was getting "C" and "D" scores on many of my missions, even though I was doing substantial damage to the enemy force and keeping my casualties low.
Another minor negative is that most of the game's settings, including key/button bindings and A/V settings are set by an application that runs outside the game.  You can't adjust game controls, sound or video settings within the main game.  Fortunately, the game does not have a huge number of controls, and the default mappings are for the most part intelligently assigned, so you probably won't have much of a need to change control mappings in-game.  However, when I'm learning a new game, I'll often use the keybinding UI as a reference,  and the split nature of the settings vs. game apps preculdes doing this.
Don't let my few negative comments dissuade you from giving  this game a try - they are just a few fairly minor negatives in an otherwise outstanding game.

Owlboy is a very, very well created game (So far, I'm only a number of hours into the story), that I hope doesn't end up being severely underrated.
The graphics are as described, pixel art, but of high quality, with each sprite and area design looking like it was made with lots of care and critique.
It has a certain loveable charm to it in its dialogue and characters, and presents itself almost like an old 'coming-of-age' story, and it's given well.
The music in Owlboy is also very wonderful. From simple tunes in tone with the art style to absolutely beautiful full range melodies, it really helps paint a wondrous, beautiful world to explore.
The most important factor, the gameplay, is also very strong. It's a 'sort of' platformer, with 'sort of' coming from the fact that the protagonist can fly. In addition, it also has light puzzle elements, and in a few areas, well made stealth portions that don't suck, and serve as world-painting and mood setting.
All in all, Owlboy is VERY much worth $25, and something that shouldn't be passed up, even if you're not a strong fan of platformers.

HIGHLY recommended for what it is now, and even more for what is to come from a minimal initial investment.
I have nearly 50 hours of real-world time, over a month of in-game time, and I can now say with certainty that I made the right move getting this game now. California and Nevada feel different, and they both have distinct and identifiable areas, plus plenty of fun details from food trucks to coastal basketball courts to shooting stars and even UFOs (!). Driving is challenging but relaxing. Free-roaming or taking jobs from one corner of the map to another adds up to more hours than I would have initially expected, even for those who want to feel truly immersed in the long-haul experience. I am very much looking forward to getting the upcoming Arizona expansion for free, and from how well California and Nevada were done, I expect Arizona will feel "real" enough also.
Are there issues? Absolutely. There are plenty of bugs which need workarounds, such as not being able to rest in certain places, having a horrible time turning left in AI traffic, brutally unrealistic police AI [easy and free mods available for this] and glaring omission of major cities such as San Jose. However, the SCS team still deserves applause for taking on the challenge of starting to build the USA and capture the different complexities of American trucking.
I am thoroughly addicted to my rig and look forward to stepping into the cab every time to see where the available jobs take me next. I recommend you get into one of your own and drive while SCS's team expands and gives us even more land to conquer.

Revered, exalted, wise. These are just a few of the words I would use to describe Owlboy.
The developer D-Pad Studio took about a decade to make this game from conception to finish, and thankfully their efforts have made a masterpiece. I honestly would put Owlboy among the high echelons of indie games and other amazing games that have come before it. I am talking Shovel Knight, Binding of Isaac, Limbo, Fez; games that have shaped modern PC gaming as we know it. They have combined spectacular story telling, fantastic characters, dazzling design/artstyle, and from beginning to end enjoyable gameplay. This game was an absolute treat to play and is easily one of my choices for best game of the year, 2016.
I don't say that just about any game. This game spoke to me in more ways than one, it captured my imagination and reminded me what I love about games.
Now before I continue I want to put out a bit of warning, I highly recommend this title(obviously) but if you continue to read this I will be talking about game features, characters, and the overall experience of the game. So if you are considering even for a moment of buying this game. DO IT.
Owlboy is game about courage, friendship, and adventure in the face of overwhelming odds. You play Otus, a young owl who is being tutored to join a long line of respected Owl guardian figures who protect and aid the people. Like quintessential heroes of yesteryear, poor Otus is mute and thus lacks in the self confidence department. His tutor Asio is tough and sometimes rough on Otus, expecting much from our young hero. The world was once densely populated with owls, but after a mysterious event, most of them have disappeared. When pirates show up at the village of Vellie, a trickster steals an important relic. This sets events into a spiral.
It's hard to capture the game in one genre but it's somewhere between a Metroidvania and an Action/Platformer. The game is a side scroller that lets you fly in any direction. Obviously things like walls, doors, and other obstacles prevent from accessing areas you shouldn't but it never felt unnatural in Owlboy. Matter of fact, I have to compliment Owlboy on how natural the game combines the flow of story with little secrets hidden everywhere to be discovered. You always know where to go but you can take the entire game at your own pace. One thing to keep in mind is Owlboy emphasized on its story. It does away with the hundreds of hidden upgrades/secrets for more of a linear adventure like experience. The secrets that are there however, are very challenging to find and once found reveal more of the bright and wonderful world to you.
Flying is one of the biggest treats in this game and the controls are fantastic; completely responsive. I mostly played with my keyboard/mouse but had no problems diving, dashing and swooping around my enemies and generally laying down a butt kicking. I can imagine the same could be said for a controller. Both control methods feature rebindable keys and an assortment of different control methods, even for you southpaws out there. The action is equally as riveting as you gather allies and companions giving you access to new abilities, ways to blast enemies and overcome obstacles. The action never got dull for me, as I found unique ways to deal with the many bosses of Owlboy.
So now I am going to gush over the graphics and sound/music of Owlboy. Be warned. I want you to take a moment and look at a screenshot of Owlboy's clouds. LOOK AT THEM!
I would gladly take these clouds ANY day of the year over any rendered 60FPS thing you could throw at me. The pixel art is gorgeous and there are several times throughout the game where it took my freaking breath away.  Attention to detail is at maximum here with each area/house lovingly given detail. The character designs and animations give the characters life in a joyous fantastical way. Every time Geddy would do his stupid dance, I would laugh my butt off. Don't get me wrong, this game isn't kittens and rainbows all the time. As a matter of fact there are plenty of times I was shocked by game itself and how dark things got. That never stops the game from being nonetheless a fun adventure and this is demonstrated in its art, level design, and animations. I honestly would be surprised if this game couldn't be adapted into an anime.
Moving on to the music of Owlboy, the game features an orchestral soundtrack that would make John Williams smile. There is a moment in the game where you are riding on the back of a giant mechanical lizard. The moment that part began, the music drew me in and I couldn't stop smiling. Even as I moved about, dodging debris and everything was going to hell. It was scary, exhilarating and the music just took it to the next level. It's these types of moments that are speckled all throughout the game and which do everything to enhance the story, the art, and again the gameplay.
We have arrived at that point where I usually insert something I didn't like about the game. Let me say I was HARD pressed to find anything. The game has no bugs and is extremely well made. Boss fights are challenging but not frustrating. Exploration is difficult but rewarding. The pace of the game is always moving forward at a good clip, as new abilities are given to you for you to experiment with and enjoy. Is the game perfect? Dang near but, there was one thing in combat that did grate on me sometimes. During combat, if you are struck by an enemy, an animation plays that knocks Otus out of the air and kind of stun locks you. If multiple enemies are present and attacking, you can get stun locked for quite a while and lose more health than you would like. There that's it! All I've got.
Honestly, If I haven't given you the impression of how impressed I was with this title then, there really isn't much more that I could say. This game took me back to when games were wondrous. Like the first time I played Ocarina of Time or started up Final Fantasy VII. It made me feel like a kid again and I loved every moment of it. To the point where I didn't want it to end. Owlboy is about a ten hour experience more or less. You could extend that by finding every single secret. This may add two to four hours depending on how well you do the first run through the areas. You could say that isn't very long, but any more would be cheapening to the story and experience of this game. Trust me the amount of time it takes is perfect.
Replay value is of course up to you, but I personally could see myself playing this game many times over and looking for every single detail of the art, secrets of the story, or just kicking back and listening to the music. Does the game innovate? Not necessarily. But it does refine an age-old style and mechanics perfectly. The game is priced at $24.99 which is above the usual Indie standard, but the quality is more than worth it. These are the types of games you want to see made and these are the games you want to support.
I could honestly write more about this games bosses, story, and that awesome ending but I don't want to spoil any more for you.
So thanks for reading.

Crime-fighting.  Its a difficult job.  In the world of "Speedrunners" its difficult for reasons you might not have considered.  What would happen in a world where Superheroes were as prolific as those with an AA in business?  Where only the hungry and competitive get to be employed for their unique anti-villain skillsets, while the rest are relegated to fry cook duty at the local deep fry eatery.
Speedrunners casts you as a fledgling costumed vigilante desperate to break onto the scene as 'This City's #1 Hero!"  The catch?  You are not the only one.  Thus, we come to the core of the game, which is not actually fighting crime at all; rather, its a mad dash to beat your fellow would-be champions of justice to the scene of the crime, by any means necessary.
What does this translate to?  A Mario-Kart-esque footrace across rooftops, through buildings, and any other place you could seemingly run at semi-full bore.  Players (up to 4 of them) pick their hero of choice from a multitude of excellent original characters (and YouTube personalities!), and then beat feet (and each other), picking up power ups, swinging on grappling hooks, and tripping each other as they attempt to leave their opponents in the dust.
The action is quite simple.  Heroes run in a repeating/looping level, attempting to have their opponents leave the shared screen by being outpaced.  This is accomplished with the help of numerous tools.  Players may find themselves in possession of seeker rockets to sling at opponents, remote mines, drop-able crates, and Scorpion-esque ranged grappling devices, just to name a few of the tools available.  Players are able to double jump and wall jump, as well as deploy grappling hooks to avoid obstacles (with mechanics similar to the ninja rope from Worms Armageddon). You can even build speed by manipulating gravity and centrifugal force with well-place grapples.
Once the first opponent is knocked out (by meeting an untimely end at the edge of the screen as the rest of the dynamic do-gooders race on), things really begin to heat up.  The music changes, and the edges of the screen shrink, giving the remaining players less and less room to maneuver.  This can continue to a point where skilled players continue their parkour punchfest in a screen roughly 1/3 the size of normal.  Last man standing wins the round; first to 3 wins takes the match.
Sounds delightfully simple doesn't it?  And you'd be right to think so, given the initial smattering of levels from developer tinyBuild.  The game features Steam Workshop support, and the level of complexity in some of the user generated levels can really ramp up the difficulty when it comes to twitch reactions and puzzling out the fastest, most appropriate route.  The game sports competitive multiplayer, as well as local and online play.  You may play with a keyboard or controller (the latter being this authors preference).
Having said all that, I offer you this review and endorsement with full disclosure.  Having played this game at length with people of varying skill levels, bear the following disclaimers in mind:
- There is a bit of a learning curve here, particularly in the competitive scene.  Its ok to fail, as long as its still fun, right?
- This game is in Early Access.  Its not perfect, but it is pretty darn good.
- Furniture and peripherals may be at risk during gameplay.  Specifically, gamepads and keyboards may experience stress fractures during tense matches, or become heavily moistened by an abundance of palm perspiration.  Furniture, on the other hand, may become damaged due to severe body contractions, particularly during close matches.  To elaborate, whilst racing you may experience "butt fist," a tensing ones backside that may result in loss of underwear and damage to ones gaming chair.
If I haven't scared you off with the potential dangers above, Speedrunners is a no-brainer buy.  So, what are you waiting for?  Break out your spandex, knee-high lace boots, and cape, and prepare to race..... FOR JUSTICE!!!!!!

This game was suggested to me when I said I would love a game where I can just run the shop, go off to get the things to sell all on my own, and have no worries... well in this game you have huge worries! Your dad is a low-life who left you with his loan having to pay it off with large sums of Pix (game currency) otherwise you're homeless. This snarky Fairy (Tear) bosses you around and you have to pay her so much money at the end of each week (if you don't have the money at the end of the week, "Game Over"). You have to go out which means your shop will have to be closed for a period of time, going to town to buy/delve further into the story takes up some time but going dungeon diving takes up a lot of time and the number of things you can carry are small... Don't Die (kind of die).
Once you beat the game... beat the game? You don't beat the game, you still have to make money to keep food on the table and logs in the fireplace, you keep your shop running and you progress through the story on Endless Mode, heck you can go through it again on New Game+. You most likely won't get all the Adventures your first time through (did you think you were fighting, you're way too dainty for that). Just a note, if you notice you're not going to make the loan payment by the end of the week get all the stuff you know will sell and go dungeon diving like crazy, you'll keep those things when the game pretends you were just dreaming you did all that. You'll also keep your Merchant levels and 'basically' everything else except your money. You're able to change the look, size, and layout of your store, plus vending machine so you can sell more items during the day.
I absolutely love this game, I wish I could play more and hopefully soon I will have a chance to get the rest of the adventurers. It's rather short if you play it hardcore like I did, it feels like I played a lot but the number of hours I played doesn't match up to the number of days that sped through my mind (talking game time, not real). At first, I was surprised by the amount of Pix I needed each week but I managed to get the game clear after the second go through. The game is cute and sometimes Recette can be annoying when she repeats the same phrases or a customer says things that is rude to her then she's all upset with herself but it was the customer who was in the wrong, 'Sell something to you for below it's base price? Woman, you don't risk your life for me, get out of my store!' I do believe Tear will tell you this also, if one of your adventurers come to buy an upgrade sell it cheaper than you would to someone else. You can't just give them gear, you can buy gear and put it on them while in the dungeon but they have to come to the store and purchase it themselves to own, giving it to them to wear while in the dungeon swaps what they currently have on for the new gear which takes up space in your bags.
So go now, build your item shop for the townsfolk and adventurers, be the person they turn to to get everything they need, send people into battle to fight for your items, and for goodness sake don't forget to save!

To start; I have no nostalgia for this. I didn't even know this game existed until earlier this year. With that out of the way here's my review
It's extremely good.
You'll have to install a patch to get it running, but there's a great guide explaining how to by DUNCAN DONUTS, you should be able to find it pretty easily. The installation's also really easy since the patch uses an installer. Once you've done that, just get rid of the FPS limit in the advanced options and you're good to go. Another thing to note is this is one of those older games that wasn't made for 1080p, so all the UI looks really small even on a large monitor, I recommend 720p.
All of this setup only takes about 5 minutes, it's not much of a hassle, and to be fair you should expect to have to do some kinda extra setup anyway for a game this old.
Visually the game's obviously dated, but it's not ugly, some effects like the fog and a few bits of lighting still actually look pretty decent. The visuals don't take away from the atmosphere though, the sound design is great with tons of little details like being able to hear lights humming when you get close to them, and despite the audio quality not being as good as today, none of the sound effects are painful or ear-grating. The soundtrack is great too, my favorite song so far is Shared Dig, though it definitely sounds best alongside the game rather than on it's own imo.
The gameplay's solid, it's the usual arcade shooting you'd expect from the time, each gun has an alternate fire that's decently different from it's normal use. For example the rocket launcher doubles as a grenade launcher, there's another weapon that works like a railgun, but you can also shoot a slow-moving orb instead that does more damage, it's really well put together overall.
My only main complaint so far is some of the level design, the first (technically the 2nd) level of the game is pretty large with a lot of branching paths, that kinda thing doesn't really work in a game like this, especially since only one of those paths is going to lead you to the next level. The level also just feels a lot bigger than it needs to be. Everything after that's kind of a mixed bag, some levels are great and linear enough to where you won't get lost, but still allow for some exploration and secrets to find, while others are pretty large and confusing. It's not bad enough to make the game unplayable or anything though. I think the best way to sum it up is just by saying the level design's not as bad as Turok, but not as good as Half-Life, it's just kinda in-between with some levels being better than others.
I'll put a score here once I've finished it, but for now it's an easy 4/5

A card game in which you build decks of equipment and encounters, playing against a smart-mouthed dealer who guides you from event to event, encouter to encounter, and taunts you every step of the way, goading you on until he either gloats at your failure or grumbles at your success.
That sounded pretty darn good to me, so I got Hand of Fate and played it. And I wasn't disappointed.
Hand of Fate is a fairly simple game, combining a very Batman Arkham-esque combat system with an overworld card game full of decisions and chances to both succeed and fail. The random nature of the game can put some players off, though, as in the later levels you can play a near -perfect game and still fail miserably due to poor luck. Choosing your deck well can help, but it will only get you so far when the game starts doling out the "-15 max health" -cards.
The game is occasionally a bit crude in it's visuals and animation, the dealer's card handling puts me off every time, but everything still manages to look functional and clear, easy to read and enjoyable once you get into it, and is brought together beautifully by the voice of the dealer.
Hand of Fate is an enjoyable experience and well worth it's price tag. I recommend it wholeheartedly.

Be wary though, survival means you need to take the time to gather resources/explore/kill.  If you aren't at all interested in survival games, don't get it. Most of the mechanics have already been covered by better writers and commentators than me. However, I can give my personal experience and feelings:
- The game exudes atmosphere. The excellent writing, narration, music and interface aesthetic make for an enjoyable "experience".
- The game felt "too easy" up until the halfway point. I totally got screwed with a couple of bad draws and was down on food, had a 30% reduction of health, my equipment stolen and went into the last fight against the boss and 4 others with just 17 health points. I after getting 3 of the 5. And it felt great. Trying to figure out what to do and going for it anyway was a great way to fail.
- The combat is a bit simplistic, but there's more to it than what the basics show. The Batman Arkham style counter system is there, but when you're battling against 4 ranged attackers and 6 melee you're going to take some hits. So you prioritize what you need. There is a strategy to it.
- Combat moves are generally varied. You have block/deflect, attack, special attack (varies by weapon), spell, dodge, and counter.
Overall, this is a great game for the value. With the DLC you can change the rules to suit different play styles. It fully supports controller so it's nice to sit back on the sofa and enjoy as well.
I'd have loved to see a more varied protagonist (female, ranged, melee, mage, etc.), bigger levels to add to the "adventure", and a better mouse/keyboard interface for the deck builder. But, for what it set out to do, it did well. I'm looking forward to seeing what the developer comes up with next.

Ok, so i wrote a review a while back when i first got the game, but it was basically complete crap. I feel, with 58 hours on record and only 3 or 4 bosses in, I have the experience to write a decent review.
So, Gameplay.
Valkyria Chronicles plays and works much like a standardized map based tactics game, moving and placing troops. However; that all changes once you choose a troop. Suddenly, the map-like layout zooms in rapidly and you are playing a third person shooter! As you move your troop, you have limited movement points that once out stop you in place. No backtracking either, thats for wimps
. In terms of actions, the usual troop gets two or three actions, use their gun (Which you need to aim yourself, autoaims for boring people), use ragnaid (a medkit basically; thankfully its somehow infinitely usable,
), and use a grenade (every class can do this EXCEPT the lancer and sniper(?), the engineer gets four, while everyone else gets one). Each item has its own effects and each is useful in the right scenario, granted you use it properly.
Uh, Story, then.
The story of Valkyria Chronicles is a fun one. World War 2 in a fictional world! The evil federation empire thingy has invaded the country of gallia! You play as welkin gunther, an all around nature hippy man who suddenly becomes a tank commander; Alicia
, A baker turned rifle wielding badass scout
; another scout nobody cares about, some assorted soldiers.... Basically only welkin and Alicia and the rest of squad 7 are important ok!
Uh, i went off on a tangent there, but basically you play a squad of people who attempt to fend off the evil empire federation dude bros and take back your country by lethal force. Think if sweden singlehandedly drove off germany and retook their country after it was overrun.
Uh, Performance?
Performance wise, Valkyria Chronicles is great. I rarely see lag or bugs, and any that I HAVE encountered
were entirely on me. Theres tons of options for making the game run smoother or look better, and apps like HiAlgo work with it too so its not like all hope is lost if you're me and have a laptop running a 3rd person shooter like a maniac.
All in all, this game is incredible. Easily one of my favourite games right beside okami, star ocean second evolution, and all those great games.
Have a wonderful day, have a wonderful life, hope my review was funny and helpful.

Pros: If you want to see what American Roads look like in the West Coast of the USA, then this is definitely for you. Peterbuilt and Kenworth are the two Truck Companies so far, with two modern trucks. The roads and cities are actually quite well done, considering that they could not put everything from each city into the game. Being a Las Vegas native I found that they did not add Las Vegas Boulevard, the road that the Strip lies upon. This game is basically the same as ETS on the engine, menus and graphics, so nothing new to learn there. What is new are the Police, Weight Stations, and parking difficulty selection, all nice additions, but could use some finishing work to iron out the problems. Scenery of all places are pretty much spot on, only people native to those places would know what is missing.
Cons: Ticket prices for crashes and speeding are a little high. There is quite a bit of time compression that is really only noticeable once you have done about 35-40 deliveries. I'm sure this is just the same as ETS, but there are a lot less citites right now to compensate for this. Parking could have been just a slight bit different, honestly just moving one or two of the spots I had major issue with a few inches over is all I am talking about.
Summarize:
This is a great game for the 20 USD that I spent. It will be constantly updated and DLC made frequently as well. What you're paying 20 USD for is a great base game for future DLC, Mods and other items. The only game I have seen so far besides ETS to allow the user to stream their own internet radio stations during gameplay as a standard game function. The only game that will calm you as you play, something about the road, the music.
Hardcore fans of ETS and other Sims may not be pleased with the initial release, but because I am American and have always loved the Trucking Culture, I bought this game. I look at it like this; it will be patched often, mods are released daily for this game, and more areas will be coming soon as well.

This game is a very fun gameplay experience for some very light squad based strategy. It is horribly unbalanced, and a good chunk of the missions boil down to memorizing enemy tactics, but it is still worth playing through for the fun of being able to wipe out an enemy squad.
Each match will take you 30 minutes to an hour unless you are rushing a skirmish. With appropriate levelling and a relaxed pace, you'll finish the main campaign between 25 and 30 hours. Wait until New Game+ to play the DLC.
DO NOT buy this for the story, realism, or balanced gameplay. All the characters are single note with no depth. The plot is bogged down by tired anime cliches, lazy writing, and an otherwise derivative narrative, all of which get worse and more apparent as you approach the ending.
The reward system is totally out of balance, and essentially necessitates the "Scout Rush" tactic if you want a decent grade and the rewards that said grade entails. The only way to play this game with any real challenge is to force yourself to use a scout only once per turn, and even that gives you a significant advantage if you are keeping up with levelling.
One of my requirements for a recomendation on a PC game is the ability to customize system settings. In this game, you can play with controls, volume (sound and music seperately,) and sensitivity (an Xbox controlelr is highly recommended for unit movement.) This is more than many PC ports will do, which is a point in its favor.
In summary, if you can tolerate a sacharrine, anime storyline and a less that balanced gameplay mechanic; and you enjoy JRPG's and strategy games; then Valkyria Chronicles is worth your time, especially for the price.

This game so far is amazing.

The game is a 2D action/puzzle game. Most of the puzzles are straight forward Zelda-esq type things, as are the bosses. The game gives you a lot of movement freedom, but is a more linear story line.
Controls are responsive, and everything plays great. You can't adjust the controller mapping and it Only recognises XBOX or Playstation controllers, which might be a problem for some. Mouse and keyboard works fine too though, and can be changed.
This is surely a game that had the developer's heart and soul pooled into it, and you can feel it with every minute you play. Definately glad I picked this one up.
Edit: After clearing the game, I can safely say I only wish it was a bit longer, I cleared it with most stuff gathered in about 10 hours or so. Other than that, it was an amazing ride from start to finish and I would certainly recommend it to my friends either now or on sale- you definately have to play it sometime.

Metro: Last Light Redux defines the standard of what the atmosphere of modern-day games should be. With gorgeous visuals and realistic gameplay mechanics, the game deserves an 8/10.
The visual content in this game is beautiful. It probably is on par with its predecessor - Metro: 2033 Redux - in terms of graphics. The amount of detail had always made my jaw drop. If I run the game at max settings, the main menu runs at 30 FPS on a GTX 1070. Why? As I said, the visuals are amazing. I had to lower some post-processing settings in order to triple my FPS.
The game's story was very risky for the developers. A post-apocalyptic world wherein most of the enemies were humans could have not worked. But it did, and I applaud the developers for this feat.
I have to say, I am disappointed with the game's difficulty. Metro: Last Light Redux is easier than its predecessor. This is probably due to the fact that I faced more human enemies than mutated monsters in this game and that I could easily get the weapons I want.
Overall, Metro: Last Light Redux is an excellent game. This game is a must-have if you loved the previous installment of the series - Metro: 2033 Redux.

Hand of Fate is a truly unique game.
On the surface, it's a fantasy-themed deck builder, with customizable decks of cards for equipment, encounters, enemies, blessings, and curses.
However, there are a ton of facets that transform this straightforward concept into a sparkling gem. The player isn't simply reacting to a series of pseudorandomly-selected cards; she is testing her abilities against the cunning of the mysterious dealer, who maintains a running dialogue throughout the game - often questioning the player's choices, grumbling about the player's luck, and quietly gloating over the player's failures. Combat with enemies is a realtime hack-and-slash affair, with the player able to block attacks, perform timing-sensitive deflections and counters, and unleash mystical powers granted by blessings and aggregated paraphernalia. Opponents are ranked and classified in suits (
), adding to the overall coherence of the theme.
Finally, in the vein of a CCG or LCG, the game continually nourishes the player with a drip-feed of new content, unlocked not by buying packs of cards, but through exploration: provide a peasant family with food to survive the coming winter, contribute capital toward the elimination of the ratman menace (
), bring down the necromantic Jack of Skulls. Failed on your quest? Perhaps the discoveries you made during this attempt will turn the tide for the next one.
Hand of Fate is definitely recommended for fans of CCGs and LCGs, fantasy roleplaying, and anyone who's looking for a refreshingly innovative gaming experience.

- Combat is not the usual kind, that fights are quick and twitchy. The enemies take a fair bit of damage, and it makes for longer and more interesting fights. I'd propably not really like it if weapons had realistic damage.
- Gunplay feels quite nice. (with 227 patch UT99 based sounds, the original weapon sounds are quite subtile) Weapons have a suitable recoil in the animations and you get some shake too from shooting the weapons. Automag's bang, minigun and rifle's sharp blasts are perhaps the best sounds.
- Great weapon variety..only 3 conventional firearms, them being a handgun, sniper rifle and a minigun with pointlessly fiddly but cool barrel setup. Rest of the weapons include a bolt type energy pistol, a crystal spike firing nailgun analogy, beam energy rifle, multi barrel rocket launcher, a huge shotgun like cannon that fires rather large metal chunks in a spread similarly to a shotgun, 3 bladed disc launcher, a device that fires sticky and volatile green goop. Every weapon has an altfire, here I described only primary firemodes. So yeah a lot of depth in the gunplay.
- The atmosphere..wonderful. The music, art style, sounds and premise/lore itself mesh together in a way that creates a really excellent sensation/perception of the game's feel. It rivals the first S.T.A.L.K.E.R I even dare say..
- Great soundtrack. There are somber, moody, energized and calming tunes all, every of them fitting the level perfectly. Neve's crossing and Bounds of Foundry tunes in particular..are just MAGICAL.
- Graphics have held up pretty well for being about 20 years old. I mean yeah, there sure isn't advanced shaders or post processing effects and the environments are blocky but the developers made the most of their beautiful creation, the Unreal Engine. I can perfectly picture how the places would look in real life, how the water would shimmer and shine, how the sky would look and so on.
- Multiplayer is great, coop is my favorite gamemode. But sadly not a lot of players active..
The bad:
Developers cut some really great maps that were in the 1997 beta..thankfully though some of them were retouched and reimplemented in the expansion pack.

Murdered: Soul Suspect has you playing as an undead ghost cop who needs to solve his own murder case in order to get into heaven. It's an interesting mash-up of ghosts, buddy cops and murder mysteries that will keep you busy for a while. The gameplay is centered mostly around relatively easy puzzle solving and deduction, though the game breaks this up by sprinkling in relentless demons that won't rest until they suck your soul and kill you again.'
Personally, i HATE the demons, they're like a Xenomorph from Alien, crossed with the Dementors from Harry Potter with some glowing TRON lights thrown in for good measure. Normally this wouldn't bother me but the demons quickly get annoying and they have no real purpose, they're not in cahoots with the main antagonist, the mysterious Bell Killer, it's clear they're only in the game to lengthen it.
Otherwise, the rest of the game is pretty good! The detective parts are the best, although the answers are a bit obvious. The locations are pretty fitting if not a bit cliche. Your ghost powers are pretty fun to mess with and make a cool gimick.
Unfortunately, the game has almost no replay value unless you want to get all the collectables you may have missed or if you want to 100% the achievements.
The collectables themselves are fairly decent, containing ghost stories, character thoughts and background info. My favourite would have to be unlocking the ghost stories in the different locations.
Pros:
-Good story
-Ghost powers
-Detective parts
-some good collectables
Cons:
-Cliche locations
-Those %$#@!#$@%! DEMONS!!!
-Obvious answers
-some bad collectables
Overall i would recomend this game for the story and the side cases and if it doesn't bother your morals, than you can easily find a way to get rid of those demons.

I was really hoping for a bit more from this game. I snagged it in a humble bundle and was so excited to finally play. The graphics are pretty fanstastic, the controls can be a little clunky, the story has a lot of intrigue and the overall difficulty isn't that high (even if increase it in-game).
The part that let me down was the "action" aspect of this game that revolves around hiding from demons in the whisp trails left behind by other ghosts. That's it. You walk around, possess people, find historical tidbits to complete achievements, and hide from the occassional demon.  The story, however, is engaging and all of the side content does add quite a bit to the game. I loved the aestetics and finishing it was very satisfying. I just with that the developer had played a bit more with the combat mechanic.

The game needs a lot of work, and I mean a lot, to be considered finished. But unlike many other similar games, there's multiple signs of competence from the developer's side. Enough to say that the game might get to a good state relatively soon.
That shouldn't be much of a surprise, seen as this time around the developer is not a random new studio or an indie but Funcom, a studio with a lot of experience and big games behind them.
But enough of that. So, why should you concider this instead of other games like it? Well, first of all, the setting! Everyone knows at least the movies and how brutal and harsh the world of Conan looks, which makes it a great set for a survival game with a lot of background lore already in place to take ideas from.
That's all nice and good but what could it possibly provide that's new? Combat! Obviously. Again, it's a freaking Conan game, and the focus on combat is apparent. Having proper fights with all kinds of beasts. Things like active dodging and power attacks, etc etc. The AI of a hyena even tried to intercept my sprint at some point! Unfortunately, right now the state of the combat is... not great. Monotonous is what I would describe it and only relies on spamming that attack button. However, if the current system is ironed out properly with tweaks here and there, it should be a lot of fun. Fortunately, Funcom seems to be aware of this as stated in their Early Access description.
Does it run well? Compared to other survival games like Ark (which uses the same Engine), it runs like butter, but that doesn't say much. Still, on my system it had no serious issues even after tweaking all the settings to max, but getting to 60fps constant was not really happening, though always above 40 and remained smooth. Since it just launched, this will probably be improved at some point, even by a small amount, but for a new Early Access game this is more than enough to show that the devs mean business.
But is it something I would recommend right now? Yes, but only if you got a friend to play with to cut on the tedious grind without cheating through admin panels. If you want to play alone or join a random server instead, I'd say you should wait a bit. If you want to throw money right now to help a project that shows competence, yeah, go right ahead!

Pros: If you want to see what American Roads look like in the West Coast of the USA, then this is definitely for you. Peterbuilt and Kenworth are the two Truck Companies so far, with two modern trucks. The roads and cities are actually quite well done, considering that they could not put everything from each city into the game. Being a Las Vegas native I found that they did not add Las Vegas Boulevard, the road that the Strip lies upon. This game is basically the same as ETS on the engine, menus and graphics, so nothing new to learn there. What is new are the Police, Weight Stations, and parking difficulty selection, all nice additions, but could use some finishing work to iron out the problems. Scenery of all places are pretty much spot on, only people native to those places would know what is missing.
Cons: Ticket prices for crashes and speeding are a little high. There is quite a bit of time compression that is really only noticeable once you have done about 35-40 deliveries. I'm sure this is just the same as ETS, but there are a lot less citites right now to compensate for this. Parking could have been just a slight bit different, honestly just moving one or two of the spots I had major issue with a few inches over is all I am talking about.
Summarize:
This is a great game for the 20 USD that I spent. It will be constantly updated and DLC made frequently as well. What you're paying 20 USD for is a great base game for future DLC, Mods and other items. The only game I have seen so far besides ETS to allow the user to stream their own internet radio stations during gameplay as a standard game function. The only game that will calm you as you play, something about the road, the music.
Hardcore fans of ETS and other Sims may not be pleased with the initial release, but because I am American and have always loved the Trucking Culture, I bought this game. I look at it like this; it will be patched often, mods are released daily for this game, and more areas will be coming soon as well.
8/10 for me, just wished for entire West Coast, and some other improvements. Game is solid! Plenty of fun for all!

In Owlboy you play as Otus, a mute young owl who ventures off in a heart-tugging emotional adventure about friendship and trust.
Here is the
(or see below for the full written review):
The story of owlboy is a simple yet warming coming of age tale.  Otus’s Owl homeland gets besieged by airborne pirates and Otus, along with his soldier buddy Geddy and a few other trusty friends, must set out to put a stop to their dastardly deeds.  Along the way you’ll team up with rebellious pirate   tand misbehaving spider Twig, using their abilities in conjunction with Geddy’s to foil the plans of those invading pirates.
The story of owlboy is a simple yet warming coming of age tale.  Otus’s Owl homeland gets besieged by airborne pirates and Otus, along with his soldier buddy Geddy and a few other trusty friends, must set out to put a stop to their dastardly deeds.  Along the way you’ll team up with rebellious pirate   tand misbehaving spider Twig, using their abilities in conjunction with Geddy’s to foil the plans of those invading pirates.
The first thing that will take you aback in this game will most likely be its refined pixel art.  This isn’t pixel art like we saw it back in the Super Nintendo era, nor is it a contemporary mashup of what most developers consider ‘throwback or retro style pixel art.’  This is sophisticated and tastefully crafted pixel art with all the dressings of high resolution graphics.
Owlboy’s gameplay is a melange of adventure platforming, aerial navigation and twin stick companion shoot-emup.  With the tap of a button, you can fly freely without any recharge mechanic, as an owl should, and on your own, you may dodge, perform a spin-attack that stuns enemies, and drag select objects around after picking them from the ground.
But the meat of the game rests when you pick up your companions.  The game then ventures into the twin stick realm, you’ll be flying with one stick and free arming with the other depending on the abilities of your counterpart.   As such, this is how ability progression plays out in Owlboy - not by purchasing new abilities or unlocking them, but by finding companions and utilizing their skill sets to add to your own.
Faults are hard to find in Owlboy, save for some tweaking that needs to be done to make the controls more responsive. It’s just a tad unresponsive, it’s a downfall yet not a catastrophic one.  Like getting an ice cream sundae and finding you didn’t get enough extra chocolate sauce.  No big deal in the end really.
The only other notable thing would be that the navigation can be tricky from time to time as you fly around the hub worlds, discover new areas and unlock barricades on past screens with special abilities.  It’s all a little bit hard to keep track off.  But nothing to mare the overall experience.
The presentation, story and character arcs are Owlboys strongest weapons.  You’ll find Twigs story arc particurlly poignant and you may find yourself open to the idea of exploring the deep character archetypes that each character is instilled with.  You’ll make friends, you’ll feel the nostalgia from the obvious Zelda influences and may gush a little when the story all comes together.  And it doesn’t hurt that the gameplay is also refreshing, diverse and satisfying.

A solid purchase for those looking for a different “platforming” experience. You were probably drawn to the game due to its striking visuals, and well, it definitely delivers in that area. There's some beautiful environments and some great character designs here, and they all complement some great animation work. That great presentation continues with the music as well, as it perfectly captures the mood of each of the gameplay sections perfectly. And that great presentation ends up complementing a rather solid story, with good set pieces and interesting characters. I loved the world that was built here, even if I wanted to see more of it in the end. There's no performance issues, as the 60 FPS never dropped a single frame, at least from what I saw. As for the gameplay, that's where the game starts to show some more faults, but that's not saying much. The “platforming” here (despite it being a game with flying), is rather solid, as it keeps things fresh by changing its traps and reconfiguring them on a regular basis. The combat controls do work and have a unique feel to them, although the lack of enemy variety in the end does end up hurting the game combat sections overall. When it does change up this combat sections, it definitely works, but I wish it did it more often. But the unique feel of the game still carries this game to a solid recommendation.

This game is just terrible. First of all, the performance is so bad that on "ultra", which still looks like an early PlayStation2 game, it chugs at an erratic and frustrating 25-30fps. Drop it down to medium and the game becomes the jaggiest polygonal game made after 1997, but at least the framerate jumps up to an erratic and annoying 50fps. It should probably be noted that my machine can do, for example, Witcher 3 on all ultra at 90fps, but apparently it can't handle a PS2-level action game with ninjas in it. At ultra low settings, the game finally stabilizes the framerate and it stops being erratic, but it hovers around 40fps (lower than medium?!) and it literally looks worse than a PS1 game. It looks like, I don't know, an N-Gage game?
But that can be forgiven if the game design is good enough. If it's fun to murder ninjas, it can be acceptable that the framerate is poor and the graphics are horrible, but that's not the case here. This is a dualstick shooter where they forgot about the second stick, so you can only toss shuriken and bombs in the direction your character is facing. I hate this design. It just forces the player to run in dumb little circles to keep recentering the character, or to simply stop moving and hurl as many shurikens as possible before dodging. It's such an inelegant design compared to just using one stick for movement and one stick for shooting (or keyboard and mouse for each if you prefer). On keyboard, you move with WASD and do all of your attacks with the other half of the keyboard, and the mouse does nothing. The worst part is that this reductive design doesn't even make any sense from a retro perspective, because the oldest dualstick ever made is Robotron: 2084. It came out in 1982 and it used two sticks, so why are people creating singlestick shooters in 2016?
It's too bad, because I like the idea. It's massive hordes of ninjas (wait, I don't think that's how ninjas worked...) storming at you and you kill dozens at a time, which is cool and sort of like a retro arcade version of Dynasty Warriors, but the horrid performance and uninteresting gameplay loop make this a hard pass. Even if they fix the performance, they'd have to redesign the whole gameplay core to make it fun. I've only played 12 minutes and that number is not going to rise.

A treacherous, greedy Catholic Patrician and Holy Roman Elector was teaching a class on Pope Innocent III, known heretic.
”Before the class begins, you must get on your knees and worship the Pope and accept that he is the leader of Catholicism, the one and only true Christian faith founded by Jesus Christ, and is even greater than Constantine the Great!”
At this moment, a brave Varangian soldier who had killed over 1500 Turks and understood the legitimacy of the Eastern Roman Empire and fully supported all its economic, social and military reforms stood up and held up a map of the Holy Land.
"Who should own this land, Brutus?"
The arrogant Venetian smirked quite Jewishly and smugly replied “The crusaders, you stupid heretic.”
”Wrong. It has been over 2000 years since Alexander the Great conquered it. If it was not owned by Arabs, and Catholics, as you say, should own the land... then the crusaders should have conquered Jerusalem by now."
The Patrician was visibly shaken, and dropped his ducats and copy of the Roman Missal. He stormed out of the room crying those ironic Catholic tears. The same tears Catholics cry for “the poor Crusaders” (who today live in such luxury that most bathe daily). There is no doubt that at this point our Patrician, Enrico Dandolo, wished he had been Orthodox and supported the Komnenoi in their struggle against the Turks. He wished so much that he had the Imperial Sword to kill himself from embarrassment, but he himself had pawned it off to the Capetians!
The students applauded and all applied for Roman citizenship that day and accepted Manuel Komnenos as their Basileus. A double-headed eagle named “Byzantium” flew into the room and perched atop the Hagia Sophia and shed a tear on the chalk board. The Epitaph of Seikilos was sung several times, and Constantine the Great himself showed up and converted all Catholics to Orthodoxy.
The Patrician lost all his merchant ships in a storm sent by God. He fled to the Turkish sultan but even the Turks abhorred his Venetian treachery and he died in a Seljuk dungeon.
