You've changed the world. Christianity is over. The Viking  Empire, the Great Fylkirate of the reformed Norse Faith, has long since sacked both Rome and Constantinople, and has spread outward to subvert and subdue all those nations who adhere to the White Christ. Your great great grandfather started this campaign by establishing the Fylkirate and declaring Holy War on greater Italia, and now after generations of toil and sacrifice, of endless war and bloodshed, the work is complete, and the near entirety of Europe answers the call of the Thunderer. The Muslims dare not offer challenge now that Chistendom has fallen, their internal conflicts consuming them. The Fylkirate need not war with the Muslim kingdoms directly, simply waiting for rebelious factions to emerge and claim lands as their own, then putting down these Muslim rebels and taking their place, the Caliphate hard-pressed to complain about the lost territory when they were already on the verge of losing it.
Things are going well, and as a young man and new inheretor of the throne, you've turned your eye to India, a lush land with an industrious people you intend to bring into the fold. Managing a massive empire is growing increasingly difficult however, tugging up the weeds of rebellion becoming a full time job for your soldiers, and India being too far to travel for the bulk of your forces to conquer it entirely. Inspecting the Royal family in India, you discover they have only a single son and four daughters. Inspiration strikes. You deploy your chancellor to a little province in the core of India, directly beside their capital. A few years pass before he can establish a claim, but once he does you act swiftly: proclaiming the land yours and deploying a large contingent of soldiers to the Indian coast. A deadly game of cat and mouse allows you to evade and re-direct the massive Indian defense force, compelling them to form one massive unit. You split your forces abruptly, sending your best combat generals to continue the cat-and-mouse for as long possible, while the other half of your force, led by your seige-masters, invades the disputed territory. Though the sacrifices are profound, the ploy pays off, and before the Indian defense force can crush you, the Royals concede the territory, one tiny province in the very center of the Indian heartland.
You give that province to your most powerful vassel, to whom the bulk of western europe was granted, and he diverts the near entirety of his force there. Within the week you've commenced raids on the surrounding provinces, with a particular focus on the Indian capital itself. Within four months, you've abducted the oldest daughter of the king of India, and have taken her into your personal tuteledge. As the years go by her views change drastically, and soon she's a devoted Norse, skilled in the ways of diplomacy and insightful regarding her faith, much like yourself. On the day of her eighteenth Birthday, your finest assassins do their insidious work on both the Indian Sultan and his son. Releasing your long-time captive, you grant her India itself as a birthday gift. If your plan is to come to full fruition however, more sacrifices must be made. A few months go by as your assassins travel back to the mainland, and in time they are deployed against not only your own wife, but your own son as well, the only male heir to your kingdom. It's a dark deed, and one you engage in reluctantly, but over the generations the Fylkir has had to make many such sacrifices with his children in order to maintain the integrity of the Empire under the rule of One. Obstacles removed, you marry your former protege who is all too willing, and begin the proccess of assisting her in squashing all rebelion against the sudden change of religious leadership in Indian society. In a matter of months India is looking more and more like a Norse nation, and you bask in your own cunning.
You then discover your wife is pregnant. While you'd hoped for this, there's a problem, in that you have grave suspicions the child is not yours, but have no way to prove it. The child is born, it's a boy, and thus your heir entire; but although you have no way of exposing him, you're -certain- he's not yours. While the Empire would survive an impostor on the throne, you cannot abide your blessed bloodline being usurped by a pretender. The boy must die. Your trusty assassins go about the task and achieve it to the letter, but alas grow sloppy on the retreat, and are soon discovered.  You hope for the best, and when your unfaithful bride petitions you for help against a rebel force, you assume you've been forgiven, and agree in relief.
The next day, you're assassinated. With only daughters remaining in your line, your grand Empire is divided amongst the five of them into a disjointed collection of smaller entities. Contention rapidly develops between the sisters, their vassels, and one another. The muslims smell blood. You struggle, as the eldest daughter, to re-unify the Empire, to bring some sense of order back to this chaos, but all around you your sisters are falling to internal strife or conquering forces, the hard work of long generations seeing your great and holy empire diminished to a shadow of its former self. After a near two centuries of global dominance, you are reduced to a second-rate power once more.

I've been intrigued by this mish mash of CCG/beat em' up since It first appeared on kickstarter, and I am so glad it turned out to be just as well conceived and addictive as I hoped it would be. First the
pros:
1.) Incredibly fast and fluid gameplay mechanics, simple combat but rewarding combat, excellent balance of card based mechanics and strategy elements.
2.) I love the voice actor for the enigmatic dungeon master who is your constant companion throughout the game. He adds so much personality to the game and just makes you want to keep coming back just to see him alone.
3.) the entire experience from the univerally woodcut artwork on the cards to the beautiful fable-inspired 3d graphics are all very beautiful and just ooze a sense of fantasy inspiration.
4.) absolutely tons of cards to unlock and collect
5.) addiction, seriously I bought this game on 4/29 and i've put in about 3-4 hours that day alone! I can't stop playing it.
Cons:
1.) the balance can be slightly unforgiving at times, it rewards cautious play rahter than risky behavior, as at times the downsides can be game-ending. Though this is part of the rouge-genre.
2.) the "card shuffling" mini game is a bit of a mixed bag. One the one hand it's kind of addictive learning how to follow the cards on the other hand it adds an element of unpredictability to the game that takes some of the control out of your hands which makes certain pitfalls seem unfair. Which leads to frustration.
3.) there are only 12 levels, which initially seems rather short, but there is an inclusion of an endless mode which is where the real meat of the game is at.
In conclusion:
HoF is definitely worth the buy. It's one of the most enjoyable games of the year thus far and has potential to be played for years if steam opens up a curated workshop for custom mods OR if the dev releases more dlc and more cards. Seriously they're on to something with this game. :) Pick it up.

Hand of Fate is a unique blend of deck building, RPG, and action/adventure with a good, if vague, story and a lot of replayability. It's quite fun and different than most games in any of its genres. It's not without issues but I would highly recommend this game.
Pros:
•	Well blended combination of gameplay from its three different genres
•	Excellent soundtrack and voice work
•	The random dungeons reward exploration while avoiding any grind due to the wide variety of encounters
•	Each gameplay session is a different story in and of itself
•	Excellent difficulty curve
Cons:
•	I'm only going to put one thing here: the combat. Now don't get me wrong, I enjoy the combat, it's not broken, nor does it make the game unplayable. The problem is that it goes for counter-based combat of the Arkham variety. Unfortunately do to the fact that this is an indie game they didn't have the animation budget of something like Arkham City or Shadows of Mordor. As a result the combat is often feels janky as your character suddenly breaks off his combo to block the attack of an enemy behind him. While this is largely a visual thing it also effects the gameplay. At times it can be hard to tell whether or not an attack will hit you, it can also lead to you combat rolling into an enemies attack rather than away from it. Fortunately the combat doesn't outstay its welcome and the game as a whole is solid.
To summarize: I loved this game! The combat was a bit of a hiccup but it's functional and the exploration and aesthetic more than make up for it. Plus the new DLC adds more play options each with their own twist. Buy this game because, if nothing else, you won't play anything else like it!

The fable games have a truly unique feel to them, with a classic British Monty python esque sense of humour, and a generally laid back chill, cosy, warm, charming..atmosphere that I'm struggling to describe concisely. Fable: The lost chapters in my opinion is the best game of the series, a series which has sadly ended.
The gameplay and controls are pleasingly simple, its not a game that will challenge your skill directly, but with things like the combat multiplier, quest boasting and mini-games allow you to test your skill and reap large rewards.
You have various skills and abilities to unlock, and truly unique weapons, and armours to find in the world, each with a backstory. The world itself isn't open like Skyrim, its split into zones, all of which have their own feel and are well designed in that they feel just large enough to lose yourself in, and find new areas in places you thought you had explored.
The story itself is like the gameplay simple, but in a good way. It is essentially a parody of your typical RPG tropes countering the typical "your parents were killed by bandits, and you are now the chosen one" origin story, with its distinct surreal humour, effectively delivered through amazing and memorable voice acting.
The graphics are dated, but yet due to Fables art style still somehow seem just as relevant today as they did back when it came out. If however you do want a graphical improvement, you can get Fable: anniversary, however that is more expensive.
Further info:
-Combat multiplier is a combo that builds during combat, the less you're hit the higher it gets and the more XP you get.
-Quest boasting is what it says on the tin, you pick up a quest and make a boast, for example you will do the quest naked etc, you gain extra gold and XP.

Valkyria Chronicles tells the story of an alternate Europe. You're set within a small country that is caught between two large empires that are about to have an all out war. The small country Gallia is not known for it's military strength but for their large amount of ragnite minerals. Ragnite is the source of power for the whole continent. As a player you're commanding a small unit trying to survive in this bloody conflict and getting dragged into political affairs. Valkyria Chronicles is a tactical role-playing game, which allows the player to command every unit and also carry out their attacks. The game is a little bit slow and it takes time to get into it. Especially when failing a mission or loosing some important character means starting the last mission all over again. Therefore the difficulty can be frustrating at times.
Nonetheless It's challenging without being unfair, tells a very touching story and has a beautiful art design. Definitely a gem worth trying for everyone who likes JRPG and wants something a little bit different, than the usual amnesia, silent hero character that goes on to save the world.

I enjoyed playing all of them, especially the secret bonus levels that you can unlock at the end (if you figure out how.) The gameplay music is rather nice, so it makes gameplay relaxing. I wish there were more tracks available, but if you become bored with it, the option to mute the music is available.
The best thing I love about this game is the option to create your own puzzles as well as be able to play puzzles other users have created. This literally opens up endless gameplay. I have a great time seeing what other players can create!
The only thing I would love to see different is bigger puzzles. While 25x25 can be challenging, I really love challenges, so the 25s where not as much of a challenge as I'd hope for. I'd love to see 30, 40, or even 50x size puzzles in the future!
Overall, I'd give this a 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Imagine this: Fallout is boasting how great of an post apocalypse game it is and then Metro comes in and smashes a Vodka bottle over its head and stands triumphantly with a tricked out AK-74--the Metro series puts Fallout to absolute shame.
This game has a test range, arena, and museum modes! Try out weapons and attachments against troops, targets, or dummies at 10, 20, or 30 meters, pit monsters verses monsters or humans and join a side and fight in little skirmishes. There's also a cassette player on the table with a couple songs you can cycle through and shoot up targets while listening to them. Never expected this from a FPS survival horror.
There are also single missions you can play as different characters, some which are your enemies! One mission is acutally a mission from the main story replayed from the eyes of another person.
Fantastic, involving storyline with memorable characters, this is something you don't usually get in a FPS. The pacing and how everything unfolds is very well done.
The atmosphere is very dark and gritty, crazy attention to detail, fantastic set dressing, and amazing graphics and animations thanks to the redux. Both 2033 and Last Light have compelling linear story-lines. Playing stealthily is a very satisfying option and in my opinion the best way to play since you experience things you otherwise wouldn't have going in guns blazing. Moral points can be earned as well, moral points dictate which ending you'll get. Basically make ethical choices and you'll be good to go. Knock enemies out instead of killing them--press "E" instead of "V." The screen will flash blue and you'll hear a certain sound when you earn a positive point.
This a survival FPS so there's no eating food or drinking water to stay alive, instead it's saving ammo and gas mask filters, and sneaking around enemies. Even though this review is on Last Light it can also be applied a far amount to 2033.
The attention to detail is something which has to be mentioned, as you sneak around, enemy conversations can be heard which can actually help you in the missions. In one instance there was a small guard team near a large airlock in a section of the metro tunnel talking about why a patrol was in the other section, if I thought about it and actually given a damn I would have realized hat patrol was to come back, find the guard I had killed and then they would go in complete search and full auto mode. It didn't go smoothly, my character is hiding, patrol is moving up, 5 second away from discovering the bodies, try to take them out, melee one of them right when the two other find the dead guards, turn around and ka-boom.
At another time I had my sights on two enemies when they start talking, no spoilers but after I hear one of them through I actually spared him.
Looting--even this has depth. You can simply pick up ammo but you can also pick up ammo from guns laying around.
Regardless of where you look they'll always be something worthwhile to observe. Metro tunnels with rubble, fog, flickering lights, dark and spooky trains all make the player think what was here before. People walked here once, used these machines, and took refuge during the war.
As an FPS it needs weapons to handle and act well and they do. You have a fair amount of weapons and a handful of attachments. RPKs with drum magazines, an anti-material rifle, the classic AK-74, throwing knives and more.
Control are top notice and the default keyboard layout is very sensible. I started off the game on Ranger difficultly which turns off 90-95% HUD and I didn't have a problem figuring out what does what--it's all where it should be.
The graphics are amazing. Lighting is great and 4A really put effort into it and it really paid off, in a game with environments this dark realistic lighting matters a lot. Any modern graphics card can run it on very high settings and still have at least 50-60% headroom.
But keep in mind tessellation and Physx will drag it down a lot. For tessellation I have it set on Normal for the in-game setting and also have it locked at x8 in Radoen settings. Physx is tricky, majority of the time it won't make a huge impact but on one mission with a ton of fire every CPU core on an i5 was almost maxed out and lead to FPS drops sometimes. Large firefights with debris and explosions might effect performance as well. Nvidia actually made a great guide for the games settings:
One thing I really don't like is the save system. It's all automatic and there's no way to make manual saves and the strangest thing of all is: let's say you're in the middle of the storyline and you decide to go play one of the single missions or the test range--your autosave will be overwritten. You'll proceed up to that storyline mission but any checkpoint in the mission will be lost and you'll have to restart. There are no seperate saves. Another strange thing is difficulty levels are global. If I start a single mission on Ranger Hardcore it'll carry over to the storyline missions which makes no sense. I'd recommend playing the single missions and test range after completing the storyline.
Last Light is a continuation of 2033's story and it'll make more sense if you play that first. I strongly recommend you buy the bundle, when it's on sale for $7 it's an absolute steal.

The original version of Metro: Last Light was released in 2013 by developer 4A Games, and publisher Deep Silver. Alongside the reissue of Metro 2033, this successor also got a Redux version upgrade in mid-2014. Whereas its predecessor was based off of the best selling novel of the same name, Metro: Last Light is not actually inspired by any book from Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky, but rather it's a direct sequel to the first game. In fact, a majority of the ideas for Metro: Last Light came from 4A Games themselves, though done so with heavy input from Glukhovsky, who also wrote all of the dialogue for it, alongside a brief outline of the story.
First up, for owners of the original Metro: Last Light, is the Redux worth it? Since the graphics were already better in 2013, the striking difference between the original and the Redux is not felt as profoundly as the striking differences between the 2010 version of Metro 2033 and its subsequent Redux. That's not to say that the game isn't beautiful, because it is. The engine is also a lot smoother, and gameplay is definitely more fluid. However, I wouldn't say pay full price for it if you own the original release; if you do grab it, get it on one of its frequent $5 sales. If you're new to the series, read on.
Metro 2033 had two endings, and depending on where your hidden karma meter landed you, you either got the good or bad one. The bad ending for Last Light's older brother, wherein Artyom ends up bombing the Dark Ones and eviscerating them with missiles, was chosen to be cannon, and this title picks up one year after that fateful event. Main protagonist Artyom has been promoted to a Ranger, and his crew have since occupied the D6 military facility that he discovered in the first game. Due to the mysterious and legendary status of the D6 bunker, rumors of it housing great riches spread throughout the metro, and rival factions have set out to seize the area for themselves. Though that isn't the sole basis of Metro: Last Light, Artyom soon discovers that one Dark One has survived the barrage of explosive devastation that was meant to kill them all.
If you played the first installment in the series, you'll already know what to expect with Metro: Last Light Redux; as stated previously, the engines are the same, as are the mechanics. To its credit, it does feel like a direct continuation of the first game in every sense. However, while the senior title focused more on a guns-blazing approach, this release really centers around stealth, especially in the beginning. There's also more of a focus on the horror elements, rather than survival mechanics. The 30 levels across its 13-15 hour campaign are also a lot more linear, and despite having more missions, it has fewer collectibles and a lot less attention to detail in regard to background chatter and NPCs. The first half of Last Light is rather uneventful, which may turn off some players, but where it shines are within its segments where Artyom is completely alone. There are some really memorable moments here, and if you're patient they will eventually come.
To its discredit, Metro: Last Light Redux ends up leaving the series feeling exhausted once you've reached the end of its long campaign, especially if you're continuing onward right after playing Metro 2033. Though the developer wanted a direct sequel, literally nothing within the gameplay itself has changed, there are only a few new creatures to contend with, and a couple of new weapons. The linear progression and lack of NPC immersion that was present in the first game also really holds this follow-up back.
This Redux does include all of the DLC that was previously released, which includes the Developer level that's like a mini-museum for the game, Anna, Kahn, and Pavel specific missions that are mini-stories, the Spider Tunnels mission where you must traverse a deep dark dungeon alone and weaponless, the scavenger level Kshatriya where you fetch specific items from around a map, and the Tower which is a wave-based survival/shooter challenge. This content alone lasts for a good 3-5 hours, depending on your skill level, and the character specific mini-stories are some of the best content that Metro: Last Light Redux has to offer.
When it boils right down to it, Metro: Last Light Redux is a good game, but it's nowhere close to being as fantastic as Metro 2033. It's missing far too much of the immersion that was primarily given from listening to NPCs banter, and the story does take a while to pick up; the soundtrack and ambiance are also lacking. It's very easy to tell that it's a direct sequel to its predecessor, which is what the developer intended, but it also feels like a reskinned Metro 2033 game since nothing really has changed; if it weren't for its immense length, it would've been better off released as DLC. If you do grab this one, do so on sale and play a game or two in between the first installment and this title.

Speed runners is an indie developed, 2D sidescrolling, racing game that is fit for all ages due to its unique appearance, availability and 'quick to pick-up' controls. This combined with its fast paced gameplay and short game length allows it to be played anywhere and anytime (i myself am guilty of sneaking it in and about while doing homework and assignments,"just 1 more match!") which can explain its overwhelmingly positive feedback even while it is still in 'Beta' development. Included with this gameplay is the intergration of the ranking system which involves the use of the leaderboard which tracks players in you league and how many points they have which allows the player to check their standings compared to others which allows for a competitive environment that increase the games longegevity and also seperates casual players to more serious ones.
Speed runners appearance is fit for all ages due to its bright and bold colour palette which distinguishes the background from the runners that the players control, giving the game a 'quirky' and fun feeling. Its availability comes from its low price of 10 dollars while not on sale and 2 dollars while on sale which is a cheap price compared to most other games in the market that usually range from 15 to 25 dollars. Speed runners is also a 'quick to pick-up' game letting players get into the game faster and also making it less daunting for newer players to the genre. This combined with its cheap price and colourful appearance sets this game up for long-term success due to its wide target market and the fact that cartoons are better than realism long-term due to realism always being outdated while cartoons itself are a unique and personalize genre of presentation.
Its rank system involves the use of leagues which are different groups that players are placed in due to their skill. Its uses a point system which is the way you rank up to a higher league in Speed Runners in which points are earned according to you succes in matches. However you may ask how they balance out the points lost or gained if you in a match with higher ranked people? Speed Runners makes it so that if your vsing a higher ranked person, the points you lose in the match are decreased and if you vsing a lower rank person, the points you lose are increased. This, combined with the quick matches that speed runners offer makes the ranking environment, friendly and less daunting for any player.

There are the reasons why Speed Runners in my opinion is worthy of a 7/10 rating which can be improved through increased content, different styles of gameplay e.g. new gamemodes, perhaps a unique character customisation (might be going a bit too far xD) and general bug fixes which i strongly believe will be achieved when this game is out on full release (maybe not the character customization).

I played Unreal when it first came out in 1997. At the time, it was revolutionary in terms of its engine and capabilities, standing shoulder to shoulder with the likes of Quake. At that time, I was young and played it with cheats on - just wanting a power trip I suppose.
I picked it up again in a Steam sale and it languished in my library for several years. Laterly, I've been going over that library and picking titles to get into and actually complete. Unreal Gold caught my eye and I decided to give it a go. Fairly this time - no cheats and medium difficulty. I don't have all the time in the world to struggle through the hardest difficulty, but I still want a challenge.
I know a lot of people on Steam try to give marks for various portions of the game - gameplay, graphics, sound, etc. I don't think I can quantify any game in that manner. All I can give are my impressions of it and how much fun it was to play. Overall, Unreal and the expansion campaign was entertaining. Gunplay was quick and generally responsive; the need to collect and manage both ammo and health were a hallmark of the 90s FPS genre. The guns themselves were ok, but they lacked any real impact. Sometimes, it seemed like I was firing marshmellows at the Skaarj rather than hot lead. The Eightball launcher was particularly lacking in that feel of something dangerous being thrown around. Levels were varied to an extent, but I caught myself thinking, more than once during the campaign, that the levels were almost like a slog to get through, rather than fun. Some seemed to stretch on and on, and a few were confusing enough that I had to consult the Internet to figure out where to go. In a linear FPS, that's rather strange. I like the lack of hand holding, but searching an area for 20 minutes to figure out where I am to go or find what moved when I pressed a button was irritating.
My other complaint was the lack of light in the game. There were places that were terribly dark, and the ingame flashlight was woefully inadequate to illuminating these. Flares were ok, but too few.
Despite these complaints, the game was enjoyable overall. While gunplay suffered a bit, the Flak Cannon more than made up for that. Killing your way around Na Pali was still a romp I would recommend at least once. Grab this on a sale if you like the "old school" shooters of years past.

I originally played this game back when it was released in 1998.  I bought it whenever I bought it on steam more recently (probably a few years ago) and probably never played through it because of various life events and just adulthood in general, but I fired it up again recently and was immediately reminded why I love this game.
It is, to this day, one of the most enthralling games I've ever played.  Much like Half-Life (which was released soon after) this game tells it's story and moves the player forward directly through the gameplay, without cutscenes or very much dialogue.  You get a PDA like device which is used to read things written by other "characters" in the game or just messages in the world/translating a sign written in an alien language.
Like the store page says, you start as a prisoner (from what I can gather) and that's what I really love about the story in this game; the protagonist is just a piece of flesh that was discarded by a society.  They aren't the chosen one, a spy on a special mission or an elite spec ops soldier (even though there are subtle and maybe not-so-subtle religious overtones that suggest otherwise).  No one within a thousand of light years from where you are cares about you.  You're not special.  You're garbage.  It's beautifully grave and nihilistic.  Don't get me wrong; there are certain aspects of the narrative that kind of give you an ego boost in a roundabout way, but the game pretty much lets on that you are just the wrong person at the right time.
As far as the gameplay itself, you can definitely see how in an alternate universe, that this game could have been the single player phenom that half-life turned out to be:  Super fast paced combat against agile, unforgiving enemies that take lots of rounds to kill, interspersed with moments of unease as you tread through dark and quiet maze-like hallways, changing to more open outdoor areas and puzzles that span large sections of a maps.
Obviously, by todays standards, this game is going to look extremely dated, but that only makes the theatricality of the setpieces that much more impressive. Lastly, while other games that had come out at that time used every chance they could to use colored lighting in the tackiest possible way, the artists in this game used a much more subtle and "thematic" approach that really lets that first version of the Unreal Engine show it's worth for that era.
And for those of you who, like myself, like to lose hours upon hours into a game, then this has that covered.  It is NOT a 5-6 hour quickie like a lot of modern FPS campaigns.  There's a lot of action and exploring to be had.

Unreal is a game I started playing over a year ago, but didn't really get into at the time. I finally got around to restarting it recently, and my thoughts are as follows.
Gameplay-wise, Unreal is decent. It's an Old-School FPS, but it forgoes a lot of the trappings of the genre. A lot of the weapons don't fit into any of the usual FPS weapon categories (shotgun, machine gun, etc.), instead filling roles that they just made up on the spot. The default infinite-ammo pistol is actually quite useful, and it only gets better over the course of the game with the help of collectible upgrades (which I apparently missed, like, three of). Besides that, there's a solid variety of weapons, each with a clear and identifiable function (and an alternate fire, which is neat), and all of them feel pretty good to use. There's a lot of overlap with Unreal Tournament (including the Flak Cannon, God Among Firearms), although they all look different.
On the other side of the gunplay, the enemies can be goddamn annoying. They all have too much health, really hard-to-avoid AoE attacks, and/or frustratingly unpredictable dodges, and sometimes the game will just send a seemingly unlimited steam of them at you. One or two at a time is fine, but more than that feels like tossing ammo into a bottomless pit in the hopes that doing so for long enough will grant progress. The higher-level Skaarj in particular can get ♥♥♥♥ed.
However, gameplay in Unreal takes a backseat to world-building, and that element of the game is noticeably better. It's really atmospheric, and everything seems weird, unsettling, vaguely hostile, and alien. Not just the alien planet that you're on, either—that would be expected. Even your weird, hard-to-classify weapons seem like they don't belong, and you shouldn't be using them. The first level in particular, once you get out into the open air, makes you feel really vulnerable and unsafe, even though there aren't any enemies around. The game also plays with some ideas that Half-Life would use to greater effect later in the year, like friendly NPCs, areas with little to no combat, and seamless level transitions, and the way they make the world seem more real only makes the alien-ness more convincing and threatening. It's a wonderfully crafted atmosphere, and the game manages to more or less keep it up throughout.
Actually, both the gameplay and world-building take a backseat to the engine, because Unreal is primarily a tech demo for the now-ubiquitous Unreal Engine. It has some fairly impressive features for the time of its release, and it can't wait to show you its transparent water, colored lighting, and high polygon counts. Sometimes it gets a little obvious that certain areas exist only to show off engine capabilities, but mostly it's pretty innocuous. Early 3D physics are still annoying, though.
Unreal also clearly wants to be Quake 2 so hard it burns inside. You have an infinite-ammo pistol instead of a melee weapon, there are blocks of text tacking goals onto your otherwise-meaningless button-pushing (without a use button), there's anger-inducingly mazy level design and no map, and overall the two games just feel very similar in a lot of ways.
The player character is female, which you don't really see enough in this genre. The fact that it completely doesn't matter and you can only tell if you look in a mirror or get injured reinforces my belief that developers should put more racial and gender diversity in FPS, because it doesn't hurt the game at all and more diversity is always nice.
Unreal has a lot of issues, and I wouldn't say that it's an especially good game, but I almost never felt frustrated while playing it. The gameplay isn't that fun, and it's not memorable at all except when it's being dickish with the enemy distribution, but the atmosphere is good enough to make up for that. Overall, it's worth a purchase, but if you have to choose between this and its immediate sequel, head for the latter without hesitation.

Short Preliminary Review:
This game is Great!!
Why?..  --
-- Runs on 'toasters' !!  ( I desperately wanted to find something that could pull me away from the con-artistry that 'Gems of War' was, (but was still 'addictive' to play), and this was it!!   My tablet that I'm currently stuck on can actually play this at reduced settings, for a game that's 3d, well-modeled and not designed like a cheap 'retro' game, this is fantastic!! )
-- Mellow atmosphere, yet 'action-oriented' game-play     (Again, I was stuck on Gems of War due to it's simple, yet effective, game design, and it's very difficult to find games that can both be 'immersive and fun' yet allow you to look at videos, play one-handed, and basically allow for you to do other things (somewhat) at the same time.
This game has a fantastic end-of-the-night mellow feel yet still has the action and intensity to keep you up and focused.
-- Massive amounts of 'completionist' level/item/stat "grinding" !!   (Game has tons to build up, do and explore in terms of character building -- this gives it massive replay value (random dungeons etc as well), which again is perfect for it's repetitive 'play while focusing on something else'  value.

You always end a game session feeling like you accomplished something, which, in a time of cheap money-grab 'random' loot games and horrendous pvp mechanics, this is saying a lot!
-- Fantastic item crafting    (You can easily build -and- level up items using crystals you find during your dungeon runs.  No weird 'scam' loot tables and 'pay-to-win' mechanics. )
-- Fluid controls including 'AWSD' movement and directional-mouse shooting.  You can 'click' on an enemy but it basically soft targets from directional aiming with the mouse - fantastic.  Full action controls but still relatively simple if you're not paying full attention.
-- NO 'pay-to-win'.  Sure the game costs a few dollars but it's worth it for what it is, far more actually.  (There are absolutely no 'transactions' in the game.)
Again, this game is -perfect- for those that need to have a game 'going' while they're on the computer, while they do something else such as viewing videos or potentially taking breaks from reading etc.
People should support games like these it's a great 'mold-breaker' and there's 100s of lame copy-cat 'click-your-enemy' top-down trash games meanwhile this has run-and-gun mechanics, fluid gameplay and great character building and item/loot design.
Much better than most games yet few have heard about this.
Note it was designed with tons of co-op multiplayer features (including guilds, rankings, etc) but since so few know about this game almost nobody is on.
Note I'm not the type to hold that against a game, I feel people should spread the word if a game is good and get others to play, not leave the game in hopes of finding something 'better'.

Verdict - Give this game a shot if you want something mellow yet satisfying to play at the end of the night or while you do stuff on the computer, it's far better than most (in the category of simple yet deep, inexpensive games).

-Played hundreds of hours, just not through Steam-
I WANT to like this game, I really do. That's part of the reason I'm wiring this, to finally convince myself that I should never come back to this game, which is unfortunate, because the game has a fantastic premise.
You have a massive world to explore. This includes multiple large continents, various smaller islands, the open sea, and even the sea floor. You can explore the world through various ships (from rowbots to gallions), vehicles (farm carts and sports cars), mounts, and gliders. But the best part about this massive world is everything is open to PVP between the two main continents. There’s even some ship based combat—and let me just say, you haven’t lived until you’ve dropped a meteor spell on a massive enemy ship.
Speaking of spells, how you choose to defend yourself is up to you, as your “class” is decided upon which of the 3 skill trees you choose. This means you have a total of 120 potential “classes” to choose from.
Here lie the beginnings of the sour taste left in my mouth after playing this game. You can certainly pick any class/combination of skill tress you want to, but that hardly means every class is viable much less possible. This issue here is due to the way skills derive their power from the weapons you wield. Every weapon is capable of dealing damage; however, not every weapon provides the additional buffs a class may need.
Let’s say you want to play a warrior who casts some spells on the side, then you need to find a way to work a spell power weapon into your arsenal, most likely meaning you’re now wielding a one-handed sword and an off-hand scepter for magic damage.  Or, maybe you want to be a stealthy rogue who can also do some minor healing? Well, good luck with that, because the only weapons the provide bonus healing are clubs and two-handed hammers.
While these may seem like viable alternatives to the uninitiated, they are NOT. Not only are these hybrid builds not at all viable, they’re not even marginable. By mixing classes you gimp yourself to a point where even PVE can be daunting. And GabeN help you if you attempt to mix the least-synergistic tree, ranger, with anything that wants non-range weapons.
The sourness continues into the crafting system. At first, the potential to plant and harvest crops wherever you so choose is fascinating. Though doing so will likely be your first introduction to the labor points system. To quickly summarize this system: Any planting, harvesting, or crafting requires a variable amount of labor points. Points are earned by remaining logged in; 10 points for 10 minutes. If you’re a subscriber or member then you earn double that amount per 5 minutes, with additional labor earned while not logged in. Free players can have a maximum amount of labor with subscribers having a higher cap.
So, free to play users are clearly at a disadvantage. But it doesn’t stop there. You crops, should you have the labor to plant them, can actually be stolen by both friends and enemies. This is another really cool concept that encourages exploration. Additionally, stealing crops is an in-game offence, and enough of those could land you in jail or make you an aggressive-to-everyone pirate. But again, the members have a distinct advantage when growing resources because they can actually claim land. Oh, you wanted a player owned home and special plot to grow your crops? Go pay a monthly fee. Then no one will be able to touch anything you grow in your plot.
This negative is made exponentially worse when the trade skills used for harvesting and crafting, such as woodcutting and armor smithing, require hundreds of thousands of resources to level up. So those non-members are left planting crops and hoping they don’t get stolen, and their precious labor points wasted.
Furthering this tragedy is the RNG involved in crafting. The items you make can vary in quality. Meaning if you’re hoping for a top tier quality of an item then you will likely be stuck making hundreds if not thousands of that item.
Let’s take a second to review all these labor costs while keeping in mind that you only get 5 labor every 5 minutes; plant your crop, harvest your crop (if it hasn’t been stolen), refine your materials, craft your item. If the item isn’t the quality you want: rinse and repeat. Crying optional.
Speaking of crying, the main story is also something you’ll likely cry over. Not due to its quality, but because it’s painfully short, and rather cheesy. Unless it has recently changed, the story barely carries you to half of the current level cap.
I WANT you like you ArcheAge, I really do. Your fast paced, massive PVP has made some of my best mmo memories. And your economy made me feel like I was a part of the actual world. A world I spent hours exploring and sailing in. Some of you skill trees were so cool in theory, but so lack-luster in practice. And don’t even get me started on my cow mount, Moonalisa, who has a cow pie skill.
But what it comes down to is this: ArcheAge is one giant slot machine, with your log in time being the accepted currency. You can play the odds and pay $15 a month or spend in game cash to buy membership, but that won’t change the odds so heavily stacked in favor of the house.

Valkyria Chronicles is a game with fantastic gameplay, and maybe even a decent story, if you can get past the atrocious script and very anime-esque. . . everything.
The main gameplay element, the BLiTZ system, is actually fairly interesting and fun to play, combining TBS tactics and Action RPG fun. I found myself wondering if a similar system might be beneficial for other games, which seems like a star in VC's book. The fact that each individual soldier at your command came with a backstory and unique set of traits, even ones that had no story significance whatsoever (and that's a lot) was also impressive, and it made me want to keep everyone alive.
The biggest problem I had with this game was its awful, AWFUL script. It's sometimes cute, but worth cringing at at least half the time. Character personalities and motivations also end up being pretty flat, but there's at least enough to kee[ the ball rolling; it's not Star Ocean bad. The Steam port suffers from a couple of glitches, but nothing I found was immediately game breaking, so hopefully you won't have any problems either.
If you don't mind cheesy dialogue and anime out of every orifice, then this game is fun the whole way through, and I entirely recommend it.
The game had a really good story with lots of clues to find and some side mysteries to solve.

The devs, after having a long term hiatus with the game, have finally come out with some form of a mega patch. I was really excited the moment I read the comment to see thinking that lots of the games issues have changed. Sadly, this is not the case.
Before you go "well this game is early access" there is a point where a game has bugs, and a point where the bugs prevent you from enjoying the game.
First of all.... The servers won't load multiplayer games, so I don't even know if my previous robots  are playable. I just get an indefinite loading screen when trying the online play. This is something disappointing because I did enjoy the little bits of content the game had. It's disappointing that the robot I made cannot be played currently.
Objects on the ground still sometimes float over your walking surface. I don't know if it is intentional, as most of them are eyeballs. It seems out of place because I can walk right through them, just like some of the props I see in the game. It really takes away from the otherwise unseen art style of the ARPG genre, which usually consists of very grim color palettes.
One of the biggest issues I have with this game is the fact you can walk off the edge of a map. Sometimes it's the literal edge where there is a physical cliff that you can walk off. Some of them are obvious others are not. If you walk off them, sometimes you can get back into the gameworld but sometimes you cannot. If you're unfortunate, you have to end your run early, preventing you from obtaining any potential rewards. This can be really frustrating if you just fall off the game world. I am not talking about the cliffs that kill your character either. I am talking about the ones that keep you alive when you walk off them, either accidentally or intentionally.
Some of the tips are not really tips. "Upgrade your weapons for more damage" is not really a tip. That is sort of commonplace for RPG's and some ARPG's. People familiar with the genres (like myself) are well aware of what upgrades are for. Tips like that feel more like handholding, rather than something useful. A better tip would be to tell me where I can upgrade my weapons, as the new hub map is a little large and confusing (more on that later).
I do not recommend playing this game with sound. The sound of weapons are generic and not sounding like they deal much damage. Not to mention some of the enemies do not have sound. This I don't find to be much of a problem though, as more ARPG's I play (because of their own nature are often grindy) with no sound. I would say listen to some of your music. I cannot speak for the game's music because I keep all the sound muted. If there is music, I have yet to hear some in all of this game's recent playtime I have.
Some of the weapons aren't what the name's suggest. The starting weapon is a "minigun" but has a very low rate of fire. This is contradictive to the real life counterpart. I am not saying video games are "unrealistic" or "need to be more realistic." What I am saying though is some weapons names' need a quick name change. Change "minigun" to "heavy machine gun/HMG." I don't know about any of you guys, but I don't know of a minigun that fires roughly 5 rounds per second (which is way slower than most modern assault rifles). I would be much happier knowing that this weapon is not a minigun, otherwise I fear for the weapons status in this game. I don't want to have a "double barrel" shotgun that fires fully auto, as that would not make very much sense.
The dash button is cool and all, but your overall unupgraded mobility is really slow (it's still really slow when upgraded; because to my knowledge, the maximum is +10% movement speed, with some marginal upgrades coming from armor I am not aware of the cap[movement speed maximum], but as far as I know, you still move very slow). Especially when you have to do backtracking because you missed an objective that was not very clear to find. I think if your robot has not been in combat for say, 5-15 seconds that you should get a speed increase. Somewhere between 20%-40%. That way you can find your next objective much easier. It woud also help fix this games tendancy to backtrack to locations (back when I played this game I recalled doing a  lot of backtracking).
I really dislike how skills in this game lack impact. The first skill you get slightly increases your rate of fire. It should be more impactful than a roughly 20% increase to your rate of fire. It does not even make a sound when you use it. That is just sad. Even any ole out of place royalty free or stock sound would make that better. I don't care if it's a clown honking it's horn, just make a sound for your skills. It's things like that which cross a very thin line between "early access" and "not ready for early access."
The duel wielding of weapons are lackluster. Because some of the weapons don't feel very impactful, they don't feel better when shooting both of them. The ole addage of "2 is better than 1" does not apply here. Especially when the fire rate is synchronised with each other. Each weapon fires at  the same time. Regardless of the type. Weapons with slower fire rates just fire on other times weapons shoot (so if a weapon has a fire rate of 10/second and another fires at 5/second, the slower firing weapon will sync up to every 2nd round fired from the faster firing weapon). The way to fix this it to make firing intermediate, or in other words, staggered from each other. It would give the illusion (if you're using the same weapon in both slots) that you double your rate of fire. That would be way better than just seeing to bullets fly across my screen in a parallel fashion.
I really do not like the half second delay it takes for your weapons to fire. That just makes the game clunkier than it needs to be and I am pretty sure that it's an easy fix. I also do not like how there is no animation for you to "ready your weapon." They just instantly pop up after about a half second delay and starts shooting.
Upgrades in this game are very cookie cutter. Very small percentage based bonus to general stats. This could be fixed by say something like, instead of having +2% weapon damage per skill level, it could be +5/10% damage for rapid fire weapons (like the "minigun"). This would allow you to specialize in certain areas and almost create a whole new tier system, based on your armor design. It would be like adding a subclass into the game.
The lockon mechanic is a great idea, just not fully realized as a component to the game yet. It forces you to attack the target that is only locked on, not allowing you to hit another target, even if it is beside it. If there was a button on your keyboad that you could press to allow you to lockon to the nearest target, that would be interesting. It would allow for some interesting mechanics for boss fights or fighting enemies (tough or weak) by themselves.
I felt compelled to let people know of the games flaws first. All games have them, but some people shoehorn them at the end, so people can make games sound better. I disagree with that method, but alas, I digress.
Despite everything mentioned above, I still think this game has potential. I think if the development team considers some of the things in my review the game would be much easier for me to recommend. Now, onto the stuff I enjoy in this game.
I really like the art style in this game. It is unlike every ARPG I have ever seen. I've played my fair share of them. The bright and colorful lights is something enjoyable to see for this otherwise grim and dark genre.
I like the addition of the hub world. It's nicer to look at instead of menus.
In the game's current state, it is hard to recommend, so I won't. I really want to though. I hope the devs continue to refine this game, as the potential of this game exceeds the sky in its current state.

The original version of Metro: Last Light was released in 2013 by developer 4A Games, and publisher Deep Silver. Alongside the reissue of Metro 2033, this successor also got a Redux version upgrade in mid-2014. Whereas its predecessor was based off of the best selling novel of the same name, Metro: Last Light is not actually inspired by any book from Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky, but rather it's a direct sequel to the first game. In fact, a majority of the ideas for Metro: Last Light came from 4A Games themselves, though done so with heavy input from Glukhovsky, who also wrote all of the dialogue for it, alongside a brief outline of the story.
First up, for owners of the original Metro: Last Light, is the Redux worth it? Since the graphics were already better in 2013, the striking difference between the original and the Redux is not felt as profoundly as the striking differences between the 2010 version of Metro 2033 and its subsequent Redux. That's not to say that the game isn't beautiful, because it is. The engine is also a lot smoother, and gameplay is definitely more fluid. However, I wouldn't say pay full price for it if you own the original release; if you do grab it, get it on one of its frequent $5 sales. If you're new to the series, read on.
Metro 2033 had two endings, and depending on where your hidden karma meter landed you, you either got the good or bad one. The bad ending for Last Light's older brother, wherein Artyom ends up bombing the Dark Ones and eviscerating them with missiles, was chosen to be cannon, and this title picks up one year after that fateful event. Main protagonist Artyom has been promoted to a Ranger, and his crew have since occupied the D6 military facility that he discovered in the first game. Due to the mysterious and legendary status of the D6 bunker, rumors of it housing great riches spread throughout the metro, and rival factions have set out to seize the area for themselves. Though that isn't the sole basis of Metro: Last Light, Artyom soon discovers that one Dark One has survived the barrage of explosive devastation that was meant to kill them all.
If you played the first installment in the series, you'll already know what to expect with Metro: Last Light Redux; as stated previously, the engines are the same, as are the mechanics. To its credit, it does feel like a direct continuation of the first game in every sense. However, while the senior title focused more on a guns-blazing approach, this release really centers around stealth, especially in the beginning. There's also more of a focus on the horror elements, rather than survival mechanics. The 30 levels across its 13-15 hour campaign are also a lot more linear, and despite having more missions, it has fewer collectibles and a lot less attention to detail in regard to background chatter and NPCs. The first half of Last Light is rather uneventful, which may turn off some players, but where it shines are within its segments where Artyom is completely alone. There are some really memorable moments here, and if you're patient they will eventually come.
To its discredit, Metro: Last Light Redux ends up leaving the series feeling exhausted once you've reached the end of its long campaign, especially if you're continuing onward right after playing Metro 2033. Though the developer wanted a direct sequel, literally nothing within the gameplay itself has changed, there are only a few new creatures to contend with, and a couple of new weapons. The linear progression and lack of NPC immersion that was present in the first game also really holds this follow-up back.
This Redux does include all of the DLC that was previously released, which includes the Developer level that's like a mini-museum for the game, Anna, Kahn, and Pavel specific missions that are mini-stories, the Spider Tunnels mission where you must traverse a deep dark dungeon alone and weaponless, the scavenger level Kshatriya where you fetch specific items from around a map, and the Tower which is a wave-based survival/shooter challenge. This content alone lasts for a good 3-5 hours, depending on your skill level, and the character specific mini-stories are some of the best content that Metro: Last Light Redux has to offer.
When it boils right down to it, Metro: Last Light Redux is a good game, but it's nowhere close to being as fantastic as Metro 2033. It's missing far too much of the immersion that was primarily given from listening to NPCs banter, and the story does take a while to pick up; the soundtrack and ambiance are also lacking. It's very easy to tell that it's a direct sequel to its predecessor, which is what the developer intended, but it also feels like a reskinned Metro 2033 game since nothing really has changed; if it weren't for its immense length, it would've been better off released as DLC. If you do grab this one, do so on sale and play a game or two in between the first installment and this title.

A Well told story in a FPS is all the rage these days.  This game seems to hit the nail on the head, specifically because it is based on a book of the same name.
I like the fact that it doesn't require too powerful of a PC to run it and look decent, but if you want 4K and everything Maxed, you are going to need a decent Video card.  My system is somewhere between the Min and Max, and runs the game at a smooth 30-40 fps at 1080p.  I know with just a GPU upgrade it would look amazing... so with looks out of the way, lets move on.
I turn the music off in video games... I see almost no reason for a game like this to have anything aside from ambient noise.
Gameplay.  Well, boundaries exist in the game, and they are VERY hard boundaries.  Traversing an open wasteland, should not be prevented by an invisible wall... but it commonly is.  The gun play is on point, with a few exceptions.  You cannot turn fast enough to follow certain enemies, which conveniently disappear into holes in the wall/floor.  Headshots frequently fail to kill enemies, Even when 10 feet away with a shotgun, multiple headshots just make them dance... though when the game feels like it, every headshot you land, at any range with any gun, will drop entire squads.
Bugs, Same bugs as its predecessor, while playing, you will randomly get locked into a cyclic issue, that dying or quitting the game is the only resolve.  I fell through the water on one mission, and had to quit out.  Reloading fixed the issue.
Bosses... Boss battles are annoying more than they are difficult.  I had no issues dispatching this entire game in a single day, and still had time to go back in and get some screenshots.
I got this game as part of the Redux Bundle, and for the price, I was definitely entertained... But there is no way that a 10-15 hour campaign was worth $60 when the game released.  I only recommend this game based on its current $ per hour, and I can find plenty of value in <50 cents per hour.

+ Well-designed environments (nothing to say, everything fits really well especially with the music)
+ Music (Alexander Brandon and Michael Van Den Bos did a great job for Epic games as usual, I'd recommend to listen to the stuff that they've created for another games too like (Jazz Jackrabbit, Deus Ex and etc.) or even check out the games themselves because they're pretty awesome too.
+ Story and the lore overall
+ Comfy UE1 rendering (even better with the dx12 overhaul)
+ Editor is a masterpiece (You build the map with special "brushes", which are basically 3D primitives which means that you don't actually have to know anything about 3D modelling in order to build your own map, the engine supports special archives where you can store your custom textures and use them for your own maps, however if you in example were to change some built-in 3D models, scripts, sounds (?), you would probably need to recompile a half of the game. As I understood, modding UE1 games is a great challenge because you need the exact version of the engine the game was compiled on + some of the developers were modifying the engine to have some extra features they wanted to see in their games, which means, I guess, that without any kind of reverse-engenering skills modifying the game is from hard to impossible, also the engine is proprietary.
- Shooting mechanics (it's kind of clunky, great variety of weapons, however after beating the game I didn't manage to figure out the purpose of each weapon (if they even have any or just designed for the player to have a wide choice)

- Some levels (near the end of the game) took me a lot of time because of running in circles, trying to understand where to go.
To sum up, this is a great demo for Unreal engine, especially for its time, also the game without any kind of huge letdowns. For the best experience I would recommend to play on easy or something like that, because I don't really feel like this can be a really interesting and challenging experience from the point of the actual game mechanics today. Updated review based on further play and updates:
This game had the potential to be brilliant, and indeed, it starts out that way; fresh, original and challanging, it draws you into it's world, rewarding skill and punishing carelessness in a way that feels balanced and well thought out.
The presentation and voice acting is sublime. I loved the dealer and his snarky little remarks. The VO is superb and I hope to see more of this kind of thing in future games. Another good point are the mechanics of the game; Easy to grasp and introduced smoothly and clearly. If you have any exposure to card or tabletop board games at all then you already know how to play this game, it is that intuitive.
The game is hard, unforgivingly so in later levels, but the 'cheapness' and unfairness seems to have been toned down a bit. The brilliance seen at the start now shines through at all points of the game, something I am immensly pleased about.
5 Hanged man cards in a row? Yes, that will happen again and again. Nightmare Golem Hunting party cards? Yup, over and over! If this doesn't kill you then the game will just start throwing bosses at you whenever it feels like it; "Oh I see you are approaching a shop....KING OF DUST AND A DOZEN MOBS!!!!!!!!" This will come after some unlikely card removes your best weapon of course. Do not think this is exaggeration, it is impossible to exaggerate how much this game enjoys shafting the player.
At first I thought this later spike in difficulty and cheating ruined the game, but on reflection I think it adds longevity and I suppose it is in keeping with the theme. Some of the more outrageous BS does seem to have been 'dialed back' which is defintely a positive move. I do not mind losing a game, but losing through no fault of my own, again and again was getting galling.
Overall this is unlike any other game you will play. It has absolutely massive replayability and the charm of the presentation, and fun of the core game is enduring, never outstaying it's welcome.
I will be keeping and eye on this developer if this is the standard of game they put out!

The first BioWare game I ever played was Knights of the Old Republic. I admittedly picked it up mostly cause, you know, it's Star Wars! But I actually thought it was mostly a pretty good game. Then Mass Effect came out. I freaking LOVED the first Mass Effect game. Even without the Star Wars license, it was an undeniable improvement over KOTOR in every way. It had a much more interesting and engaging combat system, it had more impactful narrative decision making, and it had more interesting characters and better told story. But maybe most important of all is that the in-game world felt so real and immersive. It had massive lore and backstory and I could read as much or as little about all of the locations and technologies as I wanted. The voice acting and writing was excellent and the game pulled off humor and sarcasm better than most other games at the time. Plus the game looked (and still looks) pretty darn impressive.
Mass Effect 2 is all of these things and more. I believe it to be the epitome of the Mass Effect franchise. ME3 is a good game too, but it didn't feel as refined or complete of a game as ME2. It seemed like one of the design goals of ME2 was to trim a lot of the excess fat that was present in the first Mass Effect. Gone are the clunky vehicle sections. Gone are the annoying canisters of useless extra weapons and armor that you trip over every 5 steps. But returning is the excellent writing and character design. The crewmates on the ship were so varied and interesting, even more so than ME1. Arguably the least interesting characters were the ones that returned from the first game which isn't so much a slight of the first game as much as it is a compliment to the excellent character design of the second. I loved that you also got to see some of the impact of the decisions you made in the first game. It's also a nice reminder that the impact of a lot of the important decisions you make in ME2 will be felt in the next game. Or at least felt at the end of ME2.
Perhaps the most notable improvement in Mass Effect 2 is the combat system. Combat in the first game was somewhat clunky and awkward. It was sometimes hard to tell if you were actually hitting your target and shots tended to clip into invisible barriers or sometimes seem to miss for no reason at all. The combat in ME2 is much more polished and visceral. You KNOW when you get a kill and it feels satisfying. My favorite change in the combat system is with the different weapon types. It's much more rare when you acquire a new weapon, so it feels more exciting. And it's not simply a binary "Is this gun better or worse?" like in ME1. The weapons are all different and have varied strengths and weaknesses. They all play and feel fundamentally differently with different reload speeds, ammo clip sizes, range, and also varied damage and accuracy. You have to play around with the weapons a little to see which one best suits your playstyle. And I love that. Also the excellent level design in ME2 facilitates constant changing of weapons. Some levels are close quarters with lots of short hallways that are perfect for strong shotguns while others can be long, open courtyards perfect for sniper rifles. And the refined abilities and powers are a nice added touch that separates Mass Effect from other action-shooter games.
While the refinements to the combat system are nice, the real reason I come to ME2 is to get my story on. I loved the darker or at least somewhat more mysterious themes of ME2. I liked that Commander Shepard was no longer a pawn of the Alliance, but was a renegade in league with Cerberus who were villains in the previous game. Sure, Shepard sort of takes orders from the mysterious "Elusive Man" throughout the game, but you're always free to pick your own destinations on the map and unfold the story at your own pace. It gives the game a more open-ended "explore the galaxy on your own terms" kind of feel. The game seems thematically closer to Star Trek than Star Wars which is ironic considering the development team's pedigree. But I loved exploring and discovering the game world in ME2 and the set pieces are all so well written and memorable. Especially at the end of the game. I won't spoil what happens for those who still haven't played it, but ME2 nicely and meaningfully wraps up all of the choices and decisions you've made in the game up to that point. And it does it in a way that is both exciting and memorable.
Mass Effect 2 is a great example of a perfect marriage between excellent gameplay and storytelling. It's an excellent sequel that refines everything that was good about the first game in the series and trims out everything else that was not. It should be a must-play game for fans of shooters and fans of great storytelling alike

The game that made Epic epic. This review is based heavily on the CD ROM and
(DRM-free) releases of Unreal Gold. So my Steam time with Unreal doesn't even come close to my experience with this time-tested classic.
While Unreal Tournament gets damn near all the spot light for Epic, and understandably so, it really started as an add-on for Unreal. Unreal Tournament was originally an expansion for the, admittedly weak, multiplayer component of Unreal. However, Unreal's single player core game is phenominal. In fact, the core mechanics, graphics engine, and weapon functions that made Unreal Tournament a masterpiece were first introduced in Unreal.
Unreal's single player experience has aged like the finest of wines. The minimalist story practically tells itself via the environment. The atmosphere draws the player into a fully realized world. The music sets the mood for much of what's going on, and even drops out altogether at some points allowing a vaccuum to add tension or calm. While the graphics definitely show their age, they get the job done and almost lend a "vintage" feel to a game from a ground breaking era. In single player, Unreal is neck-and-neck with Quake.
In this era of dumbed down, "hyper realistic" military themed FPSes with tacked on single player campaigns, I've grown to appreciate Unreal Gold more than ever.

Each unit has their own traits that affect them in minor ways in combat, and backstory which get revealed with time in the field. Outside of combat, there are upgrade trees to attune your units to typically play in a particular way. It is not super extensive and mostly likely increases a stat or employ a new weapon attack. These work on entire class units, not individual.
The story is pretty straight forward, you play the role of Welkins, son of a hero general, whose small nation is caught between two heated super powers. However, it is a enjoying experience, that makes you want to know more of whats happening in the world with its little surprises. The characters are enjoyable with their own quirks, where you might hate or like them.
Of course as the first of a IP, there are some minor inconveniences.
The sketchbook filter can be annoying at first but is something that is easily ignored and warm up to. It can even potentially be useful in missions. There are no options to turn it off.
The prebattle map isn't very useful, for such things as elevation, obstacles and enemy locations.
It makes it difficult to decide the most optimal placements of different units. There are save features where you can save at any instance, even every turn, for those who need to save scum.
These were my gripes, nothing large, minor hiderances.
It is also a pretty good port, recommend a controller.
A good first iteration of a series, and perhaps the best.
TL;DR: Good game with a neatly enjoyable story, fun characters, pretty tight unique style of gameplay, and challenging missions.

I've been waiting for American Truck Simulator for a few years, and I was hyped to hear about it's release! I grew up with Wheels of Steel: Long Haul and a few of the games to come in the following years until I finally bought Euro Truck Simulator 2, which I have been playing ever since. ETS2 is a fantastic game and I thought ATS would just be an American reskin.
I was wrong.
ATS introduces loads of new features and gameplay elements that make it so much more enjoyable. Sure, the map is a lot smaller, but ETS2 was a lot smaller when that first came out... it's just a baby, it'll grow in the coming years; Arizona is not too far away! There are so many things that I'm excited about in ATS, and while it's not a perfect game, it's very fun.
The ETS2 world of Europe was catered to trucking. Cities are small and only filled with warehouses, truck dealers, and recruitment agencies, there are no shopping malls, supermarkets, or life in general, and the urban enviroments are empty and baren. A lot of things don't make sense. Thankfully ATS is nothing like that:
Cities are much larger and full of life, there are more delivery locations (for example, gas stations, grocery stores, road side construction sites, ports, and many more) that are logically located in enviroments that make more sense in a real-world setting. When I pull out of a warehouse with a trailer, it feels like a real warehouse which is not placed in the middle of a busy city. There are delivery locations in the middle of no where, which I appreciate, along with the mountian passes, the beach-front roads, and the small one-stop-light towns which aren't much more than a small intersection. It's the small things that make a big game better.
The game does still have imperfections, such as buggy AI, lots of repeated assests, duplicated buildings that have just been rebranded, small truck rouster, but when you look at the big picture, they are minor things. They don't break the game. Maybe they'll be addressed in the future, but if not, the game will still be fun.
Would I recommend this game? Hella yes.
