Bought this game during the Winter Sale, but it's definitely worth full price! A truly great video game experience, and my favorite in recent gaming history. Spoiler-free review for the potential buyer; inspired by my recent completion of the main story for the first time, I feel it necessary to gush out my first impressions.
Buy it full price. Even for a now 8-year-old game, it's still a standout.
The fact must be addressed that this PC version of the game is a port from the PS3. It is, however, one of the best ports I've ever played. There's unparalleled amounts of input control, and the game engine scales to any resolution and framerate you computer provides, so it maintains graphical quality without being held back by arbitrary rendering limits. It might be a relatively dated game limited by the graphical fidelity capable on a PS3, but it's gorgeous to run on a PC nonetheless. The only thing I could find to complain about are the unintuitive UI controls, which take a little while to acclimate to.
The gameplay is a unique hybrid of top-down, turn-based strategy and third-person shooter. As the commander of Squad 7, you choose 20 members of the Gallian militia from a large roster of individuals, broken down into 4 classes, to fight in your operations. You're given a set number of Command Points to use per turn to control your units. You're also given access to various Orders that let you affect the battlefield in different ways.
However, the great part about your units is that they're all
, even the non-plot relevant ones, each complete with their own unique character models, voice-actors, personalities, "Potentials", which are positive or negative stat changes that affect that individual based on certain criteria during battle, and even opinions on which other members of the militia they like. Despite this, stat progression is based on class development, so you don't have to worry about one member needed to catch up to another if one is used in combat frequently and one isn't; they all progress equally.
The humanity of these people that you fight with is no more apparent than when they die; if you lose a member during combat (knocked out for three consecutive turns without medical aid), then they're gone for good, and losing a member, even one you're not particular fond of, is usually a heart-wrenching affair. Only five main characters get plot armor here; you have to be very careful of how you position people and use them in combat in this game.
Because of this, the gameplay is not for the the impatient or headstrong, and greatly rewards taking advantage of the strengths and weaknesses of individuals in your squad, like the aforementioned Potentials, among a plethora of other details. Another factor you are recommended to take advantage of individual control over weapon distribution; as you put the game currency you earn from ops into Research & Development, multiple weapon types become available to you; some are good at some things, and some others, and having different people carry different weapons can further accentuate their role on the battlefield.
One thing that cuts down the gameplay score for me, however, is the rank system. The success of your ops is, in contrast to the actual, tactical nature of the game, solely determined by how quickly you can complete them. The highest ranks, and therefore the best rewards, involve abusing cheesy tactics to get things done quicker, and ultimately missing out on some awesome battles. My advice is to ignore ranks on your first playthrough, and supplement your XP and currency gains by toying around with the challenges and skirmishes that are available to you at any time, and can be replayed, unlike the narrative operations.
Speaking of cheesy tactics, a couple of the narrative operations involve opposing some tremendously difficult...nay, completely overpowered bosses who will definitely give you a headache. The necessity of re-trying these battles over and over to get them right makes me lament the lack of an autosave feature, although you are capable of saving at any time.
The combination of the rank system and those outrageously difficult moments in the game makes the gameplay less than perfect, and detracts from an other awesome experience, where the fact that there are more members on the roster than you can fit in your squad and that there are a myriad of ways to complete ops keeps the replay value high.
Alright, now to the other stuff!
To be fair, this game does have its fair share of cliches in it, but after playing through it the first time, I realized it accomplishes some things I didn't really expect it to: first of all, I cared about the characters and their stories. There's development, there's relationships, the main characters get fleshed out quite a bit, and there's excellently sparing use of the fantasy element, just enough to keep it interesting. The universe is convincing and engrossing, and although there was no lack of detail, the world is interesting enough that you still want to know more about every aspect of it and its history.
The story is told through animations and animated-comic-book-like segments, with the actual operations taking place in-between. I felt like there was a nice balance between the two.
Another thing to consider is that the story has a blend of typical anime tropes, mixed in with decidedly dark takes on the reality of war; a strange contrast, but one that I think ties in nicely with the overall theme of humanity in the narrative.
Absolutely stunning compositions by renowned video game composer Hitoshi Sakimoto, which really complement both the elements of action and humanity throughout the game. You'll definitely get used to the same music over and over as you open up the game, start battles, and flip through menus, but its all appropriate and beautiful music.

There's something really beautiful about the way information is presented in this game, which is via the Glossary, Weapons, and Personnel tabs in the book. The book, which recounts the tales of Squad 7, is the medium by which the whole game is told. I love the intricite details for every weapon, and the evolving biographies of your militia members, which grow as the story progresses. Something worth merit, I believe.
In anime, one classic, age-old argument is subtitles versus English dubbing. Well, for the first time in my life, I can heartily recommend dubbing as my preferred way of experiencing the game. The voice-acting is top-notch, and seeing as how English is my native language, it's easier for me to pick up on the vocal inflections that make each voice unique, which makes the characters stronger, in my opinion.
One particular thing of note is that I decided to try the dub because the sub wasn't precise; the subtitles are a word-for-word of the dub, and not a translation of the Japanese. This means that the only way of truly experiencing the Japanese dialogue, which could be completely different than the dub, as far as I know, is without subtitles in raw Japanese. Maybe not important to many, but I figured I should mention it.
Beautiful stuff. The painted canvas effect is gorgeous.
Flawless? No, of course not. But it definitely deserves a place in any gamer's Steam library. Get it, ASAP! Even if you're not typically into strategy games, maybe the human element of this game will change your mind.

What is Crusader Kings 2? You ask as you boot up the game for the very first time. 6 hours later you are involved in a plot to kill your brother, crusading for the holy land, and your uncle is leading a revolt to lower your crown authority.
Crusader Kings 2 is a grand strategy game developed by Paradox that lets you play as a count, duke, king, or emperor during the timeframe of 1066 to 1453. Instead of most grand strategy games where your ruler lives forever, in Crusader Kings 2 your character will die and then you will continue to play has their heir until your dynasty is killed off or the game ends. In fact the entire game is based around you running your dynasty rather than your country. Good traits, prestige, and wealth are all passed down so it is important that you maintain good bloodlines, even if you need to kill a few family members off. The second part of the game is religion. When a Crusade or Jihad is called, you are expected to join and fight or suffer the consequences. Rulers of the same faith will tend not to go to war with each other while the opposites will. There is a lot more stuff I didn't mention but you are going to just have to play to find out.
The game, unfortunately, has the "Paradox Plague" meaning that if you want to do anything (custom character/country) you are going to need to pay for the dlc. Even major things like playing as Islamic characters requires a dlc. Granted they are cheap and go on sale quite often, but it is still content that should already be in the game, or at least a free update. Thankfully the game has great mod support so you can play user created content.
Crusader kings 2 is worth your time and you will sink a ton of hours into it. There is a learning curve, but once you get over that you will be ruling with the best of them.

Let my start out by saying finding a dedicated developer these days is not easy in anyway. Now you might be thinking what the hell is this guy on about?! Well since i picked up this game I haven't been playing anything else at all, and spending time on the official discord of this game and talking with one of the developers, who told me they've been working on this game for 2 years, and here is the kicker, without any pay WHAT SO EVER.
So these 5 guys from Greece have my respect and my thanks for keeping up moral and working so hard on this amazing game.
Now that to me is dedication beyond anything.
Now let's get to the nitty gritty of this game shall we?
D&R is a nice mix of ARPG mixed with some Twin Stick Shooter elements, and yes there is LOOT! (LOOT you say?!) SOLD!
It's a pretty basic game, you start a mission on one of 5 difficulty settings (ofc you need better gear to advance) and then you run through the dungeon completing your objectives.
- Easy - Normal - Hard - Insane - Legendary - The first 3 difficulty settings can be played solo allthough I would recommend playing hard and up with a friend, but like I allready wrote you will need better gear to advance. Ofc the game also has a leveling system, once you level you get 2 stats points, that can be placed into different trees that give you an increase in either dmg, crit or hp regen etc.
Like any ARPG the gear goes from uncommon - common - unique too legendary being the last tier of gear, gear can be obtained in game, but most of it is obtained by crafting. Crafting gear requires pure crystals which are obtained throught the game (yes there is alot of grinding) but too me that is not an issue, since hard work in this game is rewarded.
As you craft, your crafting level will increase giving you access to better types of armor and weapons. So far there are 3 types of armor, light, medic and heavy.
Light: Your standard dps if you want a light armored dps that is, also with light armor you have the advantage of being faster
Medic: Shouldn't need to much explanation.
Heavy: You're a damage sponge or if you don't want to be a damage sponge you can also be a dmg dealer. Disadvantage of being a heavy is you are slow.
You can also craft weapons and there are quiet a few, so far I have encountered missle launchers, ray guns, miniguns and flamethrowers.
Crafting as with any other game is very RNG based, RNG based to a certain degree as increasing  your crafting level helps.
Before I forgot some or most of the items you obtain have attachment slots, where you can equip crystals, that grant you passive stats such as attack speed, damage and hp regen etc.
Each armor also has a certain amount of skill slots, skills are found in game only, and they can grant you, or your entire team a quick boost of attack speed or hp. These skills also vary in quality and like I allready said some are single target, which benefit only you, others are mass ofc meaning the whole team.
Graphics: Amazing I absolutly love every dungeon I have been in so far, with that said there isn't a huge variation yet, but the devs are currently working on a big patch. But like I said the graphics are colorful and then dungeons are really well designed,
Sound: Well as of now they have some sound issues, that are being worked on, but taking that out of the mix, I do find the sound effects to be very very good.
Music: Amazing music that changes depending on the dungeon you are in, too really set the "mood"
Controls: Controls are good and responsive, the targeting system (lock on) can sometimes be somewhat weird, but again something that is being worked on. There are
Overall this game is a solid ARPG / Twin Stick Shooter it does have some bugs, but like I allready wrote, the devlopers are working on a big patch changeing and fixing issues that are currently present in the game.
Would I recommend this game? Absolutly if you are into ARPG games and also love twin stick shooters, this gem is a must have in your collection

TL:DR - 12hr run time if you hunt for collectables. Average plot, decent but not groundbreaking and ultimately predictable. Decent mechanics and character abilities. Reasonably well written characters. All of this is hindered and spoiled by the frustrating need to kill demons when the kill sequence is buggy as hell and only serves to slow the game down and annoy you. Still worth playing, but be prepared to be thoroughly annoyed for about a quarter of the game.
Overall it's got a decent plot, decent set design, interesting game mechanics. The Investigation side of things is pretty typical, doesn't stretch very far from the conventions of the genre but does involve a few quirks to give it it's own identity (e.g. you can uncover clues and information through possessing people and manipulating them into giving up information).
The plot is, for the most part, pretty predictable. For example, *minor spoiler, no specific details*,
.The only real twists and turns occur right at the end and even then don't do much to flip the story on it's head, they just make the overall story a little more original. Around halfway through the story, a lot of people will figure out the second half of the plot pretty quickly and then will just have to play through the game and wait for confirmation of what is sadly quite obvious.
All that aside, the biggest detractor from the game is the BLOODY DEMONS. A few sections of the game require you to get your stealth hat on and exorcise demons from behind by distracting them, triggering a quicktime event, and hoping that the stars and planets are correctly aligned when you press the buttons, because the system is buggy as hell. For starters, this style of gameplay is totally unecessary and poorly implemented. There's absolutely no flow to it and it just seems like something the developers put in to make the game last a little longer and make it more exciting/different (which it does the exact opposite of). For a dectective game, it really kills the immersion and slows the pace right down. It's incredibly frustrating when all you want to do is get on with the investigation.
Basically, if you're drawn to this game and like detective games, go ahead and play it. It's pretty fun and pretty clever at times. Just don't expect to be blown away by the story, although it has some pretty good moments. And definately expect to get extremely fed up with BLOODY DEMONS.

Metro games were games upon their release that were inaccessible to me due to my potato computer I had at the time. Now with the redux version I have a decent rig that allows me to try them. Lately I have been very disappoited with too many games hyped up to death and then have underwhelming release. Not with Metro. The excellent mix of pure fps action with atmospheric and tense post apocalyptic exploration in a narrative driven game is what surprised me positively and truly felt like breath of fresh air after many disappointments. Metro is a game that proves you don't need groundbreaking innovation or mechanics to make a thoroughly enjoyable game. The game does not offer anything that has not been seen before in gaming, yet it does everything with such balanced and enjoyable execution that it feels fresh all the time. The general precision of all the pieces coming together in this game that work so well together is what makes it into a winner. You have solid and deeply atmospheric graphics and excellent world/level design. I was shocked to see a game this old look this good and atmospheric even as a redux version. The sound is spot on and you can choose Russian or English language if you prefer the authentic experience. Subs can be any language while choosing the audio language separately. The world of metro makes you believe you are in this world and makes you invested in it and wanting to find out more. It also breaks the fps elements by adding witcher like characters and npc:s who share the world with you, allowing you to take balanced breaks from exploration/fps action. While the game does not allow you to choose different dialogue with characters, almost every person is part of the universe and responds to you in ways that makes you feel like you're getting to know them and even care for them. There are two different styles of playing options besides the difficulty settings. The original that emphasises survival aspects and forces you to sneak and count every bullet while exploring and scavenging for supplies and items to sell and buy. Radiation takes a part as well as freezing cold and toxic air. Depending on your choice, it will directly affect your game progression. For instance you have to decide can you afford to kill someone or rather spare your ammo or filters for gas mask so that further in game you don't end up in trouble.
The other option makes for more dynamic combat that for some may seem more enjoyable option. The battles can get very tense and ammo will run out forcing you to run for your life grabbing ammo from corpses while in heat of combat. I myself am playing this option currently and enjoy it. You still explore and do all the things as in the previous option but the emphasis is more on the fighting, producing tense combat scenarios and more of the fps feeling. It does not however become an straight brainless fps shooter even when this option is chosen. I may draw some ire from fans of the series for saying this but if I may, I would like to compare the streamlined combat to Mass effect 2, even though the titles are not comparable by any means, but the difference in the combat being streamlined to produce more tense and action packed fast combat, over the meticulous one offered in the first option.
The story is interesting and the world under ground in metro tunnels is engaging. I love how the story paints how despite humanity being destroyed by nuclear war, still manage to find ways to restart the same cycle of hatred between each other and essentially being at war with not only against the mutated hordes that live above ground, but with each other. At a time when they should be united for survival of the human kind. It's a narrative of the human condition and it's ironic to see the communists vs. neo nazis who are also Russian and the clan you belong to be at utter war with each other despite being all survivors of the same fate, having a united enemy as threat. This game brings out the best and worst of humanity to the table in a tongue in cheek post apocalyptic Russian setting. What also reminds me of witcher is the adult themes expored in here, along with the exploration aspect. It's a game on rails that avoids feeling like it was on rails and sometimes even feels like a semi open world game without being one. Sure you can't escape the linearity of it and some elements are more linear than others, such as the tunnel sequences whre you literally are on rails. But these are also so well made that it does not become boring or distracting. It works well in the theme and story of the game.
For the price it has and especially if you can get it on sale, definitely recommended for all who enjoy post apocalyptic action oriented games that have strong story and tense atmosphere. If you like games as S.T.A.L.K.E.R or similar, definitely give this one a try. The only gripe I have is the lack of variety in the mutants and also with the way the encounters with them tend to turn into hordes where it feels like a set number of enemies need to be slain untill they simply run out and you can progress. By this I mean last man standing type of scenarios. This game builds upon the continuation of the original metro 2033 game and is enhanced both graphically and execution wise. I definitely recommend getting both games as a bundle while waiting for the new game in production.

I am really torn between giving this game a thumbs up or down, but I chose thumbs down for two big reasons.  The first is that there are only a handful of maps, and it simply gets boring fast, I am sure this will change with updates however.  The second and largest reason is that it seems to be too difficult.  Let me explain: as with every golf game the goal is to get the ball in the hole in as few moves as possible and each hole has par, anything less is a good score and anything more is a bad score.  The problem is that it's almost impossible to hit the ball with the right amount of force because the ball either rolls a lot or a very little and is hard to get the exact force you want.  Secondly you have to be a perfectionist when playing, there are several holes where if you make one mistake you'll get over par.  There are also some holes where it is almost impossible to get under par because the hole is seemingly designed to make you go out of bounds or get lost.  I'm looking at you egyptian level.

Its still as amazing as ever! I had originally gotten this on my Xbox360 and it was a ton of fun. I saw it on sale during the Halloween 2015 sale and picked it up pretty cheep, considering the original price.
I love ghost stories, horror, and killing demons (Diablo). This game has ghosts and demons (which you can choose to avoid or execute, depending on where you are), I found I actually had to execute them to continue at some spots further in.The game begins with Ronan falling through a window and narrating a bit, you also get to learn more about Ronan's (life/ backstory). Considering the fact that he's the main hero and the playable character thats a good thing and its also important.
Gameplay is what really got really got me hooked. The town of Salem has areas for doing detective work and its freeroam in the Hub section and the areas (To an extent, its not Final Fantasy or anything, but you do get to explore). The character is always seen in the third person point of view (camera is behind the character).
Interactive- You can go around and talk to certain people or listen in on their conversations. You can "investigate" and search for clues- which you'd then use to solve a case or continue on in the story.
Collectables are always fun, but can be a pain to collect as they are actually hiding and not always in a typical spot.
Cutscenes are interactive! You can usually choose what you want Ronan to say or ask next. Nothing major, but heck its something.
Powers, well you get to do a lot of stuff later, but when you just start off you can already possess people and cats (no, seriously). You can also mind read or try to manipulate their thoughts.
Story? Spoilers! You die first thing and become a ghost- woot! You're also a detective of the Salem police department. You also have to try to solve your own murder and many others.
The game is great and recomendable, but I do have one problem. I had chugging/ lag while on my Xbox and was hoping that'd be fixed on the pc version. That was not the case, and I still have the same annoying chugging/ lag. Its not always while going to a different section of the Hub town, but it does happen a lot in the Hub area. It also happens in other spots, but it rarely happens in places like the graveyard or appartments. So, thats a bit of a bummer, but its still a great game.

So I am going to start off this review with a side note. I have more hours in the game then what is posted. exactly how much? I dont really know but after a while i downloaded the standalone version of the game and have logged hundreds of hours into the game.
Game Play:
I think that one of the best parts about this game is how fluid the combat feels. It really feels like when you are using a combo or skill you are actually DOING something. I have developed a very strong prejudice towards games that dont make the fighting seem impactful/real. Elsword delivers in every area in this aspect. Not only are "most" of the attacks amazing but every single job specilization feelws very unique. Unique enough to the point hwere i can make a new character i havent tried yet and feel like i am starting the game all over again.
I was also not the biggest fan of side-scro0lling when i came into the game but I forgot about that in about 5 minutes.
Graphics:
For the most part I feel like this game does very well with its graphics. They feel very crisp while at the same time not requiring a beefy computer to trun them. This in part is because of the anime style it has.
There are a few situations where you might encounter frame drops but these are few and far inbetween. Usually the only time in experince them is during a raid with a full party while everybody uses hyperactives.
PvP:
The PvP starts off pretty nice. E-S rank all feel pretty balanced but as you start to get into the higher ranks the bad side of this game starts to show. Gearing is extremely important in this game and most gear is attainable through hard work and persistence. However due to the game using an enhancement system to improve gear, they start loosing the balance when they let people pay to attain +10 +11 +12 and soon to be +13 amulets to amke there gear better. These arn't even small differences either. The % at which the stats increase scales the higher the enhancement. Overall though I still think that PvP is really fun but just dont take it tlo seriosly or you will probably uninstall the game in frustration. I advise KoG to take out this enhancement system or find a non P2W equivilant in the future. I also advise that they make getting costumes without real money a more regular thing.
Story:
Meh... Its pretty interesting but with the amount of time you will be creating new characters it gets old after a while.
Overall:
I do think that this game deserves a lot more praise then it gets from the community. What it set out to do it has done quite well and just has a few tweaks that i think need to be made in the future.
I rate this game with an overall score of 7.8/10.
If the P2W if removed in the future this rating will become a 9/10

Updated review based on further play and updates:
This game had the potential to be brilliant, and indeed, it starts out that way; fresh, original and challanging, it draws you into it's world, rewarding skill and punishing carelessness in a way that feels balanced and well thought out.
The presentation and voice acting is sublime. I loved the dealer and his snarky little remarks. The VO is superb and I hope to see more of this kind of thing in future games. Another good point are the mechanics of the game; Easy to grasp and introduced smoothly and clearly. If you have any exposure to card or tabletop board games at all then you already know how to play this game, it is that intuitive.
The game is hard, unforgivingly so in later levels, but the 'cheapness' and unfairness seems to have been toned down a bit. The brilliance seen at the start now shines through at all points of the game, something I am immensly pleased about.
5 Hanged man cards in a row? Yes, that will happen again and again. Nightmare Golem Hunting party cards? Yup, over and over! If this doesn't kill you then the game will just start throwing bosses at you whenever it feels like it; "Oh I see you are approaching a shop....KING OF DUST AND A DOZEN MOBS!!!!!!!!" This will come after some unlikely card removes your best weapon of course. Do not think this is exaggeration, it is impossible to exaggerate how much this game enjoys shafting the player.
At first I thought this later spike in difficulty and cheating ruined the game, but on reflection I think it adds longevity and I suppose it is in keeping with the theme. Some of the more outrageous BS does seem to have been 'dialed back' which is defintely a positive move. I do not mind losing a game, but losing through no fault of my own, again and again was getting galling.
Overall this is unlike any other game you will play. It has absolutely massive replayability and the charm of the presentation, and fun of the core game is enduring, never outstaying it's welcome.
I will be keeping and eye on this developer if this is the standard of game they put out!

**Please keep in mind that, at the time I write this review, the game is still in Early-Access Beta.** That being said, unless some fundamental things about this game change, I don't foresee myself changing my recommendation.
Firstly, I have seen this game compared in several videos and written reviews to “Mario Kart, but on foot”. This game would better serve its players if that truly was the case.
In Mario Kart, you are able to do laps on courses. You aren't kicked out of the race because you aren't as good as someone else on the track. The camera stays with you, and you progress through the track with the ultimate goal of being first, but getting to finish the race and learn the track regardless.
In SpeedRunners, the camera isn't focused on you, but, rather, whatever section of the track is occupied on average by most of the players. If you honestly insist on comparing it to a Mario game, imagine New Super Mario Bros. Wii, but instead of getting pushed up to the pack via a magic bubble when you find yourself lagging behind in your multi-player match, you just die and then wait for everyone else to do the same 'til someone wins the round, the first to three rounds winning the match.
This lends itself, potentially, to a lot of down time. I say this because you are not consistently matched with people of your same rank (a particularly frustrating issue in Ranked Matches where points are on the line). Therefor, you're left sometimes watching more of a match than you are actually playing it because someone two ranks higher than you knows the map much better than you.
[Since this is the first point I'm making, one reading this might believe I'm writing the review as some frustrated noob put off by all the higher ranked players kicking my a**. Not the case. At the time I wrote this, I was a Bronze League player with just under 180 hours logged. And, while I am certainly not the best player at the game, the grievances I am going to express here come from both excessively winning and losing at it.]
And, yes, there is something to be said about observing those higher ranked players and learning from them in your downtime. But, as most anyone will tell you, repetition and being able to immediately apply and put into practice what you have observed are pivotal to learning it yourself. For instance, if you're playing Mario Kart and you witness someone taking a shortcut you just missed, to be able to come around the next lap and give it a go yourself is essential to developing your skills.
But imagine seeing a player in SpeedRunners take a short cut, in turn knocking you out of the round. Then someone wins the match, and the next race gets voted on and isn't even the same map... you're not given that opportunity to better yourself with hands-on experience. That is, unless you create a custom match with a bunch of bots so you have complete control of the map and play it by yourself, which, I don't know about you, but that doesn't sound like loads of fun to me.
Racing a fixed number of laps vs. winning a number of rounds would better facilitate player development.
Secondly, there is the matter of the options menu needing a severe upgrade. Things like toggling the on-screen chat on or off before you even join a match, electing whether or not you want to join matches where custom maps or weapons are turned on or off... these would all be beneficial to players in having a much more enjoyable experience.
(Note: You can “mute” the players in the on-screen chat from within the match once the match has started, but your only opportunities to do this really would be once you have died in a round, as the 3-second window between rounds is hardly enough to do it if you are winning; plus, if you are actively attempting to use the on-screen chat or the in-game menu to mute the people in it, you render yourself unable to control your character. This is why all these options need to be moved to a menu prior to joining a match.)
Spend any amount of time playing this game, and you will come across players who complain about being subjected to playing “custom maps” that they didn't vote on, or how “you must really want to win if you used a bomb”. As if to say that a player should be expected to not utilize certain aspects of the game just because it is an inconvenience to what is usually a higher ranked player of the game.
Yes, you can just mute them once the match gets going (as previously explained, not the most user-friendly process) and their complaints will fall on deaf ears, but it would make much more sense to give people the option to turn such features in the matches they join on/off. For instance, if you're the creator of a room, you have the ability in non-ranked matches to control the existence and features of a sort of “bonus wheel” that effects the forthcoming match. It wouldn't take much more to apply these same privileges to turning off bombs or custom maps if you really don't want them in your gaming experience.
But, instead, what you have at this point in the game's development is a bunch of whiny players, usually Expert League and higher, who cry when you hit 'em with a bomb or pick a map they may not know like the back of their hand.
Lastly, there is the just fundamentally flawed-at-times gameplay. Instances in which you'll be in the lead and suddenly the game will kill you because you touched the FRONT of the screen (an issue that wouldn't exist if, again, the game were based on winning by laps and the camera stayed with you). Or times where, because the game allows people to join matches already in progress, people entering or leaving the room will cause the game to lag and, when it's caught up with itself, you're dead. This is especially frustrating in Ranked Matches wherein someone joining mid-match (who, because they joined mid-match, won't even be eligible for points) causes the game to lag and, ultimately, costs you points. The ability to join a match already in progress needs to be completely disabled for Ranked Matches, and it needs to be an option whether to allow players to join mid-game in non-Ranked matches.
And while the physics of the characters themselves and how they interact with the map seem to have been thought out fairly well, the physics of how a weapon effects a character is preposterously off. Examples include getting shot from behind w/a missile and then getting flung IN THE DIRECTION the missile came from, or the great inconsistency of how a player may or may not even be stopped in the first place by a bomb or missile that clearly made contact (the game will even confirm contact with an audible cry of pain from your opponent, but your opponent just keeps running).
All in all, I have reached a breaking point with the game. It's no longer fun for me, personally, as I find it difficult to gain the experience I need to reach the next step as players more advanced than me get frustrated when they are exposed to bombs and custom maps and they just quit. (If you find yourself asking "Well, how did they get their ranks? Clearly, you're just BEHD!"... yes, you're probably right. XD But, also, the implementation of custom maps in Ranked Maps, for instance, is part of the ever-changing landscape of this game. Some of the more tenured players who can't deal with change will just rage quit these days, making it hard to gain experience.) Of my friends who played this game, I held out the longest, only just now acknowledging the frustrations that led them to abandoning the game months ago.
It's worth a play, and the forthcoming offline/party mode where you can avoid the toxicity of the majority of this game's online community (it's a rage-inducing game for some) and play with people at home is something to look forward to. But it's going to take really willing to♥♥♥♥♥♥off this game's pampered players & change some long-held core aspects of the game for me to give it a solid recommendation.

The original Unreal joins the ranks of Doom, Quake, and Duke Nukem 3D as one of the best "classic FPS games" from the 1990s. It truly was groundbreaking at its release back in 1998 and it really set the foundations for games for the next millenium. Except for mouse acceleration (which I believe can be fixed by a mod? I don't know), the gameplay still holds up compared to modern games. Most enemies are able to dodge projectiles quite well and never stand still. Some of them even use a variety of weapons too. Every single weapon and item you pick up is still useable up to the very end of the game, and the game doesn't hold your hand and take you to your destination; you have to figure out where to go and what to do all by yourself.
All of the levels look incredible - to vast caverns and plains, dangerous cliffs and ancient alien temples with familiar yet weird and fantastic architecture filled with intricate hallways, and futuristic spaceships, with a unique soundtrack to go with it. However if you're looking for more of a "cinematic" experience, this game doesn't have it. Story is mostly told through your personal experience and observations from simply playing the game and through journals that you pick up. Proper characters and dialogue are not present at all.
I want everyone to experience this game because It truly is a great game that every FPS fan deserves to play. It was one giant step forward for the video game industry back in the day and although people probably won't appreciate it like I did back when I first played it at 10 years old, it's still a great "retro" experience if anything.

The first BioWare game I ever played was Knights of the Old Republic. I admittedly picked it up mostly cause, you know, it's Star Wars! But I actually thought it was mostly a pretty good game. Then Mass Effect came out. I freaking LOVED the first Mass Effect game. Even without the Star Wars license, it was an undeniable improvement over KOTOR in every way. It had a much more interesting and engaging combat system, it had more impactful narrative decision making, and it had more interesting characters and better told story. But maybe most important of all is that the in-game world felt so real and immersive. It had massive lore and backstory and I could read as much or as little about all of the locations and technologies as I wanted. The voice acting and writing was excellent and the game pulled off humor and sarcasm better than most other games at the time. Plus the game looked (and still looks) pretty darn impressive.
Mass Effect 2 is all of these things and more. I believe it to be the epitome of the Mass Effect franchise. ME3 is a good game too, but it didn't feel as refined or complete of a game as ME2. It seemed like one of the design goals of ME2 was to trim a lot of the excess fat that was present in the first Mass Effect. Gone are the clunky vehicle sections. Gone are the annoying canisters of useless extra weapons and armor that you trip over every 5 steps. But returning is the excellent writing and character design. The crewmates on the ship were so varied and interesting, even more so than ME1. Arguably the least interesting characters were the ones that returned from the first game which isn't so much a slight of the first game as much as it is a compliment to the excellent character design of the second. I loved that you also got to see some of the impact of the decisions you made in the first game. It's also a nice reminder that the impact of a lot of the important decisions you make in ME2 will be felt in the next game. Or at least felt at the end of ME2.
Perhaps the most notable improvement in Mass Effect 2 is the combat system. Combat in the first game was somewhat clunky and awkward. It was sometimes hard to tell if you were actually hitting your target and shots tended to clip into invisible barriers or sometimes seem to miss for no reason at all. The combat in ME2 is much more polished and visceral. You KNOW when you get a kill and it feels satisfying. My favorite change in the combat system is with the different weapon types. It's much more rare when you acquire a new weapon, so it feels more exciting. And it's not simply a binary "Is this gun better or worse?" like in ME1. The weapons are all different and have varied strengths and weaknesses. They all play and feel fundamentally differently with different reload speeds, ammo clip sizes, range, and also varied damage and accuracy. You have to play around with the weapons a little to see which one best suits your playstyle. And I love that. Also the excellent level design in ME2 facilitates constant changing of weapons. Some levels are close quarters with lots of short hallways that are perfect for strong shotguns while others can be long, open courtyards perfect for sniper rifles. And the refined abilities and powers are a nice added touch that separates Mass Effect from other action-shooter games.
While the refinements to the combat system are nice, the real reason I come to ME2 is to get my story on. I loved the darker or at least somewhat more mysterious themes of ME2. I liked that Commander Shepard was no longer a pawn of the Alliance, but was a renegade in league with Cerberus who were villains in the previous game. Sure, Shepard sort of takes orders from the mysterious "Elusive Man" throughout the game, but you're always free to pick your own destinations on the map and unfold the story at your own pace. It gives the game a more open-ended "explore the galaxy on your own terms" kind of feel. The game seems thematically closer to Star Trek than Star Wars which is ironic considering the development team's pedigree. But I loved exploring and discovering the game world in ME2 and the set pieces are all so well written and memorable. Especially at the end of the game. Verdict: Surprisingly addictive game with a charismatic antagonist and charming (though sometimes frustrating) mechanics
To be blunt, this game is not what I expected. Then again, what was there to expect from a game that advertises with being a "card game" with action game mechanics. When I first saw it, I figured it had to be something like "Persona" series of games, and to SOME extent, this holds true. The random nature of each "dungeon" is what you might say these have in common. The similarities end, however, when you actually play the game. If I had to compare it with something people already knew, I'd say it is a weird hybrid between a "Make your own adventure" game, mixed with a collectible (sort of) trading card game, some D&D and a pinch of Arkham Asylum - if that makes any sense.
The gist of the game is this: You are a nameless Adventurer that battles against a mystic card dealer that sets you up with a different dungeon every time you start a new mission. Your adventurer is actually represented by a small golden gaming piece that you can move about the track of cards layed out before you. The cards obviously face down, and the moment you step on it, it is turned to reveal your fate - and behold there is quite alot to be revealed. The scenes are described using text in a the fashion you'd see a dungeon master read from them in any kind of fantasy rpg. "Action" in these scenes is usually resolved by being presented some choices and depending on which one is picked, some event happens. An example would be the "Angry Guildmaster": He bullies you out of the way with his horse, and you have the option to either "Humbly apologize", or try and steal from him. While the first option lets you continue on your way, the second lets you pick 1 of 4 cards to see how things develope. Dragin a "success" card will net you a reward card (coming in the form of food, gold, health potions and such), whereas a failure might result in you getting thrown into a dungeon, having to fight your way out against a number of opponents, which - you guessed it - is determined by the pick of a card.
You'd be surprised how littel "action" there is actually going on. Only a minority of cards (still plentiful, mind you) actually leads to you being set into an action scene to fight. The game has a few set areas or stages where combat might take place, depending on where the descriptive card you landed on told you you were. There is quite a bunch of them, and some of them are trap-ridden and require keen awareness and movement.
The combat itself is basically Arkham Asylum's Reflex system, where you have three different actions. Attack, counter, shieldbash. It is, literally, the same thing, but it works quite well and you rarely get the feeling you are not in control. It is nothing new or astonishing, but have you ever heard someone complain about AA's combat system? Me neither.
As for items and such, you get a pretty standard array of axes, hammers and swords, a couple of rings, shields and armours, a bit of magic through "artifacts", pretty much standard fantasy stuff. Again, it works well enough to keep you entertained and allow for some meta-gaming.
Now, you might wonder, what is my goal in this game and how does this card thing come into play appart from being a random mechanic? The longer you play, the more cards you unlock through "tokens", which are attached to some cards. Resolve the card in the intended way successfully, and you get new cards. You can then use these cards to build your decks: One is for all your own goodies like weapons and armour, the other for possible encounters - that's right, you get to determine what encounters you might have in your adventure! But beware, the sinister card dealer has a word in this, too. With every new adventure, he puts in increasingly more challenging cards. Also, each of the story mission comes with some kind of "mutation": Sometimes everyone moves faster and receives double damage, another one might forbid certain actions, make things more expensive, etc. It will keep things fresh for quite a while, at least for the "story mode", which is, essentially, just you wandering from card to card until you reach the next boss. When story mode is not enough, you can always try endless, where anything goes and you continue until you are dead.
Now, with the card game mechanics come some things you'd might expect that make the whole experience a little... tainted. Especially in the later stages of the game, you might simply be unlucky and die without being able to do much about it. I had an especially annoying series of events that left me with ONE max HP (that is right: My maximum HP have been reduced from 100 to 1!), no food left (you lose Hitpoint when moving your piece without having food from "starvation) and nothing to redeem myself. In essence, the game just laughed at me. Now, these extreme cases seem to be very, very rare, but there are other cases where you realize you will probably not stand a chance against the upcomming boss because you simply had no chance of drawing equipment cards, never receiving gold or food, or the dealer drawing two old bosses (once bosses are beaten, they can be drawn as "regular" enemies in encounters) very early in the game, causing you to either die or losing many hitpoints. Also, while it caters to the games charm, it is not always clear what the developers intended with certain events and what a certain choice might lead to. This "trial and error" principle is probably there to pad out the game a little bit (which would fall a little short in content, otherwise), but be aware that this game sometimes just doesn't seem to "play it fair".
I also find it a little disappointing that the action sequences are so limited and that the majority of the game takes place "at the table". The game does make up with SUPERB voice acting by Anthony Skordi, whom you might recall from voicing the more cockney'esque Dark Elves in The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. He also has quite the number of lines to boot, but still, it would have been much nicer if there had been a smoother transition between the card play and the actual action.
Also, the overall card and deckbuilding mechanics fall short once you have unlocked all the cards. There is no ways to get "doubles" (apart from what the game gives you), or winning "boosters" to alter up or otherwhise improve your deck. The developers have already released one DLC, but need to bring more options if they want to bring longevity to this game.
Of course, you have to consider that this is a kickstarter game and much of what I critisized could never be expected from the limited scope of ressourced the developers had at their disposal. The game is also budget-priced, so again, the equation fits. It is hard to do this game justice and it is a shame they do not provide a demo. It was a blind pick for me and I was pleasantly surprised, but it is hard to say whether this game will be to your liking or not. It is a fresh idea where the result is greater than the sum of its parts.

I actually played this game through glyph, and started playing on day 1 of the NA alpha.   I invested a little over $200 and played at least 150 hours’ worth (pretty sure way more).  I'm writing this review after trying the game one "last" time after several month "frustration" hiatus.  This review will mostly be a supplement and to reaffirm the current and more informative negative reviews.
The Good (kinda)
The game is a great sandbox game with the exception of instanced dungeons. It has pvp, pve, and the usual redundant quests.  Sadly, few mmos put any true work in their quests and Archeage is not the exception.  The sea and land pvp/pve are one the major positive aspects of the game.  The character customization is good, but I'll rate overall customization as moderate because you can get stuck with a lot of generic armor unless you really shovel out the $$ and time. House and land customization is one of the highlights of the game (if you can find/buy land from a player).
The Bad
Land is insanely limited and open to player trolling (i.e. bots grabbing land, uneven spacing of plots etc.).  Again, the quests are redundant and the feel is a grind.  You can level via crafting, but it gets expensive fast, especially if you don't have any land.   Players who have arrived before you "will" attack you in the pvp areas so if you're a solo player this isn't the game for you.  The game has been plagued with crashing and constant disconnects since day one for many if not most players.  Lastly, while the game is free don't expect to get very far without putting some real money into it.
The Ugly
Great game, horrible management…  As I'm sure will be a reoccurring theme in prior and future reviews the games management is by far its most negative attribute.  Player neglect, day one problems never being solved, devs punishing players for what they consider "negative" feedback, and what feels like and probably is a "we'll be with you in just a moment" attitude *queue the eternal  we don't care about you hold music.*
The game has (had?) great potential, but overall was a flop of an investment for me and many others.  Maybe not for you, but be cautious when deciding to invest in this game.  Try it out for free, but don't put a lot of money in it till you're absolutely sure.  However, my recommendation for this game will be a "No."

You should buy this game in a sale, get comfy, and prepare for a cliche story, endearing and memorable characters and some unique gameplay.

Hands down,
has got to be the best "Picross Puzzler" I've ever played, at least on the computer, perhaps overall.
It plays more like the famous Picross E series and its puzzles feel similar to them as well. Not only do you get a plethora of fully colored Picross puzzles by default, it also has workshop support, meaning, essentially, an infinite supply of presumably well-made picross puzzles, all in full color.
Are you still wary of this particular Picross puzzler? Or perhaps you're new to Picross and are wondering what the heck it even is?
Well, addressing the latter part first, Picross is, of course, a type of puzzle game. I find it similar to Sudoku, but completely different and with pictures. Essentially, you have a box with numbers on the outside of it. According to these numbers you fill in squares in the box, attempting to make a picture, hence the name "Picross", each square you fill in gives you more hints as to what you need to fill in next, so on. It's one of those "easy to learn, hard to master" kinda things, and it's
.
Now, for those experienced players or even new players who want to know why they should spend the wallet-destroying seven USD to get this Picross puzzler when there're likely countless free ones that you could choose instead, I'll explain more.
First off, did I mention the puzzles are colored? Pretty sure I did, and most of the free Picross games I've seen for computer, or phones too even, tend to, you know, not be colored. I dunno about you, but it just doesn't feel the same to me without being rewarded with a full color pixel art image after completing a rather tricky 25x25 puzzle.
Also, like I've said, workshop support. I don't even know how many puzzles there are made by the community as of writing this, I do remember there's 76 pages, but I forgot how many puzzles for a page, oops. But I'm assuming its at least 760, that makes sense. Think about that for a minute, 760 puzzles, do you know how much that is? Hint: it's 760. That's a lot, and most of the community made puzzles tend to be between 15x15 to 25x25 too.
Now you might be thinking: "Natalie, that's pretty dang cool and all, but there's still so many free Picross puzzlers out there that I could just play all of those instead, why should I pay 7 dollars?" Well, first off, remember that the famous Picross E series is somewhere around 7 dollars per game, and they're considered one of the best Picross puzzlers there are out there, and if you think about it
, you'll also remember that they have far less content than Pictopix, due to lack of workshop, since that's literally not a thing on the 3DS, well, at least by default. And these aren't some shoddy puzzles like that one free one on Steam, they're actually good, and difficult at times, perhaps not as hard as some of the more advanced of the E series, but in some cases they do tend to be actually.
The controls are also
, you've got controller support, proper mouse controls, and keyboard controls, so basically everything you could possibly want pretty much. And it also has stuff like auto-fading numbers and hints as to what columns/rows can be filled, if you're into that, though they're both considered 'hints' or 'cheats' and will deduct from your crown score. Honestly, I see near nothing bad about it.
That being said, there are some limitations. For instance, there can only be 5-25 puzzles, even in the workshop. Some really massive puzzles would be interesting in my opinion, but still, 5-25 is pretty standard and I wouldn't deduct points from this game for that.
There's also some things I think could be added that'd make it a bit more interesting or easy to use, for instance, making it so the placed squares while making the puzzle don't have to be white. I mean it's probably just me, but all that white hurts my eyes, can't I get something darker?? Also, I'd love to see stuff like the rather gimicky "Mega Picross", but I can see why it's not included.
The only real downside of this game is that the music does tend to get old, in my opinion. Otherwise, I'd give this Picross Puzzler a solid
.
If you like Picross, or are looking for an interesting new puzzle game, go get Pictopix, what're you waiting for?!

Metro games were games upon their release that were inaccessible to me due to my potato computer I had at the time. Now with the redux version I have a decent rig that allows me to try them. Lately I have been very disappoited with too many games hyped up to death and then have underwhelming release. Not with Metro. The excellent mix of pure fps action with atmospheric and tense post apocalyptic exploration in a narrative driven game is what surprised me positively and truly felt like breath of fresh air after many disappointments. Metro is a game that proves you don't need groundbreaking innovation or mechanics to make a thoroughly enjoyable game. The game does not offer anything that has not been seen before in gaming, yet it does everything with such balanced and enjoyable execution that it feels fresh all the time. The general precision of all the pieces coming together in this game that work so well together is what makes it into a winner. You have solid and deeply atmospheric graphics and excellent world/level design. I was shocked to see a game this old look this good and atmospheric even as a redux version. The sound is spot on and you can choose Russian or English language if you prefer the authentic experience. Subs can be any language while choosing the audio language separately. The world of metro makes you believe you are in this world and makes you invested in it and wanting to find out more. It also breaks the fps elements by adding witcher like characters and npc:s who share the world with you, allowing you to take balanced breaks from exploration/fps action. While the game does not allow you to choose different dialogue with characters, almost every person is part of the universe and responds to you in ways that makes you feel like you're getting to know them and even care for them. There are two different styles of playing options besides the difficulty settings. The original that emphasises survival aspects and forces you to sneak and count every bullet while exploring and scavenging for supplies and items to sell and buy. Radiation takes a part as well as freezing cold and toxic air. Depending on your choice, it will directly affect your game progression. For instance you have to decide can you afford to kill someone or rather spare your ammo or filters for gas mask so that further in game you don't end up in trouble.
The other option makes for more dynamic combat that for some may seem more enjoyable option. The battles can get very tense and ammo will run out forcing you to run for your life grabbing ammo from corpses while in heat of combat. I myself am playing this option currently and enjoy it. You still explore and do all the things as in the previous option but the emphasis is more on the fighting, producing tense combat scenarios and more of the fps feeling. It does not however become an straight brainless fps shooter even when this option is chosen. I may draw some ire from fans of the series for saying this but if I may, I would like to compare the streamlined combat to Mass effect 2, even though the titles are not comparable by any means, but the difference in the combat being streamlined to produce more tense and action packed fast combat, over the meticulous one offered in the first option.
The story is interesting and the world under ground in metro tunnels is engaging. I love how the story paints how despite humanity being destroyed by nuclear war, still manage to find ways to restart the same cycle of hatred between each other and essentially being at war with not only against the mutated hordes that live above ground, but with each other. At a time when they should be united for survival of the human kind. It's a narrative of the human condition and it's ironic to see the communists vs. neo nazis who are also Russian and the clan you belong to be at utter war with each other despite being all survivors of the same fate, having a united enemy as threat. This game brings out the best and worst of humanity to the table in a tongue in cheek post apocalyptic Russian setting. What also reminds me of witcher is the adult themes expored in here, along with the exploration aspect. It's a game on rails that avoids feeling like it was on rails and sometimes even feels like a semi open world game without being one. Sure you can't escape the linearity of it and some elements are more linear than others, such as the tunnel sequences whre you literally are on rails. But these are also so well made that it does not become boring or distracting. It works well in the theme and story of the game.
For the price it has and especially if you can get it on sale, definitely recommended for all who enjoy post apocalyptic action oriented games that have strong story and tense atmosphere. If you like games as S.T.A.L.K.E.R or similar, definitely give this one a try. The only gripe I have is the lack of variety in the mutants and also with the way the encounters with them tend to turn into hordes where it feels like a set number of enemies need to be slain untill they simply run out and you can progress. By this I mean last man standing type of scenarios. This game builds upon the continuation of the original metro 2033 game and is enhanced both graphically and execution wise. I definitely recommend getting both games as a bundle while waiting for the new game in production.

Now this is a darn fine game.
Valkyria Chronicles is a gorgeous, fascinating combination of strategy and third person shooter.  The game takes place in an allegorical version of Europe in World War II and follows the citizen soldiers of Squad Seven as their country of Gallia is invaded by the much larger Empire.  I found the characters extremely likable and the story to be engaging.
As solid as the story is, however, the traits that stood out the most to me were the presentation and gameplay.  As is evidenced by the screenshots, the game is flat out gorgeous.  The entire thing looking like a pencil drawing that is as majestic in motion as it is in stills.  And the combination of a top-down turn-based tactical map that transitions into a real-time third person view works astoundingly well.
When Valkyria Chronicles was a PS3 exclusive, I recommended it to everyone I could.  Now that it’s on Steam, I’m excited to do the same again.

You were wise to come to the negative reviews, dear reader, because you are about to be spared a regrettable purchase.
Do NOT be fooled by the Very Positive rating on this game; it is shovelware, plain and simple.
If you're looking for a nonograms game that will challenge you, move along. Puzzles never get any larger than 25x25, which might be acceptable for an activity book you can buy at the supermarket, but not for a video game, where you ought to have such functionalities like zooming in and out, or scrolling around.
Hell, it's worse than an activity book. With an activity book, you can play the puzzles in any order you like, and completely skip over the ones that are too easy for your liking. In Pictopix, you MUST slog through all of the easy puzzles before you are allowed to try your hand at the harder ones. And a slog it is, because at the end of every puzzle, you are treated to an 8-second long, unskippable "Well Done" sequence (which I suspect exists solely to try to run you past Steam's refund limit.)
The mouse controls are also quite sloppy. Common to most nonogram puzzles, you have some "gimme clues" at the start (rows which are either zero or the full length of the grid). Unfortunately, the click-and-drag controls have a tendency to skip over tiles you're trying to mark, if you move your mouse too quickly. In a properly-programmed game, clicking-and-dragging would simply affect all tiles in a row or column between the start and end points of the click-drag. In this game, you have to slow down your mouse to make sure that it marks all the tiles. Trust me, it feels more annoying to play than you would think.
And don't be fooled by the screenshots on the store page. You might see what looks like a multicolor puzzle, but there are no multicolor puzzles to be found in this game. When you complete a puzzle, the monochrome grid changes into colored pixel art. You can't actually play with multiple colors in any of the puzzles.
Oh, and I hope you weren't expecting anything in the music department. As you are solving puzzles, you will be treated to the same 1:30 music loop again and again, until you mute it in frustration. Considering that this is a simple puzzle game, a good soundtrack is essential for getting your players into a relaxed, thinking mood. This maddeningly repetitive music is inexcusable.
Here's the kicker. Google search for a game called Picma. You can play it online for free. It has much larger puzzles, and multicolor puzzles, and better aesthetic, and community-contributed puzzles. Pictopix doesn't even offer half as much as Picma (or Picma Squared, which is also free), and these developers have the gall to charge $7. Unacceptable.
Hopefully, you will learn from my mistake and avoid doing business with these disreputable developers.

I've heard that CK has only four devs left working on it, I can beleive it. I was promised a dynasty simulator, and now I have given up on ever getting that, and ever giving paradox money again.

I am judging this review based on its full price and therefore cannot recommend it. I would only recommend getting this game when there is a deep sale.

.
Murdered: Soul Suspect is a detective adventure game where you play as Ronan, an ex-con badass who became a cop to atone for his wrong doings. You get killed by a man in a hoodie and become a ghost. You learn that you need to find clues to figure out who killed you in order to complete your "unfinished business" and be at peace. This game had so much potential to be something great but fell short and left me with an unsatisfactory experience.
Gameplay
This is a detective game where you play as a ghost in the mortal world. Think about all the things you can do as a ghost, it's going to be awesome!.. Or at least that's what you are led to believe. You start off the game learning that can you can walk through walls, only to realise that there are "ghost walls" all over the town Salem that you can't walk through. These walls are just there to hinder you from exploring the town of Salem and become extremely annoying after a while. Next you learn that you could possess random people and read their minds, only for it to get boring and repetitive after 20 minutes. The people around the town were bland and shamelessly copy pasted and the only thing you get from reading their minds were always something along the lines of "Oh dear a murder, that’s terrible" or "I wish it wasn't so cold". It's the same thing over and over again and eventually you just won't bother with the possessions. Their scripted dialogue with each other is pretty interesting to listen to though.
The core gameplay has you travel from place to place in order to investigate scenes and solve puzzles. You have to find a couple of clues and then come to a conclusion about what the killer was doing or where he was going to next, much like the crime scene investigations in L.A Noire . However the puzzles are so painfully simple and boring that it doesn't take you long to come to a conclusion. In the end it just becomes a sort of glorified find the object game with an extremely obvious "which one of these objects are related to the crime?" conclusion (seriously, a spoon , a fork, or a key that belonged to the killer? I wonder which of these are relevant).
The combat system is an extremely basic stealth system where you have to hide from patrolling demons and then execute them when they weren't looking at you. However, like most of the game, demons pose little to no challenge and are just there to hinder you and fill time. The combat didn't evolve over the course of the game and after the 4th or 5th time I heard the demons arrive I just thought to myself "ugh not again".
You also have several dialogue options to choose from during the story, but these have no effect on the story at all. There are also side quests where you go about helping other ghosts to finish their business and these quests are rather interesting.
There are collectibles hidden all around the map for you to collect, these will allow you to learn about the town of Salem, Ronan's background as well as give some insight on the killer. Unfortunately there is no map function and also no way for you to check which collectible you already have and which ones you still need to find.  I enjoyed listening and reading the stories about the artifacts I collected and make exploring the town enjoyable, I just wished the damned ghost walls weren't so restrictive and annoying.
Graphics
The game is quite good looking and the town of Salem looks great. The ghost structures and mortal buildings complemented each other well to give this dark and gloomy feeling.
The main characters looked unique and well designed. There is a 30fps when you have v-sync on, but you can turn off v-sync in game and use v-sync from an external program such as Nvidia's control panel and the game will run at 60fps.
Sound
The music in this game was pretty good. It set the mood really well and occasionally the music would go eerily quiet to build tension. The combat music also tries its best to build excitement and tension but was unfortunately unable to complement or help the poor combat system.
The voice acting in this game was superb and was one of the only reasons why I could finish this game. I enjoyed listening to the conversations between the main characters and especially liked listening to many of Ronan's monologues.
Pros
+ Town looks great when the "ghostly" and "mortal" buildings are mixed together to form a unique hybrid look
+ Voice acting is superb
+ Interesting lore and backstory about the town as well as the protagonist
+ Good chemistry between the main characters
+ Interesting storyline
+ Side quests are a nice change of pace
Cons
- Basic and boring combat system
- Core puzzle solving is too simple and repetitive
- Extremely linear game
- Ghost walls are a hindrance
- Somewhat clunky controls
- Choices make no difference to the story's conclusion
- No replay value
In conclusion this game is an overly simplified detective game with a boring stealth combat system slapped on it. It fails to impress, and with a price tag of $30 I certainly cannot recommend it over other detective games such as L.A Noire

One of the best sci-fi action games I've ever played.
This game feels like they put up a core concept, and then just started adding their favorite mechanics from AAA titles.  From most developers, I would expect that to be a flaw in their game design, but Digital Extremes has managed to pull off a cohesion between so many different game mechanics and systems that I genuinely wouldn't know where to start with breaking them down in a review.
The best part, THIS GAME IS FREE!  WHAT?!  There has to be over 100 hours of content just in the campaign missions!  you can spend money on guns and aesthetics to accellerate your progress through the earlier missions, but so far I have only spent anything on cosmetic items and I haven't had any issue making steady progress without feeling like things have stagnated.

I know better now, but when i was brand new, i grabbed the Latron blueprint because i wanted a sniper instead of a bow, not realizing that one of the materials was unobtainable until I got to saturn.  I bought that blueprint around the 6 hour mark.  I'm now at 35 hours, and only just am getting access to the mineral i needed.  again, a tooltip may have prevented that frustration
These are small greivances, and the resources I wasted early on are pretty moot at this point.  So, honestly I cant reccommend this game enough.  I'm absolutely blown away by the immersion into this sci-fi world through small details they put in outside of missions, and just how fun the gameplay is.  the fact that this game is free and people still blow hundreds on DLC for destiny blows my mind.

This arcade style, city-navigation, character driven, jumptastic racing game is the only game I have with mouse steering and I miss it in every other driving game. And a lot of tight streets in the cities of this game require the detailed and quick steering a keyboard can never offer. Maybe the people who are buying hardcore driving simulations already have a wheel but certainly mouse steering should be standard in any game looking to appeal to a broad audience. Because the controls in Midnight Club 2 are simply superb, the game mechanics and driving feel are perfectly balanced for fun and a challenge.
To start off you might be just holding down the gas the whole way, but eventually with extremely power cars and navigating the city, the driving does feel like actually racing through a living city, just one designed for lots of jumps and high speed cornering. Some cars you will use the brake, others the handbrake instead, but getting around fast is genuinely enjoyable. And with each car having its own style, you get to chose how you'd like to play. The cars get better as the game progresses, making it part of the game to drive a few different cars or seeing how far your favorite car can get you. Once you finish the story, you can start over with all the cars unlocked.
You get three cities that each have unique neighborhoods with nice feel to them, but more importantly, huge jumps and long curves and straights for racing. The traffic can get in the way a lot of the time, but you can avoid them by going through the jumps or hidden sections of town that cut around underground, making learning the map sometimes a necessary frustration, and sometimes a ton of fun.

Interesting mix on a card-based roguelike and a 3D action brawler (reminds me of Shadows of Mordor).  It works surprisingly well.  As far as "roguelikes" go, it's fairly easy -- it's not nearly as brutal as some of the other games more true to the roguelike formula.  For me, this is good -- I can play for an hour or so and feel like I made some progress through the story mode.
Perhaps the most engaging aspect for me is the progression.  Beating bosses and quests (represented as cards) unlocks even more cards, weapons, quests, and bosses.  It's always exciting to see a quest for the first time, because beating it usually unlocks another one.  Since quests unlock other quests, often in a logical order, the result is a sort of mini-narrative as you complete quest lines through different playthroughs.  Even more interesting, quests can also influence other quests -- for instance, after completing quests and obtaining a rare artifact, a quest I'd previously seen in a previous playthrough had a totally different outcome.  There are some great dealer voiceovers as well, and it's interesting to see how he reacts to your choices/quest combinations.  It's this sense of progression that keeps me coming back for more.
I expect to get about 6-8 hours to complete the Story mode, probably more to unlock all the cards.  From there, there's also endless mode, which has a competitive aspect to it.
All-in-all, awesome game, highly recommend.
