=Pros=
It looks cool and the story's good. That's it.
And now for the bigger list. Just saying, don't let my hours spent playing fool you.
=Cons=
- Counter-intuitive mid to late-game combat goes completely against what you were taught before. If you're a newcomer to any dungeon past Feita, forget about winning without an OP party that barely gives you any opportunity to do anything.
Have fun losing your revives to a massively difficulty-spiked boss and being made fun of rather than helped.
- Community is among the worst I've seen in my life with regards to how they handle new players. They'll badger you for lucky pulls from boxes (which will come few and far between unless you open your wallet like some retard), but that's about it. Hate is tossed around between players a lot, especially where the bullsh~~ PvP is involved.
- Unholy-bad problem with class balance. This, in a nutshell, is why I quit taking PvP seriously and only do it for sh~~s and giggles with friends. While some characters are built very well, there are others such as Eve that can barely do a god-darned thing on her own and others still that are so godlike compared to everyone else that they just crush all opposition with little to no resistance (Add, Elesis, Lu/Ciel, etc).
- Unless you figure out every little trick and trigger in the book like a tryhard who has nothing better to do with their time, I'm fairly certain even going by so-called "Pay2Win" will not help you. The mid to late game will take just about every opportunity to punish you by chopping off around half your health simply for being in the wrong place at the wrong time once (which, more often than not, newcomers will not be able to tell when that is), and it doesn't help that there are way too many windows for that to happen with how long it takes to kill things later unless you have those stupid +11 weapons that are next to impossible to build anyway with how low enhancement success rates are.
- Don't play solo when aiming for levels. EVER. It takes way too freaking long, and even with a party in tow you'll find yourself repeating segments of the game way more than any sane person should.
- Annoying notifications about who did what 24/7, which by the way get in the way of your experience and stamina bars so you can't see them.
- Storage space is too small, and you have to pay to expand it. The amount of times I've had to sell, dismantle, or throw away useless armor and weapons well below my level is downright disgusting.
- I mentioned this before, but the equipment enhancement system is hands-down the WORST I have seen in ANY game. I'm convinced I could play against FF12's infamous superboss Yiazmat and (somehow) beat it, and it would not take nearly as long as it would to get a decent late-game weapon in this game because of how low enhancement success rates are, and the consequences for LUCK-BASED FAILURE are ridiculous; sometimes nothing will happen, others your equipment will LOSE a grade or even drop all the way back down to a +0, or it will outright break for no good reason.
- Same goes for enchanting effects time-wise. It takes way too long to get just one necessary material, and if you're looking for anything specific then good luck because all of the in-game ways to get them are completely random and few and far between (some of which will have you again chancing death).
I could go on for hours about how many sloppy design choices this game made. Yes, it is free to play and some things can be fun THE FIRST TIME, but with how much of a stupid grind-fest it quickly becomes and how asininely and increasingly unfair and unforgiving it becomes to newer players (Dark Souls and classic NES games are more forgiving than this game is), even if you're looking for some kind of time waster I would ultimately say... look somewhere else. This game will not do new guys any favors unless they're prepared to pour out their wallets (and I can't guarantee even that will help you). Do I find it fun? Kinda, but I'm highly doubtful you will.

It's kinda like running one of the shops in any rpg. Heroes (and sometimes very small children and elderly) come into your shop looking for a specific item to buy and you sell it to them at any price you want. However, these people are on a budget, so you can't go too high, and sometimes you might just make them mad with the price you just listed and just up and leave your store.
While making a profit is your goal (your dad went off adventuring and left you with his debt of millions), you need to aquire the items for your shop. You get these from dungeon crawling (99% of the time), and this is where the meat of the game is. It's a top-down view of a dungeon with you and a hero/mercenary/cyborg fighting monsters and taking the loot they drop. This is how you make the most money but it's also the riskiest method because if you die you can only bring back a single item rather than a whole pouchful.
Everything is on a timer, you have a limited amount of time to do stuff (though time stops if you're only just browsing). You have a limited amount of time to pay off larger and larger installments of your debt and it gets pretty hard near the end, but the best thing is that if you fail to do so, you keep any items you had and merchant levels you gained from successfully negotiating with customers. This makes the next playthrough easier and allows you to get farther into dungeons for rarer items. The game is meant to be beaten in multiple tries so don't feel bad if you fail over and over.
Also the translation is probably the best thing ever, but that's just a personal preference because I'm a fan of terrible puns.
I like this game and it doesn't really feel that niche so I feel like I can recommend it to just about anyone who likes economics and dungeon exploration.

This game lives or dies by its atmosphere and presentation. Lucky for it, Hand of Fate nails both. The voice-acting for the dealer is spectacular and easily on-par with Triple-A developers. The card dealing mechanic is well-delivered and helps keep the game feeling quite different with each runthrough. Missing a chance to earn a token is heartbreaking, mostly because you don't know what little nugget of the game was just pulled out of your grasp and how you could have used or played it in a future game run.
The game isn't without its issues, and most of them are related to combat. Using a controller just isn't an option for me personally. It doesn't feel right. But nor is the mouse-and-keyboard combo ideal, given you're restricted to just the eight cardinal directions. But pulling off a serious combo is still satisfying, and ultimately, the combat system is just a vessel for the greater card-dealing system, which is the meat of this game. Combat, ultimately, is passable. It doesn't bog the game down.
Oh. And the music. Yes, that music.

I hugely recommend you to get Metro 2033 Redux first and finish that game before playing this, should take you around 8-10 hours to finish it. I regret finished this game before the Metro 2033 one. Dungeons & Robots is a hidden gem.
Gameplay-wise, it's a lot of fun. You get to make your own set of robots from various parts that you loot or craft and you can swap between them during missions. Loot is abundant and you can mix 'n match weapons. You even get to loot equippable skills.
Crafting feels satisfying, especially when you get a good roll, as items are totally random, and you can recycle the ones you don't want.
Co-op is where the game truly shines and you are actually rewarded for teaming up. There are also skills to support your teammates : healing, shields, etc.
Graphics are pleasing and are reminiscent of the late Darkspore. There isn't a huge variety of scenery or monsters, but since levels are randomly generated, it keeps things fresh. The explosions and various particle effects are well done.
The music feels a bit too quiet for this type of game, but it's good. The sound effects serve their purpose, nothing too fancy here.
Many of the issues mentioned in the previous reviews have since been fixed. The devs are very close to their community and listen to suggestions and bug reports. I've reported bugs that got fixed within a few hours.
All in all, it is a great pastime, especially for the price tag. The co-op is fun and bullets fly everywhere.
I recommend this game !

As of the moment I've never completed this game to the end. When I do - and I'm sure eventually I will as I do enjoy it - I'll probably redo this review. But for the time being it has left me with an impression.
I won't spoil anything in detail.
You basically take control of a trio of protagonists in this game. Laharl (prince of the underworld), Etna (one of the prince's demon vassals), and Flonne (an angel). The basic jist of the story is Laharl spends his time in the game exerting how awesome he is by winning fights - which is pretty accurate to how the player themself probably feels as well. The other two protagonists mostly spend their time trying to bring about a softer side to the prince. There are a ton of plot holes throughout the game's story but I don't feel they matter since the game never tries to take itself seriously. It's always cute, silly, or badass. Things as random as having to fight the Power Rangers takes place in this game after all. It's never really
- at least not as far as I've gotten.
The designs of the characters are adorable and cute. I absolutely love them! Not just the protagonists' designs - though those as well. Every class character in this game has a nice bit of style to them. They feel slightly demonic, a bit cute and/or sexy (the humanlike ones anyway), and they're all unique enough to see elsewhere and tell instantly
. I was even excited to see Prinny hats come out in TF2 (which incidently became my latest favorite hat in
game).
The gameplay is good. Turn-based strategy is something I have a fondness for when I feel like a relaxing type of game. I found that having the ability to build a team adds a lot to how much I actually care about my team. Having so many ways to arm the team and work them up to little beefcakes. Then breaking them out for moments you were unable to best previously. It makes you think of various strategies while also just looking for ways to strengthen current ones with better gear.
The voice acting is hit and miss. I hardly ever feel any of the characters are talking like they'd talk in real life yet I also don't feel epic moments or sincere moments through the voice acting - like something you'd hear Ash Ketchum or Goku say. It just feels like acting. This could partially be due to the formula of the cutscenes though; characters react to each other much later than they would in a video or in real life due to having to wait on the text boxes to catch up before it goes to the next line. When a character is interrupted by another character it feels especially jarring since one character just cuts off in the middle of what they're saying and then the other character starts talking about 2 seconds later. At moments it has honestly made me cringe. I tend to turn my sound down or wear headphones when I get to a cutscene for the slight embarassment of others hearing this game's dialouge.
As cheesy as the story is, as bad as the voice acting may be, and even as unfair as some of the situations in the game can be it's truely a charming game. I can totally understand why there's a following for this. If I'm honest the cheesiness of the story even appeals to me. I quite like my character being a badass badguy that's coming around to being a goodguy.
I absorbed myself in the team building; attempting to make at least one of everything. Even now I'm longing for stronger monsters to beat a level I've been stuck on.
This game feels like a good staple for overhead strategy. It has things I like about it. It also has things I dislike about it. Most of the things I dislike are temporary though - such as a badly voiced line, or a cheap stage stacked against me. I thoroughly enjoy playing the game when I'm in the mood for a game that doesn't rush me.

I loved Metro 2033, but hated this one. Gameplay isn't changed much, but the levels and enemies were far worse.
Indoor sections felt limited: every area can basically be boiled-down into: "two hallways, connected by vents/doors. When you see a guy in hallway A, sneak through hallway B to kill him." This also makes it pretty boring during firefights: crouch behind cover, wait for an enemy to try and flank/charge you, and take them out.
Outdoor sections were empty. Creatures seemed to just be placed randomly out in the open, where you could easily pick them off without ever being in much danger.
The enemy variety is a huge step back from 2033. There's some new "shrimp" monsters that are basically identical to the standard nosalis except they can swim. You won't find any new, interesting stuff like the blobs or librarians from the first game.
They also decided to add terrible boss fights for some reason.
The story also seemed like a step back. The weird, mysterious supernatural stuff is mostly gone. No ghost trains, creepy shadow ghosts, deadly anomalies, etc. There's some flashbacks and some dream sequences with the Dark Ones, but it's just cutscenes. The characters only seem to exist to tell you where you need to go, or tell you how terrible the world is. There's none of the interesting world building or philosophical discussions from 2033.
Even if Metro 2033 was one of your favorite FPS games, you might want to skip Last Light.

Well, I did not know who Airtight Games was up until now but doing 2 consecutive walkthroughs of Soul Suspect will certainly make me remember them for a while! This is a third-person view adventure game that employs some stealth elements and lots of crime scene investigation gameplay mechanics.
The story follows Ronan, a con-turned-detective who has just been murdered and whose soul - for some reason - cannot leave this world and proceed to Heaven where his wife awaits. We soon learn his killer is the one he was originally after - a couple of cutscenes later his memory is refreshed and he is certain he needs to solve the mystery of the Bell Killer who has been haunting his residential town for a while so that by solving the murder case he can peacefully enter Paradise.
Now, when playing this game I was constantly thinking of the adventure games released by Telltale Games. Why? Because the puzzles are easy and there is a great emphasis on the story immersion. Unlike those Telltale adventures Murdered allows you to control the protagonist and freely walk around in Salem.
Still, I wouldn't really call this an open-world journey as many places are only accessible if the story demands it - the "hub area" is mainly for collectibles and a couple of side missions where you help other ghosts finish their business and ascend once and for all.
Then come the demons. Certain sections require you to hide from the beasts and approach them while they turn away - execution is not mandatory but collecting evidence and other "artifacts" in the areas require you to rid Salem of them for good.
While the game is not difficult, at all, and lacks any real combat it does have a great story. I almost completed it in one sitting as I really wanted to see the antagonist dealt with. Murdered has a great atmosphere which is accompanied by a great score and very well done voice acting.
To summarise: if you are in for a great story and for something new and you do not mind that one playthrough gives you all the experience (a 2nd should only be done for the collectibles) then Soul Suspect is an easy grab - especially with a discount!

One of the best sci-fi action games I've ever played.
This game feels like they put up a core concept, and then just started adding their favorite mechanics from AAA titles.  From most developers, I would expect that to be a flaw in their game design, but Digital Extremes has managed to pull off a cohesion between so many different game mechanics and systems that I genuinely wouldn't know where to start with breaking them down in a review.
The best part, THIS GAME IS FREE!  WHAT?!  There has to be over 100 hours of content just in the campaign missions!  you can spend money on guns and aesthetics to accellerate your progress through the earlier missions, but so far I have only spent anything on cosmetic items and I haven't had any issue making steady progress without feeling like things have stagnated.
Some critiques:  I shouldn't need to use a wiki to find out where certain crafting materials appear.  tooltips would be nice for a game with such a vast ammount of content and customizability.
Second, why do I have access to weapon blueprints which I cant get materials for until later in the game?  I know better now, but when i was brand new, i grabbed the Latron blueprint because i wanted a sniper instead of a bow, not realizing that one of the materials was unobtainable until I got to saturn.  I bought that blueprint around the 6 hour mark.  I'm now at 35 hours, and only just am getting access to the mineral i needed.  again, a tooltip may have prevented that frustration
These are small greivances, and the resources I wasted early on are pretty moot at this point.  So, honestly I cant reccommend this game enough.  I'm absolutely blown away by the immersion into this sci-fi world through small details they put in outside of missions, and just how fun the gameplay is.  the fact that this game is free and people still blow hundreds on DLC for destiny blows my mind.

is a one shot wonder coming from Airtight Games; the last game they developed before closing their doors in July 2014. It is a wondrous detective story with a supernatural background that takes place in the timeline of one evening in Salem, present time. Salem? Does that ring any "bells"?
Aside my unintentionally cheesy joke, this game is about Ronan O'Connor, an ex-con and street dog turned his way straight and decided to become a detective to atone for all his past misdeeds, with a pretty gal for him to impress in the mix, of course. The events of our game start with the untimely demise of our main character. We watch Ronan as his life passes before his eyes in a stream of memories - recorded on his body as tattoos representing milestones in his life. The Bell Killer, notorious serial killer who was terrorizing Salem for months now, killed Ronan. But surprisingly, this is the beginning for him rather than an end. Now, he is a ghost, stuck in between worlds until he manages to solve his own murder. Ronan's persistence to seek the truth will take him through an old, dark ordeal in Salem history: Salem Witch Trials.
As I continue, I have to note that I loved the character of Ronan O'Connor himself. Aside being an ordinary bad boy, he has vulnerabilities, character flaws and a short temper. His death isn't even heroic as most main characters in video games as we see nowadays. He just ventures out, without having anything to loose and without a thought; and bang! He ends up getting hunted and falling to his death. We are able to read an in-depth backstory for Ronan, with Julie's perception from many collectible memory notes within the game, and put together, it portrays the story of a life. I salute developers for presenting Ronan as an original character, different from any darkened vigilante or street thug. As I was playing, I found myself recalling Mickey O'Neil, a gypsy character that Brad Pitt portrayed in Guy Ritchie's
: a reckless and wild rascal, a swindler with a golden heart. He feels much real than any old book knight in shining armor, at least for me.
If we are to talk about the atmosphere, well, sure. It is a success. Graphics and textures are impressive, alongside the modelling of each and every character. The game manages to present you the feel of an open world: the ghostly, dark remains of the old Salem clashing with the modern, physical environment, Airtight presents us a ghost's perception. It is uncanny and impressive. Combined with a successful voice acting for all characters present: this game is basically L.A. Noire quality with less action packed and more on the supernatural side.
Gameplay? Sure, it's nothing extraordinary. We run about the town - collecting a huge number of collectibles for either background story, or some independent creepy ghost stories, or trivial facts about Salem history if we feel like so, by the way - and try to predict the movements of the killer. We even gain a living side-kick as we progress: Joy, a snarky teenage who will become our involuntary aid in the world of the living. There are three defining elements to the game: item collecting, demon hunting and investigation. None of these parts are incredibly well-put, but the story being absorbing, you keep playing. Investigations are quite basic, with little to no chance of guessing wrong and combat section consists of a basic stealth kill for some demons in each new area. Could have been much more, but I won't complain.
Is it worth your time? It surely is, but still I'd recommend grabbing it on sale, so 30 dollars would be a grand exaggeration for what you're getting yourself. The greatest plus of the game for me, was its story. For one time, I really wasn't able to guess the ending, and the precise position of characters involved. I so hope that Ronan's story wouldn't end here. Would it be so much to hope for? Well, we'll see.

I was delighted to see that this game was on steam, having spent a ton of time in both the PS2 and DS versions I was sure that I would be spending quite a bit of time in this version as well. That is not the point with this version. The first time I started it up it crashed to desktop instantly. I thought "Well it happens sometimes, I will just restart it." So I did and it worked fine, I was able to set up the options I wanted in the options menu and away I went. The first chapter went by pretty fast, and the game with everything set to it's highest settings allowed ran like a dream. It was great! I decided that it was time to take a break for the night, I could return tomorrow. So the next day rolls around and I start the game up again, it immediately crashes. I restart it figuring it would be like the night before and the game just keeps crashing and crashing. I looked up many of the solutions and tried out all of them, and with the help of Pretty Prinny was finally able to get the game running again. Once again I am happy, and get to play through the second chapter of the game. I come up to the part where you need to get a level 10 item to advance. That means having to delve into the item world and subdue the masters and level up your items. About halfway through the first dungeon the game crashes once again. I am a bit annoyed, but decide it might have just been a one time thing. I go back to the game and proceed to do item world once again and this time not even into the second floor of the item the game crashes. At this point I am pretty frustrated. While crashes in the main storyline aren't too bad, in the item world it can be really bad considering you cannot save during the process. (There is an item you can get which lets you teleport out but I am sure it is limited and you have to purchase more from what I remember from the other versions.)
So here I find myself writing this review, at the current time this game is really not worth it at all conidering how many problems I have had with it. It maybe an isolated case, but upon reading other peoples reviews and forum posts this game does crash quite a bit. Hopefully someday this will fix these problems.

Midnight Club 2, good ol' racing game from the PS2 era and what is considered to be by some fans, including myself, as one of the best Midnight Club games in the series. I'll try to make this detailed without it being too lenthy, so let's get this started.
If you enjoy racing games on the PC, this is one of those games you should definitely try out, especially since it's normally only $10. Mind you, the game is almost 11 years old as of this review, so comparing it to modern-day racing games and reviewing based on that would be silly, right? For it's time, it's a very fun-filled and possibly addictive game with fast cars and racers who are willing to give you a run for your money, or the occasional cops super speeding to prevent you from winning the race. Three cities, Los Angeles, Paris, and Tokyo, and racers on the streets every night waiting for a challenger to follow them to the start of the race, Career Mode is worthwhile once you get the rivals' cars and break top speeds with them. As you progress, you'll have more access to cars to run around in Cruise in Arcade Mode. The physics are very loose, and to a certain degree, exaggerated, but that only adds to the fun of driving around the streets, dodging traffic cars and clearing checkpoints. There's several other things you can do while playing the game, but I'll talk about that another time. Besides, who doesn't like going at their top speed, hitting the nitrous, and hitting local pedestrians that walk around for you to hit them while racing, or cruising? Don't worry, they all live anyway, even if they don't ever move again. Also, the soundtrack is pretty damn good, and it seems that every racer has their own songs that you'll race in with them, and then listen to later after you beat them. Being an old game, I wasn't expecting the graphics to be as clean as they are. They must've re-added some nice quality textures at some point in the recent years, because it looks very clean for an aged game like this!
Even though the game is very enjoyable to Midnight Club fans, it can be at times annoying difficult, or give you one of those "WTH" moments for anyone. Probably because I still haven't gotten my MC2 Driver's License yet (I might have made that up), I've played this game on the consoles for years, and still tend to find certain parts of the game to be a pain at times, learning the controls on the PC only adds to it. For anyone who plays this game, those moments could be from heavy traffic, hitting poles that stops your car completely and, if you're lucky, send your car's back end up in the air, getting tipped over from cutting certain corners or oversteering with the wrong car at certain terrain, and let's not forget the occasional driver who doesn't use their blinkers before switching lanes. For newer players, you may have to learn the whole track before you can increase your chance of winning certain races, because sometimes checkpoint arrangements can offer too much freedom to where you miss a shorter route or have no clue where to go, or you miss it because you were a few inches away from the checkpoint radius. Oh, almost forgot about the multiplayer! It's...... dead, understandably.
Overall, the game would have to take some getting used to, but it can be very joyful while you do it, especially if you're a racing gamer who just loves driving around in fast cars. And for that reason, I recommend this to those who are into these kind of games! Like I said earlier though, it's an old game, from 2003, so if I see any of you badmouth it and say it's not as good as Need for Speed: Rivals or Most Wanted (either one), I'll take out one of my earned cars from MC2 and run you over with it!
Sincerely,

This game came up in my recommendations list with a lot of positive reviews and looked interesting so I gave it a shot.  Very glad I did, this game is really good.
It's a deck builder - a card game where you gain more, better cards to add to your deck as you progress through the game.  You sit at a table facing a hooded mage who controls the cards and narrated the story.  The voice acting is very good and once you have drawn the same card a couple of times the narration for that card is muted so you don't end up running through the same dialoque game after game.  It's kind of like playing a single player RPG with the mage as DM expanding the story around the cards drawn.  The voice (and the image of the DM to a degree) put me in mind of John Hurt which is cool.
The DM deals out a number of cards in a pattern depicting the path (or paths) you have to travel before meeting the final enemy.  You can choose which way to go by which cards you turn over on the path (although some are straight so no choice) and you can be lucky and find the exit to the next level quickly meaning you can skip forward but possibly miss out on finding a shop or other useful encounter.  I prefer to take my chances of drawing a bad encounter for the benefits of potentially better equipment/more cards.
The decks consist of armour, weapons, enchantments and food as well as enounters both good and bad.  Some enounters involve a test of luck where you have to choose a 'success' card from a selection of four cards.  These are displayed before being shuffled so there is a chance you can follow the best card before they are dealt face down.  Winning encounters let you draw cards from your deck giving you the chance to upgrade your armour, weapons or giving you more food (needed to heal)
It's not just a static card game however.  The battles are actually played out as a third person skirmish with you controlling your character fighting, blocking and using any special abilities granted by your equipment.  This is the part that really marks the game out as different and deepens your sense of involvement - you're not just sat at a table playing cards, you are truly part of the story which is unfolding.
Completing the final enemy grants you additional cards for your deck and every fourth quest grants you an item from the DM levelling up both your character and the enemies you will face.
If you are unfamiliar with deckbuilding or just want to progress to the next game quickly, at the start of each quest you have the option of using a recommended deck based on y0our cards.  If you wish, you can then go in and edit the deck to your satisfaction although newly gained cards will not reveal their effects until they have been played.
There is the skill of choosing which cards you own will be best suited to the upcoming quest.  This gets more important the further you progress and the more cards you have.
Overall, a very enjoyable and quite relaxing game, definitely worth the money.

Essentialy you must buy seeds, pick a plot of land to plant them in then either wait for them to grow or water them to speed up the process, after all that you can then harvest but actualy gaining crops is not guarrenteed so it seems like a huge time sink. As a side note some crops takes litteral hours to grow, i think wheat was listed at over two and half hours for a single crop.
Gaining any resource in the world such as iron ore requires what the game refers to as "labor points" essentialy this an arbitrarty point system that add's nothing but forces players to save up points thus missing out on items and loot, if you choose to save points eventualy you will be able to spend them on somthing good like a house but i have no idea how many hundreds of hours that would take, Points are generated all the time whilst logged on i believe you gain five points per five minuets of play, it is simply a bad system that punishes players for no reason.
This final point is probably the biggest nail in the coffin though, the community is non existant, in the five hours i played i never once saw a single other player or saw anyone typing messages in chat, i even asked "is anyone else playing right now" multiple times and never recieved a reply.

When I thought about games that stand the test of time, the first game that came to my mind was Fable- The Lost Chapters. It was one of the first games I played and I spent hours upon hours playing it. So when I bought it on steam, I was somewhat sceptic. Would it live up to my childhood nostalgia or would it ruin a fond memory?
You might have already guessed the answer from the intro, and you're right - it did live up to the nostalgia.
The game have a certain charm I haven't found in another game. I personally love the skill/magic/combat system and how the leveling functions. The gameplay is very accepting, yet it's challenging in some parts of the story/game. You'll have a relaxing and fun experience with it.

There is a moral "dilemma" in the game, do you walk righteous path of a saint or do you walk the path of evil and slaughter? I very much enjoy this dilemma. Sure, it is very simple and there has since been countless games with similar and more "advanced" systems implemented. Yet, I still tend to like the one in Fable more. It affects your interaction with npc's, some game mechanics, clothing, your character and parts of the story. Throughout the game, you'll have some big and some smaller choices (e.g. in the beginning of the game, you can find a fellow cheating on his wife. You can decide to tell his wife - good, or you can keep a secret and get money - evil).
As this was my first review, it might lack in certain areas but bear with me.
All in all, I 100% recommend this pearl. Yes, it does fall short in some aspects due to its age and it might not have the same effect on you as it had on me, but give it a chance. You will not be disappointed.

You start the game off as a prisoner...no this is not ElderScrolls.
Its not made clear what you are imprisoned for. Assault, murder, genocide, jaywalking? Who knows.

During the prisoners transport, the spacecraft crashes onto the planet Na Pali.
The natives (Nali) are non hostile. They help you find secrets if you keep them alive.
But they have been invaded and are being tormented by an evil race.
And you may or may not be their savior, their “Messiah”
You dont have much of an objective. You're basically exploring this planet.
Locations vary. There are indoor and outdoor locations.
Outdoor is better since you are able to dodge enemy projectiles easier. Also its brighter and more colorful.
The transition from level to level feels natural and makes sense. There is an actual sense of progression. It wont feel like its just a bunch of random levels one after the other.
This game's level design and variety puts today's games to shame.
Enemies take a lot of hits and require a lot of dodging.
The enemies themselves also dodge your attacks.
The weapons vary.
Its amazing how such an old game (1998) still holds up today.
This is helped by, of course, unofficial patches and mods.
NEGATIVES:
-Getting through some levels the first time can be hard because of the graphics some areas do look alike.
-Other than a a stained glass image of Vandora Goddess of Lightning, there are no female models of the Nali. Reminds me of the lack of female models in Half Life also released in 1998. This game has other similarities with Half-Life (this is a good thing not a bad thing). But they are still 2 different games.

Let me start by saying that I have been watching this game for a while and decided to pick it up recently when it went on sale. It has so many good features that I look for in this type of game. It is kind of like a ARPG but with guns and robots! Here are some of the things I like currently, and some I don't.
Like

-Changeable skills, you have 4 slots for skills, you find them while playing. Each skill has a solo version and a team version which is awesome.
-Guild System.
-Crafting system with ranks.
-Leaderboards.
-Global, party, and system chat.
-Seasons, you can rank up in the season and rise up on the leaderboards.
-Pretty good UI along with character stats.
-5 different proflies, kind of like different loadouts you can switch between on the fly or at a beacon inside dungeons.
-Survival mode, I love this, you clear a level, then kill the boss. Then you get sent to the next level and things get harder and harder with better drops.
-*Adding on day 2 of playing* I encountered a rare game breaking bug and posted it to the bug report section of the fourms, not 5 minutes later a dev contacted me about the issue and fixed my account within the hour. The devs are hands on and doing so much, you don't see that often.
Dislike
-Not a lot of things are explained.
-Hard to tell what is highlighted in the UI sometimes.
-Not very many different monsters and bosses.
-Not much map diveristy, seems like the same map over and over at the start.
-Some bosses hit too hard.
-Not many players currently.
-No story.

This game is not for the faint of heart of those who lack patience. It has one of the highest learning curves in a Grand Strategy game. This ain't Civilization. You've been warned.
Crusader Kings II is a Grand Strategy game from Paradox Interactive. It was released in 2012 and has been very heavily supported with various expansions via Paradox as well as mod support.
You don't play as a country in this game. You play as a dynasty in the Middle Ages. You choose a person and have to rule over your land as well as make sure you have a successor to your dynasty. You may start of as a minor feudal lord, a petty king, a king of a large country or an emperor. In this game you have to learn how to manipulate the political landscape, as well as engage in large scale wars and run your county/kingdom/empire.
The game is not the most accessible game to those unfamiliar with previous Paradox Grand Strategy titles. Even those who would say they are Civilization experts can find themselves overwhelmed by the sheer amount of info that the game displays. There is a tutorial campaign, but watching lets plays will definately help new players figure out the more advanced tactics that can be accomplished in the game. I personally reccomend watching LPs on YouTube by Northernlion, Arumba, MathasGames and quill18.
To help describe the amount of detail you can influence in this game, there is a genetic system as well as an education system in the game that I'll breifly explain. You're children will gain the genetic traits of yourself as well as your spouse in the game, like a sickness of an affinity for intelligence. This also includes statistics to attributes not unlike a tabletop RPG. The education system allows you to have your child taught different behavioural triats that boost or negate those stats. This is important to be aware of because in the event of your character dying (whether it be by poison in your wine, being killed in battle, or of old age) your child will be your successor. This isn't always the case due to different succession laws that can be enacted, but in the end, your dynasty has to survive.
The game's interface as seen on the store page takes place on a map of mainly Western Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. (Eastern countries like India are included in DLC). Time can be paused and sped up at any time during the game.
You will have to be wary as factions can cause an uprising if you run your land like a tyrant, or even if a morally ambiguous party who would see to take your throne from you. You can however use ditry tactics as well, such as bribery, assassination, plotting individuals againts one another. Sometimes you get away with these acts, sometimes your involvment gets discovered, harming your reputation.
The game itself has no set campaigns, which works to its advantage as it is a historical sandbox. You can influence the entire world in ways that aren't historically correct but still plausible, like taking over Constantinople causes the Crusades to start hundreds of years before their historical date.
This game will take time to learn, but when you do learn it, Crusader Kings II is one of the most rewarding titles to be on the PC in a very long time.
If you find games like Civ too easy, give this game a shot. It's on sale often as well.

Murdered: Soul Suspect takes a fascinating part of American history and pairs it with a supernatural detective story.  The environment and plot is very creative and unique and kept me interested until the end.  The game is fairly short and doesn't overstay its welcome, yet still provides a lot of character and plot development as well as a few twists.
That being said, there are two minor downfalls to this game.
The first is the overuse of collectibles.  While the collectibles are easy enough to find and doesn't require too much 'post game time' to sit down and sniff them out, there are still a ton of them.  Over 170 in fact.  Each collectible gives some sort of backstory to the world or relevent major characters, but the sheer number of them will have you running to pick them up first before doing the actual story missions.  I feel this can really take the player out of the setting and mood Murdered: Soul Suspect tried to create, with its old, colonial, haunted theme.  If you are the type of player to skip right over collectibles and not be bothered, then this isn't a problem for you.  But if you are OCD, have to get them all, hear every backstory, learn every secret, then this will probably get on your nerves a bit.
The other issue to this game is that some of the puzzles are unclear as to how you should go about solving them.  While this has only happened to me about maybe 15% of the puzzles in the game, it is still frustrating to look up the answer and say to yourself 'How does that make sense?'.  The game does give hints if you get the puzzle wrong, but sometimes the hints aren't that clear.  With some trial and error, you should be ok though.
Overall, I enjoyed this game.  I picked it up when it was $4 and would have gladly paid $20 for it.  The setting and plot were really unique and I liked all of the ghost mechanics that were added into the game.  It is definitely a game to play when you are looking to get a good story with some amusing puzzles.  I rate this game a 9/10.

The thing that you have to understand about Hand of Fate is that it is NOT a "deckbuilding" or "card game", even less than Ticket To Ride is a train simulator. In both cases there is some thematic resemblance to some other genre, but really the core mechanics are thoroughly different and in order to enjoy yourself, you need to understand what the game really is.
In order to qualify as a "card game", the primary device of the game should be cards. In a typical card game, you might have a hand of cards to select from, or you might play cards to achieve certain effects. On a mechanical level, Hand of Fate is instead more like a roguelike beat-em-up. A game consists of a series of randomly-selected encounters, most of which culminate either in a 3d third-person combat scene, or in a "select the good outcome" shell game. Your goal is to plow through the encounters, managing your resources of health and food, to get to the end, where you fight a boss. Hand of Fate uses "cards" as its theme and narrative -- encounters and equipment are represented by cards, and you can customize the "decks" before play -- but otherwise it bears no similarity to card games whatsoever.
But despite that, it's still an enjoyable game. Some encounters unlock other encounters, and there's a certain charm to trying to focus on some resource like food in order to try to be in a good position to "win" some encounter. Of course, it can be extremely frustrating when you're all set up, only to get wiped out by an unlucky "draw". Like most roguelikes, it can be punishing and it has quite a bit of replay value.
The biggest problem with the game is tedium, which sets in around the 400th combat. I'm not sure if it's something about my computer or what, but it takes a long time to "load" certain of the (admittedly quite beautiful) encounters, and many of the combats cease to be challenging after you've played them enough. Because so few of the encounters give you resources, you need to be pretty lucky to have a round where it's even possible to "beat" some of the final encounters. And of the encounters that do give you resources, many of them are combats, which (again) lose their charm after a while.
All in all I'd probably give HoF a 6.5/10. It's entertaining (and somehow I'm addicted to it), but you can safely skip it.
[N.B. This is before the recent update adding "fates", so maybe things have changed a little bit.]

EDIT: Now that Steam has public 'reviews' for games, I figured I shoud rewrite this for public information.
Midnight Club 2 is a fun, flashy arcade racing game released in 2003. What you're looking at here is wild speed boosted racer with TONS of replay value w/ plenty of 23 cars to choose from, races, courses, game modes, in three cities (Los Angeles, Paris and Tokyo), which also applies to the (pretty dead) online mode which also increases the amount of replay value with custom races. It's insanely easy to pick up and play with no kind of learning.
Story Mode / Carrer Mode in this game isn't exactly 'story' based, nor connected to anything, you rather just beat challenge by challenge in order to progress with better cars and move to other cities. The further you get, the more cars you have unlocked and ready to use in any game mode.
Racing in this game is a very arcade like experience, 'wonky' steering, air physics, and etc. Races are checkpoint powered (which is obvious) which can go from head to head racing to beat the clock racing. Sometimes their'll also be races where you're able to choose your own path to get to one checkpoint and back to the start. The map design also helps. In LA to Tokyo, you have cities that are filled with hidden paths, shortcuts, and alt paths to help you race to victory.
The sound in this game is very basic, but it's what'd you expect in a racing game. There's a very nice and memorable soundtrack collection in this game (as long as you have love for Electronic and Rap / Hip Hop) that differs from all three Cities. LA with Hip Hop / Rap and Electronic / House, Paris with House / Techno (that's a genre guise), and Tokyo with Trance / Hard Dance and some ambient tracks. (Please correct me if I'm wrong about the genres!)
The enviroment and graphical capabilities isn't much compared to now, but it was something very nice in 2003. The frame rate isn't hard locked (I don't recall it being hard locked at least), shiny cars, detailed enviroments, and so on.
What makes me so happy about this game though, is the evolution of Midnight Club. Midnight Club: Street Racing was a pretty damn mediocre racing game but was addicting to play, though it was just missing tons of features and was very slow. What I really love is that Angel Studios (which is now Rockstar San Diego) completely upgraded the code of the original game which managed to turn into this, and I love the direction they went, and how much the production value of the game went up compared to the last they had.
You should also check out the latest Midnight Club game if you own an Xbox 360 or PS3, Midnight Club: Los Angeles. (which I wish was on PC....I hope they make another on the PC platform!)
Now, as I said in the original review:
Buy it. It's fun, original, and it's worth what you're paying even for a 2003 video game.

It doesn't have a combat as good as other FPS games from the 90s, or the best plot ever, but that doesn't stop Unreal from being one of the best games released in 1998.
It was a technical masterpiece back in the day, and while the graphics are dated in this day and age, the game still manages to look good, with well placed lighting and colors, but most importantly, the world of Na Pali still retains a good atmosphere, and a sense of wonder as you explore ancient ruins and hi-tech starships.
The level design is what you would normally see in other FPSes from the time. Complex layouts that give with little to no directions, which allows for heavy exploration as well as a lot of oportunities to get lost, although some are more linear and don't really leave any room for confusion. Not the most consistant level design, but it works.
There are some other interesting details, like an AI that was quite advanced for the time, and a device that lets you read logs from dead humans as well as ancient messages in temples, among other things.
TL;DR: Atmosphere and environments are its strong point, and it manages to keep the old school FPS formula without feeling like a reskinned version of older titles.

First of all, Ark is a great game and I've played it about 200 hours. Ark is the obvious comparison to Conan Exiles and is also the most similar game to Conan Exiles that I have played.
That said...
Ark developers (whom are fantastic nonetheless) seem to favor adding new content rather than spending time refining gameplay. In just my first few minutes of Conan Exiles, it became apparent just how much more intuitive the basic gameplay is over Ark.
The inventory user interface manages to fit everything on one screen except for skills. Skills have a seperate menu, however, inventory items and craftables are on one page. Ark is annoyingly clunky when trying to select a craftable.
Also, if there are any free spots in your hotbar in Conan, then newly crafted items will automatically fill the next spot in the row. In Ark, I would have to make the item, then drag it onto my hotbar. Very minor, but I don't like spending unnecessary time in menus.
Also, hugely important are the default player stats. When you make a character in Ark, the default encumbrance, stamina, health, and just about everything are confoundingly poor. Your character can't survive a two-foot fall. You can't run 50 ft without needing water, food, and a nap. While stat drain and everything CAN be tweaked manually, default levels SHOULD be reasonably balanced.
In Conan, I was able to immediately start playing the game. I could run a reasonably long time without needing to take a rest. It is reasonable to be able to run just long enough time to escape a predator or similar situation at a default level. In Conan, I can survive a 5-10 foot jump without injury, just like real life. In Ark, a ten-foot drop is almost certain to be deadly, even at higher levels.
There are many slight annoyances in Ark that, individually don't bother me too much, but I frequently experience the perfect storm of BS that makes me want to just shut off the game.
The Conan Exiles developers seem to care a lot about creating solid gameplay first and I appreciate that. I don't have very much time in the game yet, but my experience has been very positive so far.
p.s. I don't mean to rag on Ark, but it's THE comparison game. There is room for both Ark and Conan Exiles in my favorites list.

Interestingly bizarre. Surprisingly, this is a sequel to Beauty Bounce. Negating whatever ending you earned in the previous game, the main character is leaving the bank after settling his negotiations, walking back towards the resort to tell everyone the good news, when a car almost strikes him. Luckily, a woman passing by pushes him out of the way, leaving the two with injuries, specifically a head injury for the main character. What he doesn't know is that that incident induces him into a coma of some sort and he starts to hallucinate. Where in reality he's in a hospital bed, unresponsive, yet acting out externally, in his mind he's gone back to the resort and sees every person he comes across clad in sexy clothing. Not only that, but in his fantasy, you can choose to romance the main girls, as he happens to hallucinate them being extremely horny. Depending on your choices, I believe there are two good and bad endings, or maybe three good one bad, or one good three bad. I got the last one which is where you realize that he's just insane and suffered horrible brain damage after his accident. Not happy, but still provided closure and makes a lot of sense. Undeserved, absolutely, yet I feel it's fitting. He had♥♥♥♥♥♥going against him from the beginning. Life decides to throw something good at him and then completely ♥♥♥♥ up any chance at redemption. He already had the success and wasn't a scummy person, but his fate seemed predisposed. Where as the first game pointed at business stereotypes, this one takes a jab at circumstance. Additionally, it sorta emphasises the saying of doing whatever you can with your life and taking some sort of control before it's gone, because life is truly too short and usually not what we expect. Kinda like how I didn't expect to pull something like this out of a game whose predecessor offered next to nothing and is comparably bland. How about that?

If you enjoy picross (or nonograms, or whatever other name you may know these pixel-art logic puzzles), Pictopix is a game you need to buy. Until now, Jupiter Corporation – creators of Mario’s Picross and Picross e, among others – is the only developer that’s really done this puzzle form justice. Thanks to Thomas Leroy, there’s finally a PC picross game with the same degree of polish and professionalism, and I can’t recommend it highly enough.
As far as video games go, picross shouldn’t be too difficult to adapt. It’s quite simple on a mechanical level; the challenge is in the design of the puzzles themselves, and plenty of people have been able to rise to that challenge in the numerous printed books and magazines that are around. And yet, Jupiter Corp is one of the only devs that’s really been able to make it work, and with their focus almost exclusively on Nintendo 3DS these days, options for playing their games are limited.
That’s part of what makes Pictopix such a welcome game: it’s very reminiscent of Picross e in terms of quality, but it’s a PC game with such low system requirements that it should be able to run on just about any machine. Finally, there’s a well-made picross game that’s available to the masses.
And it really is a high-quality game. The user interface is slick and minimalist, allowing you to enjoy the puzzle solving with as few distractions as possible. The controls are simple – left click to fill a square, right click to put a cross (indicating a blank space). Controller and keyboard are supported, too, but I never actually tried them because the mouse controls work so intuitively.
There’s a lot of effort put into making Pictopix as user-friendly and approachable as possible, but all of that would be moot without good puzzles. Luckily, that’s not a problem that this game has – the puzzle design is impeccable, never relying on guesswork the way so many picross games do. Pictopix has 150 puzzles, ranging from 5×5 to 25×25 in size, and covering all manner of themes and pictures.
If that’s not enough, there’s also a workshop mode that allows players to create and share their own puzzles. This really is Pictopix’s standout feature: not only does it allow for a potentially endless supply of new puzzles (assuming the community keeps creating), it’s also a great tool for budding puzzle designers to get started. The workshop can check for solvability, which is vital, and also allows you to import PNG files to form the basis of your puzzles.
Pictopix is a delightful game that anyone with any interested in picross should buy. Its clean, simple, intuitive UI and control scheme removes all distractions from solving puzzles, and that’s exactly what you want out of a game like this. Top that off with a massive collection of puzzles and a fantastic workshop mode, and you’ve got one of the best picross games available. Jupiter Corporation finally has some competition.

Disgaea PC is a turn based tactics game with ridiculous animations, and interesting story line, and some light rpg elements. For now, I am done with this game - so the amount of hours listed on my review is a rough estimate of how many hours I've spent doing both the main story and a majority of the side-stuff.
Important Note: I turned off all animations during my playthrough. I'm familiar with this game, so I never cared to see the animations. Turning off the animations will reduce your in game play time by a significant amount. So my account with its 40-60 hours has as much actual playtime as an account with 60+ hours. It's up to you if you want the animations, I turned them off because I know how much of a grind this game is and doing so saved me many hours to do other things while still enjoying the game.

I got interested in Warframe after seeing a video review that praised imensely both the game and the small team that built it. I think the guy doing the review deserves at least 1M$ from the publisher. I am sure his review alone added 10 times that ammount in revenue numbers.
However... I played the game 100+ hours, mostly solo, unlocked all relays, and all quests, leveled several warframes and weapons to max. Here is what I think.
Pros:
-best f2p monetization schema of late. I bet Blizzard/Activision is envious they did not manage to do the same for WoW.
-very decent graphics and beautiful combat system
-definetely a game that merits to be seen
-last but not least, huge number of players, and a comunity that is kind of nice and helpful
Cons:
-there is no concept of clearing a map, just always swimming through a sea of enemies. Spawning mechanics is a design failure imo, and unfortunately one that it's too late be fixed, because it ended defining the game.
-archwing(space fights) is a pain that no one is happy to play (imo), but the developers insist.
-stealth play is there for everyone, ...but somehting is missing, and it is buggy. Sometimes enemies turn on alarms instantly, other times they dont see you when almost in front of them.
-the in-game directions system is something without which the game had been unplayable, yet you may still find yourself lost in a maze quite often.
-good looking but less functional menus. For instance when building stuff one cannot see item attributes there, must go to codex section and then come back
...and of course small annoyng bugs, infinite loops when caught on the wrong side of a portal, infinite falling when you die in wrong places, etc.
Conclusion:
I definetely have a mixed feeling about the game, nothing like the review I spoke about in the beginning(which insisted that this is a game either you'll love it, or you'll hate it).
I for one, kind of do both. I still think the spawning mechanics is the bigest failure of the game, making it unrealistic in a dumb way.
Another thing to mention is that people prone to motion sickness will most likely have a problem with this game. Not a con, just a fact.

If you play strategy games, perhaps you know what I mean when I say that playing a strategy game is like being a relationship with someone you REALLY like, but who has one or several traits that annoy you because they remind you of a previous girlfriend who did those same annoying things. The problem is that the rest of the relationship is really good and you don't want to break it off--but you can't stand those annoying traits so it creates problems every time they come up. You two are an on-again, off-again couple and everybody thinks it's not going to work out, until you finally get sick of those awful traits.
Just when you've broken things off with Strategy--this time, for good, you swear--this other girl walks in the door and you realize immediately she has all the amazing traits of your former ex-girlfriend (we'll call her "FPS") and all the awesome traits of your recently-made ex girlfriend (her name is "Strategy"), and yet this new girl seems to have none of the flaws of either.
To put the icing on the cake, she isn't what most people would describe as "beautiful" or "stunning," but to you she has a unique enough appearance that as time goes on you are remarkably attracted to her and yet feel she is completely approachable and not trying too hard to be beautiful, which is all the more attactive to you.  Without knowing how or when it happened, you realize you two have gotten close--closer than you intended, you never meant to rebound--so you decide to start dating this new girl.
Things go strangely at first; you're not sure it's working out, but you're not sure it isn't. You're always worried that she's got something underneath the surface that is going to let you down, you just haven't seen it yet. Sure, she is kind of goofy at times, but you secretly like it and enjoy being able to be yourself without feeling judged, so you decide to go with it. Time passes, and you decide that in spite of whatever may be wrong with this new girl or what flaws she has, you love her in spite of, or maybe because of, those flaws, and that you find them acceptable because you just love spending time together and can't imagine her not in your life anymore.
After a while, however, you just wish there was more you could do together, like hang out with eacht other's friends while you're together. Sometimes your routines are a bit dull, so after a while you two just drift apart...
That, my friends, is Valkyria Chronicles.
TL:DR  Worth every penny, play the campaign a couple times, then set aside for a while until you feel nostalgic.

Let me start off buy saying this game is NOT for everyone. THe reason for this is the INSANE learning curve this game has, driving away lots of new players. BUT, if you take the time to acctually learn the mechanics and all of the games intricacy's. I gaurentee you will enjoy the game. To help you figure out wether you will like the game or not im going to give a rundown of the core mechanics.
-Classes-
Chivalry features four unique and interesting classes.
Knight
Knight is the strongest and slowest moving class. But dont let that fool you. Knight is the most vercitile class in my opninion, it has the widest variety of weapons, with each weapom having its own set of strenghts and weaknesses.
Vangaurd
Vangaurd is the class in the middle. Medium armor and medium speed. Combine this with there long weapons and low htk ratio and they become very deadly on the battlefield.
Man at arms
Man at arms is the fastest class, his intire arsenal is 1h weapons making his ht ratio high, but his speed higher. Man at arms also has acess to a dodge abilty which is bindable to any key you want. All of this combined makes man at arms extremely powerfull in duels, but considerably weaker in team objective than all other classes.
Archer
Archers fill the ranged roll of chivalry, They have extrmemely low armour thus they can be 1shoted by most of the knight and vangaurds weapons, but... thats assuming they can get close to you. The archer has a wide variter of ranged weapons at his deisposal, anythig from a sling, to crossbow that 1shots everyclass to the head, to a Longbow.
Which class should I play?
Overall its up to you, But for learning how to play, I cabt express how much I recomend playing 2h Knight longsword.
Playing this setup forces you to master all of the games core mechanics to sucseed. You must have good footwork, and learn to Drag, parry,riposte, and feint properly (I will cover all of these topics later in my review!!). Even after 800 hours of playing I still enjoy Longsword the most, for its combonation of quick attacks and slow drags.
-Health, Damage & damage types-
Damage is hadled very well in Chivalry taking into acount many variables. First off there are 3 damage zones, head, torso, and feet/legs. Head dealing the most damage, then torso, then feet. This can be really powerfull if you learn your weapons damage types so you know what combonations of moves will kill people.
There are also 3 different damage types Blunt, pierce, and cut. Each weapon and even there individual swings deal different damage types. Learning what classes are weak to which damage types helps deal with enemies quicker. For example Vangaurds are weak to piers damage so when fighting them with the Sword of War, you are going to want use your stab strike as much as possible because it will 2shot them because of its piercing damage, while the overhead will take 3 shots even thought the base damage of the overhead is stronger.
All of this ties in really well with the dragging system which I will cover next
-Dragging-
Dragging is by far my favourite part of this game. I cant stress how amazing this mechanic is, it seperates Chivalry from everysingle other mideival combat simulator out there. Dragging is the name given to a technique that invovles precise mouse movements that allow you to reshape, slow down, or even speed up your attacks. Chivalry feature real time swings, this means by pulling your mouse in the opposite direction of your swing you can slow it down, by looking into your swing you can speed it up, and depending on the strike you are using change its direction completely. This allows for some interesting scenarios. An example of this would be as follows. You are stuck in a 1v1 with a knight, You have already hit him with 2 overheads to the head so you know one more will finish him off, But he is expecting you to aim for the head so he is prepared for it. Do you do a slow drag down to his feet? or do you do a fast overhead riposte to try and finish him?
This concept is incerdibily hard to explain on paper so if you are having trouble understanding it feel free to add me and I can do my best to show you in game.

I really want to give this game a positive recommendation. Its innovative card / action battle structure has all the makings of a totally addictive and fun experience. I want more cards, want to find out what they do, and am on the edge of my seat with every move forward onto the next encounter.
But there are two really big flaws, which I suspect will limit how much time I put into the game. The first is a clunky and sometimes non-intuitive interface, with lots of unnecessary and repetitive micro-pauses. Every time you hit a merchant, you have to wait for a few seconds as the game transitions to the same 3D rendering of the merchant cart, before you are allowed to get on with the transaction. Fine the first time, really annoying by the 20th time. Ditto with shuffling the cards before making one of the game's very frequent 4-hidden-card choice routines.
The second big flaw is the tactical combat. It just feels fuzzy, with a lack of precise control over your character that it already turning me off. It's not like Diablo 3, with it's crisp and immediately responsive controls. It's more like playing Diablo 3 drunk while wearing ski mittens. I would have preferred a crisp isometric 2D action sequence, or even a turn-based battle approach, rather than the sluggish and woozy 3D battles here.
Maybe some fine tuning is all that's needed to turn this into a very fun game. For now, though, it's not going to be on my play a lot list.

TL:DR Great game, unique premise, tonnes of replayability. One of the few kickstarter success stories, definitely worth your time and money.
Basically, the premise of the game is that you are playing a card game against "The Dealer", the game is based around "Encounter" cards, this may be you finding a treasure chest but needing to go through a series of obstacles to get to it, being ambushed by skeletons or going to a demon clubhouse and gambling your soul after getting drunk. There are loads of them and they are very varied.
The encounters usually come in sets, miniture stories that unlock as you complete each card in the sequence, which is dead cool and a good reason to keep unlocking cards. For every action in an encounter (that isn't directly combat) you pick from a set of four dealer shuffled cards, which indicate how much you failed or succeeded at the action, which adds a nice RNG element to the game (you can follow the card shuffle with your eyes, so not ENTIRELY luck based) and keeps things interesting.
Your characters equipment and blessings/curses can also interact with some of the encounters, suprising me even 20+ hours in with new paths in the old cards I thought I knew. Even once you are finished with the story there is an endless mode which uses all the cards you have unlocked to create a neverending run which gets harder the longer you play. The replay value is huge.
The combat is Arkham styled (counter system and very flowy in how you move between enemies), here the equipment from encounters will really come into play, it's fairly simple in terms of what you can do but gets quite tactical, as the battlegrounds can have traps and the enemies get harder and more complex as the game goes on. The dealers starts adding curses and difficult encounters to the deck, making the later levels very difficult.
The game never feels like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t or cheating, pretty much every encounter can be run away from/refused and the combat can be difficult but it never feels like any enemy is particularly over powered, it's always down to your own skill. Due to the huge number of encounters and equipment, your freedom to choose and balance risk/reward, and the RNG element every run feels unique, the only downside I would add is that the combat is fairly simplistic, but considering this is an indie development, it's a very impressive accomplishment.
One of the few kickstarter success stories, definitely worth your time and money.

Instead of typing out a long description, i'll give you a (long) bulleted list of Pros and Cons.  I'm not going to include a bulleted list on the cons that come with the card game aspect and "random drawings" form a constructed deck", those shortcomings should be apparent and are what make some of the Pros, possible. I am only @ 13hrs right now and the game still holds a great deal of playing value as it is. That said:
Pros:
+Never the same adventure.
+The Dealer is some of the best voice work i've heard in years.
+Combat is tightly done and you are forced to pay attention to your surroundings. (Traps)
+Forced to learn to use various weapons due to the random nature of obtaining them. (You put them in your deck and draw them/buy them in the game)
+Building your deck is fairly simple but still enjoyable.
+Different enemy types have different attack patterns, don't pay attention to them and risk dying quickly. (especially later on)
+Becoming good at the combat will make your life MUCH easier and you're rewarded by not getting crushed in the inevitably hectic combat, making your placement and strategy in combat when you come upon a difficult (and some get crazy) encounter.
+Game keeps you off-balance, so even if you become well-off you never feel overpowered.
+Card shuffling is NOT random, meaning you can watch the cards a la shell game (and pay attention to the top card)
+The tokens that require you to go through the entire encounter make you read what's going on, and hence draw you in. Sometimes it is counter-intuitive and you have to solve it a different way than what may be the obvious method.
+There are separate decks for blessings, curses, "Gains", Creatures, Equipment and Encounters, which the game couldn't work without most of them separated, however, you won't run into "Draw 2 cards, keep 1 if it's an equip" but rather simply "Draw 1 Equipment" or even "Draw 1 weapon card".
(Note: You only construct two of these decks: Equipment and Encounters)
+As you progress in the story, you get bonuses that aid you, and the game in turn gets more challenging by upping the difficulty in a concise manner.
Cons:
-Some of the enemy attacks have a slightly larger than normal hitbox and priority (Minotaur i'm looking at you.), by no means unfair but sometimes I scratched my head.
-I'm not too big on the rings that only have their effect when you sell them. I can see some of them being useful, but in a game where it thrives on imperinence already, having to ditch gear to get the effect of it can make that item undesirable, in my opinion.
-Combat itself can still be a bit simple and repetitive sometimes.
-Your character fell down the top of the tallest ugly tree that exists in the ugly tree sanctuary and hit every branch of every one of the trees on the way down and landed face first on the protuding roots.
-Those branches then fell off the trees and landed on him, followed by the trees themselves.
-The lumber created from those trees was used to build a boat, and that boat would run ashore on a beach he was visting one day and smack h-
-You see where i'm going with this. Your character is not very pretty. At all. You can't change how he looks either.
Overall, I am loving the game and it is honestly full of flavor. Don't go into it expecting to get something different than what it says it is: A game of Constructed Chance, balanced further by your skills, resource managment and ingenuity. Because it is a game that uses chance, be ready for the inevitable "Bad Draw", because that's where this game REALLY shines, making you over come that Bad Draw.
Wanting to hear the Dealer will bring you back time and time again, and the gameplay is solid enough to bring you back but not wear you out. When you get a new weapon or piece of gear, you'll want to jump in and try it out and when you lose (and you will lose), you will have to seriously go back and think how you could build your deck differently to turn the tables in your favor. I look forward to playing the game once i've unlocked everything to pass the time and also can see how EASY it is for them to expand on this already great game. I am very happy with my purchase.

Going to try to sum up MY experience of the game, please don't take my opinion as facts.
Pros:
* Large open world with minimum zoning, seamless borders.

* Class system is great, mix and match with whatever you like. Abilties level up as you earn XP in battle
* Pet system, everyone can use pet that can be used in battles. Different pets has different abilties and level up as you use the pet.
* Player housing, actually build the structure of a house by getting materials, build it and decorate it
* Labor-cap, almost everything you do requires "labor" (not fighting or exploring). All players have a labor pool that decreases as you craft , open coinpurses (loot) or use any other skill related to proficiency (tradeskill). The cap prevents rich players, at least in theory, to get a gigantic leap ahead
* Loyalty points, if you become "patron" (subscription) you get loyalty points which you can use in an ingame story to purchase special goods like mounts, pets etc.
* Proficiency, probably the best tradeskill game out there, again in theory. There is SO MUCH you can do. You have the standard mmo tradeskills like weapon and armor crafting, cooking, alchemy etc but also some great unusual fun skills like "composition" where you can write music and actually play them on crafted instruments like drums, guitar, flute etc. You have a "construction" and "machining" tradeskill where you can make vehicles, ship-parts or housing items. Even "commerce" is a tradeskill that you level up as you trade items or use the ingame auction house. It is no doubt the games selling point.
* Naval, you can build and use ships and submarines and sail the seas. Fishing boats to master your fishing tradeskill or large galleons to engage your enemies in.
* Gliders, no flying mounts here but a glider can keep you up for a decent amount of time and can be equipped with boosters, cannons and lazers...pew pew...well, maybe not lasers then!
* PvP, whether you like it or not, you are going to get engaged in pvp. There are some safe zones but eventually you going to run into the contested zones where open pvp takes place, even from same faction.
*Crime system, If you engage your own faction, steal someones property you "earn" crime points. Eventually you will stand for your crimes and be trialed infront of an Jury (that actually are other players signed up for jury-duty). They decide the outcome of your deeds and you could be sent to jail, literrally. There is an island where your character gets locked up, dressed in classic white/black striped pyjamas. There you will sit for the XX minutes the jury sentenced you to...unless...you escape :)
* Pirates arrggh, lets say you didn't learn from your time in jail and continue on your path of crime, you eventually will be outcast from your faction and can't visit the major cities. Good thing is, if this is really what you want to do, there is a place for outcasts like you. A small island in between the large continents where you and your pirate friends can settle.
* Cross faction language barrier, yes this is good thing to me. You can't talk trash to the other faction, they won't understand a word you say and you won't understand them....unless, you learn and level up in "language" proficiency. Great feature.
* Player driven economy, the players create most tradeable goods in the game, which all can be directly traded or via AH. Now this is a good thing in theory, more below under cons.
* Traderoutes, when crafted, refined or farmed something you can make it into a tradepack. These tradepacks shall be delivered to a trader NPC located throughout the world. As longer away from the crafted goods home the higher the payout. There is only one thing, you actually need to carry it. If you carry it on your back your movement speed will be considerably slower. You can take public transportation which requires you to wait on "bus stops" for the carriages or airships, you can create your own carts or ships that will get you to the destination faster, but not neccessarily safer. Remember open pvp :) If you get killed your hard earned trade pack is up for grabs.

=There's not much to the story, and what there is can only be found out through data logs left behind by dead crew members or through translations of alien text. The story in the Return to Na Pali expansion is better explained as it gets actual voice acting.
