Velvet Sundown pulls you in with catchy visuals and a brilliant concept.
Then you load up the game.
The graphics are actually pretty bad and the controls are as minimal as needed to allow players to move around a small virtual world and interact with other players. The good news is, the interaction can be overwhelmingly positive, but on the other side, it can be overwhelmingly negative as well. If you get in to a game with trolls, it's over from the beginning, and when you get in with roleplayers who play their part well, there still isn't much to really do.
At the beginning it basically tells you your characters biography and whether or not you did it and why. After that, it either gives you real or fake evidence or just a pen. The pen is used at the only interactable item in the world to write down who you think did it. Whether you did it or not at the end doesn't even matter, it just says if you went to prison as an innocent, a guilty party or if you got away with it or didn't catch the culprit. The downside of the gameplay is, since it isn't a majority vote to end the game, everyone has to vote. If someone refuses, you sit there the entire time and wait for it to end, which can be annoying. If someone leaves the game, it doesn't end, but you can't figure out if they had evidence or not, though you can leave the game too.
During gameplay you simply go meet up with people (or try to), and exchange or show your evidence and try to figure out who did it, and who is lying. When a conclusion is found, everyone (hopefully) writes their choice of who is guilty in to the journal, and the game ends with a chat at the end letting you discuss who did it, etc, though this is rarely used appropriately. During the game, all words typed are vocalized with various Microsoft Sam voices and no other form of communication is present. The game doesn't censor ANYTHING, so be prepared before entering. Though there is little context or content, it can be interesting to play when everyone plays their roles perfectly, though once again, this hardly ever happens.
Another downside to the game is the fact that to troll, you simply spam in a chat with another player, and every other player nearby; whether in conversation with you or not, is forced to hear your spam. Due to so many negatives and so little positives, it's hard to give the game a good review, but I felt inclined to tell everyone how great the concept is, if only it was a little more fleshed out, especially the content. The game has been out for months, only features 3 situations and 2 of them are locked to premium users at any given time. Every week they rotate which one is free, a week. A week bound to the same scenario with the same limited interactions. Longevity is not prevalent here, but you're not here for replayability and a story, you're here to discover. And sometimes we have to make those sacrifices. There should be lobbies so you can see who is connecting, and learn who to avoid. Instead, you click on a scenario and wait for the minimum players required.
So to sum it up, we have poor graphics that get by because they are the bare minimum required to catch players in this day and age. The controls are horrible compared to a non porn based video game and only allow you to interact with logbooks, your evidence and with players at a communication level. The content amount is so small that it barely seems to exist and the rest of the game is premium based for a mere two new levels. The player base is very tiny with half being either trolls or bored and the level design is nonexistent. There is no real replayability, even if you didn't commit the crime, nothing really changes each new game. The concept and idea is fresh and I find it endearing to see that it made it's way in to a game, but this idea needs to be fleshed out a lot more before you can actually consider it as a full fledged and finished game.

Unreal is basically my favourite game of all time. Levels range from enclosed to outdoor and many intermediate areas inbetween and I obviously encourage anyone to buy Unreal. This version of Unreal (Unreal Gold) comes equipped with the official expansion pack - Return to Na Pali. I don't think return to na pali is quite as good and as long as the main game, but it is still a relatively decent experience none the less.
What I mainly like about Unreal is the extensive content creation capabilities, you can basically create new anything with this game such as worlds/maps, models, skins, textures, sounds, weapons, items, music and mods as the game comes packed with the developer tools, which have been expanded upon with the 227 patch, which also fixes almost every issue with the game, improves performance, adds new capabilities for content creation, adds new tech (such as character shadows) and some supplementary new effects. The patch, created with the permission of Epic games, can be found in the downloads section of
, it is sort of compulsary to obtain and install the patch otherwise multiplayer is inaccessable since the gamespy shut down (which shut down the gamespy master servers for multiplayer games), and the patch also updates Unreal to connect to the new masterserver. Multiplayer also allows a hotlink to custom created content, which can be downloaded from that server on the spot simply by connecting to it, over Unreal itself. This means it is very easy to create custom content and share it just by adding it to your server, this is a feature that alot of games from this era (including most games in the current generation) do not have, as usually mods for such games must be downloaded outside of the game + placed and configured in the correct folders, which then afterwoods you can connect to a server if you have done all that correctly, unlike Unreal which downloads everything over the game just by connecting to a server, and runs it from the cache + is already configured.
The 227 patch is actively updated, so new iterations of the patch will come out subsequently, adding more capabilities and more features.
If you haven't experienced Unreal yet, I urge you to. It's always nice to see new faces in the community!
Edit : Also nominated Unreal Gold for the 'Test of Time' steam award.

I want to start this off by saying that the game is promising. It's a nice concept and the base for all the really good stuff is already there. When or if this game comes further along, I'll likely change my review. I intentionally played the game for under 2 hour so I would have the ability to refund it later if I did not think it was going to go anywhere.
PROS:
-Aesthetics:
It looks ♥♥♥♥ing great. Honestly, it does. The low poly style goes really nice with robots, although I can't say the same for some of the enemies.
-Customization:
Building your robot with different parts, although currently limited is actually really fun, and there are some pretty cool characters you can make. The game does let you have 5 different equipment set ups, that you're able to swap through in the menu and at a little pad near the start of each level.
-Ability to refund skill points
Skill points can be refunded for no cost any time. This is really great, as you can mess around and see which stats you think work the best for you.
CONS:
That's about it for what's good. For the rest of what I say, I wouldn't take it as why the game is bad, but rather what would make the game better. The only real reason I'm not playing more of this game right now is due to its clear lack of content and extremely repetitive "missions".
-Repetitive "Missions":
I'm going to chalk this one up to the game still being fairly new. Currently there are only two modes, PvP and Explore. I have not been able to play PvP yet, as basically no one plays this game (got to about rank 50 world after 1.5 hours). Explore is really misleading, because it's not exploration at all. You just walk through a very linear cave system filled with enemies, and you're offered two goals. The main goal is always the same, although they give them different names, you're basically just going up to objectives and pressing F. Once you've pressed F on enough different objectives, you head to the boss and leave. You can go to the boss before hand, but you won't get any loot if you haven't completed at least one objective. The sub objectives are really well done, they're basically just a small randomized goal. Collect X amount of X crafting materials, crit X number of times or don't change your loadout during the mission. These accomplish their goal pretty well, and offer an extra chance at loot when completed.
-Artificial difficulty:
The game never actually becomes more challenging. Just harder to do the same exact thing you were doing. More enemies with higher stats. It gets to the point where you'll just be swarmed and killed in the same spot over and over again unless you press the 'escape' button and select the suicide command, which teleports you to some spot back on the map. There's more to this swarming issue, but I'll bring that back up in a bit. I don't mind the enemies getting more stats, it makes sense because I do much more damage when I get better gear. But making boss fights and side rooms with loot just swarm with enemies is really annoying. They will block you in, stunlock you and just kill you over and over again. In harder levels, it's better to just ignore all the enemies and run past everything while completing the objectives. You don't get anything for killing them anyways, except 1 random crafting material sometimes. With the game being called an action rpg you would think fighting would be the main focus. If combat in a combat centered game become something you'd rather just avoid altogether, then there is very little reason to keep playing.
-Basic attacks cost power:
This really got me upset, and I put up with it because I wanted to get a better feel for the game before I wrote a review. There is a power system in the game, which is basically the equivalent of a mana bar in any rpg. Your skills use power, but their cooldowns are so long (and for a good reason, they're mostly pretty strong) that it's basically negligible. Because of this, you're left to just shoot your left and right guns most of the game, which is what is shown in all the trailers so I expected as much. The issue is that your basic attacks cost power. I can't tell if this was supposed to be something you were supposed to "strategically work around" or learn how to manage, but it basically just leaves you kiting enemies for half the time you're in the dungeon since you're literally unable to do anything but walk around. Usually in mmos, when you were out of mana or your skills are on cooldown, you'd use basic attacks for filler. In this game, since your skills are on a super long cooldown, your basic attacks are basically your spells and there's nothing you can even do for filler except run away until it's back up. I suppose this wouldn't be an issue if power regenerated quickly, but even with the regeneration stat almost maxed out and multiple pieces of regeneration gear you run into really long down times on certain weapons. It doesn't add to any sort of difficulty or level of skill, it's just frustrating.
I'm not a game developer myself, so I can't really say what they should do instead, but I have a pretty good idea. I'll include it at the end.
-Skills are bland:
I don't mean your active abilities, these skills are what you use your skill points on when you level up. They are the equivalent of your stats or attributes in other games. It was obvious at first look, there wasn't a ton of thought behind this. Like I said earlier, I'm not a game developer so I can't say what they should do instead. Usually when I play an rpg one of the most fun things is min maxing and creating cool builds. These skills offer very little in that aspect and its pretty obvious what you want to put points into, which leads to everyone ending up with basically the same stats. Tanks will probably differ from DPS, but within each category everyone will basically be the exact same.
BUGS:
The unintentional cons of early access games. I expected a few of these.
Can't jump, but can get on different Z-levels? What?:
So remember when I said that there is more to getting swarmed than just dying a lot? Well yeah, the enemies will just push you onto themselves or terrain and move you vertically up off the map. It's impossible to move some of the time and you can't shoot them at all since you're on a separate Z-level, but since the enemies can hit you and they will kill you in the same spot until your use the suicide option to reset your position. This also assists players in completely ignoring fights all together. If you get trapped only by a few, you can get yourself pushed on top of terrain and then just bypass large groups of enemies to grab objectives and leave the mission with very little risk. This needs to be fixed.
Honestly this is the only bug I really even noticed, but it was a pretty big deal. Otherwise, this game seems to be pretty polished in that aspect.
SUGGESTIONS:
I'll say it again: I'm not a game developer myself, so I can't really say what they should do instead. But I'm going to anyways.
Power? How about overheating:
The power mechanic is frustrating and sucks. It'd be easier to and a lot more fun to just change it to an overheat system. The support abilities' power costs are virtually nonexistent, and it's not like they should have any when they already have really long cool downs. As far as basic attacks consuming power, it just looks as though the developers wanted to make sure people couldn't just spray their guns forever. Which makes sense, that'd make the game kinda easy. An overheat mechanic would take out the massive amount of downtime where players have to kite for 20 - 30 seconds at a time while waiting for a decent amount of power to regenerate. Managing your weapons heat levels is also a lot more fun (in a challenging sense).
Option to disable robot voices:
This is just my opinion, but they're really annoying.

Pictopix is another great addition to the nonogram/picross type puzzle game genre.  Nothing too crazy or surprising in this one!  The puzzles are quite enjoyable, and can all be solved without resorting to proof-by-contradiction.  There's a handy "mark" feature available with the middle mouse button which can aid in counting out squares, and there's a superb feature called "smart slide" which restricts click-and-drag marking to a single row/column, which is quite handy for not accidentally making marks you hadn't intended.  All nonogram puzzle games should include that feature!
The in-game puzzle editor works great, and the workshop/community integration lets you upload your own puzzles, and play other users' puzzles, if you're so inclined.  Works great on Linux as well!  The game is well worth the money if you enjoy this kind of puzzle.
There are two minor things I don't like about it, neither of which should discourage anyone from checking it out, but I'll mention 'em for posterity:
1) You get "crown" ratings for each puzzle based on some criteria (mostly to do with what "hints" you have enabled in the options), but the third crown can be missed if you accidentally misclick too often (which would require re-playing the puzzle if you want the third crown).  The threshhold for losing the third crown has been increased quite a bit in the most recent version (to the point where I never ran into the problem again after the patch), but it still feels wrong to punish misclicks in a puzzle like this, especially if you're able to recover from them and solve the puzzle anyway!
2) It's a common convenience in computer nonogram puzzles to mark rows/columns as "complete" once there's an appropriate sequence of marks on the row/col (regardless of whether it's correct or not).  Pictopix considers that a "hint," though, and you'll be unable to get all three crowns if you have this enabled.  In practice I didn't miss it too much, but it's something I always appreciate in other nonogram games.
Still, those are quite minor, and the game's quite enjoyable.  I'd definitely recommend it!

Well it's certainly a little treat.
If you've played really complex games like spectral souls, it's... it's not as complex as it.  A little wiki checking for figuring out how to get a few classes and that's about it really.  The combat is smooth, and I can see why people tell me that this is the 'worst' in terms of combat and they only improved on it, it's very solid with a cute lift system.
I'm by no means insulting a jrpg for it's simplicity, it's a breath of fresh air and in fact, it's what made it so addictive.  I could sit through ten missions because often they'd only take a turn or two to complete.  Three or four if I was lining up for a geo-d combo to get sweet sweet bonus points.
The story line clearly has it's fair share of humor, it's a humor based game after all.  While a some of the jokes made me smile or chuckle (nin-nin-nin), others are more... japanese zaney humor that might not really stick with the audience that cares little for anime.  Myself included, not a big fan of anime things really.
Each weapon type feels unique and fluent and you can equip any weapon on humanoid classes, though some weapons fit more naturally for some classes, you can feel free to experiment. (I gave a female warrior an axe for example, while tossing a theif a bow and arrow).
You'll probably be revisiting a lot of places to grind for stuff, but my suggestion is to save the game, then go ham on item worlds, it's easy money, easy exp, and above all, they're procedulally generated so you'll get new spices and strategies occasionally thrown in.

TL;DR: Mediocre game, do not buy.
As its predecessor, this game has a wonderful dark post-apocalyptic setting, presumably an interesting story and decent graphics. Unfortunately, it also shares all negative aspects of its predecessor such as: linear yet confusing level design, not comprehensible light-darkness-conditions, frustrating passages, and HORRIBLY placed auto-save points. Seriously, an automated save right in a Demon's attacking sequence? Although it's getting frequent updates, it's becoming more and more impossible to play the game.  Monsters are getting tougher with each update which is all fine and well, but 350 damage weapons that consume massive amounts of energy deal a tenth of that to monsters who have several thousand hit points. It's not even possible to kill things anymore without being in a group but there aren't enough people playing to group up. While I felt this game had a bit of potential, they're making things worse with the updates instead of fixing the issues at hand and while they're fixing bugs, that doesn't account for much when you can't play the game bug free anyways.
- Weapons: they're terribly balanced. Some are just outright useless (Laser, Flamethrower) with the minigun being easily the best. It has almost as much damage per hit as the other weapons, is the most cost effective on Energy VS. DPS, and with the highest attack speed by far it's easily the highest DPS. there are also only 5 weapon types in the game at the moment, and one of them is pure support and the only possible substitute over miniguns so variety is slim.
- Frames: The light frames are poorly balanced as of now having little to no purpose on being in the game aside from your starter frame. They accel in neither tanking ability nor energy, and their default skill is useless compared to some others.
The medic has roughly the same hp/armor values and significantly higher energy allowing you to sustain damage longer along with a skill that full restores hp/energy to yourself and nearby allies letting them outshine light mechs who can only invuln for a bit until hit/hitting something or the 10 seconds are up.
Heavy mechs are definitely the tankiest but with how negligable armor feels right now and the inability to put their high weight limit to the task since there really isn't anything extremely heavy in the game.. they feel slightly underwhelming compared to medic frames, all the more so considering their slow speed causes them to take significantly longer on completing missions and often getting left behind. Heavier weapons with much higher values and the armor actually giving a significant decrease to damage taken would allow them to shine a bit more and giving them a higher regen value would also help so fingers crossed they actually give them a good purpose.
Stats - Health and armor can help slightly but with how hard mobs hit you'll want to be putting most of your effort into dodging, regeneration rates are the same across all frames and hp is so low that past a certain point it becomes nearly negligable. Energy regen being a flat 20 (28 with full upgrades to it from levels) also leaves no room for thought. That leaves you with mobility and energy values, and since energy is basically your amunition it easily takes priority to ensure you've enough sustained damage to kill things efficiently. Mobility is your best tool for survival so that does take some priority but any of the mechs can move around well enough to dodge most things without focusing too heavily on it (and with a high enough mobility it can actually be detrimental to your survivability causing you to run into things you can normally walk straight around) It further enhances the singular aspect of the game where you just want as much energy as possible with enough hp to take a couple hits in order to sustain your damage.

It's a disappointing ending to a great series. My biggest problem isn't the fact that the game is short (it took me about 4 hours to finish) but the way the story plays out. In the previous two games you were presented with a handfull of characters and situations and you could try and romance each girl to get to a number of good and bad endings with a few surprises along the way. Not so in this one. Your only romance option is Yuuki, no matter what decissions you make. And while I do like her, I'm disappointed I can't choose an ending with any of the other girls. Some of the girls from the previous games are also absent so if you had any favorites, they are likely missing. Chasing the other girls will influence the ending you'll get with Yuuki, which makes sense within the narative but I felt cheated anyway. There are also no hidden characters or surprise endings like in the previous games. The CG's are as good like in the previous games but there are only six girls and you get only one encounter which each of them. So the total number of pictures is also much less than in the previous games.
All in all it's not a bad game per se, but it's presented as the conclusion to the Beach Bounce trilogy. And as such it's very disappointing. I expected more from the last entry in the Beach Bounce trilogy. More girls to choose from instead of less, more different endings like in the first game instead of four largely similar endings with the same girl.

Are you a count and are under the command of a king? Is your army pathetically small and weak compared to your liege? Then you can't seize his throne through force, nor can you fight him for independence. Well then, perhaps you should start a faction, and make its goal to put you in power and deplace him. Then send your councilors out to ruin diplomatic relations between him and his vassals, so that they will despise him and join your faction. Once enough of his vassals has joined your faction, you can merge your armies and declare war. If you have gained enough support to have a bigger army, or if you manage to outmaneuver and outwit him, then you shall win. Now you are a king, in control of a large country, and all of your vassals like you. What now? Oh look, that country next to you are infidels. Their religion isn't your religion. You want more lands don't you? Well then declare a holy war on them, allowing you to seize a giant swathe of land from their possesion if your army proves victorious over them. As soon as the war is over, you realize hey! That was good fun! Shouldn't I declare war and attack him again before his army rebuilds? But oh no, you've signed a treaty with him, and it would cost you the majority of your prestige. You can't afford to lose that! And the treaty lasts for 10 years! Wait a minute, the treaty was between him and I. Not between our countries. Well then you should plot to kill him! Begin the plot, and invite people from his court, maybe even his council and perhaps even his own family! The closer they are to him and the higher their intrigue skill, the more power they will add to your plot, and the more likely you are to succeed in your assassination  attempts. A year passes, and you receive news that the enemy infidel leader has perished, poisoned by the wine he drunk at his yearly feast. Now you can declare war again, to seize the remaining lands of the infidel country, and you won't have to wait another 9 years. And I'm just getting started! This game, is just enormous in the possibilites and the things you can do. There are hundreds of different plots you can start or join, different religions you can convert to, so many titles you can claim and hold, so many different counties, baronies, duchies, kingdoms, and empires to conquer! So many different mercenary companies to choose from! And there are many different time periods you can choose to start from too! There's even more! Have you started a game, and played as one character and his country for 30 years? You saved your game, and went to sleep. As you get up in the morning you decide to play Crusader Kings II again, because you just can't get enough of it. Well as you load your save game, you look at the map before you click to play. You realize you are in a terrible position, or maybe you are bored of your country. So choose a different character! You can switch your character at anytime, if you feel like you want to mix things up a bit. Now you have control over a different dynasty, a different country. All of your progress of your previous country will be the same. You are resuming your save game, just playing as a different character! It makes for a wonderful game, full of limitless possibilites. Plus if you just want to relax, have some fun, maybe mop the floor with the ai, the cheats on singleplayer are just MARVELOUS. I play with cheats from time to time, when I want to have fun with the ai and just enjoy even more possibilites! Want unlimited money? Just type ` to bring up the console, then type cash 100000000000 and your money will max out. And thats only one cheat my friend. But there is nothing more satisfying than working for 4 hours as a count, and then going to bed at night a king. And then the next night you snuggle down with a smile for you are now an Emperor. The next day if you are just an absolute nightmare at the game, perhaps you will rule all of Europe, and rule all the known world. So many possibilites, I give this game a 10/10 and thats not being generous enough. Not sure if you want to pay $40? Well download the demo they have on offer. The possibilities are much more limited in the demo of course, but just the demo alone will convince you, that you need to buy this game. It's what I did. If you're a poor fellow like myself, then perhaps you should add it to your wishlist and wait for it to go on sale. Not to mention there are so many DLC's to this game, and they open up EVEN more possibilites, they add more countries, more religions, more music, more units, more customizable options, etc. A great game, worth the cost, and I'll definitely be playing this for years to come, if I don't die of a heart attack first.

>Insane and odd weapons combined with a movement system create a game that actually makes you feel like a crazy space ninja.
>Multiple game modes including open-world, instanced randomly generated, and PvP ensure enormous amounts of hours of fun
>Story missions that are enormously surprising in their quality, given the game's focus on combat
>End game grind that never allows you to abandon having fun while flipping around like a space ninja
>Aesthetics that are gorgeous while also being incredibly easy to run - allowing even my 1070 to run at a solid 4k 60fps
>"Healthy" microtransactions that bring a trove of good content, including community made beauties, and no P2W.
>Player marketplace that allows those who won't/can't pony up $ to trade for real money currency. Those willing to put in the effort can easily find themselves shopping the microtransactions with no money investment.
>Customization to allow even the most niche build or worst weapon to be viable. Say NO to cookie cutters.
TL;DR Great game made through sweat and hard labor, supported by microtransactions that allow even the peniless to partake, all while flipping around like a badass space ninja.

A very pleasant surprise, mixing light combat with rpg, and deckbuilding elements. Grab it if it sounds right, because it is.
- Excellent and fresh concept: The mix works well, giving the player some of all worlds.
voice acting: Top notch and plenty of commentary from the GM. This is how it should be done.
- Gorgeous graphics of the cards and coherent one within the 3d-fighting world.
- Well written cards with sometimes alternate texts, the perfect amount of reading required.
- A real chance to influence the random elements of the game when you draw one of four cards that were shuffled.
- Plays really well with PC xbox-gamepad controller. I recommend using a gamepad for this.
- It's fun! Yups, that counts...
- Feels little too easy the first 3-4 chapters, but becomes harder, and that's in the very start of the game.
- Lacks adjustable difficulty settings, but makes that in part up by having an eternal mode. The game is geared towards the casual leaning to intermediate player or the experienced ones searching for some fun and well paced action. Hence, this doesn't have to be a con.
- The combat system could possibly have gotten an overhaul for the more demanding players: It's somewhat too simplistic even if it is indeed challenging in it's own right. Feels too static now despite the fact that this wasn't ever aiming to be the next Arkham et.c.
- When the shuffle is done it is sometimes impossible to understand where the card went mainly to how the shuffling is represented.
- Workshop support: Let the community create custom cards and/or campaigns. The game will never die then and keep getting followers.
- DLC:s - this game has way more to offer within the already established framework. I'm certain that those who enjoyed it will want more of it.

A fairly unique experience, Chivalry: Medieval Warrior's hilariously fun first person sword combat is the bedrock on which the rest of the mutiplayer-only game is centered. Four classes, ranging from the agile archer to the tanky knight, and a variety of weapons make for a wide range of player choice in terms of play style. The warrior customization, while not quite as nice overall as some games like the Forza Motorsport series, is a nice addition, allowing for experienced players to make their warrior their own. Chivalry is a game easily worth its price.

This is nearly a GREAT game. Unfortunately, only nearly. Some of the problems are unfixable. My biggest gripe is: NO ONE TALKS. Even if you talk to another player, 9 times out of 10 they don't talk back because they're too busy grinding something whether it be gilda, crafting, gold or combat. For me personally, that's most of what the game could be down the toilet instantly. Without any regular meaningful communication with other players how exactly do players of this MMO actually relate to each other? Running dungeon raids together or by murdering you mainly. And I have no problem with PVP, in fact I am in favour of it but without any positive form of relating to players to balance it out this game really ends up, despite the wonderful structure it has in place, being just a boring grind and hoard fest.
Also, most  of the early-game's adventuring spirit was entirely anhilated by an unfortunate need to have to do a gazillion tedious quests to level up which mostly consisted of boshing mobs that are standing around all over the damn place like a bunch of cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, waiting for you to abuse them. Then when you finally have reached level 50 you've seen nearly the whole map and don't really feel like adventuring anymore. It is also then when you realise that even though you have reached level 50, it's the level 55s with the♥♥♥♥♥♥hot gear and the finely tuned derivative build who are still going to be butt-♥♥♥♥ing you at their whim.
What I would like to see future developers do is: Get rid of the grind altogether - it's♥♥♥♥♥♥ Give us ultimate freedom. To do this, remove levelling. Start the game at the highest level. And get rid of ridiculously expensive/hard to find items - they're pointless and only encourage further grinding. Get rid of quests too, they feel too much like they're telling you what to do, directing you too much, and take away from your own feeling of freedom, inventing your own quests (or perhaps discovering secret/subtly written in quests). With all that♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the way, focus on one thing only - making a good end-game. Also consider ways in which to encourage players to interact with each other in ways that don't ONLY include grinding dungeons and killing each other. If a developer considers all these things we might get a good game. Archeage has a lot of great features, unfortunately they all come to diddly when overshadowed by the grind and total lack of meaningful relations between players.

Prepare yourself for one of the greatest FPS games of all time, alongside Doom and Duke Nukem 3D.
Unreal puts you in the shoes of Prisoner 849, an otherwise nameless character with no dialogue or emotion, who was a prisoner on the prison ship Vortex Rikers that crash landed on the planet Na Pali.
You emerge from the crashed ship and take a gander at the vivid detail of the amazing landscape around you.  Fight your way through tough enemies that can appear from anywhere just to find out what happened to the rest of the crew and what your options for survival are.  As you progress through the world you learn more about what happened to everyone and how far they made it, what happened to the planet natives, and who the alien invaders are and what they want.  Gather new weapons and discover the right tool for the job as you face new and bigger enemies.  You'll quickly find out that some weapons have the ability to completely explode an enemy, sending body parts flying and bouncing with a trail of blood, while others can sever limbs with the same outcome.
When you finish the game and discover your final outcome you have the pleasure of going back and playing again on harder difficulties.  Harder difficulties not only make the enemies stronger and your weapons weaker, the enemies are faster, come in greater numbers, and (my favorite) they become SMARTER.  Smarter, meaning they hide, ambush, fake their deaths, and mislead you down the wrong path.
The multiplayer aspect is much appreciated.  Play online (if the servers are still running) or go against the computer in a botmatch and make the match you want to play, with maps inspired by levels from the main story.
Built back in 1998 on the brand-new Unreal Engine the game takes your breath away with amazing detail and a breath-taking score to compliment the variety of environments throughout the game.  Customize your controls with action-mapping and fine-tuning sensitivity, while also changing the HUD to need your desired style.
The only downside to this game is the lack of detail and textures when you get up close to an object or environment wall.  According to an interview with developers, this was the result of a time and budget constraint.  Just imagine what they could have accomplished without those constraints and how different our games would be today.  Many games and development companies use a variant of the original Unreal Engine, such as Battlefield, Borderlands, Life is Strange, Duke Nukem Forever, BioShock, Dirty Bomb, and many, many, many more.
I originally got this game not long after it came out and was blown away by everything and immediately fell in love with it.  I would highly recommend this for anyone that is up for a challenge and appreciates old, revolutionary games that changed the way we game today.

This game is a gem.
It is an interesting twist on turn based strategy with the units controlled from an over-the-shoulder, 3rd person perspective. This allows for nuances like taking cover behind your tank or putting a tree between you and a sniper to be viable tactics. The story is an impressive telling of an alternate version of World War 2 from the perspective of a local militia. It keeps you interested and has several good twists. One of the games strongest points is its diversity of missions. While you are using basically the same units each battle, every mission presents you with new and challenging situations. You are forced to come up with new tactics and uses for what you have available to you. While chance elements occationally give you a lucky long shot or a wrench to deal with, tactical positioning and optimized use of resources play a much larger role in victory. The graphics are simple, but have held up very well. They have an elegant, almost painted, look to them. The controls and menus are a little clunky and show signs of their console origin, but are manageable.

This game has the seed of a potentially good idea (online auto-moderated salon-style LARP - never mind that "online" and "LA*" are contradictory).  However, the execution on that idea is irredeemably flawed.  There are three major things lacking:
- game size:  the free instances are typically limited to 5-6 players, and zero NPCs; it looks like premium scenarios are the same scenarios, with roughly doubled instance sizes.  The available scenarios all feel like they would start to get interesting at around 20 players
- environmental interaction:  Every player starts the game with 2-5 items (which are always the same items in a given scenario, though the character/item match does get shuffled).  There are not any other items in the game.  There is a big yacht to walk around on, but there's never any reason to.  Games tend to devolve quickly into everyone standing around in the same conversation, at which point the setting might as well be a stopped elevator.
- depth of plot:  Since everything that exists or can exist within the instance starts out in the hands of a small group of people, and nothing happens in the environment, the possible interactions within a scene are usually exhausted inside of 5 minutes.  This makes the remaining 25 minutes until the scene actually *ends* (always by the clock running out) quite tedious.
There are also small but crucial mistakes, such as the murder mystery scenario always giving the same piece of evidence to the killer.  Figure out what that is, and the mystery becomes really simple:  each player has one piece of evidence, so whoever has that one, or refuses to share what they have, must be the killer.

TL;DR: Mediocre game, do not buy.
As its predecessor, this game has a wonderful dark post-apocalyptic setting, presumably an interesting story and decent graphics. Unfortunately, it also shares all negative aspects of its predecessor such as: linear yet confusing level design, not comprehensible light-darkness-conditions, frustrating passages, and HORRIBLY placed auto-save points. This very poor game design couples perfectly with said frustrating passages and makes playing Metro Last Light quite a pain to play. I actually started a new game on the game's easiest settings (Spartan, Normal) after exiting Reich to give it a second chance, but due to its mediocrity, I decided to prematurely end the game at the Sundown level which is the manifestation of nearly all the negative aspects I mentioned before. Although there were no eastereggs pointing at the STALKER series like they were in Metro 2033, Metro: Last Light does also appear as a try-hard poor copy of respective games.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is one of the games I missed out on when it was released, in fact, I hadn't even heard about it until I got it in a bundle pack on sale.  Turns out, I loved this game.
It takes place in a pretty nice noir setting.  The graphics are alright, but nothing amazing and certainly not groundbreaking for 2014.  The game suffers from a few issues, one of which being the copy-pasted NPC models and voice-acting, and another being the choices you make have virtually no effect on the outcome of the story.  The game features little to no replay value, due to its linearity as well.
That said, the story of the game was very well done, and the events that take place are really well thought out and the gameplay mechanics are very well done, so the game is still worth it, I think.  The main character, Ronan, isn't exactly a very complex character, but his inner demons and his relationship with his wife Joy, really give him some depth.  There is pretty great character development in this story, and the whole thing has a very distinct movie-like feel to it.    The evidence finding and general detective mechanics are pretty fun and the atmosphere they managed to create with the ghosts and seeing Salems past through the eyes of Ronan makes for some really cool effects and storytelling.
One of the highlights of the game is the phenomenal voice acting and character lip-syncing to the voices, which often goes pretty underrated.  However a downside of the title is that there is a 30 FPS lock on the game, but I honestly wasn't able to notice, very similar to the way L.A. Noire has a 30 FPS lock as well.
I highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys paranormal/ghost stories as well as noir/detective games with dark-ish atmospheres.  It is certainly worth the time.

This game is a really fun top-down ARPG shooter, it has an excellent concept and I highly recommend this game to those that want to join, play the game, and make it the best.
I would like to note that currently this game is very alpha.  There will be bugs and glitches.  The game does need some serious quick polish to get it to at least beta status.  BUT the core concept of the game is great, it has some really huge potential.  So I would only buy this game if you really want to help the game improve, otherwise I would follow and wait for some patches to roll out.
As I said above, the game is a top-down/isometric shooter.  What makes this fun is that you don't click to move, you do so by using WASD and you shoot your guns with left click and right click, which makes combat very interactive.  You have 4 skills that you can have and equip, an example is one that increases your attack speed and you have 1 armor ability that you get when you wear certain armors.
There are two game modes currently, defense mode where you defend a certain object against waves of enemies.  The other one is explorer mode where you get a random objective and have to complete them, an example is to collect X amount, or escorting a person to the exit.  For combat it all boils down to pretty much kiting and shooting aliens until they are dead, they have some variety in their attacks, but not that much.
For character customization there are a lot of things you can do.  Each character has a skill list where you can put points, into a variety of different stats such as increase damage, increase health, increase armor, etc... Best thing is you can re-roll your points any time you want (when you're not in a game), this allows you to experiement with different builds.  You earn these skill points by leveling up your character and to level up you complete mission objectives and gain experience at the end.
Another great thing is you can customize the looks of your robot.  You can find different armor and weapon pieces when you play, they are random drops in the level, and they change your looks.  Another great thing is that these pieces have random stats on them, so not every piece is the same, this will give you further character customization.  Also you can craft gear by finding crystals in the dungeon and have a chance to make a rare.
Lastly with regarding modifications, you can upgrade your armor and weapon pieces, they increase defense and attack respectively.  There can be other modifications too, but that I haven't discoverd yet.
One feature this game has that I'm not too fond of and I'm sure other as well, is an
game, there is currently no option for offline (no internet) play.  Reason is there are online features in this game such as guilds, auction house (will be in game in the future), and various co op modes.  For this price though I can look past this feature, but if it were any higher I wouldn't have bought it as I really don't like online only games.
From a singleplayer standpoint, the game is very playable.  I have been playing exclusively solo and been doing just fine.  Although the game is geared more towards co-op play though, but not needed if you don't want to.
From a hours:gameplay value, you will definitely get your money's worth and more.  Content-wise as in levels there isn't much at the moment (will be more soon), the hours come from farming for crystals, finding items, and crafting awesome gear for your character.
Overall the game has been great and really the sky's the limit, again, such huge potential.  Also, the devs are very active with the community.  Quick response and fixes, I don't know many games that have this kind of dev interaction, more games need to be like this.
I hope this review helps you in deciding if you should purchase the game or not.

King Oddball:
~~~~~~~~~~
My dear fellow gamers, this is the story of King Oddball!
Once upon a time . . . wait, what am I doing? Let’s get straight to the point - Oddball does not like humans at the best of times. He pretty much wants to destroy them and that’s exactly what he is going to do. So, which one of you is ready to become the terrifying King Oddball?
King Oddball is a 2D/Casual/ Puzzle game in which you play a pivoting head in the middle of the sky and your goal is to eliminate all human military forces by throwing rocks using your tongue. The game starts with the king at the bottom of a map. This map has nine large squares and within each of them you have another sixteen squares where nasty human units are located and will need to be destroyed. As you progress during the game some of the squares have other icons on them, like a grenade. They are basically challenges and instead of throwing rocks, you’ll throw grenades or different items.
The gameplay is really fun. You have units (soldiers, helicopters and tanks) stationed on each level to be eliminated with the pivoting King Oddball, which sits in the middle of the sky. In some levels, you might have four throws but it is usually three. If you manage to destroy over three units with one throw, you’ll earn an extra go and this may help you the clear the level.
Nice 2D graphics and the game is very easy to play.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice 2D graphics
-	Plenty of levels and challenges
-	Ease to play
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	It is repetitive
King Oddball is a fun and original casual/puzzle game. Great way to pass the time.
7/10

Imagine taking the Sims. Now, make every character in the Sims religious and despising every one else that's not their religion. Then make them ten times more evil. You control a king or doge and guide his actions and rulership. Be a tyrant, be a ruler of a docile disposition. Just keep a hold of your vassals, win the elections, and make sure to kill that kid that has a claim on your title.

I'm still working my way through the introduction of the game (haven't gotten past the first city), but so far I'm loving it! I'm playing on the Classic difficulty, and there are two difficulties higher than this one.  My characters are now level 7, but this is still an early review, as I have yet to complete act 1.
Pros:
1.) Combat is incredibly tactical. There have been a couple of fights where I got my butt handed to me because I didn't think to exploit the terrain or the destructibles placed in the battlefield.  Height matters a lot more in this game, especially if you have a huntsman.
2.) Oddly, the soundscape is amazing.  Walking through town you can hear the bustling of people walking around. It sounds great when you're in a dungeon, along the beach, and everywhere.
3.) Voiceovers, world building, and characters has been spot on so far.  I have found some characters to be really funny, and others to be incredibly intriguing, such as Losche.
4.) The game doesn't prevent you from doing things out of order.  Once you escape from Fort Joy, it really opens up and allows you to wander around the map in any direction.
Cons:
1.) Don't get me wrong, the UI is pretty well done in this game.  However, there are some UI'isms that I would like improved.  Such as being able to send all of my "wares" to one character (who has the highest bartering skill).
2.) Saved game bloat bug.  Right now there is an issue with saved games getting extremely bloated to the point where it can take a long time for my computer to upload the saved games to the cloud.
Closing Thoughts:
This is definitely a CRPG that has had a lot of love and time put into it.  It will ask a lot of you (time wise) to get going, but so far, it has been a really enjoyable ride!  I definitely recommend it so far, and I will update as I get further into the game.

Few games lately have made me feel such wonder, had played many as videogames are my main passtime. But what makes this game so special? So unique? Well, it is a card game, and there are plenty of card games. It is an action game, and there are plenty of action games. And yet this game can suspend my disbelief like no other.
This game just want to make you fell like you are... playing a game, and in this simplicity lies its brilliance. It does not try to suspend your disbelief to great heights and in doing that it brings an incredible immersion. All I need to feel is that I am playing a game with that strtange fellow in front of me. A fellow that, like no other character, I wish to pull of the screen just to have a chat over some beverages. Or maybe... a game of cards.
It is impressive how a game that does not create anything new, but just mixes what we have already seen in a way we have never seen can fell so fresh, so different.
As for the game itself, it plays as a roguelite. The randomness, the decisions based on your circinstances, the reset after a failure. Failure that does not bring the game back to the beggining, as the bosses you already defeated will remain defeated, but the entire board of the one you are chasing gets reset. Failure that can still reveal some minor rewards as you unlock tokens. Or even just comments from the dealer.
And I press forward. Not for a quest to save the world, but for the wonder of discovery after each new card. Or even some old ones. Or just to spend some more time with this intriguing character that feels almost real.

A true gem. It's quirky, cute, and all around fun. The concept is simple: stock your item store to earn money and pay off a loan. However, it quickly becomes much more in depth. You can buy items when the prices drop and sell them for a profit later, or hire an adventurer and head off to the dungeons in search of treasure! If you've ever been a fan of games like Rune Factory, Harvest Moon, Summon Nights or other hand held games like those, you'll probably love this game. There's something about it that becomes truly addictive, trying to stock the store, get cool new items all while trying to earn (and keep) enough to pay off those weekly loan payments! Even more, it has some of the most interesting and entertaining characters, who you really begin to learn more about and see dynamics between them all, in and out of your shop. The game itself has personality, as off the wall phrases like "Capitalism, ho!" make their presence known in the game.
However, there are some short comings: at my point in the game, it appears as the story is rather short, but I anticipate a lot of "end game" styled content (I'll update my review once I know for sure). As well, the combat isn't the most exciting thing, but it is still fun getting to use and level different characters. There isn't a whole lot of exploration feeling in the dungeons, either. They're randomly generated each time on entry as you search for an exit to the floor (however, so far they're pretty small in scale). If you aren't a fan of: JRPGs, cutesish anime characters/story/tone, addictive slightly repetitive mechanics/objectives, reaching unknown goals, grinding loot, selling items, or capitalism, then I wouldn't recommend this game to you.
If you are, even with some of the shortcomings, I can definitely say with confidence you'll enjoy it if you give it a chance, it's definitely worth the buy. If it goes on sale, grab it!

EXILED TO EARLY ACCESS
Funcom has exiled it’s first sandbox survival game into the wasteland known Early-Access. Now vulnerable to the uninformed hatred of curious by-standers who decided to spend 30 bucks and the possibility of banishing it’s chances to reach freedom as a complete title. Nonetheless, Funcom is a well-established company with a few major MMO’s under it’s belt including The Secret World and Age of Conan.
While still falling in lines with most survival games it’s apparent that Funcom is attempting to take the next steps of providing the unscripted enjoyment from Minecraft with the grindy competition seen in most MMO’s. A game that in retrospect should be able to satisfy a handful of gamers; however while the potential is there, my feeble attempts at survival are on par with it’s current state.
CONNECTIVITY CONS
First off, let’s get the connectivity issues out of the way. Unfinished network code and server crashing are all too common with online early access titles but that doesn’t make it acceptable. Getting kicked out of a server at the worst possible time is frustrating, multiple failed attempts at joining a server is head banging and “rubberbanding” (all the cool kids are saying it) is eye gouging but we have played early access games with similar issues and we know they won’t last forever. As the game smooths out over the coming weeks those issues will be reserved for those special few who will have to complain while everyone else is having fun.
As far as negatives regarding gameplay the two issues that have me worried is the damage/xp scaling and combat mechanics. Most rpg peeps tend to focus on attributes that fit with their play style, yet the damage stats like Strength and Accuracy when both tested with 12 points in each seem to produce little to no increase in damage. This could be an issue on my playthrough but with a medicore stats system, I fear that the hardcore pvpers and pve players will find a new world to through points at a computer monitor.
PRIMITIVE BRUTALITY
The combat has promising variety in weapons and alternative attack abilities but the core mechanics of movements just aren’t there to support just yet. Slashing and gashing through hordes of enemies is more enjoyable then most surival games and with the Conan universe to play with we are sure to be in for some brutally satisfying moments.
AN OASIS IN THE DESERT
And for me that is what is going to keep this game rolling. The world of Conan is rich with lore, dynamic environments, and battle. From the moment you set foot in the desert you will see mysterious structures that will pull you in to discover, and from that point on your adventure begins. The initial zone for Early Access consists of a sprawling desert, a lush oasis, and an abandoned wasteland all presenting different challenges towards your survival. I am really looking forward to exploring more of the world and uncovering its secrets.
It is yet to be said that discovering the world with a friend is highly recommended. One of the major improvements made by Funcom is that natural cooperation that tends to happen while crossing the wasteland. From the easy to use base building mechanics and the clan system working together with people in Conan Exiles surprisingly feels really good.
With a massive following on Twitch and Steam, Funcom is off to a great start. In a recent article in VG 24/7 they stated that in “no more than a year” players will be able to tame mounts, develop siege weapons, travel to new biomes and even study in dark magic. If devs find a steady pace of releasing content (as seen with successful survival games before) most everything is possible. Minus back end issues Age of Conan manages to bring an enjoyable experience that looks to only improve on it’s early access build.

I really wanted to like this game, as the plot seemed interesting, but honestly the gameplay was just too awful for it to be enjoyable at all. I appreciated the story as far as I've gotten thus far, and I can overlook some of the cheesiness of the characters and their actions, however, every fight feels like a struggle not against enemy units, but against chance. A big point in all of the battles is that the protagonists are fighting against the odds, and are frequently outnumbered and outgunned, but the fact that any move you take can have a high chance of failure makes combat a significant frustration. Your snipers will miss nearly point blank headshots, your lancers will miss tanks all day, and if you try to get close enough to have a good chance of hitting, well then you just ran in to a horde of enemies. And if you try to clear said horde of enemies so that you can approach your enemies in order to have a decent chance of hitting them, then either their tanks will destroy you, or they'll just call for more reinforcements. Now by all means, combat isn't impossible. You can beat most missions in one attempt, even if you're not that great, but the gameplay in and of itself is absolutely frustrating, and unless you grind experience doing skirmishes, you may find yourself irritated when your plan backfires because all of your units missed.
If you can overlook gameplay for story, then I do recommend this game, at least based on how far I've gotten at the time I wrote this review. If you don't find that sort of gameplay discouraging, then I would suggest considering this game, as it certainly has its merits, but personally I cannot stand the frustration of losing by chance, or getting a lower rank purely based on randomness.
As an aside, how the hell does getting hit by a bullet that "lowers your attack" make your gun or rocket launcher somehow go from killing a tank in 4 shots to killing a tank in 37 shots?

As other reviews of this game have mentioned, Unreal is phenomenal! Of the first person shooters I've played, this one is way better than most. The amazingly rich environments suck you deep into the plight of the peaceful Nali and the cruel world of their oppressors. When you awaken in your cell, you are alone, the bodies of your shipmates bloodied and lifeless. Many are torn in two. Sirens and garbled voice recordings break the uneasy silence, as you crawl through the battered remains of the ship, only to find that you are the sole survivor, lost on a planet full of hostile beings intent on your demise. That is only the beginning, though. Your travels to escape the planet will lead you through many varied locations that are very easy to differentiate from one another, each one more visually stunning than the last. That is definately one of Unreal's strong points.
The brilliant designers do not allow for the levels to become tediously repetitive. Each environment has it's own personality. Another strong point, and perhaps most important, is the enemy. Long gone are the days of Doom when enemies would simply stand their ground, and trade fire with you. These enemies are much more cunning than that. They will use cover, snipe at you from high perches, duck fire, dodge and even call for back-up if neccessary. Some of your enemies will even try to draw you into traps and ambushes.
This game is exceptionally challenging and rewarding, making most shooters pale in comparison. I was most impressed with the dramatic lighting, ambient sound and music, utilized to it's full potential, making this lengthy epic bristle with life and tension. This is an ideal purchase for anyone who does'nt already have this classic in their library. You can take or leave the included expansion pack, as it simply doesn't offer much more variety to the original experience, but don't over-look this title due to it's now ridiculously low price. For unparalleled on-line battle, check out Unreal tournament.

This is a fun F2P game for a while, as long as you aren't too picky.  Not worth putting as much time in as I have, but definitely worth at least playing.  In general, there are some really cool features, but they're too poorly executed to really take the game seriously.
The economy has a cool premise: make gold however you want to, and do whatever you want with it.  You can  buy a plot of land and farm crops; or you can be a merchant and deliver trade goods by land or overseas; or you can be a pirate who sinks merchant ships and steals their goods; or you can craft and regrade items and sell them at a huge profit.  And so on.  There are a lot of cool things you can do in the game, and the naval side of it is pretty unique.
There are quite a few downsides, though.  Things that make it obvious the developers never really bothered to think anything through, and endgame suffers immensely.
- Seriously pay to win.  Almost everything can be purchased with gold, and you can buy gold with real money via Apex tokens.  Fortunately, you can choose to earn the same items legitimately in-game, so real money purchases are not technically required.
- PvP is a horrible CC-fest.  CC is a huge annoying problem in most MMOs, but i've never seen it as bad as it is in ArcheAge.  Most classes aren't viable because only certain ones have CC or CC-breakers, and that's all that matters.  Also, more than half of the game world is open pvp, and there's no way you can opt-out.  Carebears beware.
- Suuuuuuuuuuper grindy.  Almost every single quest is "kill X monsters", and the last few levels have exactly 1 good way to get XP: kill literally thousands of monsters in your choice of exactly one endgame dungeon.  Professions in most games tend to have a level cap of a few hundred levels, in AA it's 180,000.
- The road to powerful items is paved with gambling, dumb luck, and horrible gold sinks.  You "regrade" them by spending an ungodly amount of gold, which may make it more powerful, or do nothing, or actually get weaker.  Or, if you're really unlucky, your very valuable item gets completely destroyed.
- Zero balancing polish.  The numbers for mana cost, crop grow time, drop rates, you name it, it's a joke.  Dungeons are the very worst in this regard: the monsters are way too powerful, but they're so glitchy that instead of Tank/Healer/DPS, the roles are Glitcher/DPS.
So, I listed a lot of criticism, but like I said, don't set your standards too high and it can be fun for a little while.  If your goal is endgame, skip ArcheAge, because it has little to offer in that regard.  But if you tend to just level up a few alts then quit an MMO, this game does have some unique features that are worth at least trying since it is free to play.

I'm playing devils advocate a bit here but bear with me...
I remember being in awe of this game as a kid, especially when I went into my local CEX and they had a dozen PC's running the demo on a loop. The graphics were at the time genuinely amazing. However if I remember back a bit harder I also remember never finishing it, and playing it again now I'm not the least bit surprised.
The level design is poor. If you're of the opinion that the mid - late 90's was the golden age of level design and has subsequently gone downhill then comparing to something contemporary like quake the level design is doubly poor. Storytelling breaks the golden rule of "show don't tell" by being accoumplished through innumerable, slightly-awkward-to-access message dialogues. Enemies are wooden and moronic (again compare to quake, or even doom,) and with the notable exception 1 or 2 well loved weapons (read: flak cannon) these is absolutely nothing here beyond a cookie-cutter shooter. Albeit one that happened to look very pretty at the time.
The whole thing could written off as a glorified tech demo, and unsurprisingly that's what the name "unreal" has come to mean to most gamers, it's an engine, not a game.
Add into the mix the usual retro-gaming bug bears such as no auto save or widescreen support, awkward default key-binds and proprietary surround sound and you have an experience that IMHO it isn't worth going back to. Let fond memories be fond memories.

I will make this one very simple for you: Do you love collecting♥♥♥♥♥♥ I mean, really REALLY love collecting♥♥♥♥♥♥ Is all you ask of a game that you push a button, hear a pleasing jingle, and see the "X out of Y" counter increment? Because if you do, you will love this game. And if you don't... well, let's talk.
Murdered is the tale of the tragically-named Ronan O'Connor, loose cannon of the Salem PD with nothing to lose. The game opens with him getting ventilated by the world's least-subtle-slash-least-catchable murderer, the Bell Killer, and you spend the rest of the running time trying to figure out why. Well, that's a lie. You spend most of the running time wandering around Salem, ghosting through walls and people in search of the 242 collectable knick-knacks scattered throughout the city. While some require your ghostly powers to reach or reveal, most are just sitting out, waiting for you to mash X on. Each one gives you a tiny snippet of backstory on the characters or Salem if you bother to open the menu, and a few let you hear a cute creepypasta story if you collect the whole set.
If you're wondering why I haven't talked about the core gameplay yet, that's because it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. No lie, the investigations in Murdered are probably the worst of their kind. At every major story beat, you have a crime scene you need to investigate for clues to answer a specific question. Around the scene you'll find plenty more doodads sitting out for you to mash X on, each giving you a clue. After finding all the clues, you have to pick the clues that are the most relevant to answering the question at hand. This is where it all falls apart, because the expectations of the developers in picking answers ranges from so obvious you'll miss it to absolutely non-nonsensical. You're either going to breeze through every investigation or stumble over every answer depending on how well your brain is wired like the developers. Not that it matters either way, because there is literally no penalty for ♥♥♥♥ing up an answer, you just try again.
So that's how Murdered plays, terrible detective sequences broken up by fits of collection-sperging. If that was all, we could flip it the bird and move on with our lives. The weird part is, everything else about the game is fantastic. The graphics are gorgeous and detailed, bringing the town of Salem and its residents (living or dead) alive. Sound direction is on point with satisfying effects and a moody, fitting soundtrack. The characters are charming and memorable despite what seems like every effort to make them obnoxious. Bad-boy Ronan is vulnerable and compassionate, manic goth-girl Joy is plucky and nuanced, and the entire supporting cast is interesting in their own ways. Your ghost powers also keep things fresh, allowing you to possess people to intrude on their idle thoughts, or poltergeist their appliances to freak them out. There's even some stealth combat against some pretty horrifying demons that's simple, engaging, and a welcome break from the running and collecting.
I'm not going to pretend Murdered is a great game, or great for everyone. But even after identifying its flaws, I had a blast with it. Full disclosure, I watched my buddy stream the entire game months ago, and still had enough fun with it to play through the whole thing myself. A lot of your enjoyment is certainly going to hinge on the collect-a-thon aspect, but if you get into the story and learn to love Salem and its characters, there's a perfectly good game to be had here.

A dark and epic post-apocalyptic shooter. A great sequel.
If you haven't played Metro: 2033 yet, stop and go buy that game and play it first, since this is the second chapter of the same story and the storyline is dark and epic. Metro: Last Light improves on the first game in almost every way. Same dark, oppressive post-apocalyptic atmosphere, one of the best in the genre. Same mutant, bandit, commie, and Neo-nazi enemies, which have competetive AI. Same reliance on exploration and resource conservation. However, this game has a larger variety of weaponry and extensive upgrades.
Also there is an extensive section in which you run a diesel-punk rail buggy through the dark tunnels, which made me realize I want an open-world game set in the Metro universe in which the play moves through the subway on a customizeable rail buggy.
In this game, Artyom is now a ranger, guarding the mysterious bunker they captured in the last game. However, he discovers a surviving "dark one" from the previous game, which he must either save or hunt, a decision he struggles with. Furthermore, the war between the Commies and Neo-nazis begins to threaten the rest of the subway settlements. This leads to a number of narrative twists and turns and ends with the most epic last-stand final battle of any game.
This game features the same, complex morality system as the first that makes an enormous difference to the end of the game and lends itself well to multiple replays.
All in all, a must have for post-apocalyptic and survival horror fans, like the first game.

I tried to enjoy this game. I gave it a chance. But I can't recommend this.
Disgaea 1 is an extremely grindy SRPG. Anytime you create a new character, he or she is level 1. You need to either grind levels you've already beaten or grind item world in order to make them stronger, or else they won't be fit for upcoming missions. Added to this, item world itself is both a requirement to continue the game at a certain point and also an unfair grindy mess in its own right. There comes a point in the game's story where you aren't allowed to continue unless you have a level 10 weapon. In order to level up weapons, you need to go through 10 floors of item world, which is a world inside any and all items in the game that has 10 floors of randomly generated maps of enemies to fight. You have to clear floors of these in order to level up your weapon. If things get too difficult, you can just move from one map to the next via a floor tile that's placed in a random spot on the map. The problem is is that each floor you go through has progressively harder enemies; even high leveled well equipped units can fall once you get to a certain point. The enemies increase in difficulty very quickly, and if your party starts wearing down, the only way to truly escape the dungeon is to use an item called "Mr. Gency's Exit", which frustratingly enough, can only be obtained after clearing 10 floors in item world. Add this to the annoying tedium that are geo crystals, random crystals found on maps that change the stats of units on certain tiles, and the whole thing becomes exceedingly annoying.
Outside of this, the plot itself is silly and ridiculous, and as a result its difficult to find the characters in this game relatable. The game is full of slapstick humor and dark humor involving characters making fun of each other or torturing prinnies and so on. None of the characters act as you would expect a real person to. It detaches them from reality in a way. I realize most of the characters in this game are demons, so its not expected of them to act like normal humans, but it just makes it harder to think much of them. That said, I do think there's some appeal to the humor and a likable character or two. Etna in particular is what pushed me to continue playing this game really; she's a sexy self-serving demon that, while strong, lacks the attitude of her friend (and the main character), Laharl. But a character cannot save a game, and I just could not enjoy this game. It doesn't help that the graphics are a bit dated and the music is boring and repetitive.
If you're looking for a fun SRPG from NIS, I would suggest you look towards Phantom Brave PC rather than this. It has a better PC port anyways. Or perhaps wait for later Disgaea games to get ported, as I hear the series improved with later entries. This game was my first plunge into Disgaea, and it was overall unpleasant in my opinion.

This is truly one of my favorite games of all time, if not the very favorite. I've probably played through it 4 or 5 times on console and just had to do it again on PC. This game is absolutely incredible. You're seriously cheating yourself out of a great game if you pass this one by.
The graphics are amazing, even for the continous progress of graphics in newer games. The soundtrack is unbeatable. Jack Wall did a terrific job on this game and everything you hear fits the atmosphere and intesity of whatever given situation you're in nearly perfectly. The story is inspiring and as deep as you care to make it. I don't want to reveal content, it's best to experience on your own and take it is as you go along. Aside from base story, every character has their own personalities, dialouges, and loyalty missions. You really grow connected to your crew and want to get to know them, and ultimately survive with them. I don't really think you find this degree of character connection anywhere else. Bioware really nailed it. If you haven't played the first game, I recommend it, but it isn't at all necessary. Story is filled in early on and you shouldn't feel confused or lost at all. On top of all this, Mass Effect 2 is completely replayable with different courses of action and character builds. My 22 hours were only a single completion run, and there is room for much more entertainment than that from this game.
If nothing else, give this game a try. It's a masterpeice that shouldn't be ignored.

Did you know there’s a game where you can come back from death, blow up prisons, take on three factions of mercenaries, deal with wars between species, survive a Suicide Mission and get in a relationship with the hot alien you want? Nominated as the best game of the generation, winning 150 awards of Game of the Year of 2010 and building so much hype that its sequel couldn’t be more than disappointing, Mass Effect 2 is a game you have to play.
Even if you didn’t play the first one, you won’t be left in the dark, people will tell you what’s the deal and the codex has all the extra details. If you played the first one, then you’ll enjoy the fact that your choices carry over and have some weight on what’s happening.
The combat involves 3rd person camera, using your class specific abilities and guns and giving commands to your squadmates and it has an interface made for PC. There are 6 classes and each of them are varied enough for every playthrough to feel like a fresh experience. Some are more power based, other weapon focused, but all of them do damage and are awesome and you’ll definitely find your type, whether you like to make shockwaves in the enemy lines, hack the robots, pull them in a singularity, cloak yourself and shoot them in the back or simply slow down time to shoot them while they wonder what’s happening with them. There are difficulties that vary from casual from insanity, so whether you play games for their story or want to dominate the dominators, you’ll find what you want.
Many will say the story is great. I say it’s a good one, but that its characters make it to be one of the best. 80% of it you recruit team members and gain their loyalty(only if you want to). They all prove themselves to be interesting and you’ll have enough dialogue options to find out what makes them tick. On your ship, there is going to be the hyperactive mad(ish) scientist, the hot secretary, the crazy all powerful ♥♥♥♥♥, the assassin with regrets, the best friend who took a rocket in his face and is 99% of the time in the middle of some calibrations, a lizard hulk who calles himself “Grunt”, the gun expert that does 663 abs each day,  the cute engineer whose face you’ll never see and some more. You’ll have the options to get involved in their lives. Some of them will argue and you’ll be the one to settle the conflict.
Depending on your gender, some of them are available and open to ideas.
The last mission a.k.a. The Suicide Mission is what makes everything in the game pay off. It’s the place where the catharsis is unleashed. The place where your love for this game will be cemented.  Whatever you’ve done, there will be consequences and by that time, you’ll care.  If you’ll fail hard, you’ll cry hard. But if you’ve upgraded the ship and made the smart choices throughout the game and in the last minutes, you’ll be overjoyed and feel like you’ve won 1 million dollars.
All in all, Mass Effect  2 is a great experience, when you’ll play it you’ll live your second life, one where you’re saving the galaxy you enjoy being into.

While there are definitely a handful of things that could improve the game, the experience as a whole is a very cool, unique, and fun game play concept that hasn't really been done before, and for that I very much look forward to future installments.
The execution is very clean, from the music, voice acting, card design, environment, etc. Some of the issues are with the mechanics though, like the inability to rotate the camera in battle, how the "counter" system works, and other foundation level things like that.
My one main complaint was the lack of a feeling of progression as you go through the levels. Every single level, you start with basically the same default gear. Sure it upgrades as you progress, but the point being, there isn't any of the enjoyment/excitement/satisfaction of finding new loot, at least in the traditional sense. You may get a card for a new awesome weapon, but there is a good chance you won't get to use it any time soon, or technically speaking, you could make it through the rest of the game without getting a particular equipment card that you've unlocked. Because of that, I don't really view this as much of an RPG, instead it's more of fantasy game wrapped around an action framework.
All and all, I loved the fresh approach, and many aspects of the game, enough that I would in fact recommend it. In hindsight, I wish I had got it on sale for $10-15, but have enjoyed the experience of it all.
