When I was given the option to create a character, I decided to make a personified version of me. Surprisingly enough, I actually managed to create a perfect representation of myself with accurate statistics. Needless to say he was a scrawny, unintelligent man of little worth and terrible aim. However as I played the game with my character, I roughly began to build him up. Slowly but surely he began to grow in both strength and endurance. Then one day, when he was decently strong and had defeated a great deal of demons, he took it upon himself to take in a vassal of his own. She was a succubus, and like him she started from the bottom and worked her way under his wing.
As I named, outfitted, and grinded these characters I felt a connection between them all. Having braved against deceased historical monarchs, fairy tale characters, spiritual entities, and even spanish milk drinks to name a few. Then you remember you can just bring them back from the dead with a quick check up at the convienient hospital that is inside your home. But regardless this game is a great way to show just how successful your fake self can be with a weapon that shouldn't even fit his preferences. It will make you laugh, and it will make you cry; and then there are moments where you think one unit is too obsessed with thowing his chili at you. Oh and there's also something about a sadist redhead, a bumbling blonde otaku, and an arrogant prince who wants to become an overlord but has a crap tolerance to boobs. I would recommend this game if only so I could butt stab a dragon with a penguin wielding a crab claw one more time.
P.S. Grind your charcters to level 10 before you fight the first boss. Trust me when I say you do not want to see what happens when you lose.

To do anything in this game you need a thing called labor points, any action you do such as cooking, farming, planting, building, breaking etc, you need to spend these points. Unreal is a very difficult (provided you play on the later difficulties) and classic FPS from the late 90s. The AI in Unreal and Unreal Tournament 1999 is very advanced, as they become better at dodging rockets and predicting your own movements, which means they'll aim their rockets and other projectiles not directly at you (at least not 100% of the time), but where you're headed, with surprising accuracy. The AI is actually better than most people I've seen play FPSs, and not because their accuracy and HP stats were raised 200% like most games. You, as the player, are also able to use agile dodging moves like the enemies you face. Because of this, and the fact the levels are very large with plenty of secret areas to explore, and a ton of inventory items and weapons to find, Unreal is very fun to play. The graphics are great, and the music is, too. It has most of the same composers as Deus Ex and Unreal Tournament 1999 (obviously).
If you're one of the people who likes a bit of story in their games, Unreal offers a lot of that in the form of a universal translator the player can use to read alien texts and carvings, while also reading the diaries of humans also stranded on the planet you're on.
Music:
Overall, the game is excellent, and for the $10 price tag, you'd be silly not to pick it up.

Unreal Gold is
first-person shooter and sadly overlooked by other lesser FPS games of 1998 as well as other genre defining classics. This game stands heads and shoulders above all other shooters with a believeable and intriguing world, easily some of the best design in gaming history, incredible sound design with a killer soundtrack and some seriously fantastic visuals that more than hold up 20 years later.
:
++Not only did this look visually stunning for the year in contrast to everything else, as well as introducing an engine that would go to run some of the best games ever released (i.e. Deus Ex, UT99, Rune) the game looks fantastic today with some really impressive lighting and colourful landscapes.
++Alexander Brandon and Michiel van den Bos' work on the soundtrack is honestly half of the game. The music provides such an incredibly otherworldy atmosphere and provides some of the best music ever heard in a video game. No exaggeration.
++The sound design is rivaled only by Thief the Dark Project when it was released. Mixed with OpenAL, it adds to some really believable environments with realistic high quality sounds that suit the games atmosphere.
++Unreal's multiplayer may have been made redundant by Unreal Tournament but the game features some great experimental maps and includes bots, which were very uncommon for a PC shooter back in the day as well as lots of options and game modes.
++There's a reason the weapon array of this game has gone largely unchanged through every iteration of the series, including the latest released in progress since 2014. The weapon array is probably the best I've ever had the joy of using. Every single weapon is useful and each one suits a given task but not only that, the sound design offers some meaty feeling weapons on the more realistic side but also makes the more sci-fi weapons feel great and bassy. These weapons were entirely original as well. The majority of these weapons are stuff you really just won't find anywhere else.
++The level design is this games biggest strength. The utterly gigantic expanses of land and breath-taking views and vista's add to the feeling that you really are on a foreign planet. Everything is so interesting
++This game has a pretty unique way of handling story providing most of it through your handy translator. This provides back-story as well as information on how to continue your journey in a believable way. The game is also one of the few I've played that is entirely seamless. It feels like a journey from start to finish and everything connects naturally.
++Enemy design is interesting and thoroughly varied. This game also boasts to having some of the best AI ever, and to this day, that's still true.
:
+The games engine holds up well on modern PC's as long as you use DirectX9. Getting the fan-made 227i patch also helps as well allowing high resolutions and a FOV slider, as well as a bug list too numerous to mention, and more.
+The game is long, really, really long. This isn't a bad thing because the pacing is so fantastic and the gameplay is so refined you'll never feel bored. This is actually a big strength. It also means lots of replayability.
+Multiplayer options are great and online multiplayer is still supported through the 227i patch. The server browser is really well done.
+The game gets better and better as it goes, which is saying something with such a breathtaking intro.
+Movement is fluid and easy and the games unique dodging ability is helpful and adds another layer of depth.
+The game is challenging without ever feeling unfair or atificial. Enemies aren't bullet sponges on the hardest difficulty. (Note: The 227i patch offers a few more harder difficulties harder than the default games hardest. These difficulties have a big problem of bullet sponging enemy types. The original games hardest (Very Hard) does not.)
+Return to Napali is decent
:
+-The level design may be the games biggest strength, but sometimes with so many levers being pulled I'm not always entirely sure how I even progressed in the first place. You will get stuck sometimes in these large environments, but honestly it's not so much of a big deal for it to really be an issue.

I was fortunate enough to get this game gifted to by a friend, and I was very excited to try it out after seeing all the powerful positive reception. I was very satisfied with my experience, and this has easily become one of my top (local) multiplayer games.
If you like comedic racing with item pickups (in the vein of games like Mario Kart and Crash Team Racing), then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are good - the detail in the environment is nice, and the artsyle is colorful and matches the tempo of the game. The different character models are well-done, and some of them have interesting jump animations (ex: the shark character dives forward and the cat character rides a broom). The music and sounds are very good, however, I usually play my own music to add to the intensity of the gameplay.
Controls are simple and easy to familiarize yourself with. I strongly recommend playing with a controller - especially if you are doing local multiplayer. The tutorial is quick and very helpful in showing you all the game mechanics. The learning curve is mostly minimal, however, mastering the game and understanding each map takes some time. Maintaining momentum is critical to success, and practice will really help you understand the most efficient way to traverse through each map (ex: knowing when to jump vs. double-jump to get across a section). Whenever I play with my friends, we like to start from the first map and play through all the available ones (they are ranked in ascending order of difficulty).
Gameplay really shines if you can play (local or online) with a few friends - this is my top local multiplayer game at the moment of writing this review. As you race, the screen gradually shrinks toward the middle, and touching the red edges (usually happens if you are trailing behind) will cause you to explode and be knocked out. Interestingly, there have been rare moments where being in the lead too much has caused me to die (but I think it's because I touched the "ceiling" before the lagging players could be knocked out. 4 players can play at a time, and the round ends whenever only one player remains - the first to 3 points wins the map. Whenever a round ends, all players will respawn in the immediate area (this can cause hilarious situations if the starting point is somewhere very inconvenient - like a multiple wall-jumping area). My friends and I have gotten the screen to shrink into an extremely tiny square in the middle (we don't know if there is an upper limit for how small the screen can get) before someone won.
Throughout the map, there are hazards like spikes/lasers (they will stun you for a few crucial seconds), boxes (usually a set of them in a row), and drops (insta-death). Boxes respawn, and a common technique is to let someone take the lead initially if you are unfamiliar with the map - especially since momentum can cause you to hit multiple boxes if you aren't fast enough in recovering. Usually, there are switches throughout the map that allow the person in the lead to manipulate the field a bit. For example, triggering a switch (you just need to run over it) may cause a route to be blocked off, opening a new one for the people behind you that is longer/more difficult. Sometimes, however, it is a better idea to avoid the switch, as they may also open routes that act as shortcuts for people lagging behind.
There are also items you can pick up, and this is my favorite part of the game - I am an item ♥♥♥♥♥, and will purposely go for items just to see what I randomly get. Pickups may be things like homing rockets, a set of boxes you can drop, a pulling hook (switched places between you and the person in the lead), or a freezing beam. I do not know if this is a bug, but something I've encountered is a delay when you use the ice beam right before a round ends - instead of having the item wasted, it seems to activate right after the next round starts, freezing anyone in front of you.
There are white areas on the ceilings that allow you to use your grappling hook to swing around. Some advanced techniques include swinging to propel yourself up a wall-jumping area and swinging to redirect your forward momentum (in the right direction). Boost areas also litter the map, and using a boost will make your character move considerably faster. Your boost gauge carries over even after death, so one technique I use it to save my boost for an ideal situation (ex: don't waste it if I am extremely far behind).
All of the DLC's are for purely cosmetic - there are no differences between characters except for the movement animations. From what I've experienced, the online multiplayer community is both active and friendly.
Overall, the game is fantastic for anyone who enjoys comedic, fun racing. It is currently a steam daily deal, and this price is honestly a steal - even if you were to treat it as a finished product with no future developer support.
Strongly recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

Truly majestic FPS whose epic single player campaign remain in many ways unique to this day.
Unreal is a fantastic, atmospheric journey through beautifully realised alien world, one filled with a sense of mystery and wonder.  It is also a genuine visual and aural feast, and a game that presents level and specific sort of challenge that simply isn't seen anymore.
As is fitting for game's adventurous feel, its levels tend to be huge and exploration-heavy, and often require reading of various clues and careful scrutiny of one's environment in order to proceed. They are always expertly crafted and pleasing to the eye, be they ancient temples and moody ruins with their exquisite architecture, dark spaceship interiors or, especially, Na Pali's unforgettable outdoor locales. Many of Unreal's environments look genuinely beautiful to this day, which is no small feat.
Another expertly crafted element is the soundtrack, which simply cannot be praised enough. Whether the tracks are subtle and evocative, perfectly fitting for game's slower and exploratory sections, or fast and pumping ones that enhance many of game's intense gunfights, they are always excellent and memorable.
Now, game's gunfight are perhaps its most unusual part, one that will make it or break it for most players. Unreal opted for something quite different from the norm: while it has its share of simpler enemies that are focused on simply attacking the player while moving in his general direction (say, some of Na Pali's native fauna), major part of the game is exact opposite from mowing thru hordes of uninteligent meat. Unreal's most dangerous enemies are sparsely placed through its spacious maps, they are agile, hard hitting, constantly in motion and surprisingly intelligent (they will dodge your projectiles, run to cover, fake death etc). Surviving your encounters with these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s requires fast reflexes, awareness of your immediate surroundings and understanding the nuances of game's varied and creative (and highly satisfying, if one allows it to be) weapon arsenal.
This is a must play, and for a particular kind of player that can fully appreciate it, Unreal remains truly one of a kind game: one that was unique back in the day, and one that is even more special today.

Amazing setting: The Mass Effect universe is rich and interesting. I love its lore, settings, and characters. This is the main reason to play the game.
Decent story: The main story is amateur and doesn't fit in with the first game, despite the entire trilogy being planned ahead of time. Bioware threw away a great opportunity here for no reason. It's crazy. But the supporting side missions and stories are interesting, as you would expect from a Bioware title. The Mass Effect universe is still great.
Fun combat mechanics: It's a huge improvement over Mass Effect 1's mediocre combat. I'm actually enjoying it this time rather than skipping through it as fast as possible. Unfortunately, as with all Bioware games, stealth mechanics are completely broken, so don't try to make a stealthy character.
Abysmal PC port: The game's interface is a giant, embarassing mess. It's even worse than Mass Effect 1. The mouse scroll wheel doesn't work anywhere. Text boxes are difficult and clunky. I have a full keyboard with over 100 keys, which can compose into thousands of possible chords, but the game requires binding 3 unrelated actions onto a single key. It's limiting me to the same number of bindings as a console gamepad. Ugh. Instead of taking cover, it keeps trying to open safes or talk to teamates during combat. It's frustrating and makes the game into a chore. Also, what idiot decided to make the skip conversation button be the same as the select response button? How did this make it past QA? Did they even do QA? It doesn't look like it.
Awful third-party DRM: You have to log into EA with an Origin account to use the content you bought on Steam. The text boxes for logging in are broken (see above). The text box used for entering CD keys doesn't support the clipboard, so you ave to manually type in all three keys. Worst of all, the auto-login is broken, so it complains about not being able to log in every single time you start the game. What a god damn embarassment. How could this not be fixed after all these years? What's going on at Bioware and EA? Is everyone asleep?

This is a stat-based strategy game based on officer & city development, with a lot of depth & replayability. For now this game is very similar to several of Koei's strategy games... I see similarities with old games like "Bandit Kings of Ancient China" (e.g. hunting for bears, tigers, wolves). This game was the first one in the genre for me and the one that hooked me up... Of course, there are many similarities with the Romance of the Three Kingdoms games apart from the setting. I will give some examples, but there are really too many parallels to sum up:
-Sieges & land battles are much like RTK IV, but with more options. Why do I compare it with RTK IV? Battles proceed after the end of the month, you can have a lieutenant in your army, the sieges really have a similar feel, etc.
-The city view reminds me of RTK VII and VIII with the people walking around to interact with.
I have to agree with another review that duels are in the style of RTK XIII, but they really need improvement as you cannot modify your actions once the duel has started. Furthermore, you don't know anything about the moves of the opponent. This is probably still being worked on (as the officers' "character types" still have to be implemented).
-Prisoner management is like RTK IX or XI where the officer's loyalty decreases over time, so that you can employ some of them if you are lucky.
All in all the game feels to me as a nice blend of the RTK games, but the AI is still stupid at times... However, this is still early access, and again, some features like the officer's character types are still in development, which might explain that leaders at this point still rush to their deaths... I hope this game will get more influences from RTK VIII as well, as it is my all-time favourite!
In short, this game has a lot of potential, I already like it, and I'm sure any RTK fan will have a great time with it once it is finished. For those who don't know the RTK games, watch a video and get ready for a lot of stats and detailed characters that allow for replayability... I have confidence in the developers. This review will be updated as the game develops further, mainly because I think it is worth it and (as a modder) I like a nice comunity.

This game is alright, but there are some flaws that need to be addressed first.
First, the gameplay.  You can only play as a ruler, that's fine, but the problem is that the Ruler only gets to control one city directly, every other city you have to delegate to a governor.  There's just something really funny about taking a city and immediately afterwards someone else controls it.  You CAN move to another city (Moving capital) to control it, but it costs gold and it's not a small sum since I was never able to do it in my playthrough. (Oh and have I mentioned that it doesn't actually tell you how much it is?)
The game has no tutorials atm, and no help files.  I am kinda just running blind, though I did manage to figure things out for the most part, there are some things I can't seem to do (like creating siege weapons) I wonder if it's because it's not implemented yet or something.
The battles are ok, feels like a mix of ROTK 4 and ROTK 11.  You move your unit and you get to perform an action after you moved.  You can attack, you can use up "Morale" to perform tactics and strategies, cavalry units can dismount, you cannot ask for duels though.  You can have a unit become AI controlled (But they won't perform an action for that turn)  It's not bad, but not super exciting either.  The AI looks to be as bad as the ones in ROTK - Cao Cao is the commander and he just willingly walks up and puts himself in danger.  I find it funny that his army barely helped him, considering the fact that upon defeating Cao Cao the battle was immediately over....
The duels are no good.  Of all the things you could've copied, you copied ROTK 13's terrible dueling system of selecting 5 moves before a fight (Well okay it was something Sangoku Taisen did first but still) and unlike ROTK 13 you don't even have any hints as to what the enemy will throw, so it's completely RNG - You somehow managed to top ROTK 13's terrible dueling system.
There's no interactions between officers and very little between officers and you, the ruler even refers you as the ruler rather than himself.  There's not much flavor to this game at it's current state, rather bland and lifeless.
The graphics, the officer portraits at it's current state is no good, there's not much emotion or anything to tell them apart except for the most famous of generals, but even then some of them look really really sad.
My conclusion is that this game is banking too much on past ROTK games.  Though it did tickle the nostalgia a little, the gameplay doesn't feel all that exciting because there wasn't much about it that is truly unique.  Adding to the flaws the game has I just can't recommend this game at it's current state.   I realize that this game is still in Early Access, but for all the hype and nostagia there really isn't anything that draws me in and keep me there - when there are FREE demos that actually grips you.
The current Chinese reviews of this game seems to be rated positively because they are Chinese (but most of them also points out the same flaws I pointed out) but I am going to have to rate this game negative BECAUSE I am Chinese and I would much rather have a good and well polished game representing us.
I will change my review once early access is over if things change for the better.

When I was given the option to create a character, I decided to make a personified version of me. She was a succubus, and like him she started from the bottom and worked her way under his wing.
As I named, outfitted, and grinded these characters I felt a connection between them all. Having braved against deceased historical monarchs, fairy tale characters, spiritual entities, and even spanish milk drinks to name a few. Then you remember you can just bring them back from the dead with a quick check up at the convienient hospital that is inside your home. But regardless this game is a great way to show just how successful your fake self can be with a weapon that shouldn't even fit his preferences. It will make you laugh, and it will make you cry; and then there are moments where you think one unit is too obsessed with thowing his chili at you. Oh and there's also something about a sadist redhead, a bumbling blonde otaku, and an arrogant prince who wants to become an overlord but has a crap tolerance to boobs. I would recommend this game if only so I could butt stab a dragon with a penguin wielding a crab claw one more time.
P.S. Grind your charcters to level 10 before you fight the first boss. Trust me when I say you do not want to see what happens when you lose.

Oh, how I love this game. Seriously, this is the type of game you can just have fun with, relax, and laugh maniacally when you sell an item that has a price increase (that you found in a dungeon or bought at a decreased price, of course). It might seem like this type of game would get boring after a while, but even when I take a break from it to play a more typical RPG or an action game, I keep finding myself coming back to this.
There are different options you can take, as well. You can dungeon crawl (which you will probably eventually do, if only for the ingredients) but you can just as easily not go into a dungeon at all and just "buy low, sell high". Even when you finish paying off your debt (which was actually my least favorite part) you can keep playing, or play over again with the items you have from that game, or play a survivor mode where you keep going through higher and higher payments. Point is, there are plenty of things for everyone to enjoy.
If you're not sure if this is the game for you, go ahead and play the demo. You get to keep your save data if you choose to buy it, plus there's a little bonus ending that isn't in the full game, if you beat said demo.

You know, it really is a shame. This game had a lot going for it. I can't express how disappointed I am.
I went into playing this game with little hope to begin with. Another lame F2P MMO. What can I say? I'm a die hard WoW fan that is rarely ever impressed, much less interested in anything else. Call it personal preference or obsession, whatever suits you. But after playing ArcheAge for a few weeks, I actually started to enjoy myself, little by little. Until I realized a few things about it.
For starters, this is not a F2P MMO. They like to make you think so. But if you want to do anything substantial in this game, you'd better have cash and be prepared to spend big. At the very least, you need a paid account if you want to get involved in trading profitably. That's a real downer for those who just wanted to enjoy the game they had marketed to them as F2P.
Another big hit that eventually lead me away from ArcheAge was the community. I played for several months on NA Calleil. I don't know how things are on all the other servers, but the community in Calleil is horrible. People are downright cruel to one another. As cool as some of the game mechanics are, it's the perfect set up for people to be hateful to their fellow players. If you want to keep any shred of faith in humanity, don't play.
I still maintain a small hint of interest, simply due to the naval side of the game. Let's face it, having your own boat is pretty damned cool. So you might just run across me, out there in the war torn waters, trying to catch a stupid fish that will probably get stolen along with my boat. But, don't count on it.
TL;DR ArcheAge is not F2P, ArcheAge kills faith in humanity.

I was fortunate enough to get this game gifted to by a friend, and I was very excited to try it out after seeing all the powerful positive reception. I was very satisfied with my experience, and this has easily become one of my top (local) multiplayer games.
If you like comedic racing with item pickups (in the vein of games like Mario Kart and Crash Team Racing), then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are good - the detail in the environment is nice, and the artsyle is colorful and matches the tempo of the game. The different character models are well-done, and some of them have interesting jump animations (ex: the shark character dives forward and the cat character rides a broom). The music and sounds are very good, however, I usually play my own music to add to the intensity of the gameplay.
Controls are simple and easy to familiarize yourself with. I strongly recommend playing with a controller - especially if you are doing local multiplayer. The tutorial is quick and very helpful in showing you all the game mechanics. The learning curve is mostly minimal, however, mastering the game and understanding each map takes some time. Maintaining momentum is critical to success, and practice will really help you understand the most efficient way to traverse through each map (ex: knowing when to jump vs. double-jump to get across a section). Whenever I play with my friends, we like to start from the first map and play through all the available ones (they are ranked in ascending order of difficulty).
Gameplay really shines if you can play (local or online) with a few friends - this is my top local multiplayer game at the moment of writing this review. As you race, the screen gradually shrinks toward the middle, and touching the red edges (usually happens if you are trailing behind) will cause you to explode and be knocked out. Interestingly, there have been rare moments where being in the lead too much has caused me to die (but I think it's because I touched the "ceiling" before the lagging players could be knocked out. 4 players can play at a time, and the round ends whenever only one player remains - the first to 3 points wins the map. Whenever a round ends, all players will respawn in the immediate area (this can cause hilarious situations if the starting point is somewhere very inconvenient - like a multiple wall-jumping area). My friends and I have gotten the screen to shrink into an extremely tiny square in the middle (we don't know if there is an upper limit for how small the screen can get) before someone won.
Throughout the map, there are hazards like spikes/lasers (they will stun you for a few crucial seconds), boxes (usually a set of them in a row), and drops (insta-death). Boxes respawn, and a common technique is to let someone take the lead initially if you are unfamiliar with the map - especially since momentum can cause you to hit multiple boxes if you aren't fast enough in recovering. Usually, there are switches throughout the map that allow the person in the lead to manipulate the field a bit. For example, triggering a switch (you just need to run over it) may cause a route to be blocked off, opening a new one for the people behind you that is longer/more difficult. Sometimes, however, it is a better idea to avoid the switch, as they may also open routes that act as shortcuts for people lagging behind.
There are also items you can pick up, and this is my favorite part of the game - I am an item ♥♥♥♥♥, and will purposely go for items just to see what I randomly get. Pickups may be things like homing rockets, a set of boxes you can drop, a pulling hook (switched places between you and the person in the lead), or a freezing beam. I do not know if this is a bug, but something I've encountered is a delay when you use the ice beam right before a round ends - instead of having the item wasted, it seems to activate right after the next round starts, freezing anyone in front of you.
There are white areas on the ceilings that allow you to use your grappling hook to swing around. Some advanced techniques include swinging to propel yourself up a wall-jumping area and swinging to redirect your forward momentum (in the right direction). Boost areas also litter the map, and using a boost will make your character move considerably faster. Your boost gauge carries over even after death, so one technique I use it to save my boost for an ideal situation (ex: don't waste it if I am extremely far behind).
All of the DLC's are for purely cosmetic - there are no differences between characters except for the movement animations. From what I've experienced, the online multiplayer community is both active and friendly.
Overall, the game is fantastic for anyone who enjoys comedic, fun racing. It is currently a steam daily deal, and this price is honestly a steal - even if you were to treat it as a finished product with no future developer support.
Strongly recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

I'm usually not a big fan of ARPG, i only like those that bring something new and/or have an interesting gameplay. That's why i was slightly worried by Recettear childish artstyle and similing basic dungeon exploration. But i tried the demo, and was instantly convinced. Recettear definitely brings something different than other ARPG, and it ended up as my third most played game on Steam.
Recette is a small girl (10-12 years old ?) who is contacted by a fairy that tell her...She is in debt and must reimburse it immediately, because her father has disappeared ! Since the small Recette doesn't have a single penny, the fairy offers her to teach her to handle an item shop for adventurers so she can raise money and pay her debt.
Despite the dramatic beginning, this is actually a very cute/child-friendly game. Recette is extremely cute and has some memorable quotes, but you will also meet a lot of funny characters along the way. The dialogues are well written, and the overall story is very enjoyable.
The gameplay itself is divided in two parts. Though you will have to do a bit of both parts to finish the story, you're more or less free to focus on the aspect you most wanna play because both give you ways to get money to clear your debt.
The first part is a basic dungeon exploration to try to get new items. Top-down, ARPG-style realtime combat. Though it's fairly standard, and enemies variety is a bit lacking, on the whole it's still a fun experience. The point of the dungeon runs is to get the rare items you need to craft high level equipments to be used or sold as you wish. You run through the dungeon by playing the hero of your choice with Recette following automatically behind.
Each hero has a different weapon and skill sets, which mean each hero play differently. This allows you to pick hero that suits your playstyle, or challenge yourself by trying to clear all dungeons with all the different heroes. By the way, for players who enjoy a bit of challenge, clearing the (optional) last dungeon is a very fun undertaking. It's not required to finish the story, but if you want some tougher fights, you will definitely find them in that dungeon.
The second part is the "Item shop". You have a shop, that you fill with items you got in dungeons or at the merchant's guild, and try to get the most money out of them. The value of items may go up or down during certain days, so you will, as usual try to buy low and sell high. Everytime you open your shop, customers will pour in, and if they find an item they like, you will be able to negociate the price.
Though the item shop gameplay is simple, it's a lot more fun than i expected it to be. You have to set up your shop the right way to get the right customers, and try to get combos of successful transactions to level up your shop, giving you more space and opportunities to get even more gold.
On the whole, i really enjoyed both parts of the game. It can sometimes get repetitive, but since you can pretty much switch from one task to another whenever you feel like it, you can usually find something fun to do. I spent more than 80h of this game, and would gladly play some more.
If you're unsure about this game like i was, try the demo. You will immediately know whether you like the game or not. It gives you a basic idea of the gameplay is. The whole game is a lot bigger and richer than what is in the demo, so if you liked the demo, you will like the game.

Like Dwarf Fortress, Crusader Kings 2 is a game with several layers of simulation and data that is best played without micromanaging every detail.  There is the potential for surprising events if you allow a degree of inefficiency.

Disgaea is a wonderful game. The artwork and character design is charming, the story can hook you right from the beginning, and the combat system is fun and interesting.
Disgaea PC, unfortunately, is a bad version of the game. It crashes every twenty minutes, sometimes the voice acting disappears, and it suffers from screen tearing at the larger resolution of a full-screen mode. The buttons for controller keybinding are labeled with numbers instead of letters, and while there's an option for Japanese voice-acting, choosing it means you get no voice acting.
Honestly, I've enjoyed what I could play of the game. Despite frequent crashes and forced restarts, I've cleared the tutorial, created a new minion (a cleric), and enjoyed myself immensely. So I'm torn between returning it because the crashes make it nearly unplayable, and keeping it because what little I can play has been deeply enjoyable.
So I'm not recommending this game, but if the game gets a new patch (the developers are still working at it) that fixes the crashing, that will change in a heartbeat.

Before you dive into positive reviews take a look at amount of time reviewers spent in this game. Most of them have approx. 6 hours and I would leave positive review too if I didn't spent a bit more time in this game.
Only 2.6% of player base completed this game and there is reason behind this. The more you play the more game becomes annoying rather than enjoying. Yes, narrator's voice is beatiful, music is beatufil too, aesthetics is good, but this game some serious gameplay problems.
First of all, the way diffuclty inrecreases is absolutly irratating - new "event" cards become a lot more diffulty in terms of randomness or difficulty of combat. For example, there is event card which will reduce your max HP by 66% if you fail to pass 25% roll. So you can have almost a perfect run and ruin it just by failing this event. And it's a pretty big deal, because it's not like winning an event grants you perma win, you work really hard trying to accumilate as much equipment as possible, but it still wouldn't be enough to win a final fight, becase of this - the combat system is really bad.
When you play for the first time, combat seems fine, of course, it's not outstanding, but it's fine for this type of game, but later, when you unlock more events, combat becomes pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ because there is a huge change that you face a pretty big amount of tough enemies while wielding ♥♥♥♥♥♥ rusty axe. And it's boring. It's boring to fight 6 enemies when each of them requires at least 20 hits to kill. I'm not even taking in consideration fact that you can encounter mini-bosses who will heal allies and has twice as much hp.
There is no variety in weapons - no 2h weapons, no duals, no ranged - only 1h and shield. All bosses have pretty much the same skill set, there is also no variety in that. There is also very annoying things like "unblockable" attacks and amount of enemies who can do that increases with amount you play, it's verry annoing because some of them is faster then your counter attack animation so it can lead to a situation where you receive almost guarnteed damage, combine it with fact that combo counter (thing that will increase your damage for some weapons) seems to be broken because it  sometimes resets when you roll (the only way to dodge unblockable attack) and sometimes it's not, sometimes you can make a few steps with combo still active, sometimes it's resets when you stop attacking for a few moments.
For me this game feels like pretty mediocore early access title, it needs a lot more polishing and variety which is not the case right now.
Buy it only if you want to enjoy narrator's voice and music for 6h hours and then never launch it again.

Have played more than a thousand hours since Alpha as a paid subscriber. In my opinion, one of the best MMOs available 2014/2015, although it's not without its flaws.
Marketed as free to play with an added subscription, it's difficult to say just how long an average gamer would spend on a free account without either paying or doing the necessary money making grind to keep up the subscription paid for with in-game gold. It's entirely possible to do so, however it involves playing on both regions and transferring the wealth generated by the labor system. If you're determined to play for free, or have a little extra to spend on the in-game store without adding real money, it's certainly worth the time. I imagine most are a little lazier and, like myself, pay the sub, and forget about it. In that respect, it's like EVE's plex system. Do you build up half a billion ISK to buy a month, or do you just sub and spend your game time having fun. Unlike EVE however, there's no skillpoint system, so it's entirely possible to dump a bunch of cash and have the best everything. It'd take a LOT of cash, and the know-how, but it does sour personal acomplishments, knowing they can be acheived faster laying down a lot more money.
P2W is one of those dirty phrases to a lot of gamers and I don't think it directly applies here, along with all its negative connotations. Those that wish to come top of any sort of in-game leaderboard will have to spend big. For most players this simply isn't a concern, a wealthy existence can be had with a subscription, doing the regular things the game offers. One of the most attractive features since launch has been land ownership in a persistant world. Houses in varying sizes, farms and a huge variety of ships are what most players aspire to. Naval combat has recently seen a massive overhaul, widely perceived as being excellent by the community.
This is a game that's had a lot of mixed reviews because it suffered a lot of issues initially. Hacking, server stability and a lack of presence from developers and GMs were perhaps the biggest problems. Thankfully all have been long resolved and many fans have come out to defend it in force.

The advertised feature of this is the combat.
It is relentlessly shallow.
You press a WASD in the direction of an enemy, and then left-click until a green icon appears, and then you press Q. If a red icon appears, you press space.
That's it. That is all that there is to combat. WASD to an enemy. Left-click if no-icon. Q if green icon. Space if red icon. You do not need any weapons or powers to defeat every level without getting hit once.
This is almost a good game. But the combat sequences are the worst part of it. They're also the hyped feature, which leaves this being a trashy gimmick. Oh and, by the way? If the crummy combat wasn't bad enough? You also gotta wait for it to load into each one. The worst part of the game takes the best part of your time.
There's a bit of fun with exploration, cash and food. But you will never, ever, ever, run out of food. And the cash bonuses are who-cares weak, because they only affect combat. Which, again, is so easy that you've got to be mentally-deficient to actually take any damage during.
There are occasional trap-gauntlets. Those are sorta fun, just because the controls are so wonky that it's basically random whether you'll get hit or not. I almost came close to getting halfway towards fifty-percent of my health, in a trap room that lagged like butt, one time.
Just pass on it.

Could the game be more than a game? For decades we had been saturated with games without ever satisfying our desires to experience the reality within virtual reality. Many games, unfortunately, have yet to ascend from the generic cookie cutter approaches to appealing the public, with mouth-opening graphics and ear-flinching sounds. With endless Steam sales and seemingly eternal fountain of games in our game lists, we always feel the emptiness in our gaming mind, highly cultivated by some of games we will never forget and always compare to newer generations of gaming.
Velvet Sundown however takes a different approach to how we must play the game; some could hastily make a judgment that this game is not a game but Velvet Sundown is following the new trend of lifeful experience of reality ithin virtual reality. This game is the path of enlightenment of any gamers who felt like the gaming industy has failed them--which most of gamers could agree that gun-blazing battlefield and immersive fantasy world no longer seem appeal compared to their very first games back in old time when there was just a gamer and the game. Velvet Sundown stretches from the basic concept of gaming in alternative path by bringing the reality we often ignore to focus on virtual reality. With such intricate interactions between players, the game endlessly provides the mindless gamers who had been used to quick-time events and pay-to-win freemium games. Of course, I'm not simply comparing other social-based sandbox games such as the Second Life, but Velvet Sundown intelligently centralized players' view points into realistic social simulation yet supplied with superb quality of hyper-reality experience. The perfect balance between how much players can induce their abilities, assuming the gamer fully understands the critical essence of the Velvet Sundown, and how much game prebuilds the foundation of players' abilities, not just provide the playground to play in.
It is deeply unfortunate that not many gamers find this game truly enjoyable and interesting. Such judgment is rather a pinpoint representation of how gaming industry have dumbed gamer communities to controller holding press-to-win gameplay foil-wrapped by foul storylines and pointless service scene only to entice erecting pleasure, not the mind-cultivating pleasure we have enjoyed far before the birth of gaming. Do we truly understand what we want? Do we play the games because it was 75% off? Do we buy consoles to participate in sponsored gaming events and monotonously scream at the screen? In the age of regression of gaming community, Velvet Sundown is the game we must intake to awaken our senses and ultimately relinquish bondage of vile medication of gaming industry from what we call "the gamer's soul."

For the $7.49 that I spent on this game, I would say it's worth it.  The story is the only thing that you are coming to this game for.  The gameplay is largely just going around and collecting items that are either needed to solve murders from a spree killer, or just your standard collectable affair.  If you are looking for some sort of groundbreaking gameplay, avoid this game like the plague.
The story is so-so, but the setting is interesting, and given that you are a ghost that can only interact with certain people/items, it was enough to keep me moving along.  Set in a modern day Salem, Mass. your character is, just as the name states, Murdered, and you then spend the night traveling around this sleepy town, with a storied past, trying to find out why you were killed and who they actually were.  You meet some mediums, you kill some demons, and it all raps up, nice and preety, in under 10 hours.  The only reason I took longer was I felt compelled to get all the achievements in this game, something I haven't tried to do in years.  Like i said, the achievements are mostly just collectables, but I refused to delete the game before I had a 100% for this title.
Also, I want to see more games in this genre.  We don't see to many crime-solving detective games, and I really like the premise.  Now, of course, the games would need more than whay we saw on display here, but I would love to see something like LA: Noire again.

Disclosure: I like spooky stuff, and I got this game heavily on sale.
I enjoyed this game and would recommend it while voicing some STRONG CAUTIONS.  Particularly, cautions that aspects of this game are unpolished on PC, and that some aspects of the game probably could have been better.  However, beyond some faults, the game seemed pretty reasonable.  The price tag of $29 (statement made 8/22/2015) seems a bit steep for a PC game of this caliber, so I would recommend folks take into consideration what they'd pay for this, and possibly keep an eye open for Steam's sales.
Apparently, the developer went defunct one month after the game's release, and I have not yet read anywhere about whether or not they managed to patch any of the game's issues.  Here's some of the things I experienced.
----For example, in the first 20 minutes, I was prompted to click a selection of words and discovered that all controls had locked up, requiring me to CTRL+ALT+DEL and manually close the program.  Whether it was coincidence or not, I arbitrarily took a forum-goer's advice to turn off the V-Sync function, and did not see the problem anywhere else.
----Keyboard controls for navigating the UI seemed unusually poor.  For example, in the Tab menu, keys Q and E often change selections left and right, but W and S do not change selections up and down.  The Up and Down arrow keys could change selections  up and down, but Left and Right did nothing.  The mouse could point at interface selections, but on some UI, clicking would only sporadically function, besides making the selection icon flash.  Most Yes/No UI prompts required clicking, but confirmation prompts would not respond to clicking and demanded pressing either Enter or Esc keys.
----Frequently, depending on where I steered the protagonist, he often stepped on a "ground clutter" object and would go into an infinite falling animation until I steered him again.
I thought the setting of the game seemed interesting: playing as a ghost, wandering Salem, solving some mysteries, seeing some weird stuff.  It showed some flavor, with the protagonist suddenly becoming incorporeal to most of the mortal world, and suddenly hemmed in by fleeting spectres and the haunted rubble of generations past.
In my opinion the gameplay wasn't very deep, but was a change of pace that challenged the expectations I've built up playing other games.  For example, at one point in the story I found the protagonist's path blocked by a fence, with no clear way to cross it.  For a moment, I racked my brain looking for an alternate path around or over the fence.  Eventually I remembered "DERP, I forgot, this character is a ghost" and simply walked through it.
One thing I'd consider both a strength and weakness of the game would be "item collection"  mechanics.  The game's environments are peppered with objects that reveal tiny snippets of flavor text upon inspection.  This does help flesh out the story, characters and locations, and does give some motivation to explore.  As it is implemented, I can picture some downsides, particularly in regards to game design.  I would say the setting is one of the game's most interesting aspects, and that the item collection mechanics took away from it.
----Those items demanded level/map design to heavily focus on incorporating inconsequential nooks and crannies.  In my opinion, that development effort could have been used to make the levels/maps feel more cohesive or detailed.
----Much of the details provided by flavor text probably could have been woven into the story in a more interesting way.
----The game has a few creepier ghost short-stories in it, which unlock after collecting a certain amount of items native to an area, items that inherently do not have flavor text.  If someone does not reach the quota, that means there's an interesting piece of story that soaked up more development and writing but ultimately contributes less to the player's experience.
----The flow of the story contains some "points of no return", meaning that making another attempt at finding an elusive tidbit of story or component of an achievement might mean starting from scratch, or needing to revisit a location long after it has been forgotten.
----Given the UI problems mentioned earlier in this review, I found myself waiting until after I finished the game to look through most of the accumulated flavor text.  Reading text right after it is discovered often meant continuously being exposed to that UI, or interrupting cutscenes to make use of the briefly-available chance to enter and exit UI simply using the TAB key.
In regards to graphics, I would say they seemed well-optimized.  My computer is a bit older (statement made 8/22/2015), and newer 3D games would often demand I turn down some settings (such as shadows) in order to render reasonably.  Barring the limited number of NPC models, this game's graphics looked reasonable and at a reasonable framerate from the moment I turned it on, without me tweaking settings.
Overall, I got the game for cheap, enjoyed it, and have few regrets besides thoughts about lost potential.

Don't get me wrong, I've played all three VC games and watched the anime. So forget my actual playtime. Valkyria Chronicles, or VC, is by far my favorite alternate ww2 like world that i will always love and cherish. Not only do i support the game because of anime, but also my endless love for this story especially. The first VC truelly had a story worth tears from a manly man such as myself, filled with trials, triumphs, racial acceptance and the feeling of loss... Oh the feeling of loss. So here are my PROS & CONS to better brief you my lovely players on the game Valkyria Chronicles!
Pros -
1-Story - Whether you are saving private Ryan or gathering your band o' brothers, this is a definite 'must experience' No high school reunion romance senpai simulator here. The story will grip you by the balls, and make you grow another pair just in case.
2-Art - Art has always been a nitpickky thing for me. And when i first saw the game for VC i thought, 'crayons?' Boy was i wrong as the sketched like art of VC was Beautiful and Immersive to the story and setting of that world.
3-gameplay - Ever played and loved fire emblem? Well this game is like Fire emblem and battlefield had a baby to smack you full o' fun. You control your squad, which you get to pick who you want prior to mission start, and go on a turn based battle where you control your characters movement and attack. Whether your rushing towards defensive sand bags under enemy fire or risking it to get behind the enemy tank and fire a salvo, you control your characters in a turn based fashion in a real time environment. Moving around infront of enemy troops will have them turning you into cheese if you mess around.
Cons -
1-A few bugs here and there. Crashes can be terrible so save often.
Conclusion - I'd still buy it if the price was 60$, and now its 20$ so even better. You'll be bonding with characters as you get to know them more, while fighting a war. I really recommend this to those who love anime, fire emblem, turn based tactical shooters, etc and even those who feel like giving a new game a try. This has story elements, but really good core gameplay mechanics as well so dont write this off as some visual novel. I cant wait for them to release the other 2 for steam, and i hope this review helped you in spotlighting this game in a new shine.

TL;DR A worthy sequel to ME1. The grittier feel extends to all areas, including a shift from 'futuristic blue' menus to 'diarrhea yellow' menus. The simplified mechanics are a mixed blessing.
Mass Effect 2 is very much the 'gritty second installment' of the Mass Effect series. Think The Empire Strikes Back compared to A New Hope - the whole game takes a darker tone, from the locations you visit, the characters you meet, the urgency of the story and the significance of the choices you make. A warning, though - there is much more language and blood/violence.
Due to a surprise attack by an unknown spaceship at the beginning of the game, you are forced to work for the pro-human activists Cerberus. Remember those guys from the first game? They did genetic experiments on aliens and killed a pro-alien human officer who got in their way. Things are a little awkward as you, erstwhile saviour of the galaxy take up arms alongside the space-Nazis.
Having defeated the lone Reaper in the first game, the Council believes that the Reaper threat is over, and refuses to acknowledge there are more out there. However, since they are sending their minions to capture human colonies, Cerberus sends you to investigate. In the course of your adventure, you visit all sorts of places, from the poorer areas of the Citadel to the Krogan homeworld, the corrupt but glamourous Asari world of Illium and even the notorial criminal capital of Omega. You recruit a new team, composed of some of your old comrades, but also a whole host of new characters. Some of the new characters are not as developed as the old ones, but on the whole, the calibre of storytelling is consistent.
The combat system has been completely revamped, and the controls alone can take a couple of levels to get used to, but overall, they're mostly an improvement, as things are generally simplified. The loot/inventory system has also been changed. Instead of picking up millions of useless weapons, you research new types at your ship, which can then be used by anyone. The weapons are all subtly different, even within a certain type - ie, instead of each successive sniper being marginally more powerful, the first is a standard rifle, the second is a higher capacity one which fires 3 shots at once (useful for groups) and the third is a slow firing but amazingly powerful anti-material rifle.
A new feature is research. In a special lab in your ship, you are able to research upgrades for you and your squadmates weapons, armour and abilities. Armour upgrades are different, in that you can switch components like your helmet, shoulder pads, leg armour, etc for ones with different bonuses, rather than the whole suit at once. You can also buy research from shops, unlike the first, where I never used a shop at all!
Research takes minerals/rare metals, and this leads us to one of the worst elements of the game. Mining. You take the ship into orbit, and fire probes at a planet until it's depleted. Over. And over. And over again. I preferred the Mako.
The game has also been divided up into 'hub' type areas, where no enemies ever appear, and 'mission' areas, where everyone you meet is an enemy. I feel this is a bit of a step backwards. Fortunately the tactical combat part of the game is significantly better, so fighting is much more enjoyable.
One of the best bits of the game is the final mission. it, again, follows a general storyline, but depending upon choices you made during the game and during the last mission itself, there are any number of interesting variables. One interesting thing is that you can die and still beat the game...I've not seen that often in video games.

To be honest, I expected something bad coming into this game. But, coming out with about six hours played, this game is actually decent.
PROS
- There's quite a decent length in terms of gameplay.

THE STUFF I'M NEUTRAL ON
- The graphics are ok. It's go a decent style but it's a bit weirdly shaped and the textures are a bit low quality.
- The cutscenes in the game are a bit stupid. I get a giggle once or twice, and it might be that I'm not used to that "hue hue BR" humor, but it's a bit stupid.
MINOR THINGS THAT BOTHER ME
- Whenever you encounter a new character, after their cutscene thing, you have to start the level over. Would've been better if you continued from where you were.
- The controller support is a bit weird. The controller I used was a Logitech F310. To pause/start, you press B, and you can't start a level controller. The D-Pad controls for it also didn't feel to right.
CONS
- The game lags quite a bit, and this has happened to a lot of people, mostly because of how much is on screen.
- There aren't any in-game options, which sucks if you want to listen to something else while playing the game.
- Some of the enemy designs are kind of ugly and bizarre.
Overall, especially for the price, I recommend this game.

-Permadeath mode.

-Potentially even more mods.

TL;DR:
Hand of Fate is two repetitive, hardly innovative, unfortunately vague, sometimes-working games stuck together in a way that's at least pretty. Don't buy it without doing your homework.
FULL REVIEW:
Hand of Fate boasts an aesthetically gripping melding of two unlike games into a single experience that varies from unplayable to underwhelming. On their own, each of the ‘games’ of Hand of Fate fall far from being worthwhile. Together, the card game and the three-dimensional fighting game intermingle in a way that works just enough to keep players invested in a fairly transparent skinner box.
Players are subjected to a deck-building card game that rewards repetitive play with a larger card base and challenges players through proper resource management. Game-to-game rewards are meted out through a shell game that is either too easy or too hard, an aspect that belies the RNG nature of the card game. Overarching rewards are given after successfully completing ‘token’ cards, which have a variety of conditions to complete (some of which are obvious, some obscure, almost all of them lacking explanation). Common issues of RNG exist and are easy to overlook, but there are some more severe instances such as stumbling upon very difficult encounters too early on that force a player have to quit a run of the game or even completely reset their progression overall. Card balance is a huge issue, with several cards being outright stronger than others regardless of situation. Furthermore, the encounter deck that the player must create is a vague collection—there are no indicators of what the encounters do, and some encounters seem variable in their options and outcomes. This makes constructing an encounter deck a chore of either looking up each card online or simply not knowing what each encounter brings in terms of challenge and reward unless the player has drawn that encounter several times. Hand of Fate seems to beckon players to experiment to discover what works and what doesn’t, while punishing players every time that it does not work out both in their current game played and across multiple future games.
The fighting game, unfortunately, has even more severe issues. Combat is without weight, several mechanics of the system go unexplained, difficulty of encounters has to be inferred, some arenas are far too unforgiving, and so on. There is a simple system of click-to-attack, click-to-counter incoming moves that’s been popularly attributed to the Arkham series of games. Here, it barely works, as most encounters find the player vastly outnumbered by enemies that constantly attack. It is often difficult to even land two attacks in a row on an enemy without being interrupted in some way, giving combat a hectic and choppy flow. Camera angles can be a detriment to properly positioning the character, especially as some arenas feature traps and enemies can attack the player from off-screen. There’s a rolling maneuver that the player is intended to use to avoid several of the heavier attacks in the game, but the roll often comes out too late and does not offer much in terms of defense thanks to aforementioned issues along with painfully awkward hitboxes. Enemies take far too many hits, with the exception of when the player has specifically itemized to defeat an enemy type, and then combat becomes laughably easy against said enemies. There simply is no middle-ground, though. To further frustrate things, rewards are tied to number of monster cards drawn rather than individual monster difficulty--sometimes beating four skeletons can be just as fruitful as overcoming ten skeletons and a boss you fought before. Overall, combat is a mess, ranging from repetitive and easy to punishingly difficult thanks to a culmination of issues that are out of the player’s hands.
Throughout the whole of the game, there simply is a lack of clarity—how much damage am I actually doing? How much damage does my gear reduce? What does an ice-cone attack even do? Is holy damage only extra-effective against undead? Who are these various characters? What does this encounter card even do? What is the purpose? Too many aspects are left to be inferred, both in terms of narrative and mechanics (an appendix would help, even). Oft-times, I find myself recursively fighting through boring encounters, hoping that I actually win the shell games this time around, so that I can unlock more shell games and progress to just being done. There isn’t a gripping narrative arc that makes me want to continue to play to the end. The gameplay from moment to moment is droll and forgettable. There’s nothing that stands out.
This all goes without mentioning the several issues the game has just running. It outright crashes on startup, it crashes when loading some encounters, it sees framerate dips on some machines; so on and so forth. Thankfully, the support team for the game has been working on patching out and addressing these issues, mostly via their forums.
This isn’t to say it’s all bad. I’d be kidding myself if I said the style of the game and the goals it sets out for aren’t awesome. There’s a very strong aesthetic that permeates the game just as there’s something refreshing about having these two genres put together in such a way that one doesn’t get too boring before the other takes over. Sure, dialogue gets repetitive and lore is a bit sparse at times and obfuscated at times, but it’s charming and interesting when it isn’t.
All in all, Hand of Fate is promising, but lacks polish. There are plenty of options that can be fixed, plenty that can be clarified, and several aspects that can be advanced. Sadly, it seems that a complete overhaul would need to be done to each of the games that exist within Hand of Fate for them to work on their own. If you’d like to pick up two flawed, repetitive games that can distract from their flaws and repetition by means of alternation, go for it. If you’re a sucker for how a game looks rather than how it plays, buy the game like I did. If you want a worthwhile playing experience that’s rewarding outside of just earning more stuff in the game, though? Look to spend your money elsewhere.

A really good game that shows a  developer with talent can achieve great things with Unity. And also that you don't have to spend $60 on a game for it to be fun and compelling.
Hand of Fate offers a nice mix of card game and roguelike-like and does so brilliantly. The graphics are really nice, in sort of a dark/cartoonish style that I find really easy on the eyes. It runs really well, obviously, given that it doesn't try to go into the spectacular visuals with tons of shaders and post-effects. Instead it offers a solid, stylized presentation where nothing feels out of place. The voice acting is quite good, too, and helps set the mood, with the card dealer commenting on your choices and their consequences. There probably aren't hundreds of hours of recorded audio, but what little there is is quality voice acting and writing.
Gameplay wise, it's mostly a tarrot game of sorts with some third-person Batman-like brawling action to spice things up from time to time. The action scenes are relatively well executed, as in they're functional (if not grandiose) and offer a fun way to see your bonus/equipment cards in action. They also help adding some manner of player agency in a game that's mainly RNG vs. you. TLDR: the actions scenes, while not the best brawling gameplay you can find, are well integrated and end up making the game a better, more varied experience as a whole.
All in all, Hand of Fate feels like a very well crafted little game, that's not yet another 16bit pixel style roguelite, and asks very little $ for what it has to deliver.

In most RPGs, card games are a staple mini-game where you can use the cards collected in random encounters. Sometimes, these games are fun like tetra master in FFIX, but most of the time they are just a distraction and play-time-extenders.
With this game, however, it's the other way around. Collecting and playing cards is the main part, while the hack-and-slay-style encounters and bosses are fun, but do not compare to the excitement of unlocking new cards and the adventures and mysteries they hold.
It all comes together when a round ends: Regardless of the outcome, each token acquired in the game unlocks new cards that have effects that are yet unknown - you have to uncover their meaning in-game. Then, the dealer invites you to play another game. He let's all your cards hover in a cloud above the table and you just have to click to start another round to get to know your new acquisitions...
Highly recommended, especially for players that cannot resist an innovative rogue-like or card-game with many collectibles.

It's a subtle spell that American Truck Simulator casts, yet one whose alchemy can be surprisingly complex. The roads are filled with more traffic than prior games, and it's dictated by convincing AI; fellow road-users are beholden to the same everyday rule-set as you, stopping at traffic lights and observing a speed limit that fluctuates as you cross state-lines and keeping an eye out for patrolling police cars that enforce the laws of the road. Negotiating busy highways offers its own challenge, the mirror-signal-manoeuvre that precedes a lane-change becoming a part of your vocabulary as trusty as Street Fighter's quarter-circle fireballs.
Ticking beneath all this like a diesel thrum are the systems that piece each journey together; the acquisition of XP that sees you level up and opens up more trucks and more parts, the growing income that allows you to buy more garages, to hire more drivers and to take on more jobs. There's a satisfying sense of progression that sits neatly alongside your excursions, which themselves can escalate as you move on: longer journeys see you battling fatigue and looking for rest-stops lest you fall asleep at the wheel.
If that all sounds familiar, well it is. Beyond the shift in location and a handful of very minor tweaks - those patrolling police cars, the ability to haul longer cargo and a slightly fancier GPS unit - this is quite simply Euro Truck Simulator 2 with a new lick of chrome and transposed to America, with the front-end and all the slow crawl of empire building it enables near-identical. In many ways, it's a more limited game, too.
More is on its way, and given how Euro Truck Simulator 2 quickly expanded thanks to SCS Software and the modding community's efforts, it's safe to assume American Truck Simulator will slowly fill out. Right now, though, it's an openly modest game - with a £14.99 price tag to reflect that - rather than a full-blown sequel. What you're currently buying into is the pull of those American roads, and the slightly mysterious promise of where they'll head next; Arizona is next on the menu, and after that there's the hope that SCS Software could head all the way to the midwest and beyond.

This game is more like "L.A. Noire" than anything else, and I really enjoyed it. Then again, I enjoy games with decent stories more than a lot of people seem to do, and the story for "Murdered: Soul Suspect" had enough twists and kept my intrigue enough to see it the whole way through without too many regrets. There was potential for it to be a "horror" game (which I hate), but fortunately any scares were more in the environment and feeling of the game than through outright scares.  Some people seem to put more value on time spent, so for those kind of people this game at $30 (as I write this) might not be of value. But if you enjoyed "L.A. Noire", this game is at least worth getting on a Steam sale.
There are enough other reviews (should this one ever be read by anyone) that I'm going to spare yet another description of the story and get to what I think are the pluses and minuses of the game.
Pluses:
+ Non-linear with respect to being able to visit previous locations
+ Intriguing story placed in Salem, MA and linked to the historic witch trials
+ Dark, brooding atmosphere without necessarily crossing the line into "horror"
+ Good acting and voice work
+ No jump scares (for the most part)
+ Roughly 8-10 hour play time doesn't require too much commitment
+ No achievement mandating that all of the mysteries are solved PEFECTLY (unlike "L.A. Noire")
+ Side quests while not required provided some well-written ghost stories
+ Some interesting plot twists
Minuses:
- Demons felt like they were added for pointless stealth/action gameplay
- Too many collectibles for a game of this size
- No way to track how many collectibles still remain in a particular location
- End sequence stops somewhat abruptly
If you can put up with the pointless demons, which don't show up very often anyway, and you can deal with not having to find *every* collectible, you'll probably find this game worthwhile, although the $30 price tag (as of writing) might be a bit too much for some people, based on the returns. This is definitely worth picking up on a Steam sale, though.

There was also an unusual amount of walking back and forth for no real reason. It's not an Open World, you can only go from one scene to another, so why make the player walk through the same parts of town X times?
The Clue-finding and Conclusion-Drawing mechanics were very railroaded and often left me wondering just how slow the protagonist must be, to take so long to figure it out. It's tough to write a "no" review, but my internal rating of 5/10 just doesn't justify recommending this game.

TL;DR A worthy sequel to ME1. The grittier feel extends to all areas, including a shift from 'futuristic blue' menus to 'diarrhea yellow' menus. The simplified mechanics are a mixed blessing.
Mass Effect 2 is very much the 'gritty second installment' of the Mass Effect series. Think The Empire Strikes Back compared to A New Hope - the whole game takes a darker tone, from the locations you visit, the characters you meet, the urgency of the story and the significance of the choices you make. A warning, though - there is much more language and blood/violence.
Due to a surprise attack by an unknown spaceship at the beginning of the game, you are forced to work for the pro-human activists Cerberus. Remember those guys from the first game? They did genetic experiments on aliens and killed a pro-alien human officer who got in their way. Things are a little awkward as you, erstwhile saviour of the galaxy take up arms alongside the space-Nazis.
Having defeated the lone Reaper in the first game, the Council believes that the Reaper threat is over, and refuses to acknowledge there are more out there. However, since they are sending their minions to capture human colonies, Cerberus sends you to investigate. In the course of your adventure, you visit all sorts of places, from the poorer areas of the Citadel to the Krogan homeworld, the corrupt but glamourous Asari world of Illium and even the notorial criminal capital of Omega. You recruit a new team, composed of some of your old comrades, but also a whole host of new characters. Some of the new characters are not as developed as the old ones, but on the whole, the calibre of storytelling is consistent.
The combat system has been completely revamped, and the controls alone can take a couple of levels to get used to, but overall, they're mostly an improvement, as things are generally simplified. The loot/inventory system has also been changed. Instead of picking up millions of useless weapons, you research new types at your ship, which can then be used by anyone. The weapons are all subtly different, even within a certain type - ie, instead of each successive sniper being marginally more powerful, the first is a standard rifle, the second is a higher capacity one which fires 3 shots at once (useful for groups) and the third is a slow firing but amazingly powerful anti-material rifle.
A new feature is research. In a special lab in your ship, you are able to research upgrades for you and your squadmates weapons, armour and abilities. Armour upgrades are different, in that you can switch components like your helmet, shoulder pads, leg armour, etc for ones with different bonuses, rather than the whole suit at once. You can also buy research from shops, unlike the first, where I never used a shop at all!
Research takes minerals/rare metals, and this leads us to one of the worst elements of the game. Mining. You take the ship into orbit, and fire probes at a planet until it's depleted. Over. And over. And over again. I preferred the Mako.
The game has also been divided up into 'hub' type areas, where no enemies ever appear, and 'mission' areas, where everyone you meet is an enemy. I feel this is a bit of a step backwards. Fortunately the tactical combat part of the game is significantly better, so fighting is much more enjoyable.
One of the best bits of the game is the final mission. it, again, follows a general storyline, but depending upon choices you made during the game and during the last mission itself, there are any number of interesting variables. One interesting thing is that you can die and still beat the game...I've not seen that often in video games.

Pros:
1) This game is a very good game as an introduction to the strategy genre. I find it amazing how they set up the system for selecting soldiers to bring with you into combat, and I love how they make it so that each character has their own strengths and weaknesses. For example, a teammate may be powerful, but they have allergies, so they can't hide in tall grasses. Or, a character might feel comfortable on roads, which increases their attack when their on sidewalks and streets, but they don't like being around nature, so their attack would go down if they were near grass.
2) The combat mechanics are nice. Basically, each turn, you can move your troops a certain amount of times. What units you move, and where you go with that movement is up to you, but you have a limited amount of stamina, so you can't move around forever. You can shoot enemies during your movement, and depending on what part of their body you aim at, the amount of hits you get on them and the damage you dish out are different.
3) The art style is fantastic. Everything looks (and I'm pretty sure it is) handrawn, and it makes everything ingame look beautiful. I also find that this artstyle helps to broaden the amount of details on characters and models. All of the troops that you can add to your squad have unique designs, and that includes small details on their faces. It's amazing how great this style is, yet SEGA hasn't used it more often.
Cons:
1) The gameplay of the game doesn't start until 5-10 minutes ingame. Although I do enjoy the cutscenes (mostly due to the artstyle), I find that they can get to be quite long. I wouldn't mind this if there were less cutscenes, but it seems like the cutscene-to-gameplay ratio (at least up to chapter 2) is 3:1. Again, if you do not like story in games, and just want to get this for the gameplay, I do not recommend this for you.
2) Nothing. Really, I try to keep my reviews even so I have an equal amount of positive and negative points, but I can't see any other glaring issues about this game. It's that good.
So, would you like this game? If you are interested in the strategy genre, and don't mind lots of story, I'd say that the answer is a definitive, "Yes!" However, if you aren't really interested in any of the story and just want to play it for the strategy parts, be forewarned that a large majority of this game will shove story down your throat. However, there are side-missions that you can play that have no impact or relation to the plot whatsoever, if that strikes your fancy.
Overall, I'd say that this game is worth getting, just to try it out.
