Other players will claim that this is not "Pay to Win". It definitely is.
Good F2P games don't force microtransactions on you, but rather make you want to spend money. However, Warframe makes you pay for inventory slots with platinum, the ingame currency acquired with real money. As experience is tied to equipment, leveling up equipment is the only way to proceed, making inventory slots absolutely vital.
One alternative to directly buying more inventory is selling old equipment - including warframes - to make room. However, as the whole point of Warframe is collecting equipment, this pretty much directly serves to undermine that goal. Another is selling anything rare and good you find and grind for. The way I felt about this was pretty much like a peasant serving more worthy players with money. It's not fun, and it definitely doesn't make you feel being on equal ground with others, which is exactly the feeling to make you consider buying platinum with real money.
And as incentives go, platinum is not cheap, nor are the items bought with it. I'm now at a point, where to skip the inventory grind, I'm considering the cheapest way to do so: buying a "Hydroid Prime Access Pack". This includes 3990 platinum, which would be enough, as around 3000 is needed to unlock the whole inventory. The current discounted price is 125,99€, with real price reported as whopping 342€ !
With that kind of money involved, it's time to seriously think if the game is worth it. By the start of the game, you have enough inventory to last about as much as I have, and it's been fun. The maps have been fresh, so has the lore, and I've felt like a space ninja goddess among mortals. Especially fun is to play with friends or your bf / gf. The game emphasises this by design, as many of the missions are far easier when done with a group, and nigh impossible to solo without end-game equipment. By the psychology of "microtransactions", I've been "sucked in", and kept playing by group pressure.
However, now the wall has been hit. The maps repeat constantly, I've met all the four types of enemies in the game, and the only thing that's left is serving players with money by grinding. To get enough platinum, this would easily take hundreds, if not thousands of hours. The alternative is paying to have fun, and make no mistake it's what Warframe wants you to do.
// Edit 15.12.2017: When I said the wall had been hit, it was about 120 hours in. Now, I'm 414 hours in. Suffice to say, I bought one of the Prime Accesses for 72 euros. Right afterwards I got a -75% platinum price discount, and got the most expensive package for 50 euros. Afterwards, the game has been fun, and I'm still playing.
Even though there are significant problems with the game, some of which I'd say is misleading marketing, exorbitant prices for ingame currency you're basically forced to pay for, manipulative discount algorithm, high prices for many of the cosmetics to customize your character - including more than basic colours, and vaulting of the "prime" gear to milk more money into the game, I'm still changing my recommendation to Yes.
I cannot in good conscience not recommend a game, when I'm still having fun after over 400 hours of gametime. End of Edit 15.12.2017. //

Remember how the most fun to be had in Skyrim was trying to get the maximum most valuable loot from every dungeon, cackling with glee as you then sell it off to about five different shops, amassing huge amounts of cash, so much that money becomes meaningless to you, the glorious and unstoppable trillionaire Dragonborn?
Yeah, me too.
If, however, methodical and obsessive treasure selling and cash hoarding is actually
among your favorite RPG memories, your mileage with this game may very.
Forget robotic NPCs, dragon hunting, falling off mountains. This game cuts out all the extraneous crud, leaving you with only the very best: treasure hoarding, buying and selling. All the cackling with glee, none of the frustration. Nothing to stand between you and the rapidly increasing numbers, the juggling and sorting of a thousand little items, the excitment and joys of haggling and customer service. It's the game you never knew you needed but always secretly wanted in your heart of hearts. You might stare at the screen in disbelief, thinking no game about just buying and selling items has any right to be so dang fun. But I never stop loving the ring of that cash register, or high-fiving the nearest living human or cat or whatever's nearby when I amass 500,000+ moneys in one day because sweets were on sale, and just sitting and smiling as I enter dungeons with my wizard friend, exploding enemies in bursts of beautiful fire so we can gather
items. It's addictive and fun and basically the best thing ever.
Of course, because this game truly knows the joys of the methodical and obssessive item seller, it knows you'll get burnt out if all you do is sit behind a counter and watch numbers roll, no matter how satsifying and enjoyable that may be for a while. So it's the delightful writing and characters, the brief but highly enjoyable story events, that truly make this one of the best games I've ever played. You've got a lovely cast of truly charming characters keeping things interesting, and stories of just the right size, scale, and length, that add to the game without detracting from it. You've got simple but fairly fun dungeon diving that manages to not be too tedious. And the game is drowning in humor, and some inexplicable, surprising things that can be delightful to stumble across (fish? FISH?!). The game is laughing. You're laughing. We're all laughing. It's even got a corny theme song. How can you
love it, I ask you!? Only some fiend who hates items would hate this game. Begone, fiend! Stick to your mountains and troll slaying, why don't you! Ride away on your dragon! We'll be rolling around on our mountains of cash, partying with our customers, buying awesome new decor and counters and books about DOOOOMSDAAAAY. You won't be missed.
One thing I was worried about was replay value, and just how long this thing could actually go on and still be fun. My fears, however, were soothed! There is a surprisingly large amount of story content, enough to last you for months (mabye even years, I don't know, I'm not there yet) if you don't binge-play the game too intensely. There's more than one game mode and lots of items to collect and dungeon diving to do and you can just keep trying to get better and better at haggling and learning all the characters and basically there's all sorts of goals you can strive for and stuff that'll keep you busy and invested. So that's good! I was dreading that it would all come to a halt or wind up boring but nope, it just stays awesome forever. Dream come true.
I also like that it's casual enough that I don't have to invest huge amounts of brainpower to it, but deep enough that I can dive in and have fun and it's still a satisfying experience. If you're a busy person you can devote a few hours to it (or even thirty minutes, fifteen minutes, you can save whenver you want) and it probably won't suck your life away. YAY
TL;DR: play this game if you like items and/or selling stuff and/or numbers/moneys

This port is basically just like what you get on a PSP emulator, except you can't tweak the bugs out. Disappointing.

1. UI
Menus for crafting, character sheets and so on are obstructive. Terrain such as bridges, overhanging cliffs etc block nearly all vision of your party which makes it difficult to navigate through streets and valleys. Sometimes you can end up walking all the way up a hill and through a an environment hazard because you clicked on a random cliff edge above wherever your characters were.
2. Combat and quests
Unless you thoroughly go through each area and soak up as many quests as possible you will be underleveled and undergeared. This, in combination with the ruthless AI, makes combat an absolute chore that requires savescumming.
Element interactions and environmental hazards are poorly explained and require experimentation to fully understand. So much can be going on during a fight that it is difficult to gauge what is happening at any given time. Aiming up and down cliffs also seems to have random restrictions placed on what you can and cannot hit (spells can't go over banisters, but arrows act like ICBM's when shot up from the first floor).
3. Camera
The camera is at the perfect level of awkwardness where it requires you to zoom allll the way out to see where you're going but demands you zoom back in to pixel hunt for objects. It's easy to lose track of dead bodies in tall grass or behind bushes unless you outline them with fire spells first. Sometimes a combination of bad geometry and camera angles will make it impossible for you to see enemy NPC's at all. It is very frustrating to walk into a random ambush after failing to manually save the game.
4. Map design
Maps act like extended corridors for the sake of staging ambushes. Walk into an area -> autosave function triggers -> hostile NPC gives you 1-3 responses which almost always end up in a fight.
5. Skills, attributes
The effectiveness of any given build during a blind run comes down to dumb luck.
Example: I ran into some lava slugs in a cavern. Unless I had taken the trait that allowed me to diplomatically talk to slugs/dogs/cats I would have had to fight them with a butter knife and wool clothes. I had literally no idea that would be useful prior to that situation.
There are a bunch of other, smaller issues I could also talk about but these are the core problems I have had with the game over six hours.
Edit
Whoever designed the second act boat fight is a goddamned sadist. Enemies moving before their turn, necro fire spam, inability to place my healers next to the NPC... what the ♥♥♥♥. It's like I'm playing Final Fantasy Tactics Advance for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.

Love the game.  Early access is early access, so yeah there is lag, performance issues and the need for impromptu patching and server reboots.  But the core of what they are working with is fantastic.  They've taken some of the best elements from other games (don't be salty Ark, take it as a compliment) and improved on them by enhancing story and experience.  Right off the bat there is great story that immerses you.  The look and feel is great.  Solid crafting options to start with.  They diety/religion system creates instant replayability because you can see what the options are with a different diety/shrine.  From day zero they have dedicated server options so you can tweak the game and play with friends if you want to avoid public server drama and challenges.
If you're interested in the survival genre, I'd definitely recommend this.  The Conan theme is solid.  The playability is fantastic for being early access.  For $30 you'll get a lot of game time either single or multi-player before you feel like you've explored most of the map or learned all the crafting.
If you have no tollerance for early access games then I'm not sure why you'd bother.  Don't expect the game to be a AA vetted title when it's clearly early access (but still solid even as early access).  Wait 3-6 months for the likely vast improvements to stability and play then.  If you enjoy the quick updates and developer interaction of early access though, I'd say it's well worth it!

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is an RPG game wherein you take on the role of the Monopolist~ Err, Capitalistic entreprenuer known as Recette as she takes on the mantle of an item shop owner in order to pay back a substantial debt owed due to her father.
While sweet at first and lighthearted, this game quickly turns into an all-out battle for survival as your debt increment grows and grows, leaving the player to have to make smart business decisions in a VERY fluctuating market.
Those weapons you just bought that you'd been making all the money with? Guess what? They just turned worthless. Those treasures that you were sure you'd make a killing off of? It's a shame that they're worthless too.
Oh it's okay though; Candy is always in boom. And the supply of Little Girls is seemingly endless. You could always make money off of them, I guess.
Digressing, the game does have a fitting storyline if people are willing to work for it, the dungeon-roaming offers a sort of different pace for the game after it's central hub-bub of a market place gets tiring. The character's that come to your shop all have unique personalities (Minus the Townsfolk, who are stock characters) and preferences that you, as the shopkeeper, must abide to, which adds a twist to your usual marketing strategy.
For instance, modeling your store to appeal to different types of people may have you gain business with some, but lose others. If you want to truly master the ways of the monopol~ Err, Capitalistic society that you've been given, then you must attain a delicate balance in building trusts with NPC's, and lining your pockets with coin.
All in all, this game provides a solid challenge while giving a rather entertaining set of characters to keep you along the baseline journey. Further delving in the story reveals darker bits of the world that they live in that you might have otherwise not known unless you pieced it together from the text, which gives you a bit of lore to put in your cap too.
I would most definitely recommend this game, as it's been an experience like no other.

It's a subtle spell that American Truck Simulator casts, yet one whose alchemy can be surprisingly complex. The roads are filled with more traffic than prior games, and it's dictated by convincing AI; fellow road-users are beholden to the same everyday rule-set as you, stopping at traffic lights and observing a speed limit that fluctuates as you cross state-lines and keeping an eye out for patrolling police cars that enforce the laws of the road. Negotiating busy highways offers its own challenge, the mirror-signal-manoeuvre that precedes a lane-change becoming a part of your vocabulary as trusty as Street Fighter's quarter-circle fireballs.
Ticking beneath all this like a diesel thrum are the systems that piece each journey together; the acquisition of XP that sees you level up and opens up more trucks and more parts, the growing income that allows you to buy more garages, to hire more drivers and to take on more jobs. There's a satisfying sense of progression that sits neatly alongside your excursions, which themselves can escalate as you move on: longer journeys see you battling fatigue and looking for rest-stops lest you fall asleep at the wheel.
If that all sounds familiar, well it is. Beyond the shift in location and a handful of very minor tweaks - those patrolling police cars, the ability to haul longer cargo and a slightly fancier GPS unit - this is quite simply Euro Truck Simulator 2 with a new lick of chrome and transposed to America, with the front-end and all the slow crawl of empire building it enables near-identical. In many ways, it's a more limited game, too.
More is on its way, and given how Euro Truck Simulator 2 quickly expanded thanks to SCS Software and the modding community's efforts, it's safe to assume American Truck Simulator will slowly fill out. Right now, though, it's an openly modest game - with a £14.99 price tag to reflect that - rather than a full-blown sequel. What you're currently buying into is the pull of those American roads, and the slightly mysterious promise of where they'll head next; Arizona is next on the menu, and after that there's the hope that SCS Software could head all the way to the midwest and beyond.

Unreal is an absolute classic and is up there with Quake 2 and Half Life. You play the game as Prisoner 849, who was on a transport ship going to a Moon base prison. However something happens and you awaken with the ship crash landed on a mysterious planet. You blast your way through the game with a whole range of different creative weapons, whilst exploring the planet and trying to figure out what happened to the transport ship by reading varies journals, as well as figuring out a way off the planet.
For its time the graphics were unreal, with amazing looking environments, lighting and textures, which are more well detailed, especially up close. The levels vary from large open fields with a few houses or caves to explore to smaller areas such as a spaceship or a temple. Each area looks unique and it’s easy to distinguish one area from another. The weapons are fun and unique to use such as the bio rifle which shoots green toxic globs and the flak cannon which shoots out shrapnel, which can ricochet off any surface. The enemies vary from slow moving aliens which fire rocket launchers, to fast moving enemies which shoot projectiles at you, almost every enemy in the game shoots a projectile, only a few will use hit scan weapons. The enemy AI is extremely good and are very challenging. You will find yourself dodging left to right to avoid enemy projectiles whilst shooting them down, which can get very intense. From beginning to end this game is a wild ride and is worth a playthrough.
The expansion Return to Na Pali is good but doesn’t live up to the main game. You get a few new weapons, which whilst fun to use aren’t that interesting and some new enemies. The story is told a lot more straight forward, through cut scenes and audio blogs from prisoner 849 if you play as a female. The levels for the most part well designed however the level layout makes no sense, in one level you’re in a base which is located in the middle of a cliff and the next level you’re in the mountains. Worth playing through if you have finished the main game.

Welcome to Salem!
Notoriously known for the witch trails that took place in the late 1600's.
You play as Ronin, a cop who got a lead on a case that has caused quite a stir around Salem as of late.
If you watch the video you'll come to the understanding that, well your dead and trying to find your killer.
There are aspects to this game that make it enjoyable and others not so much.
The game gives you an interesting take on what it is like to be ghost/geist/specter. I also like the mystery and gathering of clues. You can gather a few clues and try to come to a conclusion, or you can gather more clues and solve it with more probable outcome.
Besides the the main mission there are also side missions or should I say ghosts who want closure. You can either aid them and find out what happened to them or you can leave them and just focus on your case.
There is a few hiding go seek instances where you interact with hostile ghosts "Demons". You have to avoid them until they look in a different location. You can then perform an "Exorcism" and purge the demon from the world. If you mess up and they spot you will have to play hiding go seek. Which then has you jumping from a ghostly hole into another,  and into another to avoid the demon.
I wouldn't really classify this as horror but more of a mystery. Townsfolk that you interact with have two lines that they usually say. When you load into a new area. That theme continues.
I'll give this a thumbs up due to the story being enjoyable. Voice acting was tolerable, mechanics were alright.
I would recommend picking this up on a steam sale if it interests you. Wait for it to fall under 10$. Without strolling around helping other ghosts or looking for collectibles. This game is easily 3.5 - 4 hours long.

An amazingly cinematic game with great graphics, plot, and gameplay.
For those who have played STALKER, it's thematically very similar in almost every way, but instead of being open-world, you're railroaded on set pieces. The game has many moments of down time and exposition.
It's also noticeably easier than Metro 2033. Higher difficulty settings may be recommended primarily because many of the human opponents are exceptionally easy to take down. Mutants, less so.
Also it's wroth noting that the game can get very disgusting at times, but that's more of a personal preference. For people that play a decent amount of horror games, it's not scary in the slightest, but there are some tense moments. For people creeped out by horror anything or find spiders to be unbearable, this may be an issue.
Fans of stealth may find the system a bit easy with throwing knives being the go-to. However, achievements discourage killing, so there is replayability there.
Overall, it's thematic and wholly recommendable for people that like this type of game.

The core values are kept for Last Light well (narrative, visualization of the post-apocalyptic world/society). You will visit a lovely crafted world with so much attention to detail, immersion at its best.
Metro Last Light Redux is superior in the level design and in the tactical combat. The chapters are still directed as a FPS gauntlet, but there are far more options for tactical combat, even during encounters with mutants.
Both parts share same game play mechanics after the Redux, thus there are no surprises. Be prepared to experiment with the video settings though.
My final verdict on Metro Last Light Redux:
The story gets nicely twisted in Last Light, but it would be too shallow without the narrative from 2033. I fully recommend playing both parts in the designed order. After the Redux they melt nicely together visually too.

TLDR: Glitchy and Poorly Designed Game Mechanics - More Frustrating Trial and Error than Fulfilling "Strategy". Do not recommend.
1. Too Many Cutscenes
I'll start with the smallest gripe I have. Most of the game is wasted on cut scenes. Although you can skip them, actual gameplay is few and far between. Unless you are a fan, I definitely would not recommend this.
2. Glitchy Gameplay and Lack of Actual Strategy
Gameplay is glitchy and mechanics are frustratingly wonky. There is little actual strategy as the game functions like an overly complicated version of rock-paper-scissors styled combat; this is unacceptable for a strategy game (explained below).
2a. Inconsistent and Unreliable Mechanics Which Foil Any Attempts at Strategy
Gameplay mechanics are inconsistent and unreliable, resulting in a reliance on luck and trial and error rather than actual strategy.
Units that are specialised for certain situations rarely work in practice. Snipers miss that crucial shot 60% of the time, Anti-Tank units miss huge tanks 50% of the time - these penalties do not apply to enemy units who hit almost 100% of the time.
The entire "counter-attack and return fire mechanic" is inconsistent and undependable and cannot actually be relied upon in positioning your squad or setting up kill zones because you can never be sure if your units will counter or get slaughtered. Or whether that sturdy looking rock counts as cover or if it would magically allow bullets to fly through. Each turn therefore becomes an exercise in trial and error.
Summary: Imagine playing rock-paper-scissors without being able to control your hand, now add a blindfold. I would recommend saving your money and just playing rock-paper-scissors with a friend instead.
3. Poor Controls and Navigation
Controls are poor with the tank (your most powerful unit). It is difficult to move around the map because the keyboard and mouse controls were lazily designed. You'll find your tank moving in circles, using up your precious movement resources, and then inexplicably getting stuck in the groundmesh while exposing its weak spot to the enemy. You then get one shotted, costing you the 2 hour battle you were until that point winning since you lose immediately if your tank is destroyed.
The lack of visual cues for what actually counts as cover has been dealt with above - but this is further complicated by the fact that path readability and mapping are not always clear. This is extremely frustrating since you get a limited number of steps per turn. You'll find yourself wasting entire turns attempting to run towards that "crack in a rock" or that log which looks like it could be stepped over only to find an invisible wall mesh, wasting a turn trying to snipe through a crumbling building only to see your shot get blocked by more hidden wall mesh, or even running across flat ground for a backstab only to suddenly encounter an inexplicable "No Entry" message and being forced to waste two more turns going back the way you came.
4. Lazy Mission Design and Explanation
Each mission is poorly explained and becomes an exercise in trial and error rather than actual strategy. Poor mapping of the navmesh and visual readability (explained above) aside, you'll find yourself doing 2 hour "trial runs" to figure out the intricacies of vaguely hinted at mechanics which are crucial to a successful mission. Once you realise what is required you will have to restart and replay the entire mission over again. This is a pain since most missions take more than an hour.
Example 1:
You will encounter vague plot points without any actual notification that they will affect the mission in any way. For example you might get a conversation in your second turn of a 20-turn mission where you are told that "the enemy is crossing the bridge!". You chalk this up to dramatic effect and continue as planned. Suddenly you find out on turn 7 that you have only 3 turns left (instead of  the originally displayed 13) because now "the enemy is almost here". By this time you probably would not have enough time to finish the mission objectives because you had been planning based on double the number of turns instead. So you end up having to restart and ignore the mission briefing which still says "20-turns".
Example 2:
There was a desert mission to cross a large span of open space under fire by enemy snipers. After about an hour of slow and steady work moving meticulously from cover to cover, the screen fills with flying sand and the game tells you that a sandstorm is happening and "now is your chance to run across". So you start rushing your entire squad out from their cover before the sandstorm ends - only for everyone of them to get shot dead in the next turn as if there was no sandstorm at all.
I actually had to google this one.
Turns out the game meant was that the "sandstorm" would reduce accuracy for most units - which generally doesn't help when you have 4 snipers trained on your team; essentially the "sandstorm" was a lie, you were still supposed to stick to cover but you could now try to hit the more exposed shorter ranged enemy units rather than running across in the open. Which begs the question - why would the game tell you that "now is your chance to run across" as if that was what you were supposed to do?
Bottomline: Congrats you get to start over on 2 hours of blindfolded rock-paper-scissors because the game neglected to explain this rather important distinction clearly. This was the point that I quit playing entirely.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is an RPG game wherein you take on the role of the Monopolist~ Err, Capitalistic entreprenuer known as Recette as she takes on the mantle of an item shop owner in order to pay back a substantial debt owed due to her father.
While sweet at first and lighthearted, this game quickly turns into an all-out battle for survival as your debt increment grows and grows, leaving the player to have to make smart business decisions in a VERY fluctuating market.
Those weapons you just bought that you'd been making all the money with? Guess what? They just turned worthless. Those treasures that you were sure you'd make a killing off of? It's a shame that they're worthless too.
Oh it's okay though; Candy is always in boom. And the supply of Little Girls is seemingly endless. You could always make money off of them, I guess.
Digressing, the game does have a fitting storyline if people are willing to work for it, the dungeon-roaming offers a sort of different pace for the game after it's central hub-bub of a market place gets tiring. The character's that come to your shop all have unique personalities (Minus the Townsfolk, who are stock characters) and preferences that you, as the shopkeeper, must abide to, which adds a twist to your usual marketing strategy.
For instance, modeling your store to appeal to different types of people may have you gain business with some, but lose others. If you want to truly master the ways of the monopol~ Err, Capitalistic society that you've been given, then you must attain a delicate balance in building trusts with NPC's, and lining your pockets with coin.
All in all, this game provides a solid challenge while giving a rather entertaining set of characters to keep you along the baseline journey. Further delving in the story reveals darker bits of the world that they live in that you might have otherwise not known unless you pieced it together from the text, which gives you a bit of lore to put in your cap too.
I would most definitely recommend this game, as it's been an experience like no other.

==Tech Stuff==
Day 1, it was broken mess for many.
Month later, it was getting better but there were still random crash here and there.
Now today ( FOUR MONTH after the release ) , it's been fixed and it supposedly run without crashes.
==Music Stuff==
Probably the best point of the game. Music from NIS / Tenpei Sato are of excellent quality
==Graph Stuff==
10+ years ago, it was acceptable at best. nowadays, it's the kind of thing you'd expect from low budget indie game.
While there has been a few enhancement here and there from the PSP version, it's still far from being up to nowadays standard
==Scenario==
Mostly comedy with some seriousness here and there. Decent but nothing exceptionnal to see here.
==Gameplay Stuff==
Basic is a good word for it. There's nothing exceptionnal here.
If you played a more recent Disgaea game on PS3/4 or Vita, then you'll most likely find this installement horribly lackluster.
==Replayability==
Wholly depend wether you intend to grind for the post game or not.
10 to 15 hours top are plenty enough to clear the storyline.
Add 15 to 40 hours of stats/item grinding/leveling to defeat the last Ex Boss depending of wether you know what you're doing or not.
==Overall==
10+ years ago, this game was a solid hit and worth its price.
Today, it's decent. Not exceptionnal since the system itself is badly primitive/poor/outdated , but it's decent.
Give it a try during a sales period, you might enjoy it.

Once upon a time there was a little game called Quake.  It was pretty badass with something like 64 different shades of brown.  Then once day this company named Epic asked themselves, "What if we created a similar engine and used it to run a game with colors and maybe a few trees?"
After some development, Unreal was born.  The engine itself has gone trhough many overhauls and is the groundwork for some of the biggest and most badass games.  Quake engine however didn't get near as much support from outside developers.
The story isn't all that special and graphics haven't aged all that well, but the gameplay is balanced and guns are fairly creative.  Most of what you'll see in Unreal Tournament's arsenal started here.  Do yourself a favor and bump difficulty up a bit from normal as you wont see any difficulty until about midway through the game.  Also have a heart and don't shoot the goofy looking guys with 4 arms.  They have enough problems to deal with, read the popups from your scanner and you'll understand.
Do buy and enjoy.  You'll feel good about yourself after.

Metro: Last Light Redux is a short, but well-paced and action-driven FPS set in the dystopian Russian Metro tunnels after some undetermined global nuclear annihilation event. Strong gameplay elements, coupled with with a distinct setting are the strong selling points for this game.
Pros:
-Excellent gun-play; the game feels very responsive to your every action.
-The narrative-driven story is well above average, continuing the events of Metro 2033.
-The game engine is phenominal; turning up all of the graphical settings really shows off how beatiful the dystopian setting is. High elements of detail and good animations really suck you into the environment and make you feel a part of the Metro.
-Distinct art style for weapons, settings, and characters for those long time fans of post-apocalyptic games. Specifically, the weapons look almost steampunk like, kind of like weapons made of scavenged parts and made to "make do with" (I call it junkpunk). Each Metro City has its own unique theme as well.
-New secrets added in for the Redux version that did not appear in the original version of Last Light.
Cons:
-The game crashes hard. It can be fixed by reinstallaling the C++ redistributable (vcredist_x64.exe in the Metro Last Light folder of your Steam Library directory) in most cases, but still. It's pretty bad to crash straight to desktop with no warning; and seemingly at random.
-Awkward nudity. Not really a fan of nudity in video games; especially not in narrative-driven games were it comes out of the blue and is mostly irrelevant. I'd be okay with it being in the game if it could be skipped as per the player's decision.
-Not being able to skip the startup cinematics. They are pretty long, and there are two of them. Once when you start the game and another with you press any key to go to the menu.
-Pavel. You'll see why, or you already know.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Technical Rating: 8/10 -- Playing the game is a blast, and the 4A Engine really shows what a FPS can look like, but the crashes are still pretty unacceptable.
Enjoyment Rating: 10/10 -- Even with the crashes, I still wanted to play more. I had already played the non-Redux version before, and thoroughly enjoyed it then; the second playthrough was still just as good. Lots of inspired level designs, dynamic stealth-to-action gameplay that does not suck, and a wonderfully fleshed-out game world that leaves you wanting the sequel today. Highly recommended to anyone that wants a quick, fun, but good FPS experience; or anyone just looking for a good story with a semi-futuristic; dystopian setting.

I played a few hours of Metro 2033 before starting Last Light and haven't read any of the books. I am not familiar with this universe and its character so here are my thoughts exclusively on the game Metro: Last Light. Since I played this game in 2017 and considering the game is a few years old by now, I will try to be considerate.
First person story driven game. Most of the game takes place underground between metro tunnels and stations. If you don't like claustrophobic settings, stay away from this. What I expect from a game like this: good mechanics, decent AI, great weapon feel and some level of interesting story. What did I actually get? Not much sadly. The weapons don't feel great when I compare it to even older games such as Crysis. AI is horrendously stupid.
Okay...
The post-apocalyptic plot involves metro nazis, aliens, mutated dogs and crabs in radioactive environment, some deadly virus, communism and metro politics... What???
As I said, most levels are based in underground metro tunnels and so its almost dark all the time. When you do go out in occassions, you get a very limited area to explore. Few things that threw me off: When you fall in water, you can't manoeuvre. Instead, you just emerge on the land at the point where you dived in. Second: When you try to go slightly off-limits in the outside, you die by some un-explained radioactive waves.
To me, what makes the characters interesting: good character arcs, some level of development, some back-story and good voice acting. What this game has: No single character that I gave a damn about. The voice acting is terrible and the facial expressions are non-existent.

Disgaea is one of those games that really changed the genre. When it first came out on the PS2 it was pretty unique with it's focus on super grinding. I did not care for it back then, having been an SRPG player since the very beginning with Shining Force 1 and 2...played on an actual Sega system. When the PS1 came out, it was flooded with tons of great games with that feel: Final Fantasy Tactics, Vanguard Bandits, Vandal Hearts, Tactics Ogre, etc. etc. By the time the PS2 came out it felt like the genre as a whole was drying up. So you can imagine my excitement when this was released. Of course, Disgaea is really its own beast and I did not appreciate the charm it had at the time.
When it was re-released on the PSP I decided to give it more of a fair shake. I took the time to grind characters and unlock the secret levels/endings. I gotta say, it was worth it. I ended up really enjoying the game. It had the trappings of the SRPG genre that I loved so much, with a kind of general absurdity to it that ended up being very entertaining. If you accept Disgaea for what it is, it is a genre unto itself.
When I saw they were porting it to the PC with the content from Afternoon of Darkness, I was pretty excited. Getting to play that on a normal sized screen again with a controller sounded aces to me. I have not been disappointed so far. This is one of those games where, if you have the time, you can easily waste 5+ hours in a single sitting as you grind out levels or explore the depths of the Item World. All the charm is still there with a slightly nicer looking interface. Is it worth it if you still own the original or the PSP version? Probably not, they really did very little to it. But if this is your first foray into the series or you need a cheap copy to play, then go for it. You really need to experience this game at least once.

It's somewhat difficult to say what makes Unreal one of my favorite FPSes ever. Certainly it's not the gameplay. As a classic FPS it can be excused for being mechanically little more than a long string of bullets being introduced to faces, with the bosses being able to take more bullets to the face than most. Admittedly that's a bit of an undersell, since compared to things like the Dark Forces Saga the enemies are pretty varied in their attack forms. But even then only the Skaarj (quick-moving backflip enthusiasts) and Mercenaries (with their shields) have much in the way of techniques that warrant a change in strategy beyond "pull out a bigger gun."
But for some reason that's apparently the appeal of classic FPSes, sprinting at high speeds while commiting genocide. In which case that's kind of hard to fault. But it's not my preference, so why my love for this game?
The answer would have to be "atmosphere." Like with Morrowind and Metroid Prime, I'm a sucker for games with a strong sense of place and meaning. Unreal has a sort of psuedo-fantastical feel to it that, along with its minimalist storytelling, gives the game a somewhat mythic feel that's hard not to love. And while the particulars of the layout tend to be fairly nonsensical and "gamey," Unreal's level design is based largely around huge locales that let you explore the ins and outs of them in a way that gives a very tangible sense of scale.
It's not perfect, and in many ways has not really aged well, but whatever mechanical failures Unreal has is eclipsed by the wonderful weight of its atmosphere. It's still second to Metroid Prime in my not entirely humble opinion, but if it was visually brought up to speed and given the gameplay quality of, say, Half-Life... that'd be hard to top.

Unreal, a game made in 1998. A game that I am sure of many people will remember for it's amazing graphics at the time. Even now in 2015 as I am writing this review, I can still say that Unreal is a great looking game with an amazing plot.
Unreal is a fast paced 1st person shooter with a huge campaign, as well as the possibility to fight in deathmatches, capture the flag and many more gamemodes with bots. The levels in this game can be quite difficult to navigate trough and have many secrets to be revealed, but are all extremely well made. There is a large variety of weapons that you'll aquire troughout the game as well as a large variety of enemies that you'll encounter in Unreal's large amount of levels, giving you the possibility to shoot your way out in every way imaginable.
A thing I should also mention is the difficulty of this game. There are 4 different difficulty settings in this game, easy being the easiest setting and 'unreal' being the hardest. What they did is actually improve the enemies' AI, increase their damage and decrease the amount of ammo, health and upgrades you will find troughout the levels. This is something you'll rarely encounter in nowadays' games where they will just increase the damage you'll take and decrease the damage you deal. Unreal has a great way of spicing up things by making it more difficult in different ways.
Like any other game, it needs music. The music in this game is not just some lousy drums and some silly beeps here and there. No no, there's a lot more to it than just that in Unreal. Each and every track is extremely well made and adds a lot more to just a simple level where you pass a cave or tunnel. As soon as you'll enter a spaceship for example, you'll notice the music will change to a more electronic style which fits really well with the level.
All in all, Unreal is a great fast paced futuristic shooter with a nice variety of weapons, great enemy A.I. and an amazing storyline that I could reccomend to anyone that doesn't care about graphics, but about gameplay instead.

This game is an excellent example of story and investigation blending together to create a unique experience. It provides an original approach to the idea of using ghosts in video games, while making use of Salem's historical background to create an immersive and interesting story.
A particular thing about this game which I found great is your "mind reading" ability. By seeing what people think in the middle of conversations creates very authentic characters and atmosphere.
The investigation methods and the gameplay overall bear a lot of similarity to The Vanishing of Ethan Carter and players who have enjoyed that game are likely to enjoy this one as well.
Pros:
+brilliant story which is revealed through flashbacks and investigation
+intuitive means of investigation
+very authentic atmosphere which cleverly links the past with the present, allowing you to see ghostly bits of walls and objects all around Salem
+side stories are creepy and fun to discover
+gathering clues to solve investigations and the ability in which you can get answers (hell, who doesn't love flashbacks when you're looking for info?) based on your own deductions is great (somewhat similar to that of The Testament of Sherlock Holmes)
+based on your ghostly abilities and the way in which you are encouraged to explore in order to find clues and collectibles, it's very immersive (after playing the game for like 3 hrs, I actually tried to pass through a wall in my house. I was very disappointed to discover that it didn't work like it does in Salem.)
Cons:
-no replayability value at all (except when you miss some collectibles in the first playthrough, which may or may not happen depending how much attention you pay to your surroundings)
-linear level design, makes you know what to expect from most parts of the game in terms of gameplay
-it isn't that much of a challenge to complete, only real threat are the demons, but they are not a constant presence throughout the game
-except for the menu song, there is no soundtrack at all
Overall, I'd say it deserves a 9/10, for the way in which it blends intuitive means of investigation, ghost powers and a mysterious and interesting story.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a supernatural crime thriller about Ronan, a man with a criminal history who became a detective then found himself a victim of the bell killer when following a lead in the case. The game has a sense of uniqueness that has to be appreciated in just its premise. The character is full of quirks and remarks throughout the game as well as some of the other characters. This is all delivered rather nicely in it voice acting which is very solidly done. The controls are very simple and straightforward nothing to complicate things which lends itself well to the games puzzle-esque ways. Combat doest really exist out side of exorcising demons which is mostly optional bit is always pulled of by one of the movement (WASD) keys and right or left mouse button click so it feels a bit gimicky and like its trying to be pattern like but feels out of place in some way, at least for me. The plot and story are the absolute best  part in this game by far and with quite a few twists and turns that leave you scratching your head at who is behind it all then promptly smacking your ideas of the suspect. The only thing I feel they could have done better is making me feel more emotionally invested in some of the character which would have lent itself well in other aspects of the game in terms of impact. There are side things that can be done BUT due to auto save ONLY with no manual save control of your own if you want to colllect and/or solve all side things do so before reaching the end of the game otherwise that has to be done in a new game. Despite being a rather small and short game Murdered: Soul Suspect still deserves a try and it has its handful of problems but any I've run into felt very minor to the point it felt like might be me being picky so I say give this a go as it deserves a little more attention and love.

As a 6 hour experience for about 5 bucks, Murdered tells an ok story. As a game though it falls down in almost all departments. Boring and repetitive stealth sections make up the only actual gameplay part of the experience. The rest of it is simply walking around rooms to find clues and push the story forward, in an almost visual novel sort of experience. While a fan of these kinds of games myself, such as the Ace Attorney series, I dont think this is what Murdered was trying to do, and instead it fails at being a good action/mystery game or a good visual novel too.
In conclusion I can't really recommend the title, as it does nothing particularly interesting with its unique premise, sadly turning a very intriguing concept into a run of the mill point and click adventure style murder mystery without a satisfying story to hold it up.

OCULUS REVIEW + LOGITECH G27 STEERING WHEEL REVIEW:
So I played this on Oculus. I just have a few things to say.
1) It is so ♥♥♥♥ing cool. It actually feels like you are driving a big truck. I know when I drive my truck in real life I am constantly checking my mirrors. You'd think I am having a seizure looking back and forth at my mirrors. Doing that with the mouse and a steering wheel is near impossible. Using the steering wheel and oculus to look around = perfect.
2) Graphics just need to be better optimized and upgraded. In oculus, I get super motion sick because of how wonky the graphics look. So much stuff is pixelated and hard to see.
3) Steering wheel + shifter is the way to go. Being able to shift gears with a clutch while playing this game is just so cool and makes it so worth it.
Not much else to say, it is just amazing. I will warn that the motion sickness on oculus for this game is a solid 8/10 on the puking scale. I can't play for more than an hour or I feel super ill.

So yeah, this game brings back hardcore nostalgia, we're talking every RPG I play ends up leading to me downloading this masterpiece and playing through for hours. Definitely download it if you haven't tried it

I'm extremely disappointed about the condition of this game. I realize that it's still in early access, but according to the news on the store page, full launch is expected by April 2016. It's because of this fact, and the posts indicating patches and updates that I decided that this was finally the time to take a look at it. I had really high hopes, even though I was expecting a minor glitch or two.
What I found instead was a game that I simply cannot play. Firstly, the game does not have full controller support, as indicated. At best, it's got partial support. I was unable to start the game, or even go to full-screen, without using the mouse. The menu didn't function correctly, and it appeared as if perhaps this was one of the features that had not yet been finished.
I began with the tutorial option, but it didn't work for me, so I decided to just try the play option. Again, I had to use the mouse to begin the game with "Book 1," and when the game did start, I experienced several difficulties and oddities.
Firstly, the screen would waver, like a mirror image or looking through water. I have no idea if this is intentional or because of a design issue, but it made it impossible for me to see my character and what I was doing. All the while, though, this side-scrolling platformer is continuing to move, so that resulted in "sudden death."
The next thing I noticed was a sudden slowing of animations and movement on the screen. This most often occurred for me while my character was in motion or in the air in mid-jump.
I attempted several times to finish the first level but couldn't, so I had the idea to see if I could go to "Book 2" without having actually finished "Book 1." It turned out that I could, though it's probably not a good thing that this was possible. Again turning to the mouse to launch the level, I made a few successful jumps, popped off a couple shots with my gun and noticed that the shots seemed to be moving much slower than they probably should. I figured that I could deal with that and just kept jumping, determined to play this game that I'd been anticipating.
This is when my screen started wavering yet again and then a very odd thing happened. I'd landed onto a lower building, but a split-second later, the building disappeared. My character remained stuck in an odd position in the middle of my screen, and everything just froze. I couldn't believe I was actually seeing what I was seeing, so I took a screen shot and then tried to restart the level.
Unfortunately, I was unable to use any of the controls or the mouse. I hit Alt+Tab and closed the game screen, but even that didn't work. Next, I tried to close Steam, but I kept getting an error message that Steam couldn't close because Guardians of Victoria was running. With no game screen to close, and no option to force quit, I had no choice but to reboot in order to regain control over my laptop.
I can't even express how disappointed I am. I love indie games, steampunk, and platformers, so I was truly excited about this game. I can see from some of the posts that the developer has had quite a struggle with this game, and I sympathize with that. Unfortunately, though, I really cannot recommend the game in it's current state. I will, however, invite the developer to reach out to me when the game is truly finished. At that point, I will absolutely give the game another try and revise my review.

SpeedRunners is an interesting hybrid between Sonic the Hedgehog, Ninja Gaiden, the Batman: Arkham games, and Mario Kart... which is to say it's a hectic mess of crazy fun.
Oftentimes, the game becomes so insanely fast that you can't tell what's going on, but it never becomes frustrating or annoying.
After one opponent is left in the dust (off screen), it sets off an explosion that begins to shrink the field of view, which makes long matches intense.
As you try to outwit, outrun, and outluck your opponents, you can gain weapons with various effects (a homing missile that chases down nearby foes, a claw that yanks your opponent out of place and flings you ahead, a freeze ray, etc.). These can all be used brilliantly to mess up your opponents (or occasionally yourself if you're unfortunate).
There's also your typical boosts, and the excellent grappling hook to help even the odds when you're falling behind, which adds even more to the fun.
The graphics are simplistic but fitting. It's well animated, and has a very clean look. The downside is, when someone is far behind, the screen zooms out and makes it somewhat hard to see, or when the match has lasted for a great amount of time, it can be a bit difficult to see what's ahead as the screen closes in. However, this isn't a huge detriment.
The audio sounds good and fitting, except the music is very repetitious. There's only one song while racing, and while it's catchy, it does grow old after a while.
The vanilla stages are well designed, and have well placed shortcuts and traps, and have a very well placed risk-versus-reward-style layout for each one. The Workshop also provides random stages, which have varying levels of quality (naturally).
Simply put, this game has a few flaws, but it's a blast, especially with a group of friends. It's a perfect example of a party game.

There's a lot that seems antiquated or unpolished, but I found myself wanting to continue and complete the game.
The dealer is a neat character, and the way the game is setup, through trading cards, adds an excellent storyline and backstory: the card drawn is a 2 of lava golems, so the player must fight 2 lava golems.  That's meant as praise to the intriguing minimalist game tableau rather than as lambastment.
The combat is more engaging than it initially seems.  This is batman's combat without gadgets, without control of the camera, without special moves, and with movement that always feels erratic.  There is 1 attack, 1 shield bash, a batman-style autocounter, and a dodge.  The challenge of the combat is chaining long combos, which deal increasing per-blow damage and add a minigame to the simple action.  Continuing combo chains becomes difficult in the later levels with boss monsters, unblockable attacks, and constant projectiles interrupting player combos.  It's simple, but it keeps the attention.
The graphics are wince worthy.  Blur effects are often more a nuisance than a graphical enhancement, and the in-combat graphics feel 10-years-ago. Annoying shop load times and card shuffle animations really emphasize that this was meant to be a text-based game.
Overall, I've been wavering between thumbs up and thumbs down.  The game has so little, but I keep going back to try to collect more tokens and beat the last levels.  Thumbs up with reservations.

Ok ! I think 400 hours are enough for a review, right? Well here goes nothing.
( ! Spoiler Alert ! )
Warframe is basically a space ninja(TENNO) third person shooter game with some pretty decent melee action if you'd preffer that to ranged power guns or pee shooters; extremely repetitive and grindy, with real time crafting which in a weird way adds to the flavour of the game. Now here's something you might think is wrong but it all makes sense considering the type of game this is. Everything is instance based, yes you heard me, including the new big update which known as Plains of Eidolon. So the Plains were supposed to be an open world area, well it's not. What the Plains of Eidolon update added is just a BIG instance where you can have a crapton of fun hunting these big things called Eidolon Teralysts, somewhat of a  Focus tree rework and some additions to the Operator mode which make this boring yet in a way extremely fun highly repetitive game stellar in my honest opinion.
I am a returning player, a veteran. I have played this game about 2 years ago and came back to it as soon as I saw the Plains of Eidolon update being announced a couple of weeks before launch.
If you're looking for one of the biggest and baddest Free 2 Play game on the market then look no further because you've reached your destination my friends. Also do not be fooled this game is completely free, you do not have to purchase Platinum because you can trade these so called Prime items which consist of prime warframes and prime weapons with other players in order to get that juicy ,juicy "real life", but in-game ,cash.
Note: This game will not hold your hand. You have to learn everything by yourself , although there are chat moderators that will help you with your questions and the community is EXTREMELY friendly compared to most games out there nowadays.
As a new player you need to know the Codex on your ship is and to constantly research on the warframe wiki to enhance your knowledge about the game.
This game does somewhat reward the "Stealth" approach, although I would highly recommend you don't bother with stealth unless you plan on farming "exterminate;spy" missions.
Also let's not forget about the so called Mastery Rank, which our beloved developers somewhat forgot to introduce to us in the beggining, it being hidden in the game's Menu and all that and  not much explained unless you read the patch notes or the warframe wiki.(note that I have no idea if this has been recently introduced into a tutorial for new players nowadays since I did start playing this game like 2-3 years ago). Weapons are mastery rank locked , crafting said weapons is also mastery rank locked , this meaning you will not be able to craft and use said weapons untill you reach said mastery rank which you get by leveling up warframes,weapons and companions. The name for experience warframe uses is known as Affinity which it all goes from leveling your items to your mastery rank and when you want to advance to the next rank you HAVE to pass a so called mastery rank test.
You do want to complete the quests as they introduce new powerful warframes and an awesome story , one which you do not want to miss out on, TRUST ME, you need that story for the "end game" of warframe , tenno.
Note that some warframes, weapons and resources you can only get at the CLAN DOJO and some
MODS which are used to upgrade your warframes and weapons/companions from syndicates.
There are many other things this game doesn't tell you , or at least it didn't in my first days of play which i can not explain in a review because it would literally take too much of my warframe time, now being Night/Day cycles out on the Plains and all.
Now, this being said, I DEMAND YOU PLAY THIS GAME. You shall not regret it.  Warframe is basically the next World of Warcraft only it's completely 100% free. (YOU WILL WANT TO BUY platinum and steam items from Tennogen with real life cash, it's too tempting after a while and you give in to your TENNO urges).
See you out on the fields fellow Tenno and may the Lotus be with you.

My review on Strikey Sisters
I must say that DYA Games done again an amazing job in making such a well polished game.  When I started up the game, it brought me into that memory of my youth when played those many arcade games back in the days, which they where all great times for me.  This game from DYA Games, has given me so much motivation to go and create a full cabinet arcade system to have at home.
Strikey Sisters brings many other game element styles into the mix.  You got the map to choose which levels areas you want to start off from. just like Super Mario Brothers 3.  With the gameplay style of Brick Breaker arcade gameplay, which i was very impress that this game was that kind of gameplay, but with action style in the mix.  It also give that pixel arcade style feel and look.  That fans of retro games, will surely enjoy, with good sound effects and good music too.
The game is also a local two player co-op, which you and friend can play as ether one of the two sisters.  Marie and Elene.  Which they both do the same attack style when you press the attack button.  But they do not look or sound the same.  The story of the game, is very interesting and funny.  All character designs and look, just give you those old time nostlagia feel when playing a game back in the days on the consoles like nintendo & sega genesis system.
Art design of the game is so right on with the pixel graphic look, of those retro games back in the days.  As i mention before anyone enjoy the retro games of times past before, will feel right at home with this game.  The game also as many other features, such as changing the difficult from easy to hard and etc.
Now to the pros and cons
Pros+
+Good Story
+Amainzg Pixel Art Style
+Good Soundtrack & Sound Effects
+Great Fun Gameplay
+Hours of play
+Local 2 Player Co-op
Cons-
-Nothing to complain
So this is my review of the Strikey Sisters.  Would i recommend this game to a family or friend?  Yes i would, is it worth the full price?  Yes it is, but if you are still unsure if paying full price is worth it.  Then wait for a sale but in honest truth, it not that pricey which wouldn't break your wallet or purse at all.
Hope this helps anyone that has been wondering if the game is worth it or not.

Laggy, freezing and crashes? Servers can desync and creatures can glitch out by randomly teleporting while running. Freezing can occur during random times when the servers get crazy. Randomly, when joining a server the game can have the possibility of crashing to the desktop.
FPS? While I was playing with the recommended 'Auto' video settings at the start, with a mixture of all High settings except for 2 Medium settings (General Shadows and Foliage Shadows) the game ran between 100+ FPS at the start, then when I went into more dense areas the FPS can drop down to 30 FPS. These video settings were being played on an i5-6600 and a GTX 950 FTW. I played in all Mediums settings except for Texture Detail (I put this to High) and it mostly ran the game in 30+ FPS in dense areas, outside of dense areas the FPS can go up to 70+.

Based on what I stated, it's only recommended to buy if it's on a sale since the game is in 'Early Access' and anything can change. There are games you want to play and then there are games you have to play.  This is a game you have to play.

Roughly 100 hours later, my S/O hates this game, my front lawn is a little over grown and I have a sink full of dishes.
I still have a lot to do in the game but I think I can say without hesitation that this is the best tactical RPG I have ever played.

The comedic story, beautiful sprites and endless game play make this one a real keeper.
I can see myself playing this one for years to come.
The only gripe is that you WILL need the strat guide AND gamefaqs to understand all the systems and mechanics in the game because, holy hell, are they neumerous and complex.
A few hints to make your life better:
Turn off Anti Aliasing if you get a multicolored rainbow line in the middle of your screen.
Turn on Vsync if your screen is tearing.
Leave the edge blur effects off.
You can throw enemies onto geo prizims to 1 shot destory them.
Dont worry about leveling up more than 4 or 5 characters your first time through the story.
Do not mess around with the item world until you beat the game (unless you have to for the story).
Ditch your starter prinnies asap, and level a male fist user, a mage, healer, a theif, and male warrior  with your main characters these will all you need on your first play through.
Do not worry about starting new characters with perfect stats or better versions of the class you currently have, you can restart them later as any new class and carry stats from their current level over as many times as you want (google transmigrating disgaea).
On first playthrough, angelic main character is the best one to ask the assembly for a healer and a mage because of next tip.
Once a character creates another one at the assembly, it can learn all of their spells by standing beside the new character in battle and casting the new character\'s spell(s) 5 times; this works with all spells at all levels.
Bribes in the dark assembly are cumulative, that is, the more you bribe, the higher your influence gets over time.
The dark assembly can be entered and exited at no penalty to re roll influence for that session.
Talk to your all of your castle's vassals in each chapter, they sometimes reward you.

Despite the fact I was initially skeptical of this game due to its appearance, Recettear has to be one of the most addicting games I've played. Recettear tells the story of Recette, a young girl whose dad disappeared leaving behind a massive debt for her to deal with. In order to pay the debt back and save her home from being claimed by the bank, she converts it into her own shop to earn the money.
The game combines two main gameplay elements: operating your shop, and dungeon diving to find items to sell or use to craft something even more valuable. Running the shop is very fun, surprisingly so even, and personally I found the dungeons to be fun, at times fairly challenging, and a great to mix things up from time to time. The characters of Recettear are also loveable, with some very charming and quirky personalities, which make for some seriously funny moments. Overall a great game, and definitely worth the price (especially if you buy it on sale)!

Unreal is an FPS from 98' that lives up to it's name, one of the most aesthetically pleasing games to date which  spawned the fantastic Unreal Tournament 99, which is still hands down the master of arena shooters thanks to Unreals flawless engine, extremely talented mappers and great mechanics.. This is one of those games that you NEED to experience before you kick the bucket as it's pretty much the pinnacle of FPS before the massive decline.
The story is pretty simple, you're an inmate who's prisoner transport ship crash landed on an alien planet and you'll need to explore lengthy, non-linear levels to progress, you can learn some of the games interesting lore by reading messages left on the dead bodies of humans, reading diaries and scripture on walls, similar to that in Metroid Prime where you learn all the lore from scanning objects and alien text on walls.
The graphics are incredible, especially being that it was originally released in 98', which was one of the best years for gaming in my opinion. The sound is superb, the weapons sound deadly and powerful. The atmosphere is relentlessly amazing through-out largely thanks to the sound effects, music, scenery, amazing lighting effects and all round amazingly designed levels which see you exploring large layouts, filled with many paths and many hidden secrets while fighting bad♥♥♥♥♥enemies that fake their death, dodge your attacks and have different behavioural attributes.
The weapons in Unreal are varied and each behaves in a very unique way, my personal favourite being the Flak Cannon which sends shards of flak at your opponents, shredding them to pieces and has an alternate fire of a grenade that explodes on impact.
I honestly envy you if you haven't played this yet, I'd kill to be able to see everything in this game for the first time again, it's an experience made by true masters who took so many obscure factors into consideration that its scary, this is one solid shooter you don't want to miss out on.

The scenery was breathtaking on release, and still doesn't look that bad today. The levels are almost always well designed to reward exploration, and often have multiple ways of getting around. The music is exceptional, and worth a listen to even if you don't own the game. The story does its job well, and the atmosphere is superb.
My few complaints would be that some of the mechanisms for opening doors can be arbitrary and confusing at times, as are the few points where you have to kill a certain amount of enemies to progress.
Overall, you won't be disappointed with this game.

Archeage is a title that exemplifies the phrase "Jack of all trades, master of none." The game has tons of things to do, regardless of whether you want to PvE, PvP, craft, trade, raid, run dungeons, fish, explore the seas, or do some home decorating. However, I can't imagine anyone claiming that Archeage does any one of those things the best. Furthermore, while the game does allow for 120 different class combinations, it feels as though little effort was put into making all the class combos viable options. For instance, any hope you may have had of creating a magic warrior should be suspended, as it is virtually impossible. Not only do melee and magic rely on totally different stats, but mages rely on the bonus to magic damage afforded by staffs and scepters (which are useless to warriors) to increase damage output.  Some form of STR-based magic or possibly and spell which added elemental damage to a weapon could have made this combo a possibility.
Despite my misgivings, however, I do think the game has merit. While it doesn't do anything the best, it does do most of it well and few games available these days try to implement such a breadth of gameplay options. At the very least, it's worth a look.

In Murdered:  Soul Suspect, you play a ghost.  You can walk through walls, affect things like lights and TVs, and blow papers on the floor.  You can possess people, but you can't really make them do very much.  Mostly, you just access their memories or influence them a little.
This is a murder mystery, and you're trying to solve not only your own murder, but a series of murders you were investigating before you died.
Along the way, you'll meet other ghosts, and some of them will help you, some will haunt you, and some will need your help.  Many of the ghosts have stories that they want to tell, and in a few cases, you will solve other murders.
This is a beautiful and emotional game with a LOT of depth to it.  It was creative.  It was original.  It was intelligent.  Not flawless.  Not perfect.  But beautiful, and I don't mean graphics.  I mean this is a game where someone put some real love into developing it into something unique.
There were only two things I didn't like about this game:
1.  The name.  I think they should have just called it "Murdered".  More mysterious and dark that way.
2.  The demons.  There are these demons that float around, and if they see you they will attack, and then it's game over.  I went into the config file and blinded them all.  I felt they went against the tone and feel of the game.  It's spooky having them their, but this, in my opinion, is not a game that needed action or combat.  So I essentially turned them off, and they became just more creepy atmosphere.
Overall, I highly recommend this game.

There's a lot that seems antiquated or unpolished, but I found myself wanting to continue and complete the game.
The dealer is a neat character, and the way the game is setup, through trading cards, adds an excellent storyline and backstory: the card drawn is a 2 of lava golems, so the player must fight 2 lava golems.  That's meant as praise to the intriguing minimalist game tableau rather than as lambastment.
The combat is more engaging than it initially seems.  This is batman's combat without gadgets, without control of the camera, without special moves, and with movement that always feels erratic.  There is 1 attack, 1 shield bash, a batman-style autocounter, and a dodge.  The challenge of the combat is chaining long combos, which deal increasing per-blow damage and add a minigame to the simple action.  Continuing combo chains becomes difficult in the later levels with boss monsters, unblockable attacks, and constant projectiles interrupting player combos.  It's simple, but it keeps the attention.
The graphics are wince worthy.  Blur effects are often more a nuisance than a graphical enhancement, and the in-combat graphics feel 10-years-ago. Annoying shop load times and card shuffle animations really emphasize that this was meant to be a text-based game.
Overall, I've been wavering between thumbs up and thumbs down.  The game has so little, but I keep going back to try to collect more tokens and beat the last levels.  Thumbs up with reservations.

When i first started playing this game, i was really impressed by how immersive the world was, and how much effort was put into making the underground society feel like a living breathing world. The FPS gameplay is solid, but the game suffers from a few issues that really kill the immersive experience and turn the game into a rather annoying chore.
The developers give you absolutely NO sense of direction when it comes to level design. Most of the time you are simply dropped into a massive maze, and expected to simply know where you're supposed to go or what you're supposed to do next. This is a HUGE issue for a game that often requires you to race against the clock in order to not run out of oxygen and DIE. Some people might call this a challenge, but in a linear FPS the only challenge should be killing things before they kill you, not trying to figure out what button you need to press or what specific direction you need to move towards in order to progress.
The game will even purposefully screw you over by presenting false pathways that lead to dead ends or random boss-like enemies that don't need to be killed just so you can waste your ammo or waste your time and eventually come to a point where you can no longer progress without starting all over because your resources have been wasted.
The game creates a false sense of difficulty by simply not providing the player with enough equipment or ammo to progress in the game. Even the toughest games will give their player enough ammo or health before a major battle. But Metro will literally lock you into areas that have NO ammo and a TUN of enemies (via checkpoints) so when you run out of ammo you have to start the entire level all over again. I shouldnt have to stop in the middle of playing a game and think "a few minutes from now i am going to die and theres nothing i can do about it so i better quit". I never feel like i am failing because of my own fault, i just feel like i am being screwed over.
The game world has an interesting concept and looks great, it reels you in with it's epic environments and animations, but later on you realise that the story is mostly nonsense and the developers make no attempt to provide any exposition. Characters will reference things that are never explained, and the main character is silent which doesnt exactly help. It also doesnt help that most of the characters you interact with are bland and extremely forgettable, making the game feel like a wasted opportunity.
Its very easy for people to love these edgy post apocalypse games where the cover has a picture of a guy wearing a gas mask while holding a rifle (SO EDGY) but i don't think Metro has anything good to offer here. It's boring, pointless, annoying, random and forgettable.

There is a feeling you get on discovering a new world that cannot be duplicated. Like stepping through the wardrobe, falling down the rabbit hole, or having been spat in the eye by a Hobgoblin; when you first see the curtain drop, and the landscape come into focus, excitement akin to Christmas morning overtakes all other senses.
Such was my experience long ago when, on a whim, I picked up Suikoden II at my local flea market. To me it looked like your average game at the time. Pixel graphics. Promise of amazing story on the back. I had no great expectations.
I've never been more wrong in my life.
As many who love RPGs have found, the Suikoden series is one of the best if not THEE best in the history of the genre. When I popped that disc into my old PS1 and heard the opening, named my avatar, and within the first hour was betrayed?! Hah! I was eight years old again, unopened red an green boxes sat before me under the tree.
Fast forward about 15 years and that same jolt of excitement strikes again. This time in the form of an indie game I picked up on Steam called 'Hand of Fate'.
Brought to us by Defiant Development - a small Studio based in Brisbane, Australia - greenlit by the Steam community, and funded on Kickstarter; the game could not be more Indie if you gave it a whip and put it above a pit of snakes.
55,000 dollars was all it took to see this masterpiece come into being. A drop in the bucket compared to the triple A titles being produced these days. Yet, as I play the game, I don't notice the difference. The voice acting is superb, the graphics are breath taking, and the combat animations are so satisfying you feel like yelling out, "GET REKT!!" whenever your shield connects with an NPC's face.
What truly makes this game stand out however is not the RPG elements, nor the brawling. No, they are but two of the ingredients Deviant Development decided to toss in the pot. You also have a table top experience that's like a Tarot card reading mixed with Magic the Gathering. Deck building that reminds you more of 'choose your own adventure' books. Mazes reminiscent of classic dungeon crawlers. With all of it wrapped in a game of luck to the style of 'choose your card, any card'.
Most of the deaths I've had in game has been due to choosing the wrong card and having my health eaten away. Or my food depleted, adding to the RPG experience of resource managing. Every single move has you on the edge of your seat because of this. With the fights actually a nice respite, and chance to catch your breath.
Now, that isn't to say the fighting isn't challenging. Think Assassin's Creed, but with an element of luck thrown in. As all your armor and weapons are picked up by chance. Sometimes taken away as well. As was the case one round when Goblins came and stole my shield. Leaving me with just an axe to try and defeat a veritable army of bandits.
There literally isn't one BAD thing to say about the experience this game brings to the table. One can only nitpick at the few misspelled words, or similarities in Boss appearance. None of which diminish the shear enjoyment one gets from traversing the ever changing game board, unlocking new cards, and dodge rolling around trap-filled arenas with fire-breathing lizards, musket-toting skeletons, and kung-fu ratmen all hot on your tail.
At launch the game was 20 USD. It's since gone up to 25 USD. Would I recommend people wait for a sale to pick up what I'd describe as the biggest surprise in gaming since the early 2000s? No. A resounding NO! Go, buy it now. Play it, enjoy it. You're welcome!
