Love this game! It's not like all those other first person shooters and it's not one of those terrible sword fighting games.
This game is amazing because of the high skill cap. There are players who play hours every week just dueling 1v1. Sounds boring but there are so many different types of attacks and ways to react.  It's not one of those games where you can spam RMB and expect to kill someone skilled. Speaking of the mechanics here are a couple things that you learn how to do:
1. Read your opponent. When you see them attacking you on the left, you have to move your mouse to the left to block the attack. A skilled player can actually start attacking one direction then swerve and trick you into parrying the wrong way.
2. Timing. Timing and footwork is another skill you learn. If you block at the wrong moment you'll still get hit. Timing also comes in when attacking. You want to time your stabs and slashes just right.
3. Position is another huge aspect of the game. If you're on a team, if you rush out and leave your team behind you'll most likely get slaughtered by several enemies at once. Fighting two players at once is extremely hard to do since when you attack one person you make yourself vulnerable to the other player.
4. Similar to real life fencing you actually fight in turns. One person attacks then the other person attacks; somebody who just swings their sword back and forth can easily be parried and killed.
5. You really have to have fast reaction times. Chivalry is the only game I've ever played in which I can notice if someone has a 50+ ms connection. I only play in rooms where I can get <50 ping, usually 20 ms or so. In fact, when I'm dueling i always check the other player's ping, if it's higher than 80 then I usually change my fighting style.
6. Speaking of style, every player you fight has their own special fighting style. For example, there's this one vanguard player who usually runs hard left after attacking to avoid an attack. Once you catch on to this you can anticipate and attack left. There are a few players that I don't even have to see their username to know who they are; their style and gear choice makes it very clear. You don't get that with most FPS games. Usually style isn't seen as much.
7. I've seen some players do this but you can actually bend your body around to avoid getting hit. I'm still trying to learn this one.
All these variables make every game different and interesting. Because of things like this there are many times where a low rank will kill me because he has a strange fighting style that I don't understand.
There are a couple annoying things though. People abuse the mechanics of the game. One of the most powerful attacks is a 180 back swing attack. When timed right you can actually start the attack while inside the other player; making it impossible to block. Another abuse is "dragging" moving your mouse in the direction of attack to make your swing even faster or slower; moving your mouse in the opposite direction of attack (much more commonly used) to throw the other guy off.

I had never written any gaming reviews before but this had to be done.
Firstly I'm not a serious gamer and pretty average in English but I'm writing this down for my own satisfaction.
So this is my experience of Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light Redux:
Well, as I said I'm not a serious gamer and never played any game for eight hours straight. Until today.
When you find yourself glued to a game for eight hours you know you're experiencing something amazing and surreal (The only breaks I took when I felt the need to relax myself from the emotional roller coaster that the games were putting me through). Firstly this is not a fancy game. You won't be able to jump rooftops, ride horses or grapple and beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your enemies with swords and fancy Laser guns. The games provide you with a real humanly experience in an unearthly and mysterious environment. The games are about survival. Its about what you will do if you are put into such an environment and trust me you would have done the exact same things which Artyom (the protagonist) did throughout his journey. The games will put you through the exact same emotional trauma which Artyom experienced. You'll be so engrossed while playing that you'll feel the 'need' for survival yourself. I often found myself gaping in awe or cheering in joy literally ninety percent of the time. That's the level of engagement you'll feel while playing Metro and that's where lies the success of the games. Metro will suck you inside. You'll forget everything and keep playing, you'll keep try to find out what happens next.
Putting you in an imaginary world full of deadly monsters (and The Dark One) and engaging each and every nerve and the emotional epicenters of a gamer into it throughout the journey? Not so easy. But Metro has achieved that flawlessly. There was not a single moment in the game where I felt bored or felt the things happening in the game are part of some fantasy novel written by Dmitry Glukhovsky. This felt so REAL

Many of the "chance" card choices you are required to make with increasing frequency later in the game don't really seem fair, and the penalties for not getting lucky are very harsh. Overall, I wish the game had a lot more fighting, and a lot less hoping to get lucky through picking arbitrary cards.  This is really the only mechanic that gives the game replay value; in that you hope you won't get terribly unlucky to make it to the next level.

In addition to control your ball you also have to evade the ordinary enemies and their attacks, as well as the bosses' attacks all the while trying to hit the bosses with your measly sized ball while they move around. While the 4 sequels does a lot of things better than this slightly improved release of Disgaea 1 does, you're still in for a real treat if you like SRPGs/Tactics games and are new to the series. Disgaea is one of the most freeform games ever. Distribute 10 actions over a turn freely, from 10 separate turns in a row to a Rube Goldenberg-esque chain attack that devastates your target(s). Level up your characters with traditional grinding, or tweak your items with random-dungeon crawling to make them twice as powerful as normally or more. Are the plot-based characters too boring? Create your own! Do you think archers would be cooler if they ran around with axes and longswords? Why, just give them some!
Disgaea doesn't just have a single way to play it - you can do anything you want, and still succeed (well, as long as you did something remotely sensible), and that's why I love it. It also is extremely rich in content - you can easily lose hours in the random dungeons, and getting to the normal final boss doesn't even show you half the stuff you can come across. There are several bonus stages to take on once you're done with the normal story, and the story's final boss' level of 105 pales in comparison to the ultimate secret boss Baal's towering Lv.4000 figure - not to mention there's no end to the power of the random dungeon enemies' and bosses' strengths. Between powering up your party, micro-managing your equipment, and taking on new bonus challenges, you'll easily lose a few hundred of hours in this game, and feel entertained and rewarded all the way through. Slow-paced enough that you can watch videos and eat while playing, fast-paced enough to never get boring.

Overall a good game, minor flaws nonwithstanding, buy it.
-----------------------
-
- The item shop and dungeon delving aspects of the game synergize well, creating a difference in find that rarely leave you bored.
-
- minor flaws in explaining game mechanics: there are several instances where some semi-essential mechanics are left unexplained (or at least, I never found suitable explanation in game). I will fill in this information further down for you.
- Pacing issues: it didn't seem very possible to both enjoy the story and beat the game: I found myself skipping all story events just to complete the game. However, this is alleviated by the "endless mode" option, that will allow you to continue the game (to my knowledge you do not lose any of the narrative).
---------------------------
- The item shop aspect of the game is very well polished: it is quick, fun and it also serves well to flesh out different characters and allow you to bond with them emotionally.
- Many mechanics that make running the store interesting
- As said before, some semi-essential unexplained mechanics.
-----------------------
- It is true that each character is different in combat as it says in the blurb. Not only are the characters different numerically, but handling each one feels unique and comes with its own challenges and advantages.
- the dungeons start out relatively easy; however, they become quite difficult (in my opinion) in the post-content: it's the good kind of difficult, it is rarely unfair, although, since the dungeons are random it is up to the luck of the draw.
- Combat rewards skill
- Leveling is not grindy and happens naturally for the most part. In fact, since player skill and items are major foundations of the character, leveling is not entirely necessary to do advanced dungeons, allowing for relatively fast leveling of characters.

Fable: The Lost Chapters is a 2005 re-release of the 2004 killer app Fable, brought to you by Lionhead studios - a studio famous for this, having Molyneux as a creative director, and having Molyneux as a creative director who lies.
Luckily the 2005 release places it outside of recent memory, so we can ignore all promises of real-time tree growth, multiplayer and multiple guilds, and get on with the game proper.
This is not a blind review. First played this game near release, and remembered it being incredibly mediocre. How's that for a first impression? As it turns out, it was just the memory that was mediocre.
- Guildmaster
By combining all three virtues/playstyles - Strength, Skill, Will - you'll end up with a character that forms many unfinished wholes into an Ultron of tolerability. Going for a specific "build" is not fun, limiting yourself is not fun, the only way to really squeeze some playability out of it is to throw it into a smoothie. Abandon all delusions of sticking to a single path, you're a spellswordbowman.
With that out of the way, the game has more to it than you'd initially expect. Will gives you a dozen tools for every situation, Strength keeps you in the action with little touches like rolling having i-frames and the guard-breaking flourishes that I swear trigger at random, and Skill supplements the other two with speed and money.
At times, especially during endgame when you've completely broken the game to become a regular munchkin, I was having legitimate fun with the gameplay alone. Something not expected from the half-remembered aeons of strafing/kiting at a distance, or continually bouncing off an enemy's impregnable defense.
But it's sloppier than a pig's feeding trough.
Movement isn't remotely 1-1, there's no combos beyond mash attack, no way to play gracefully or precise at all. Enemy attacks either telegraph from a mile away, have just enough startup to seemingly knock you out of wailing on them, or in some amazing circumstances are completely messy distance attacks with no way to predict them at all, just react.
Accept that you will be spamming your go-to preferred glorified macro lategame and you'll be happier.
- Guildmaster
What's there is there, but Fable has largely sold itself on character morphing.
Which is okay. A bit ridiculous, you'll end up twice the size of the average character and shrivelled to a prune while the tykes at the local school still take their first lessons. There's not nearly as much character customization as you'd think - maybe 25 outfits, 10 haircuts and a handful of supplementary aspects, you'll rest easy in the knowledge that your super special Hero is going to turn out about the same as everyone else's.
The only real morphing here is of your expectations, and with no way to roll back level upgrades you're probably going to end up with a stature you're unhappy with regardless.
It's fundementally a silly game, which is fine except that means that any attempt to appear serious falls flat on its face. All the lore ends in abrupt handwaves with no payoff (Did you know that Jack of Blades is a primordial horror-demon, despite just being a smug trickster ingame you trip over and OHKO?), all the character art angles more towards the era's World of Warcraft domineered sensibilities instead of more traditional aesthetics - fine if you like that - and all the music is consistently great there's no dissing these tunes.
- Guildmaster
Ultimately what Fable is, is a surprisingly mechanically fun but otherwise shallow and cliched RPG. Much like Molyneux's hopes and dreams, it aimed for the moon and landed amongst the dirt.

I daresay that Recettear is one of my all-time favorite games. Having played well over fifty hours of the game at this point, I feel the need to update my review (which was already positive).
In Recettear, you play as a young girl named Recette, whose father went missing while out adventuring and left behind a mountain of debt. When a faerie named Tear comes to collect on that debt, she suggests that Recette convert part of her home into a shop in order to come up with the money or risk losing the house outright. That's where the game begins.
There's so much more to Recettear than buying low, selling high and scouring dungeons for loot to sell at 100% profit. The game *does* revolve around buying/selling and dungeon-crawling, but these two different aspects of the game complement one another in several meaningful ways.
Dungeon-crawling will definitely net you plenty of items, but they're usually not very valuable. However, you can find ingredients that you can, in turn, fuse together at the guild to create more valuable items. Also, you'll meet new adventurers in dungeons, and they'll eventually become regular customers at your shop.
Buying from and selling to the aforementioned adventurers in your shop allows you to build relationships with them while also allowing them to gradually spend more money at your shop. They'll purchase equipment from you for use in dungeons, as well, freeing up space in their inventories that you'd probably otherwise use when lending them equipment.
There's more to managing your store than just buying and selling items, though. You can change the carpets, counters, flooring and walls of your store to attract different customers. You can expand the size of your store to allow you to stock more items. You can put different items in your display windows to attract different customers. You can take advantage of local fads in order to sell certain types of items in large numbers while also attracting more customers.
Even more interesting, in addition to buying and selling based on regular market fluctuations, you'll find that you can influence pricing to some extent by outright "crashing" the value of some items by selling too many of them. While this may initially sound like a bad thing, you'll have a while to purchase said item(s) at ridiculously low costs while waiting for the demand on them to bounce back. Really nice touch.
While Recettear has enough to offer in terms of depth to warrant a purchase, I daresay that the game's charm is what makes it something really special. Recette's kindness and naivety makes her a really fun character, and Tear acts as an excellent foil to her in terms of personality. The various adventurers and townspeople interact with Recette and Tear throughout the game, and their individual personalities do a lot to better flesh out Recette and Tear. I can't say enough about this game's charm. The entire experience is just so great.
Before I close this review, I'd like to make a recommendation to new players (or existing players who have issues with certain customers, namely the little girl who breaks your damn combos): Use a guide that outright tells you which percentages to use when buying/selling. The game does make the mistake of giving you some rotten advice at the start, and following this advice will prevent customers from leveling up and having access to higher budgets.
If you're concerned about a guide spoiling the game for you, then don't be. The percentages are a very small part of the game. It's still very challenging, as you'll still often find yourself having to take chances by spending 90-95% of your money when you're just a few thousand pix away from making your weekly payment goal in order to come back and blow past your goal, giving you an incredible sense of satisfaction. You still have to play the market intelligently to win.

This is NOT a farming game.  It is, in fact, a factory game, the use of farm products as widgets notwithstanding.
If that's fine with you, then great.  Personally I want a FARMING game - without the "social" junk imposed by Farmville.
There is no continuity in this game whatsoever.  You are not building a farm, you are not planting crops, you are not able to choose for yourself which farm buildings you want or where they will be placed.
It's a series of hoops you have to jump through with a set goal, imposed by the game, and totally linear.  The only thing that is valued is how fast you can do things.  They place the buildings at random so at each new "level", none of which last more than a few minutes, you are starting over with some random initial conditions.  Within each level, the initial settings will be the same, but from one level to the next, you are starting with different buildings placed in varying and seemingly random locations, and with a variable number of farm animals and varying amounts of startup cash.
You are never building on what's gone before.  Doesn't matter if you bought a sausage factory in the last 28 levels, you'll have to buy it again the next level.
There is zero replay value.  Once you've hit the end, you've hit the end - and each new "challenge" is the same as the last.  Do things FAST and count on starting from scratch at the next level.
I wish somebody out there would make an actual farming game that does not rely on - or even PERMIT - access to social media.
If you're looking for an actual farming game, this is NOT it.
Also there are a ton of small but very annoying bugs in the game.  Firstly, in order to get it to run at all, I had to go and disable Tablet PC Input Service, even though it was set for Manual only startup.  I have no idea why; I have never started that service ever, as I would have to specifically do when a service is set for Manual.  But nothing would satisfy the stupid game except that it be actually disabled.  That's just bad programming on the game developer's part.
Then, everytime it starts up, it is screwing up the configuration check and tells me that my PC "does not meet the minimum requirement" - when in fact it exceeds them.  I can run Dragon Age and The Elder Scrolls Oblivion on here - heck, I can run all of the Witcher series on this but The Witcher 3, which is the most advanced game I own and needs way more graphics power than I have on this system.  But apparently not Farm Frenzy 4, even though this machine exceeds the listed system requirements.
Then, it will lock up once in a while for no apparent reason.  If you have too many animals, you have to watch how much grass you put out - because if you put down too much grass, the pigs will go to sleep as if there were no grass at all out.  The music on startup will sound like a stuck record, playing the same 2 or 3 notes over and over and over again while its loading the startup screen.
And the English translations are among the worst I've ever been forced to deal with.  You would think they could find one person in Japan or whereever this game comes from who can actually speak English to do their translations, or at least check the translations.  It's not QUITE of "all your base are belong to us" quality, but its close.
If you would be happy with a game called "Factory Frenzy" then this game may be for you.
But if you want an actual farming game, this isn't it.

This is a fine example of style over substance. The voice acting is solid, the writing is generally okay (it's cliched at times, but has some decent moments) and it looks good.
Unfortunately, it is hampered by gameplay which ranges from mediocre to bad.
On the mediocre side, you are given a mere handful of skills, which are used remarkably infrequently and only in very obvious situations. The detective aspect has some good aspects, but while it mostly avoids LA Noire's tendency towards arbitrary and frustrating sleuthing, it does so by making things terribly obvious and having no consequences for failure. My favourite was a scene where you have to find a key. Not only does the game tell you how to go about getting to the key, it then presents you with a puzzle to pick it up, where you have to choose between the key, a fork and a spoon. Spoiler: the correct answer is the key.
As for the bad, the combat is hideous. Awkward controls, very limited options and overwhelming noise make for a frustrating experience.
There's plenty of collectables in the game, some of which are at least a mild challenge to get, but unless you're really into that aspect of it, you're better off just watching the story on YouTube.

Not so much a runner as an auto-scrolling platformer - think of the Mario levels where the screen keeps moving to the right, and you lose a life if you're left behind.

There are some excellent songs in the soundtrack, and the art is mostly charming.
IF you choose to buy the game now, know that it's in VERY early access.  Some of the basics are missing - menus don't work as they should, control is a bit sluggish, some enemies are unintentionally immortal, many key animations aren't in place yet, most levels are missing and so on.
Despite that, the groundwork is there for a true gem, and I think the current price (about $3 USD) is fair for what's currently in place.
The devs have shown themselves to be very responsive to feedback, and have already massively updated the game in response to user input in the few days it's been out.
This is definitely one to watch.
Recommended for anyone who likes the idea of the game and is willing to put up with a VERY early access product. HIGHLY recommended for those who enjoy giving constructive feedback.

This game is based on a clever idea - a turn-based card game with mini-arpg battles mixed in.
But the gimmick wears off after a couple hours.
Many of the "chance" card choices you are required to make with increasing frequency later in the game don't really seem fair, and the penalties for not getting lucky are very harsh.  While this is somewhat entertaining in the beginning of the game, it can be frustrating to the point of making the game unplayable later on.
Overall, I wish the game had a lot more fighting, and a lot less hoping to get lucky through picking arbitrary cards.  This is really the only mechanic that gives the game replay value; in that you hope you won't get terribly unlucky to make it to the next level.

Probably the best game I've played since Fallout NV was released, and I put over 1000 hours into that thing. The story is unmatched in modern Sci-Fi, the gameplay is action packed enough to not become boring, but you can't just run into a room blind and start shooting from the hip and expect to last more than a nano-second. The DLC is weird, as you have to go through Bioware's website, and have to buy these stupid Bioware Points - akin to Microsoft points - to buy any content besides the game itself. Be prepared to dedicate a week or more - minimum - to get near 80-90% completion in all games on a single character, as these games are some of the longest I've played in a long time. Also prepare for a massive shift in mechanics between the first and second, as the second / third go for a more action RPG style akin to Deus Ex: HR, while the first game is a straight up space RPG. The "Moral Choice" system is also pretty stupid. You can either choose to Galatic Commander Jesus and be showered in love, money and good endings, or be Space Captain McDouche, with no support, good endings or rewards. It's worth every dollar plus one hundred more though, definitely would recommend it.

For a free to play title that came out years ago, Warframe is pretty decent. I played for a few good weeks in its early years, but now i've started to play again and invest a little bit of time into it once more.
First off, the customization in the game itself is amazing. You can customize your frame, your weapons, your ship, your pets and companions. There's ton of color palettes that'll help you customize your frame even better, some skins, helmets, sigils & regalias, syandana or capes, you name it. Heck, you can even decorate the inside of your ship! you can even build your own Dojo or Clan house and design and decorate it as you wish! It's almost guaranteed that you'll never come across someone with the same customization and taste in fashion. #fashionframe
Second, the gameplay. Gameplay is fluid. You can play the game however you like. Either go in guns blazing, play it stealthy, or just hack n' slash your way towards the objective and then to extraction. You also get to do awesome maneuvers on foot or in air. Bullet time? That's some Max Payne♥♥♥♥♥♥that makes it even better! It's combat and parkour at its finest. You wanna play as a tank, support or dps? The game's got you! Different frames and loadouts for different occasions and playstyles!
Third, the content. There's lots to do in warframe, it can be a little overwhelming at first but everyone gets the hang of it. You'll be unlocking planets, warframes, weapons and a lot of other stuff either through quests, alerts or events in game. I just can't write about most of it right now since I feel like I might choke on the content just by thinking about it.
Fourth, the community. The community is quite helpful and welcoming. Even the moderators in game are quite engaged in the community. You can just ask questions in region chat and people will gladly answer. Ask for help and people will. I've never even seen a bit of toxicity in-game, other than that of weapon mods and Saryn. kek
So is it worth playing? Definitely.
It's one of those games that continue to compete against other titles, old or new. Heck it might've given other recent AAA titles a run for their money. You know what it is. :D

I wouldn't recommend this title based on several aspects of the games mechanics:
- This isn't a "turn-based" strategy game as enemy combatants respond in real time while the player is limited to single actions during turns. Final Fantasy Tactics or even XCOM would be much better examples of how to effectively manage enemy reaction patterns in a strategy game.
- The class/weapon leveling system is capped based on story progression. Replaying scenarios is the only means to properly equip characters prior to story missions.
- Grinding in scenarios is as awfully repetitive as it is boring. You often are required to keep fighting the same scenario on the same map with the same objectives before gaining enough experience to level your units.
- Units are leveled as a whole class and not as an individual character. This makes each character feel disposable in a setting where everyone is supposed to matter.
Overall, the game is overly repetitive with little/no rewards to keep a player coming back for more with an awkward learning curve to boot. There are a lot of tropes that are forced into the narrative to give life to the characters but it falls short with the feel of copy/paste writing.

I feel bad for not recommending this game, because it is brilliant, charismatic and understands that grinding isn't something that RPG fans want rid of. However, what we have here is yet another example of a classic JRPG ported sloppily to PC.
I've just under two days worth of playing time in Disgaea PC, and I've enjoyed enormously about 40% of that duration. The rest was spent worring that the game was going to crash at any moment (a serious problem in the "Item World" where you can go long periods without the opportunity to save) and being driven mad by the suttering, lagging-behind-visuals sound (music, effects and voice acting were all effected). The second problem was actually the most enjoyment destroying, as both the music and voice acting are wonderful, while I managed to devise ways of getting round the crashing problem.
I might return to this game sometime in the future, in the hope that these problems are fixed by those responsible. However, as of the writing of this review Disgaea PC seems to have been abandoned, so my hopes are low.

I hate to say it, because I was so sure I was going to love this game, but I am actually very disappointed in how bad it is. (From a gameplay perspective. Visually, it looks great.) If you are the kind of person who likes a more masochistic experience (e.g. XCOM), then you may find something about this game appealing, but after playing several scenarios, I can honestly say that, for a game that is supposedly tactical, there are too many things about the combat and systems that are incoherent or just plain bad.
For starters, this is not actually a tactical RPG. It is a "guess what the developer was thinking" puzzle game. In most tactical games, you are rewarded for making good strategic decisions and making efficient use of available resources. Not in Valkyria Chronicles, though. This game gives you a "grade" at the end of every encounter, which determines the quality and quanitity of the spoils you receive. You lose points off your grade for taking too many rounds and are rewarded for using as few rounds as possible. This accomplishes two things from a gameplay perspective, both of which in my opinion are terrible: 1) It incentivizes you to make rash decisions, which is antithetical to tactics/strategy, 2) It assumes you want to replay the scenario over and over again until you trial-and-error work out the most efficient way to accomplish the victory condition in the fewest rounds. (Which I absolutely f***ing do not want to do.) So like I said, it is basically a "guess what strategy the developer likes" puzzle game.
But another thing that doesn't make sense to me about this game is that you are literally always being shot. It is supposedly a turn-based game, which implies that the opponents take turns. But the enemies are almost always in a state of shooting you. They shoot you on their turn AND on your turn. In a typical tactical type game---hell even in XCOM which is a game I loathe---you typically have time on your turn to plan and strategize your next move, like a game of chess. If you have consumed your first action point and are deciding what to do with your second, you can typically at least look around, think about your options, etc. You know, STRATEGIZE. But in Valkyria Chronicles, if you consume your first action point, and are thinking about what to do with your second action point, enemies will just stand there and shoot you repeatedly the whole time you are thinking it out, then they'll KEEP shooting you once you actually take an action. It is literally possible for enemies to shoot you to death while you are just trying to turn your character around to face the other direction so that you can perform an attack. What makes it especially egregious for me, though, is that turns don’t end automatically. You have to manually declare that your turn is over, so even if you consume all your actions points and it is literally impossible for you to take any more actions, you had better remember to manually declare that your turn is over, because every second that you don't declare that your turn is over, the enemy will be shooting you to death. This results in the ridiculous situation where I will command a unit to attack, and then the whole time the attack is being executed, I am furiously tapping B so that the "end turn?" prompt comes up as soon as possible so that I can minimize how many times I get shot for not declaring my turn is over fast enough. Who thought this was a good idea? Why do so many people think this is a good idea? It seems like such an obviously bad idea to me.
But then there are other little annoyances, too, like how you always want to end your turn by running up to a sand bag wall to take cover, but if you keep holding foward as you approach the wall, your unit will just JUMP OVER the wall and get shot. So this means you have to run up to the wall to take cover, but be very very careful not to walk TOO close to the wall or you’ll do the exact OPPOSITE of taking cover--namely to jump out in front of the wall and ask the enemy to please shoot you as much as possible. This, too, seems like the worst possible way to configure this aspect of the combat. And then other weird things like units getting a defense bonus for being behind a sandbag wall, even if you just jumped over the sandbag wall and are shooting them right in the face? Sure, okay.
But the point where it dawned on me that maybe this game was going to be kind of bad instead of amazing was one of the very first scenarios. In one of the early missions, there is a part midway through the encounter where a tank randomly shows up that you had no idea was going to be there. The game takes the liberty of moving all of your units directly next to the tank, regardless of where you had placed them, so that the tank can shoot them.(For drama, I guess?) I replayed the scenario to make sure it wasn't MY mistake, and tried being extra careful to keep my units far away from where the tank would inevitably enter, but this proved to be a waste of effort, because even though I kept my units 200 feet away from the tank's point of entry, the game played the cutscene of the tank arriving, and when the cutscene was over, my units were inexplicably and arbitrarily all right there, next to the tank once again, which of course promptly shot them with a tank shell. Yeah, sure, okay, makes sense. Much strategy. Very tactics.
Also, the only reason I can think of for a game to make me manually select each successive cutscenes to view from a storybook style menu is to obfuscate the length of what would otherwise be some really damn long cutscenes. At least if they had just made it one really long cutscene I would only have to press "skip" once instead of eight times.
I just don't get it. I want to like it SO HARD, but it is an incomprehensible mess to me. I just do not understand it.
I'd like to see the rest of the titles in the series be released for PC as well. Fantastic port.

Unreal Gold is a sci-fi fps made in 1998 by Epic Games, you play as an escaped prisoner on an alien planet, there are over 47 maps on single player and extra maps in the Return to Na Pali expansion pack, which comes bundled with this version of the game. There are several different types of aliens to shoot from shark-like creatures to huge titan beasts, there are also upto 13 different types of weapon with alt fire modes. As you progress through the game, you find new weapons and power-ups which can be useful, there are also ammo, armor and health packs which you have to use wisely to conserve resources. When you first buy the game, make sure you adjust the settings to your preferances and optimize the game to run best on your device, I recommend changing the graphical/audio settings, character models, controlls and interface settings before you start playing. There is also multiplayer and bot matches, which host about 20 additional maps, you can set up a match with your friends or if you don't want the fuss just start a bot match and practice, get a hang of the maps and weapons to learn while you progress.

I've played quite a bit of this game.
I bought it on the Holiday Sale after seeing some YouTubers play it and I've been in love with it ever since. Speedrunners is a surprisingly fun game that is fun for both casual and serious gamers, with the "Quick Match" or the "Ranked Match" multiplayer system. You can also create custom games and invite your friends to play.
While this game is incredibly fun and is totally deserving of the money, in my experience I have experienced a few glitches that actually cause the game to break and/or crash. These glitches are actually pretty hilarious (and they aren't too frequent for me), so I really don't mind them personally, it's just something for you to keep in mind before you make the decision to purchase it.

The game's weaknesses are mostly forgivable due to the strength of the story and worldbuilding and collectibles. I didn't run into any technical problems, and looking back at the reviews, I think they're a lot harsher than the game deserved. It's worth noting that Steam reviews are very positive, sitting a 82% rather than the critic average of 59%. I found the game engaging and interesting, and I thoroughly enjoyed messing with video game conventions of character interaction with walls.

I'm gonna start out by saying that I do enjoy and recommend the game overall, but we'll see some back and forth in the review.
I initially played this game on my Xbox One and loved it for about 15 hours before it got repetitive and boring, but after hearing the announcement of a Plains of Eidolon open-world feature I came back to the game but on PC this time. After playng for about 5 hours I had already gone further than my Xbox account, and I finally began collecting cooler weapons and Warframes. The movement in the game is extremely satisfying and, when combined with trying out new weapons or abilities, the game is really fun.
However, the game can get quickly repetitive. There are around 4 or 5 structures to missions and they get boring quite quickly. The only factors keeping me playing occasionally are making new Warframes and weapons, as well as helping out my friends. On top of that, Plains of Eidolon was a huge disappointment. At the moment it's merely a blank canvas waiting to be filled with actual content. This is made worse by the dreadful loading management. You have to stand in front of the gate to enter the plains for a good 40 seconds before it recognises what you're doing, and one time it took 4 minutes to load me into a story mission on the plains. My final complaint is that gaining platinum seems almost impossible because everyone in the market wants to gain platinum but nobody wants to buy anything, so there needs to be an alternative in-game method of gaining platinum, even if it has to be very slow so that the developers can still make money off of the game.
To conclude, I recommend this game, as it's very fun to play for about the first 20 hours, but it can get repetitive and stale very quickly.

I've got to do a full review here, because this is probably one of the best games ive ever played. The only other RPG I've been this engrossed in since childhood is probably Witcher 3. I legitimately am just looking forward to the end of my shifts at work because I want to just go back to playing D:OS2.
First, the side quests are super fleshed out and frankly revolutionary in a way that I hope sets precedents for future RPGs. Remember how we all praised witcher 3 for having a lot of side quests but none of them being simple mindless fetch-quests like in Bethseda RPGs? This game has one-upped that: the game is jampacked with side quests, none of them are fetch quests, and you have a variety of ways of completing them that can change how the quest develops and rewards you without the options being inherently wrong.
There are ways to fail the sidequests, sure, but there's also fleshed out ways of completing quests (read: It's not '"You get Dialogue B instead of Dialogue A because you clicked text Option B instead of Option A). You have unique ways that make the story of the side quest finish in unique ways which end in unique rewards. In fact, the way you complete one side quest can have a domino effect that can change other things in the game including the options you have to complete other quests. It makes the world feel alive and dynamic and I hope this becomes a RPG staple.
Second, the combat is exquisite. It's everything great about the tactical and in-depth customization Original Sin 1 had but better. New classes, a more balanced AP system, etc. Basically, you get four action points per turn that can be used to attack, to move, cast spells, etc. Typical S-RPG stuff. However, the depth of the tactics you can pull off is pretty much the best there is gaming. Just to give you an idea of how the combo system works: If you use a fire spell, the spot you hit will now be 'burning'. Walking over it will cause fire damage and set a burning DOT condition. Use a water spell? Well now it's extinguished! But there will be a steam cloud, and if you use lightning on it you can stun everyone inside that cloud. That's a small sample of what you can do: You can fly, teleport, ram, sneak, whatever you want through combat and the amount of combos and unique interactions you can find are limitless. It feels like every single 'quintessential' fantasy rpg archetype was lovingly crafted into the combat.
The game came out like a week ago and I already have 60 hours in it. All I think about when I'm at work is how much longer until I can play Divinity again. I haven't felt this way about a video game since I was a little kid. My main save has about 30 hours in it and I'm probably like 1/4 through the game (also got a 2nd save for the co-op). I haven't even touched Game Master mode (which is basically Dungeons and Dragons with full control of basically every asset in the game) and Arena (PVP) yet. I could see myself easily logging hundreds of hours on this game.
This is hands down game of the year and hands down one of the best games I've ever played. I had huge hopes for this game and was really worried it wouldn't live up to the hype. But this is hands down everything I could have wanted from a sequel to D:OS1. You're missing out if you don't get it.

Mass Effect 2, I think, is the best game in the Mass Effect Trilogy. In ME2, you still get missions by actually taking to other characters, rather than walking by them and over hearing them in ME3. ME2 has more of your conversations with your squad mates actually be conversations, rather than simply ambient dialogue in ME3.
ME3 had it merits, but ME2 was the overall better game.
Being that ME2 is older now and I'm mainly writing this because I'm currently replying the franchise again, I'm not going to spend a lot of time writing about the nitty grity details of the gameplay. But I do want to talk about things that should be much better.
1) Why is there no 'Gold' edition that includes all the DLC and content packs? Mass Effect 2 is several years old now, and no more DLC is being made for it. Even on Origin, there's no AIO type package. You have to buy the game, then buy the story DLC using the always stupid 'Bioware Points.'
2) Buying the DLC for ME2 is about as clumsy as it seems to get. You buy the game on Steam, buy the DLC from Bioware, install it outside of steam through self-installers, then access that DLC only if you've logged into the Cerberus Network in game with your Bioware/EA credentials. If you're not going to make an AIO pack, at least let me get all the content from one place with as few clicks as possible.

Full Version:
[This review has some minor spoilers about the game]
Well, if you're reading this, Valkyria Chronicles (or Senjou no Valkyria, in Japanese) has already picked your interest. Be it because some of your friends have, or because of the massive amount of people who liked it, because you like RPGs and want something fresh or because Sega has some broad range games that commonly goes on sale. Either way, VC is a prime example of how RPGs can still evolve and implement new things without sacrificing the story-telling.
STORY
The story revolves around a conflict between nations during the Second European War (EWII), in which nations of the Empire (East) and the Federation (West) battles between each other for power, territory and resources. One specific nation, Gallia, tries its best to remain neutral, but it is still taken amidst the conflict with the invasion of the Empire forces. Welkin Gunther, the main protagonist, is one of the inhabitants that is caught on this invasion in his home city, Bruhl, but with the guidance of Alicia Melchiott, the town watch captain, they manage to evacuate the city to the capital city of Randgriz. There, they join (compulsorily) the 7th squadron of the town's militia, and from then on you must complete some missions that end up engulfing the entire squadron against the Empire's best forces, including even a Valkyria, a being of mystical powers that can basically one-shot-kill tanks and is virtually invincible.
It has loads of references to WWII and Cold War in real life: alliances battling for oil (or, in this case, ragnite); wanting other nations to join their cause (and even deal with backstabbing); massive destruction weapons (did I hear nuclear bomb?) and, of course, the sense that stronger weapons and more soldier numbers meaning better army getting crushed with intelligence and strategy. Some Japanese elements are still there to soften the mood sometimes, but be sure, the story itself is marvelous.
Along those lines, an obvious love story evolves between Welkin and Alicia, but in a heartwarming and slow way instead of it being rubbed in your face every mission. Even if some plot points you can see from miles away, some are genuinely breathtaking (like one of your squad members that is killed along the main plot). The main story has some 20 chapters neatly divided as sub-chapters of a book, each containing a certain cutscene or sequence of dialogues... oh, and the book wasn't a figure of speech, you can even change tabs if you want to read more about the squad members, weapons, cities and even see some side events.
GAMEPLAY
I was really impressed when I read "mix of real and turn-based strategy RPG" on the game's description, but it's exactly how you play in every mission. Basicaly you are the commander who can spend command points (CP) to control individual units around the battlefield (that can suffer damage if nearby units or turrets see you while you move), but once you raise your sights to aim at the enemy, all enemy units halt their actions and it works like a 1vs1 battle.
There are lots of mechanics between my explanation, really: your unit consumes AP points (which differs from each class) to move around, and once it depletes, you'll be stuck; you can move units multiple times, but you must spend a CP everytime you want to move a unit, and as you select the same unit over and over, their available AP drops, meaning they're getting tired and will walk less further; you have classes that counters each other (shocktroopers deals lots of damage to less defensive classes like Scouts, but they also have less AP than Scouts; Lancers are good against tanks, but are slow and have low accuracy; Snipers deal tremendous headshot damage but are also slow and fragile; engineers can disable mines and heal tanks, but aren't good at the battlefront), along with RPG elements like status ailments and "orders" that can raise units status briefly. It's really complex, but the game introduces those mechanics little by little, so you'll have plenty of time to practice and master those. Just be sure to save inside missions, as some of them can easily take up over an hour depending on your luck.
THE GOOD
- Dual audio available with English subtitles
- The sense of danger and challenge of the missions
- Plentiful of things to do with EXP and money earned
- Combat feels balanced for the most part
- The story (and the satisfying ending!)
- Quite a few things to do and read besides the main story
- Around 20-30 hours of gameplay just for the main story
THE BAD
- No online play
- Some plot points are just rubbed on your face too much (yes, that member that dies)
- Not saving inside missions can lead to frustration due to bad unit positioning
- Luck is quite a factor to be considered in this game (from acurracy of shots to enemy unit spawn)
- Takes a little while for you to become used to the terms and political movements
- It feels like some missions must be started a couple of times to get the hang of what exatcly you must do and how fast to proceed
- I WANT A VALKYRIA UNIT TO OWN EVERYONE ELSE!!
OVERALL
8/10
An awesome story, equally nice combat mechanics, sense of challenge in almost every mission and the broad range of things to be done and accomplishments to... erm... accomplish, Valkyria Chronicles is a must for every RPG lover, or even those who don't like sole turn-based strategy games. Definitely worth buying even without any multiplayer (because, really, if it existed, each game would take up hours easily). Just keep your eyes peeled in case the PSP exclusive's Valkyria Chronicles 2 is ever ported to PC, because it's even better!!

All the ingredients for a solid game are here, but unfortunately I'm finding it a little frustrating. The stages are too small vertically. You play very close to the blocks, which means it's easy to toss the ball behind you accidentally, and the unbreakable blocks tend to be annoyingly in the way too often. I would also argue that you move too slow. Especially if you consider getting all the coins. Each block drops a coin down to you when broken, and each level shows you how many coins you've collected in it. Getting all of them in one stage is frustrating and takes a lot away from the fun of the game, because using power ups can cause blocks to break all over the place and you'll never be able to get all of them at once, not to mention the need to catch the ball. Getting 100% completion would be a nightmare.
Aesthetically this game is fantastic. Looks, sounds and feels like a 16-bit arcade classic. I would guess that the game was inspired by the SNES game Firestriker, because it's sort of a beefed up version of that, although not so much in terms of gameplay. I was actually really hoping it would be more like Firestriker, because that game did this sort of thing incredibly well, in my opinion. But the premise here is still good. And for the $1.13 I spent on it I'm willing to look past some of things I'd consider flaws and recommend it.

This game features one of the greatest engines ever made, the Unreal Engine.  Without it, countless games are nonexistant.
When this game came out back in '98 I was floored by the scenery.  Escape from the crashed ship and take a minute to look around the world, take in the rich pallet of colors and textures that add so much to the game.  Listen to the score, it's right up there with something by John Williams or Jesper Kyd.  A few years ago they released an Unreal collection that included a cd of the game score, which gets regular play when I'm driving.  I've spent many hours on this alien planet.  It has lots of replay value because of its four difficulty levels.  They don't just make the enemies stronger and your weapons weaker; they make the enemies SMARTER, stronger, and faster, and there's more of them.  There is not much story to the game.  You are a prisoner on the worst prison ship in the galaxy, you have no name, only a number, and the ship crashes on an alien planet.  Your goal is to survive and escape.  No dialog, no cut-scenes, the tutorial is in the manual and if you don't like the default controls you action map them.  Multiplayer is the godfather of Unreal Tournament and its sequels.  This one only has DM, player vs player with or without bots, or player vs bots.  And these bots can get just as brutal as the enemies in single player.
The game has few negative qualities to it.  If you look at it from today's perspective the polygons that make up the world and its inhabitants are obvious and they have no textures when you get up close.  According to an interview with developers, time and budget constraints prevented them from putting better textures on objects when you got up close.  What they did get right is the blood and gore aspect.  Shooting an enemy in the head can result in the head flying off and bouncing around while the body tries to stop the bleeding from the neck.  Explosives can render whole bodies (alive or dead) into bloody chunks that get launched across the room.  Try doing that in Battlefield or Mass Effect.
Bottom line: This game has stood the test of time.  It put time in the camel clutch and made time humble.  If you're stuck on a deserted island this is one of the 3 games to have.

I'm going to not recommend this game, primarily because it is just too short and has too many small issues with it; however, I do still think this is worth a play through.
In Murdered: Soul Suspect, you play Ronin; a not-so-cleverly named man who is dead and searching for his killer. Through the game, you will help some random ghosts in what is I think some of the most interesting gameplay, and run around in crime scenes solving hide-and-seek puzzle games. The major flaw in this game comes with the very short play time and annoying time wasting monster encounters.
Throughout the game you will have encounters with "daemons" who are your typical Metal Gear style pathed guards; they can only be killed from behind with a simple QTE and are more of a nusanse than actually being a challenge. By the end of the game, I went into the config and made it so they just didn't see me so I wouldn't have to fight them. It's not that fighting daemons is hard, it's just annoying and by the end of the game if you don't know where the escape rooms are you can just die if you screw up.
The final encounter is lame and very confusing, I had to look up the solution. Again, like the daemons, this wasn't because it was hard, it was because the prompt wasn't clear on what I should do.
The story has some decent writing in small parts. The noir monologue at the entrance to each game section is a neat touch. The two main characters are interesting, and there seems to be a decent about of background lore on Ronin (the PC). The collectables are interesting as they expand on the murder case and also include background about Salem (the town in which the game takes place). I have no idea if any of the lore is true, but it is nice they put it in. The hidden collectables are unique as they are just ghost/horror stories that have no connection to the main plot - its nice.
Over all I think the game is worth a play through if you can pick it up for under $10. There is enough there to keep you entertained for an evening and if you like ghost stories than you should have a good time.

People in other reviews say that it is like Mario Karts with legs, and they'd be right, when you're low skill.
Now this isn't to insult anyone who's new to playing the game, but when you've learnt all the mechanics, unlike mario karts there is a way to counter every single item you come across, only sometimes would you need another item to counter. Also unlike mario karts, items are not the largest part about it. There are 4 things that make you go fast 1: those boats that give you boost which you can use at any time 2: the bubbles that are in some parts of levels 3: If you have alot of velocity downward and you grapple you get alot of horizontal velocity 4: Same applies with number 3 but with slopes(stairs included) that are in the level.
3 & 4 is where I say that high-skilled players are separated from the low-skill that makes it unlike mario karts. Because most people who are new to the game don't know this(you should probably add it somewhere in the tutorial devs, or choose a different level that demonstrates these 2 well).  Anyways, these 2 important mechanics are what most of the useful tricks in speedrunners are basically derived from, it basicallys makes up the speed in speedrunners. Its these 2 mechanics that make it fairly different from mario kart, because in mario kart, without the items its basically who knows the map's parts and who's learned which kart is best to use and how to do the turns well(which isn't very in depth).
That's what I wanted to say about how this game is not mario karts. This game is extremely fun and very competitive. I've been playing it for at least a few hours every day. I've put 229.5 hours into this game, just the last 2 weeks I've put 21.9 hours(which is more than what other people writing these reviews as of now have even ever played).
Sometimes speedrunners is buggy, and perhaps it could use some more maps, but this game is top-notch, no doubt about it.

I have played many of the trucking sims out on the market for many years.  Then about a year ago I bought Euro Truck Sim 2.  Very quickly found that I enjoyed the realism in the driving experience and really appreciated the Dev Group's work on improving and adding more maps and trucks to the game.  So when American Truck Simulator was announced I didn't hesitate.  SCS has not let me down at all with this newest version of their work.  Many people will complain about lack of truck choices and map size at the moment.  Please put it into perspective,  It takes time to get licenses to show the actual different makes of trucks in this game.  Most companies want their equipment painted in the best possible light so SCS has to make sure to do their best work on every truck, not just looks but function and capabilities.  As for the map some are saying that the highway driving doesn't seem long enough but please realize when the full USA is complete it will take an estimated 1 hr or more of real time to go coast to coast.  This is because of the sheer size of our country.  At this point I have zero complaints with the game and am just patiently waiting for the new updates that will come.
I do have some things I would like to see in the American version of this game but will post it to Dev's.
P.S.  I am a real life OTR Trucker so if I can enjoy it then you can too.

Hand of Fate is many thing. It is a collectible card game, a deck builder, a board game, an action RPG, and a roguelike. It features a bizarre combination of elements and manages to make an excellent game with what it has. The CCG aspect comes from exploring new cards and unlocking the tokens, which is done by completing a certain requirement for each. You collect your tokens and whether you win or lose, you get the prizes inside. Which happen to be equipment cards for your own deck, or more encounters to unlock more cards, or to help you journey through each level. You get to build two different decks in this game, one featuring all of the equipment you can get, from simple weapons and armor, to magical gear in the form of weapons, armor, rings, helms, and artefacts. The second deck you build is the encounters deck. It features all the cards that you can come across in the board game element. From a poorly disguisted goblin who only wants to help you, to a dangerous river crossing, to being captured by lizardmen, and much more. Each encounter card can play out in multiple ways. Giving blessings at one time, to curses at another. Filling your pockets with food and gold, or stripping it away. The board game has you choosing which way you want to go, unknown encounter cards lay ahead while you move one card at a time trying to find your way to the exit to eventually face the boss of the level. Hopefully aquiring the gear from your equipment deck along the way, or piling on curses and misfortune as your food and health are stripped away. Moving your piece on the board will always take one food. If you run out you begin to starve. The action RPG elements come into play when your encounter happens to be against a monster, drawn from a deck that only the dealer has access to. At the start of the battle all the pieces are placed, and the cards your gear resides on descend over your character to equip him. Battle begins, arguably the weakest aspect of the game, but easily looked over because of how well everything else is done. A simplistic Arkham combat is used here. Only one attack, a counter, and a roll. With access to a weapon power or artefact if you have either. Early in the game combat is good and quick. As you get to the later levels and with poor luck combat drags on, mostly turning into a roll fest while you dodge enemies and wait for an opening.
If you survive all your encounters and make your way to the final boss of the level, either a Jack, Queen, or King then you win, opening all the new tokens that you have obtained for that run, the same happens if fate is not with you and you fall in battle. The tokens open to reveal new goodies, all of which you must see on the game board while playing to learn what they do.
While each element that is in play here may not be the best done version, how all of them come together into a wonderful game. Excellent presentation from the art work and writing on the cards, to the dealers narration, to showing your progression in the room you are in by the slow burning of a candle, and destruction of the area around you. Having put 17 hours into my first time playing the game has only made me want to go back in and unlock more cards that I have not yet seen, and my head races with ideas that could be expanded upon hopefully in a sequel. Every time I start a new level it feels like a short game of Dungeons and Dragons is about to begin, making my way through an adventure, the cards deteremining how the story goes.
if you like turn based RPG, just buy it, dont think twice, you wont regret and will love it.

A mixed bag of a breakout clone, but the sum of its parts ultimately makes it a good purchase.  DYA games tends to make very fun pixel games with an arcade feel and Strikey Sisters is no different. It has a nice, upbeat soundtrack, fun additions to the breakout gameplay with the spells and abilities added in, collectibles galore, and some truly interesting boss battles.  I also give the game credit for having full voice acting.  It is hit and miss in places, going at times too shrill anime, but...credit for trying, some of it is pretty fun.
Now, the mixed bag part.  This is a breakout game through and through, which means it has all the frustrations of hitting a ball over and over again to try and kill the last enemy hiding in a corner or the last block hidden in a corner.  That is incredibly lame.  Also, while the abilities and additions are nice, there aren't enough evolutions to remove the frustration.  Likewise, it's annoying that some enemies can just hit the ball away or hide with their back to the wall to prevent you from advancing.  Finally, you can get multiple of the less fun upgrades, of which only about half are really enjoyable.  Also, despite having collectibles, aside from the bestiary, you can't tell how many emeralds you've got, keys, or whatever from each stage.  All you get is an arbitrary percentage marker.
So, frustrations aside, do I recommend?  Well, yeah.  It's oozing with charm and if you like Breakout, you can do much worse.  Frankly, I like the arcade gameplay better than Wizorb or other Breakout contemporaries.  Buy it if you can deal with Breakout and all its issues because it's a pretty fun.

Choosing different units and then actually moving them in 3rd person view and aiming their shots makes for a more engaging experience than if you only watched from above like a godly commander. The level maps are really well designed as there are often multiple routes and you sometimes have to coordinate separate teams to achieve a goal. The art style is really nice to look at but a bit too clean for the war theme at times. Music is very good but the limited number of tracks start to feel a bit repetitive after a while. The characters are likeable and the story has enough twists to keep you playing. Its combination of war and fantasy is a bit goofy but mostly works in a JRPG context. This is one of the few games in recent memory where I skipped sleep on a weekend because I just had to play one more level.
A slight annoying thing is the lack of a quick restart option. Loading a game is fairly quick so it's not a big deal but the extra button presses to do it could've been avoided. I often restarted because when you start a level for the first time it becomes obvious very quickly if you didn't choose the right units or if you made a really bad move that you won't be able to recover from. It's also bit of a drag having to watch the computer play its turn at normal speed. A fast-forward option would've been nice. There are also some minor control issues like rotating the tanks and one outright level bug where climbing certain ladders in one of the later levels causes your character to fall though the floor endlessly. It can be avoided though but it's bothersome for sure. Generally though the controls work well with a gamepad.
I recommend the game but I can't say much on who I think would enjoy it most. Based on reviews and videos I saw, I really wasn't sure if I was going to like it. I've enjoyed a few JRPGs before but more for the stories and less for the gameplay. The story was engaging for me. I won't say it's the greatest story ever but I think it does enough to get you to care about the characters. Luckily, I enjoyed the gameplay just as much if not more than the story. I've already begun speculating how this game could be played by two players cooperatively and against each other. That tells me that the strategy gameplay is one worth exploring more in further games.

A rather simple, yet enjoyable, little game about a young girl forced into the Item Shop business by her missing fathers rather ludicrous amount of debt. Over the span of 5 weeks she must make ever increasing weekly payments to pay off this debt by stocking her item shop and hoping to make enough money through the sales.
While the base of this game is the management of the item shop in an attempt to make money, how you get stock is left up to the player. While they originally allow you to buy stock from the Merchant Guild, this will quickly fall away and you'll begin to dungeon delve with one of the various adventurers (starting with Louie the Swordsman) in an attempt to get large amounts of high priced items to sell.
This game is a balancing act, attempting to balance the amount of cash your selling things for in an attempt to pay your debt while also not overcharging for items and losing customers. On top of that equipment sold to your adventuring friends makes their gear within the dungeon better, so do you sell Louie that sword for 130% or do you charge him a mere 110% to ensure he buys it and gets a better weapon next time you enter the dungeon.
While not by any means a HARD game, its still fun and a good use of your time.

Even without the helpful filter of the nostalgia goggles this is a game that has aged exceptionally well; its gunplay is sharp, the AI is smarter than the usual gun-wank, the story is minimalist but compelling and a great example of environmental story-telling in a pre-Fallout 3 FPS. It's also something that is still a little unique for an FPS with no RPG elements, it's very much a shooter that plays like an adventure game, relying on all of that genre's tropes and cliches rather than those set by its doom-like predecessors.
Where the game doesn't hold up is in graphical fidelity; to be expected for a game made in 1998, but for a title that sold itself on the strength of its scenery and set design it's a little disappointing when you realize you can play it on two rocks ducktaped to a piece of glass so long as it was assembled after 2008. I suppose that's nitpicking though, the atmosphere is great and its not hard to see why the scenery was considered some of the best for its time.
The long and short of this review is get it, it's historically important and cheap even if it wasn't a fantastic game. The fact that Epic declined to continue making games for this series and instead focused solely on Unreal Tournament is one of the biggest disappointments in all of gaming.

Free Will: Illusion vs. Reality
I will try to deny plot spoilers in this discussion, and instead focus on generalities. Strictly speaking you begin Mass Effect 2 as Commander Shepard and due to some circumstances are bound to the illusive man to help save humanity and the universe by revealing and exploring ways to defeat the Reapers. Starting out you are immediately tied to the destiny of a group of individuals and are made responsible for the survival of the universe.
Of course it's implied multiple times that Shepard is the only one that can unite and save everyone. And so the responsibility is solely placed on your character. This is just the first choice that is denied you, the choice of responsibility. However that choice was made before even loading up the game, as you the player are already taking into your hands and putting on your screen a universe that you are taking responsibility for. Consent to become a savior is implicit in installing the game. It is your choice to play and when you play you are bound by the rules of the world you inhabit, the first one being that you must save the universe or doom it. That is your burden.
You'll like this game if: You enjoy space opera science fiction and like light bloom effects on literally everything. You may also enjoy the illusion of choice without having it or shooting black holes at people.

As someone who's played Elsword for a long time, I must note that Elsword has gone down a few leagues in the last few years in terms of playability. It's really fun and all, but it's absolutely lacking in endgame material. Endgame gear is a matter of "Do this single dungeon 50 times." as well as a general lack of leeway for unique setups in pvp. With the recent updates. I might as well note a few of my observations as well as widely accepted information from my peers who also play the game.
PVP is much more centered around stats than skills, and money is a key part of this process. Players without premium currency will find it practically impossible to hit over +8 "Enhancement" (The process of increasing equipment stats by a given % which increases in increments each level, from 3% increments to up to 40% at the moment) for their precious endgame gear unless they don't mind it resetting, or breaking (Which at that rate, you must spend premium currency to FIX the item.)
The max enhancement level is +12, which allows players spending cash to be infinitely stronger than those without it, seeing a 135% higher difference in stats (This is actual data as well.) To increase enhancement levels without risk of reset or breaking, players must spend a small fortune on "Fluorite ore" and premium currency ore that makes enhancement far easier. Players are known to spend up to 600$ just to get one item to +12.
Onto gameplay, in PVE enemies are usually just the same AI with a different model, and eventually you notice a very obvious pattern in the story that'd feel about as repetitive as Bravely Default was with its 5 worlds mechanic. Early game is actually the most unique part of Elsword, which is rather ironic with how bleak it quickly gets. In later areas, the main reason anyone desires to replay dungeons is to obtain ED, which is spent in the economy. The newest area, Elysion, is the only exception to this. Sadly, this is only for players who are 5 levels from the cap and finished a long story quest around the other regions with their usual "Copy-Paste" style of gameplay.
With economy on Elsword, everything is horrendously unbalanced. Every run in the final dungeon gives you around, 300,000 Currency. On the other hand, any costume piece will go from 40 to 600 Million currency. This doesn't include Ice Burner sets, KoG's gacha for Elsword. These sets, which are usually priced at horrendous levels, can cost over a billion for the accessories, and 5-6 billion for the sets. I wish I was joking about this but unfortunately as a player of over 4 years, I can't. To go back on this, that'd be doing about....20,000 runs to obtain an Ice Burner set. Endgame equipment is also given the same treatment, usually being about 1-2.5bil for the full sets.
Combos aren't nearly as fulfilling as they seem at first as you may quickly realize that the best combos are the shortest. In pvp, the meta is known for "Loops" an infinite combo where the player simply inputs the same command over and over to ensure you cannot be knocked down. With the +12 mechanic for players who can afford its insane costs, pvp is simply a matter of who loops who first, and whether or not they've the money to kill the other quickly with the loop.
For a beginner, Elsword is a really fun game, and I in no way condemn anyone for trying it. But the game's flaws are cleverly hidden until you go further in, and the results as I can personally say, are as unpleasant as it gets. Elsword was much more exciting years back, when it had the playability and focus more on skill, than the money you spent on making your gear too strong. Originally, the top enhancement level was in fact +8. I noticed the game started making a turn in the wrong direction for long-time players the moment +11 became the new max, and +12 later. It no longer had nearly as high replayability.

People in other reviews say that it is like Mario Karts with legs, and they'd be right, when you're low skill.
Now this isn't to insult anyone who's new to playing the game, but when you've learnt all the mechanics, unlike mario karts there is a way to counter every single item you come across, only sometimes would you need another item to counter. Also unlike mario karts, items are not the largest part about it. There are 4 things that make you go fast 1: those boats that give you boost which you can use at any time 2: the bubbles that are in some parts of levels 3: If you have alot of velocity downward and you grapple you get alot of horizontal velocity 4: Same applies with number 3 but with slopes(stairs included) that are in the level.
3 & 4 is where I say that high-skilled players are separated from the low-skill that makes it unlike mario karts. Because most people who are new to the game don't know this(you should probably add it somewhere in the tutorial devs, or choose a different level that demonstrates these 2 well).  Anyways, these 2 important mechanics are what most of the useful tricks in speedrunners are basically derived from, it basicallys makes up the speed in speedrunners. Its these 2 mechanics that make it fairly different from mario kart, because in mario kart, without the items its basically who knows the map's parts and who's learned which kart is best to use and how to do the turns well(which isn't very in depth).
That's what I wanted to say about how this game is not mario karts. This game is extremely fun and very competitive. I've been playing it for at least a few hours every day. I've put 229.5 hours into this game, just the last 2 weeks I've put 21.9 hours(which is more than what other people writing these reviews as of now have even ever played).
Sometimes speedrunners is buggy, and perhaps it could use some more maps, but this game is top-notch, no doubt about it.
the characters also amuse me. 10/10.

Ah, Soul Suspect. The trailer alone had me clapping my hands from excitement. However, there's a lot to say about the game itself.
The concept seems unique at first; a murdered cop who is forced to solve his own murder before he can pass on to the other side, where he can be reunited with his dead wife. It's not an angle you see often. That being said, the game feels empty when it comes to gameplay and the semi-original plot can't make up for it. It feels like all your abilities seem to have huge potential and you have fun playing with them for an hour or so, excited about what more you can do along the way. Then you realise that you're limited to distracting people with flashing lights and walking through a wall (but not all walls, only some walls, obviously) every now and again.
You also have the ability to possess people, which seems wicked awesome at first. You can possess pretty much anyone you meet and you have the options of mind reading or influencing them. However, the reality of possession is that you possess a person, read their mind and they're like "Oh man, it's sort of chilly today" or "I hate my job" and you lose interest pretty fast when that's all you hear.
In the end, I'm unsure about whether or not to recommend this game. It's visually pleasing, the voice acting is decent and the idea behind it is worth the time. But the final product is just not satisfying in the long run.
Murdered: Soul Suspect is another one of those games that you should get if it's 60-75% off, but it's not worth the full price. Overall, it's like a lukewarm bowl of pudding. It's not entirely done and feels a little lacking, but hey, it's still pudding in the end.

I have played many of the trucking sims out on the market for many years.  Then about a year ago I bought Euro Truck Sim 2.  Very quickly found that I enjoyed the realism in the driving experience and really appreciated the Dev Group's work on improving and adding more maps and trucks to the game.  So when American Truck Simulator was announced I didn't hesitate.  SCS has not let me down at all with this newest version of their work.  Many people will complain about lack of truck choices and map size at the moment.  Please put it into perspective,  It takes time to get licenses to show the actual different makes of trucks in this game.  Most companies want their equipment painted in the best possible light so SCS has to make sure to do their best work on every truck, not just looks but function and capabilities.  As for the map some are saying that the highway driving doesn't seem long enough but please realize when the full USA is complete it will take an estimated 1 hr or more of real time to go coast to coast.  This is because of the sheer size of our country.  At this point I have zero complaints with the game and am just patiently waiting for the new updates that will come.
I do have some things I would like to see in the American version of this game but will post it to Dev's.
P.S.  I am a real life OTR Trucker so if I can enjoy it then you can too.
