I was going to pass this game by as yet another boring card game until I looked at the screenshots and saw what looked like an RPG element. This seemed interesting so I bought it, and am quite glad that I did. Not only does it have a card game element, but also a board game element (like "Monopoly!") and a RPG element. This makes it quite unique and better yet, all of these elements intermesh nicely. On top of that the game is executed superbly, which is a testement to the game designers skills. The difficulty of the game increases at a frustrating, yet manageable rate. At first it seemed that the lack of a saving the game and keeping your items was a weakness, but in the end it was a strength. It made it mandatory to use different item combinations early in each new game to survive, which often produced unexpected results leading to an advancement path that I likely would not have otherwise tried. The crucial dealer character is well done and appropriately sarcastic and arrogant at times, and other  times cajoling and supportive of your efforts. That made his inevitable defeat most satisfying.  The final battle I thought was well done, whereas in other games it is a disappointing afterthought. I am still playing the game to round up the last few tokens I havent gotten and intend to play the endless mode from time to time for amusement. Be warned this game is highly addictive and you can expect to lose a whole weekend or week before you are satisfied. The only question I have is how long do I have to wait for the sequel?

An absolutely charming game. Roguelike real-time combat meets card game with an engaging campaign which may seem very easy at first, but soon enough ramps up the difficulty. You craft both your own deck and the dealer's and progress your collection through your interactions with the cards during play, unlocking new cards which are often thematic "sequels" of the card before it.
New conditions apply each round and the dealer adds in fixed cards for each campaign step, making you re-think your decks and what you need. You know you'll get a curse every level? Add a ring to your deck that raises your damage for each curse you're suffering - an example of many.
The dealer is your mysterious opponent, always with a quip ready for your struggles and he has you continually second-guess the nature of the game and he himself with droplets of exposition.
While I haven't tried Endless mode, I likely will, just to unlock every last card. Campaign alone is certainly worth the price.

Strikey Sisters is, at it's core, a simple brick breaking arcade game. But the package it's wrapped in as well as lots of neat little features make it something special.
The story is simple, retro video game faire. Two witch sisters lose their beloved pet and go about beating up monsters all over a fantasy kingdom to find him. It's very goofy and doesn't take itself seriously at all, which is just fine. Reminds you of something you would see in a 90's game.
The dialogue is fully voiced over to mixed results. The two sisters, as well as many of the characters, are enjoyable but many of them deliver lines with unusual pronunciation or tone. One jarring case is when a character's name is pronounced completely differently by two different characters. Another is when an actor's dialogue is clearly supposed to be interrupted but they finished their line as a complete sentence. I also learned that one actor played all the male characters. While that's a neat credit to have and some of his performances are fine, several are also weak and I think he was stretched too thin.
At the end of the day, the gameplay is what matters and that's where Strikey Sisters shines! You move back and forth to knock a ball up and break blocks like many classic arcade games. What makes this stand out is you play in an arena full of monsters that hamper your progress. Some are simply obstacles while others attack you in interesting ways. Killing these monsters give you a variety of power ups that either enhance your ball, yourself, or affect monsters in some way. Bosses also keep things fresh and are often invincible from the front, so you must get creative in how you'll defeat them.
The simplest little feature that makes all the difference is your attack button. This one button allows you greater control of your ball's trajectory than most brick breakers. Not only that, you can use it to attack enemies close by. Not only that, you can use it to block enemy attacks. Not only THAT, you can charge your attack to hit your ball with greater force that breaks blocks and kill enemies faster. NOT ONLY THAT, your charged attack can deflect enemy projectiles. which is incredibly helpful for taking down bosses! It's a beautiful example of simple innovation. I love it when games can make one little feature very robust and useful. I think of the jump button in Downwell.
Being that the gameplay is very simple, I find it a good thing that the game isn't overly long. I beat it (not 100%) in about 5 hours, and there's still unlockable levels and a bestiary to complete! I often found myself meaning to only sit down for a level or two, then found myself totally sucked in. I also found the difficulty to be fair and steadily increases throughout the story.
The entire game has a beautiful, pixelated esthetic and is supported by catchy synth tunes! There aren't a ton of tracks but enough for the map, cutscenes, levels and boss fights and they get the job done! The entire game gave me a lot of nostalgic, warm fuzzy feelings!
Overall, I highly enjoyed Strikey Sisters throughout. While I do have some production qualms, the game does exactly what it sets out to do beautifully. Credit also has to go out to the two brothers who made it. You guys created an excellent product that you both should be very proud of and you're officially on my radar now. This game is incredibly solid and, if you take everything you learn from the feedback, your next game should be fantastic. Great work to you both, and everyone else involved!

Recettear really surprised me, it came out quite a while ago seemingly from nowhere and it didn't get much attention. The game has very anime stylized aesthetics that will, In my mind somewhat unfairly, turn some people off to it right away, and the graphics remind me of the latest 2D Final Fantasy games. The game breaks down to you becoming a shopkeeper unwillingly and needing to buy/find/sell/and haggle in order to pay the bills and stop the bank from taking your family's house. The game feels to me like animal crossing in a way, as you can customize your store/item layout often placing things in the window to draw the attention of the people on the street, that and the fact that you start out having to repay a massive debt. The game has a very interesting dungeon system where you can hire adventurers that you take control of to go into these dungeons and fight monsters/bosses in order to obtain rare items for your store, the dungeons play out like the original Legend of Zelda game with that kind of fighting, and a  randomized dungeon each time you enter, making it less tedious if you fail the boss fights and or fail to escape. The game plays solid and starts out quite easy but almost immediately ramps up the difficulty making you have to be more cautious with haggling and be more efficient with your time if you want to keep playing. The game is fun and has very few drawbacks other than the rather sharp learning curve after your first few payments (and the dumb little girl who always tries to haggle you down below your bottom line), but even that doesn't detract from it too much as you keep your stock when you fail so you can start over with a leg up next time. My experience with this game was rather positive and it is VERY addicting, just like the games it seems to take inspiration from. If you can get it for a good price it's definitely worth your time.

The year is 1935, you are the small independant country of Gallia in Europa. To the East is the Empire, an autocracy nation and to the west is the Federation. Both nations are at a 2nd world war with eachother and both nations depend on a rare material called ragnite for their needs. Gallia happens to have rich ammounts of ragnite in their soils, and thus The Empire invades the small country for this precious mineral.
You take on the role as Welkin Gunther, who is in love with nature, who is the leader of squad 7 in the Gallian malitia, from here you can customise who is in your squad, level up a certain classes with xp, learn special commands, read the news and upgrade your tank and weapons.
All the characters have their own personaility, rememorable and are fun to watch.
Art style for this game is beautiful and unique, everything looks like it came out of an pencil sketch
Music is fantastic, not a single moment I hated any of the music
The gameplay involves a tactical view of the area of operations, where you can see you whole squad on the map and any enimies in their line of sight, you then use CP (command points) to chose one of your soldiers to move and shoot within the same CP, tanks however use 2 CP. One of the cataches is that whenever you use the same soldier within the same turn, their movement speed decreases each time you use them.
Speaking of PC ports, the port is fantastic, runs at a constant 60fps, has keyboard and mouse support and feels great.

After playing the excellent Bot Vice here on Steam, I was looking forward to seeing the developer DYA Games' next game. Now it's here, and while I think that Bot Vice is still the better game of the two, Strikey Sisters is worth checking out for anyone who's interested in retro action!
Strikey Sisters is a pretty fun game that could be seen as a mix of action games and classic brick breaker style games.
Your characters are stuck at the bottom of the playing field (can only move left and right), and your job is to destroy all bricks and monsters by using the ball that bounces around. You'll also find several power-ups and attack spells to help you. If the enemies get close enough, you can still also melee attack them. Just like in classic brick breaking games, you are not allowed to let the ball go off screen, you will lose health if you do, so you'll need to be careful to not let that happen.
+ Fun gameplay
+ Good pixel art
+ Good music
+ Two player co-op
+ Funny story and dialog that doesn't take itself too seriously. Cutscenes also have voice acting. It is not always that great, but at least the main characters' voice actresses did a very good job. I'm actually really glad that the devs decided to have voice acting both in this game and Bot Vice, because it just gives the game so much personality!
+ Generally it's a polished game, just what I would expect from DYA games!
- Can get repeative after playing a while
- There can be moments when the ball is bouncing around in the back of the stage for a long times before it comes back to you, and meanwhile you don't really have much to do. It can also get frustrating when there is one unbroken brick left at some tricky location and you keep hitting the ball for a long time until you finally get it broken

The combat is choppy, sometimes the AI just stands there taunting you or not reacting at all. I'm sure I'll find more as I keep playing but that's the most noticeable.
Conan Exiles brings some unique features to the survival, heres to hoping they're determined to iron out the bugs that pop up and keep adding content over the coming months. Brick breaker games have been around for a long time but you've never seen them like this before, welcome to Strikey Sisters.
From the get-go your strong attack will be your best friend. It will break bricks faster and reflect projectiles. Enemies will drop power ups and respawn until every brick has been destroyed. Power ups will come pouring down the screen, ranging from freezing enemies, lighting attacks, fire balls, bombs, and more. Not only will you need to collect power ups, but bricks will also drop coins which are needed to unlock treasure chests containing keys for secret levels and a monster catching ability. There is a cutscene and boss battle every 4 stages which are even more frantic and fun. Don't worry, missing your ball or getting hit 3 times only makes you restart the stage. The retro synth soundtrack fits perfectly with the charming pixel-art style.
DYA Games has done a fantastic job revamping an old time classic into a modern day action arcade brick-break breakout!

Man, I loved this game! This is from the same Team that made Bot Vice which I also really enjoyed.
The graphical style is similar with great pixel-art sprites and backgrounds. The gameplay is considerably different though. I found Bot Vice a bit more difficult too.
This one is a breakout/arkanoid style game where you smack a ball back and forth to destroy blocks while also fighting enemies and dodging their attacks. The goal in regular stages is to destroy all the blocks and then the remaining enemies who will keep respawning, trying to kill you, so long as there are still blocks on screen. You actually hit the ball with a slashing attack so you can control its direction if you hit it at certain angles. You can also charge your slash to hit the ball faster and also use it to reflect most enemy attacks which is very usefull.
Then there's a boss battle every so often where you only have to diminish the boss's health bar instead of destroying every block. Boss battles are alot of fun and can be a bit intense IMO. Some of them I had to retry quite a few times. lol.
It has a light-hearted story with voiced cutscenes which I found amusing. The scenes are mostly before you fight one of the bosses.
The soundtrack rocks too. I felt the need to pick it up off bandcamp almost immediately lol. They brought back the same guy that did Bot Vice's music.
It's even got a 2 player local co-op mode which is great if you have a buddy to play with! I've tried it both ways and enjoyed playing solo just as much personally. The main game's story lasted me about 8 hours and it took me another 2-3 to go back and collect all the achievements. I imagine I'll be revisiting it every so often since it's fun to play in short bursts.

Metro: Last Light ties into Metro 2033 so strongly, they may as well be the same game. Compared to the first game the gameplay is largely untouched just like the technical side and that's a great thing. Everything works just like in the first Metro; You run, sneak, shoot and scavenge your way through the Metro once again and follow Artyom's story further. This time though the gameplay changes a bit more drastically from level to level, since the story takes a lot of twists and turns that routinely get you in difficult situations with sub-par equipment. You can always rely on the tried and true basic gameplay concepts, but often you'll have to improvise a fair bit to accomodate the peculiarities of the level at hand and your current equipment.
All the technical strengths of its predecessor are still here in Metro: Last Light. The levels are just as gorgeous as ever, maybe even moreso. The sounds and animations breathe a ton of soul into the populated parts of the Metro and especially the lighting system makes even the most deserted tunnels a sight to behold. Trips to the surface shine especially brightly this time since there seems to be more vegetation around than last time.
Storywise, Last Light continues Metro 2033's story decently and brings the different factions more into the limelight. Again it delivers a relatively simple but well-written and well-acted plot that keeps you going throughout the whole game. And again there are a couple of curveballs that keep you on your toes not only in terms of surviving the hostile environment, but also in terms of understanding the fragile situation the factions find themselves in.
It's a worthy successor to Metro 2033 that expands on its strengths without rocking the boat too much. Another easy recommendation and a must-play for people interested in atmospheric shooters. Ranger Mode strongly recommended.

An absolutely charming game. Roguelike real-time combat meets card game with an engaging campaign which may seem very easy at first, but soon enough ramps up the difficulty. You craft both your own deck and the dealer's and progress your collection through your interactions with the cards during play, unlocking new cards which are often thematic "sequels" of the card before it.
New conditions apply each round and the dealer adds in fixed cards for each campaign step, making you re-think your decks and what you need. You know you'll get a curse every level? Add a ring to your deck that raises your damage for each curse you're suffering - an example of many.
The dealer is your mysterious opponent, always with a quip ready for your struggles and he has you continually second-guess the nature of the game and he himself with droplets of exposition.
While I haven't tried Endless mode, I likely will, just to unlock every last card. Campaign alone is certainly worth the price.

Some pretty severe balancing problems really hurt this game on the harder difficulties at the moment I write this review. It definitely seems like melee-heavy parties are not very viable. I've restarted three times now and reduced my party's melee investment with each restart and I've been progressively enjoying the combat more as a result. Basically, melee at least so far in the first act, do not have mobility skills they need to do anything. Attacks of opportunity require a trait investment, which is kind of lame. It doesn't help armored enemies mitigate a lot of melee damage and that getting magic resistance as a fighter is difficult, resulting in a lot of annoying CC from numerous enemies.
I've had to cheese a lot of my fights to win them (abusing conversation mechanics mostly) and it feels kind of bad.
The game is still fun, but I would advise doing research about party composition before investing a lot of XP.
Also, this game commits a lot of "cardinal sins" for me:
1. Persuading people down from fights...results in a net XP loss and no notable change in the story's outcome (at least so far); as far as I can tell, being a murderous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is the best way to play this (by far, even). Aside from meager barter prices I don't see a point in making a charismatic character.
2. You're encouarged to fight and kill trash for XP; at multiple parts in the first act instead of advancing the story like I wanted to, I was compelled to scour the area for more things to kill. If you like this, then this is the game for you. Reminds me a lot of Baldur's Gate in that regard.
3. Some party members, if you don't keep them on a short leash, will break quests for you by doing naughty things to NPCs.
4. Quests break...and there's no notification about it. It's basically a missing thread. It's kind of interesting this way, leaving you to figure out how to resolve the quest, but if there's no way to resolve it, you'll never know for sure. So be careful when you go murdering people who might be connected with a quest.
This is definitely preferable over Skyrim's "everyone is invulnerable" bullcrap, but I'd like to know when I've royally ruined everything and should reload.
5. A lot of game mechanics aren't forshadowed at all (one of the early fights has turtles which...explode for a ton of damage when you kill them, really great surprise when you have a lot of melee in your party) and you'll be reloading after you experience them.
6. Numerous boss weapon drops so far for me have been inferior to standard stuff I find in shops. It's funny (not in a way I like), this one notable enemy I killed dropped a dagger which had a "10% bleed chance" mod on it - and that was supposed to be the draw for me using it I guess? In a turn based strategy game, "10% anything" might as well as not be there. There are a lot of other lukewarm mods on gear that might as well not be there or do anything. I've been vendoring a lot of stuff.
7. Gold isn't super abundant, so you will be picking up pots, pans, and kitchen sinks to make by. I've never liked this as it's just absolutely silly and tedious.
Depsite my gripes, this is definitely a solid RPG and tactics game, at least the most of what we can expect from 2017.

That being said, it isn't without it's little problems.  For one, the combat in this game can be a mess and seeing as how I wasn't a fan of the Arkham style fighting in the Batman games, I don't find it very appealing.  There's no real sense of fluidity or a great deal of control, just mostly button mashing.  In many instances when I would have wanted to not attack or pron target or quickly dodge an incoming assault, I would find it quite unresponsive.  On top of that, if you're not a fan of RNG (random number generator) elements, then the random chance factor of this game is likely to make your tear your hair out on more than one occasion.  That being said, I still HIGHLY recommend this game because of its interesting concept and how very well presented it is.  Regardless of its faults, I find myself eager to continue playing again and again just to see what new things I can unlock and how well I can manage through one game to the next.
...Let's just hope that any sequel strengthens that issue with combat.

This is the first Steam review I have ever written, I normally wouldn't write them, but I enjoy this game so very much that I thought I would share my thoughts.
This game is, hands down, one of the most compelling roguelike-rpg-combat games I have ever played. It has a very tight core gameplay loop, it scratches that collectable itch, and the combat is fun, with enough mechanics to keep it interesting.
But let me speak to the one feature that really sold this game to me. The Dealer. God I hate that man. But I also love him. He narrates the game, he goads you, he encourages you, he hints at a story behind why you and him are playing the game, Every snide aside and every grudging compliment I feel like I earn, and when I defeat one of his cards I literally whoop with victory.
As for the RNG (random number generator for those not familar with acronyms) aspect of the game, I never feel like it was unfair, because you can choose which cards to include in your deck. For the past 3 games I was insta killed by one particular card. Am I complaining? No, I chose to include that card specifically because I want to unlock the next card after that. I like to intentionally make the hardest deck I can, just to see if I can beat it. Because there is that element of choice, I never feel like the game is unfair.
Finally, the difficulty curve. It is rather seductive. It lures you in the first couple of bosses, and then decides to smack you around a bit. I like it, I feel like it lengthens the game. The one issue I have is that I feel like it was way too easy on the outset, so I managed to get to the 10th boss with minimal losses. That could be just me, and it is taking quite a few runs to even see the boss I am currently on.
That gets to my final point, and only criticism, such as it is. I need more. I am worried I will be running out of cards to find, of things to see, and I need more. Fortunately the game seems very well set up to add content to, and I for one will be getting whatever the developers put out. I hope they support this game for a very long time.
I wholeheartly recommend this game to players who enjoy a good dungeon crawl, who like paying for their mistakes, and especially to those who love the feel of a board game, where you can look across the table at your opponent and think, "Time to take this jacka-- down. "

I shall now proceed to write unbridled and unambiguous praise for this game.
is a triumph. It is a triumph in gameplay, style, presentation, sound design, narrative, character development, exposition and content. The game combines the illustrious production values of AAA titles with innovative gameplay quirks usually found in more obscure indie titles. Yet, it doesn’t compromise for even an inch. It delivers a style that uniquely its own and that might not appeal to everyone, but it sure has hell makes an exceptionally appealing case for itself.
If you’re a fan of turn based rpg tactics like
or
you will often find yourself in a minority crowd. It is a rather specific genre that many mainstream publishers don’t even want to look at it. Sega however took a bold stance and had
developed and published. Not only is it a turn based rpg tactics game, it also breaks the mold on that genre to become a hybrid of turn based and real time. Part shooter, and part chess. The blend is so unique there is nothing quite like it outside of the series itself.
You control a small squad of soldiers. Each turn you’re given a number of action points. By selecting a soldier you expend the point and are given real time control of the unit. You can then move around the map. You only see enemy units on the map if any of your own units currently have a clear line of sight in that area, so you might run into unforeseen threats while exploring. When you’ve found your mark, you can hit the aim button and line up a shot. Your unit will empty a clip and then the enemy might retaliate, granted that you didn’t murder him in the first place. When moving, you deplete a movement gauge. When the gauge is empty your unit will be rooted to the ground and cannot move and you’ll be forced to expend an extra command point to move your unit. You’ll have to take range into account when moving. If you run out in enemy crossfire you’ll most likely lose your unit in the next turn. Additionally, units come in different shapes and sizes. Scouts are fast and nimble, but generally miss the firepower and endurance to break enemy entrenchments. Shocktroopers are the opposite of scouts. They tire much faster, but pack a serious wallop and can take one too. Lancers specialise in destroying enemy armour units, and the engineers provide support to your own tanks and troops. The sniper unit does what it says on the tin; it takes out single units with pinpoint accuracy.
However, your units are all unique, each soldier is a character with its own traits and abilities. You develop their talents by letting them perform in the line of duty, and by training them by expending experience points. You also have to equip them with new and better gear. You’re always busy with maintaining your army, be it out in the field or back at base; a commander’s duty never ends.
The missions are also very well executed. Most maps feature a unique obstacle that needs to be overcome. This keeps the gameplay fresh as you make your way through the enemy ranks. You’ll fight in the desert, the streets, beaches, forests, canyons and in fortresses. The variety is excellent and you’ll quickly learn to adapt you tactics and squad accordingly.
Speaking of the commander, the game’s story focusses on Lieutenant Welkin Gunther and his squad of militia men and women. The small nation of Gallia is caught amidst a continent wide conflict as the eastern Europan Empire invades and begins to violently subjugate the nation. Welkin and his fellow countrymen are drafted into service to repel the invaders. At the same time they discover important clues about the country’s history and its former rulers: The Valkyria; near mythical people with incredible powers.
The setting draws parallels with our own Second World War. Complete with ethnic scourges and totalitarian ideologies. Furthermore, the game takes its time to give you exposition. Many of the secondary characters get room to develop alongside the main man and lady. Most stages are bookended, with intro cut scenes beforehand, and an outro afterward. All cut scenes are fully voiced by an anime competent cast, so they’re familiar with the style of material and do an excellent job at conveying the moments the best they can. Even when the natively Japanese expositional style doesn’t exactly suit the moment. I’ve never found a need to switch the voices to Japanese. This is one of the key points where
scores. Its approach to its narrative is not like a Hollywood movie like
, but more like a TV series, like
. It takes its time and lets you experience it at your own pace.
The entire game is presented in the form of a journal. Ever chapter takes place on a set of pages, where every ‘photo’ represents a cut scene, and every map equals a stage. You can flip through the journal’s tabs to find the entries on each separate character and other glossary entries. It’s a great way of presenting the story and its lore and mythos. You’re free to explore, or never even look at it.
The book is a neat way of presenting the game, but the real captivator are the graphics. The characters and environments are fashioned in an extremely stylish and gorgeous watercolour and pencil sketch manner. Not only does it suit its anime tone, it also stands the test of time. Even now, seven after its PS3 release, the graphics hold up and will probably hold up for a long time coming.
Accompanied with the visual package comes a very smart and elegant sound design. Every sort of bullet impact has a distinct noise, so you know when your unit is in direct danger, even if you can’t see the origin of the gunfire. The music is a romantic, tense and sweeping score that really underscores the game’s every moment. From the tense high stakes cover shootouts, to the emotional and heart wrenching moments, that despite of all your tactical prowess, will inevitably befall you.
These moments are where game is at its strongest; and where the art, gameplay and sound work together in a perfectly orchestrated and coordinated union that not just elevates the game at hand, but the medium as a whole.
seizes the player for a unique experience that will change the way RPG tactics, narratives and presentation are perceived in video games

With 271 hours played, i feel comfortable in my knowledge of this game, and i feel ready to make a "review" of it. (note, the reason i call it a "review" is because it strictly is not one, it is more a summary of content)
Let me start of with this: i have not played Crusader kings 1, i also have played all the other contemporary paradox g-strategy titles, (including the somewhat aging Victoria 2 (which is great btw)) so this will be from the perspective of someone who has a good deal of experience in the different games.
Now, CKII, A game of thrones? well, other than the fact that a mod exists for that, yeah, that is the best way to describe part of this game.
You are a Medieval count/duke/king/emperor, (depending on who you start as) and have challenges to face that befits your station, as a count, you deal with the threat of the much larger kings, and in many circomstances a duke that wants your stuff, intrigue, in terms of.. well, killing the sod, is an option, improving relations is one, play the long game, and marry his daughter(or son, i dont judge) or go to war, claim your right to rule.
As a duke you deal with your somewhat unruly subordinates, often very few of them, and other than that, your real enemy is the king or emperor. You want to become one! And the king stands in your way to greatness.
Ally other rulers, use intrigue, once more, marry, make your child ruler, there are many options.
Now, on to the battle system, where i will start with talking about technology: It increases in %ages, instead of unit changes, as is the usual with EUIV, and the upgrades are less game changing than in vic 2 (dig in cap hello) but the most important in terms of millitary is the retinue upgrades (and the demesne upgrades, but that does not have to do with war, so i dont talk about it here) A retinue was a medieval following, you did not yet have (often at least) professional armies under the command of the ruler, every single lord had a personal and a land based army, the land based one was often on more or less lease to the Ruler, in defense of the realm and whatnot, in this game the personal retinue is a personal Army, separate to the Levy (or land based) army, the limit of which can be increased by technology.
Anyway, the combat is (farily) simple, you have three parts to your force, the right, the left, and the center flanks. each with a commander, who each gives their combat modifiers to their respective force, other factors that play in are Attacker/Defender, Terrain, Straight crossings, boat landings, the like.
Every territory you have or conquer is part of your Demesne, or Held land, each territory holds a number of "holdings" which include Churches, Towns, and Castles (baronies) each with their own need for upgrades, people to keep happy, and different rewards to be gained, Castles provide large levies, towns provide cash cows, and churches provide faith, gold and levy, in my experience, i go for towns in most provinces and go for castles in the ones with higher limits of holdings.
You have a demesne limit, this is based upon your stewardship skill, wife (or husband)'s stewardship, and technology, you start seeing minuses to tax income and the like if you go over it, but dont be afraid to do so, it can sometimes save your hide.
Now i wont say much more, as i would have to get into expansions, but ill be safe to say, there are tons of events, religions, and effects based on that, Crusades happen, Jihads happen, and great holy wars (for other religions) happen.
This is a game with a steep learning curve, so dont be discouraged by losses, it takes some time to get used to.
Sieze your birthright lord, for you can rise to greatness. Rise Imperator, for your time has come. Rise Pagans, for riches untold. Rise Raja, for lands untold.

Crusader Kings 2 is, at its core, a GRAND strategy game. The world is massive and massively detailed, and the possibilities are endless. At the time of writing this review I have about 315 hours logged in the game, and when you consider that I am just the type of person who can rarely log 100 without getting bored, that is saying something.
The focus of this game is to build your dynasty in feudal Europe, but the game also include some parts of Africa, the whole Middle East, and India (only playable with the Rajas of India DLC). The timeline for this game is truely massive, with just the base game you can play from 1066 to 1453, just over 400 years. In that time you will play as a single ruler, then your ruler's heir, then their heir, and so on. This is a game about forging your path into the history books. If you want to play as a Viking and conquer India, you can. If you want to play the manipulating vassal of the Holy Roman Emperor, you can do that too. There is almost nothing you can't do.
If you get tired of conquering the same old Afro-Eurasia again and again, then there are always mods. CK2 features a native system to easily activate and deactivate mods, as well as Steam Workshop support. In addition to the well crafted framework for mods, the modding community around this game is enormous. For instance, the Game of Thrones mod. A full overhaul to set the same Feudal Dynasty simulator into the world of Westeros, and that is just one of thousands.
Overall, this is my second favorite game of all time, right behind Europa Universalis IV, another title from the same developers. This game is one of the best I have ever seen, and the devs are still releasing patches and massive updates.

I had bought this game on a recommendation from a friend of mine; telling me that I wouldn't regret it. I didn't. This was by-far the greatest $19.99 I've spent on Steam to date. The characters are charming, and the gameplay get more challenging as time progresses. 11/10 would buy again.

+ Conan is VERY similar to ARK Survival Evolved in many aspects. If you've played ARK you should be able to easily understand how to play. In comparison, instead of dinosaurs you are fighting a large array of mythological beasts.
+ Visually the game is gorgeous, and quite stunning for a multiplayer game. (I was playing on Ultra)
+ The Map / World is HUGE, you can spend many hours exploring the world.
+ Very challening. The game is setup so you star in the south-eastern corner, and as you slowly progress to the north-west you will find more difficult foes which can track you down from a distance and are impossible to outrun. You really have to plan accordingly and build up your gear before venturing out.
+ Great crafting system (again almost identicle to ARK), where you earn experience from gathering/killing monsters/building stuff, and when you level you can improve your character and learn new crafting recipes.
+ Full nudity (you can even choose how long your slong is)
+ Lots of interesting creatures to slay
+ Very intuitive building system which let's you build great looking homes or bases easily.
+ The combat system is decent. It mainly involves swinging a sword wildly, but you can also block with a shield or shoot arrows from a distance.
- The game is very demanding even on high-end PCs, so you may experience frame drops in certain areas or even freeze for a few seconds.
- I've heard that multiplayer servers have quite a few lag /  rubber banding issues. Even on a single player server hosted on your own PC you will get some moments of lag or a few seconds where the game will just freeze.

Altogether this is a pretty cute slight twist on a brick-breaker style game.
Two things stand out as not-so-great, though.
There is a "power attack" where you hold the button to charge, but releasing does not attack.. an entirely second button press is necessary and constantly mashing and holding and tapping was kinda un-intuitive from what one would expect from normal gameplay tendencies and design.. not a huge one, but it was oddly annoying.
Second, the voice overs are incredibly unnecessary and downright annoying/bad. All of it is constant and lame pop-culture, fourth-wall breaking, etc.  Which isn't bad in and of itself, but bosses, for example, say their one or two "hilarious" references EVERY TIME they use an attack. The little bits of story are delivered via dialog and cutscenes of sorts, and is decently done, but so tacky and 'humor' focused that I just skipped it.
Honestly without the attempted humor that falls flat I'd recommend this more strongly, and all in all it's my feeling that it takes away from the game rather than add to it.
Sometimes there are too many projectiles and moving bits on screen such that the ball becomes utterly lost, but overall it's pretty fun. I'd liken it to Wizorb and that sorta thing. I didn't try the local co-op, but that's an option.
Ultimately I'd recommend it for what it does well - a pretty tightly controlled block breaker with a few twists - spells, attacks (you can charge-up and reflect enemy attacks, giving you more options to break/damage than just the ball(s)), even if the game is hindered a bit by a super over-the-top and bad attempt at humor, unnecessary voice overs that don't add anything, and the same tired, overdone constant barrage of stupid pop culture - repeated every few seconds by each boss to the point of ad nauseum.

I have never played any of the prior Farm Frenzy games except the demos. FF4 is a surprisingly addictive game. I am used to buying and playing high-budget AAA games and playing a "casual" game like FF4 is a different experience for me.
I was introduced to "time-management" games recently and I am enjoying this genre because it requires a bit of fast-paced thinking, not just clicking.  FF4 can get a little hectic and it takes a while to get through the entire campaign. It is very difficult to collect all the Steam Achievements due to how many rounds there are in the entire campaign.
As many reviewers have noted, the broken English in the game used is pretty bad. It is a bit distracting if you are trying to immerse yourself in this game.  How hard can it be to find one American editor to clean up the broken English?
The sound effects are good and functional. The cartoony graphics works for this game.  Again, my biggest criticism is the poor English being used. I am not a grammar Nazi, I simply object to what appears to be laziness on the developer's part to find someone who knows conversational English to edit the text.
Aside from that quibble, I have no regrets getting FF4. As usual, I wait for a 66%-75% sale before I buy as to minimize the risk of paying money for a bad game. Yes, I know Steam does refunds but with all the games I have and available today, I am simply not into paying full retail price for most games.
FF4 is a cute but challenging time-management/strategy game.  Don't let the cutesy graphics fool you. It does require some strategy to get through to the very end. I highly recommend FF4.
UPDATE: I still prefer FF4. It is still the best version of the FF. I tried the sequels after FF4 and I really disliked the style and the mini-games. I was greatly disappointed in them which reinforces my love of FF4.

This unique ball-breaking puzzle fantasy action game is basically Arkanoid meets Popful Mail (or insert some other classic, charming Japanese action-RPG). It's fun, addictive & gorgeous... but

I USED to have some slight issues, but they've all been cleaned up! Now the bounce physics & collision seem fair, predictable... they seem as good as they possibly could be. There's no more times when the ball will go flying in seemingly the wrong direction when you hit it while moving. There's no more instances where the ball seems to clip on corners and fly off in surprising ways. There's even a better drop rate for items like recovery chickens, and they even tweaked the amount of hits it takes to bust blocks in single player or multi player modes to improve the pace of each match and cut down on the tedium early on where you just want to destroy blocks to get some breathing room. Rounds no longer feel like they last a tad too long. This is now super polished and genuinely seems like an ideal version of the game they wanted to execute, and we all wanted it to be.
:)
The player controls are really fantastic, and its one of those games where it's just fun to control the main character of your choice. There might be
of a learning curve here, but after short while, this goes from "pretty good" to "super fun and addictive". It can get difficult in places (at least until you learn to always prioritize ball return instead of going for power-ups), and you may take awhile to focus on the ball when there's VFX and particles going off everywhere during boss fights, but there's always lots of opportunities to get back in the game thanks to the power-ups enemies and blocks drop anyway. There's no big penalty for failing in the first place (just instantly try again). Its one of those games you end up just playing a bunch without noticing. Even when I lose, I'm finding myself going right back and retrying stages.
The main mode is also a bit of an "RPG Lite"-style design. With a world map and location "nodes", and a simple premise about going to find your pet presented via cute little cutscenes with sharp, funny dialogue. Its the kind of thing I wish WAY more arcadey games have, since I dug this kind of thing in games like Mario Tennis Power Tour for the GBA or Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes. Its super welcome to see Srikey Sister also frames its arcadey block-breaking action goodness in a mode like that :)
Basically, Strikey Sisters delivers some big, BIG fun. It sports some really gorgeous faux 16-bit sprite art (no lo-fi, minimalist crap pixel art here!), and absolutely bleeds 90's Japanese game charm (the voiceover work even recalls charming 90's anime too!). Its also got some rocking chiptunes. This is just a really good design, whether you want some arcadey fun for a few hours or to just pick-up-and-play (and lose sometimes, and try again, and again, etc.).

So after reading the reviews.  I decided to try this game out to see if it was truly Pay 2 Win.  If you are on the fence because of that well I will tell you right now this game is not pay 2 win.  There is actually only two things that you can pay for that will give you a direct advantage over other players.  Those are Patron status(monthly sub) and Apex.
Personally I think if you are going to stick around and play the game for a while you SHOULD subscribe to the game.  If you are just going to be a freeloader then I don't think you really get an opinion.  Secondly,  the subscription doesn't automatically equate to you becoming a PvP monster.  You still have to put in the time for character development just like other MMOs.
Apex is the only thing that is sold that can give you a direct advantage.  Problem is it costs 100 dollars per item just to get buy, in gold, the items you would need to to farm the materials to get the end game stuff.  If you still insist on pay cash for the truly end game items it is 350 dollars per item.  BTW,  both of those figures don't include the upgrades.
Or the cost should you blow your item to pieces trying to upgrade it.
Secondly,  The Auction House isn't over run with end game items.  I've litterally seen the same items on the AH for several days now.  So they arn't getting bought up.
So,  The game really isn't that easy or cheap to pay 2 win.
Really,  The people who are kicking♥♥♥♥♥in the game paid attention to the economy and the crafting system in the game.  If you are smart enough you can actually look in there and see that YOU can craft the end game items simply by playing and collecting the materials.  WHICH ARE NOT PROVIDE IN THE CASH SHOP.
So what really is the biggest horse crap reason you shouldn't play this game?  Well the fact is unless you want to constantly grind mobs for coin purses to make 'okay' money then you are going to need land to create materials for crafting.  Which can either correlate to end game gear materials,  selling materials for gold, or grow materials to create packs.
BTW,  land is at a premium in this game.  With the exception of a few little scraps that are missed out there most of it is taken up.  To get a decent plot is going to cost you some serious gold.  since it is a limited resource.  It'll really chap your♥♥♥♥♥  when you walk in to a housing area and realize that a large portion of it is owned by the same person or guild.
So in reality the game is not P2W in the least.  While there are avenues there that can increase the speed of getting to the end game players still have to grind their♥♥♥♥♥off to make it there.  And if you are smart and can work this games economy you actually can do better than a player who payed the cash to get to a point where they have a powerful character but still doesn't know the ends and outs of the game.  Essentially,  you can make bank in game off of the people who are paying 2 win,  because they have to covert it in to gold to buy your items.
Really,  the only people complaining about P2W,  don't understand the economy and probably got destroyed in PvP because they either suck at it or don't understand the economy of the game.   Like I said the biggest pain in the♥♥♥♥♥is getting the land you need to create the materials that you and everybody else needs,  including the people paying cash to get ahead.

I've been thinking what to write about this game for a while. Let me just start by saying that when I first tried it, I disliked it. I started it directly after the original Mass Effect and I noticed several changes. The RPG-ish system from the first Mass Effect game changed a lot. The game is more shooter-like, the inventory doesn't exist anymore, you suddenly need "ammo". All these changes made me very bitter about this game. But I continued playing and soon began to get used to this system, maybe even prefer it. You don't have to freak out every time you're nearing the item limit for your inventory like in the original ME. The combat is more intuitive and requires less franctic running around. The ammo thing, you can get used to it, at least the weapons don't overheat anymore. The only downside I found was the overly simplified skill system. Not bad, but I preferred the original one.
Story-wise, the game is superb. Not because of the main plot (which is also quite good), but because of the characters. I rarely find any games that include characters this life-like and believable, with great voice acting and consistent character. The customization options for your character (Commander Shepard) are also very good, no complaints there. Music is also very well-done, atmospheric and memorable.
There is only one thing I dislike very much about this game - the DLC system. Unfortunately, you can't buy the DLC here so you have to use Origin. And the DLCs are quite expensive and essential for the story.
To conclude - buy this. I don't think there is any other game on Steam I would recommend this much. For 20 Euros, you will get a memorable space adventure with rich story and characters and a great gameplay and music.

For anyone who is a fan of medieval combat games, Chivalry is an absolute must. This especially holds true if you are a veteran of the Mount & Blade games. While you lose a large degree of the customization that M&B gives you, Chivalry's combat system is vastly superior in everything except archery. The real-time blocking beats the arrow-key based directional blocking that used to drive me up the wall when playing M&B. Chivalry doesn't have any real Single Player content, sadly, but the multiplayer is quite fun and the Team Objective missions add just a hint of story and strategy to the game.
Pros:
+ Good combat system. It's challeging, but beats any other medieval combat systems I've seen to date.
+ Solid graphics and performance overall.
+ A fairly authentic assortment of weapons.
+ Amusing humor in the voice acting.
+ It's generally fun to play once you get the hang of it. That said, it can also be really frustrating if you approach it the wrong way.
Cons:
- Some players find ways to exploit the combat system in annoying ways. That's fairly typical of any game.
- Customization is mostly limited to color schemes. Doesn't affect gameplay, but I'm a sucker for good customization.
- The community is pretty bad, particularly in how much they constantly complain about the devs.
- The game is still kind of unreliable in terms of crashing, though it's far better now than when I first bought it. When I first bought it, it was the most unstable game I owned. It might still be, but it isn't near as bad now.

I can't decide if the story of this game did or did not make up for things I disliked.
I enjoyed the side stories and as someone who likes searching every nook and cranny of a world I enjoyed hunting for the extra pieces of evidence and items to find the stories. Sometimes it was frustrating having to be standing right next to something for it to have the option to interact with it but most of the time it was solid.....except once where my game glitched and I had to reload before it would let me interact with anything again. I was also a little annoyed that we couldn't revisit investigations. Again being someone who likes to be thorough, when I noticed I'd accidentally missed a clue out of an investigation you can imagine who annoying that stain on the record was when I realised I couldn't revisit it to find the clue I'd missed. Could not have some "Recall Investigation" feature been added?
My main gripe about the game was the combat system against the enemies. Using a mouse and keyboard, I really disliked how they used the wasd keys and a left or right button click to dispence of enemies. If I was in a panic, I would have to wait around for ages to go through the malarky of it again hoping I don't miss-click or press the wrong key again. I didn't feel like it was a very rewarding system in that respect and just frustrated me more than anything. The enemies were just an annoyance rather than a "Alright! Lets deal with these evil demons!"
Little disappointed with the ending. I feel like you found out only half of the story...the twist of who the killer was, I thought, was very interesting but they didn't go into it enough at the last minute. I felt through the whole game we didn't have a clue who the killer was and at the end they just went "Hey lets have this person". I don't even think I understand why the killer did it. I understand she was murdered for accusing witchcraft...but why had she accused them in the first place? What was her reason for that? The bell didn't really have much significance either. I just feel a bit underwhelmed. I also never appreciate a game which doesn't allow you to skip the credits!
Overall, I am glad I played the game (even though it probably doesn't sound like it!) but it was a little....meh. I don't think I'll be playing it again in a hurry to find things I missed.

This game builds on Mass Effect in every way. The critical feature of the series is save file transfer, where decisions you made in previous games have an effect on the later games. If you are just getting into the series and looking for gameplay over story, I would recommend this over Mass Effect. If you prefer a story, you really should play Mass Effect first.
This game is more action oriented than the first. Gone are the cooldown periods of guns from the first game, instead weapons have 'thermal clips', which are basically ammo in a gameplay sense. No thermal clips, no firing. Abilities also share a short, common cooldown, rather than having longer individual cooldowns. One downside is you are restricted in what weapons you can use based on your class, unlike the first game where you could at least use un-skilled weapons at a penalty. You do get the ability to choose an additional weapon class later in the game.
I fully recommend this game.

Right, Crusader Kings 2. This game is a masterpiece of a grand strategy sandbox. You play as the head of a medieval dynsasty, and must guide your family over the centuries towards prosperity and glorly. I will attempt to describe the game without going into the complex game mechanics, which I highly recommened you watch some youtube tutorials and chech out the CKII wikia to understand. If i went into detail about these game mechanics, this review would be far to long.
Crusader kings 2 is a vast historical sandbox in which you can play any character/culture/faction and do anything. Want to play as a viking warlord and turn the germmanic (norse) faith into a modern religion rivaling christianity? You can do that! Want to break up the Holy Roman Empire? That's doable. Want to revive the Persian empire AND the Zoroastrian faith? Incredibly difficult, but it can be done! Recreate the Roman Empire and reunify christianity? Yup, totally doable. Want to create a Jewish kingdom of Israel? Challenging, but possible.
The point is, you can do nearly anything in this game. You can try to recreate history as best you can, but even that takes effort. Half of the fun of this game is seeing what weird things happened while you weren't paying attention (like a successful Islamic invasion of France). No playthrough of this game will be the same. The replayability is endless. I've sunk in hundreds of hours, and will likely sink in hundreds more.
Are there problems? Of course. The battle mechanics are a little wonky. The AI is not always very bright (though they can be rather clever at times). Court intrigue and and assassinations need some work. Current versions (as of 28/12/2014) have given rise to oddly stable massive blob kingdoms, though not as bad as some previous versions. And some other nit picky details.
Overall though, this is a brilliant game. Especially because 10 hours in you realize you're plotting the deaths of your 8 year old nephew so you can inherit his land and titles.
Just... buy this game. I also recommened you at least buy The Old Gods DLC, as it pushed that start date back to 867, and adds a lot of depth to the pagan religions. It also allows you to play as VIKINGS, and they are a blast to play as. Especially because now you can sacrifice THE POPE to pagan gods if you manage to capture him. Sword of Islam is also good, though you can do without Rajas of India unless you want to play in India. Way of Life is fantastic, and adds more depth to roleplaying and characters, and isn't that expensive. Charlemagne isn't bad, though the start date isn't as interesting as 867, and Charlemagne's story triggers are a little wonky. Still fun to screw with history by preventing his rise to power, however. The game regularly goes on sale, but even at full price it is worth buying.
If you buy this game, you will get hundreds of hours of entertainment out of it. You may even learn some history while you are at it!

"The big space mess" lacks everything. Game design, development, art, producing, in every way, this game is baaad. This is the kind of game you would have expected from a beginner developper. As a "space shooter" demo, it is fun. As a full  comercial game, the joke isn't. There are good ideas here: the bonuses are well thought, the animations are great, but there is soooo much to complain about: The introduction is horrible, the gravity engine from unity is so underexploited, the story board is not existent (even tho it's the game's big selling point for some reason), the environment is sooo WTF, the game is soo unbalanced, Usibility-wise the game is horrible, same thing psycology-wise, the language menu is useless and i could continue on and on...
But the thing is this: It is not a game to play. It is a game the developpers have made in order to improve -or at least it looks like it-. It is the kind of project, we, developpers, do for our own, and have never the intention to sell to public. Selling is exactly what they have done.
Normally, i don't like to give a hard time to indie developpers, our games are not perfect and could easily be done better. It's not about giving a hard time to the developpers, it is about getting things right! As a developper myself, i cannot recomend to buy a game that never should had passed Steams approval -at least in this form-. I would enjoy playing it and gived a positive feedback, if it was what it should be: a free Demo. Now, this is not a full game, and even less a game worth an euro. There are hundreds if not thousands of indie games that are soooo much more fun and worth than this one, and still cost less or even nothing.
It is imposible for me to recommend this game. I shouldn't be on Steam, and it shouln't be sold.

While I was initially turned off from the game, because it performed very poorly, I have since re-bought the game, at full price even, as I had an itch to play it and was informed it worked better than it did.  I can thankfully say, that this is worth the $20 and works great now.
This is a review for people who don't know what this game all has.  Keep in mind, I am not an anime fan in the slightest, because of this, I'm very happy that there's a skip storyline option.  Something to note on this though, it doesn't skip introductions and outros for episodes, but it does kill all the filler before battles in the story.  You'll mostly know what's going on with the story because of this, but it does drag on.  A nice option you have with it being on PC, is you can alt-tab while it runs the story and the game will continue to go.  This is great for those especially annoying outros.
As for the game itself...ho-boy, there's a lot of content.  I've played this game pretty religiously in the past, I think the last time I beat the hardest boss I clocked in 104 hours or so.  There's a lot to this game if you really want to dive in, the story itself will take about 30-45 hours depending on how much you feel like grinding or get side tracked.  There's two story modes, one being really rushy and not that interesting, but still a nice addition and the regular campaign, as well as post-game content and something called the item world.
The story is pretty standard, you'll go through pre-determined maps to progress the storyline.  Some interesting concepts, that change pretty good to keep you thinking.  This is partly due to Geo Panels which are battlefield bonuses you can control to a certain degree.  Sometimes they're helpful, sometimes they aren't, you get a fair amount of control that's hard to explain without actually playing the game.
The post game content is presented in a similar fashion, when you unlock it, it has a few levels leading up to a boss usually.  These are side plots that can have their own ending, but often serve as very difficult encounters.  I really like these, in my opinion this is what you push content for.
Then there's the Item World, another difficult to explain concept that ends a lot of variety into the game.  It's a randomly generated map that's created when choose a weapon to enter.  The item generates floors and clearing each one is great for exp, getting new items and it also allows you to level up the weapon, making it even better than it was.  This is where you can spend a majority of the game, or you can also decide not to, I actually beat the game on my 104 hour save file without going into the item world, however if you really want to push your efficiency of your character/s as well as get the truly best gear available, you will have dive deep into the item world.
With all this there's also a court system, you can pass bills that affect the enemies, increase what you can find for items in the shop and so forth.  If you're having too easy of a time with the game, you can make the enemies harder by passing a bill, or you can make them easier, rebirth, improve your character in other ways and so forth.  It adds another layer to the game can affect all the other things to do.  What's fun too, is if you're having issues passing a bill, you can kill the senate.  These are demon politics afterall!
All in all, it's one of the best SRPGs you'll find around.  You don't have to worry about too much filler in between battles, the gameplay is very solid and there have been improvements that are found on this version.  I highly recommend it if you're into the genre, even if you don't care for anime.  And if you do, well that's good for you, will help you enjoy the story.

All the main characters are highly memorable, and even all the side-characters have their own story in the game that you can unlock. Im'ma stop myself before I spoil, but know that this is the main reason I would recommend this series to people.

Over-All: 9.5/10

Unreal was the game that spawned one of the genre's most popular and enduring series. It blew everyone's mind at the time with how visually impressive it was, featuring some of the most immersive environments ever created. Of course, Halflife came out later the same year and diverted everyone's attention somewhat, but the the original Unreal remains a must play classic. Set in a futuristic techno-gothic universe with a Mayan touch, Unreal is a fairly long game (unlike many of today's) that should provide a satisfying experience in one of the most unforgettable worlds to be created. I hadn't played this in many (about 10) years, and the nostalgia overload as the second map began (stepping out of the prison ship onto the alien world, and THAT music starts) was well worth the reduced price of £2.99 I can tell you! Not all of the level design is as innovative as the outside parts, there are some Doom style dark futuristic corridoor moments to add variety, and the medieval looking parts are vaguely remeniscent of Heretic. There are some instantly memorable level designs here, and a soundtrack that in places is just unforgettable. The enemy AI was very intelligent for its time, the Skaarj and their dodging in particular will cause you to waste plenty of ammo if you don't aim well. Being that this is Unreal Gold, it includes the Return to Na Pali expansion which despite apparently not being as good, is a good addition for extra gameplay. Then of course, you get the original Unreal Botmatch. We all know what this lead to, and indeed it does work like a proto version of UT, featuring several maps (Deck 16 for example) in their original incarnations. A classic that should not be missed.

TL;DR:  Great scenery/art style.  Huge, open world, full of choices to quell your boredom.  Good combat system.  Can still win without paying, just takes longer to obtain items/materials.  You won't lose out by trying a free game, so why not?
I've always liked the idea of MMORPGs more than the execution.  I've tried several free ones, and played WoW during one of those promotional times for one month.  I'm not a wallet-warrior on any game, so after reading reviews about ArcheAge, I was leery about diving in.  I decided to just go for it, because the game looked complex and visually impressive.
I have not been disappointed.  This game is really big.  The world is big.  Your options on how to play are nearly limitless.  The scenery is gorgeous, too.  It's a really nice looking game, and it's fun to play.
Lots of grind quests (kill 20 of these, now 40 of the same thing, now 60!) sort of make you want to shove bamboo slivers under your fingernails.  The good news is, you can just  go do something else and earn XP or other resources.  If you get bored of killing mobs, take a break and go chop down some trees, or go fishing.  Better yet, scour the mountains for some illegal farms to raid.  Maybe you can go to a contested area and try to steal a trade pack from some filthy reds?
There's a whole you can do.  This game makes it fun, interesting, and really nice to look at.  Plus, it's FREE.  You don't have to spend money to have fun.  I've earned enough gold in game to pay for Patron status.  Twice.  Sure, getting geared up is easier if your Mastercard is powerful, but if you put in the time and effort, you can get geared up for free.
Just give it a try.  You won't regret it.

--Story--
[Unreal]
As Prisoner #849 of the Vortex Rikers ship, your shuttle makes an emergency crash landing on a mysterious planet of Napali, from there on you must then escape the damaged shuttle with all your crew dead and venture off to find your escape route out from the planet fighting hordes of interesting, aggressive, funny, but horrific creatures such as the Brutes, Mantas, Gasbags, enormous giant Titans, and Alien Mercanaries. But most importantly the deadly ferocious Skaarge: a capital alien race seeking complete control over Napali's resources and claiming it for their own ideal purpose as their planet with its innocent 4-armed inhabitants called the Nali, using them as slaves for their corrupted tasks. The Nali fear the skaarge and the terrors of Napali but they seek and pray for their savior where ever they may be to save them from their control from the skaarge and the threats of Napali to bring them hope and haven to their race, who is you (duh). As an ally to the Nali people they'll aid you in any way possible providing ammo, items, secret routes, and sanity from whatever that was left that they had in their home planet that is now the Hell's Sanctuary. Progressing through the vast beautiful world of Napali you'll encounter many fascinating yet horrific locations such as ancient sky temples, abandoned vandalized villages, other crashed humanoid piloted ships, and finally finding the Skaarge Mothership in order to find and destroy the "Source" and ending the Skaarge race once and for all making your escape from Napali with a low fueled but reliable escape pod and float seemingly in space hoping for someone to rescue you to safety..
[Return to Napali] (Expansion Pack)
Only realizing that your vision of "safety" turns into a return to hell when you're captured from another different human incorporated ship (The UMS Bodega Bay aka Unified Military Service) and be forced to be sent back into the hellish world that you survived again to locate the "Prometheus", a ship filled with rich and viable weapons information in which the captain of the Bodega desires for greatly and chose you as their scout due to your cunning experience and survival that you had already on the planet. Once fighting your old pals once again, you locate the ship and find the weapons information in which the Bodega demanded, only realizing after listening to a past recording of another UMS ship that provided a brief description about the Bodega's dark background of its greed and misfortune. You are later attacked by the Bodega's soldiers as they were planning to get rid of you once your mission was complete in order to let no one know about their schemes. After wiping out their attack squads you continue on your own path once again to find an escape out of Napali and getting your revenge to the Bodega. After finally locating your (more improved) mini space shuttle you then escape Napali for good and encounter the "UMS Bodega Bay" tricking their attack upon your ship you manage to take down their ship and thus escape with victory and hope that you'll finally find your safe "Haven"...
--My Opinions--
As a childhood classic of mine, I strongly recommend this game for those who love both FPS and are adventurous and love suspense, mystery, and survival in a game. As I already briefly explained the plots to both the game and its expansion pack (or DLC), I can't give it any more other reason to why this old but still decent work of spanktacular beauty, excitement, and challenge is not worth the buy. Already with its amazing architecture, creatures, and story, it is filled with such well composed music that truly brings you with the feeling of sparking your imagination for exploration, survival, and adventure. Despite its exciting intense gameplay, it does have some tedious puzzles that may take some time and thinking to pass but they aren't that bad. Lastly, it also comes with a game editor which captures the essence of its infinitive sense of creativity and exploration of a never ending journey. From designing your own world built by your imagination for the whole world or just your friends to endure your own world in the Unreal universe.

You play the ghost of a detective trying to solve his own murder. The game takes place in Salem, MA, modern day, but there are insights to the city's infamous past hidden all over Salem. As you explore looking for clues as to who murdered you and why, you find many other mysteries throughout the game.
This game is very linear aside from finding objects throughout the city and buildings. It took me eight hours to beat the game and that includes the time I spent exploring.
It is story driven and has very little action. The only action involves sneaking up on demons and attacking them, which does require some tactic. No shooting or combat, lots of hiding. Not much horror to it either. Nothing jumps out at you and the story itself isn't that creepy.
Graphics are fairly decent and controls are smooth. I used a control instead of mouse and key board.
I liked the story throughout this game and enjoyed hunting for clues. If you like story rich games and detective noir stories than perhaps this is the game for you. However I wouldn't recommend this if you're looking for an action/horror game. Also, I bought this on sale and thought it was a good deal, not sure I'd say the same buying it for $30.

What is with EA releasing first two games of a every trilogy here in Steam, but the third one is Origin exclusive. Mass Effect 3, Dead Space 3, Crysis 3. It's almost as if they don't want my money.
Anyway, back to the review.
While Mass Effect 2 is kinda unnecessary to the story and doesn't fit right in - in the first one Shepard is with the Alliance, here with Cerberus and in third one back together with the Alliance. - still is the best in the series.
Atmosphere is dark, maybe a little cyberpunkish, just the way I like it, and the characters are all, even the minor NPC, very interesting, well most of them (Miranda, I am looking at you). Fortunately you can get the unwanted characters killed if you play your cards right.
The opening of the game is somewhat stupid. Cliffhangers don't work if they are resolved five seconds later. They should have ended the last game with Normandy being shot down and Shepard dying with it. (Also killing a character and bringing him back alive later. Don't do that).
The Changed controls and new game mechanics may feel a bit alienating at first if you finished the first game just five minutes ago, but you can switch them back almost the way you like them. Also the Cerberus network is a bit of a pain in the butt.
But even so: Best game in the series.

I can see how some people might recommend this game.  There is stuff to like about it, it's playable, but as a big studio title I'm going to take the harsher route and not recommend it.  Mostly because it's so underwhelming, gameplay and story wise.
The game play is super casual.  Reduntantly casual.  Most of the game focuses around collecting clues, but you don't derive any meaning from them.   Once you've found the right clues you can opt to solve the case and the game will ask you a straight forward question like "what happened here", or "where did the killer go next" and you click on the clues that blatantly answer the question.  There's no deduction involve, just fill in the blank and then the character will summerize the obvious as though they were hit with some hard earned revelation.
There is also the hunt/be hunted aspect of the game.  Every area has one or two sections where demons emerge and you either have to navigate through them, or destroy them without them attacking you.  It was kind of like the developer was trying to include some action in the game, but it was pretty pointless.  They didn't really get any more difficult as the game progressed and they had nothing to do with the story.  It made me wonder if the developers were playing with what kind of genre they wanted the game to be and ended up not developing or cutting out any of the possibilities. Heck, even the opening scene of us trying to get back into our body uses a gimicky game play element that we don't see again for the rest of the game. It obviously wasn't an interesting enough element to use again, why is it still in there?
The story is also pretty mediocre.  I guess it's fine, it wasn't painful, it was just blah.  The superficial questions were answered, but there wasn't really any explaination as to why any of it was happening, nor was there any real character development for anyone.  The story did conclude, which is more satisfying than some games, but there wasn't really much reward for exploring so much game territory.  In fact, there were lots of smaller unrelated stories that presented themselves in the first half of the game that were probably more interesting and involving than the main plot.  I think they got tired of programming ghosts in the second half of the game or something because the NPCs that drove these side stories stopped asking for  help, and suddenly all the NPCs that had about 2 lines of original monologue each started sharing about 4 lines between all of them.
All in all, I'm sure some people will like this game.  Maybe many will find it on the positive side of mundane, but personally I found it to be an overglorified, padded, hidden object game.  It could really use some editing, and it would be a nice bonus if they actually decided on an aspect of the game to develop into something interesting.

I am not a great adventure fan, so for one of these, things might be different.
This game has some of the worst aspects of adventures, the very reasons why I do not like most adventures.
I like the graphics and the sound. I like the idea about being a ghost who searches his murderer very much. Mindreading people is fun for 10 minutes until you realize that it is good for nothing if you are not currently searching for clues.
It starts with the bad experience in the first scene, you have to search for clues. You are even told how many there are and how many you already have.
You think, "cool, searching a murder scene for clues".
You saw in a video what happened, you were thrown through a window from high above. So why is broken glass a "clue"? Why? Why is your gun a clue? You have to find.. don't know 7 or 9 clues and you get NO new info out of these clues.
And it is really as bad as in my first adventures, more than 20 years ago. You have to find the pixel which is the clue. But is worse than 20 years ago, because you do not just move your mouse, you move a character and the character has too look at the pixel.
Next scene, you have to find x/y clues. After a while you realize, it is again moving around until you get the info that you are looking at a clue. Cool...not. It gets worse. You don't believe me? It GETS worse.
You will get no hint in that direction, but sometimes, for example in the second scene, you will not find all clues, but you have to conclude from your already found "clues".
These conclusions are the worst you can imagine. Nope. That is not true. They are worse.
There is NO logic (no human logic at least) behind the decision which picture is the right to chose.
Then, after this is done, sometimes you have new sensitive pixels in the scene. Somewhere.
Sometimes it is so bad, you KNOW that there, at exact that spot has to be the pixel you want to "find" (google, walkthrough or load game), but you have to move and turn and snake around the pixel until you get it.
So, what have we until now? Pixel searching, clues which give you no clue and missing logic in the conclusions you HAVE to make.
Can it get worse?
It can.
But at least it is a taste thing. Some - adventure lovers - will see it as normal, some - as me - will start to hate.
You see, there will be puzzles. These will be of the kind: "I am a ghost and have no clue, help me". Then you search a radus of 5 meters around the ghost for x/y clues (you remember that one, right?) and will come to totally unlogic conclusions and "puff", the ghost is happy and goes away to heaven. Yeah, real police stuff, you know.
And then, then there are the demons. In a game about ghosts, why should be there no demons you ask?
Because they are used as action/stealth elements which make the game longer, have you die and get you to curse a lot.
If you find in the steam forum some message about "how to disable demons", then you know, you are not alone with your frustration. These demons do not really make sense for the story of the game. STOP! NO THEY DON'T!
They just get in your way when you want to continue with the story.
Oh oh. The story.
I have to say, the story is kind of good and interesting. But had I known how brutal the game (what is told and what you see in backflashes) will become, I would not have bought it.
I do not like brutality or sadism in my games. And I like really happy endings in my games.
I was sad when the story ended, not because the game was finished, I was so happy that I was done with it,
but I was sad because the story told about horrid fates of young friendly girls who just had wanted to help others.
If you a an adult adventure lover, get it. You will love it, I fear.
For all others, keep away, don't get it, not even cheap. Just DO NOT GET IT!
And do NOT give it to your children to play it. I think, the story is just too brutal. At least for me.
Do NOT buy!
