To be honest, I feel that this game got a lot more flack than was deserved. Is it perfect? No, but I think the criticisms were a bit extreme. Mind you, most of the criticisms I read were during the time that it was initially released and some of it had to do with bugs.
I'm guessing that by the time I bought the game (4 months after release) all those bugs were fixed because I didn't really have any of the issues that they were talking about. There were times, however, I noticed that the narration would cut out. This happened in maybe 3-5 different cutscenes were there was just no sound at all - the only way I knew what was supposed to have been said during the scene was because I always have subtitles on.
I think what hurt the game more than anything else was the story. It was okay, but I feel that it could have been better - more developed maybe. Also I feel like the characters were poorly written.
I say this because I felt no emotion towards any of them whatsover. The wife was annoying, and there were too many random collectibles of her memories with him - I'm guessing like finding pages of her diary or something scattered around. I felt myself annoyed with all of these and couldn't care less about her or their relationship.
The friendship or, partnership I guess, between Ronan and Joy felt really shallow. Since Joy is the character Ronan interacts with the most throughout the game, I was hoping for more development in their friendship.
I couldn't even find myself caring about Ronan himself. None of the characters in the game were developed enough for me to root for them or care about them in anyway.
Also I felt it was strange that all the events in the entire game takes place in one night. Why on earth was that one couple getting married in the middle of the night / wee hours of the morning?
The demons in the game were laughable. It felt like it was just thrown in at the last minute to give the game some kind of combat in it. They should have either given the combat more diversity or taken the demons out completely, in my opinion. I didn't play the game with combat in mind so I wouldn't have cared if there was no combat in this game. There are perfectly good Adventure Mystery games with absolutely no combat in it (the majority of Sherlock Holmes titles for example).
With all that negative out of the way now for the positives: I appreciate the game trying to do something different. I'm a big fan of Adventure Mystery type games and one that approaches it from the perspective of a ghost is innovative and interesting. I enjoyed walking through walls and possessing adorable felines, as well as the people around town.
It would have been great if they expanded a bit more on this - more animals to possess, control over individuals in town like how
, as well as being able to poltergeist more items.
To sum up my review, I would recommend people to give the game a go. It's enjoyable and fun and I definitely don't think it deserved 59 on metacritic. I would rate it more of a 6/10. It's worth a play through to get to play and experience something different. The mystery is also relatively engaging.
I just wouldn't get this game at full price - wait for a sale. I was able to scoop it up during one for 4.99.

Hand Of Fate:
~~~~~~~~~~~
Hand Of Fate is an  unique game which combines a fighting (hack-and-slash), role playing and a card game.
You will sit at a table opposite this story teller (he reminds me of the evil Jaffar) with his deck of cards and you will be invited to play the game of life and death! You will have to defeat 12 of his champions in the story mode or you can play an endless mode, which is play until you die.
Our nice story teller will shuffle the cards at the start of each campaign and you will receive a deck of cards which will have goodies (weapons and armour) and he will also have a deck with plenty of nasty surprises with the objective of bringing you down.
You will need to gather food; to use every time you move. Gather money to purchase weapons, to heal yourself, to remove curses or to receive a blessing.
When the cards are laid face down on the table, you will be represented by a figurine and you will have to move it to the next card. Upon arriving on the cards you may face a horde of bandits, goblins, ratmen or you might be going to the shop, talking to a priest, finding a treasure chest or even retrieving a weapon from a canyon. The ultimate goal is to go through the deck and kill the champion.
Sometimes you will face a challenge (fighting) and if you win, you will receive a token which will give you a unique card to add to your deck for your next campaign.
In terms of the controls, the gamepad is the best option in my opinion but you can use the mouse and keyboard if you want to.
All fighting maps are small but fast and challenging. And you will need a good deck of cards and plenty of skills to kill your opponents.
Graphically, the game looks great and you can put the resolution up to 2560 X 1440.  The audio is good and the narration is splendid.
So, are you ready to play the game of life and death? Your fate lays in a deck of cards ... what hand do you have?
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Unique concept and gameplay
-	Fabulous narration
-	Great Graphics
-	Generate new game after dying
-	Runs well
-	Challenging
-	Achievements
-	Trading cards
Negatives:

With 271 hours played, i feel comfortable in my knowledge of this game, and i feel ready to make a "review" of it. (note, the reason i call it a "review" is because it strictly is not one, it is more a summary of content)
Let me start of with this: i have not played Crusader kings 1, i also have played all the other contemporary paradox g-strategy titles, (including the somewhat aging Victoria 2 (which is great btw)) so this will be from the perspective of someone who has a good deal of experience in the different games.
Now, CKII, A game of thrones? well, other than the fact that a mod exists for that, yeah, that is the best way to describe part of this game.
You are a Medieval count/duke/king/emperor, (depending on who you start as) and have challenges to face that befits your station, as a count, you deal with the threat of the much larger kings, and in many circomstances a duke that wants your stuff, intrigue, in terms of.. well, killing the sod, is an option, improving relations is one, play the long game, and marry his daughter(or son, i dont judge) or go to war, claim your right to rule.
As a duke you deal with your somewhat unruly subordinates, often very few of them, and other than that, your real enemy is the king or emperor. You want to become one! And the king stands in your way to greatness.
Ally other rulers, use intrigue, once more, marry, make your child ruler, there are many options.
Now, on to the battle system, where i will start with talking about technology: It increases in %ages, instead of unit changes, as is the usual with EUIV, and the upgrades are less game changing than in vic 2 (dig in cap hello) but the most important in terms of millitary is the retinue upgrades (and the demesne upgrades, but that does not have to do with war, so i dont talk about it here) A retinue was a medieval following, you did not yet have (often at least) professional armies under the command of the ruler, every single lord had a personal and a land based army, the land based one was often on more or less lease to the Ruler, in defense of the realm and whatnot, in this game the personal retinue is a personal Army, separate to the Levy (or land based) army, the limit of which can be increased by technology.
Anyway, the combat is (farily) simple, you have three parts to your force, the right, the left, and the center flanks. each with a commander, who each gives their combat modifiers to their respective force, other factors that play in are Attacker/Defender, Terrain, Straight crossings, boat landings, the like.
Every territory you have or conquer is part of your Demesne, or Held land, each territory holds a number of "holdings" which include Churches, Towns, and Castles (baronies) each with their own need for upgrades, people to keep happy, and different rewards to be gained, Castles provide large levies, towns provide cash cows, and churches provide faith, gold and levy, in my experience, i go for towns in most provinces and go for castles in the ones with higher limits of holdings.
You have a demesne limit, this is based upon your stewardship skill, wife (or husband)'s stewardship, and technology, you start seeing minuses to tax income and the like if you go over it, but dont be afraid to do so, it can sometimes save your hide.
Now i wont say much more, as i would have to get into expansions, but ill be safe to say, there are tons of events, religions, and effects based on that, Crusades happen, Jihads happen, and great holy wars (for other religions) happen.
This is a game with a steep learning curve, so dont be discouraged by losses, it takes some time to get used to.
Sieze your birthright lord, for you can rise to greatness. Rise Imperator, for your time has come. Rise Pagans, for riches untold. Rise Raja, for lands untold.

Hand of Fate is a blast to play, but not easy to describe.
It is obviously a game with cards, but not really a card game in the usual sense. Think of it as a random adventure game where the cards are your storyline, equipment, quests, enemies, curses and blessings. And the actual battles are fought in Hack & Slash real time encounters which mirror the cards you have on hand. I hope there will soon be a Demo available for people to try it, because its really unique and should be experienced instead of described.
The strongest point of the game is probably the Narrator of the Card Dealer, very well done and highly immersive and even comments on your situation or what cards you have on hand. The second strong point is the randomness and replayability, every adventure you start will be different, depending on the cards you choose and how they are played.
The presentation is top notch, the card animations fluid and pretty. Only the switches to the Battles are a bit tiresome after a while, but they can be skipped.
There is a big luck factor in the game which makes things interesting, it can screw you over royally, but also make you come back against all odds. You will die, and you will not be successful in every quest and adventure. And you probably have not many ways to prevent it, its the luck of the cards.
If something is missing then maybe character variety, there is only the main character. At least the different equipment is displayed nicely on him.
The real time battles are short encounters against one or more groups of enemies with varying abilities and are visually pretty and also randomized. The actual fighting is not too difficult as long as you learn how to block & dodge and use the abilities. The store page says controller recommended, but i played with M&KB just fine. The Battles might be easier with a controller.

Crusader Kings 2 is, at its core, a GRAND strategy game. The world is massive and massively detailed, and the possibilities are endless. At the time of writing this review I have about 315 hours logged in the game, and when you consider that I am just the type of person who can rarely log 100 without getting bored, that is saying something.
The focus of this game is to build your dynasty in feudal Europe, but the game also include some parts of Africa, the whole Middle East, and India (only playable with the Rajas of India DLC). The timeline for this game is truely massive, with just the base game you can play from 1066 to 1453, just over 400 years. In that time you will play as a single ruler, then your ruler's heir, then their heir, and so on. This is a game about forging your path into the history books. If you want to play as a Viking and conquer India, you can. If you want to play the manipulating vassal of the Holy Roman Emperor, you can do that too. There is almost nothing you can't do.
If you get tired of conquering the same old Afro-Eurasia again and again, then there are always mods. CK2 features a native system to easily activate and deactivate mods, as well as Steam Workshop support. Hand of Fate is a breath of fresh air in the Rogue-like game style. The exploration point is fun, the challenge is descent, and the rewards for playing are surprisingly well thought out.
You are a warrior, who has traveled far, and have meet a person, which is The Dealer. He has spent time making cards. Cards based off your memories. The game takes place on a board fashioned by these upside cards. As you play the game, you unlock and discover more memories, in which you get to go in and briefly explore. It's part Choose your own Adventure, part arcade smash them up, part resource management, and the key feature is the deck building.
The deck building is a fascinating part of the game, and hints at a deeper story. You disover new magic weapons and abilities, and they go into one deck, and in the other deck are events. Often these events have a token which you can earn by running into it and passing the challenge. Pass the challenge, you get rewarded with a new card, a new memory from your past. So, the better you do, and the more tokens you unlock, the more story gets revealed.
Is the story a deep one? Is it a good one? I can't say. I've not uncovered enough. I'm kinda struggling in the middle of the game not to starve to death, but that's a good thing. It's really random how the cards are distributed after a few levels, and if you overplay events, the game takes notice and changes them up. So it pays to change your deck every now and then. It also helps to have a good eye, as part of the game is three card Monte, and if you are good at spacial awareness, you can keep track of cards as they are shuffled, which is useful.
Overall, this game is well worth the price of admission. The Journey is worthwhile, and while the combat is a tad simplistic, the exploration aspect and the gorgeous art assets make this game worth several hours of play through.

Much like most of the other great games that have come out this year so far, Hand of Fate is one of those that could have easily slipped through the cracks. It is a difficult game to categorize, but it's mix of card game mechanics, brawling and table top RPG mechanics proves to mix together very well. Let's break down each part and see how it stacks up.
The Card Game -
Easily the best part of this game. When I heard this was a card game I went into it expecting something along the lines of Hearthstone, but I couldn't have been more wrong. Your deck controls what is in each level, and gives you equipment. the dealers deck on the other hand (heh card puns) contains the monsters you fight, the prizes and punishments from encounters, and a few cards just to mess with you. Its very unique and very addicting
The Brawling -
Easily the worst part of the game. It's not bad, but if you have played Shadow of Mordor then this is going to feel quite clunky. The combat is just imprecise and the trap level that all depend on movement are hard to navigate. It should be noted though that its not BAD, just could have used some more polish and seems rushed compared to the rest of the game.
The RPG Side -
Much of the game comes down to what are essentially dice rolls from D&D, though in this case is a card pick. This is what ties the whole game together. With this system even playing the same deck time and time again will give you a different playthrough. It is a deep system and allows for almost infinite replayability, and in a time where games are getting bashed for not having replayability  *cough* The Order *cough* its good to see.
Hand of Fate is easily one of my favorite games of the year so far, and I highly recommend picking it up is you have any interest in card games.

This is a review for people who don't know what this game all has.  Keep in mind, I am not an anime fan in the slightest, because of this, I'm very happy that there's a skip storyline option.  Something to note on this though, it doesn't skip introductions and outros for episodes, but it does kill all the filler before battles in the story.  You'll mostly know what's going on with the story because of this, but it does drag on.  A nice option you have with it being on PC, is you can alt-tab while it runs the story and the game will continue to go.  This is great for those especially annoying outros.
As for the game itself...ho-boy, there's a lot of content.  I've played this game pretty religiously in the past, I think the last time I beat the hardest boss I clocked in 104 hours or so.  There's a lot to this game if you really want to dive in, the story itself will take about 30-45 hours depending on how much you feel like grinding or get side tracked.  There's two story modes, one being really rushy and not that interesting, but still a nice addition and the regular campaign, as well as post-game content and something called the item world.
The story is pretty standard, you'll go through pre-determined maps to progress the storyline.  Some interesting concepts, that change pretty good to keep you thinking.  This is partly due to Geo Panels which are battlefield bonuses you can control to a certain degree.  Sometimes they're helpful, sometimes they aren't, you get a fair amount of control that's hard to explain without actually playing the game.
The post game content is presented in a similar fashion, when you unlock it, it has a few levels leading up to a boss usually.  These are side plots that can have their own ending, but often serve as very difficult encounters.  I really like these, in my opinion this is what you push content for.
Then there's the Item World, another difficult to explain concept that ends a lot of variety into the game.  It's a randomly generated map that's created when choose a weapon to enter.  The item generates floors and clearing each one is great for exp, getting new items and it also allows you to level up the weapon, making it even better than it was.  This is where you can spend a majority of the game, or you can also decide not to, I actually beat the game on my 104 hour save file without going into the item world, however if you really want to push your efficiency of your character/s as well as get the truly best gear available, you will have dive deep into the item world.
With all this there's also a court system, you can pass bills that affect the enemies, increase what you can find for items in the shop and so forth.  If you're having too easy of a time with the game, you can make the enemies harder by passing a bill, or you can make them easier, rebirth, improve your character in other ways and so forth.  It adds another layer to the game can affect all the other things to do.  What's fun too, is if you're having issues passing a bill, you can kill the senate.  These are demon politics afterall!
All in all, it's one of the best SRPGs you'll find around.  You don't have to worry about too much filler in between battles, the gameplay is very solid and there have been improvements that are found on this version.  I highly recommend it if you're into the genre, even if you don't care for anime.  And if you do, well that's good for you, will help you enjoy the story.

I am absolutely in love with this game. It takes deck building, choose-your-own-adventure, board games, Arkham-style brawling and roguelite elements and mixes them all into a melting pot, and the atmosphere is the final ingredient that brings it all together.
You're essentially playing through an adventure, using a deck of cards as the base, with the dealer providing colorful commentary and setting the mood. It's like playing a personal, one-on-one game of DnD with someone...or like old shows like Knightmare or similar. I can not overstate how impressive the atmosphere is of the game, with each card full of flavor and every encounter interesting and exciting. You never know what you'll find!
The dealer himself is a very interesting character, who half the time seems to want to help you and half the time seems happy to watch you twist in the wind. He'll applaud you for victory, but just as quickly savor your defeat. Maybe you decide to swap out an axe for a sword? He'll snark about it, asking you if it's really what you want to do. His commentary, though sometimes cryptic, does an immense job in building the world and turns every card into a fully fleshed encounter, dripping with detail. Every monster, enemy and boss is played up with description, sometimes terrifying and sometimes mournful.
Honestly, I have no complaints about this game at all and have had no issues or bugs with it...at least so far. Some of the RNG can get truly brutal in the later encounters and the combat itself isn't exactly door-busting, but it's more than servicable and for anyone who's played the Arkham games, Assassin's Creed or the like will find it easy to learn, though the difficulty ramps up greatly.
I can already see this being one of my favorite games of the year. I sincerely hope they intend to release more content for it, as I'd love that, though between the Story mode and Endless Mode, I can see playing this for a long while yet.

Recommending this game was a close run thing.
I got it originally for the Playstation 2 back in the day, and that console died a while back. I also picked up the DS release, which had the added content of Etna's story mode. It's really no different from that release, and where it is, it's not necessarily in it's favour.
The reason I'd recommend it is the same reason I'd recommend those versions. The story is fun and engaging, the mechanics are deep enough to allow someone to really get into creating the fighters that they wish and it requires a real investment in time to get the most out of the experience.
The downside is that the steam release hasn't been done particularly well. The game is unstable, crashing out on a regular basis. This is still happening, several patches down the line. I realize that NIS are putting in the time and the effort to patch the game, and they've been doing good work on that. But frankly, a game that crashes out as often as this probably shouldn't have been released commercially yet. Half the recommended actions to increase stability involve turning off features that are meant to improve the user experience.
This game relies heavily on grinding, several of the achievements are named for exactly that. You cannot focus on grinding well when you're aware that you're likely to lose progress often, simply because the game crashed out before you can save.
Like I said, I would recommend this game, but that recommendation depends on your willingness to put up with the bugs. If they do release later titles, I'll probably get them too, but I really hope that NIS puts in more work on the port before release to ensure the game is as good as it should be.

Right, Crusader Kings 2. This game is a masterpiece of a grand strategy sandbox. You play as the head of a medieval dynsasty, and must guide your family over the centuries towards prosperity and glorly. I will attempt to describe the game without going into the complex game mechanics, which I highly recommened you watch some youtube tutorials and chech out the CKII wikia to understand. If i went into detail about these game mechanics, this review would be far to long.
Crusader kings 2 is a vast historical sandbox in which you can play any character/culture/faction and do anything. Want to play as a viking warlord and turn the germmanic (norse) faith into a modern religion rivaling christianity? You can do that! Want to break up the Holy Roman Empire? That's doable. Want to revive the Persian empire AND the Zoroastrian faith? Incredibly difficult, but it can be done! Recreate the Roman Empire and reunify christianity? Yup, totally doable. Want to create a Jewish kingdom of Israel? Challenging, but possible.
The point is, you can do nearly anything in this game. You can try to recreate history as best you can, but even that takes effort. Half of the fun of this game is seeing what weird things happened while you weren't paying attention (like a successful Islamic invasion of France). No playthrough of this game will be the same. The replayability is endless. I've sunk in hundreds of hours, and will likely sink in hundreds more.
Are there problems? Of course. The battle mechanics are a little wonky. The AI is not always very bright (though they can be rather clever at times). Court intrigue and and assassinations need some work. Current versions (as of 28/12/2014) have given rise to oddly stable massive blob kingdoms, though not as bad as some previous versions. And some other nit picky details.
Overall though, this is a brilliant game. Especially because 10 hours in you realize you're plotting the deaths of your 8 year old nephew so you can inherit his land and titles.
Just... buy this game. I also recommened you at least buy The Old Gods DLC, as it pushed that start date back to 867, and adds a lot of depth to the pagan religions. It also allows you to play as VIKINGS, and they are a blast to play as. Especially because now you can sacrifice THE POPE to pagan gods if you manage to capture him. Sword of Islam is also good, though you can do without Rajas of India unless you want to play in India. Way of Life is fantastic, and adds more depth to roleplaying and characters, and isn't that expensive. Charlemagne isn't bad, though the start date isn't as interesting as 867, and Charlemagne's story triggers are a little wonky. Still fun to screw with history by preventing his rise to power, however. The game regularly goes on sale, but even at full price it is worth buying.
If you buy this game, you will get hundreds of hours of entertainment out of it. You may even learn some history while you are at it!
Worth the 20 bucks? Probably not. Worth it on a steam sale? Yes.

A semi-adequate port.  Not bad, definitely not terrible, but when core functionality does not work properly (eg dodgy mouse controls) you cannot call it good.  Serviceable at best.
The art is nice, the music surprisingly good and the plot quite entertaining.  Humour is always YMMV, but I liked it.  It definitely helps to have at least a basic appreciation for the Japanese TV references.  The core gameplay, however, was disappointing.  It is a decent Tactical RPG, a genre barely represented on PC, but compared to its peers there are some serious issues.  The way experience is handled cripples certain classes and emphasises one or two over-powered Rambo characters over a balanced and tactial squad (the normal for the genre).  This makes a lot of the potential gameplay elements irrelevant, because attempting to explore them weakens you and makes the game more grindy/less fun.  The randomised Item World maps are an interesting concept, but can occationally be impossible to complete, resulting in wasted time.
There is a market for this game, but I think it is a very small one.  Combined with the not-so-good port, I believe this is a game most people could safely pass over.

Good god, for every small mission you get to play, Valkyria Chronicles forces you to sit through six to eight cutscenes, throughout which some strong philosophical concepts are explored but executed with all the grace of a mass-gassing. Dialog is cringe-worthy, interactions are barely above a child's Saturday special, and in that spirit everything is explained, repeated, and beaten over the player's head just to make sure we got the ♥♥♥♥ing message. And as to be expected of anything Japanese, it's unbearably saccharine featuring androgynous tweens full of angsty drama taking on diesel-punk tanks with lances. Today's McGuffin is a sort of precious metal that serves as everything from a healing agent to light source, fuel to ammunition. Can't imagine why there's a shortage of it. Which is the cop-out geo-political excuse for the evil empire, full of heartless sadistic mooks who gun down civilians and beat pregnant women, to invade Western "Europa" (♥♥♥♥ing seriously?). This criminally bloodless rebranding of WWII (it's even a "Second Europan War" in the story) does touch on some strong points; aristocracy, the unnaturalness of human conflict, philosophy of equilibrium, but it's all buried under soap opera drama and atrocious writing. Commendation is deserved for the effort put into individualizing every otherwise generic mook in your squad, but unfortunately they stuck to the typical anime formula of angst, drama, and subliminal pedophilia.
Gameplay has some innovative concepts; turn-based strategy with third-person control of your characters as you move them. But the environments seem lazily built, since you can only crouch at sandbags and even then you can't take cover in a corner to enjoy two-sided protection. You can hide in grass, even when the enemy knows you're there, which brings up the ironic situation of concealment trumping cover. Moves are pooled for your units, adding some strategy, and health and grenades regenerate between turns. There's no reloading, probably because of the most frustrating gameplay feature; constant fire. The enemy will shoot at whichever unit you're moving during your movement phase, and usually stop when you take aim. Sure, your units will do the same to them, but computers end their turn as soon as they've moved, so if you're navigating the finicky terrain in their sightlines, expect to lose a lot of health (even in cover). If you have a unit trying to duel with an enemy face-to-face (especially when they're toting an automatic), better start writing a letter to their next of kin. The tank is no better, turning unpredictably and running into obscure geometries. But worst of all to gameplay is the fact that this game is a prime example of the bad kind of port. You only ever can use the mouse to look around when controlling the units, and the arrow or WADS keys in combination with the space bar at all other times. This is most apparent in the menus, where to switch to the next tab in the main menu, you must open the mini menu and choose the tab you want to go to. As one renowned reviewer perfectly described it; it's a broken fractal spreadsheet nightmare. On the plus side, your squadmates in reserve level up along with those sent into the field, but the upgrading is linear and thus feels like busywork.

There is simply no finer game to play as a single player game than UNREAL!
I know it may sound corny, but consider that the game has come out in 1998, and the graphics still look good!
A 'proper' atmosphere, where players with an actual imagination can try out different ways of tackling any baddies, or different ways of reaching 'secret' places.
Probably the most enjoyable aspect of this game would have to be the 'physics' with respect of the character you control to its environment:
the extremely unique double sideways jump, which made the 'space' jump all but absolete, allows you to reach areas with slanted faces in almost a single movement, thus outmaneouvering opponents, especially in multiplayer LAN games, giving freedom of movement a whole new meaning.
The only other game that in my opinion would come close to this kind of control today would have to be: elder scrolls oblivion, another great game, where character control is second to none, especially the jumping ability, something that was unfortunately removed in skyrim.
However, Unreal's real strength (padon the pun, lol) lies with the adventuring and exploration of every nook and crany to find useful items on your journey to escape the planet of the Nali.
Come-on guys, that's a page turner right there, lol.
You're on your own, just crash landed on this UNREAL planet in your prison ship as the only survivor, making your way out of the ship and stepping into a completely alien world of both mysterious wonder and great danger ... now go play the game!
I don't actually play the STEAM version of this game, as I have a fully customized version of it thanks to the support of a still very large UNREAL community, like
, where people still release amazing new player maps, single or multi player ones.
I only bought this game to let the developers know that there are still seriously UNREAL fans out there, and I sincerely wish they would remake the single player game of it again using todays graphics tools and hardware available.
... imagine the eye-candy when playing Nali Castle, Spire or Bluff Eversmoke maps ...
Anyway, before I get too carried away: it's a damn great game, ESPECIALLY if you've never played it!
Get it, then get yourself the high-resolution texture packs, and for heaven's sake, lose yourself in the atmosphere ...
just for the record, I still play this game several times a year for several weeks at a time EVERY YEAR since its release, that's how damn good UNREAL really is!

So, after playing for about a week and trying out what the game has to offer. I can safely say that I would recommend giving Archeage a try. I've seen a lot of reviews on here saying that the game is "Pay to Win", which in my time playing I haven't seen that at all. Yes, I will say that it helps if you go to patron status (The games formal way of a monthly subscription). If you do decide to go with a patron status you get bonus XP and well as more then double the Labor Points. Labor Points are a in game energy so to speak. You need Labor to craft, harvest and open some bags from in game drops. Now you do get Labor points in game, about 5 every 5 minutes for the f2p model (with a max of 2,000) and 10 every 5 minutes through patron (with a max of 5,000).
Graphics in this game are amazing, if grahpics are a big selling point to you then this game is for you. I play on low settings (just cause I like to multitask and watch a livestream at the same time on the other moniter) and the game is still visually stunning.
Combat in Archeage is very smooth and feels great. I've played as a melee class and a caster class and both feel great and fun.
Character design is very nice and easy to do. You can sit there for however long you want making your character to whatever you'd like.
The only problem that I've ran into so far is when I start the game it takes about 2-3 minutes for everything to load. Not the game but the in game npc's. I'll see the nameplates but not the characters for a little bit. Which isn't that big of a problem, just sit there for a little bit and once everything around you is loaded and rendered you'll have a smooth gameplay.
Overall, I'd say give this game a try. Don't listen to the negitve reviews. The game will be different to all different people and the only one that can tell you it's a fun game is you. Archeage is a fun game in the f2p model just as much as in the patron model. If you want to play give it a week, in that time you'll probably get to max level on one character or have experienced enough of the game to decided if you like it or not.

I am a great fan of Mass Effect 1 and have played it through a number of times with different characters. However, even though I thoroughly enjoyed the game, it was never really an RPG. It was always a tactical shooter with an excellent story, great grpahics and a few RPG elements. I'd even go as far to say how bad some of the RPG aspects were (poor levelling system, awful inventory, limited character creation etc...).
Mass Effect 2 seems to have taken out all of the bits that irritated me (including those dull dull dull Mako missions) and created a much tighter playing experience. Every mission feels important to the main story and there were very few times I felt I was playing the same mission with a different background. Some of the missions were truly exciting and left me guessing what was going to happen next. The story is even better then the first. It introduces new twists to the story and I like the idea of seeing the galaxy's darker side. Even the characters seem more engaging this time round. I'll always miss Wrex, but most of the game's first charcaters left me cold.
It's not perfect however, but the faults are few and far between. I can imagine the planet scanning side game/quest for resources getting tedious, especially on a second playthrough. The inventory system, although much easier to use, could have made the player feel more involved. I just wasn't happy being told exactly what gun I could or couldn't use. Finally, I'm still undecided on whether DLC is a good thing or not. Time will tell.
Overall, I feel that some of the customer reviews on this page have been unfair. I think EA gets a great deal of unfair stick, but it is one of the companies that I think seems to take the risks (unlike Bioshock 2 or CODMW2). Mass Effect was never a true RPG so the sequel shouldn't be judged as one either. If you're looking for an excellent 80+ hour RPG then choose Dragon Age or Divine Divinity 2. If you want a fun and exciting tactical shooter with great graphics and an engrossing story, then Mass Effect 2 is simply perfect.

If you drag yourself, embittered and complaining, to the end of this game, and watch the credits roll-by (unskippable credits, too -- WHO still does that?!), it's informative, I think, about what's wrong with this game. The first name listed is the Story and Creative Director, which is fair enough, followed by aaaaaaaaaall the Square Enix producers, the Marketing directors, then their sales managers, analysts and coordinators, the interactive marketing senior manager, the traffic manager, the senior counsel, VP of HR, HR administrator, the network engineer, desktop support, senior manager officer administration, the senior accountant, the credit manager, and a whooooooole host of other Square Enix people before you finally get to the... Square Enix localisation managers, producers, teams, coordinators, brand design managers, production assistants, and then all of those for each office, the marketing in each country, the community managers, the localisation testers, functionality testers ... etc ...
What's my point? There's about 300 names (unskippable, remember) before you get to a single programmer. And therein this game's primary problem.
Early on in the game, in your rush to solve the first puzzle, you can seemingly run ahead of the game, find too many clues, and the game will effectively lock and you won't be able to progress. A check online will detail the precise order of clues to find to get past that section, but by that stage, you're pretty much over it. And this is sadly not an isolated incident. This game is riddled with problems: there are walkways you can't walk over the one-inch step on, others you cannot walk down, priests that walk through walls preventing your continuing the mission, cats walking up ramps that seem to freeze in a "I'm jumping down" pose, ...
Yet, at the core of it, this is a really good game, and if there were more QA people and fewer marketing people involved, it could have been a really great game. In investigating your own murder, you play ethereal detective, run around possessing people to help solve your murder at the hands of a seemingly unstoppable serial killer. You get to hear peoples' thoughts, read their notes, look into their lives, or even influence their thinking.
Expanded, some graded difficulty and substantially polished, this could be a real bombshell of new IP. But I am guessing SE didn't have the faith, cash or the willpower to purge the apparent stadium full of executives, producers, directors, managers and marketing people in favour of actual QA folk and programmers.
tl;dr? Good idea, poor execution.

I got this game in a Humble Bundle, so I thought I'd give it a try.
This game is something of a cross between L.A. Noire and a horror movie; it does have detective elements where you collect clues and make deductions, but many of these 'investigations' are arbitrary at best and senseless at worst. Although I did eventually 'get' the logic behind their decisions of right, it took me a while.
If this game had stuck to the detectiving as a ghost, I'd have been pleasantly surprised; even the optional 'unsolved cases' done by meeting the victims were well done. Where this game fell apart, for me at least, is in the OTT creepy theme. There was nothing full on scary and only one or two jump scares... It was just creepy. Ghostly figures and shapes that fade away when you get close, only to reappear if you look away... The goddamn f**king demons that instantly kill you if you mess up a brief QTE...
With the already-creepy setting, the heavyhanded layering on of ghostly imagery made this a difficult game to finish. I hate horror. This one ISN'T horror, but I would not recommend playing this in the dark and definitely not right before bed.
Not much to say on it, but the level design is a clusterf**k. Even the overworld hub is a labyrinth of deadends, obscured paths and greyscale buildings. The individual levels are better in that they're usually more linear, but collectible-combing is a ♥♥♥♥♥. This game could sorely have used a Tomb Raider-esque collectible tracker.
If they had dispensed with the demons, stationary figures and 'ghost buildings' everywhere, this would have been a clever, short detective game with a twist. As it is, the creepiness put me off and I only finished out of a bloodyminded determination to 100% the achievements.
Play L.A. Noire instead; the puzzles are more logic-based and it's less sleepless-creepy. The voice acting in this is top notch, though. Even from peripheral characters.

For starters I am not one for puzzle games. When I first played this game it reminded me much of the old game Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine, with the similar style of game play. There are two types of mode in this game. Arcade mode, and puzzle mode. This does add a little bit of replay value to the game, but still only really kept me interested for about 2 hours before it got a bit boring and started to become a little annoying. The controls you will be using are Ctrl and arrow keys. I'm really not sure why they chose ctrl to be their main button to select things in the main menu and to use in the game. I did have a few issues with the ctrl button, for one it's right next to the windows key for me, and pressing that minimises the game. If you then try to go back on the game it crashes. Really annoying, and couldn't find anyway to change the controls.There are two types of game modes on this game.
is basically connecting 4 of the same coloured blocks, that will get rid of them. Each level you have to get rid of a certain amount of blocks to pass the level in the time limit that is given to you. The first few levels that I played I didn't even realise that there was a time limit that I was up against. Obviously I found this out after a few levels, and this time constrain gets pretty tight on the later levels that you get into the game. There are a few elements to this game, that are again kind of similar to the old Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine game. There are brick type blocks that if your 4 blocks (or more) touch the brick block it will take it out with them, or they will fall if they are not taken out and if they have space to fall. If however there are solid blocks, they cannot be gotten rid of and doesn't have gravity to it either. These two simple elements of the game make this game get harder as it goes along. Along with the time constrain it makes it a nice challenging game that has a nice difficulty curve to set you into what the game has to offer, and doesn't drastically increase the difficulty which is really good for this type of game. The other mode that there is is called
, it is what it says it is. Basically you have a limited amount of turns to drop the blocks, and you must clear all of the blocks to pass the level. I felt like some of the later levels where way too easy then some of the levels before that one, this makes me feel clever but kind of defeats the object of a puzzle game. Both of these modes have a nice little kind of collectible, you can unlock different colours of like the hand held console thing that you play these modes on. Nice little feature.
The Art style of this game is cute, and fits in with the whole puzzle game on like a old school hand held device. There isn't really much else to talk about for the Art Style of this game.
The music for this game is not bad, although there is only one track that repeats itself over and over again. It really needs to be varied when it comes to the music because after about a hour of listening to it I decided to just mute my sound so I wouldn't have to listen to it anymore. As for the sounds they are pretty generic for this type of game, nothing else really to comment about or say.
I defiantly recommend this game to puzzle fans, and people who don't even like puzzle games. I myself I don't really like puzzle games but enjoyed my time with this game. The game play is really fun and satisfying, and if you can get over the awkward ctrl button and repetitive music this game is really fun.

Castle is a simple unique puzzle game that has a steep learning curve, low replay ability and some interesting mechanics that really bring the game to it's name. I enjoyed this game for a certain amount of time, then it just got boring because of the difficulty. I am however recommending this game because even though it has low replay value and does get boring at times, there was a nice session of when it was fun to play. I do suggest playing in short sessions though as you might get bored of this game if you keep failing.
This game is very unique in the sense of the puzzle side of things. You have to create a castle with the tiles of the castle at the top of the screen as the scroll from right to left. All you have to do is drag them into the correct places and make the castle. Simple enough right? That's what I thought. The games concept is great, don't get me wrong. I haven't seen other puzzle games that are like this. There are a few problems with this though. First off, it's easy to misjudge what piece of the castle goes where. There where many times in the game where I would put a piece on the wrong slot just because I wasn't sure if it fitted there or not. This is not a puzzle factor of the game, it's simple misjudgement. If you combine that with the enemies you have to take care of, the time limit and the lives that you have then you are always on edge of this game. There are so many things to take into consideration that makes this game so difficult. This then makes you play a single level over and over again for like half an hour and that isn't fun. That also ties in with the repetitive nature of the game as each level is basically a harder version of the previous level. They add more enemies, and bonuses you have to buy every now and then. Despite all the bad things that  have said there are some fun elements to the game that I want to talk about. They do produce a small and pretty basic graph of how many of each enemy will be on that level. This means that you can plan in advanced and buy the things that can stop them from you building, each enemy has a different type of item that you can use to get rid of them. A fireball for a bird, anvil for a knights, dynamite for a mole ect. Along with the variety of enemies there are also 3 different variations of castles to build, plain, desert and ice which kinda separates the art style.
The Art Style to this game isn't all that good or bad. It has nice, crisp and clean graphics for a cartoon like game. I personally don't really like the way this game looks, the Art Style looks too childish for me to really like it. I like some cartoon art styles but this just seems to go a bit overboard for me. I will score it fairly as I know some people do like this kind of Art Style
The music to this game is great. Although it would be better if they could add some more variation to each different type of castle, as depending on the type of castle it is will change the music accordingly to that certain castle type. This means that there are only 3 different soundtracks that play throughout the entire game. Again gets very repetitive if your playing in a longer session. As for the sounds they are okay, the sound of a anvil hitting a knight on the head is pretty satisfying to say the least, and others like when you hit a fireball on the bird.
I would recommend this game to people who like puzzle games, I suggest playing in short periods to avoid not really having as much fun as you did the first time you played it. Also the soundtracks get repetitive so there is another reason why playing in shorter sessions could benefit your gaming experience better than mine.

Castle is a very unique puzzle/building game, where you basically build a castle while being attacked by various things that either prevent you from building your castle, or they remove pieces you have already placed.
You have a bunch of hooks at the top of the screen that will place the castle pieces for you, so you drag the right shaped pieces to the right hook. You need to kep an eye out for various things that prevent you from making the castle, such as a thunder cloud that makes one of the hooks rusty so it won't work, or a chicken could swoop in and take a piece from you.
You need to do all of this quickly and accuratly, or you will lose.
Between rounds you can use in game coins to buy upgrades like faster hook drops, and items to deal with the attackers.
It's very unique, but that doesn't make a good game.
I played about 30 mins and made it to level 7, but that was enough for me.
The game is quite easy to figure out and it explains what to do, but the actual gameplay is more a chore than entertainment.
I found the whole process to be rather annoying which may be your cup of tea, but it isn't mine.
It's easy to misjudge where pieces go, and if you send the wrong piece to the wrong spot too many times, you lose.
It's always rather stressful to constantly have to watch out for problems against your castle and there is little room for error, and I'm sure it only gets worse.
While this may sound like an inexperienced player complaining becuase I wasn't very good, the issue here is, this is not fun enough to BOTHER getting good.
This is the type of game that needs a Demo, because it will certainly be a hit and miss game for people.
For me, It's a miss.

I am absolutely in love with this game. It takes deck building, choose-your-own-adventure, board games, Arkham-style brawling and roguelite elements and mixes them all into a melting pot, and the atmosphere is the final ingredient that brings it all together.
You're essentially playing through an adventure, using a deck of cards as the base, with the dealer providing colorful commentary and setting the mood. It's like playing a personal, one-on-one game of DnD with someone...or like old shows like Knightmare or similar. I can not overstate how impressive the atmosphere is of the game, with each card full of flavor and every encounter interesting and exciting. You never know what you'll find!
The dealer himself is a very interesting character, who half the time seems to want to help you and half the time seems happy to watch you twist in the wind. He'll applaud you for victory, but just as quickly savor your defeat. Maybe you decide to swap out an axe for a sword? He'll snark about it, asking you if it's really what you want to do. His commentary, though sometimes cryptic, does an immense job in building the world and turns every card into a fully fleshed encounter, dripping with detail. Every monster, enemy and boss is played up with description, sometimes terrifying and sometimes mournful.
Honestly, I have no complaints about this game at all and have had no issues or bugs with it...at least so far. Some of the RNG can get truly brutal in the later encounters and the combat itself isn't exactly door-busting, but it's more than servicable and for anyone who's played the Arkham games, Assassin's Creed or the like will find it easy to learn, though the difficulty ramps up greatly.
I can already see this being one of my favorite games of the year. I sincerely hope they intend to release more content for it, as I'd love that, though between the Story mode and Endless Mode, I can see playing this for a long while yet.

This game is obviously made for mobile and hastely ported to PC. The controls are more intuitive for a small-sized touch-screen.
The options are severely lacking, ie no sound or music sliderbar and the monitor options reset as do the audio settings each time the game is launched. I'm greeted with blaring background-music and have to go through several screens just to get to sound options to mute them... The simplistic audio mute-buttons could've been in the main menu or in the main options menu rather than an additional level deeper.
As for the screen resetting; I used 1920x1080 which is a mistake for this game because the mouse needs to travel a larger distance to place the same amount of blocks, and you have to pay attention that a slightly rotated block isn't placed somewhere it shouldn't. For me to play this longer than 5 to 10 minutes at a time, I'd need to use a super small window so I don't need to move my head / neck. ----- Now, back to reset. I tried full-screen, then windowed and it resets to the smallest wide-screen size despite the window being the proper size. The rendering engine renders 1/5th the screen when you swap; after you change the resolution in the options between one other and the larger, it renders fine. There is an issue with the game not properly rendering when it loses focus, but not minimized, which is slightly annoying too.
The game is essentially: Build a 3 to x sized puzzle using only the edge pieces, more suited for children aged 3 to 4 or younger to gauge coordination and tracking; it's too easy. To counteract it being so easy, the developer added a very short time-limit ( but you can extend it if you need more time ). If you let the time run out the round resets, but wait.. there's more.. you get back ALL of the money you spent and then some... for failing the level... The developer also made the pieces move in conveyor-fashion.
To top it off, and this is where a few interesting things were added to the bland game: enemies / traps which rust your cranes, etc... which is a good touch... But a penguin running off with tons and tons of stone by pulling the bottom layer off and then the top coming down ( although, the way they'd build castles is by alternating stone so with the loss of stone underneath, the entire thing won't come crashing down ), but then again, to "add challenge" I suppose. Fix: Rendering issue with changing resolution, annoying critters that can't be stopped ( IE moles can be stopped with tnt but not a meteor which can provide a bit more energy ) with certain tools; let certain tools be more useful...
Add: If the game has lost focus but not minimized prevent sleep or provide an option..
Games are supposed to be enjoyable / fun, they should be challenging in some cases but not to the point of being annoying ( although you could create a clause such as certain holidays, depending on the map, that particular critter is overly annoying... Groundhog day, Christmas, Halloween, etc... ) which would add flavor without being annoying all the time..
I'll revisit this review at a later date; aside from the rendering glitch and the free-money "on-purpose??", you're a winner for trying, and some of the annoying characteristics I could see this game being quite enjoyable for the incrediibly young while making them pay attention to minute differences thereby stimulating the brain. With 271 hours played, i feel comfortable in my knowledge of this game, and i feel ready to make a "review" of it. (note, the reason i call it a "review" is because it strictly is not one, it is more a summary of content)
Let me start of with this: i have not played Crusader kings 1, i also have played all the other contemporary paradox g-strategy titles, (including the somewhat aging Victoria 2 (which is great btw)) so this will be from the perspective of someone who has a good deal of experience in the different games.
Now, CKII, A game of thrones? well, other than the fact that a mod exists for that, yeah, that is the best way to describe part of this game.
You are a Medieval count/duke/king/emperor, (depending on who you start as) and have challenges to face that befits your station, as a count, you deal with the threat of the much larger kings, and in many circomstances a duke that wants your stuff, intrigue, in terms of.. well, killing the sod, is an option, improving relations is one, play the long game, and marry his daughter(or son, i dont judge) or go to war, claim your right to rule.
As a duke you deal with your somewhat unruly subordinates, often very few of them, and other than that, your real enemy is the king or emperor. You want to become one! And the king stands in your way to greatness.
Ally other rulers, use intrigue, once more, marry, make your child ruler, there are many options.
Now, on to the battle system, where i will start with talking about technology: It increases in %ages, instead of unit changes, as is the usual with EUIV, and the upgrades are less game changing than in vic 2 (dig in cap hello) but the most important in terms of millitary is the retinue upgrades (and the demesne upgrades, but that does not have to do with war, so i dont talk about it here) A retinue was a medieval following, you did not yet have (often at least) professional armies under the command of the ruler, every single lord had a personal and a land based army, the land based one was often on more or less lease to the Ruler, in defense of the realm and whatnot, in this game the personal retinue is a personal Army, separate to the Levy (or land based) army, the limit of which can be increased by technology.
Anyway, the combat is (farily) simple, you have three parts to your force, the right, the left, and the center flanks. each with a commander, who each gives their combat modifiers to their respective force, other factors that play in are Attacker/Defender, Terrain, Straight crossings, boat landings, the like.
Every territory you have or conquer is part of your Demesne, or Held land, each territory holds a number of "holdings" which include Churches, Towns, and Castles (baronies) each with their own need for upgrades, people to keep happy, and different rewards to be gained, Castles provide large levies, towns provide cash cows, and churches provide faith, gold and levy, in my experience, i go for towns in most provinces and go for castles in the ones with higher limits of holdings.
You have a demesne limit, this is based upon your stewardship skill, wife (or husband)'s stewardship, and technology, you start seeing minuses to tax income and the like if you go over it, but dont be afraid to do so, it can sometimes save your hide.
Now i wont say much more, as i would have to get into expansions, but ill be safe to say, there are tons of events, religions, and effects based on that, Crusades happen, Jihads happen, and great holy wars (for other religions) happen.
This is a game with a steep learning curve, so dont be discouraged by losses, it takes some time to get used to.
Sieze your birthright lord, for you can rise to greatness. Rise Imperator, for your time has come. Rise Pagans, for riches untold. Rise Raja, for lands untold.

Crusader Kings 2 is, at its core, a GRAND strategy game. The world is massive and massively detailed, and the possibilities are endless. At the time of writing this review I have about 315 hours logged in the game, and when you consider that I am just the type of person who can rarely log 100 without getting bored, that is saying something.
The focus of this game is to build your dynasty in feudal Europe, but the game also include some parts of Africa, the whole Middle East, and India (only playable with the Rajas of India DLC). The timeline for this game is truely massive, with just the base game you can play from 1066 to 1453, just over 400 years. In that time you will play as a single ruler, then your ruler's heir, then their heir, and so on. This is a game about forging your path into the history books. If you want to play as a Viking and conquer India, you can. If you want to play the manipulating vassal of the Holy Roman Emperor, you can do that too. There is almost nothing you can't do.
If you get tired of conquering the same old Afro-Eurasia again and again, then there are always mods. CK2 features a native system to easily activate and deactivate mods, as well as Steam Workshop support. In addition to the well crafted framework for mods, the modding community around this game is enormous. For instance, the Game of Thrones mod. A full overhaul to set the same Feudal Dynasty simulator into the world of Westeros, and that is just one of thousands.
Overall, this is my second favorite game of all time, right behind Europa Universalis IV, another title from the same developers. This game is one of the best I have ever seen, and the devs are still releasing patches and massive updates.

"Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale" is an action jrpg in with we take the role of female shop owner in a fantasy land. This original idea let's us be an NPC from with we bought items in many different games. 
The main heroin is Recette. She inherited a shop after her father. Her father passed away and she have to pay the debt that her father took. She got some help from a fairy named Tear. Well that fairy is more like a broker and she is responsible for collecting the debt that Recette have to pay. She was kind enough to split the debt in to part so that she is able to pay it. Each month you have to pay bigger chunk of the debt. If you fail to meet the deadline you lose and you have to start over from day one. When you lose you keep your items and unlockables. So each time you fail the game becomes easier. 
Main point of the game is to buy cheap and sell expensive. Each client bargains with you on your wares. If your offer is to ridiculous client will not want to talk with you no more. If your offer is reasonable they will tell you if it's to much for them. Different people have different standards when it comes to price. a girl that was sent by her mother on shopping will most likely not pay more then 90% of value of the item, but some noble man can even pay 180% of the value. We can unlock new items through dungeon running. To go to a dungeon we need to "rent" an adventurer in the guild. He will boost us through dungeon for a price and we can keep all the items that will  drop in the dungeon. Heroes vary in price depending on their skill. When we rent the adventurer we take control of him in the dungeon.
Fight in this game is similar to old snes Zelda. You move around the screen in for directions and use your basic and special attacks. Special attacks cost us mana and you can replenish mana by using items. You have the ability to borrow items to your hero. Before starting the dungeon You can chose what items you want to borrow to heroes. If the hero dies in the dungeon you will lose all the items you borrowed him.
Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale doesn't have good graphic when we are in a dungeon game looks like a game from N64 and when we navigate through town it looks like a game from Game Boy Advance. Forget about running this game in 1920x1080 resolution it's not going to happen. game is very much anime stylized. 
Sound assets are very weak and if you listen to the music for a longer time you might get a headache. Music sound like a 16 bit console music.
The game doesn't have to good of a quality, but It's original idea makes this game a lot of fun. I didn't know how much satisfaction would give me selling an item for 10x times it cost. Even though storyline in this game isn't to deep. Building the relationship with the adventures is really fun. And it's great to sell items to adventurers with whom we later go to dungeons. It's a shame that we don't have better control over what the heroes are using. 
Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is by all means worth it's price. I played it for about 18 Hours. If someone really like the concept he can get much more value by playing in endless mode and higher difficulties. If you are not bothered by the weak graphics you should definitely give it a try.

Truly a sleeper hit.  When I purchased this game I was expecting a fairly cutesy shop simulator and not much beyond that and boy howdy although I was right on that there is so much more to this.  The big part of this game that steals the show comes from the dialogue and the great translation.  It feels similar to Earthbound in that there's some quirk to it that just makes you grin, although I'd argue this does it better.  Despite having the shiny atmosphere the game is also quite challenging with the debts you must pay for the Item Shop and you will have to push yourself to ensure your income makes it in time.  In addition to managing items, selling high, and buying low you also have a side story that comes in the form of dungeon crawling which is again something I did not expect.  The dungeon crawling I'd argue is just average truth be told, cause while it does have the standard looting, random drops, and boss battles the later dungeons get enourmous and it makes navigation a royal pain since the floors are randomized and you can have as many as thirty rooms on a single floor.
TL;DR
A surprisingly engaging game with a great script, average dungeon crawling, and a good level of challenge.  Pick it up when you get the chance!

Valkyria Chronicles is trully one of the best T-RPG available on PC. Despite a "naive" outlook, it actually has a lot of depth. The scenario doesn't have many surprises (it has a few...) but holds itself together and doesn't pretend to be better than it actually is. The lore, however, is a hole other story: it really works well and bring up some interesting points about racisme, war and all their consequences. The game will make you cry at least once. It might be in a plot twist, it might be when one of your soldier dies (or child soldier, for that matter), it might even be when an ennemy soldier die, but it will happen.
Now about its gameplay... Exellent, but flawed would be te best way to describe it. The "BLITZ" system works really well as you alternate between the "tactical mode", where you plan your strategies, and the "action mode", when you put them in motion. The game suffers from an awefull balance, though: some soldiers and weapons are clearly overpowered when compared to others, and you don't even need to farm to be far stronger than your ennemy. Speaking of the ennemy, the AI is the greatest flaw of the game: it is far too scripted and make a lot of dumb move for no particular reason. It will sometime prefer to waste its turns patroling areas it knows you couldn't possibly have reached. Sometime, however, it will unleash its wrath against you and you will lose. Periode. But those moments are scripted as well and you will be prepared for it in your next try.
I probably make it look worst than it is, though: Again, it is flawed but exellent nonetheless.
Also, buy this game and live in fear of chapter seven. You have been warned.

Its Fire Emblem in first person.
That's what this game is. Its fire Emblem but in first person. FE combined the two phases that this game stresses into one chess match. Here; you're given a set pool of moves, and your foe always has more. You can kill certain dudes to lessen the amount of turns they can make, but it never matters. This movepool can be used on any unit so as long as they're 1. alive, and 2. within range. Also; each person can move a set amount per move point. Each consecutive move you take them for; they get a bit less movement range, but they always have one attack.
Your foes could feasably take one powerful unit and just destroy you. That constant threat, can also be done for me.
I can easily cheese whole forces if I have enough firepower. Take the tank; shove it into a key persons mouth; and just wait for the game over screen. The tanks shots are realistic; so its an AOE. Granted, its not that powerful of an AOE, but its enough; particularly knowing theres just nothing you can do about it unless you happen to have a tank. Its not balanced. You could've just copied FE and it would've been so much better.
I'm not a nintendrone. Nintendo games are by no means the pinicle, but when I talk about this game, I just say "Its FE but with guns and a broken battle system." Because you know. FE is the most well known in context, and also happens to actually be a fair comparison. It does a lot of things right.
The voice acting is great, just like FE, and I like how they remain pretty silent on the field unlike FE; only telling you what you need to know every three seconds. "ENIME SPOTTEED ENIME SPOTTEED ENIME SPOTTEEEED". Stand right in front of him like I did in MGS: PW and watch the man eat three of the five shots because all the guns are like creme cheese. But in MGS:PW it was a sniper rifle. And he would always die. And I'd never get noticed because its MGS:PW and it wasn't the PSP's best game.
MGS aside;

Possible-medical-fore-warning:
There has been some reports + newer-reviews mentioning something about the "current-built" of this game "flickering" quite a alot on some of the machines. While this doesn't make this game unplayable (as of writing this), some people might experience nauseating or any similar effects.
Personally, I do indeed see some consistent flickering. But I don't exprience any medical-side-effect, at least not yet.
Technical-fore-words:
It is fair to warn right away that this is indeed a very "as-it-is"-release of the originaly year-2000-build of this game, which is also mentined on one if the first pre-title-images. So there are no build-in tweakings in options-menu for windowed-mode, resolution-changes, or various other "modern" tweaking-options aside wheteher you want to turn of the sounds or not most importantly.
That being said, you're going to get one of the least amount changes suffering re-releases on Steam, only chnage being that it works on (at least most of the ) moderm machines.
You're also unfotunately forced to use another 3rd-party screen-capturing / shotting-software since due the age and un-modified nature of this game, the Steam-overlay won't be working (at least by default).
--------------
--------------
As for the game itself, "Puzzle Station" is the non-product-placement "off-spring" of Ninai Games (before Detonium Interactive) of "Drop Mania" (which eventually was "remade" as "Super Drop Mania" for Gizmondo by "Fathammer"; then there's of couse the "Rampage Puzzle Attack"-variant also by "Ninai Games").
Like the title suggest, this "Drop Mania"-variant is much more puzzle-heavy for the most part. But considering the simplistic nature of the game-mechanics (link 4 or more of the same color-blocks to "poof"-them), I for one can forgive this even if sometimes I'd like to just watch pretty explosions "without thinking" (I.E. playing without swapping the blocks with Ctrl-button).
So, is the game worth buying?
Well,  puzzle-game enthusiastics, especially those who are looking for some older titles, this is quite a good and solid one to their collection.
That's pretty much all I can say about this game, for now.
And who knows, maybe we'll see an actual new "Drop Mania"-game in future on PC.

I must admit, I had my doubts about buying the game, since I've played quite a few time management farming games in my time and felt like I've seen pretty much everything the genre had to offer. However, Farm Frenzy 4 was a pleasant surprise. Yes, basically it's the same old Farm Frenzy inside, but it does not fail to entertain you every second of the time spent playing. Lush colors, 3D, camera control - it's all pretty nice, maybe it's a matter of taste, but I liked the visuals. Music is great as well, all the rustic Country and Celtic themes somehow sound fresh and don't irritate you after hours of playing. Storyline with its mysterious take is rather good for this type of games, too.
But what really surprised me and made the game stand out of the similar farming clickers, is the attention to details and its constant aspiration to keep you occupied. I love having so much to do to find things while you're playing to up the money multiplier (I like the multiplier idea a lot. Sometimes I found my focus elsewhere rather than on my goals which created a real challenge) and the way you catch the bears is cool. All that quirky little perks like collecting things to trade them for bonuses, and animal combos leave no time to be idling about, either on levels or between them. The only complaint I'd like to voice is that it would be nice to have a little more detailed instructions on the collection items. And yes, maybe it's too easy sometimes - if you only pay attention to the primary objectives, getting the gold most of the time does not present a significant challenge. But when you've figured out the level strategy, previous Farm Frenzy got boring, and here, the fun only starts - you can hunt bears and moles, catch butterflies, collect apples and whatnot. Your mouse never rests at peace, and that feels good.
Overall, it's not the same old same old Farm Frenzy from yesteryear, but that's perfectly fine. Definitely recommend.

I found this game to be pleasantly surprising. At the very worst it could have been too flash game like, which I was afraid of (even though there are some amazing flash games out there).
Actually quite nice, crisp and clean, cartoony, with  a almost angrybirdsy-like feel. Bright but not blindly so.
I think I like the chicken graphics the best. yeah.
Pretty straightforward, and based on the level designs, some can be hard to get - but nothing that is crazy insane intense.
I still get a crazy angry birds feel from this. But each level is a fortress and you have to drop pieces of the castle in a correct place, or else you lose a life. Compound that one the enemies that will try to impeded your progress. Add the timer and you have some challenging, yet fun levels.
You can improve your skill set with money earned completing each level, with bonuses for completing levels quickly.  You can spend money on 3 stats: time increase, speed, and life.
You also need to be careful choosing what to buy, as certain levels will need items to stop enemies (however even if you don't have money, you will still get the items, you just have to wait longer in the game - something a lot of the down voters didn't even notice)
There are also 3 game modes, being the regular mode (explained above), king mode (extremely hardcore mode, lvl 10 is kicking my rear, and defender mode )
