Intro:
There are some bad reviews, but, if you read the bad reviews, most of them are by people that obviously don't understand what "Early Access" means.  Funcom even put a little disclaimer in their intro to the game, with a link address to Steam's explanation of "Early Access."  You're basically paying a company for "early access" to beta test their game for them.  Don't buy it yet if you are expecting optimized and streamlined gameplay.  It's not there yet.  But it's getting closer by the day.
Now, all that being said, I should give my own disclaimer.  I am a Conan fan.  The first novel I ever read was "Conan the Defender" by Robert Jordan, when I was 7 years old.  I snitched it from my older brother, and read it in my room and at school.  But to let you know that my review is impartial, I am also a big WH40k fan, and WH:EC was a complete disappointment, and I don't play it.  I hate it.  I was a beta tester for AoC, and that was a disappointment in that Funcom didn't deliver what they promised.  As a fan of something, I expect the company developing the game to put a fan's level of heart and soul into it.  Anyway, this is about Conan Exiles.
Review:
This is a running update review.  I check back to edit it as I feel an update is needed.
Currently at 114 hours play time, around level 40.  Some time played in single player, but that was all messing around with admin rights and stuff.
Pros:
The environment looks really nice, if you can play with high enough settings.  My settings are only at medium, and the world looks really nice.  I'm looking forward to the tax return, so I can buy a 980 or 1080 and see what that does.  Right now, I'm playing on a GTX 570.
You can set the level of nudity allowed on your server/single player game.  If your server is set to full nudity, each player can also set their own level of nudity, so you don't have to worry about what level of nudity the server is at.
Slaves.  ...I mean thralls.  It's not every game you get to go bludgeon somebody into unconciousness, and make them bend to your will.
All lag is pretty much fixed.  We have zero problems with leg anymore, except the very occasional spike that sometimes goes unnoticed.
Funcom is active and working hard to make this game worth your money.  They want this game to succeed.  They want it to be what you're looking for.
Mixed:
Progression is a little slow compared to other survival games, but on par with MMOs.  This can be tweaked in server settings, but like I said, we're playing it vanilla.
-We upped our xp to 1.5 and it's much better.  Only change thus far.
-Upped our xp to 2.0.  We're starting to get a little ground down with xp farming.
Cons:
Currently some wacky little bugs, but nothing game stopping for me.  It's EA, so these are easy to ignore, and find workarounds, or fixable by logging off and on.
-crafting bugs
-inventory bugs
-creature pathing
-you get the gist.
Spawn points are not random.  I know where to go and kill a croc, and shalebacks along the way, for easy XP grind path.  I hope that this changes.  I'd like to see wandering mobs that can travel the entire map, if they so desire.
-Gind path irrelevant due to XP required vs. XP given, but I really want wandering mobs.
-AI:  AI is very basic.  Easy to exploit animals and humans into combat situations of your choosing.  Basically, just be careful of pulling too many mobs at once, and you're okay.
-Boss Mobs:  Boss mobs are unkillable in single player.  Even if you lure them to a point where you can hit them, and they can't hit you, good luck killing them.  And yet, on the undead dragon, the story block tells you "a single man killed it."  Yeah....
-When I view the game in my library, the mods pictured show full frontal nudity, as my 4 year old son pointed out.  Not good...
-The world is too small at the current build.  They do have plans to add new biomes, but until this happens, prepare to get bored.  I couldn't even level all the way to 50.  Perhaps PvP servers are a remedy to this?  I don't know.  But the environment by itself is too small to keep one's attention.
-Not enough lore driven content.  Robert E. Howard gave Funcom enough content to build an entire world.  Add in all the other side books by Robert Jordan, Leonard Carpenter (even though I believe he was the one that had Crom take an active role in Conan's life), comic books like The Savage Sword of Conan, and you have way more than enough content to start filling a world like this with tons and tons and tons of lore.  Yet so little of it, besides the titles of NPCs and the race of your character....
Conclusion (TLDR):
Little bit of a rough start, but Funcom has been on the ball getting hotfixes out.  People are complaining about Early Access stuff, and that's why there's mixed reviews.  Stay away if you don't like beta level gaming.  Game is fun, but has small issues, nothing game breaking, unless your computer sucks, your server sucks, or your connection sucks.  Game is pretty brutal until you get a good foundation set up.  Expect to die.  A lot.  And I mean PvE.  Beautiful environment.  Once you get set up though, the game becomes a grind, and a bit of a bore.  I recommend the game to Conan fans, otherwise...  wait until more development has been implemented.

Great game. I think the title alone will help you decide if you'll like it.
Do you want to golf with your friends?? Well if that sounds good, you should probably enjoy it.
The Level design here has its flaws at times, (mainly with holes that forces you to hit your ball off walls, like the pillars in egypt or the bottle in the mansion) but it is for the most part quite forgiving and interesting. It's great for a large group of friends of all skill levels.
The controls themselves are incredibly simple but very well made. Simply click and drag where you want to go and how hard you want to hit it. There's a power bar that easily indicates how hard or soft you'll be hitting. It gets the job done efficiently, and I appreciate that.
Surprisingly, it is also got a great amount of replay ability. Coming back to maps you did and turning on jump can really change the entire game. It's broken, but it's fun. And if you really want to make things hectic, you can change the gravity, change the ball shape to all sorts of horrible things (Eggs, cones, stars, cubes, etc) which all completely change how the holes work. Luckily, they're still almost all doable!
I really enjoy this game for its simplicity. It's what you'd expect from a mini golf game. I wouldn't recommend it unless you bring a few friends along, however. The single player is nice, but would probably get stale.
Only real gripes right now are that I wish there were more levels and possibly a VERY easy to use level editor that lets you pick community levels on the fly (similar to how SpeedRunners does it). Obviously, though, there's more planned for the game, but you can never be sure when it comes to Early Access.
Even though there's only a handful of maps, I'd strongly recommend this game with friends, especially since the price is quite affordable as well.

I bought this game on sale and if you can get it for a similar price, I recommend it. The gameplay is really innovative and interesting. However, there are some issues that would prevent me from recommending it at full price. It frankly needs debugging, for one. Glitches happen (thankfully, there's fixes online). Also, there are some points where you have to find a clue, and you just can't do it unless you twist and torture the camera angle to Just The Right Spot, which can be suuuuuper annoying.
The most frustrating part for me personally was the missed story opportunities. When Ronan realizes the truth of what's going on, he doesn't break into a run or teleport or do anything to signify panic - he just sort of sets off at a leisurely pace. Jarring much? Also,
Or when you find out who the Bell Killer is, there's no "well, how did they do it?" Just easy acceptance that they did. That kind of lazy storytelling really bugs me.
Wish Squeenix had given this game like six more months to clean up the bugs and expand the story - it's on the short side, even. If it was longer, tighter and less buggy, it'd be one of my favorite games ever. But alas, it's not. So if you can get it for $4.99 or something, like I did, go for it - but not a penny more.

I am not reviewing this game in the perspective of "at the time it came out" or comparing the editions in any way. I'm reviewing this game as it is, for what it was to me playing it in 2016.
To start, the save system is an absolute disaster. You can manually save the game while you play, but when you're in a quest you can "hero save" which saves your items and stats but not your quest progress. In any case, both of them are extremely problematic. It's not actually consistent what saves and what doesn't, and the game is in no way smart about making sure it saves properly. For example, at some point the game forgot that I had completed a side quest, but it remembered that I had used the items required in the quest.... so basically, it made the quest impossible to complete. On a later save, a bunch of my money disappeared but it remembered the things I had bought during that same session. It just picks and chooses what it remembers and what it doesn't, occasionally breaking an entire storyline altogether. This alone is a game breaker.
Now to combat. Fighting against one enemy, combat is sort of fun. You lock on to your target, you can hack and roll and block to be a formidable fighter. As soon as 2+ enemies come at you, it all falls apart. Blocking becomes useless (actually, blocking performs inconsistently to begin with). The target system is supposed to let you switch between targets but doesn't realistically let you do that in a helpful way. Most players invest in a physical shield that uses mana as a defense and doesn't allow you to use your block; this to me is a screaming flaw. So to get through a wave of baddies without being seriously hurt, you need to use an overpowered spell and consume 10 mana potions? That sounds like a cheap exploit, not like enjoyable combat. In many ways, this game rewards you for overpowering easy spells and punishes you for trying to take part in actual melee or ranged combat.
The enemies seem to be very inconsistent. You will face an enemy and find it easy to mow down, then moments later you'll come across another one and it seems to have infinite health. I don't know what the basis is, exactly. When you run into some bandits on the way to a destination and it takes 5 minutes to get rid of them in the same repetitive chop chop chop get knocked over drink mana put up shield chop chop chop sequence, it just becomes tedius. You can recruit some expensive mercenaries to help you, but in my experience the auto target likes to aim at them during battle. So I'll have ten generic looking bandits, each with a totally random mystery amount of health, swarming me while my auto-target aims at my mercenary or the person I'm supposed to be escorting to safety. What? How does that help me in any way?
There are two cosmetic mechanics in the game that are really cool to a point but become rather irritating. First of all, your character ages each time you level up skills. This is an interesting mechanic, except that nothing else ages in the same way and it is way too drastic. By time you finish leveling, you look old and withered (you are 65). Meanwhile, everone else looks EXACTLY THE SAME. The children in the game are still children. This makes aging utterly meaningless; it just ruins your toon if you care about how he looks. The other mechanic is scarring: As you get damaged in battle, you develop scars over time. This is actually really cool, until you realize that your face gets cut up like butter. Given the awful combat system I mentioned, you are GOING to get attacked and after only a few hits you will get a new cut or your old cuts will become more prominent. In the end, it's just scratching up your character for no reason. The only thing that can stop it is the afforementioned mana shield which basically strips combat of any actual skill and devolves it into hacking at your opponent as fast as you can so as to avoid being hit, and gulping down mana potions if you do get hit.
The characters in this game are f***ing irritating. There were a few funny moments that genuinely made me laugh, but for each of those there are dozens of nerve grating lines of dialogue. For a game that's so cartoonish and silly, there isn't really any heart to it because the storyline is entirely cliché and there isn't a single likeable or relateable character in the game
There are a lot of small features in the game like the chance to buy and sell for profit, marriage, owning a house, etc. Unfortunately, all of them are mere distractions and offer no real depth whatsoever. Since none of the characters are actually likeable, and marrying one just involves pressing "laugh" "flirt" "show off muscles" and giving gifts, it is entirely purposeless. You buy a house so that they can live in it, or so you can rent it out for gold. Let's talk about gold: There is a memory game you can play in the tavern that is extremely easy to win and on which you can bet thousands of gold pieces. You can win all the money you need from it, making everything to do with currency in the game entirely meaningless. Why should I do quests boasts (an interestnig feature where you bet money on accomplishing quests with special limitations) if I can just make all that money from a game of memory? Why wouldn't I just buy all the best armor there is if I can get all the money I need at any time? Any progression pertaining to the spending of money is undermined. I think the best example of how this game tacks in random features to make it seem better than it is is the experience orbs: When you defeat an enemy, it leaves experience orbs which you collect for experience. Well, why the hell are they little orbs which I can miss? Why wouldn't the game just allow me to have the experience? That exemplifies how the game sort of makes "features" out of non features. Why would I choose to be evil when it'll literally be like "save this person or brutally murder them?" Why would I buy and sell for money when I can gamble for it easily? Why would I choose to be a swordsman or archer when I can just acquire some overpowered spells?
The sad thing is, for all the roleplaying features the game boasts, there is actually no real variety in how you play. Things are pretty much predetermined for you, and the choices are an illusion or a gimmick.
I dare anyone who thinks I'm not being fair to this game to look up a strategy forum. Pretty much any serious player used loopholes, exploits, or overpowered spells in order to play the game and do well. If you want to actually play the game in the way it presents itself and that has meaning to it, you will probably find it isn't worth the trouble.
Altogether, I'm glad I finally got around to playing a game from the Fable series just so I could check it out, but I don't plan to actually finish the game as there is no reason to do so.

Well, I have been spoiled in the past by another great title in the survival genre, however that game changed much after nearly 2 years. Conan Exiles has a strong foundation upon release and I do believe that in the next few months, this game is going to be awesome and a valid option for Survival fans as well as people who enjoy the overall theme/setting the game takes place. I decided to help out the project as I know it has great potential.
Considering the Early Access tag, the game just launched with its Alpha build. That means the game CURRENTLY does not look at all like the video / trailer, even on ultra settings (actually anything higher than "low" is inexistant). I can understand why as more graphics = taxing and more impact from the optimization front, which clearly needs a pass before they upgrade visually.
AI is pretty simple. It will engage you on sight and I found some animals very persistant in killing you. Chasing a long range before giving up. Some creatures I managed to out run, but felt that crocodiles ,for example, chased too far away from water sources.
I barely started a base with door, walls, foundation, celling and a cooking fire (3x3). It seems standard for the survival market, though I did enjoy the foundations as they don't stand that high from the ground and the map seems to favor a long chain of flat terrains, so at least for now it seems feasable not to over rely on pillars and can use foundations instead, this is great for builders like myself who pay attention to detail and prefer solid ground work.
Learning craftables is interesting, 2 things stood out:  Items highlight what it will unlock down the road, allowing for better planning. The other is when you learn to make structures, the game lets you craft the entire tier, thats actually smart and less tedious than learning every item individually. Grats for the vision here.
What really shows to me though, is the lore. I mean there are brief interactions but those are voiced and decently so. I found a diary from a woman and she related the horrible events she went through. Another was from a killed soldier about some creature and his fears. I like tales and survival games have adopted none to minimal story. This is were Exiles could stand apart from the rest. The pontential is great here, while still ensuring players own stories prevail.
Conclusion:
The game is on "investment phase", you will buy something only to be able to really play it 6-8 months from now (and still issues to resolve until full release). Unless you like to get involved and see the project improve over time, I would avoid it for now. On the other hand, if you like being part of the devolpement process, which could take a couple to a few years than I believe this project is solid. Funcon is known, they have good ideas and they have a good structure to handle community. Now is the time for feedbacks, first 6 months will be rough but that is Conan. I really like to see more of this game.

While I have pumped over 100 hours into the game, but I'm coming to the point where I will need to be going into item world, and doing some serious grinding, and this is where the port falls to pieces.
even though there have been several patches, they have fixed / broke / fixed / broke and not fixed some issues, the not fixed is the core crashing issue that still plagues this game. We the community are at the mercy of the devs, and IF they decide to fix this mess, but from what Kaldaien has found out, I suspect the only way to fix this mess, is probably to do a rewrite of the code. and I'm not sure that will happen.
but if this is how NIS will release games onto steam, then sadly, I can see other games falling into the same mess as Disgea.

Have you ever gotten a coffee from Dunkin’ Donuts? America runs on Dunkin’ so I know you have because no civilization exists outside of the borders of this great nation, trust me. I visited England once, there was nothing but football hooligans and CCTV cameras. Anyway, back to the dunkin’ analogy, when you start drinking it it tasted bitter, unpleasant, there’s too much milk and it’s bovine creaminess threatens to choke the breath out of you. If you manage to survive that stage you’re near the end, it’s starting to to sweeten a little and you think: ‘Maybe this is what victory tasted like.’ With only the dregs left you throw your head head back and down the last of the liquid, knowing that you’ve won and nothing will be able to stop you today.
After you’ve thrown up the sickly sweet goop that slid down the back of your throat along with the the tooth enamel it grabbed on the way past you realise that the jerk behind the counter didn’t even give the cup a shake to dissolve the sugar.
That’s kind of the inverse of this game.
It’s all a game of deception, you see, it fools you into thinking you know what you’re in for: Here’s a homeless little orphan girl, here’s her fairy manager, set up shop and do business. But hold on there, Ken-Sama, get your nose out of that doujin! That stuff will get you arrested if one of those British CCTV cameras catch you with it. They’ll sentence you to life imprisonment with nothing but American tea for sustenance. Once you get past the saccharine sweet character designs and voicework  there’s some bitter, milky gameplay to get familiar with.
There’s no fantasy here aside from the setting, you’ve got to start setting prices for your various wares won through old-fashioned dungeon crawling along with the various stupidly loyal or dangerously self-interested cohorts you’ve set loose to murder the peaceful inhabitants of said dungeons. Try as they might to defend their homes and loved ones, let none stand against your (Simplistically controlled yet still enjoyable) bladework, their property WILL be yours to peddle to the various citizens of your town.
As in real life, of course, this is the far more difficult proposition. Convincing someone to kill for you is a simple matter, maintaining domination of even a relatively docile population from behind the scenes via market control is a more trying task, just ask the Reptilian overlords deciding our fate. All I can say to that is watch out for the little girl, she may play innocent but she knows far more than she’s letting on.
Get that money, little merchant. Get that money.

tl;dr version: This is a very vaugely Tetris-y game, involving building a castle from manually dropped block pieces, that has decent-if-simple art and music, but suffers from poor presentation.
The game's refusal to give you any comprehensible feedback on game elements or mission conditions turns what seems to be a reasonably decent puzzle game into a frustrating 'guess the game's intentions' engagement.
That is, you're going to lose a level more likely because of the game not giving you the appropriate feedback, than the circumstances within the level.
Weirder still, the mid-level tips are actually fairly relevant, so it's not like the devs didn't know how to do it.
Rather than stick the tips in-between levels, maybe they could have presented them during, or via tool-tips, like most developer?
Agh.
Well, as the gameplay itself wasn't stimulating enough to keep me playing through those UI issues, I'll focus on giving you a content description rather than a more point-by-point review (Though, PRO, the music seemed simple but pleasant, and changed stage to stage, so that's a plus.)
> Puzzle tiles cycle across the top of the screen.
> You drag and drop the tiles onto claws, which then lower the tiles downward.
> Your goal is to match the tiles to the outline of a castle depicted below, matching each tile to the appropriate silhoutte location.
> Enemies pass by trying to steal your pieces, block your pieces, break your claws, etc.
You can buy a very limited number of time, life, or claw upgrades- you also HAVE to buy enemy counter item each level or you simply cannot complete a level.
This arrangement makes the purchasing system seem pretty irrelevant, since you're pretty locked into what you need to/can buy each level, and there's no real meaningful effect on gameplay past what hard-locked-per-stage items could have provided.
(Question: Why allow players to screw themselves over on required items, if the alternative is just an illusion of choice for upgrades? Feels like cooldown-based abilities and a more polished gameplay presentation would have worked far better than a shop system- and I LIKE upgrade systems.)
With no explanation given on new enemies, how to use abilities (I never could figure out how to fireball the chickens), or anything else, it's an early guessing game for a game that lacks the depth to be worth the effort.
It's essentially in that 'what you'd expect from a flash game' catagory, nothing more to it than that.
I didn't play it long enough to give a fair rating, and there seems a lot of room for subjective opinion on this one as well, so ?/5 on this one.
The game is bundled/free fairly often.
As such, if the content description above interests you, you like simple puzzle games, AND you're not easily aggravated by poor presentation, there's enough here that it may appeal to you.
Otherwise, I direct you toward Triple Town, my current 'simple puzzle' game of choice. TT doesn't have any real stage-by-stage development of note, either, NOR do the stages ever really change.
It's also more about 'not making a mistake' than about solving more and more challenging puzzles- but it's an excellent zone-out-into-it time-killer and sometimes you don't really need more than that.
For a more demanding puzzle game, I direct you toward the co-op-only Ibb & Obb, which despite some flaws, is a great brain-teaser and teamwork-tester of a game.

I guess it's legal though, because no rozzers have issued a demand on Freddytrux USA's limited funds for it.

After many years devoted to the Total War series, I decided to give the Paradox games a go when CS2 was on sale. I never expected that this game would become the single game I've played more than any other in my twenty-five years of gaming. The character/dynasty depth goes far deeper than the simple character portraits alude to. The challenge of taking a simple count and surviving, then thriving, is what I'm all about. I usually strive to form a large kingdom or empire, then I settle in with no intention of expanding. I prefer to build alliances and defend my Faith. When I inherit large swaths of territory unexpectedly, I begin decades long plans to give it up. The biggest challenge is powerful neighbors. Sometimes I am forced to wait for a hundred years or more to slowly get what I want. Timing is everything. You'll spend countless hours making plans, and twice as long struggling with unexpected calamities. Simple traits like 'craven' or 'lustful' will give you nightmares. The game deserves more than my recommendation, and I easily rate it 100/100. Hands down, the greatest game I've ever played.

Do you enjoy intrigue? Do you find your life lacking in fictional assassinations of royal houses? Do you find yourself missing a bit of crusading action on a cold winter's day?
If the answer is "yes" to any of the above questions, look no further, for Crusader Kings II is here to rescue you and bring you to the era of crusades and conquest! Beginning in 1066, Crusader Kings II lets you pick any count, duke, king, or emperor that existed in Europe at the time. You can play as William the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, before he became William the Conqueror. You can try to avert his invasion as Harold Godwineson, or play your kings right and bring the French Capet's into England.
The game features an extensive system that lets you achieve domination through intrigue, either through plotting or reckless assassinations. Another brilliant selling point? The AI doesn't play to win. It's programmed to play into its role. A lunatic character may attempt reckless tactics that wouldn't have any chance of winning. A paranoid character might imprison people left and right. So you never quite know what to expect.
Along with all these things, the game offers a whole aisle of DLC to suit your every need. The Old Gods will let you extend the timeline to the invasion of England by the Sons of Ragnar in 867, and let you reform the Norse faith and become Fylkir. The Sword of Islam lets you play a muslim leader, letting you enjoy the wonders of decadence and all that accompanies. Rajas of India brings you to India, and lets you experience Hindu and Buddhist culture first hand as you struggle to become the greatest ruler in India.
The game also features a massive amount of mods, placing you in any of a number of universes. Are you interested in  Arthurian England? There's a mod for that. Maybe you're a Song of Ice and Fire fan? You can play as the Stark or any number of their allies or enemies in the Game of Thrones mod, if that's the case. You can also drop into Bethesda's Elder Scrolls universe with the Elder Kings.
There will be endless hours of fun, that much I can almost guarantee.

Writing of Archeage is like writing about my high school dropout son, as in, I don't like doing it. I only do it as I am compelled to help him out of trouble. And my, my, is Archeage in trouble. Archeage is a KMMO in which the idea of a massively open world "sandbox" is realized with beautiful graphics and a massive open world. I would say that the way of play suits it well, and it is very different than your average MMO. I found myself vying for economic success much more than Levels, which I thought was an interesting difference. I have put a lot of time into this game, and I very much adore it.
But, it has more problems than a hooker with daddy issues.
Cons:
-Pay 2 Win: It is there. While yes, it is possible to earn your way past it with money, you basically need patron to do anything. Want a house? Patron! Want land so that you can grow crops to make money? Patron! Want to craft more than one thing before having to wait a day to continue? Patron! This was problematic, but once you get past it (you can buy Patron with in game gold) you find yourself enjoying it much more.
-Dead Servers: At the time of writing only a few of the servers are actually active in both NA and EU. Consider research before joining a server.
-Gank-Based PvP: Now here is a con I don't think everyone will agree on, but I think everyone should consider. PvP is a main aspect of the game that snakes its way into everything else that you do. From the auction house to the arena you are facing off with other players. The problem is that with actual combat it comes down to who gets the first hit. Likely you will be stunned, and put in an infinite combo until you are dead. This isn't exactly the best PvP, people.
Pros:
-This game has the most fun 1-50 of any MMO I have ever played.
- The community, while mostly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, are very entertaining in both Trial Chats and Faction Chats.
-It is an MMO that has experiences unlike many others
-It looks beautiful, like really breathtaking stuff.
Conclusion:
I recommend this game with more than a fair list of caveats. It is fun, and I think if you are looking for a new MMO you should try it out. I think it has many problematic aspects, and I wish I could say that Trion was trying to improve them. It still is great amounts of fun, however, and with a group of friends it becomes a great world to adventure around in. With all the problems it has,

Ok so if this game seems like a good idea to you.....Buy this game!
Combat - Weakest part of the game; other reviews probably have mentioned this. However, for an indie game, I think it plays a great and key part. Chances are, you will win a typical encounter with your foes. It might even be easy or a breeze. But every battle here and there will cost you SOME health. This is the point. You WILL win. But at what cost for future cards and encounters? Sure it is clunky. But it does its job.
Cards (Dungeon Crawl) - The system is great. It makes it random. It makes every run different. It can screw you sideways based on what curses you have. It makes the game great.
Cards (Encounters) - Sooooo good. So good. Wanna pick the high and holy route? You might get rewards and good gear...Wanna be a scumbag stealing and drinking at taverns? You might save some food for a stretch with no traders. You will encounter both. Both have certain rewards. This is golden.....There is no right path.....but one may get you further on a certain encounter....so good.
Deckbuilding - I was a complete novice at this. I had no idea what it meant. With this in hand, you KNOW what can come. You KNOW the enemies. You can build your encounters to give you a chance. Some cards are downright awful and once you know this, they are gone forever never to be used. Some are great and provide a chance against the end game bosses. It makes a rouge-like seem fair and impossible at the same time. Perfection.
The Dealer - Yes, he is worth a mention. The devs could have left him out and had a decent game. But he exists. He will seem friendly when you are dying, angry when you get your 3rd blessing, or hopeful based on your skill or a lucky break. You will hate and love him. Such a beautiful adddition.....
Overall - I have played FTL. It is great, but the level of random may screw you. I love Ziggurat. Its is a FPS and will make you wanna high-five yourself if you win. This is better than both. You will earn rewards. You will fight. You will die. But you will always think next round will be the miracle run. Buy it.
ADVICE - Play the bosses until you get beat on multiple runs. Then play the endless mode to unlock better stuff. Then try again at the boss that mauled you. This is where I am now, and I enjoy every part. Great game!

Hand of Fate is one of those rare games that blends several game types in to one and is successful.  You face off against a mysterious dealer who challenges you to defeat his deck of cards that contains different monsters and bosses.  As you play you collect your own cards that contain events, items, and weapons to help you defeat the dealer.  Each game you play will be different from the last with both you and the dealer have new cards.
While the cards play an important role in the game, the actual combat system uses a 3rd person hack and slash model where you control your hero.  This is actually very fun as there have been several encounters where the deck has been stacked against me, but I was able to win due to my combat abilities.   While some of the animations can be a bit jerky here and there the combat system works and adds to the fun of the game.
Overall, I think if you enjoy action rpgs or card games you should give HoF a try.  I hope the devs keep adding new content as this is truly a fun niche game.

This game is more than just get, sell, buy, sell... It's more of an RPG.
The trading part of the game is just the ultimate goal of the adventure.
You see, to trade things and earn money, you need to befriend adventurers, so you'll have to activate events and then level them up. Once you've befriended an adventurer you get his/her card, once you have their card, you can start the loop over, and still have them available!
Then it get's a bit complicated; the more you level them up, the more they will cost. Except the adventurer you start out with, he'll cost you either a set amount, which gets higher the more you level him up, or however much money you have on you. So you'll have to step up the game to be able to get to more area's if you want to actually earn anything.
Add to that a coming disaster, when an evil magician starts to stir up some trouble, meanwhile, you're still in large debt. You'll have to defeat this evil magician and pay off your debt, if not, you'll have to start over.
But starting over isn't such a bad thing, you'll be doing it lots. If you lose, don't worry! It was all just a bad dream... Although all the stuff you got in that dream is still in your inventory. Except all that sweet, sweet money.
This game is also very much a visual novel, that means lots of reading. I like that, and if you like it, I recommend you check out "Steins;Gate", which you can buy on JList! But don't worry, it has a skip function, in case you don't like reading. What kind of visual novel is it? Slice of life and comedy.

You can equip the adventurer with items you have in your inventory. If you succeed defeating monsters & bosses on the dungeons, you can bring all items you've collected. You can do fusion at the guild. The variety & rank of items you can fusion is depend on your merchant level. The higher your level the more items, of course. The merchant level also affects what kind of items you can find on market & guild, and items dropped from the monsters on dungeons. Also, how much you can decorate your item store is depend on it too. It's also affect your haggle/bargain skill when you open your store and start selling items to your customers :)

This is my first Steam review, and I've chosen to do it about this wonderful little gem: Recettear. I have to admit that when I bought this game, I did it purely on a whim one day when it was on sale, and I really was not expecting much. But this game really ended up surprising me, and in a very good way.
You are Recette, a young girl who ends up being forced to repay her fathers debts and are accompanied by Tear, the fairy who was sent to recover the debts payment. Together the two of you open up a store, Recettear, so that you can make enough money to repay what you owe. The gameplay can be roughly divided into two parts: store management and dungeon crawling.
Each day in the game is divided into 4 time slots and you can choose what to do for each one: go to town to hit the market to stock up on goods, visit the guild to grab an adventurer for some dungeon crawling or tend to your store. Store management is the main aspect of the game and in my own opinion the most fun. It also has a surprising depth to it. Make sure to buy stock when price is low and sell items when their value is higher. Choose what to put up for sale. Barter with you customers and fulfill their special orders. Change the look of your store to suit it to certain customers preferences.
There are several adventurers you will meet and that you can take with you to do some dungeon crawling. There are several dungeons with multiple levels and bosses in the game, and exploring them will get you several items you can sell at your store or use in recipes to create better items. Exploring the dungeons also serves to advance the story which, without spoiling anything major, actually continues far beyond when you have finally managed to pay your fathers debts.
The game has a really interesting story and likable characters. Cute is really the best way to describe the way the game looks. A special mention must be given to the games english translation which is really well done. Once your debt is paid for the first time, some new game modes are unlocked, and the game has a considerable replayability value if your goal is to get all items in the game (doing so will require starting a new game once for each adventurers loyalty item). It should be noted that it is possible to start a new game and carry over all the money, items and store upgrades from your other saves. This is helpful when only trying to get each adventurers loyalty item since you do not have to worry about making enough money to pay off the debt in the early phase of the game.
There are two things I feel I should mention though: in my experience, dungeon crawling can be very tiresome and repetitive which is why I feel this is the least interesting aspect of the game. This is especially problematic if you want to get all items, which requires doing A LOT of grinding. The shop management aspect can become something you can do almost mechanically once you've upgraded the shop to the max, unlocked all possible items in the market and have gotten used to each customers characteristics when bartering. In my opinion this doesn't take any of the fun away from this aspect though.
Finally, to end this review. If you do not like anything with a cute/anime aesthetic, or if you are looking for an action packed game do not buy this. To everyone else looking for a nice little way of occupying your time, I can only fully recommend it.

(Review is completely subjective and based on my own experiences, not others.)
(I may spoil gameplay mechanics, but I won't spoil the story/key facts)
TL:DR
Storyline/Entertainment/Gameplay 9/10
Combat 2/10
Environment 9/10
Controls 9/10
Replayability 2/10
Overall: 7/10 - Would recommend to those who are more casual gamers or those interested in a interactive story, not intense action shooters.
Details:
I saw this game while browsing the steam store page. I happened to buy the humble bundle including this game, so awesome! When you enter the game you are greeted by the death of well.. yourself. The story is all about discovering who is your killer, while uncovering the hidden truths which plague the town.
Storyline/Entertainment/Gameplay:
The game presented itself as a abnormal murder mystery story where when you think you have a good lead on the killer, things suddenly get intense or theories unravel and get thrown out the window (bad storyline pun). There were very few moments where I was bored during this playthrough, mainly the walking between areas of the map, although this space was filled with side-quests or objectives. During gameplay i had only one immersion-breaking bug, which was when i was in an area and explored off deeper in the area following the plot, but upon return to the beginning of the area the game was like "ERRR, where was this guy before? Oh well, just play all the cut-scenes again until we get to where he is now!" Per good storylines, I was not expecting the ending. It was also nice that the main character was able to piece together elaborate stories from a few hints, and conviently explain them to the other characters (and the player). The only infuriating part of the gameplay is having to find the right spot to click or where to find the next hidden clue to progress the game.
Combat:
This game felt as though combat was a last minute idea to add challenge to the game. The only combat in the game was when ghost/spirits obstructed your path and maneuvering around them was too much of a pain, so a quick-time event is needed to rid of these.
Environment:
All the scenery and graphics were visually appealing, although at times i thought to myself, "If im playing on max settings, why isn't it as pretty as in the trailer?". Though, i guess companies ramp up graphics in trailers to boost sales. Each area had about 7-20 (maybe) little pick-ups which, when collecting them all, gives a side-story/backstory to the game.
Controls:
Not much to say for controls. At times, I couldn't hit keys at the right time during quick-time events, but its much more a personal thing then key-mapping. I didn't encounter too many issues otherwise, nothing which was immersion-breaking.
Replayability:
Since this game is linear and follows the same storyline each time (to the best of my knowledge), there is no point to re-play the game unless a period of time has past and you want to re-live the story, or to 100% the game by finding all the little hints.

Unreal was a massive technical achievement for it's time. While not the first game to implement skyboxes, it was one of the first to show what one could do with them.
The game takes place in the alien landscape of Na Pali. You explore this rough foreign location while dealing with the locals that get in your way. Unreal's engine was very innovative for the time. It tried to do a lot of things to stand out compared to it's main competition: Quake 2.
While Quake 2 was a corridor shooter taking place in futuristic bunkers and facilities. Unreal took place in jungles, and temples worshipping long dead gods. You find a universal translator early on in the game and the raw detail that goes into the backstory of Na Pali is extraordinary. You can see this legacy continued in later games such as Morrowind and Halo.
The Gold Pack comes with the core game, plus it's expansion pack. All updated to UT1's engine, so you know mostly what to expect if you've played that game.

Imagine if Alexander the Great's empire hadn't collapsed, but managed to hold onto and encompass everything east of the Ural Mountains. Then in the 1930s, the Emperor becomes Hitler sans Final Solution and starts World War II. Oh, and there's magic-based nukes and a legendary race of sexy Jedi ladies (no I'm not making that up). Thus is the world of Valkyria Chronicles.
It's hard to give this game a recommendation. As much as I'm enjoying the gameplay, there's so many little problems with the mechanics that add up to a big leech on that enjoyment. First and foremost is the lack of saving during battles. This wouldn't be an issue if the gameplay were faster, or at least more fluid. Even in the early game, one battle can take well over an hour to finish. Sometimes you just don't have that much time to waste on a game. A simple addition of checkpoint saves would have taken care of the problem nicely. Alas, you must slog through each battle start to finish. Because JRPG, I guess.
Secondly, the cover system is a joke. Why only sandbag barricades? Why can't I crouch behind a waist-high crate? WHY, GAME???
Third, grenades are an even bigger joke. With an effective range of maybe 20 feet, getting close enough to hit someone with one puts you WELL within range of endless gunfire. Their only purpose seems to be destroying sandbag barricades and artillery—and nothing else, not even wooden boxes.
GRENADES DO NOT WORK THAT WAY. Good night.
Other than that, the game is all right. It doesn't bog you down with a huge amount of different units and mechanics, easy for even beginners to strategy games to get into. There is a fair amount of grinding required to get your unit/equipment levels up, but that's JRPGs for you.
On the plus side, if you hate anime storylines, you can skip through 95% of the cutscenes and just get to the shooty-shooty-bang-bang.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare will always be among my favorites from the past but never again. I saw how old and outdated my original review was so here's my updated one for those new and curious.
The gameplay for Chivalry is done really well and makes you feel like you're a part of a real medieval battle. The battle system is simple but effective and fun. Left click is how you swing, throw and shoot arrows and right click is how you do a timed block. You can customize how you'll look and what you want to carry with you during your battles. Choose a bow, a 2 handed sword, 1 handed sword, shield, spears or axes. Upgrade and get more weapon choices by getting kills with said weapons and become even deadlier later on. What I really like about the combat is you can do different attacks rather than just slash around. Swing left and right, thrust or do an overhead attack. Easy to learn, somewhat difficult to master.
Graphics are done well. Maps, knights and archers are all polished and menacing to look at and see. There isn't much detail I can really give on this.
The sounds in Chivalry are good, bad and sometimes outright hilarious. The voice capturing equipment was clearly bad; but the voice acting itself isn't too shabby. And the shouts are amazing. I really loved shouting and it was both funny and inspiring hearing all those around you join in on your battlecry. The sounds of arrows firing, armor clanking and swords clashing are all spot on and great to hear. You get a good adrenaline rush every match you play.
-First off, I realized pretty early on that the developers did not care about their game. I dealt with it starting off, but it became way too apparent that they would not fix their bugs or create more problems than they fix.
-Second, there was usually a problem with lag. Hits and blocks wouldn't always register and I've witnessed teammates getting killed behind walls or after a swing to an enemies head when the victor of the fight was clear. This goes for myself as well.
-Third, the game had a few exploits. The most infamous one is the dreaded backward overhead swing. What players realized is that they could bend over backwards with a 2 handed sword and do an overhead thrust which almost immediately hits you and does maximum damage. The second exploit is absolutely ridiculous: players can look down and not get hit by your swing. I actually found this out by accident when my mouse jumped and I looked down really fast in the middle of an enemies swing. The worst part is, there isn't a "duck" to it and it'll look like you hit them (on your end if you're swinging).
On top of all of this, most of the community ended up with lazy elitists really fast who instead of fighting each other, work together to kill all of the newer players. Or at least those they deemed "less skilled". I also noticed that some matches ended up not being a match at all. Literally. I've gone into matches where no one even played and just stood around using the in game chat. God forbid you actually do what you're supposed to and attack or kill one of them. They will grief you until the end.
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a great game ruined by lazy developers, bugs and elitists. It had so much potential and to this day wish these problems were fixed. If you want a good medieval fix, I recommend getting Mount and Blade: Warband or look into the upcoming game For Honor.

I just finished my first playthrough of ME2. I could immediately see why it's such a classic trilogy in the gaming world. It added a lot of dynamics to the game which were and still are somewhat uncommon in shooters. It's very similar to a Gears of War combat system, except with the ability to pause, review your surroundings, and command your allies to execute attacks or movements. That alone added an element of strategy with an excellent and unique cover system.
The character development was also a treat. I was always running to my allies, wanting to talk to them and uncover their individual opinions and pasts. Each character was likeable in their own way, having a bit of complexity that never fit into a stereotypical mold, and a visual appearance that was distinctly original.
The dialogue options and the lasting effects of choices, especially if you've played through the first game, made the dialogue more interesting. It's funny because the actual gameplay is seldom affected by your choices, much to the regret of many ME3 players. Without the expectation of some grandiose conclusion based on my actions, I was able to see the game for what it was. It's a present experience, not a build-up, and it does it extremely well. Like a good book when you're done, you wish that you have that anticipation back that you had as you read it. It just proves that the story was very compelling.
My only complaint was the research gathering system, which took several hours of my time for a very uninteresting mechanic added ot the game. I'll admit that it adds a reward for exploration in that sense, and it gives a way to interact with things in space, but the very limited scope of it is more of a time sink to justify the upgrades. I'd rather that the more you used certain characters, the more experience it added to the upgrade. It would've given incentive to change up your party members and have them use different weapons.
I'd personally give this game a 8.5 / 10. I really enjoyed the story and gameplay, which were captivating enough for me to actually finish a game for once, I felt like the experiences were linear, although very original and interesting, full of background information on each character and always relevant to some immediate concern. I never wanted to get something "over with." Every part of the game was enjoyable (except a certain Hacking mission in a city). I think that if the game incorporated some of the last mission choices into other areas of the game, it would've made things feel a lot more dynamic and weighty. Excellent game, looking forward to ME4!

First Review in my career.  I have more like 60 hours as the internet went out for a while as oppossed to the 40+ that is shown.  I have played through the game 2 times once (and most recently) as a male Shepard and another as a female Shepard.  Copnstructive critism is wlcome as well as advice because I plan to review some of the other games I have.  So please, enjoy.
Disputably, this is the superior game in the Mass Effect Series.  Personally I hold this opinion, but do NOT just buy this game.  In order to get totally immersed in the story and develop connections to the characters, purchase the original Mass Effect and possibly Mass Effect 3 (but use Origin at your own peril).
The story itself is extremely engaging.  Traveling the galaxy and assembling a suicide squad is interesting as each character is found in different places and missions associated with the character's loyalty to you are also unique.  I never once came across a moment when I thought "I've seen this before".  While enemies are mild repeats (you will be fighting armored aliens, sheilded ones, boss ones, and various types of mechs), the NPCs are always very interesting even if they are flat.
The role-playing aspects of the game are handled well.  When starting the game, you can choose between 6 different types of combat styles which range from being a pure biotic (using magic), an infiltrator (turning invisible), and being a soldier (regular combat grunt/bad***).  Each of those classes have 5 upgradable abilities that either give you interesting ammo mods or special attacks like slamming a person to the ground or turning invisible for a short time.  On top of that once you chose your character class, you can select another special ability from a list.  Every time you level up, you recieve one point for spending it on abilities.  Initially, all of them cost 1 point and once they are upgraded, they incriment (go up) by 1.  At the end of the skill bar for each skill you can chose a significant bonus ability.  For an ammo mod, this could be giving yourself an upgraded form of it or allowing your entire squad to partake in it.  The latter thing I find most useful because I tend to hang back and pick off enemies from range and let my squand soak up most of the enemy fire.
Speaking of combat, I love this 3rd-person style.  It leans heavily on cover and utilizing the abilities of your allies.  You can direct your 2 squad members simply pressing a key (one per member).  To use your abilities and your squad member's, you hold down a button and select the ones you wish to use.  Your team can deploy at most 3 separate abilities (one per person).  Aside from that, regular combat with guns is point, aim, shoot.  You can hold a maximum of 6 guns, however this depends on which class you pick in the beginning.  The adept class doesn't even carry weapons while the soldier can hold all 6.  You can have a sniper rifle, assult rifle, shotgun, speical weapon (missile launcher,mini-nuke launcher, etc), pistol, and submachine gun.  Acquring of these weapons range from finding them in levels, recieving them, and making them. There is melee combat, but it is rather sloppy.  If you were to use it (which I don't) you leave yourself open to enemy fire which will destory you if you aren't in cover even on the easiest difficulty.  The enemy A.I. is capable of flanking, putting down suppressive fire, and charging indescriminantly, so it always keeps you on your toes.  Sometimes the enemies get stuck behind obstacles, but the pathing for them are solid.  They use cover and can go through your suad members quickly.
The graphics are exceptional even for a game from 2010.  The textures are good, but in combat it really shines.  The laser beams, mass-effect bullets, and ammo mods are a sight to behold when they are flying everywhere.  The sounds are also good.  The soundtrack is also pretty good.
The place where this game falls short is the map system.  Like from the previous game, you travel across the galaxy using Mass Relays.  That is carrried over, but the actual physical exploration of planets and moons from the previous installment is scraped in favor of a mining minigame which is tedious to do for an extended period of time.  It is also worthwhile though as the resources you get from mining is used for upgrades which are found in the course of missions and from purchashing them.
The upgrades are rather significant improvements which range from increased damage to reduced cooldowns to even additional equipment for the ship.  I highly recommend consulting your team for ship upgrades because they will make the difference between life and death in the late game.  Some do cost a lot of stuff, so you will get aquainted with the mining monstrosity.
However, this is overshadowed by the characters you interact with.  While I briefly went over this in the beginning, I feel I must describe how great it is.  Every character on your ship have a story, opinions, and remarks about your progress.  And yes, the infamous romance options are back and "better" than ever.  I will let you explore them to see for yourself because I have not explored them yet.
The lore is wonderfully explained to you through the codex, accessable via the pause menu.  As you interact with more things, the condex articles explain everything.
Overall, I give this game a 9 out of 10.  The strong character customization/upgrading system teamed with the strong graphics, good teamwork elements, and the immaculate NPC collection are what make this game a must-own for Sci-Fi fans.   If you are bored by generic first-person shooters and want a more engaging combat system, this is a good game to look into.
I know that there is a multiplayer to the game as well, but I have not exlpored it.  I would suggest skipping it.  To me, this is a single-player experience through and through.
So long and good luck.

Where do I start. This game is addictive as all hell. It is a pure character role play orientated game where you play generation from generation of your family throughout the dark ages with everything revolving around how YOU as the player mould your character and his/her successors. This does mean that a single playthrough from just 1066 to 1453 can take in the excess of sevral days.
Have you ever wanted to play as a Spaniard with Russian culture who is a staunch believer of the Zoroastrian faith and conquer Germany? In this game, you can! That is just the tip off the iceberg of insanity. I have had a succession war with my 1st born son who was also the SPAWN OF SATAN, literally a hell baby.
Now understand this game can be daunting to new players especially because there are no real good tutorials provided by the game. That is definitely a shortfall and has to be made up with Youtube tutorials or experienced friends who play the game. The other problem is how random some events can be which can royally screw over a fresh game. I wont go into details but I am sure many of my fellow players can recount situations the destroyed their games. Also It pretty much a requirement to get game mechanic DLC such as Old Gods and the Republic to get the most out of the game.
That is the only real problems I can think of with the game. Otherwise its an excellent game with challenges and character driven role play. Fantastic modding community always re-inventing the game and extending the hours of life this game has. I don’t think this game can be adequately compared to any other just because how unique it is.

Archeage, what can I say. It is an amazing game that allows you to own a piece of property within a vitrual expanding and everchanging world. The sea combat is awesome, the crafting system/trade pack system is awesome. The biggest problem I see with people reviewing this game is thier inability to comprehend what a "P2W" game really is. Yes, Archeage has a "Patron" system in place, but I ask how is this different than any other sub. based MMO? The Patron program has been in place since launch, this should be no suprise to people that if you pay a monthly fee you get certain perks. These perks however do not make you super competitive, honestly the only major benefit is land, which free accounts can still farm in the temp. farm locations. And yes farming is a big part of making money in Archeage!!! As for Apex and the Marketplace, they do not offer any advantage other than time saved. Honestly most Marketplace items are cosmetic in nature, and if you are truly butthurt about someone having a cooler mount or costume than you, then I say good riddance to you and the game will be truly better without your presence!!! I mean seriously if you consider someone having a costume or mount a "P2W" advantage than by all means Archeage is "P2W" but if you want a game that is challeging in the end game, offers a level playing field for all when it comes to attaining usable and vauled gear, and a game that makes you feel like you are contributing to an evolving fantasy world, then please click install. 10/10

Hand of fate has interesting ideas bunched into a suprisingly good deck building action RPG. The game is very rogue-like since no adventure/dungeon is the same which gives it a great amount of replay value and the game has endless mode aswell. Narrator/dealer has good dialogue and pretty much comments on everything. Which can lead to situations where some dialogue gets repeated if you don't which up your deck from time to time, writen dialogue is really good aswell. In overall the games music, dialogue and narration creates a rather great, foreboding atmosphere.
On minus side: combat is clunky and has a tendency to get rather repetetive in longer adventures. Might be worth mentioning that once the game actually went into a infinite animation loop during one of the boss encounters forcing me to forfeit the dungeon.
Games "story" seem to be rather short. After 5,6hrs I have killed 7 of the 12 boss encounters and opened half of both the equipment deck and the event deck.
If you like the idea of a action brawler with heavy emphasis on deck building with light RPG elements, this game is a good purchase.

Fable is a game I've played several times, and at first I thought it was fantastic. I loved the story, the world, and it was really one of the first RPG's I really got into. I owned it on Xbox, and after losing it I thought I'd buy it again on steam. And after playing and beating Fable for the hundredth time, I've only just now began to realize this game is far from perfect.
Don't get me wrong, Fable is still a good game, and decent RPG overall. The graphics hold up pretty well today, which is impressive for a game that's going on 12 years old. But that's really where Fable ends, "Good" and "Decent" The story has really weird pacing, the game's length is far from impressive, and the games lack of side quests really detract from replay value. Another thing I've come to dislike about fable is how simple it is. The game has very few deep and interesting mechanics, and some of the ones that are there are broken (ex. the morality and ageing systems)
It may seem like I'm harping on it, but I would still recommend Fable to both casual gamers, and fans of action RPGs. While it may seem lack luster, Fable is still a solid experience with great combat, good characters, an interesting world to explore, and plenty of chickens to kick. It was a fantastic third person action RPG experience back in 2004, and while it has aged over the years, I think Falble is a purchase that you won't regret.

This is my first Steam review, and I've chosen to do it about this wonderful little gem: Recettear. I have to admit that when I bought this game, I did it purely on a whim one day when it was on sale, and I really was not expecting much. But this game really ended up surprising me, and in a very good way.
You are Recette, a young girl who ends up being forced to repay her fathers debts and are accompanied by Tear, the fairy who was sent to recover the debts payment. Together the two of you open up a store, Recettear, so that you can make enough money to repay what you owe. The gameplay can be roughly divided into two parts: store management and dungeon crawling.
Each day in the game is divided into 4 time slots and you can choose what to do for each one: go to town to hit the market to stock up on goods, visit the guild to grab an adventurer for some dungeon crawling or tend to your store. Store management is the main aspect of the game and in my own opinion the most fun. It also has a surprising depth to it. Make sure to buy stock when price is low and sell items when their value is higher. Choose what to put up for sale. Barter with you customers and fulfill their special orders. Change the look of your store to suit it to certain customers preferences.
There are several adventurers you will meet and that you can take with you to do some dungeon crawling. There are several dungeons with multiple levels and bosses in the game, and exploring them will get you several items you can sell at your store or use in recipes to create better items. Exploring the dungeons also serves to advance the story which, without spoiling anything major, actually continues far beyond when you have finally managed to pay your fathers debts.
The game has a really interesting story and likable characters. Cute is really the best way to describe the way the game looks. A special mention must be given to the games english translation which is really well done. Once your debt is paid for the first time, some new game modes are unlocked, and the game has a considerable replayability value if your goal is to get all items in the game (doing so will require starting a new game once for each adventurers loyalty item). It should be noted that it is possible to start a new game and carry over all the money, items and store upgrades from your other saves. This is helpful when only trying to get each adventurers loyalty item since you do not have to worry about making enough money to pay off the debt in the early phase of the game.
There are two things I feel I should mention though: in my experience, dungeon crawling can be very tiresome and repetitive which is why I feel this is the least interesting aspect of the game. This is especially problematic if you want to get all items, which requires doing A LOT of grinding. The shop management aspect can become something you can do almost mechanically once you've upgraded the shop to the max, unlocked all possible items in the market and have gotten used to each customers characteristics when bartering. In my opinion this doesn't take any of the fun away from this aspect though.
Finally, to end this review. If you do not like anything with a cute/anime aesthetic, or if you are looking for an action packed game do not buy this. To everyone else looking for a nice little way of occupying your time, I can only fully recommend it.

This is THE GAME.
On a personal note, I've never enjoyed any game as much as this one.
The story... is facinating and makes you want to pursue it all the way to the end without boring you even for a minute. Most quests also give you several choices during them which in turn make your status more evil or more good while twisting the means and/or the end result of quests.
Character customization... is well done. You can add tatoos, change your hairstyle, wear different clothes, have battle scars, get older... and all these together decide how NPCs see you and react upon your arrival. You can also get married which usually requires your character to be more attractive and renown.
Combat system... your combat skills don't advance along those lame "skill trees" you often see in RPG games. In Fable you can choose everything yourself. If you want to max out all possible skills, go on. If you want to specialize as a combat mage, archer or whatever, you can do it. Also your status will show your combat class depending on which skills you invested your experience into, and there are a lot of classes. Scout, rogue, spellwarrior, witch hunter, fighter, warrior. Just to name a few of them. It's even possible to choose never to train your skills and stay as an "apprentice" all the way to the end game, though this being an expert level challenge.
As an action RPG, the game allows you to fully decide how you move, use skills and take on enemy attacks during combat. Changing from spell to another, or from bow to your sword is very simple and doesn't require you to memorize dozens of different buttons for different commands. For a game about a upbeat lackadasical girl with a dream and her straight man in the form of a sligtly cynical lone shark fairy girl that likes to curse prodominatly in french. I would say what more could you expect from this little gem of a game? It is a great examination of the whole omnipresent all powerful iteam shop in video games, because really how did that merchant really get the bottom of the large monstrous final dungeon, filled with monsters that feed on the crush hopes and dreams of small orphans that took you an hour to get through? How did they get that magical "God-Slaying" Sword of Summoning Swedeish Super Models? Well Recettear, tries its best to give you an idea. You go from punching and slicing your way through a more traditonal randomly genereated dungeon crawl, to get better and more expensive items, But then you spend the rest of the time going through town, meeting new people (especialy new adventures to help you with said dungeon crawl), and most importantly barting and haggling with the best of them as you run your item shop.
And the iteam shop gameplay is just as engaging as the combat, as would be expected for a game about an item shop.  The game gives you freedom to express however you want your iteam shop to be. You're the one to decied what goes in the shop window display case, if that old muffler is too tacky etc. And the game does not punish you either way, even providing a fancy little graphic which tells you how Plain/Guady, Dark/Light your shop is respectivly. Which of course attracts diffrent people to your shop and diffrent adventures. And then comes the sweet, sweet revenge that Recettear provides for long time RPG fans. It is up to you to barter and sell your items, no longer will you be the one to be rob blind by the crazy old man that needs 1,000 Gold Dragon's Feet to get your phoenix down, or potion, or stick of better hitting. Now it is you that is profiting from these adventures and excavations, not through life lessons learned but through gold and wealth! And the game does push you to be a good salesmen though, be too agressive with your bartering and you will lose costumers, be too leinent and try to make everyone happy? You won't make enough money by the end of your dead line to keep the shop open!
All in all though Recettear is a fun little game, does it have the best graphics, sound design, etc? No of course it does not, but it follows true to the type of game it is trying to be and these design elements help compliment the cute and yes even whimiscal feel about the game. In the end Recettear is funny, happy, cute and unbashfully selfaware of its self. But that does not stop it from telling you a story about friendship, and from being honest and real with you as well. What else can I really say? Try the demo, if you like the feel of it well then you got nothing to lose now do you? I belive firmly that the pricepoint it is it is fair, and well the rest is up to you.
This is Griffin reminding you something that Reccettear is proud to hold as its mantra;
Capitalism Ho!

A great game with a caring dev team behind it, despite the release day shame and seemingly high amount of impulse-refund kiddy negative reviews, the game has been patched and has solved the more glaring issues. The dev team is continuing to work on patches and improving player experience with each patch, as of today pretty much all of the negative reviews are irrelevant.
Game itself has been improved form previous versions offering new textures, filters, and the pretty UI from newer games, recommended to fans of the series and people who enjoy SRPGs. As a real fan of the series I'm glad to be able to support this project and see it improve, hopefully we can receive more games of the series on the PC in the future.
For newcomers and curious people, disgaea is a japanese SRPG featuring a colorful cast of likeable and unique characters, a ton of different classes/units to create to customize your party, a lot of over-the-top skills, the ability to reach incredible levels and damage numbers.
You can rebirth your units to go back to level one, keeping most of your stats and skills while getting stronger and advancing to a new tier, you can also attempt randomly-generated dungeons within each ITEM to level it up and increase its stats further, there's a lot of fun grind to do and things to find, obviously optional.
Even 13 years later, Disgaea 1 is still a joy to play and I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys or has enjoyed the genre, and to people who are interested in getting into the genre.

There's a noticeable lack of good detective games out there: LA Noire, Sherlock Holmes series, a bit of Batman - and that's it. And there're even fewer concepts as interesting and original from the gaming perspective as this one. However, you must clearly understand what you're getting yourself into: this game definitely is a walking simulator, with the only gameplay being two-button fatalities against demons (which are not all that hard) and the actual detective routine, which consists of loooking for clues, analyzing them and being led to even more clues as a result.
Also, Murdered: Soul Suspect is a dream game for any munchkin: there's an abundance of different collectibles in every area of the game and, to the developers' credit, all of those actually contain some story. Those stories (as well as the main one) are obviously and heavily influenced by Stephen King's styled "creepiness", and are well told and fairly unpredictable. In addition, voice acting is surprisingly decent for a not-AAA project.
---
Summarizing, Murdered: Soul Suspect entertained me for three whole evenings, which is definitely worth those $15 it's asking for right now. The gameplay simply doesn't have enough time to become repetative, and the story is being told with good pace and plenty of intrigue, concluding itself right when it should. Great voice acting gives the finishing touch to the game. Enjoy.

I got the game on sale and I think it was okay, but the full price is ridiculous. I like the game but it's not worth the full price and you should go through more reviews or gameplays even if it's on some 50 % off.
I'd say most of the game is okay. And that's exactly the word. It's not great but it's not bad either. The general feeling when you finish the game will probably be something like... yeah, I had fun but it could (and should) have been much more fun.
The story is fine but not breathtaking. It uses a lot of clichés but what really makes it dull is that there are too few characters. It's a detective story and you have like two possible suspects, not much mystery there.
The detective part is... ehm. You collect clues and then you are supposed to draw some conclusion. Unfortunatelly, all you need to do is to click on the most obvious stuff you can and it's usualy the right answer. Sometimes, you even "discover" something you (as a player) must have thought before you started investigating because it's so flippin obvious.
The stealth and fights with demons are really easy once you get a hang of it. Not much to say about it, the stealth parts could have been great but they ended up just dull. The demons are really creepy though, they look a bit as if they were dancing... but they wanna eat you... creepy.
There are many collectibles. Some of them add to the story, which is great. Each area of the game has a ghost story which plays only if you find all related collectibles. These are great. Unfortunatelly, many collectibles just give you an achievement and that's is annoying. I also ended up with one or two collectibles missing in some catogories which brings me to...
The saving system. It works fine, there are autosaves and even if you die, you dont lose much progress. But there is no way to make a hard save and once you reach a certain point in the game, you cannot enter most areas. So if you dont have all collectibles by the endgame, you will not get them unless you play again. And even then you'd have to go through almost the whole game because areas of the game open as you progress in the story.
The few puzzles you encounter are really easy. You have some great mechanics (possessing people and cats, messing with electronics to make people move and get you through areas you cannot cross) but the creators really didnt use all the potential. I know puzzles weren't the point of the game but they could have add a lot of fun to the gameplay.
I generally enjoyed the game, it's has a lot of genuine creepiness in it and it's mostly fun. But it gets repetitive even of it's a rather short game (I think I have like 12 hours with almost all collectibles, I think people do it faster) and you will be left with the feeling you expected more from it.

(Love it when those spiders can target you in water throwing poison bubbles at you and still hitting you). The extreme aggro radius also remains a constant worry along with respawn times (you just killed a mob and poof you are getting killed by its respawn. Ain't it just lovely ??) .
As of the crafting system a lot needs to be adjusted / tweaked. Lag online does not seem to be an issue anymore though I would definitly stir away from PingPerfect which suspended the server side support .
PingPerfect's website showing the item as "out of stock which in server side parlance means service suspended , The official servers being hosted by PingPerfect there are no official Funcom Servers past the first 24 hours of release  (i wonder why??) . PingPerfect being funcom's partner in Early Access Phase ... Of course there is always the solution of running your own service if you want.
Otherwise the game looks GREAT for an early access game. The whole shebang looks interesting and I expect great content coming up past the first kinks have been polised out of the game. I would definitly recommend the game if you are a patient person that can afford to wait for the game to be polished properly regarding its mechanical bits.  If on the other hand you expect a polished AAA title out of Early Access you should not consider Conan Exile at this point.
(Official release is already in the works and i would not expect EVERY aspect solved).
Funcom is stirring away from the old and tired MMO model and this is definitly a good move. Moving the server side costs to the public is a good idea in general especially since the MMO genre is hitting the rocks since F2P has become the rule for the Genre and P2O/S2P (Pay to Own / Suscribe to Play) models are becoming a thing of the past. F2P turns unfortunately rapidly in P2W there days either malignantly (GuildWars 2) or blatantly (Skyforge). S2P models still do exist but with their own share of difficulties when it comes to maitainning the title / community alive.
Would i recommend Conan Exiles ... Definitly yes but to the general public of gamers at large the product will look rushed out of the window which is definitly NOT the case. Funcom delivers a good product in its early stages . For myself i think the pricing is right for an early stage product. I would expect things to go smoothly past the first kinks we have so far encountered in-game.
One thing that would be great to get in the clear is the planning for modding / expansions model . But all in due time.
