Fascism (/fæʃɪzəm/) is a form of radical authoritarian nationalism[1][2] that came to prominence in early 20th-century Europe. Influenced by national syndicalism, fascism originated in Italy during World War I, combining more typically right-wing positions with elements of left-wing politics,[3] in opposition to liberalism, Marxism, and traditional conservatism. Fascism is often placed on the far-right within the traditional left–right spectrum, but several academics have said that the description is inadequate.[4][5]
Fascists have identified World War I as having been a revolution. It brought revolutionary changes in the nature of war, society, the state, and technology. The advent of total war and total mass mobilization of society had broken down the distinction between civilian and combatant. A "military citizenship" arose in which all citizens were involved to the military in some manner during the war.[6][7] The war had resulted in the rise of a powerful state capable of mobilizing millions of people to serve on the front lines or provide economic production and logistics to support those on the front lines, as well as having unprecedented authority to intervene in the lives of citizens.[6][7] Fascists view World War I as having made liberal democracy obsolete and regard total mobilization of society led by a totalitarian single-party state as necessary for a nation to be prepared for armed conflict and to respond effectively to economic difficulties, such a totalitarian state is led by a strong leader as a dictator and a martial government composed of the members of the governing fascist party to forge national unity and maintain a stable and orderly society.[8] Fascism rejects assertions of violence automatically being negative in nature and views political violence, war, and imperialism as means that can achieve national rejuvenation.[9][10][11][12]
Fascism borrowed theories and terminology from socialism but replaced socialism's focus on class conflict with a focus on conflict between nations and races.[13] Fascists advocate a mixed economy, with the principal goal of achieving autarky to secure national self-sufficiency and independence through protectionist and interventionist economic policies.[14] Following World War II, few parties have openly described themselves as fascist, and the term is usually used pejoratively by political opponents. The terms neo-fascist or post-fascist are sometimes applied more formally to describe parties of the far right with ideological similarities to, or roots in, 20th century fascist movements. [15]

Etymology
The Italian term fascismo derives from fascio meaning a bundle of hay, ultimately from the Latin word fasces.[16] This was the name given to political organizations in Italy known as fasci, groups similar to guilds or syndicates and at first applied mainly to organisations on the Left. Mussolini founded the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in Milan in 1919 which became the Partito Nazionale Fascista (National Fascist Party) in 1921. The Fascists came to associate the name with the ancient Roman fasces or fascio littorio,[17] which consisted of a bundle of rods that were tied around an axe,[18] an ancient Roman symbol of the authority of the civic magistrate[19] carried by his lictors which could be used for corporal and capital punishment at his command.[20][21]
The symbolism of the fasces suggested strength through unity: a single rod is easily broken, while the bundle is difficult to break.[22] Similar symbols were developed by different fascist movements: for example the Falange symbol is five arrows joined together by a yoke.[23]
Definitions
Main article: Definitions of fascism
Historians, political scientists and other scholars have long debated the exact nature of fascism.[24] Each form of fascism is distinct, leaving many definitions too wide or narrow.[25][26]
One common definition of fascism focuses on three concepts: the fascist negations of anti-liberalism, anti-communism and anti-conservatism; nationalist authoritarian goals of creating a regulated economic structure to transform social relations within a modern, self-determined culture; and a political aesthetic of romantic symbolism, mass mobilization, a positive view of violence, and promotion of masculinity, youth and charismatic leadership.[27][28][29] According to many scholars, fascism — especially once in power — has historically attacked communism, conservatism and parliamentary liberalism, attracting support primarily from the far right.[30]
Roger Griffin describes fascism as "a genus of political ideology whose mythic core in its various permutations is a palingenetic form of populist ultranationalism".[31] Griffin describes the ideology as having three core components: "(i) the rebirth myth, (ii) populist ultra-nationalism and (iii) the myth of decadence".[32] Fascism is "a genuinely revolutionary, trans-class form of anti-liberal, and in the last analysis, anti-conservative nationalism" built on a complex range of theoretical and cultural influences. He distinguishes an inter-war period in which it manifested itself in elite-led but populist "armed party" politics opposing socialism and liberalism and promising radical politics to rescue the nation from decadence.[33]
Robert Paxton says that fascism is "a form of political behavior marked by obsessive preoccupation with community decline, humiliation, or victimhood and by compensatory cults of unity, energy, and purity, in which a mass-based party of committed nationalist militants, working in uneasy but effective collaboration with traditional elites, abandons democratic liberties and pursues with redemptive violence and without ethical or legal restraints goals of internal cleansing and external expansion."[34]
Position in the political spectrum
Fascism is commonly described as far right on the political spectrum,[35][36] although some writers have found placing fascism on a conventional left-right political spectrum difficult.[37][38][39][40][41]
Fascism was influenced by both left and right, conservative and anti-conservative, national and supranational, rational and anti-rational.[39] A number of historians have regarded fascism either as a revolutionary centrist doctrine, as a doctrine which mixes philosophies of the left and the right, or as both of those things.[40][41] Fascism was founded during World War I by Italian national syndicalists who combined left-wing and right-wing political views.

If you're looking for a game review, you've come to the wrong place. But if you're looking for a fantastic Banana-Bread recipe, you've come to the right place.
Tips
No need for a mixer for this recipe! Clean-up is easy too, if you want,
you can mix everything in one bowl.
The best bananas to use for banana bread are those that are over-ripe. The yellow peels should be at least half browned, and the bananas inside squishy and browning.
Ingredients
- 2 to 3 very ripe bananas, peeled
- 1/3 cup melted butter
- 1 teaspoon baking soda
- Pinch of salt
- 3/4 cup sugar (1/2 cup if you would like it less sweet, 1 cup if more sweet)
- 1 large egg, beaten
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
Method
1. Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
2. In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until completely smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
3. Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
4. Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 50 minutes to 1 hour at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
5. Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

The oldest game in the series, and as such is not as complex as the other games in the series. Despite being an inferior game to it's sequels in almost every way Disgaea 1 is still an amazing game that can get a lot of mileage out of anyone willing to spend time on it.
Often times I hear people complaining about grind and how it's never a good thing, but really grind is at the core of the Disgaea series, but it's been refined in such a good way. It's as if someone out there went through the effort of figuring out how to make grind appealing.
I can't really pinpoint one thing in particular that makes the mundane task of grinding much more entertaining, but if I had to compare it to something it'd be the progression in things like Cookie Clicker without the whole clicking or automatic aspect. I mean this in the sense that when things seem like they're about to slow down there were typically many ways to make the game go faster. But really, I suppose that the best thing about all of this is that grinding is completely optional and if you strategize properly you'll never have to grind for anything in the storyline. There are many end game bosses that require bosses, but you'll never be absolutely required to grind unless you strategize poorly and end up getting your characters massacred every time you play.
One of the neat features this game has is something called the "Item World" and what that is is a world inside of an item in the game, and every single item in the game has it's own item world which is 100% randomized every single time. These item worlds have monsters that progressively get stronger based off of the quality of the item you're in as well as the floor you're on. Items can have upwards of 100 floors based on their rarity, and going up in floors increases the stats of items and grants you a chance at running into the "Residents" of the world. Completely seperate from the enemies you will encounter in the item world, Residents are things that can be subdued and transferred from item to item and give really good bonuses such as elemental resistance, higher stats, and increased EXP gains.
Reincarnation is another feature that this game has to offer. Although the level cap is 9999 you can still go even further, with reincarnation resetting your level but netting you extra points to spec into your stats depending on what your total level was. You'll also get a bonus to your base stats depending on how high they were when you reincarnated. Reincarnating as a generic may also allow you to promote that unit to a higher ranking if they meet the requirements, which allows you access to higher stats, sometimes better spells, and if applicable better weapon mastery.
There's really so much to this game that I could go on for days. The game is amazing and if you're looking for a way into the series this is probably one of the better places to start since it's all uphill from here. Disgaea 1 also has the best story and cast in the entire series and everything else after it in that regard isn't as good, so I really hope you're not looking for story in the later titles because they might as well not be there.

The character models have some obvious flaws, but much better in comparison to Fable anniversary. Don't bother with anniversary, the price tag does not justify the very minor undates to grahpics and the other problems that came along with it.

Do I recommend the game: yes and if all you're looking for is another possitive opinion then that's all I have to say to you - move on.
For the rest of you: be aware that this isn't a flawless game by any emans; the Tanks control like♥♥♥♥♥♥ randomlty changing the direction they turn in based on their position relative to the camera and eat movement just to turn on the spot; the character balance is off with many of the characters being literally useless and you can just Alicia rush most levels with minimal sniper support. Some of the cut scenes definitely drag on too long, you can play anime cliche bingo with the plot and for all the effort that went into characterising the various squaddies with unique traits to reflevct their personality - they kick in so randomly that they's almost meaningless; there's no truly memorable, classic characters in here except your usual preferred loadout. The plot has pretenses at depath but it's really just Anime World War 2 that may as well be constantly yelling "HEY! THE DARCSENS ARE THE JEWS! HEY! DO YOU GET IT!" - I'm all for games trying to tackle sensitive subjects but writing this blunt isn't doing the game a favor. However as the combat eats up the majority of the play time. perhaps the biggest problem is that Valkyria Chroinicle's main source of challenge is to just not tell you important things like for example critical mission details that ultimately force you to reload a save after the first attempt flounders in the first 3 turns. The last boss deserves a special mention because although it's not difficult per se miss more than a handful of shots and you quickly get trapped in a grind.
...that said; for all it's warts; it's a game of simple pleasures, excellent mechanics, a charming personality and fantastic depth. If you want to you can go for A rank in every misison which is very challenging in many cases but honestly I just enjoy the game's missions for what they are - fun mixed turnn based and RTS combat and don't even consider replaying the skirmishes grinding (even though they are), I just enjoy it. Although the potentials are a bit too random for my taste, they are still a great way of flavouring the characters who are in turn a wonderfully eclectic bunch so you'll definitely end up with favourites (Jane, Nadine, Marina, Jann and Aika were mine). The new game plus is well developed too; offering you harder challenges, new characters, filled out backstories on all your favourites and a chance to push for all those A Ranks (many of which are still hard even at level 20) with your new insight and toys.
Overall, for all it's shortcomings, it's just good fun and a genuinely enjoyable game that's spawned a devoted community with good reason - I love it to bits and will probably be playing the occasional skirmish at random for years to come.

Beauttiful game, setting, story, and gameplay. I'm only a few hours in and I'm fully emersed in the story. I care about the characters, their country, why they fight, and understand their relationships with their fellow troops. Don't expect this to be one of those games you just play from beginning to end. Everything has layers.
While the turn based/FPS format is interesting as it is unique, it can be a bit clunky at times. Simply stopping enemy troops from "free firing" after your aim phase would've resolved the issue. Instead, you can get stuck taking unecessary damage when you simply want to end your turn or reposition yourself after attacking.
The cover system is a bit flawed too as you can only hide behind sand bags and hide in tall grass. (Assuming the unit in question doesn't have allergies.)
Even with its shortcomings, combat is complex, fair, and deeper the more you progress. Every unit type has their given usefulness, strenghts, and weaknesses. All of which can be modified further by their potentials, relationships with other units, and the layout of the given map you're on. One aspect that I really like is that progression is streamlined, allowing you to allocate experience points to an entire unit type. This cuts prevents power creep and the need to grind levels with less favorible troops. Everyone levels up at the same time and when you want them to. I actually hope to see a growth/progression format simmilar to this in other turn based strategy games.
I'd reccomend Valkyria Chronicles to JRPG and turn based strategy fans. If you're both, then you probably already have it in your library.

I love that Chivalry and War of the Roses have tried to replicate sword combat in a game instead of giving you a series of preset skills and letting you cycle through a dps order.
Chivalry tried to design a game that would make use of feinting and trickery to outsmart your opponents, which would have been great but they failed in two major ways.
1.  The animations do not do a very good enough job of syncing up with the actual gameplay, its needs to be pretty much bang on unlike other types of games to preserve the integrity of the system.
2. When you program a game in which precise movement is key like this, even 50 ms of lag from a player will ruin it, and you cant get away from lag online.
The end result is a game in which players find ways to exploit the incorrect animations and lag to make their movements difficult to predict visually.  You will see players doing 360 spins at you, fighting you while bent 90 degrees backward, you will get hit by a guy whos animation says hes blocking instead of swinging.  You will see knights in full armor jump 1 foot in the air to avoid a blade 3ft high that passes straight through their body and worse.
I really want to see a good game like this, I hope the next guys get it right.

I have over 100 hrs on ETS2, so I thought I'd write about my experiences with ATS.
I live in Canada, so playing ETS2 was fun, but I had no clue whether or not what I was seeing was realistic or authentic. Now, since Canada and the US have very similar city layouts and stores, I was able to judge more ffectively whether or not what I was seeing was convincing. I was delivering a load and saw I was taking it to a grocery store. A big name grocery store, exactly like the ones I've seen accross the US and Canada. Something about this rather mundane experience seemed so immersive and realistic.The building of the store, the parking lot out front, and the loading dock in the back.
Now to address the criticism of the lack of content. I do not fault them one bit. I don't want to steal the words of Daniel Hardcastle (Nerd3) so I'll summarize his explanation in this review, as he framed it in the most convincing manner I have heard yet. ETS2 has 2 previous games worth of content behind it, ETS and German Truck Simulator. This is a completely new venture, and the cities are much more fleshed out than in ETS2. So whereas only a few cities actually had many roads, now even smaller cities have a ton of roads and actual area you can drive around in, as opposed to seeing the rest in the distance.
At the end of the day, it is NOT a revolutionary change from ETS2. But to anyone who complains of that, I have no idea what you were expecting.
Overall, it's a good looking, reasonably priced and actively developing game and I can't be more excited for the future!

Before I begin, a word of warning: This game will very likely end up causing you to spend more hours than you might even have thought - especially if you've never played Disgaea before.
That said, I'll start with my review :)
I remember playing Disgaea HOD on the PS2. My first impressions of the game were that the character designs and the animations were nothing short of amazing. The storyline was engaging, and full of hilarious and downright silly moments. The environments that you play throughout the stages were vast, ranging from snow covered mountaintops to the burning embers of volcanic ash to even a baseball field (yes, you read that right).
If you, like me, enjoyed Final Fantasy Tactics, you'll be pleased to know that Disgaea also boasts of myriad character classes for you to choose from - and customize as you see fit. (You can equip any class with any weapon/armor build, though most classes have a particular preferred set, but you're free to divert away from the latter if you so desire). Character classes comprise of the common warrior (very tanky) classes and mage (high damage, low def) classes to the more unorthodox classes (Scouts - able to change environmental bonuses, Angels - my personal favourite, excels in almost everything, and the completely imba Majin - demon(?) class behemoths than have virtually no weaknesses).
And when you think you've leveled your characters high enough, the game also allows you to reset your character completely by a process called Transmigration that returns said character to level 1, with a modest boost to his/her base stats. The change pays off when you've transmigrated your character a couple of times and you'll begin to see the difference when your character grows from a struggling demon to a all-netherworld-will-fear-me demon (or human, or angel, or monster, or whatever-you-want-to-add-in-this-space) slayer.
While many have commented about the technical bugs with the vanilla release, the recent update seems to have fixed many (if not all)  of the performance issues, and I've been running the game with a steady 60fps even during heavily animated scenes.
All in all, Disgaea is a gem of a game, and I'm glad that they did a wonderful job porting this to the PC after so many years.
Also, Disgaea was the game that, to my knowledge, first introduced the word "dood" and the world of prinnies. That, in my opinion, is worthy of a thumbs up. <3
Just remember to get out of the house for a while. ;)

Excellent strategy/tactics rpg with, as many others have said, endless replayability.  Super fun and unique mechanics that let you dive into the game as deep as you want to go.  The story is very entertaining, and can be completed with relative ease, even if you don't want to get characters to level 3000+.  The graphic update is actually nicer than it's showcased, and gives the player a decent amount of options to find a graphical style that they like.  For example, you can take off smoothing around the character sprites, which gives them a 16-bit look (my preference).  There were initially a lot of graphical bugs and horrible framerate issue, but these were all patched within a week of release (which is insanely fast).  I'm hopeful that NIS will make an effort to at least port Disgaea 3 in the future, until then, this is the most light-hearted, fun and addicting strategy rpg you can get on PC.

I've started playing this game quite a long time ago, and this game came a long way, at the time, it was an above average game, now, it is oustanding. Let's see why.
The gameplay in this game is extremely well executed. Moving is intuitive, fast pace, and satisfying, it is extremely easy to make your 'frame do what you want it to.
Shooting is extremely solid too, from your sidearm to your rocket launcher, every weapons seems to work as it should, and it never feels out of place.
The abilities of your 'frame can change the tide of the battlefield, you can support your team, dish out a lot of damage, become invisible, etc etc, each frame have a specific ''feel'' to it, and their abilities can be quite enjoyable to use.
One of the best selling point of warframe is the content, there's quest, events, challenges, secondary bosses, end-game content, a ♥♥♥♥ ton of weapons / 'frame to plat with, thousands of mods for them. Actually there is so much to do in this game it can be overwhelming at time, but if you just take your time with learning how things works, then you should be just fine.
Customisation-wise, the game can be pretty fun there too, you can switch the color of specific areas on your frame/weapons, giving them specific looks/feels, you also have access to thousands of mods to further customize their fighting abilities, maybe you want your weapons to dish out critical damage ? or maybe you'd rather deal with elemental damage ? Maybe you want your 'frame to be more resistant, or maybe you want her to deal more damages with her abilities, etc etc.
This game is free, so you might expect it, microtransactions are present.
they are far from necessary, thanks to the trading system. Quite early in the game you unlock the ability to trade with other players, and this allows you to trade goods for platinum (the paid currency), depending on what you are trading you can get quite an amount of platinum. This sytem is pretty much enough to pay for everything that you will need in game (weapons / warframe slots, wich are not unlimited).

I'm very into deck building card games at the moment so there was a lot of appeal going in for Hand of Fate.  The price is also reasonable so I figured I'd give it a try.
I've played through the first three bosses and I have to say I really like Hand of Fate.  There's something very exciting about it.  Let me walk you through the game play.  You and your mysterious opponent both have several decks of cards to choose from (that you can customize after the first run through the dungeon).  These cards represent the journey you'll take to get to the boss.  They also hold encounters and equipment you can gain to upgrade you hero.  You hero starts with basic equipment (a sword and light armor), 100 hit points, and some food.  The stranger places the cards on the table to represent the path to the boss.
Then you'll move from card to card dealing with whatever you find there.  Sometimes it's a peaceful ecounter with a friendly merchant, sometimes it's a trap, other times it's an encounter with a powerful demon.  You hero must deal with each card and continue along until they get to and defeat the boss enemy.  When it comes time to battle you zoom into a battle ground and you see your cards turn into your hero complete with all of the equipment you've found to this point.  Then you fight whatever was on the card you drew.  It's a lot of fun.
The thing that probably makes this game for me is the dialog of the mysterious stranger and the music.  It really sets the tone and atmosphere of the game.
If you like rpgs, choose your own adventures, deck building, or adventure games you may find something to like here.  I would definitely recommend this title.

Amazing game to be carried away by. Feature rich, good menu system (not the toned-down, controller optimized stuff you normally get these days), an amazing turn-based battle system, very good music and sound in general, very compelling graphics and art style. Characters are, as it's normal for the Divinity series, quite quirky sometimes, but the humor works well and already made me chuckle a few times.
You'll probably not like this game if you have a short attention span, since it can be a tad verbose and it's easy to miss a clue for a side quest if you don't dig into this verbosity. Other than that, I feel it does a better job than its (still lovely) predecessor when it comes to introducing the player to its world: a proper journal keeps track of the adventures and right off the bat the game rewards thinking out of the box, being it in combat or while exploring the world.
4 player co-op and the gamemaster mode are the cherry on top this rather well rounded package. Although, granted, this particular cherry is made of solid gold and provides endless posibilities and replayability.
So far, 10 out of 10. Would talk to a dog again.

Conan Exiles is an early access game. Let me start by saying that we should all know what that means by now. It means it isn't finished, that they don't have everything ironed out, that they havent tested it in a major way, and it might not work as expected. There will be bugs. If you're concerned by the current mixed rating on steam, read through the negative reviews. Some have legitimate opinions, most folks are giving negative reviews over it feeling unfinished, buggy, or not optimal. Well no♥♥♥♥♥♥- Early Access. Duh.
With that being said, I had a blast with it last night. My load times were good, my gameplay experience was fun, even though there was some noticable lag and glitches. I will say that as overpowered as my rig is, singleplayer had way more noticeable stutter than the multiplayer server I rented after about an hour of playing it.
I think that the game has a lot of potential, and the platforms that exist in the game give it a strong path ahead should Funcom choose to take advantage of the myriad of tools they've given themsevles for making this game truly something special.
I'd recommend it to anyone looking to have some fun with friends. It's not Rust, it's not an Ark clone - it's Conan Exiles. It feels unique. Looking forward to loosing a couple hundred hours of my life into this.

My experience with Conan Exiles has been a pleasant and enjoyable one so far. Stunning graphics, fun multiplayer, well thought out crafting system, great physics and combat that is decent for the time being (and will hopefully be tightened and polished in future patches). I have experienced a few minor bugs and glitches here and there but nothing game-breaking. The major issues of the community seem to be the server list and lag on servers. After the first update, the game has run smoothly for me with minimal lag. The server list has remained buggy but there is a quick fix for that while it's broken, and it is to simply use the Steam Server List to connect to servers.
For a game that has only been some 12-13 months in development before its early access release, it is nothing short of impressive. I have high expectations for this game in the future, as it already seems like a very solid start and already has quite an amount of content, which is often lacking in early access game.

The Movement is turn based but combat is FPS/RTS as the enemy/player get to react to one another during the combat.  The attacker/mover turn gets to pick its targets and aim at those targets. A fresh and vibrant concept that marries platforming and racing in an almost seamless manner.
It took me a while to really try SpeedRunners, and that was on a whim after watching several Youtubers and Twitch streamers play the game. It seemed like really great fun to play with some friends, and it proved to be as such.
Another gem published by tinyBuild games (wow, they're really starting to make a name for themselves in the world of publishing) and developed by DoubleDutch games (I checked, they are based in the Netherlands, hence their name...LOL), SpeedRunners tells the story of up to 4 superheroes all racing and sabotaging each other in order to get to crimes the fastest. (And yet, the funny thing is that every map is basically all the runners going in a loop without actually getting to a crime scene...)
The game does seem like it needs more polish, despite the great concept here at play. Once in a while I get the occasional game crash, sometimes I find (oddly) that the game doesn't respond to my controls, there are a few weird bugs here and there where I am eliminated from a round a lot earlier than expected...
Refer to my edits at the top of this review.
Otherwise, the core elements of this game are incredibly great. There are a wide variety of powerups to frustrate your opponents with and slow them down or pull them back. Not that many official maps but there is a theoretically infinite supply with in-built Steam Workshop support. If you can grab a few friends to play a few rounds of multiplayer, you're probably going to have a fun time. (Or you might end up becoming ex-friends with those friends. It can swing either way.)
If you don't have any friends to play with, and/or cannot be bothered to play online with other people, you can actually practice your skills using bots.
This has been replaced with a new story mode where you race bots. Very decent alternatives that are adequately able to account for any lack of real life hoomanz.
The game has been bundled a few times; the cheapest it has gone is 75% off. Quite worth picking it up from these sources/at these prices, it's great. :)

However, I stopped to think about it. How many different types of trucks do I really see out on the road, myself?
I start off with a "Duty-Day Cab". Fairly basic. Either Kenworth or Peterbilt. I see other options unlocked as I level, such as lights, mirrors, Sleep-Cabs, wheels. Items to make my truck look like any number of trucks I see out on the roads.
Only 2 states. 3rd is coming soon for free. Yeah. Not too thrilled about that as it makes it sound like that's the end of free DLC. We'll have to be patient and hope that's not the case.
The 2 states, California and Nevada can take more time to get through at first. I don't have a wheel, just an old xbox360 controller that likes to drift to the right a lot, and going the speed limit, a good job can take a good 10-15 minutes to complete.
I'm terrible at backing up and parking. However, this is a good thing, as it's a challenge for me to overcome and get bettwr reards from.
The streaming of music is great too. Real radio stations with real bands. Jammed to Megadeth and Volbeat down the Fresno Interstate. It was awesome.
The game overall is gorgeous. I don't have much time in it, but I want to see what else there is to it as well.

Maybe not for everyone, but I don't regret it at all.

Sequel to the critically acclaimed game Mass Effect, Mass Effect 2 takes the beloved franchise from great to magnificent. The storyline, voice acting, visuals, and the 3rd-person combat system with a sci-fi twist work flawlessly. It is a masterpiece of our generation, to say the least.
In this sci-fi action RPG the player takes on the role of Commander Shepard who must save the world once again, this time from mysterious beings called “The Collectors”. Before they destroy humanity, Shepard must travel the universe and recruit a team of humans and aliens, gain their loyalty, research the enemy, and stop the Collectors at all cost.
In many ways Mass Effect 2 embodies what Bioware is all about. Players will appreciate not only the top quality storyline and voice acting -- Martin Sheen steals the show -- but also the lengths Bioware went to listen to their fans and improve on the flaws of the previous game. One example of such improvement is the switch from the cool-down weapons to the traditional magazine-reload weapons. While many developers would have kept their old “innovative” system, due to either pride or laziness, Bioware went the extra mile to make the changes -- and it paid off. Other changes such as simpler weapon customization and tighter combat controls make for a more satisfying experience overall compared to its predecessor. The save file from the previous game carries over as well, which is another welcome trademark of Bioware.
The presentation of the game is flawless. Including everything from visuals, audio, and writing, Mass Effect 2 does not fail in the “epic experience” department, the most impressive aspect being the characters themselves. Bioware has taken the time to create such compelling characters that I had no choice but to care about every single one of them. The universe of Mass Effect 2 is deep, thoughtfully-crafted, and engaging, just like its predecessor, which is full of codex entries that pull the players deeper still into the futuristic world. Add to it the attention to detail such as the great soundtrack and the subtle biblical references throughout the game and you get yourself an unforgettable experience.
The 3rd-person combat is very satisfying as well. Not only is the gunplay improved compared to the previous game, but the use of special skills has tightened up as well, giving much more incentive for the player to try out classes other than the gun expert Soldier class (being an Adept with telekinetic powers is incredibly satisfying, not to mention all the other classes).
Ironically, the weak point of this game is also its selling point -- the morality system. Yes, it does have a morality system that very much controls the tone of the playthrough; but it lacks the complexity and the ambiguity that makes such systems… well… so delicious (Dragon Age, a Bioware game with such deliciousness, comes to mind). The player’s choices are always presented in a very clear manner that just boils them down to “good” or “bad” in the end. In my first playthrough I was interested in what Sheperd would do in a given situation but after a while I found myself just clicking the “good” option (as I was playing the “good” character) without even reading the actual response, which made me much less appreciative of the morality system. Other weak points include the sub-par vehicular DLC “Firewalker Pack” and the shallow and two-dimensional “romance” system.
Mass Effect 2 is one of the few games in which I began a second playthrough immediately after the first one. It is a game I’ll revisit at least once a year, like a classic book that gets better each time you read it. Is it the morality system that changes the tone of the game? Is it the compelling characters that I can’t keep away from? Maybe it is the engaging combat with multiple classes to choose from. Or maybe it is just the sheer polish of the script and voice acting. Whatever it is, there is no denying that Mass Effect 2 is something special. Even if you are not a sci-fi fan, even if you are not an RPG fan, or even if you are not a third person shooter fan, it would be a damn shame if I didn’t recommend this game with all my heart.

I'm very into deck building card games at the moment so there was a lot of appeal going in for Hand of Fate.  The price is also reasonable so I figured I'd give it a try.
I've played through the first three bosses and I have to say I really like Hand of Fate.  There's something very exciting about it.  Let me walk you through the game play.  You and your mysterious opponent both have several decks of cards to choose from (that you can customize after the first run through the dungeon).  These cards represent the journey you'll take to get to the boss.  They also hold encounters and equipment you can gain to upgrade you hero.  You hero starts with basic equipment (a sword and light armor), 100 hit points, and some food.  The stranger places the cards on the table to represent the path to the boss.
Then you'll move from card to card dealing with whatever you find there.  Sometimes it's a peaceful ecounter with a friendly merchant, sometimes it's a trap, other times it's an encounter with a powerful demon.  You hero must deal with each card and continue along until they get to and defeat the boss enemy.  When it comes time to battle you zoom into a battle ground and you see your cards turn into your hero complete with all of the equipment you've found to this point.  Then you fight whatever was on the card you drew.  It's a lot of fun.
The thing that probably makes this game for me is the dialog of the mysterious stranger and the music.  It really sets the tone and atmosphere of the game.
If you like rpgs, choose your own adventures, deck building, or adventure games you may find something to like here.  I would definitely recommend this title.

I don't write a lot of reviews, but this is a good game and warrants one. It's one of the better indies I've played recently with a lot more depth and fun than it seems to posses at first glance. The story is interesting with you playing against a rival for some unknown treasure; the skill ramp is slow, which gives you time to learnt he mechanics; and the gameplay is extremely varied.
There's a nice mix of ranomness, luck, and skill to each play session. Combat is twitch based, though not overally aggressive; the deck building is fun; and the overall story is interesting. I especially like how cards can have stories that unlock additional cards as you succeed at their demands.
The animations can be a little jerky in some spots and there's a few odd bugs (ex: change categories in a story, right click and then hit ESC (thinking it will close the window) and your cursor disppears. For those that his this, simply alt-tab and then alt-tab back to the game and your cursor will come back).
I'd recommend this game anyone getting tired of the rouge-clones that are popping up and looking for something fun and engaging.

Mouse control is good most of the time, but occasionally super finicky. Keyboard controls are good. Runs great on my i3 & R7 370 desktop. The game itself is the same it always was, so you'll either love it or hate it. I'm glad I bought it.

A really strange mix between a beat'em all and an RPG.
The narrative part is very well done and you unlock differents parts of various stories as you complete challenges given by cards.
Each card presents an event or an equipement, and each game shuffle your deck of events randomly to give you a challenge.
The battle system is inspired by the Batman Arkham series and if not perfect (because it stays pretty basic), does its job.
The RNG is present and sometimes can be a ♥♥♥♥♥. (Davy Jones, give me back my soul !).
But the more vicious challenges tends to give the more interesting rewards (and if it's too hard, don't keep them in the deck).
Several challenges are kept in the deck in order to unlock others events so you end up by keeping the difficult one only to complete them once.
For an indie game, graphics are also really great and animations well executed. Presentation is top notch. The amount of work in this gem should have been huge.

I usually avoid writing reviews so early in a game's life cycle, or with such short playtime. However I feel many of the reviews are bias and would like to share my (short) in game experience.
I am very, VERY happy to report this is exactly everything I was expecting. The trailers made it out to be a combination of many survival games over the past three years, but with some nice little twists. It's important to note that the environment is VERY deadly. I am pleased that it's not just players, that there are creatures that do not hesitate ruining your day. To me this is a first in the survival genre, the amount of threat you are under from NPC's as soon as you spawn is almost overwhelming.
I've died five times, having not seen a single player. The first time I spent too much time at spawn looking at shiny things and died of thirst. The second time I ran straight into a bandit camp (They cut my head off). The third time some turtle/dog jumped on my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The fourth and fifth deaths were at night and I couldnt see much, only heard the beasts rip my flesh asunder. This game is hard, but not unfair.
Performance is an issue but that is to be expected with Early Access. I'm aware people can't see servers and of some of the structure placement issues are questionable but so far I'm very impressed. This game has the potential to be one of the greatest survival games and I believe that is because of it's heavy reliance on non typical survival game elements.
My verdict: With technical issues aside this is a fantastic survival game that adds new twists on the typical formula. (Gods, NPC threats, NPC structure defenses, dungeons)

Truth: Disorder. The name of the game really doesn't make a lot of sense. Unfortunately, I didn't get much more out of the story either. Basically a guy lives alone and has his meals and medications delivered every morning by a schoolgirl. At the end you get to decide if you want to stay in and take the pills or go out and see what happens. That's pretty much it. I was underwhelmed, even at 1.99 USD.
So, a very short (~30 minutes for all achievements and both endings) visual novel with two short branches right at the end that lead to each ending. Suffers from a pretty poor translation, which slows the read, so it's likely even shorter if read in it's native language (Russian?). Made using Ren'Py. I'm not real familiar with what comes with the engine as far as premade sprites and backgrounds, but the sprites especially look familiar. Otherwise, sprites, and backgrounds are pretty basic and uninspired. No CGs. The BGM was a single track repeated, which if it had gone longer than 30 minutes likely would have had grave psychological effects to the listener. No voice acting. There are Steam achievements for those who are interested in them, but no trading cards at this point. Overall, there are better VNs out there, including a lot of free ones. This title isn't really worth the time or money invested. I can't even think of a niche that I would recommend this to. Sorry to leave a bad review for a new VN company, but I can't in good conscious recommend this. Thanks for reading and I hope this helps people make an informed decision on buying or not.

Murdered: Soul Suspect was easily the biggest surprise of 2015 for me, and I think the last game that really blew away my expectations to the same extent was the psychologically assaulting trek through the sands of Spec Ops: The Line. Now of course that comparison gives Soul Suspect a lot more credit than it deserves, it’s a far from perfect game and certainly won’t be looked back on as a game design milestone. But while I expected a more or less point and click hidden object game with fancy 3D graphics and bizarrely contrived QTE’s, what I got was a decent story entwined in a fascinating and well fleshed out word with fantastic mechanics to handle action sequences.
Honestly, yes. If I had to boil this game down into a single genre I would have to go with a point and click adventure. The main backbone of the game is walking from crime scene to crime scene and pressing X when you spot a clue. There is certainly nothing revolutionary about the mechanic but the content of the clues- and to a much larger extent the collectibles- brings to light a remarkably well imagined world. Now I’m not well versed in the history of Salem and the details of the witch trials, but I think the writers put in a good amount of creative effort bringing an engaging fictional story into a very real place and time. Typically the little factoids littered around the game world only appeal to completionist minded individuals like myself, however I found myself on a multitude of occasions scouring the town for that last entry to figure out the end of a story.
The visuals of the game are adequate, nothing that I didn’t expect after looking at 2 or 3 screenshots. I was able to run the game mostly maxed out on my 680 and the framerate was stable and consistent.
Here is the thing that made the game for me: the “final boss”. Don’t worry I will not spoil a thing, and it was actually the absence of something which made it utterly refreshing and a huge relief. Aside from a handful of action-y stealth segments with demons, the game is slow and narrative driven. As I felt the story come closer and closer to a close I got this feeling of dread. You see I know how AAA games go nowadays, every fiber of my being was expecting this dreadful quick time event unfair boss fight that has no continuity with the entire rest of the game. I was even tempted to not finish the game myself and watch the ending online because I didn’t want to walk away from such a great experience with a terrible taste in my mouth. Yet the developers NAILED it. No it’s not a spectacle and no it’s not brutally difficult, but it was satisfying and conclusive to the narrative. The amount of relief I felt at the ending was overwhelming.
I’ve harped a lot on a very little point of the game, but it was a big reason this game left me with such a positive view of it. Murdered: Soul Suspect is not perfect but it’s a breath of fresh air for narrative centric games and it kept me engaged and entertained the whole way through.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is cute and fun game. For me, this game is perfect collection of genres, combining a shop sim, a dungeon crawling action RPG, and visual novel style segments all into one game.
The basics of the plot is that you are Recette, a young girl who's adventurer father disappears and leave behind a crippling debt that threatens to take away your home and everything in it. So you along with Tear, the fairy loan officer responsible for you paying the debt back, open an item shop. From there on out you can go out into town to buy stock and meet people, or hire an adventurer to bring items you can sell back from dungeons.
The difficulty curve can be intense, with your payments going up exponentially. However, I would consider this to be a medium difficulty game. Neither the shop segments or the dungeons are too difficult, though they still can be hard and tricky.
There are 8 adventurers that you can unlock over the course of the game for the dungeon portions and each has a unique combat style and abilities from one another, so there is plenty of variety whether you want to change things up or find a style that suits you best. There are also 6 dungeons, each one harder that the first but providing better drops progressively.
The plot is presented in very cute visual novel style segments and is quite light and relaxed despite the goal to pay off an ever increasing debt. I find it fits the medium difficulty game play segments very well. To trigger most of the story segments requires you to leave the shop and waste a chunk of your time, but the characters are all unique, fun and quirky. It's also the only way to unlock some of your potential adventures, so it can be worth your time.
All in all, I love this game. It's not to difficult to pick up and has a lot of content available so you can keep playing for hours.

This is another one of those games that makes you want to kill your friends, like Super Smash Bros. In fact, the best way to describe Speedrunners is "Mario Kart meets Super Smash Bros."
The gameplay is essentially one huge looping race, and you have to outrun your opponents until they hit the border, and thus killing them.Each math has 3 rounds, and if you win 3, you win the match. The game has a lot of Parkour-esque platforming that is really enjoyable and fun; double jumping, wall-jumping, sliding and grappling your way to victory.
The real fun comes with the items though, as you can use these to mess up the other players and  get in their way. Every item is useful, and every item needs to be used correctly. They also require precise timing to hit, and precise timing to dodge. Every item in the game can be countered, making none of the items feel overpowered at any point whatsoever.
Much like the item usage, everything in this game is precise. You need precisely timed button presses and jumps in order to win. You usually have no one to blame but yourself for losing, and it's great...usually. One of the major issues is the lag when playing online. On several occasions, I died due to horrible lag in the game. Luckily, this only happens while playing online with random players. When playing with friends or locally, it seems to run just fine.
The level design is fantastic; every stage looks great, and they are well-though out, with multple shortcuts, and how to get them, along with many traps. Sometimes, these traps can feel a bit cheap (the spikes in particualr are really bad), but they are overall pretty good. The character designs are also pretty awesome, as every character looks cool, and you want to play as all of them jut to see what their animations are. However, I wish that the characters played differently from eachother. There is zero difference in playstyle between characters, and that is disappointing to say the least. No stats, no special abilities, nothing. It makes the game feel devoid of strategy and tactics. And while most of the game is reaction and skill-based, it would've been nice to have some strategy involved, outside of item usage.
Something else that's disappointing is a lack of a story mode. I like stories in video games, and if the game doesn't have a story, that's understandable. But the problem is that the characters and the stages are so well designed, hat I would like to know about the world. In fact, during loading screens, you'll occasionally see characters making a remark or two about another character, and it just makes me wonder what is going on in this world. But comparatively, that's a minor complaint, as the gameplay is good enough to make up for it.
The gmae also lacks content, as every race is pretty straightforward. I would've liked to see a few extra modes such as a battle mode, or something to mix up the gameplay. I also think that the game is very had, as you start out in the entry league, and so you are matched up wih players who are also in the entry league, and are more or less just as good as you are at the game. If you win a match, you get around 40 to 60 points, but losing will make you lose around 5 to 20 points. And trust me, you'll be losing ALOT at first, due to the slightly confusing controls and play style that takes alot of getting used to. This makes it almost impossible to reach higher rankings and be paired up with people who are really good at the game to get some challenge every now and then.
However, despite all my complaints with the game, I still highly recommend Speedrunners. The gameplay, while it has a learning curve, is extremely fun and addictive. You'll play for hours on end, not realizing that you just wasted 3 hours of your life away. The complaints, though plentiful, aren't that bad and they are outwieghed by the good that the game has. And frankly, most of these issues come from this game being an Early Access title. Most of these issues will most likely be fixed down the road. Speedrunners is definately worth your time, and for $10, you'll definately get your money's worth out of it. I rate it an 8/10.

Sequel to the critically acclaimed game Mass Effect, Mass Effect 2 takes the beloved franchise from great to magnificent. The storyline, voice acting, visuals, and the 3rd-person combat system with a sci-fi twist work flawlessly. It is a masterpiece of our generation, to say the least.
In this sci-fi action RPG the player takes on the role of Commander Shepard who must save the world once again, this time from mysterious beings called “The Collectors”. Before they destroy humanity, Shepard must travel the universe and recruit a team of humans and aliens, gain their loyalty, research the enemy, and stop the Collectors at all cost.
In many ways Mass Effect 2 embodies what Bioware is all about. Players will appreciate not only the top quality storyline and voice acting -- Martin Sheen steals the show -- but also the lengths Bioware went to listen to their fans and improve on the flaws of the previous game. One example of such improvement is the switch from the cool-down weapons to the traditional magazine-reload weapons. While many developers would have kept their old “innovative” system, due to either pride or laziness, Bioware went the extra mile to make the changes -- and it paid off. Other changes such as simpler weapon customization and tighter combat controls make for a more satisfying experience overall compared to its predecessor. The save file from the previous game carries over as well, which is another welcome trademark of Bioware.
The presentation of the game is flawless. Including everything from visuals, audio, and writing, Mass Effect 2 does not fail in the “epic experience” department, the most impressive aspect being the characters themselves. Bioware has taken the time to create such compelling characters that I had no choice but to care about every single one of them. The universe of Mass Effect 2 is deep, thoughtfully-crafted, and engaging, just like its predecessor, which is full of codex entries that pull the players deeper still into the futuristic world. Add to it the attention to detail such as the great soundtrack and the subtle biblical references throughout the game and you get yourself an unforgettable experience.
The 3rd-person combat is very satisfying as well. Not only is the gunplay improved compared to the previous game, but the use of special skills has tightened up as well, giving much more incentive for the player to try out classes other than the gun expert Soldier class (being an Adept with telekinetic powers is incredibly satisfying, not to mention all the other classes).
Ironically, the weak point of this game is also its selling point -- the morality system. Yes, it does have a morality system that very much controls the tone of the playthrough; but it lacks the complexity and the ambiguity that makes such systems… well… so delicious (Dragon Age, a Bioware game with such deliciousness, comes to mind). The player’s choices are always presented in a very clear manner that just boils them down to “good” or “bad” in the end. In my first playthrough I was interested in what Sheperd would do in a given situation but after a while I found myself just clicking the “good” option (as I was playing the “good” character) without even reading the actual response, which made me much less appreciative of the morality system. Other weak points include the sub-par vehicular DLC “Firewalker Pack” and the shallow and two-dimensional “romance” system.
Mass Effect 2 is one of the few games in which I began a second playthrough immediately after the first one. It is a game I’ll revisit at least once a year, like a classic book that gets better each time you read it. Is it the morality system that changes the tone of the game? Is it the compelling characters that I can’t keep away from? Maybe it is the engaging combat with multiple classes to choose from. Or maybe it is just the sheer polish of the script and voice acting. Whatever it is, there is no denying that Mass Effect 2 is something special. Even if you are not a sci-fi fan, even if you are not an RPG fan, or even if you are not a third person shooter fan, it would be a damn shame if I didn’t recommend this game with all my heart.

Metro: Last Light Redux
+ Good shooting, each gun has its uses in different situations and you really feel the power of the weapons. You'll get access to modifiable pistols, shotguns, rifles and a number of explosive devices. Stealth is encouraged and is a viable approach to many missions.
+ Very detailed, atmospheric environments, traversing the dilapidated Metro stations and nuclear waste swamps on the surface was great. I enjoyed the seemingly insignificant, yet immersive graphical effects of Metro: Last Light Redux, where raindrops blocked your view when it was pouring down, or dirt splashed all across your screen when you waded through irradiated marshes.
+ The story is interesting but it's also a bit hard to follow, even with diary entries found within each level. Picking up from the events that occurred in Metro: 2033, Artyom is sent to eliminate the last known surviving 'dark one', but ultimately ends up embarking on a journey of self-understanding and reflection on humanity.
~ Some of the DLC is fun and some of it isn't. For example, in Sniper Team you'll infiltrate a Nazi compound, relying on a high powered sniper rifle to neutralise enemies from afar. In spider lair you're recruited for an expedition to charter the metro tunnels. After a few days, you wake from unconsciousness stuck in a giant web of silk - now you must survive and find your two partners in the spiders' den. The mission in Kshatriya, where you scavenge the libraries of Moscow on the surface for cultural and technological artifacts is also good. Returning to base camp you will be paid for the items you retrieve so you can re-stock for future trips. The goal is to acquire a secret map of the subway somewhere on the surface, which will aid your cause.
Other parts of the DLC like 'Heavy Squad' and 'The Tower' are very boring, amounting to nothing more than mindless "survive the wave of enemies" combat levels.
- I dislike how my decisions in the game weren't appreciated by the developers. I made choices for the self-preservation of the Rangers in D6 who I serve, doing what was necessary for the safety of the Metro as a whole and killing any hostile mutated creatures. The plotline was so predictable, I could tell I was going to receive a "bad ending", even though morally my decisions were entirely justifiable and logical. This was a very shallow and sad design implementation by the game's developers.
- Dumb, scripted 'boss fights', where creatures or humans take an abnormal amount of bullets or cannot die until a certain condition has been triggered. Unrealistic!
- I wish there were more levels for the surface and more opportunities to explore it. Unfortunately most of the time you are rushed, trying to delicately balance the filter timing in your gas mask with exploration (if it runs out you will suffocate). I still managed to thoroughly search the surface every chance I had, but it's the feeling of time pressure which is annoying. Metro: Last Light Redux looks so amazing and the surface is one of the best areas of the game, so it's disappointing that you feel hurried in these sections.
- Microstuttering on a high end PC - GTX 970 4GB, 8 GB RAM, i7 CPU, not fixed by developers.

This game is a very well done mix of a deck builder and an action rpg. You start each game with a basic hero (non-cusomazable likeness, if it's a deal breaker for you) and you live a small adventure that is brought to life by uncovering the cards on a map.
It's fun, casual, quick, everchanging, and original enough while adhhering to all the apects you'd expect from a fantasy adventure.
Let's talk about generla mechanics first.
There are two kinds of decks that you build and carry from mission to mission: events and equipment. Events are those cards that are laid out on the table to represent the map, your journey, and you uncover them while you travel.
Equipments are weapons, armours, artifacts and whatever makes your hero more powerful, and they are added to your hero by surviving events.
The dealer (your opponent) has other decks from which he gets monsters when required, bonuses and maluses, blessing and curses for you hero every time an event goes your way or the other.
Each time you meet a new event or defeat a new opponent, you are rewarded with more cards to add to your events and equipment decks. The events can be as easy as picking successful or failing in a random mishap, or complex like making multiple choices.
Now for the cool twist: the most fun events require you to actually change screens and take control of your character ina a third person adventure -style game (a little bit like the combat system from Fable).
So you won't be sitting there picking carda and making choices, you will also fight, dodge, deflect magic attacks and stomp skeletons, outlaws and lizardmen.
So, the game is tons of fun, and the added benefit is that of being very replayable: the same events change the way they are presented and the way they unfold, and the maps are generated at random, plus they are generated from you deck of events plus the cards the dealer slips in it... this makes the game infinetely replayable.

I'm going to begin by saying that this review was written after playing the first level beyond the tutorial, so I might not have a full handle of the games nuances.
First and foremost, this is a deck-building game. The cards are not just a creative way to stylize the game, they are the source of your equipment and your challenges. Before each level you assemble two sets of cards. Your equipment deck, and your encounter deck. Now, you don't start with any of these cards, these are the cards that are going to be on the board for you to gather or miss depending on chance. The Equipment is your assortment of weapons, armor, and special abilities. And the Encounter deck is your encounters in the level (duh), of scaling severity. From the farmer, to the goblins, to the hall of traps, to the ambush. While these can hurt you, they can just as easily reward you. At the end of the hall of traps, is treasure. At the end of the ambush, loot. This brings us to the core gameplay
After building your decks, you begin the game, where cards are shuffled and laid face down on the table in random assortment. This acts like a board to a tabletop game, where you can only move one space (or card) at a time, and each card is an encounter. And just because you built an encounter deck doesnt mean that's all you'll face, The Dealer (or Game Master) peppers his own cards in there as well. The encounters for me so far have either been text blocks with multiple choice answers, or action phases where you navigate hazards or fight enemies.
The combat reminds me of the Batman: Arkham series. While not reliant so heavily on combos, there is an assortment of enemy types and a dodge and counter system that is very similar, if not identical. Special abilites are earned through cards and do things like generate gold on hit or throw a fan of knives.
After winning encounters and navigating the board, you make your way to the boss, which, after the battle, you collect the tokens you've earned up to that point. These work as booster packs for your deck, giving you random equipment and encounter cards, which can be used for the levels ahead. New cards however, remain somewhat of a mystery, because while you have the name of the card like say, Scavanger's Helm, you don't know exactly what it does until you aquire during a level. (probably something involving loot)
Death is going to be common, but, much like the game Rogue Legacy, death isn't the end. It's a chance to do better next time, with the new cards you've earned from tokens during the round, and a new assortment of cards that might be more (or less) favorable to you.
During the game, The Dealer will taunt you and will make comments on the cards you draw. It can really draw you into the game and give the immersion that you're really in a card duel with a (slightly overdramatic) snarky wizard, trying to beat him at (literally) his own game.
Overall, This game has my complete approval. Being a very creative and well exicuted concept I would love to see more of it.

This one is right on the line. Expeditions: Conquistador would be a good mod, but as a feature-length game it isn't quite satisfying. It makes a lot of good, small decisions with its design, but fumbles the stuff that the player interacts with the most. Writing, portrait art, and a lot of scenario elements are all really strong. Game feel, game flow, and the UI are not. The end result is a kind of clunky game that's worth tolerating, but only if you've played through all your other SRPGs and are looking for something else to scratch that itch.
Conquistador is like a head-on collision between Blackguards and Legends of Eisenwald, with Eisenwald's overworld and exploration, but Blackguards' combat. And if that sounds like an unpleasant matchup, yes. It kind of is.
On an overworld full of obscuring jungle cover, your camera is glued to the back of a tiny man on a horse. To move, you scroll to the edge of what you can see, find a clickable pixel, hammer your mouse cursor on it until it selects, and then watch five seconds of animation as your expedition trots over to the point. In a single 'turn', or game day, you're going to do this about four or five times. After that you camp, manually tweak your duties roster, switch people from hunting to perserving meat and back again, twiddle with a few percentage values, and see if half of your resources walked away in the night.
This is all clog.
Every single part of the overworld is pure tediousness that keeps you from getting to the game's good bits.
Something like Banner Saga's or Hard West's interface would have served Conquistador well, as it could have streamlined the plot into one satisfying flow. Instead, you spend most of your time piloting your claustrophobic camera and tiny horse into spots that look like they might lead somewhere, and then wheeling the camera in search of clickable pixels.
When you do get into combat, the balance isn't bad, but it is pretty unforgiving, and everything is for keeps. If you make a bad perk pick on one of your core units, or if you lose a bunch of equipment points, the finale can be *very* unforgiving.  In a game where your characters have fairly low damage output, the succession of "kill every enemy by turn X" battles (with anyone who gets dropped being unusable in any of the following fights) is somewhat frustrating. Add in the huge numbers of enemies and slow pace of each combat round, and it becomes the sort of experience where you'd be getting up to get a beer after each end of turn, if you didn't watch the enemy's actions to make sure they don't suddenly swarm around one of your best troops.
Combat balance is kind of fun, kind of iffy, with a meta that revolves around guaranteed hit melee attacks and percentage chance ranged attacks. Of course, only one class has any chance of hitting with their ranged attacks, so the game turns into straight melee unless you carefully build your hunters so that they can double-tap their muskets at close-range for guaranteed criticals if the shot connects. Even then, all your troops feel fragile, so a lot of combat is desperately body-walling around injured troops in the hopes that maybe they won't get targeted with a bow or blowgun.
The story is actually pretty good, but the gonzo bits stand out as *really gonzo* against the otherwise fairly serious historical approach the game takes. Being able to double-tap with your (apparently semi-automatic?) muskets is nothing next to the temple full of Aztec robot-skeletons protecting the fountain of youth, or the actual dog-headed god of the underworld who lets you sell people for skulls. The fact that these two moments even show up is a little strange, but they felt like the game at its strongest. A slow-burning supernatural undercurrent culminating in a dive into the Aztec underworld to rescue the captain would have been really cool, but instead Mesoamerican Anubis is an optional side-encounter, and it's easy to play the game without ever finding any of the weirder content.
In the end, this is not an objectively bad game, but it's not quite good enough for me to recommend when there are so many other, better games in the genre. Even if what you specifically want is a south-american conquistador-era expedition-based SRPG, there's a section of Hard West that is exactly that, with a better UI, better resource-management, and a more gripping story.
Don't be scared off by the 'no' vote if you really want to try this out, but I'd say wait for a 75% sale before picking it up.

Hand of Fate is a game I've been seeing around lately, hearing a lot of solid words from trusted sources and fellow gamers, and of course some harsh criticisms, which is to be expected, but the one theme that keeps popping up is that it is addicting as hell. Combining elements from card games such as Hearthstone and Magic the Gathering, board games like Dungeons and Dragons, as well as RPGs like Skyrim, Diablo, and The Witcher, this game has all the elements to be the meth of gaming, a blend of a lot of different things making for a hell of a drug, but is it fun? Let's find out, shall we?
Gameplay: 93/100 A-
As I mentioned in the intro, Hand of Fate is a mix of a lot of different things, taking the best aspects of each and nearly seamlessly melding them into one, a feat that is hard enough to do separately, let alone flowing from one to another, but it is an achievement that Defiant have successfully done. Playing through the cards and planning ahead with equipment, magic, traps, all the standards that you can find in other card games, but then the RPG side comes in a bit as you can trade with caravans, should you draw that card, and finally landing on the combat, which is fairly simple to get used to. Attack, blocking, countering, all can be done and the game does flow like water over river stones in the spring time.
Audio: 94/100 A-
The sound effects and music is also done very well. It was never intrusive or overwhelming, Calm when it needed to be and action packed elsewhere. The voice acting has to be the crowning jewel here, where listening to your "trainer" felt real. For example, leave the game playing during a turn or when picking cards, he may start babbling or criticizing you for taking too much time. It's an organic feel that I really welcomed and made me chuckle a few times. The combat sounds and ambience is also very well produced, a solid effort on this end.
Visuals: 94/100 A-
Hand of Fate is good to look at, even at the lowest settings. There is of course clipping issues here and there, but I feel like that's going to be an issue in gaming for at least another generation and a half. Anyways, the colors are all done well and placed in logical locations, things look like they belong as well as drawing inspirations from all the genres that are mashed together in the game: medieval fantasy, gothic dark ages, D&D, it all comes together quite nicely, giving Hand of Fate a distinct style.
Content: 95/100 A
There are a LOT of cards to play with here, easily competing with other big dogs in the market, both old and new, couple that with the other elements of the game and you're into a lot of replayability, but with that also comes some repetitiveness, and while the latter is annoying, it is also expecting in a game that uses themes from other games which rely on such a large selection of options and randomness. But the game works well together, keeping me interested even when things became repetitive. It is something you come back just in case that awesome moment happens this time around and you get that ultra rare thing you've always wanted.
Design: 96/100 A+
Like I said, the game flows very well together. Everything is done in moderation and not one aspect of the game overwhelms or overpowers another and I think that is the key to Hand of Fate's popularity, despite the often complicated genres that it takes inspiration from. A testament to Defiant's understanding of the multiple elements they've taken from.
Performance: 80/100 B-
Now we get into the issues I ran into. While the game itself is brilliant in combining everything together, the technical side of things are a bit choppy. Again, this is from my experience on my machine, got it? The biggest issue I had, first, involved the Steam overlay glitching and remaining on the screen when I took screenshots. Another issue was often times during the loading of the combat scenes took ages to load, often making me think that the game had frozen, only to come alive suddenly. There was some detection issues with the combat as well, but that could just be my suckiness at said combat. Not to mention glitches here and there bugged me in many ways, but the game is good, so I just learned to ignore them and kept going.
Verdict: 93/100 A-
At the end of it all, you can't deny the strokes of brilliance in Hand of Fate. The developers picked and chose the right things from each genre melded them together, where they would be most effective and instead of falling flat, it stands tall, albeit a little shaky with a lot of polishing needed, it is still a great start. The potential for this game is through the roof.

Hand of Fate has a very unique approach to action RPG. As the player, you will find yourself sitting at a table and across the table you will find a robed individual with rather large hands. This masked man has plucked and manipulated your very memories in order to set the stage. Cards are used to construct levels, provide gear, health, or pain. Part story, part combat this game brings both worlds together to give the player a interesting taste of the characters life through the dealer's eyes.
The player progresses through the game by moving from the starting position to the stairs, cave, boat or basically the exit point for that level. With each move the player consumes one food. If you do not have food than the player loses 10 health. Each move delivers a new encounter for the player as he lands on a card. These cards are determined by what cards were included by the player and the cards added by the dealer. There are more player cards than dealer cards for the campaign. The encounters can be everything from rat men, humans, skeletons to an old woman that asks the player to bring her husband home.
The combat system is rather simple. Counter green indicators, dodge red ones and use shield bash to get past their block. Melee is confined to one button and feels  semi fluid. I've been playing Elsword for a long time, even before it released in North America, since 2010. I even played the Chinese knock off Fists of Fu, or East Fantasy Online. I wouldn't be exaggerating if I said I had well over 20,000 hours. From 2010 to early 2014 this game was my life. And thankfully I kicked this bad habit of a game and haven't played it since 2014. Yet somehow this game is still on my mind, it's just a scar on my life I can't seem to forget.
Avoid this game like the plague if you're weak willed like I was, it will suck you in and turn you into a salty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with an empty wallet.
Pros-
In it's prime it had some of the best PvP I've ever ever seen. I've still yet to find a game with a comparable combination of ultra quick cancels and combos.
Cons-
One of the most vile communities I've ever seen. Especially horrible if you're not a fan of Weeaboos.
"Events" consist of either PvP with a GM which isn't nearly as fun as it may sound, or an opportunity to drop $100 on costumes.
Terrible netcode, in a game that requires such precise movements this is unnaceptable. It's also peer to peer, and they've merged servers before, so expect ping in the 100s quite frequently.
Recently Reduced FPS cap, speed is tied to framerate in this game. With the 60FPS cap movement isn't nearly as quick as it was before, some combos can't even be pulled off anymore. It almost seems as if KOG is progressivly modifiying the game to make combat worse,
As pay to win as you can possibly get. Not only will paying players have double your stats, but they'll have a total of eight skills to use, while a non-paying player is stuck with four.
Completely Unbalenced,
Old classes are completely outdated, (Wind Sneaker being the exception, her concept alone has been broken since she was released years ago) they recently released a character that literally replaces Elsword himself.
Leveling up consists of doing the same dungeon 3 times or more. A casual player will probably take an entire year or more to reach the level cap because of this. The PvE is so painfully repetitive that you'll most likely be happy with any alternative you can find. chatting or roleplaying with weeaboos in the vile section of the game called "sparring" is usually what most end up doing.
In my opinion the only reason this game is still alive is because a small group of unlucky people who enjoy collecting Ice Burner Sets. Ice Burner sets contribute to the pay to win aspect of this game, you spend $1 on an Ice Burner, this Ice Burner has like an incredibly low chance to give you a single piece of a costume set that changes on monthly basis. These costumes don't replace your armor, so the incredibly high stats on them after socketing give quite an obnoxious advantage over those who don't have them. These collectors often buy in bulk, usually $300 at a time, I've been playing long enough to not only see others do this, but actually do it myself. Less fortunate people look at collectors like gods. Hoping that their $5 charge will get them something (It wont).
If you have a low spec PC, steam has so many better options than this terrible game. Do yourself a big favor and forget this one exists. The PVP videos on YouTube might seem really attractive, but it's really not worth trying.
