There are two things which appeal to me in particular about Expeditions: Conquistador..
Firstly that it feels different to other games I've played. It feels like an honest attempt to make a more unique experience, and though I wasn't sure at first whether I was going to like it, I quickly settled in past the tutorial phase and realised it was refreshingly different.
Secondly the overall feel of the new-world. The game is split into two sections, the first taking place on Hispaniola, and the second in Mexico. The lore and historical accuracy is all well founded and researched, making the experience look and feel genuine. The artwork for events and conversations is nice and adds to the atmosphere and feel. Hand painted artwork really adds to the era feel.
The game does lack in minor areas due to the small development team, needing some polish across the board, but nothing I can be too critical about. The graphics could be alot better, but personally I'll take gameplay over graphics any day of the week.

You can make barricades, traps etc., to use in combat, and there are various classes with can be levelled up, some being alot better than others in combat. I've played games with better and worse hex combat, but the battles were enjoyable none-the-less.
Overall a good game made by a small team. Not for everyone, but an absolute steal when it goes on sale.

RIP 1:
In RIP 1, you are a turret. You can't move, and you are usually located in the center of a small map. Enemies come at you from all directions, most of the time in groups and in formation, and attack you. That's it. There is nothing else to the game. Looking at the screenshots you may think, “this looks like it was made in the early 90s even though it was released in 2007.” You may be right, but it does manage to be mildly fun. As you progress through the 40 levels, you will unlock perks, and there are also about five or so weapons available to you in each level. Sometimes you will have access to three or four of these weapons, and you may choose which one you will use. By trial and error you will figure out that depending on the level, some weapons are much better than others. It took me about one hour to beat the game, and I would say that it was a decent hour of simple, yet fun top down horde shooter action. There is no reason to play through it again, but what it provided in that hour was enough.
RIP 2 - Strike Back:
RIP 2 takes your character of choice out of the turret and makes the game much more twin-stick-shooter-like. With that said, there are still a few levels that require you to use the turret, and they have also added two vehicles you could use in several levels. There is a tank and a cumbersome helicopter. In addition to the vehicles and new control mechanics, the developers also added some new enemies and a few bosses scattered throughout the 60 levels. RIP 2 is noticeably more difficult than the first game in the series, but it's still manageable with the exception of having to repeat one or two levels several times in order to beat them. The enemy pathfinding problems are still there, and because some levels have many more obstacles than on the first game, it becomes much more obvious to notice that the game's AI leaves much to be desired. RIP 2 is basically 60 more levels of the original game with the addition of a few things here and there. It's virtually the same game, but with more levels and some new mechanics. With that said, it's comparable in enjoyment to RIP 1.
RIP 3 - The Last Hero:
This is the first game in the series to actually make an attempt at fleshing out the story. This adds nothing to the quality of the game, even though some of the cutscene artwork is decent if you like their 90s style. The AI and pathfinding problems are much more noticeable in RIP 3 than in the two previous games. This has more to do with the level design being generally worse than in the other two games. Strangely enough, even though it may seem like the developers spent more time with this third installment by adding a few more interesting weapons and polishing the graphics and overall presentation a bit, the game suffers technically, as the AI's behavior is erratic at best, and extremely boring at its worst. Not much has been done to make it better than the other games. It's as if the development team had the urge to make the third game, but very little interest in attempting to make it better. RIP 3 is the least enjoyable of the three games, as it steps down in quality quite frequently through the 100 levels.
The other reviews of RIP - Trilogy are quite harsh. I agree that these games aren't good, but the amount of negativity seems to be coming from people who didn't even give it a chance. If you like simplistic, retro style arcade action, this package is at an OK price and will provide you with a few hours of fun.

Valkyria Chronicles has a very well written story that explores war (specifically world war II) from the viewpoint of the militia. Mass Effect 2 is one of those games you can see yourself grow up with. I first played this game on the Xbox 360 in 2010 when first released. It was new to me and wasnt a generic shooter. But I never fully comprehended the decisions aspect of this game, and resulted in me not caring about the consequences. Consider it being that I just wanted to skip the decisions and get to the combat. Now being that its 2014, and I have matured much since then, I wanted to give the game another chance and give it my best shot.
I purchased 1 and 2 on PC (The bundle) and launched 2 because I already beat 1. After playing it for a while, I was deeply involved in the decisions and actually disliked the combat. I wanted to make those high priority decisions, and wanted to strip combat out of the game. But then I noticed that combat was a catalyst to keep you playing. Without the combat, or without decisions, it would have been a generic game. Combat influenced what skills deserved the points from my leveling, what materials I should go hunting for next, what missions I decided to do. Some missions didnt even involve combat, you had to rely on either your diplomacy or force of words. Combat was indeed repetitive at times, but made the game what it was. It was the perfect mix of Action and RPG moments. Hense the phrase Action RPG.
Playing 2 again was a complete shock to me. I have never played a game that made me feel decisions had consequences down the road. Hell (SPOILER) The first quarian you find in the game that hit from the collectors at the human colony, shows up when you are doing the loyality mission for Tali and reacts based on what you did to him. If you gave him to Cerberus he will literally say you are the devil. And that was a good amount of time that passed from the first mission to Tali's loyalty mission. Every decision has a consequence, being good or bad.
Now I dont want to make this extremely long, but please if you have time, and you love RPG's, purchase this game. Just purchase it. Dont forget about the Space Hampster or fishees, feed them or you die.

There's a definite wall at times attached to strategy games. Sid Meier's Ace Patrol sidesteps these stigmas to a fault, Designed for iOS devices originally, Ace Patrol is a dogfighting game set in WWI. With a series of manuevers to intense air combat is engaged over a battlefield of hexagonal grids. Using simple mouse commands,  players execute everything from strafing to swooping dives, hard banking, the Immelman turn and other expert maneuvers and that is it. My Pros and Cons
PROS
A: Simple easy tutorial, very streamlined tactic, you can name pilots, promote, and simply follow the action on different skill levels.
B: Atfer a while it is more planning than executing as you start to recongnize patterns in the enemy.
C: You feel like an ACE at times because of the simple dynamics of Ace Patrol. Even my 5 year old got it.
D:  It does not try to do too much. Missions are straight forward and easy to pick up
E: The look is simple, colors to customize your planes, and good solid sound effects and graphics. even if they are old school.
CONS
A; Its positive is it's negative. Not much of a challenge beyond the missions and goals. There is no strategy features like building up your squadron size, no real story mode of the pilots you select. It is too simple for its own good
B: The enemy is too redundant and not fun enough. Since you stay fighter pilots, you don't get to have fun being a bomber, or torpedo plane, execute full mission goals, like an actual stragey WW1. This is just flying and shooting, which may turn off players.
C: The game quit on me a few times and then reloaded on its own, with the quick save, you never lose your place. However, annoying
D: Like many other Firaxis missed an opportunity to have a true ww1 strategy game. They could have doubled down and make a real neat WWI strategy turn based game like PTO, Instead chose one aspect and streamlined that. Their loss
OVERALL: Ace Patrol does its job, perhaps too well to simplify things. I finished the game in several hours in easy mode, BUT found it more fun on higher level skills. Keep that in mind. Again, go to the discussion, see VIDEO of gameplay before you buy. For the price or a few dollars. Worth adding for some simple fun
OVERALL: 3 out of 5 stars

A bit of role-playing, a good slice of exploration, and a great deal of trial-and-error turn-based skirmish goodness. What's not to love ?
Starting as a hopeful conquistadore with a (more or less) trusty band of followers by your side, the coasts, jungles and mountains of the new world open before the feet and hooves of your expedition. While the beginning of your journey is driven by colonial errands, exploring the land and uncovering the map quickly becomes the mainstay of the game, with a gentle prod of the main questline or one of several side quests to push you forward when simple exploration would become routine. Your traveling companions quickly acquire a personality of their own, and you find yourself favoring some and more or less subtly relegating others to menial duties - but, favored or not, all hands are useful and all skills matter when the difference between success and a starving, disease-ridden death lies in the survival expertise of your company.
Both exploration and combat are turn-based : exploration is day-by-day and each day allows your party to cover a predefined distance - modified by the roughness of terrain. During your travels, you can find resources, discover hidden locations of interest, and meet both natives and "fellow" conquistadores. At the end of the day, you set camp and assign people to forage, guard, scout and craft duties. You quickly learn to specialise your companions so that you have a robust team in each required area of expertise, but secondary proficiencies are always useful to substitute for a sudden illness or battle wound.
Speaking of battle, a good deal of their variety comes from the initial setup and terrain: sometimes you hae to hold the line at any cost (especially when ambushed during the night at your camp), but in other cases you will have to engage in a running match to prevent your opponents from escaping, or steadily advance on one side while delaying the onslaught on the other. While some combat role combinations can usually be relied upon, you find yourself having to fiddle with your lineup and standard battle plans quite often, and, because of the specific mix of the opposing forces, sometimes have to shoehorn some of your warriors in less than optimal positions and roles. Environmental conditions (nighttime, rain, fog) also come into play, favoring some weapons and combat styles and making others less effective - but a trusty medic is always reliable and handy, as long as he can dress battle wounds without interruptions.
Individual character development occurs on different axes - combat skills (ranged, melee, defense) which translate as new, more powerful equipment use, outdoors skills to help your party survive, and specific talents (think RPG feats) that provide unique advantages. Additionally, there is a social progression as well, with a reputation-like map between your character and all her expedition companions. This affects their efficiency in the field, but also leads to several interesting conversations and arguments, which add to the feeling that your band of conquistadores is more than a set of skills and have some personality meeat on their combat bones.
As you can probably guess, I like this game. On the downside, exploration becomes a bit stale at times, mostly because there are only so many surprise events the devs could spring on your party and because some quests require you to litterally clear the whole damn map, but if your camping routine is fast enough, you can cruise from one point of interest to the next without too much hassle. Graphics are OK if unremarkable, and the soundtrack is discreet if fairly repetitive.
Overall, a thumbs up if you like turn-based tactical / exploration games with a side of team management and development and a smattering of role-playing. The fact that it takes place in a low-magic, quasi-historical setting is a nice break fromthe usual high-fantasy or tactical sci-fi game.

A turn-based combat, exploratory cRPG, as advertised.
The real interesting points are the historical basis of the scenario ( a close-enough thematic placeholder for Hernando Cortes ) and the "choices" you get to make, or not make, during the conquest of New Spain.
There's enough historical bite to satisfy players who also read, but enough fantastical adventure to satiate readers who game.
The choices you make ( as the invisible expedition leader ) do actually affect the plot of the game, as well as party morale and party composition throughout the game, but one gripe is that your persona never appears in battle maps and you're only leading your followers.
Also, the combat can seem a bit tedious and overwhelming, but some practice can result in sound tactical plots and plans that made me smile when executed properly ( with, of course, help from the RNG in the sky ).
All in all, I greatly enjoyed my playthroughs, as explorer, trader, conqueror and ( mostly ) doomed Spainards. Ironman option is punishing, yet rewarding if you can keep the focus.
Recommended whole-heartedly.

: The concept of this game is relatively simple but unless you've played poker before it can get a little tough.
However there is a Tutorial that covers a lot of the bases for gamers new to poker.
Best of all. You aren't spending any money in the game itself.  There are a variety of modes to choose from and you can be sure there are good times to be had in this game.
:  There is a jam-pack plethora of musical numbers, various voices, all the right sounds to cover what would be a real game of poker going on.  It's marvelous to listen to the different mixes going on, though you also have an option to choose one specific sound for a match if you want to.   The music tracks are seriously nice though. They really keep the groove alive for a game of cards.
8 out of 10.
There are aesthetics to the game visually.  The focus on the cards, table and environmental backgrounds are pretty well done.  My only complaint here is that there are no physical models of people sitting around this card table. you clearly hear their voices, but the game provides zero actual people sitting around the table to play. That detracts a little from the overall experience of a real game of poker and I'm kind of surprised that the developer didn't add this on.
7 out of 10
I did play quite a few sessions, trying out some of the modes, especially the first person experience which was good in my overall thoughts.  You are going to do a lot of mouse clicking with this game and so fingers may get tired after a while. So do take yourself a break from the game once in a while. I really enjoyed playing a good few games and there are a lot of useful things with this game. For one thing you aren't spending real money in the game, so that's a plus.  For a second, the music is really good.  And it does help teach you to recognize certain things like when to bluff.   Or when to fold.  I enjoyed it and I'm pretty certain a lot of you card players who are into poker, or if you want to learn, can certainly play it.
: 7 out of 10.
This game is certainly engaging and fun for card players and families, just be sure to take a break though.

Worth buying at at least 50% off via my "Never buy games at full price" motto and "Percentage-to-hours" hypothesis (accounting hours played and enjoyment in regards to the absolute lowest percentage that I would consider buying it at if I suddenly lost the game and had to rebuy it).
Pros:
Fantastic game to play with friends that doesn't kill friendships ala Mario Party or Monopoly. The game runs off Workshop content, so the game doesn't get repetitive because the levels are pretty much endless. You can find multiplayer games really easily, as well as ranked games when the servers are available. The story provides a good challenge in a Trackmania style with times to beat to get certain medals. Also has "boots" you need to collect all of in a level (as well as Gold medals) to unlock the last level of SP mode, which adds a bit of replayability (that ends when you get them all, see Cons for more). There are DLC but it's only cosmetics and is not necessary to play with. It is a game that doesn't require much of your time, so it can be picked up and exited at almost any time outside of Ranked. Ranked is good because skill level matches up very well leading to competitive matches most of the time. Powerups initially looked overpowered but are very much balanced. Has some achievements that allow for achievement hunting and extending replayability. Controls can be remapped and the game works well with XBOX 360 controllers.
Cons:
Singleplayer after completing the "story" is basically non existent, and playing with bots is not as good as in other games like Chivalry or Dota 2.  SP mode can be completed in about an hour or two, so you need to be active with multiplayer. Game can be dropped out freely, so you'll often go games without 4 people due to angry and salty players saddened with the prosect of losing (though Ranked has penalties for dropping out). Game has a few bugs and clustered UI. Game sometimes randomly crashes after choosing a level.
Overall I rate this game 8/10. It's a multiplayer game (up to 4 players) that doesn't ruin friendships AND is replayable with a fairly good tutorial. Needs some matchmaking experience to know the nooks and crannies, but is generally welcoming while retaining depth, very similar to Chivalry in that aspect.

The world seems to have a rich history but the overarching story itself is a little bit lacking compared to the rest of the game.
Overall, one of my favorite games. A good choice if you would enjoy a semi-casual tactics game and definitely worth a try if you like JRPGs in general.

First and foremost this is behavior we should applaud from a publisher. Even a big one. And even if that publisher takes notoriously bad approaches with other games (DLC's, etc). This one, they got it right. They brought a "cult hit" PS3 exclusive to the PC and took the time to do it right, without DLC's, and at a reasonable price. I hope it had (and continues to have) great sales and the publisher takes note.
With that out of the way, on to the game. The port to PC is fantastic! I cannot undersell that at all. Obviously gamepad controls are flawless but the keyboard and mouse controls are fluid and what I used. Frame rate never dips below 60 and the game looks superb in modern PC resolutions. The game itself  is a slow paced tactical, turn-based, strategy game that looks beautiful and has a rich and deep storyline and characters. But it isn't without it's flaws and is probably going to be an "acquired taste" for many, if not most. I will touch on a few things below.
Technical hiccups I encountered personally;
-I had some crash on exit issues that seem to be related to Steam Overlay. Turning Overlay off stopped it. Though I often just dealt with it because I wanted Overlay for screenshots. And crashing on exit isn't the end of the world, I was exiting anyway!
-Minimal tearing on some cutscenes. Non-issue for me personally but I mention it for the sticklers out there.
-Steam now recommends a bunch of pervy anime games to me since I poured over 40hrs into this.
Gameplay issues some might have. "Fair warning" stuff basically;
-It IS slow. And failing a mission means going through the same slow steps again.
-The game will breed impatience in some. Every mission does have an "A" rank way to beat it swiftly. So there is this inherent "feeling" that you can be brazen and act swiftly to beat any level. BUT, these tactics are mostly reserved for the second playthrough with a much much more powerful squad at your fingertips. Patience and caution is the name of the game the first playthrough!
-Also on that note, the game will throw new obstacles, tactics, and effects at you each mission. Especially in the second half of the game. Not taking the time to read (also read between the lines of) warnings and plan ahead will result in what feels like a "cheap" death. But in reality the game lays everything out and you have the time to learn "on the fly" as long as you're taking your time. I learned my lesson the hard way more times than I care to admit before I slowed down my pace and started thinking like Welkin (protagonist) rather than me the modern impatient gamer.
Regardless of any neglible issue or "fair warning", with sales at multiple online gaming outlets and here already reaching as low as $4.99USD it's worth the throwaway just to support the developer's behavior on this approach. Even if the publisher doesn't need the money and is huge. This is a rare (maybe only) moment where I can recommend a purchase even if you have no intention of playing. That said, if you DO play it and DO take your time to "acquire the taste" you will be handsomely rewarded for your efforts. This game was a thoroughly satisfying play and experience and ranks atop my short list of all time favorites. Yes, ALL TIME FAVORITES. It is damn good. The game is fun, lengthy, deeply well written, well voice-acted, beautiful, and smooth. A pleasure. I had great fun in my 40+ hours of play and I still have extras, hard and expert modes, and more left to enjoy should I want to! One last random note; I've never watched an anime outside of Cowboy Bebop so I can say with emphasis that the art style goes beyond that crowd. It really is a lovely game visually.

Jokes aside
Getting deeper into the game, this is what i found on setting.
Vsync: on might cause fps drop alongside with game speed for some, while set it off can fix fps drop, it cause tearing instead.
User interface: change your UI to old one, there's no noticable impact on peformance
Character filter: change how character rendered. Off means it will be pixelated, while on means your char gonna blur. Given this is a PS2 port, such graphic is normal. No noticable impact on peformance.
Map texture: change the look on nearly all background. No noticable impact, so just pick one that suits you.
Shadow: just like all normal games, render shadow for most object. Might cause fps drop on some rig
Screen end blur: gonna makes edge of your screen blur, no noticable impact.
Depth of field: blur some object that either too far or too high from your char. Not so sure, didn't affect me, but might be for some.
SSAO: Now this what i call a failed setting. Gonna break your texture, didn't even know what this setting supposed to do, since this always cause problem every time it's on
Normal map: just like character filter, but it affect map instead. Make it blur if you set it on.
Important note:
Opt out of beta client fix most of fps drop bug. You can kept Vsync on to avoid tearing without cause fps drop.
Still didn't help with SSAO though
And all above is based on my personal experience. Different rig might get different results.

A fun, casual strategy game.
Gameplay is turn-based dog-fighting set in WW1. It's not very deep, but still satisfying. You have a variety of maneuvers available to your pilots, and as they level up you gain access to fancier abilities. Missions are never too difficult but if you're careless, your pilots will get shot down quickly, resulting in capture or injury.
The overarching campaign is relatively simplistic, with several chapters. Victory is determined by whether or not you won enough missions in a chapter. If you win enough chapters, you win the war.
Unlocking new planes and upgrading planes brings variety.
Overall, this game is more than just a time waster, but not really heavy strategy. I would love to see a more complex game built on these mechanics.

I have only played few hours, so my review is based on a first impression. I have only play one other game similar to this, and thats Eve Online. This is a very interesting concept. However, while some details are well thought out, there are  other things that look and feel either out of place, or unpolished.
The graphics is nice in the sky, not so much on the ground. But then again, its a flying game, not a driving one.
Sound is just bad. Its either anoying humming sound of an "engine" or silence, with occasional deafening roar of fly by patrol planes. it needs more ambient sounds and maybe flopping sounds of propellers, instead of an engine hum.
Camera has a mind of its own and sometimes it feels like im fighting it, to point where i want it to.
Shooting weapons is not designed for this game. 3rd person game with autopilot movements does not go we ll with first person shooting to me. Wouldve been much btter to have a tab targetting attacks, concidering how laggy it gets during the combat.
First I was loving the ship designs, with a steampunk theme and I thought thats how the rest of the ship are going to be. Thats until I saw some screenshots of more "advanced" vessels. Some are just litteral ships, that float in the air, whout a a hot-air baloon. And the most advanced ones are just flat out modern cruisers, again, without any hot-air baloons. Now why would you take a dump on your own game theme like that?
To me, the UI is the most frustrating aspect of this game. It has a very nice steampunk theme, but it handles like a bad website from 1990s. Every time you change graphics setting, you need to restart the game. Some graphics setting refuse to switch on or off, no matter what you do. The UI has some serious issues with scaling, mening if you scale it down enough, things start overlapping instead of scaling down. The "talent tree" menu... does it really need to be so long and wide? Does it really need to feel like a bad Excel spreadheet?.
Despite all the negative things, I am gonna vote yes and hope this game gets some improvements, because the concept is nice.

I was a huge fan of the last game Divinity: Original Sin and loved it, but had the small critique that I felt that the start of the game suffered from some pacing issues. Issues that might be a turn-off for more "casual gamers" in the first few hours of the game. I liked that it didn't hold your hand, but you spent alot of time walking around town talking to people, and didn't feel like there were many combat oprotunities untill later.
This game Divinity: Original Sin 2 seems to smooth all that out with a nice balance of tutorial for new players, combat, and talking to people right in the beginning. Definitely feels like it will hook players earlier in my opinion, which I think will be great for the casual audience (aka some of my friends). So far it seems to find that nice balance of challenge, engaging story, and learning curve.
These games can be played at your own pace thanks to the turn-based natture of combat, and it emulates what a session of table top Dungeons and Dragons feels like to me...closer than any other video game out there. It's not the same for sure, but grab a friend and play your saved game together over the course of a few months when you can get together on a couch, or online, and you'll feel the tablet top RPG-feels.
Way easier to get into than Neverwinter, Baulder's Gate, Tyranny, or Pillars in my opinion (which are all great games) and it has a range of difficulty settings that makes it playable for a wide-variety of gamers.
Haven't finished the game yet obviously, but I wanted to give a review for this awesome developer and their amazing game since I really do love it. Loved the first Original Sin, and 2 so far is an improvement in so many aspects.
Best wishes to Larian Studios.

In the Middle of 1600.
A new World discovered.
Ships from spain are taking over.
Men and women on the search for adventurers and gold.
YOU are one of them, leading them, beeing a conquistador.
Expeditions:Conquistador is an interesting turn based strategy game with many tactical elements.
I`am a big fan of BETRAYER, also set in this timelime, so my interesting was awaked.
Also the impressive Game Trailer made me wanting it.
In one of the monday sales i got this and was ready to play.
In the beginning you are planing your Expedition. You are choosing between more then 30 Characters, each one with special abilitys. Choose wisely a balanced team, because you are going to make more decissions, then you like.
Decissions that influence the path you will be going.
After choosing your team, you arrive in the new world and are ready for discovering.
Leaving the first City a big card is waiting for you.
While you explore the new world in turn basing mode you have to manage Ressources and Motivation of your Expedition. Your Team is very unexperienced in the beginning but will rise. And you decide what.
So, Glory is waiting for you ...... or death.
What i like in this game, is the atmosphere. The Game feels really detailled in that timelime. You will feel with your Expedition. Each character has it own background story what make each one special. If one dies, it will not leave you cold if you got deeper in this game like i did.
As i said before, the game leaves you also the choice what to do. Slay the indians or help them is one of it. Nearly each decission has consequences. Thats something that makes the game more playable.
Speaking of decissions, each time you have the choice of diplomacy to avoid battles, but you can not escape every time from it. When it finally comes to battle the game changes into a JAGGED ALLIANCE Style and you have to move each character for itself. For me the battles where sometimes really tough and challenging and sometimes they feel a little bit unbalanced but to be honest, what was easy in that times. Each battle can be won and are not impossible.
The Game has 2 Campagnes and each one is excited. It is really fun to explore the map to discover the secrets and read the events. The game has also a muiltiplayer.
I have this game in a monday sale, but it is definitly worth its full prize. The Devs did a very good job with this game and it has very much content to bound you for many hours. Much more then many "full prize" games.
What can i say more. The time of the Conquistadors was not the gloriest chapter of human history but it still polarizes.
If you want to dive into this timelime and like turnbased games, this is for you.
Go on Expedetion or die trying....
Thank you for reading.

...is a turned-based tactical RPG. Along with your company of soldiers, you embark on a voyage for the New World to conquer and tame its lands and native people for the glory of Spain.
You play as a company leader of noble birth, taking the place of Hernán Cortés as you board your ship to map America. The first chapter will have you land on Hispaniola to deal with problems facing Santo Domingo, then move on to Mexico where you meet the Aztec Empire. As the story unfolds, the choices you make will branch out into a few paths and different endings to the game.
After creating your leader character, you build a party by picking from a list of doctors, hunters, scholars, scouts and soldiers. You will also encounter additional optional characters during your game. Each class has its own skills, and each character has a unique back story and various personality traits that will determine their interactions with you and how your decisions affect their morale.
When moving across the map, you regularly need to set camp, manage food reserves, and give tasks for your party members. Fighting is done on a hex-grid map of your location, moving your units around to attack in ranged or melee combat, taking cover behind obstacles when needed. You'll sometimes come across traps or obstacles. You can craft your own traps to be used if the encounter allows you time to prepare for battle.
You gain party experience from completing quests and battles. This experience can then be spent on leveling up (or promoting) party members, picking additional skills and adding attribute points. You are limited to three Level-4 characters and one Level-5 character in your party.
This is a very unique setting that doesn't often get explored. A pre-colonization America with its people, tribal wars and beliefs or folklore. Each encounter, whether a scripted or a random camping event, includes flavor text to explore the attitude of awe, or suspicion, local tribesmen have when meeting you, as well as delving into the city life some of these empires had.
Attributes are quite a departure from traditional RPGs. Your leader has his specific set of attributes which will not change during the game. These determine how likely some conversation choices are to succeed. Your party members have completely different attributes reflecting their use at specific camping tasks (guarding, hunting, healing, etc.). It is all very different from the typical Strenght, Perception, etc. attributes such games usually take.
When travelling, you'll find random loot boxes of resources or crafting material. When camping, you'll assign tasks to your party member: guarding, hunting, crafting, or contextual tasks like fishing if you're camping by a river, or assembling maps from various landmarks you discovered. Camping will sometimes result in random events happenning during the night, such as party member story development, or sneak attacks by natives.
Inventory management is oversimplified. You don't manage armors and weapons, you simply have "equipment", which acts as a quantity of points you can distribute (and redistribute at will) to boost armor or weapons of party members. Survival is also basic: have "rations" to feed your party, have "medicinal herbs" for a doctor to heal injuries, have a lot of "valuables" to determine how rich you are.
The game feels rooted in an attempt at a realistic historical RPG with no magic or belief in things other than The Church, yet sometimes dives in the supernatural. Sure, a wave of disease afflicting those who stole a so-called "cursed treasure" can be shoved off as party members superstitions, but coming across a Dog-Headed God to whom you can sacrifice a party member really kicks you out of the realistic context.
While the combat maps are pretty, they are too static. Besides traps, there are no interactive map elements. I wish there were swampy floors, movable boulders, something. Also, there's no indicator to make it clear whether you have proper cover from ranged attacks.
I've had a nice enough experience for me to recommend this game. It's not the strongest tactical RPG and the story could've had a lot more depth, yet I'm now looking forward to
If you're itching for an uncomplicated tactical RPG you haven't tried, this might be it.

An xbox classic. In retrospect, Fable is not the great game I remember, but a solid game nevertheless. Fable is an action RPG surrounding what starts out appearing nothing but a simple boy who had lost his family and his village, but the plot thickens instensely throughout the game to become much more.
Fable was based around the idea of "for every choice, a consequence", but don't let that motto fool you. There isn't a whole lot of choice besides "what's your combat preference" and "good or evil", but the quests, combat, and loot selection are unique enough to still feel fun.
I've played enough of Fable to see through it (I have way more hours on xbox than here), but if you haven't picked it up yet and are considering it, $10 is more than fair for your time. I will say though, do purchase *this* version and *not* the anniversary edition; as much I would like to love the anniversary edition, the clunky GUI and un-updated animations make the game more of a crappy retelling than a welcomed overhaul. Fable TLC is still graphically fidelic to be appealing today as it was when it released.
Overall, if you like action RPGs, visit the world of Albion is it's oldest (and arguably, best) incarnation of the series.

First and foremost this is behavior we should applaud from a publisher. Even a big one. And even if that publisher takes notoriously bad approaches with other games (DLC's, etc). This one, they got it right. They brought a "cult hit" PS3 exclusive to the PC and took the time to do it right, without DLC's, and at a reasonable price. I hope it had (and continues to have) great sales and the publisher takes note.
With that out of the way, on to the game. The port to PC is fantastic! I cannot undersell that at all. Obviously gamepad controls are flawless but the keyboard and mouse controls are fluid and what I used. Frame rate never dips below 60 and the game looks superb in modern PC resolutions. The game itself  is a slow paced tactical, turn-based, strategy game that looks beautiful and has a rich and deep storyline and characters. But it isn't without it's flaws and is probably going to be an "acquired taste" for many, if not most. I will touch on a few things below.
Technical hiccups I encountered personally;
-I had some crash on exit issues that seem to be related to Steam Overlay. Turning Overlay off stopped it. Though I often just dealt with it because I wanted Overlay for screenshots. And crashing on exit isn't the end of the world, I was exiting anyway!
-Minimal tearing on some cutscenes. Non-issue for me personally but I mention it for the sticklers out there.
-Steam now recommends a bunch of pervy anime games to me since I poured over 40hrs into this.
Gameplay issues some might have. "Fair warning" stuff basically;
-It IS slow. And failing a mission means going through the same slow steps again.
-The game will breed impatience in some. Every mission does have an "A" rank way to beat it swiftly. So there is this inherent "feeling" that you can be brazen and act swiftly to beat any level. BUT, these tactics are mostly reserved for the second playthrough with a much much more powerful squad at your fingertips. Patience and caution is the name of the game the first playthrough!
-Also on that note, the game will throw new obstacles, tactics, and effects at you each mission. Especially in the second half of the game. Not taking the time to read (also read between the lines of) warnings and plan ahead will result in what feels like a "cheap" death. But in reality the game lays everything out and you have the time to learn "on the fly" as long as you're taking your time. I learned my lesson the hard way more times than I care to admit before I slowed down my pace and started thinking like Welkin (protagonist) rather than me the modern impatient gamer.
Regardless of any neglible issue or "fair warning", with sales at multiple online gaming outlets and here already reaching as low as $4.99USD it's worth the throwaway just to support the developer's behavior on this approach. Even if the publisher doesn't need the money and is huge. This is a rare (maybe only) moment where I can recommend a purchase even if you have no intention of playing. That said, if you DO play it and DO take your time to "acquire the taste" you will be handsomely rewarded for your efforts. This game was a thoroughly satisfying play and experience and ranks atop my short list of all time favorites. Yes, ALL TIME FAVORITES. It is damn good. The game is fun, lengthy, deeply well written, well voice-acted, beautiful, and smooth. A pleasure. I had great fun in my 40+ hours of play and I still have extras, hard and expert modes, and more left to enjoy should I want to! One last random note; I've never watched an anime outside of Cowboy Bebop so I can say with emphasis that the art style goes beyond that crowd. It really is a lovely game visually.
Easily recommended.

*NO SPOILERS*
I already had this game on my last steam account, but I got a new one and I liked this game so much, that I had to buy it again.
I've played it like 5 times (4 times I wanted to make a different decision at the end, but I just couldn't. That kind of shows how deep and emotional this game is).
The game could be described as a 3rd person Shooter, but that doesn't hit it very well, because the best things on ME2 aren't shooting and RPG. Sure, the gunplay is good (every weapon feels different) and on the RPG side it's also a game slightly above the average, because unlike most new RPGs new skills for you and your charackter can really change the game.
But the thing, that makes ME2 such a great game are it's characters, the "interactive" storytelling and it's presentation.
Let me get through all of this points:
-The characters
The Mass Effect series has in my opinion the best characters in gaming history. You really want to know everything about every single crew member. You can always go to them and have a conversation. They are sometimes deep, badass, sad, arrogant and so on. I can't imagine one single emotion, which wasn't shown in crew members actions and I always felt like "I can understand that", "I'm so sorry for you", "Let's take revenge!" etc.
Every single person you've hired has its own mission with a great story behind it. You can always do this mission your way or the way the crew member wants to do it. You can change your crew members opinions or even act against them if you think, that it would be the best for your crew member.Those missions change the loyalty of your crew members and that's extremely important for the last mission. I will come back to that later.
-Storytelling and presentation
The special thing about the Mass Effect series was always, that you can choose which way you're going to face the situation. In every single conversation you can choose your answers and try to change some characters opinion. Every time you're making a decision you are getting renegade or paragon points and if you have enough of them you are getting new options to solve conversations. But you can't just only have goddamn well written conversations, no you can make some actions in your conversation sometimes (my favorite one was to punch that ♥♥♥♥♥y journalist from ME1 in the face).
To the presentation: I've never ever seen a game with such a great presentation. Like I said the conversations are goddamn well written but it gets far more better with all those beautiful backgrounds and perfect music.
Especially in the last mission the music is unbelievable perfect.
To the last mission: I won't spoiler, but I can tell you, that it's the best mission ever made in a videogame. I can just say this without spoliers, but I can SAY that you'll always remember the so called "Suicide Mission".
I probably forgot a lot of things, because ME2 s such a huge game, but I just gave you the main reasons, why Mass Effect 2 is (in my opinion) the best videogame ever made.
I'm from Germany, so I apologize for every grammatical error I've made in this review and I hope it didn't disturb you that much.
Thanks for reading and thanks BioWare

This game is fun and engaging.  The combat system from the first one has only been enhanced and the story continues to deliver top quality content that encourages you to replay the game over an over.  For anyone who loves story driven RPG's this game takes the cake.

As for this game, I personally think it has some of the better game design choices that most indie companies can't always spend time thinking of. I personally think some triple A companies could get a lesson out of this.
The iteration playability is outstanding. You can get mauled by the RNG in the deck though you can put the RNG in your favour by unlocking and stacking the deck with cards with better chances and results. What makes this not painful at all is the short iteration time. Even when you do die, you can get right back into playing another game. If you are going to have a game that kills you pretty often you need to shorten iteration time which this does.
Rewarding in this game is pretty spot on. Even when you die 10 cards into a match you still feel like you got something out of it. As you progress you get tokens from cards, which unlock more cards. So even when you die, you get to unlock tokens and get more cards to make your character feel stronger without actually making them any stronger.
The story is kind of weak, but the narrative from the story is very strong. You get a feeling of the dealer teaching you life lessons as well as the idea that he is just a proxy for the devs telling us their darkest thoughts on the game.
The combat system is very similar to that we find in The Batman Games. I find it interesting a smaller company was able to replicate this system with a smaller budget, however it is very much the same.
The learning curve in this game is very good. It does not hold your hand too much in regards of most games, but it gives you enough to start, then you start to learn on your own. As you get your first cards you learn mostly how the game works, but they are a gateway into unlocking better cards that get more complicated and give you more choices on how to proceed in your adventure. So the beginning cards are gateways to better cards.
The only real bad thing about this game I can find is the character looks dumb to me, and the game play time is not very long if you are good at Batman style games. However, the good things far outnumber the bad things. The developers did amazing to get rid of a lot of annoying things we see in games that just infuriate us, while still putting in good game/level design. This is far more polished and far more intelligent on a gamewide scale than most triple A games I play. I would highly reccomend this game over Darkest Dungeon.

TL;DWTR - A tactics RPG with ridiculous stat capping, humorous/goofy dialogue, and enough grind to last hundreds of hours. Recommended.
------------------------
As always, my recommendation comes with a disclaimer that your experiences will vary. Please read through at least the next paragraph.
Let's tackle everyone's main issue with this port... performance. Good God, launch day was a disaster for a lot of players, even those with high-spec PCs. But, interestingly enough, I have a mid-tier rig running 2.5-year-old hardware (i5-4460 3.2GHz + R7 260X 2GB), and Disgaea PC works fine. I'm honestly not sure where everyone's frame drops are coming from. I tested using new/old map textures, SSAO (which I didn't like personally, but it still didn't impact my performance too much), and all the other minor graphical tweaks...no sudden drop in FPS for me. So I'm probably really lucky that it runs perfectly fine... and as such I'm going to ignore factoring in performance for my review. Just be warned that if the game doesn't run smoothly for you, the rest of this review is pointless and you should return this game until NISA (Nippon Ichi Software, America) sorts things out.
Disgaea PC is a port of Afternoon of Darkness on the PSP, which is an enhanced remake of the original PS2 title, Hour of Darkness. This is the third remake of Hour of Darkness, after Afternoon of Darkness and Disgaea DS for Nintendo DS systems.
Disgaea (the series) is a tactical RPG (grid-based, turn-based, action points, the usual deal) with its key selling point being the ability to grind out your stats and level to absurd highs. The caps for stats and level are insanely high (~20 million for each stat in Disgaea PC and 9999 for level). There's a lot of bonus maps, content, and endings to access that the game acknowledges how many New Game Pluses you've done. I love grindy games, and so I figured Disgaea was right up my alley. Sure enough, I've played and enjoyed the hell out of Hour of Darkness and Cursed Memories. Haven't played 3, 4, D2, or 5 yet since I don't own a PS3/4.
Another highlight of the Disgaea franchise is the Item World, a completely randomized dungeon crawl generated from items you collect in the game. By exploring the Item World, you can grab more items, grind out EXP, and improve that item's stats. Each item contains an expansive dungeon of 30, 60, or 100 floors, depending on the item's rarity.
I'd have to argue a minor problem with the mechanics is just how many different systems they've jammed into this game. There's the tactical combat, which is simple enough to understand... then they introduce Geo Panels and Effects, Lifting and Throwing allies, enemies, and Geo Effects...the Dark Assembly, Pupils, Skill/Stat Inheritance between Master and Pupil, the Item World, Reincarnation (Transmigration in this version), and some mechanics the game doesn't even cover such as Elemental Affinities (Fire, Wind, Ice), Status Effects, and Weapon Masteries. For a newcomer this may seem like a daunting amount of things to learn about... and believe me, it is. However, all of these things don't need to be used...in fact the game even tells you, you can beat the game with "minimal game knowledge". The systems are there to provide hardcore players the means to be more efficient in grinding out those stats.
I won't go into nor analyze the story (because I suck at analysis and not spoiling), but I will say it's decent and humorous enough to suffice as an RPG plot. I also will not criticize the graphics because I don't really care for them, but the port made the map and character art look better than the PS2 graphics. There is also an option to change the graphics back to the old PS2 game, for that old nostalgic feel (I guess). EDIT: I completely forgot about the Keyboard+Mouse (the mouse kinda messed the cursor movement up for me, so I turned it off...but you could technically play the game using just the mouse if you wanted to... also mouse click detection is a bit bugged) and Gamepad support (which is a little clunky to detect). That's there as well. I suppose I should also add that the port added custom resolution support. (you can resize the screen to your desire)
Overall, I'd give this game a solid 8/10. Good for RPG fans, grind-fest lovers, and people who just want a lot of content for their buck.
Score Breakdown:
Story/Plot/Characters: 9/10
(each character seems unique in their own way, dialogue gave me a couple laughs, story was dramatic at times - but not overly so when it was)
Music: 8/10
(pretty good soundtrack, still waiting for my digital dood/pre-order soundtrack bonus)
Graphics/Art: 5/10
(has a nice theme to it, but even with the new textures the game looks dated, plus the new character filter thing just blurs the pixels so your characters look like a smudge on the screen... wtf?)
Mechanics: 8/10
(lots of cheesing you can do with unit movement, lifting, and AoE attacks, probably intentionally made to be cheesed... overall great but slightly clunky mechanics)
Value: 10/10
(hours and hours and hours and hours of content and grind)
Performance: 8/10
(works fine on my rig - stays notably above 60fps most of the time - others not so much... EDIT: I am now getting crashes more often, and I'm not sure why. Maybe the math and numbers are getting too high? Either way, dropping 2 points off performance. It shouldn't be crashing because of memory leaks or integer over/underflow.)
Oh yeah, I should add: Buy it for the Prinnies, dood!

This is due to how the developers created the cash shop to include items which you can either sell for the in-game currency or use them to make more money for example labor potions, premium beds etc. Players most often stop playing not because they get bored, but they come into close contact with a p2w player which ruins the experience for them therefore causing them to stop playing.
However, personally i believe Archeage is not unplayeable completely. Starting off with the most obvious fact is that in order to gain overpowered items in the game it does not simply take a few hundred dolars or euros. To get the very best stuff it might take thousands. True a couple hundred, let's say euros, will get you somewhere, to an average player level, not too bad, but also not awfuly good. This already can be a good thing for the game because honestly how many people do we see around not having a problem with spending thousands on a korean MMO? True there are a few, but not a lot. I personally haven't spent any money on this game currently as i never felt the need to do so in order to enjoy the game more. It would make it slightly easier to progress, but i do not need it as i have other ways to play and progress that do not include fat wallet.
But how do i play without having to pay, you may ask. Well there are multiple solutions. First of all the reason why the game is p2w is also the reason why it's not unplayable and that is APEX. For those not knowing what that is, well it basically is a in game item that can be bought off the cash shop which gives the player 1250 credits which is the premium currency. It is pay to win as players can choose to sell it and gain quite nice amounts of gold from it allowing them to buy either gear or materials for gear depending on preference. But it makes the game playable as it allows players to get the patron status that allows players to build property, access the auction house and other things. Two APEX will give enough credits to purchase patron. The way to get APEX without paying with real money is to buy it in game off the auction house, but the problem comes in now whenp f2p players cannot afford it. And the only way to afford it is to work in game, grind to get it. Once a player unclocks patron the game becomes significantly easier for them, and it becomes much easier to make money too allowing you to get more APEX faster.
To make that gold fast I would recommend joining a friendly guild perhaps focused on farming or some other job but it will make money. This in the end is a mmo game so playing alone has no real point in my opinion.
Those APEXes can also allow normal players to access premium items from the cash shop if only they save up for them enough gold. A majority of people would get upset about that it will take ages to get APEX or all those cool items and to that my response would be that all you have left to do is grind like all other mmo games require, best if you have a team to do it with, only then i believe you can progress at a rate that won't get you bored fast and allow you to compete with some players who invested money into the game.
Of course when i say grind i don't mean just get on the game for an hour or two to kill some mobs, i mean this game truly requires dedication to be played and enjoyed. From my own experience in the game i have learnt alot of things about the way it works and through the people i met and played with i also learnt that this game can be playable without any money to be put into it. There are some dedicated players who get all the premium powerful gear and did not put a cent into the game.
Of course the game is as it is and the developers have ruined it's massive potential it had during alpha phase. This is all just in the terms of the pay2win part of the game. In conclusion I believe Archeage is still a playable game with the developers constantly updating it with new updates some of which include significant changes improving the experience for all the players. Content-wise there isn't much to say other than there is always something to do and every adventure is always a little different from the other. As an mmo sandbox I would rate this game a solid 10/10. But for the existence of the cash shop and pay2win it most definetely falls to a 6.5/10.

When I first started playing this game, I wasn't sure how well aerial combat would translate to a Turn-Based Strategy game. But, sure enough, this game is a worthy part of Sid Meier's brilliant line. I certainly enjoyed it and, while I didn't play any multiplayer, I imagine that it was enjoyable on all fronts, so here are some Pros and Cons.
PROS
- Does require thought and memory so you can't just wing it, especially on higher difficulties (no pun intended).
- Sid Meier's classic customization is present, allowing you to rename the pilots (I personally named them after characters from Avatar: Legend of Korra, RWBY, and Code Lyoko, because why not?). Also, pilots can gain upgrades and abilities as they become more experience, allowing specialization.
- Graphics and sound are great for the game.
- The mechanics of it all are fun to work out but not dreadfully challenging.
- It is very satisfying when you one-hit kill an enemy ace on higher levels. Satisfaction for a successful run increases with difficulty level.
- It has multiplayer. I'm counting that as a pro.
CONS
- Like most  games, the AI could use improvement, but this is just a minor complaint. For what it's supposed to do, the AI does well enough.
- I'll admit that, save for Germany and maybe the UK, I didn't really notice the national bonuses. But I guess 2 out of 4 isn't that bad.
Other than that, I have no complaints. If you can, you should certainly give this game a try.

This game has a great premise, haven't seen other games in this timeperiod and i love the way you can make your own, sometimes truly humorously written decisions in this RPG.
The downsides for me are that, when i compare it to XCOM enemy unknown the turn based combat isn't quite as good, the way hit chances work for ranged attacks isn't explained point by point so although you can use your common sense to figure it out (like moving closer) it's just mildly more frustrating then XCOM. Also you dont really know what counts as half cover, full cover etc. Again common sense does usually make it possible to figure out but not always, sometimes i think a rock is big enough to provide full cover but no. Make no mistake though i found all the fights in Hispaniola to be quite fun (haven't been to Mexico yet). Things like traps and such can also spice things up.
The good thing about this game though is that unlike in XCOM where i spent like 80% of my time in fights it was only 30-40% of my time in expeditions. The rest of the time im moving around on the map (which i find pretty) gathering food, exploring, making medicine etc. and making decisions when i for instance find some pirates whom can be dealt with in a variety of ways. I've seen some comments of people who find this a chore but most things in camp can be auto resolved like handing out food, setting people to do guard or hunting duty, processing herbs into medicine so it really isn't like you have to spend a lot of time doing that if you don't want to. You can also grab extra food, materials and herbs on the map but if you just grab some stuff if it's close to the road when you're travelling you should be fine.
You can also trade between settlements, it's not too complex with only 4 things you can trade (valuables, rations, medicine and equipment) but it works decently and the system makes sense so you can also make money that way. The main problems i have with this is that you really want to have a good guarding group (75% at the least) or you will lose A LOT of stuff to thieves sometimes. I seriously lost 1300 valuables to thieves a few times.
Like i said earlier the story and your companions and the way their personalities clash is quite interesting and unique but it's sad that i don't really see a lot of character progression so far. I've heard that there originally wasn't  a lot of money for this project so you can see the potential for this but it sadly wasnt completelyt implemented which stops it from becoming an awesome game. You may want to be careful not to take too many contrasting personalities with you because they can apparently desert you if their morale gets too low but i generally take good care of my team which isn't too hard you win fights often and don't act like a total♥♥♥♥♥♥(sometimes it's funny to do just that but it usually comes to bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥later.)
All things considered i find this to be a very decent game, definitely worth the 5 euro's it cost me during summer sale but looking back i would also  buy it for 10-15 euro's and quite possibly the 20 euro's it is usually. If you are a fan of turn based combat or like reading RPG's but hate all of the stuff surrounding it i would suggest buying it at a discount but this title is definitely one worth your consideration to try and see if it strikes your fancy when it's on discount.

For example, you have all melee soliders but the enemy is all range, and you are at the other end of a spiral pathway.  Lame.  And you are given a range of characters with different capabillites to pick for each battle, but no idea of what you are going up against!  The game might as well choose randomly for you.  So you need to loose a lot to figure out how to play, which isn't my idea of fun.  Sure, you can heal your team, but that means camping incessantly while looking for enough loot to do it, and dealing with food, all to get back to another battle that was poorly rolled out to the player.
- For such a numbers heavy game, it does a bad job of giving you results.  You are forced to "camp" every 60-90 real world seconds, but the results are shown only in text that fades after a couple of seconds.  So I ended up not really caring about the events of the night, and simply being annoyed at the whole process.
- The UI is quite cumbersome for how resouce intensive it is.  I often just clicked around on things to figure out how to get them to work.  While not optimal, it would have been acceptable if I was having fun elsewhere in the game to offset the drag.

Story feels kind of like a visual novel sans choices with its length and method of character development (which is pretty good if you enjoy that Japanese style of story telling). The game plays in a strange pseudo-turn based strategy RPG with shooter elements. It plays much better than it sounds.
Every turn you are allocated a specific amount of actions, each troop takes 1, tanks take 2, and you can call in buffs via "orders" which take these action points. You move each character individually, each turn consisting of a certain amount of movement possible, and a single combat action (healing, shooting, repairs, etc). When you choose to attack, the camera goes over-the-shoulder and you manually aim where you want to shoot, allowing targeting of weakpoints which can come at the risk of doing no damage at all.
The RPG elements come in the division of classes of your soldiers, the leveling and equipment system that each class takes, and with the individual strengths and weaknesses of each soldier. Every soldier has their own set of pros and cons depending on environment, proximity of enemies and allies, random chance, and so on. The quirks aren't exactly necessary to pay attention to, but they do give flavor to the characters, and can prove an insane boon at the right times. Additionally, every soldier has other soldiers that they prefer to fight with, and properly setting up soldiers with other soldiers they prefer leads to multiple soldiers attacking in a single turn, leading to a deeper strategic element to soldier choice, which sadly isn't too necessary at the basic difficulty.

Those looking for old console nostalgia may enjoy this game, but I don't recommend it to anyone who isn't already a fan of the series.  I can see where it may have been good in its time, but this game has not aged well.
The story is some of the worst anime dreck that I've ever seen.  The characters are irritating and bipolar, flipping back and forth between stoic posturing and sobbing toddlers every cut scene, and good grief there are a lot of cut scenes.  There are 4 to 8 slow, plodding cut scenes between every mission, maybe 5-6 hours worth for a 15-20 hour game.  And only a minority of them have anything to do with the plot.  Most are just weak attempts at character development that drive home how bad the writing is.
The gameplay is decent.  It would have been revolutionary in its day, but it's a little clunky by modern standards.  There are a lot of unnecessary "Are you sure?" prompts that could have been cut out to streamline the pace.  The missions seem challenging until you figure out how unbalanced one of the classes is.  From that point forward, if you use that class it feels like cheating.  All the challenge is gone and victories feel hollow.  Or you can focus on the other classes, and still have challenging, fun missions, albeit with much slower progress.
I enjoyed the missions enough to complete the game, but I'll never want to re-play it.  Even if the price drops to $2-5, you're still better off investing your time and money elsewhere.  Unless you're in it for the nostalgia, there are other much better games on Steam.

Cons:
Costs of building, in terms of Iron Reinforcement(material). It takes 30 seconds per one to make, and you need hundreds for tier2 buildings.
A lot of bugs (obvious with Early Access), such as your Thralls (tamed ones) dissappear if the server restarts. It kind of defeats the purpose AND availability to get into caves and "the city"
Early raiding seems TOO easy, doors and walls gets destroyed in seconds. The raid is over within a few minutes, and the loot is LOCKED, so you HAVE to actually destroy EVERYTHING that they own. The purpose of raiding is to get loot, not to make people quit (in early stages).
Desync and inconsistency in monster damage. Sometimes a rhino can 3 hit you, sometimes you can kite it around and kill it without losing any HP.

Many hours played, a few dollars spent.
The initial learning curve and grind to get a base running seems like an entirely uphill battle.  Once you have a base running, the real uphill battle begins, with limited (and already settled) resources to share around and a dwindling population of deserted bases.  It is hard to enjoy when to do a simple resource transfer from one base to another can not be accomplished remotely, and while you are in the air, you have no control over what is being produced in other bases.
Market griefers buy up masses of fairly priced goods to sell back to the market at unfair markups, but since the markets are so sparce the goods likely get snatched up at inflated prices by someone who, too frustrated to wait for a better offer, will buy game money with IRL money (which is deceptively cheap, leading to a real nickle-dime you FTP model) to fill their hold and go power their mighty lumber mills for half their running capacity.
So far as flight enjoyment or simulation, with a 15 minute flight time to the CLOSEST ports and clunky hands-on control (which means you spend most time on auto-pilot), the game becomes a very hands-off experience for the most part, and becomes mind-numbing and repetative.  The dragons represent almost no threat and can be felled with a single early-game round auto-fired by your vessel while you're off cleaning the kitchen or orgranizing your sock drawer.
I do not recommend this game for anyone looking for a trading sim (I highly recommend Elite: Dangerous for that craving), or a base building sim (from what I've seen Factorio looks much more rewarding), or a steam-punk RPG (the only role you play is that of a confused, bored airship captain).
Unfortunately most of Alexey Pehov's works are not translated to English, but the series that has been, "The Chronicles of Sialia" (which is a fantastic series by the way) bares no resemblance to the game world in any shape or form.
All in all, colour me disappointed.  An interesting concept executed poorly.

What a great game, a masterpiece. If you enjoy RPGs, dont hesitate - buy it right now (but be ready that it is super addicting and takes a lot of time to beat)
Why is it so great?
+ Multiple (often unexpected) ways to complete the quests, both main and side ones. For example, first chapter takes place at Fort Joy, your objective is to escape it. Aside from obvious head on approach, there are like 5 more different ways to do it. Isnt it amazing? The same goes for every goddamn quest in the game. You can steal, fight, talk, sneak outta almost anything, discover something secret (no spoilers, but chapter 4 was mind-blowing for me lmao), talk to ghosts or animals and many more
+ Quests intertwine with each other, creating situations where completing one quest creates new opportunites in other questlines
+ Amazing and addictive combat, much more enjoyable than the first iteration (DOS1). With addition of magic/phys armor every encounter is now splits into two stages, where you first whittle down enemies' armor, then apply debuffs/stuns or whatever. Also new skilltrees!
+ A more mature plot, not as goofy as the first one (maybe its a con for someone, dunno)
+ Great characters, all of them. I recommend playing origin characters on your first playthrough, cause they have great background and stories
+ World is super reactive: many decisions that you make throughout the game will find a place in the game's world. Race matters, tags matter, your origin story, your companions and more
+ Astonishing music. Borislav Slavov had some big shoes to fill, but he had managed so greatly! What a great score to listen too both in game and out
+ Pen and paper freedom and it is not just marketing slogan, the game gives you so much freedom that sometimes it feels like even developers dont know of every possibility available to you
+ It is lengthy and feels completed
+ Great variety of multiplayer and co-op options
Some cons:
- Some journal entries and quests are buggy, but mostly towards the end (Chapter 6-7). There is no way Larian wont fix it, so not much of a con honestly
- For some the game will be difficult. I enjoy difficult games, some people dont
So, all in all, its a 10/10 for me. Try it!

This genre-bending title has impressed me.  While not a perfect game, its ingenuity and mashing of game types carries this game.  The mix of D&D tabletop and the old "Choose Your Own Adventure" books is the base of the game; however, there are a there are a few other game types fused into this title including deck building and fighting.   What is so impressive about this mix is that it feels organic.  It doesn't seem like stitched together, independent ideas fused togther.  Instead, Hand of Fate delivers a very unique experience which is unlike most other games on the market.  Due to the Hand of Fate deck system, each playthrough is different than one another.
While the game difficulty was very easy initially, I noticed that it does ramp up a bit towards the middle section of the game.   Combat, while not perfect, is very familiar as it feel much like the Batman/Shadow of Mordor combat system. While it is not as polished as the before mentioned games, but it is manageable and feels good enough.  One critque would be that it would have been nice to see more style going into the fighting system.  The moves are a little repetitive at times, and with the attention of detail Hand of Fate has, it would have been nice to see more go into making the action portion of the game pop.
Visually, the game sits in the middle of the road.  Its nothing too over the top, nor it is not something that will hurt your eyes.   Graphically, Hand of Fate does its part in making you feel like you are sitting infront of a mysterious person and playing a dark, mystical card game.   The transitions in between the game world and the table are pretty cool too!  As your character puts one every piece of equipment you have equipped before each battle.  Your character changes as it picks up the equipment also, so that is a nice touch to show your progression.
This is a very solid game.  I really hope this type of game takes hold.  I could see this type of game doing well with an already established property.  (Spawn, Marvel, D&D, Warhammer, etc.) I'd definitely recommend the game and I hope to see more games like this in the future.

In addition I have been intentionally drawing things out to try and maximize my enjoyment of my purchase. It is only fair that I note that I found this game to lean a lot more to the "Casual" side of the RPG/Tactical spectrum, if Wasteland 2 was hardcore, Expedition Conquistador is Casual.
As someone who lives or dies by the challenge a game can provide a 20+ year veteran of RPG's like myself, Expedition Conquistador definitely meets my expectations. It isn't insanely difficult like Jagged Alliance Online Reloaded, but the combat is definitely challenging, without being super fancy/complex/tactical. The combat does have a partial/full cover system, but it is hardly the main focus of combat and you will always end up fighting CQB, hand to hand by the time all is said and done. It is still fun and the game has a slough of different randomized combat scenarios that pop up at various times and challenge you to meet a certain criteria in order to complete the combat scenario. In addition, the ability to place obstacles and a wide variety of traps you make outside of combat, before the start of some combat scenarios, is a pretty original and unique feature in Expedition Conquistador, I cannot remember ever seeing anything quite like it in any other tactical RPG before.
The storyline is pretty basic and comes out in bits and pieces, but you are the one who choses how your own story is going to unfold. It is up to you if you want to be a completely genocidal maniac and merc every tribe or roving band of warriors you come across, or if you want to curry favor with the Aztecs by merc'ing the Mayan's (yeah, you heard that correctly, the Aztecs & Mayans on the same world map, hows that for historical accuracy !!! Middle Fingers Up!!!) Other than that, the game stays pretty on schedule from a historically realistic standpoint, there is  definitely no magic in this game, the closest thing would be some Healing Water you come across late game, but you only get 3 of them and then they are gone for good.
I say buy it and thank me for my review later, by clicking that little "this was helpfull" box. It is nice to see a new developer starting out so strong, in a world run amok with garbage, 60$ AAA titles. I am definitely going to buy the recently released "Expedition Vikings" in the next couple of days, according to RPG Watch, it is even better.

After reading a lot of comments about the game being average or less than average, I waited for it to become boring at some point during the gameplay, assuming it was unavoidable. I finished it and now I know that I disagree with all those opinions.
This game is exactly what it claims to be - a creepy detective story. There isn't too much action, most of the time it's looking for clues and while I heard some people saying that it gets repetative, I think they just do not grasp the idea of detective games so they can't enjoy it. It's supposed to be repetative in a way. You just walk around, looking for stuff and then make sense out of it, which helps you to search for more stuff. A bit simplified, I know, but this is more or less how it works. It's no different with this game - it's very climatic, creepy, slow but engaging if you like this sort of stuff.
I was lucky not to experience any glitches, although I hear they are not non-existent and a few claimed that some of them can be game-breaking. I don't know, I haven't met with any so I can't say.
One thing that comes to my mind that some people my not like is that this game is very linear, although personally I don't consider it a problem. There are linear and non-linear games, both types can be equally good depending where they aim.
I saw a lot of 5/10, 4/10 etc. but I think giving such low marks to the game is doing its injustice. I'm sure it deserves 7/10 and if someone is really into detective games then they may even give it 8/10.

I played this game for a good amount of time as Ironman in Very Hard difficulty,and it was rly enjoyable,challenging and punishing at the same time.
It's pretty hard to find a tactical game well balanced in this level of difficulty: if you do everything perfect (and it's not impossible) you get the best results,and it's not too much frustrating if you dont.
Pros:
-Story is fascinating and well written,they paid attention to every detail of quests,that are not the classic "bring/kill x take y",but much more deep.The historical contest is not very common if not for pirate games,and there are no pirates here.
-Gameplay is a bit intricate at start,expecially the map,but you get used to it fast.
-Tactical battle is pretty simple,but yet challenging and hard to master,probably this is the best part of the entire game
Cons:
-Songs start to be boring after a while
-Moving in the map is annoying at start and the campsite autosystem is not well optimised,you have to check every meal for every person for every night to be sure that noone is eating too much or too little
-If one of your crewman is defeated in battle he will get an "injury",but the lethality of it is totally random (it's not important if he lost by 1hp or 100hp),at least at sight
Plus there is a personal event that made me ragequit for some time,and in my opinion is not a bug or error,it's just a technical mistake easy to fix:
After 20 hours and about 15 battles playing Very Hard difficulty in Ironman mode (only autosaves) i did a single mistake and one of my crewman was defeated by a small amount. Thanks to the random lethality my man got a deadly injury,and normally it means long time to recover and a lot of medicines to spend,but that's ok,game is hard and punishing,i'm totally fine with it. Unfortunately during the main quest you will fight battle that are semi-scripted; when the battle is over you dont have the "campsite event" that normally occours every night, and i have not been able to heal my man that died the next morning. I just didnt have the possibility to heal him,that 99% of the time you have,it's just unfair. I dont think that was intended, in my opinion devs just didnt think to add the campfire (that you have to set every single damned night) after an event. I came back to play after a while,but this ruined my run,experience and achievement.
After all this is a pretty good title and I liked playing it,one of the few tactical games well balanced in higher difficulties
