Sid Meier's Ace Patrol is the first of two Ace Patrol games (the second being Pacific Skies), and is, to me at least, the better of the two games. To sum it up, Ace Patrol is a light strategy game where players control a 4 man squadron on the Western Front during the First World War. It's not a bad game, but it has it's quirks. Here's the details:
Graphics - The first thing players see, and what gives the biggest impression because of it. Graphically speaking, the game is either sort of cool or really ugly depending on your preference. A lot of people say the graphics look like a Android ported game, and, from what I understand, it's because it is an Android port. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, as the game is more about tatics and strategy than graphics. I think the cartoon esque graphics are fine, and they seem to fit the game, even if they are somewhat glitchy at times.
Rating: 3/5
Gameplay - Gameplay is fairly good. I find myself having that one more turn addiction I get from other Sid games, although not to the same affect as I would from games like Civilization. Gameplay consists of cotrolling a squadron of up to four pilots in tatical air battles over the Western Front. The goal of each mission varies, with everything from balloon busting to escort duties being available.
Squadron members can "learn" new maneuvers, which makes them more effective in combat. The same happens with enemy squadrons, which means the game gets progressively more challenging over time. Unfortunately, this means if you haven't been able to upgrade a squadron member, he\she becomes rather useless as they basically become cannon fodder. Overall though the replayability is fairly high, even if some missions are bit repetitive.
Rating: 4/5
Sound/Music - As can be expected with a game like this, music is basically non-exsistent. There's some at the beginning and end of each mission, and some for the menu and that's it. What's there isn't bad, and music isn't really needed. Sound on the other hand is really good. There's sounds for everything. From machine gun fire to explosions, it all sounds pretty good. There are a few bugs where the sound gets garbled, but this can be overlooked as it doesn't happen often.
Rating: 4/5
Overall, the game is good as long as your willing to overlook a few glitches and to some extent, depending on your taste, ugly graphics. Gameplay is solid, and the game serves it purpose of being a light strategy game. If your looking for a more casual gameplay experience, are just looking for a decent WWI game, or just want to try one of Sid Meier's gaming experiments, I recommend it. If, however, your turned off by cartoony graphics or shallow gameplay, then I would skip it.
Overall rating: 6/10

This game is fun for the time it last and for the price you pay.  Its not a complex game and I think Sid Meiers should watch more on what he puts his name on because the historic accuracy and the simplicity of the game is clearly not of a CIVILIZATION level.  I expected something more .. hmmm... ''constistant''.
The mechanic is simple.  You select a certain number of your pilots to do a mission in a choice of three missions.  The pilots gets kills and when they reach a certain level you get upgrades on them.  You also get a few upgrades on planes if you perform better.  Basically, its a turn-based positioning strategy game.  You shoot when you are in a good position and you are a pigeon when you are chased.
The game has no luck factor so its pure strategy.  Still, its way too simple to be very interesting for a long time.  I've gone through the game at the level 4 difficulty (out of 5) on my second run and sticked to it after.  There are not enough plane choices (5 per factions) and you only have 4 pilots under your command.  They can be wounded, captured or grounded by plane repairs ; reducing your missions opportunities to ZERO.  The worst of all is that you have have FEMALE pilots.  Not that I don't like women or think of them as inferiors but this REALLY cut you off from the historic immersion.  Thumbs down for this ''politically correct'' choice.
The planes have a few differences but this could have been more significant.  You can customize their skins with ''ace paintings'' but they are all dull and very generic.  There are almost nothing to unlock and replayability is limited to 4 ''goes through'' (each of the four factions).  After that, its soporific.
One of the best aspect of the game is totally lame because of the camera auto-zoom that you can't remove.  You can replay your battles in pseudo ''real-time'' to watch how the fight happened but the auto-zoom will focus on shooting then get back to field view, then refocus on shooting then come back to field view, etc... and you lose all the fun of seeing the whole battle as it switch every 4 seconds from a point of view to another one.
Really, this game had a lot of potential to be a gem but the fact it has been designed for commoners rather than history fanatics kills it.  The history side is BS, the strategy side is too easy and repetitive and the replayability is close to none.
I cannot recommend this game because it does not enter a classification to please anyone.  Its too simple for strategy fans, its too inaccurate for history fans and its too repetitive for hardcore fans... maybe for people who knows nothing about WW1 ...
Graphics : 4/10 - (Sprites, its all right but plain and dull)
Sound/music : 2/10 - (Almost inexistant or just very generic and unremarkable)
Replayability : 3/10 - (Repetitive and limited)
Fun factor : 6/10 - (For the 15 hours it will last)
OVERALL : 3/10
Conclusion : Too easy, too inacurrate compared to history, repetitive, limited.  This was probably a good Cell phone game but on PC it lacks polishing and diversity.  You paid 5$ and you get what you paid for : something to kill a few hours.

I was told if I take the time to report bugs in detail (and there are quite a few) that I would be rewarded with in game gold.  All I got was a "thank you for your support."  If you don't mind spending $20 a month, have 12hrs a day to spend moving resources from base to base just to keep your ques full then this game may work for you.  If you want to play for free and value your time, then don't waste any on this game.  The devs are content with their money sink and have not communicated any intention for future changes necessary to make this game a truly player driven market/ economy.  There are numerous ways this game is broken, besides the time commitment required.  I'll name one more major issue; it is impossible to defend your settlement unless it is on a 4K+ elevation spot.  100 bombs dropped from above 6k are undefendable otherwise.  The catch is there are only a few 4k+ spots in the game, and those are already occupied. Anyone interested in more ways this game is broken, just take a peek at the discussion board in the Luckcatchers forum.  You'll find plenty of legitimate complaints.

Capitalism, ho!
You're a cute little air-headed sweets-loving girl with a deadbeat dad, ginormous amounts of debt, and a Kuudere fairy that's trying to help you get out of it, instead of just making you homeless or eating your soul.
You've got rivals from other shops to compete with (though that doesn't play much in the game itself from my experience), and you've got a bunch of adventurers you can go dungeon crawling with. One of which is a thief that starts out pretty much as a meanie-face, and another that's a worthless and penniless adventurer wanna-be that'll ask for your stuff for around 75% of the base price (meaning you lose money when you sell to him unless you dungeon crawl with him to get items, and he'll use the items he gets from you) when he shops at your store. WORTHLESS AND PENNILESS.
Everything is cute to disguise the horribly realistic scenario of children being forced to pay their parents debts for the rest of their life, unless they're good with CAPITALISM, HO!
It's got an amusing dungeon system, though people complain about the hit boxes being bad (I haven't noticed it) or having to always attack in a linear manner (you don't, quite a number of the attacks hit everything in a half circle in front of you) they aren't real problems unless you're very, very rigid and perfectionist. It's tedious, yes, but what dungeon crawling game isn't? I have yet to run into one that doesn't become a tediously boring thing after a dozen or so floors, and this one has dialogue, plot, and new characters interspersed throughout it to keep things at least a little interesting.
If you don't like ditzy characters, cutesy dialogue, and a bunch of anime-esque plots then this probably isn't the game for you, but if you've been watching anime for a while and like to sink some time into dungeon crawling without it being the only thing to do in a game, then this game might just be for you.
Some people complain about "having to do things over and over again" and I can only say one thing: too bad, so sad. Darn near every game is like that, and always has been. The only reason it's "different" now is that you perceive it differently because it's gotten boring.

After having my eye on Expeditions: Conquistadors for many, many months, I finally bought it during its last sale and it did not disappoint.  It gave me a very satisfying roleplaying experience that was quite refreshing, offering varying ways to play my Capitain via dialogue options and it was fun exploring the different lands, and I could choose if I wanted to be a blood thirsty conquerer of the native peoples or a more benevolent explorer type.  After being strong armed into a certain archtype by most of the recent AAA rpgs of late (Bethsoft being the most primary amongst them), it was a lot of fun being able to play my character how I wanted and being given the options to do so.
However, there were aspects of the game that ended up givng me a kind of game fatigue, like the limited movement each day which could be increased via tinkering but even with it researched completely, it got to be really onerous after a while, knowing only a minute of movement later, I'd have to set up camp yet again and again and again, with periodic events to eleviate that tedium.  And I sorely missed there being any kind of inventory management, as in game it's very streamlined and only serves to provide offensive and defensive stats but that's about it. Finding chests during explorations became rather boring as well as they only contained valuables (money) or tinkering ingredients such as oil, rope, wood, etc, so looting in the game eventually became more ho-hum for me rather than oh yay, a chest!
However, even though I had some issues with the game, it was something I'm glad I got to finally play and I enjoyed it a lot, especially for the roleplaying aspect of it.

This game is sort of an alternate-universe retelling of World War II. This isn't your typical war drama, though. No, this is War Lite™, where war has been sanitized for consumption by a PG-13 audience. Heavy topics such as racism and mass murder are present, but only lightly touched upon, serving as side points to the main story which focuses on the relationships of your team, Squad 7.
This is not an inherently bad thing, but I can understand why some people may not appreciate the watered-down vision of war that the game presents. Personally, I didn't mind this too much; light and flufffy games can still be fun if they're done right, and this one is certainly no exception. If you can get over the game's anime-ness and occasional saccharine dialogue, you'll find that this game has an interesting story and likeable characters, even if they sometimes fall a little flat.
The gameplay is where Valkyria Chronicles really shines, though. It is a mash-up of turn-based strategy and 3rd-person action, and it works extremely well. You view the battlefield as an overhead tactical map first, and then you drop down into 3rd person mode when you decide to command a unit. Units have a limited range of movement and you can only perform one action per turn - so you are encouraged to consider every action carefully. Staying in cover and using the terrain to your advantage is key to keeping your units alive. If you don't, you will often find your units ruthlessly killed by snipers or ambushes when the enemy's turn comes around.
However, if you've placed your units right, you will find that they will dish out intercepting fire against the enemies and kill them off before they get a chance. This can be
satisfying. You are rewarded for smart play, and that's exactly what you want in a strategy game.
The other great aspect of this game is the attention to detail that has been given to the squad members themselves. Every soldier in the roster (and there's dozens of them) has their own distinct personality, strengths, weaknesses, and even unique voice overs (which probably explains why this game weighs in at 20 GB on the hard drive!). Some soldiers also synergize better with others, and finding the right combinations to deploy into battle is half the joy of Valkyria Chronicles.
The gameplay is not perfect, however. Tactics can be somewhat limited in the story quests, which too often rely on scripted sequences and highly linear level design (however, if you simply want to focus on the battles without that stuff getting in the way, there are repeatable "skirmish" battles available that allow you to do just that, and they still allow you to earn money and XP for your troops).
Also, this game also relies a little too heavily on gimmicky boss battles. You know the ones. You're fighting a boss, but not
, because instead of actually fighting them, you have to complete a bunch of tedious side objectives to "weaken" them or make them run away, such as destroying generators or covering them in rubble, things that have nothing to do with actually fighting them. This game does this because most of the bosses are key characters in the story that need to fulfill their roles later, but it can be a bit tiresome nonetheless. Thankfully the skirmishes have none of this.
The enemy AI also feels a little lackluster at times. Enemies who are pre-placed in cover positions are your biggest challenges, but once they're flushed out, they seem to lose their minds and run directly at your forces. Same goes for reinforcements that are spawned from enemy camps. Essentially, this game relies too heavily on thwarting the player through clever level design rather than smart behaviour from the enemies.
Another thing to note is that this game was originally designed to be played on PS3 and, like many ports, it has some problems. The most noticeable issue is with the tank controls, which are a little wonky, and the mouse movement on the tactical map can also be a bit buggy when your units are bunched together. Aside from those small issues, though, this game has been ported extremely well in all other respects.
With all that said, Valkyria Chronicles is an extremely enjoyable game, and an excellent value for your money. You'll pay about $20 USD for about thirty hours of content, and that doesn't include the side plots and DLC's (all of which are now included in the full purchase price). With those included, you're looking nearly
hours of content - Or even more if you're an achievement hunter.
I highly recommend this game. It's a must-play for any strategy game fan!

Good, bad, and the ugly.   (update time)
Good: If you like grindy games, then youll love this one.  It takes a while to get up the gold to get your first settlement and start supplying your own stuff, not to mention help other people out or start selling your own supplies and resources.  There are a few players that are always on a willing to help, and there are a few great tutorial videos on youtube.
Bad: The game either requires a lot of time, much more than Ive thrown in the get anywhere decent, or you can negate a lot of that time with your steamwallet (that being said, it actually costs very little actual cash to get a pretty decent amount of gold).  That being said, the game is somewhat pay to win, and i really hate to say that and it wasnt always so, but after "The Update", good luck unless you want to devote your life and sign a blood contract.
The Ugly: If youre reading this far, dont stop now.  The trainwreck is almost over and traffic can resume.  This game was made by a Russian development team and I dont actually mean that negatively.  However, because of this, the English players arent really listened too by the dev team, and if they are, they may not take priority.  This game has been in the works for a while now, but not for the English side so Russia pretty much dominates the map and have claimed most of the great resource plots for settlements. Pirates really dont bother too many people mainly because the player base isnt huge at all (though we help everyone as much as we can most times), unless theyre a settlement with NPC defenses.  Feedback has somewhat been ignored across the board from what ive noticed, as there have been a great deal of great ideas that shouldve been implemented but havent at all.  This game takes time.  not days, or weeks, but months most times if youre not going to throw at least a smidge of money at the game ($4.50 really aint bad and goes a pretty long way surprisingly enough) and a lot of people have been lost because times are have only been getting longer.  If you want tutorials, you have to go on youtube or take the time to have someone walk you through the game in ingame chat, which takes a while and not all of us have time to do it.
Overall, I cant really tell people one way or another to join with us or to run as far away as possible.  I love the thought behind this game with a passion and its a great idea, but the exectuion of that idea has been severly lacking.  I really want to see this game go far, but it seems like the dev crew arent focused on the areas that need to be focused on, and it seems like they dont have the dedication to make it go where we all want it too.

I’m not going to knock it for being a P2W because it’s designed to cater to its paying members and this is the business model the Developers have decided to go with, but be advised, you cannot earn enough money playing under the free umbrella to establish yourself as a legitimate competitor. The entire map is run by a few clans of people who had the opportunity to do a land grab when it first came out and establish settlements around all the cities. Everyone who comes in now has to set up their bases in the wastelands because there’s only a certain amount of spots available and the good ones have been taken. The Devs have already stated that there will not be any resets so the areas that have already been settled will never be available for new combers.  If you do earn enough money to establish a settlement in the Wasteland you will be exposed to Pirate attacks and without the protection of the city or kicking in a lot of money on defenses, can quickly be overrun.
This is a very slow paced economics game and if you are looking for action you will find very little here. Everything runs at a snail’s pace and has very few upgrades for speed. This is the kind of game you will run in the background while you’re doing something more important.
You earn money by buying, transporting and selling cargo and in the beginning they make it quite easy for you to do so. After you working your way up to level 2 things start getting a little more difficult as the easy beginner cargo runs become less frequent and by the third level it is no longer profitable. It is at this point where the free-to-play game will become stagnant and it will become abundantly clear that you are going nowhere unless you pay real-world money. In level 2 you can earn approximately 96 gold every 15-20 minutes. This is dependent on how fast you can load your cargo, how many others are competing for the same run and how fast you can turn your ships around. This is about the quickest you can earn money as a free player and because everything costs money in the game, its gone as fast as you can earn it.
The learning curve for this game is very difficult and there's not much in the way of instructions.  There is a chat where you can ask questions and sometimes you will get a coherent response. There is a basic map that you can look at but it does not show all the established trading locations. It only shows the larger cities. This map is not zoomable or customizable and in my opinion is of poor design.
You are told when you first begin that you have a 30 day grace period where you cannot be killed but it only applies if you stay within a certain distance of a city and as I said before you cannot establish a settlement anywhere near a city because the land is already been claimed.
There are people in the game who will set up a bogus cargo jobs which as a newbie you might unintentionally choose. When you attempt to complete the run you will find it to be an ambush where you will be destroyed on site.  Once you've clicked on the job you cannot go back or cancel it and if you choose not to deliver you’ll be charged a penalty fee (they call it a deposit). This dirty gameplay is not only accepted it’s promoted because it’s allowed to take place in the beginner cities where newbies are easily tricked. As a New player you cannot be expected to know the difference between a legitimate job and bogus jobs.
I’ve played this game for about 30 days so I’m not criticizing it without having given it an honest workout. There are a lot of annoying bugs that need to be worked on, details that need to be incorporated and balances that need to be set in place. As the game sits now, I cannot recommend it.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a story driven game in it's entirety.  The initial events and investigations that followed kept me interested enough to keep playing to the end.  In that regard, Murdered succeeds and is why I'm giving it a thumbs up recommendation.  However, if I was able to vote with both thumbs, it would be one up and one down... I was on the fence about this one.   Why?
On the positive side, the story of a modern murder mystery slowly unraveling as the victim himself uncovers the truth is satisfying.  It starts very strong and doesn't end the way you might expect, so that was refreshing.  But there comes a point when as a player you piece together the basic gist of what is happening but Ronan takes a while longer to 'get it'.  This is about mid-point in the game and it was quite frustrating because Ronan is supposed to be an investigator but due to his inability to make the connections before the player does, the game seems to drag until Ronan catches up.  The ending does leave a lot of 'huh?' questions in your mind and does feel a little anti-climactic.  I think this is mostly due to discovering several things all at once in once scene, then end credits.  There is no pacing to the final shocking revelations, and therefore no real chance to feel closure, empathy, relief, satisfaction... none of it.  It's there but it happens too fast.  So fast that Ronan doesn't even react to a world-shattering personal discovery.
The characters are memorable.  Pairing the main character Ronan with a mostly reticent, feisty, but intelligent teen Joy adds a lot of chemistry.  Joy is well written and performed.  For me she was the star.  Ronan was a rough and tumble kind of guy before meeting his soulmate, and the mellow, tolerant side of him is done well but that's the only side we get to see.  I was severely disappointed by the lack of strong emotion or raw aggression that could have bled through on many occassions but doesn't.  Sadly Ronan comes off as deadpan.
The environment is very well done, with a quiet moody setting where the grim nature of it's history can be seen through your dead eyes.
On the negative side, this is a game.  Or more precisely, it tries to be a game.  Almost every single game aspect  just gets in the way, slows things down, and makes you wish the substance it hides was more fleshed out.  The presence of demons and the need to evade and/or exorcise them is haphazardly thrown into the mix.  They look cool and scare the crap out of you when they start chasing you, but these notably gameplay moments seem so disjointed from the story.  It's like the developers said 'OK let's just throw some game in right here'.
There is a heavy collecting element to this game if you want your story fleshed out.  From Ronan's background, to his relationship with his lost wife, to history of the setpieces... it's all locked away in the text granted to you when you find something which is not always related.  I'd say maybe half of these were worth reading for good background info.  The rest were all useless to the story and the game.  Of special note are the area specific ghost stories you can unlock.  Most of them are interesting and I really wish they had been incorporated into the story somehow.
The investigation and possession elements were great concepts that were presented so incredibly poorly.  When you attempt to solve an investigation the premise is that you take clues and piece them together to come to a conclusion.  Among those pieces are clues that don't help.  If you get one clue wrong, it exits the minigame and you start again.  So all you have to do is keep trying each one until you get it right, and there aren't that many to choose from anyways.  It feels really pointless.  You can inhabit the body of people and read or influence their thoughts, but the thoughts are so plain and boring and the chances to influence people are few and far between.  More wasted potential.
My recommendation is to enjoy the game for the story and just follow the carrot.  The gameplay is easy enough to just get through so you can keep the main story moving along.  Collecting and killing demons and exploration are entirely not necessary (unless you want achievements in which case you will be forced to grind through everything).  The game length felt good for a story driven game; not so short that I felt ripped off but not too long that I felt it was watered down or needless.
I'd also recommend getting this at $15 or less, which I feel is a fair price point.

This is not a proper review of the game, but in its place I will tell a story. This story will include a few spoilers, but let's be honest- the game is from 2004, the story will most likely have been spoiled for you at some point.
Let us begin. There once was a boy, brought into the great Guild of Heroes at a very young age, who trained hard night and day, dedicating his life to becoming a great Hero, seeking fame and glory. Even as a child the Hero was very boastful- proud of his physical and mental prowess and always seeking recognition for his accomplishments. But then one day the Hero took a boast that would later prove to humble him; the day had come that he enter the Arena, and the prideful Hero raised himself upon the podium outside the Guild's walls, looked down into the cheering crowd below.
This was, by this time, a familiar sight, for in his search for glory the Hero was not satisfied with merely completing a Quest. He would stand upon the platform and utter the most outrageous of boasts, at one time defeating an entire pack of Balverines stark naked without taking a single scratch as a personal test of his agility. His pride knew no bounds, and the Hero took upon himself the title of the divine Avatar, claiming that he would be the sword which the Gods wielded to drive back the darkness. However, this day the Hero saw an opportunity to forge a truly legendary tale within the Arena, one which could never possibly be surpassed: he would enter the Arena and slay all that came before him, be it man or beast, completely unprotected, and without a so much as a scratch to mar his rosy skin. The crowd cheering and his chest puffed with pride, the Hero set off to the Isle of Witchwood, and the Arena therein.
The Hero entered the Arena to the roaring of a crowd that could only brought on by the anticipation of imminent bloodshed. A veteran of the bloodied sands had just fallen, adding yet another entry in the long list of those who had died in pursuit of glory through combat. The Hero made short work of an entire nest of Wasps, then of a clan of Hobbes, all singlehandedly. From the third round on he would be joined by a fellow Hero to defeat the beasts that were released upon him. The gate lowered and from beyond came his greatest rival, a Heroine by the name of Whisper who had looked upon him with disdain ever since they had begun their training together many years ago. However, the Hero was satisfied with this, as it would only add to his legend, and so together they set about cutting down a pack of Balverines to pieces. By this time he had set into the familiar groove of combat, and with spell and sword his foes fell before him.
The Hero did not blink an eye as the remains of those who had died on the sands of the Arena tore themselves from the blood soaked earth and rose to reclaim their glory in death. After dispatching the Undead, a clan of Bandits, once feared throughout all of Albion and slated for execution within the Arena several years ago were next. Methodically he dodged their blows and cut them down one by one, Whisper his constant companion this a whirlwind of blood and blade. By this point it had become apparent that group tactics were no match for the Heroes' skill, and so the master of the Arena swiftly changed tactics and introduced a matched pair of trolls to the audience. The Heroes had already faced Trolls before, so as they saw the rumbling of the earth and the giant hands of stone emerge from the sod they knew what to expect. Cool and calm, they circled their prey, waiting for the opportune moment to strike and avoiding the attacks of the other troll. First a pair of Earth Trolls fell beneath their blades, then the even tougher Rock Trolls, chipped at repeatedly by their hit and run attacks.
With the defeat of the Trolls the Heroes stood tall, knowing they could take on anything. With the end near, the question of who the gold would go to should they win, as the Arena can only have one Champion,  arose, but this thought was quickly purged from minds as a massive creature the likes of which they had never seen before clawed its way out of the sands, stinger raised and claws snapping. The beast, a gigantic scorpion, was called Arachanox, and many a Champion candidate had fallen before her, their aspirations crushed along with their bodies under its massive stinger. This threat was novel, something the Heroes had never faced before, and it took a great amount of teamwork to learn its strengths and weaknesses. Carefully, they paced around it, dodging out of the way and poking at is when they could. The Hero had managed to maintain his boast of being untouched up until this point, as familiar foes had patterns which he could exploit. But in the face of the unknown his abilities remained sharp, but even the most skilled warrior eventually makes a mistake. Learning the patterns of the great beast the Hero hacked at it with his greatsword when it was stunned, retreating from the slashing of its pincers when it freed itself. They repeated this, but the long hours of combat had begun to wear on them, and the inevitable happened: the Hero made a mistake. Thinking the beast dead after an especially powerful blow, he raised his sword to the sky in celebration, to the delight of the crowd. But Arachanox was not yet defeated, and in its death throes it struck the Hero from behind, putting an end to his long line of successful boasts. Angered by the ruin of the legend he was trying to forge, he turned and struck it down, making sure it was dead, then turned to the cheering crowd.
Above them appeared none other than the legendary Jack of Blades to commend them for their valour. However, with his praise came a final, deadly, proposition: one final round. There could only be one Champion of the Arena, Unable to refuse this challenge or lose all they had just fought for, Whisper turned to the Hero and said that she could not kill him, not after all that they had been through in the Arena. The Hero then recalled his earlier boasting, declaring that he would cut down all he faced on the sands. He was a good man at heart, but he realized that his hubris had led him to this situation. Whisper's voice broke him from his thoughts, declaring that they should at the very least put on a good show. And so they crossed blades, once rivals, then allies, and now as reluctant foes on the field of battle. Whisper's skill proved to be no match for that of the Hero in the end, and as she kneeled in the sands, beaten, the Hero had a decision to make: would he sacrifice this woman who had caused him so much anger and betray the bond forged between them in battle to salvage at least some semblance of the legend he had hoped to create? As he looked down at her, he realized that he could not take the final blow and sheathed his blade, turning from the jeers of the disappointed crowd and the pleading eyes of Whisper to walk silently through the gates. With this he took an oath to never boast again, and became a true Champion of Righteousness, rather than a slave to the battlefield, going on to forge a legacy befitting the title of Avatar.

This game is free. The fact that it is free should not detract from the quality of the game itself; the company, Digital Extreme, has made leaps and bounds from when the game originally started, experimenting with different play styles, experimental graphics design, volumetric lighting.
These all culminate into a game that appears well-polished, with a unique game mechanic and wearable entities that are affected by physics. That doesn't sound like a whole lot, but considering where the game started out, this is leaps and bounds from where it was originally.
Their newest expansion, Plains of Eidolon, allows you to explore a large, open area, which is similar to other MMOs and an idea that Digital Extreme as a company has wanted to try for awhile. After releasing their Plains of Eidolon expansion, their player base has nearly doubled, with 125,000 regular players within a week of release. This has been the second largest jump in player base in the history of MMOs.
Their low squad requirements helps reduce lag and culminates to a better game.
Each Warframe that they have all have unique powers, and these Warframes have synergies that are best found by experimenting with friends and playing within your favorite playstyle, whether it is CC, tank, DPS, healer, or something in between.
All in all, Warframe has something for everybody.
The cons of this game is it is a freemium game, allowing people who spend money to be able to progress significantly faster than other players.
The game does also have a learning curve, especially end game, which makes playing with other people publlically to be difficult.
All in all, I rate this game 7/10.
